name: Maryland Matters
title: Once a rarity, Latino candidates are now up and down the ballot in local, state races
text:
Latina connecting at Arepa Zone in College Park include, from left, Colmar Manor Mayor Monica Casañas, Del. Deni Taveras , House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk, Montgomery County register of wills candidate Barbara Ebel and Nicole Rios, a political strategist. (Photo courtesy Joseline-Peña Melnyk)When she entered public life in 1990, Ana Sol Gutierrez was a pioneer, serving two terms on the Montgomery County Board of Education before becoming Maryland’s first Latina state legislator when she was elected to the House of Delegates in 2002.
A native of El Salvador, she came to the U.S. in 1949, the daughter of a founding director of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. A systems engineer by training, she worked for NASA and was deputy administrator at the Department of Transportation in the Clinton administration. But she also saw the surge of Central Americans coming here to flee war and economic hardship.
“I saw that Latinos were not really represented. I ran with the idea that I wanted to get the Latinos registered and active in politics,” Gutierrez said recently. “I carried applications in my purse, sent [applications] to the kitchen in restaurants, and [left] four or five at the [cash] register.”
That work apparently paid off.
Today, Latinos hold state positions and local office, and work in staff positions throughout state and local government, Gutierrez said. The Maryland Democratic Party said it is following 21 Latino candidates who are running for state and local offices this fall.
Retired State Del. Ana Sol Gutiérrez (D-Montgomery), center, stays active in party politics, voter registration and fielding bilingual calls for the League of Women Voters election hotline. (Photo courtesy Ana Sol Gutiérrez)
“Nine are incumbents, six are new in safe blue seats, two in competitive races, and four in red seats,” said Carter Elliott, a senior adviser for the party. Those candidates “won their primaries for county council positions in Prince George’s, Montgomery, Frederick and Baltimore counties. This also includes multiple Democratic candidates working to flip some council seats blue.”
Afro-Latina House Speaker sets inclusive agenda
Nowhere is the advance of Latinos more evident than in House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), the first Afro-Latino and first immigrant to hold the job.
The groundwork laid by Gutierrez opened the door for Peña-Melnyk, who was elected in 2003 to the College Park City Council, and three years later was voted into the Maryland House. She was unanimously elected speaker last December.
As a child in the Dominican Republic, she was raised by a single mother in a one-room house with a leaky roof. They escaped poverty for a life in the United States, where young Joseline translated documents for her family and others trying to navigate the complex social welfare system.
“When you grow up that way, it gives you perspective on the struggles of life, and it shapes you,” said Peña-Melnyk, who said that life fueled her activism.
Like Gutierrez, when Peña-Melnyk entered political life, few looked or sounded like her. She soon got to work to change that. She and Del. David Fraser-Hidalgo (D-Montgomery) in 2014 co-founded the Maryland Legislative Latino Caucus, which today has 100 members, including eight Latinos and 92 associate members who support its agenda.
Peña-Melnyk says the effort is paying off in legislation that she says lowers energy bills, reins in prescription drug costs, and extends Medicare coverage to undocumented pregnant women — work accomplished with a greater support team.
“Today you have people that are chief of staffs, committee managers, HR directors, working in the governor’s office, in the comptroller’s office, which is so important to have not just Latinos but to have, you know, the workforce reflect the people of Maryland,” she said.
In the run-up to November, she said she has been on a seven-day-a-week campaign across Maryland to get out the vote, and fulfill a promise.
“I told my members that I was going to come to their districts, that I want to get to know all of Maryland,” she said. In late August, she organized a candidate meet-up at Arepa Zone, a Venezuelan restaurant in College Park. Dozens of activists and supporters showed up to celebrate primary victories and listen to what new candidates like 25-year-old Ruben Amaya had to say.
Getting out the youth vote
Born in the United States to Central American immigrants, Amaya’s history in politics began in high school, where he mobilized classmates to fight for gun reform, and to fix infrastructure problems at the school. By his senior year, he was president of the Baltimore County Student Council and in 2022 he ran for the House of Delegates. He finished fourth out of 12 candidates, but garnered political capital in the process.
Ruben Amaya is running for a seat on the Baltimore County Council. (Photo courtesy Robin Stevens Brody)
Amaya is currently the third vice chair of the Maryland Democratic Party and president of the Young Democrats of Maryland, while balancing a day job as an admissions counselor at Stevenson University in Baltimore. In June, he won a crowded primary race for the Baltimore County Council from District 2, and is favored to win in the heavily Democratic district.
“I’m running to be the first Latino to hold elected office in our county’s history. Also, if elected, I’ll be the first Gen Z member to hold elected office as well in Baltimore County,” Amaya said. “I think it’s a big moment, not just for Latinos, but for young people. We’ve been able to inspire a lot of young people to get involved.”
Amaya said his priorities are housing affordability, economic and food security and basic day-to-day county services, applying his known-how of what he learned from his immigrant parents.
“I think that coming to this country with nothing, their mindset was never about what can we do to just reap the benefits. It was about what we can do to contribute back,” he said.
Running for council to be an advocate
For Howard County Council nominee Jessica Nichols, her childhood in rural Texas was “very food insecure.”
“I used to call it ‘peanut butter poor’ because we would often [just] have a jar of peanut butter as the only food in our home,” Nichols said. Her parents fled poverty and violence Central America, she said, and her single mother later moved them east, for better work opportunities.
“That really did inform my service both as a teacher and as board chairperson of Columbia Community Care,” she said of the post-pandemic nonprofit she co-founded to combat food insecurity in Howard County. “Care meant that there was one less little hungry Jessica. That was very impactful to me. It still drives my involvement.”
Nichols, a social studies and resource teacher who was named 2024-25 Howard County Teacher of the Year, has become increasingly engaged in civic life over the last decade. She’s been president of the Columbia Democratic Club, a member of the Democratic Central Committee and the Howard County Education Association, the local teacher’s union.
Barbara Ebel, the Democratic nominee for Montgomery County register of wills, on Primary Election Day in Wheaton with Teresa Ramírez. (Photo courtesy Friends of Barbara Ebel)
When budget cuts threatened county education “was when I realized that the voice that was missing in the room was the voice of educators, because when the educators’ voices are in the room, there’s advocacy for children,” she said of her decision to run. “There’s advocacy for families.”
With no opponent in the Nov. 3 election, Nichols will likely sworn in Dec. 7 as the first African American woman and the first Latina in the post.
A ‘passion … to continue to help people’
Montgomery County register of wills nominee Barbara Ebel said she ran because she decided it was time, after years helping others.
“I found my passion, and it was to continue to help people,” she said at the August gathering in College Park.
Born in Puerto Rico and raised in the Dominican Republic, Ebel parlayed her bilingual skills into a job in 1996 at the Maryland Department of Labor Workforce Development Office as a career counselor, the only Latina hired at the time. Within eight years she was its Montgomery County director, serving along the way as a trainer, business developer and in supervisory positions.
She was elected to the Montgomery County Democratic Central Committee in 2022 and has also served on boards of several nonprofits that advocate for people with disabilities.
Besides the right timing, Ebel decided the job of register of wills would be a good fit. The office administers the legal process of settling a deceased person’s estate, she said. “And, because I went through the process myself, I knew I could really do this job, and, also because I have 26 years of public administration service, have implemented regulations and [am] able to interpret regulations and polices,” she said.
Ebel faces Republican nominee T. Dolores Reyes for the seat, but is favored in Montgomery County, a Democrat stronghold. If elected, she will leave the Labor Department to devote herself full-time to the new position, where she hopes to make the office easier to navigate, easier to understand and welcoming for all county families.
Ebel, who also spoke at the Latino candidate gathering in College Park, said she came away hopeful.
“It was a beautiful synergy to see so many Latinos that really want to do the people’s work. That they are putting themselves out there, running for office to serve the public and make a difference and impact in the community,” she said.
Despite the gains, Peña Melnyk says the fight for equity and representation is ongoing.
“Now more than ever, the immigrant community needs people to speak up for them, to advocate for them, to advocate for human rights. And, we cannot do it alone,” she said. “We need brothers and sisters from different backgrounds. It’s a way to keep us all connected to make sure we make life better for everyone.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: The Montana hunter’s new ‘BFF’
text:
This is an area recently acquired by American Prairie called "Pintail Flats' (Photo courtesy of American Prairie).It’s the time of “the hunt.” In Montana, it has been big deal for a very long time, a time of year when friends greeting friends no longer say, “How you doing?” 
Instead it’s, “Get your elk yet?” 
The enthusiasm for the hunt hasn’t changed for decades.  
What has changed is the hunter’s landscape. For most hunters, I should say. It hasn’t changed much for wealthy hunters who can afford pricey guided hunts on private land controlled by outfitters. It might even be better than ever for them. For hunters who depend on public land or on permission from private landowners, however, it’s tougher nowadays. More competition, less access, more regulation, less success. Every hunter knows the problems.
That’s why Montana hunters and their nonprofit organizations should be embracing their new “BFF,” American Prairie, a Montana-based nonprofit organization. 
American Prairie opened its doors in 2004 and has been making great progress toward its goal of creating one of the largest nature reserves in the United States, upwards of 3.2 million acres, to serve as a refuge for people and wildlife forever. To date, American Prairie has acquired more than 600,000 acres of north-central Montana with, undoubtedly, more acquisitions to come.  
 Before American Prairie came to Montana, almost all of these 600,000 acres were closed to hunting. Now, big game and upland game bird hunters have free access to all of it with the exception of small parcels around residential areas. 
Bison have been reintroduced to portions of the reserve with the herd growing to about 1,000 animals. American Prairie holds an annual bison hunt, the only opportunity in the entire state for hunters to have a real hunt for a wild bison in a prairie environment similar to how it was when Lewis and Clark struggled up the Missouri.
There lies the rub: American Prairie’s long-term plans envision a larger bison herd roaming free over a restored, unfenced landscape. Some –not all – local ranchers hate the idea of free-roaming bison and therefore oppose American Prairie. Even though these ranchers likely represent a very small slice of Montana’s population, they have the ear of the governor, attorney general and all four of Montana’s congressional representatives. 
This has led to political retribution. The State of Montana has paused permits to graze bison on state land leased by American Prairie, even though bison are officially classified as livestock, not wildlife, in Montana. The same politicians have convinced the U.S. Bureau of Land Management to disallow bison grazing on public land within the reserve. These two politically driven decisions combined are a devastating blow to American Prairie’s long-term goals. Consequently, the nonprofit has pursued its only remaining option, legal action, and both decisions are currently being contested in state and federal courts.   
This is why Montana hunters need to step up to the plate. Our politicians need to know that Montana hunters support American Prairie. Take a little time away from hunting to write letters or make calls to our political leaders expressing your support for American Prairie and urge them to start helping the Montana nonprofit group accomplish its goals instead of fighting it every step of the way.
Hunters should know that American Prairie’s efforts have received endorsements and support from notable Montana hunting organizations such as the Montana Wildlife Federation, Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, Montana Sportsman Alliance, Montana Backcountry Hunters and Anglers and Randy Newberg’s “Hunt Talk.”
But only silence from the big dog, the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, even though, American Prairie has opened up hundreds of thousands of acres of some the best elk country to the public and protected all that prime habitat from future development. Even when the American Prairie acquired the Anchor Ranch in the Missouri River Breaks, nearly 70,000 acres (including 45,000 acres of leased public land), and opened it to public hunting and then opened a 3.8-mile section of the Bullwhacker Road which, in turn, opened free access to another 50,000 acres of public land that had been closed to public access for many years, not a word of praise from the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation.  
Yes, there has been support from hunters, but it has been soft and not very vocal.  We need to turn up the volume.
In addition to the obvious benefits for hunters, letters could mention that American Prairie has been a major economic boost to an economically depressed section of Montana—hiring people (40+ employees), buying goods and services locally, bringing in tourists to camp and enjoy the prairie experience, and leasing much of the acquired land back to local ranchers for cattle grazing. 
In fact, about nine cows graze the reserve for every bison. American Prairie also opened a fantastic visitor center in Lewistown, the American Prairie Discovery Center, which attracts many more of tourists. 
Basically, the political panic over American Prairie seems irrational and overdone. Has American Prairie caused culture change? If so, what change? Cattle still graze there. Bison graze there, too, but for every bison nine cows graze on American Prairie land. And other Montana ranchers raise bison with no pushback to what they’ve decided to do with their private land. In fact, everything American Prairie does fits with the sacred cow of conservatism – private property rights. All acquisitions are with willing sellers who are only exercising their private property rights. 
So, what’s the problem?
One thing I’ve always liked about the sport of hunting is its politics. It has none. I’ve never seen a poll of the political preferences of Montana hunters, but I would bet my moose permit that all political parties are equally represented. In Montana, however, Republicans hold every major elected office, so clearly, it’s especially critical that our political leaders hear from their conservative-leaning constituents who enjoy hunting and worry about its future.
Bill Schneider is a retired publisher and outdoor writer living in Helena. He has no connection with American Prairie.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Senatobia officer put himself in harm’s way before fatally shooting 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, experts say
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Sarah Whites-Koditschek and Mukta Joshi are investigative reporters at Mississippi Today spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellows. They can be reached at sarah.whites-koditschek@nytimes.com and mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
Multiple experts who reviewed video footage of the police shooting in Senatobia said officers unnecessarily escalated the encounter and put themselves in harm’s way in the moments before one of them fired into a car, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley.
Six experts, including a forensic reconstructionist and five consultants in police training and use of force, said at least one of the officers clearly put himself at risk when he stepped in front of the car while pursuing two women accused of taking a box of diapers and baby clothes from Walmart.
That decision goes against training widely provided to law enforcement officers, who are taught not to stand in front of a car in an attempt to stop someone from fleeing, the experts said. 
It also appears to violate Senatobia Police Department’s use-of-force policy, which says an officer’s “first responsibility” is “to move out of the path of an on-coming vehicle.” 
“It’s just a tragedy. It could have been avoided,” said Chuck Wexler, executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, a group that advises police departments on use of force. “You don’t stand in front of the car, period. You stand off to the side.” 
Reporters for Mississippi Today and The New York Times asked six policing and use-of-force experts and an attorney who defends law enforcement to examine video footage that was collected by state law enforcement and leaked to a Mississippi news outlet this week. The footage is incomplete, but provides the most detailed insight so far into how officers came to shoot Kohen during what began as a routine shoplifting call in June.
Kohen’s death set off protests in Senatobia and sparked outrage across the country, in part because Kohen, who is Black, was shot by a white police officer, who Mississippi Today later found had been accused by two separate colleagues of making racially offensive comments toward them. 
In September, Mississippi Today revealed that Harold Vanderford, the department’s chief who had taken no action against Foster in either complaint, routinely used racist slurs in text exchanges with a colleague in the department. Vanderford was fired soon after.  
Foster resigned from his position at the department this week, and city leadership accepted his resignation late Wednesday.
A close examination of the footage, in consultation with the experts, raises questions about how the officers responded, and whether Foster’s life was in danger when the shots were fired. It also leaves critical questions unanswered, including what the officers knew about the women they were chasing and whether any of them knew a child was in the car.
Of those who reviewed the footage for Mississippi Today, only David Mastagni, an attorney who represents police, defended the officers’ tactics. He cautioned against judging their actions based on video footage, saying it appears far different than what an officer experiences in the moment. 
“It’s capturing from a perspective, and it has tranquility and hindsight and all that, where we can slow it down and look at it,” he said. 
An excerpt from Senatobia Police Department’s use-of-force policy, which warns officers that shooting at a moving vehicle is “inherently dangerous and difficult.” 
The other six experts were unanimous in many of their criticisms.
In the video, the confrontation with the officers begins after Latoya Ferrell, Vellesiya Wiley and her son Kohen have gotten into a gray sedan parked outside Walmart. An unidentified officer runs up to their driver side window and tries to open the door as the sedan pulls backward out of a parking spot. 
One officer yells, “Stop,” and the car pauses before continuing backward and slamming into an S.U.V. 
Several experts noted that this is the moment when at least two officers pull out their guns. Russ Hicks, a police consultant, former instructor and assistant commander, said the officers drew their weapons before the car drove toward them.   
“What concerns me is taking out the gun so quickly in this kind of a case,” Hicks said. “Officers only draw their guns if they believe they’re going to use them.”
The officers then surround the car, with two of them, including Foster, standing in front, in the only possible path for the driver to flee. 
Hicks called this a critical mistake that put the officers, the car’s occupants and bystanders at risk. 
“This is a provocational tactic where they’re standing in front of the cars and now saying, ‘I need to use deadly force,’” Hicks said. 
When the car moves forward, Foster appears to be in its path. The video shows the car’s front wheels turning left at the last moment in an apparent effort to avoid hitting him. As Foster pivots out of the way, he fires his gun and the car passes between him and another officer. 
Several of the experts took issue with Foster’s decision to fire. They said shooting into a car – even if it is threatening an officer’s safety – is almost always inappropriate because killing the driver is unlikely to bring the car to a stop and protect the officer.
“If you hit the driver, now you have an unguided missile,” said Geoffrey Alpert, a criminology professor at the University of South Carolina. 
Foster shoots four times, according to the experts who reviewed the video.
The officer’s first shot was fired when his right leg was in front of the car’s bumper on the passenger side, said Jeremy Bauer, a forensic reconstruction expert. By the second shot, the officer’s left hip is lined up with the right passenger mirror and his chest is parallel to the passenger side.  
In the third shot, “We actually see the evidence that he shoots into the right front passenger window,” Bauer said. “We see glass shatter.”
The final shot was fired when Foster was standing near the rear tire, he said. 
Mastagni said officers often experience a delay between facing a threat and firing. 
“It’s not uncommon that the bullet strikes at a different spot on the car than where the officer was intending to shoot at the time that they perceived the threat,” he said. 
The publication of the leaked footage set off a social media firestorm, and multiple local news outlets reported in definite language that the car had struck two officers. But the experts said it was impossible for them to determine whether the vehicle had made contact with any of the officers based on their immediate review of the video.  
In a press conference Wednesday, Gov. Tate Reeves said it was “very clear and evident” that the driver had “attempted to run over” the officer. But Reeves said he had not watched the video. 
The leaked footage does show the car coming close to Foster’s leg as it turns left away from him, but he does not appear injured after it passes. While the car is in reverse, its front bumper comes close to another officer’s foot and leg as he steps to the side away from the vehicle.
Both he and Foster join the other officers in running to their cars to continue the pursuit.
The state’s attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced her office had found the shooting to be justified, and would not pursue criminal charges against Foster. She did not provide the reasoning for her decision, saying only that there was insufficient evidence of criminal conduct to present the case to a grand jury. 
“The bar for criminal prosecutions is obviously high. It’s probably extremely high in Mississippi,” said Michael Gennaco, a former federal civil rights prosecutor and founder of the OIR group, a police oversight consultancy. “But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t wrong, or ill-advised or tactically deficient.”
Gwen Dilworth contributed reporting.

name: California
title: Los recortes a Medi-Cal podrían dejar sin cobertura a las personas mayores y con discapacidad
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Julia Feinberg siente que vive en una versión siniestra del Día de la Marmota. Por segundo año consecutivo, los legisladores de California han dificultado que las personas mayores y las personas con discapacidades puedan acceder a los beneficios de salud financiados por el estado.
Feinberg, de 37 años y quien padece un trastorno neuromuscular degenerativo, dijo que sin Medi-Cal estaría confinada a una residencia de ancianos en lugar de vivir y trabajar como terapeuta en Oakland.
“Tenemos que librar la misma batalla una y otra vez”, dijo Feinberg. Ella necesita una silla de ruedas eléctrica y aproximadamente 19 horas de cuidados al día, lo cual está cubierto por Medi-Cal.
 California está recortando Medi-Cal después de una década de expansión, como parte de los drásticos recortes federales y estatales que, según los expertos, dejarán sin cobertura a más de 2,2 millones de californianos en los próximos cuatro años, duplicando la tasa de personas sin seguro médico en el estado.
El último recorte se produjo en junio, cuando los líderes estatales aprobaron un presupuesto que reducirá el límite de activos para las personas mayores de bajos ingresos y las personas con discapacidades a 21,000 dólares para poder optar a Medi-Cal, a partir de julio de 2027. Feinberg, que ha acumulado ahorros de emergencia, tendrá que gastar unos 10,000 dólares para no superar ese límite.


 Medi-Cal: El recorte 
 Los recortes en la atención médica a nivel federal y estatal dejarán sin cobertura a millones de californianos. CalMatters está haciendo un seguimiento de estos cambios e informando sobre ellos a medida que se implementan.

 Aprende cómo prepararte para estos cambios y comparte tu historia con nosotros.
 Vean nuestro documental en colaboración con Evident.



En 2024, el estado eliminó los límites de activos vigentes para Medi-Cal, pero desde entonces los legisladores han ido reduciendo esa política. A principios de este año, los líderes estatales restablecieron un límite de activos de 130,000 dólares, y el presupuesto de junio lo redujo aún más.
 La vivienda principal y un vehículo están exentos del nuevo límite, pero las personas de 65 años o más, así como las personas con discapacidades, no pueden tener una segunda vivienda ni un segundo automóvil, y no pueden tener más de $21,000 en cuentas de ahorro, ciertas cuentas de jubilación, pólizas de seguro de vida ni siquiera parcelas funerarias . Aún deben cumplir con los límites de ingresos para acceder a Medi-Cal, que son de aproximadamente $1,800 al mes para una persona soltera.
Los activistas afirman que las normas discriminan injustamente a las personas mayores y a las personas con discapacidad.
 “Es realmente caro tener una discapacidad”, dijo Elizabette Guéçamburu, de 44 años, quien, al igual que Feinberg, padece atrofia muscular espinal y necesita una silla de ruedas eléctrica, además de cuidados diarios.
Guéçamburu comentó que está ahorrando para comprar una furgoneta usada adaptada para sillas de ruedas, que cuesta alrededor de 75,000 dólares. Las modificaciones en su casa, como la instalación de rampas y la adaptación de los baños, también cuestan decenas de miles de dólares, ninguno de los cuales está cubierto por Medi-Cal. Guéçamburu afirmó que esos gastos serían imposibles de afrontar si no pudiera ahorrar.
 Guéçamburu vive en la granja de su familia en Patterson, donde cultivan nueces, almendras y alfalfa. Trabaja a tiempo parcial como contable de la granja. En 2024, a su padre le diagnosticaron cáncer de próstata y ya no pudo cuidarla. Ese mismo año, California eliminó los límites de patrimonio para personas con discapacidad y adultos mayores; Guéçamburu lloró de alegría al poder acceder a Medi-Cal por primera vez.
 “El momento fue una bendición”, dijo. 




 La cuidadora Lexi Marsh ayuda a Elizabette Guéçamburu con diversas tareas cotidianas, como guiarla en ejercicios de circulación, ayudarla a subir a su furgoneta y darle de comer. Fotos de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
Ahora, su anciano padre no puede cuidarla si pierde su cobertura médica, y Guéçamburu se debate sobre qué hacer con el dinero que le dejó su abuela. Probablemente tendrá que depositarlo en un fideicomiso para personas con necesidades especiales administrado por un familiar y renunciar a su independencia económica. Además, ella hizo que su familia la excluyera oficialmente de la herencia de la granja centenaria. La atención domiciliaria privada cuesta miles de dólares al mes , lo que dificulta que las personas de bajos y medianos ingresos puedan pagarla de su propio bolsillo.
 “Tengo que renunciar a nuestro legado solo para tener seguridad médica y poder vivir mi vida”, dijo Guéçamburu.
 Cambio de límite de activos
 El gobernador Gavin Newsom eliminó los requisitos de patrimonio para acceder a Medi-Cal en 2024, tras una campaña de varios años por parte de defensores de los derechos de las personas mayores y con discapacidad. En un comunicado previo a la eliminación , Newsom afirmó estar orgulloso de las “audaces inversiones” que su administración estaba realizando para “proteger los ahorros y los hogares”.
Pero dos años después, ante un déficit presupuestario de 12,000 millones de dólares, Newsom propuso restablecer el límite anterior de 2,000 dólares, argumentando que se habían inscrito más del doble de personas de lo estimado previamente. La Legislatura se opuso a esa propuesta y llegó a un acuerdo con el límite actual más alto de 130,000 dólares, reduciéndolo nuevamente a 21,000 dólares a partir del próximo mes de julio.
 Lindsay Imai Hong, directora en California de Hand In Hand, un grupo de defensa que apoya a las familias que necesitan cuidados, dijo que los organizadores esperan que el próximo gobernador impulse el cambio.
 “Nos encantaría que la prueba de activos se eliminara definitivamente de la lista de posibles eliminaciones”, dijo Imai Hong.
 El candidato republicano a gobernador, Steve Hilton, declaró a CalMatters que se opone a los límites de patrimonio. Criticó al estado por extender otros beneficios de Medi-Cal más allá de sus posibilidades económicas, incluyendo la cobertura para inmigrantes indocumentados.
 “Las personas mayores y las personas con discapacidad no deberían perder su cobertura solo porque hayan logrado ahorrar dinero. Han actuado con responsabilidad. ¿Por qué castigarlos por ello?”, afirmó. 
 Elizabette Guecamburu realiza ejercicios de circulación en la sala de su casa, a las afueras de Patterson, el 16 de octubre de 2026. Guecamburu teme que los recortes al programa Medi-Cal estatal, aprobados recientemente, la descalifiquen para recibir beneficios. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
 El candidato demócrata a gobernador y favorito, Xavier Becerra, no respondió a preguntas específicas sobre la política de límite de activos, pero un portavoz de su campaña culpó a los recortes federales de la administración Trump de “apretar” el programa Medi-Cal de California.
 Becerra se centrará en “proteger el acceso a la atención médica y exigir ahorros reales, cuantificables y sostenibles”, declaró el portavoz Johnathan Underland. Durante la campaña, Becerra se ha autodenominado el próximo “gobernador de la salud” de California y anteriormente ha sugerido aumentar los impuestos para revertir los recortes a Medi-Cal, pero no ha presentado planes detallados sobre políticas de salud.
 Camille Nguyen, abogada de la Sociedad de Asistencia Legal del Condado de San Mateo, dijo que la mayoría de las personas que tienen dificultades para mantenerse dentro del límite tienen poca seguridad financiera.
 “Tienen todos sus ahorros en efectivo en lugar de una casa. Ese es su fondo de jubilación. Esa es la cantidad con la que esperan vivir el resto de sus vidas”, dijo Nguyen.
 Según datos estatales, aproximadamente 600 personas perdieron Medi-Cal cuando California restableció el límite de $130,000. Los defensores prevén que muchas más personas perderán Medi-Cal con el límite inferior, pero el estado nunca publicó estimaciones presupuestarias antes de que los legisladores aprobaran el límite de $21,000. Si el estado restableciera el límite mucho más bajo de $2,000, el Departamento de Finanzas estimó que 62,000 adultos mayores y personas con discapacidades perderían Medi-Cal en dos años.
Limitar las restricciones fomenta la ansiedad y la ira entre las personas con discapacidad
 Feinberg comentó que la posibilidad de perder Medi-Cal le preocupa especialmente porque también perdería el acceso a un programa especial para personas con discapacidad que cubre las horas adicionales de cuidados y tiene una lista de espera de varios años. Los cuidadores ayudan a Feinberg a levantarse y acostarse, a vestirse y a preparar sus comidas.
 Antes de que se eliminara el límite en 2024, Feinberg comentó que revisaba su cuenta bancaria a diario para asegurarse de que el saldo fuera bajo. En aquel entonces, Feinberg era estudiante de posgrado y no ganaba mucho dinero. Ahora, como terapeuta titulada, ha podido ahorrar algo de dinero.
 “No quiero gastar ese dinero. Quiero ahorrarlo para mi jubilación, tal vez para comprar una casa en el futuro”, dijo Feinberg. “La perspectiva de no poder tener un fondo de jubilación me inquieta mucho”.
 Guéçamburu dijo estar enojada y frustrada porque el Estado considera que los servicios para personas con discapacidad son prescindibles.
 “Es agotador tener que justificar tu existencia en cada ciclo legislativo”, dijo.
 Este programa cuenta con el apoyo de la Fundación de Atención Médica de California (CHCF), que trabaja para garantizar que las personas tengan acceso a la atención médica que necesitan, cuando la necesitan y a un precio asequible. Visite www.chcf.org para obtener más información.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Voters will decide whether to expand a tax relief program for Georgia farmers
text:
A voter card is inserted into one of Georgia's ballot-marking devices. Election workers in Bartow County, Georgia conducted their pre-election tests of the voting equipment on Oct. 6, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderGeorgia voters will have a chance to weigh in on a ballot measure that would expand a property tax relief program to include those who own larger swaths of farmland. 
The proposed constitutional amendment, which passed the Legislature in 2025 with broad bipartisan support, is the first question on the ballot. It would alter the Conservation Use Valuation Assessment, a tax relief program that allows farmers to pay property taxes based on the land’s productivity instead of the fair market value of the land, which could be much higher. Under it, landowners must keep the land in a qualifying use like agriculture or timber for 10 years in exchange for a reduced property tax rate. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
If voters approve the constitutional amendment, owners of tracts of land up to 4,000 acres could be eligible. Currently, the tax perk is limited to farmers who own up to 2,000 acres. The average farm size in Georgia is 253 acres, according to the Georgia Farm Bureau.
Proponents pitch the amendment as a necessary adjustment to a program that was first approved by voters through a 1990 constitutional amendment to help family farms, many of which are multi-generational, grapple with rising land values and development pressure. Opponents question whether the program should be expanded to include larger operations or worry that schools and local governments could see decreased revenue as a result. 
State Rep. Chas Cannon, a Moultrie Republican, said his own family has seen benefits from the original program. His family has owned the same tract of land since 1912, and he said that over the last 30 years his family has been able to avoid selling parts of their land for commercial use or redevelopment. 
“We’ve been able to hold the tract together in its entirety over 114 years …. so you’re able to keep that land together. You’re able to keep it in conservation, and I think that’s a benefit to obviously our agricultural industry and to conservation,” Cannon said.

Cannon is also Colquitt County’s county administrator, and he said that if the amendment passes, it likely won’t have a major impact on local revenue. He said that most tracts over 2,000 acres, which aren’t very many, are likely taking advantage of the program by breaking up large farmland among other individuals, like family members, to qualify for the tax relief program. 
“I think from the fiscal orientation, there really won’t be that much of an impact because, number one, there’s not that many family farms that are over 2,000 acres, and the second thing is that those that are very likely already have that land in some kind of CUVA. It’s just in a different LLC, but it’s related to the original underlying 2,000 acres,” Cannon said.
Adam Belflower with the Georgia Farm Bureau said updating the program is important because “that’s not an ideal way to have to do business,” saying that it adds layers of bureaucracy that add “headache or a barrier that you want to have to deal with.”
Ballot amendment would pave the way for dedicated funding to upgrade Georgia’s 911 system

“it kind of creates an extra level of burden on the landowner who’s trying to manage their asset portfolio,” Belflower said.
He added that only family-owned farms and individual taxpayers are eligible for the tax relief program and that large corporations and investors are barred from taking advantage of it. He added that while people tend to associate family farms with small operations, many family farms have grown to be large scale.
“There’s a lot of very successful family farms in Georgia that because of the commodity they grow, they just have a bigger operation to stay profitable. As margins get thinner; they have to scale, and they’ve got to cover more acres,” Belflower said.
According to the Georgia Conservancy, the program has been essential to preserving agricultural lands across Georgia and helping families keep their farmlands, especially at a time of soaring development that’s reaching rural parts of the state.
And while concerns were raised that many farms taking part in the program in rural areas of the state are not under threat of development like properties in more urban areas of the state, Belflower said that the program helps farmers make a profit on their land. He added that even in rural parts where there is less development, forces that could push a landowner to sell that land still exist.
“It might not be 2,000-home subdivisions like it is in metro Atlanta, but it may be a solar project,” Belflower said. “A lot of these counties down here in southwest Georgia have some of the highest acres of land going into solar of any part of the state. So there are still competing land uses and competing development uses.”
According to the Georgia Department of Revenue’s 2025 property tax administration annual report, nearly 200,000 parcels across Georgia take advantage of the existing tax relief program that together saw about $13.8 billion in property taxes eliminated in 2024. About $330 million had to be picked up by other taxpayers, like homeowners and businesses, so local governments could balance their budgets.
A spokesman for the state association that represents counties at the state Capitol said it’s unclear what impact the change would have on local government funding. 
Tim Lowrimore, the head of the Georgia Forestry Association, argued that the 2,000 acreage limit is outdated. He said that because of smaller profit margins and more costly equipment, many successful family farms have had to modernize by scaling operations and consolidating land to remain competitive.
“The program’s acreage limit hasn’t changed since voters created it in 1990, even as land values and the pressure to sell have climbed. Amendment 1 would give more of those families the option to keep their land in farming and forestry rather than selling it for development,” Lowrimore said in a statement.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Secretary of state launches complaint challenging Georgia residency of House candidate
text:
David Dillie addresses 300 people gathered outside the Effingham College & Career Academy to protest the proposed OpenAI data center in Rincon on July 23, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaSecretary of State Brad Raffensperger has filed a formal complaint against a Georgia House candidate accused of voting in two states, arguing that he does not meet the residency requirements to serve in the state House of Representatives.
David Dillie, a 24-year-old mechanic for Gulfstream, qualified to run as a Democrat for Georgia House District 161 in March and ran unopposed during the May state primary. But last month, Raffensperger’s office launched an investigation into Dillie after discovering evidence that he cast primary ballots this year in both Georgia and Nevada, where he lived until September 2024.
Dillie has denied the allegations. When the secretary of state’s investigation was announced last month, Dillie said he did not know who submitted his Nevada ballot, and cited a 2021 Nevada law requiring the state to send mail-in ballots to every registered voter as the reason why a ballot bearing his name would have been sent to his old address in the Las Vegas area.
But in a complaint filed with the Office of State Administrative Hearings on Wednesday, the secretary of state’s office said it uncovered evidence that Dillie traveled to Nevada from June 6 to 9, which overlapped with the state’s primary election, and voted while he was there. Under state law, a voter who casts a ballot in another state automatically loses their Georgia residency.
“Respondent is deemed by law to have lost his residence in the State of Georgia and does not meet the constitutional residency requirements for office,” the complaint reads.
Dillie did not respond to phone calls or emailed requests for comment.
Growth of data centers becomes a defining issue of the midterms, entangling some Georgia candidates

The Savannah-area district spans parts of Chatham and Effingham counties. Dillie has centered part of his campaign around opposition to local data center projects. Rep. Bill Hitchens, a Rincon Republican, has represented the district since 2013.
Early voting has already begun across the state, and more than 41,000 voters across Chatham and Effingham counties have already cast their ballots. Under Georgia law, parties can replace disqualified candidates until 10 days before an election, giving Democrats a narrow window of time to appoint another nominee for the office.
Aaron “Adot” Whitely, the chair of the Chatham County Democrats, said it would be up to Dillie’s campaign to decide whether to withdraw from the race.
“Should he be disqualified, it’d be a sad situation,” he said. “As long as there’s a substantive investigation, that’s all we could ask for.”
The complaint will now go to a hearing before an administrative court judge. The hearing date has not yet been announced.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: US Supreme Court ruling restores NH law blocking use of student IDs at polls
text:
All New Hampshire voters will need to produce a government issued form of identification when voting in the midterm elections next month. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire high school and college students will be barred from using their school identification cards to vote Nov. 3, after the U.S. Supreme Court overruled a New Hampshire federal judge Thursday evening.
The court’s ruling, which was unsigned, restores a 2026 New Hampshire law that removed the school ID cards from the list of acceptable documents to prove identity at the polls.
The restoration of the law means that all New Hampshire voters will need to produce a government issued form of identification when voting in the midterm elections next month.
Republican state lawmakers passed the law arguing that it would close off the potential for voter fraud using false or out-of-date student ID cards. Opponents said the restriction would deprive some young voters without passports or drivers licenses with an easy means to vote, and potentially disenfranchise those who could not get to the Division of Motor Vehicles.
The Supreme Court’s decision Thursday reversed an order issued by a New Hampshire judge earlier this month.
Judge Joseph Laplante of the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire had issued a preliminary injunction Oct. 2 freezing the law for the general election, after a voting advocacy group, Open Democracy, sued to block the law.
Open Democracy and other plaintiffs argued the student ID ban violated the 26th Amendment, which lowered the voting age to 18, and created an unlawful burden on voting in violation of the First and 14th Amendments. Defending the law, the state called it a reasonable measure to reduce fraud and increase confidence in elections that did not unlawfully burden the right to vote.
In his order, Laplante wrote that he did not believe the plaintiffs would succeed on the merits of their lawsuit. But he ruled that erroneous guidance from the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office given to local election officials in April had caused confusion and necessitated a pause on the whole law.
After the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office appealed that injunction, the First Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the freeze. The state Attorney General’s Office then requested a stay of Laplante’s order Oct. 15.
In granting the stay Thursday, the Supreme Court majority did not detail its reasoning, but the court docket indicated that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson had written a dissenting opinion. That opinion was not immediately available Thursday evening.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: U.S. Rep. Tony Wied, challenger Rick Crosson debate in 8th CD race
text:
Democratic challenger Rick Crosson and U.S. Rep. Tony Wied met Thursday for a debate in the race for Wisconsin's 8th Congressional District. (Screenshot from WFRV)Republican U.S. Rep. Tony Wied and his Democratic challenger, former Green Bay school board member and U.S. Army veteran Rick Crosson, met Thursday afternoon for a debate as the two compete for the Green Bay area’s 8th Congressional District seat. 
The 8th CD has been under Republican control since 2011 and this year the district is getting less attention and investment than the races for the 1st and 3rd Districts, which are seen as more competitive. Two years ago, the seat was open after Rep. Mike Gallagher’s departure from Congress and Democrats put significant resources into the campaign of Dr. Kristin Lyerly — who lost her race to Wied by 15 points. 
With Democrats gaining momentum in Republican-dominated districts across the country, surprises could be coming on Nov. 3, but Crosson’s challenge is still seen as a longshot. 
In the debate on Thursday Crosson sought to cast himself as a problem solver and Wied as someone who isn’t up for the job and who has “acquiesced” to the “erratic whims of the current occupant of the White House” while avoiding accountability to his constituents and using the position to personally enrich himself. 
Wied, the former owner of gas stations in the Green Bay area, worked to present himself as a good-tempered representative who has worked to improve the lives of people in northeast Wisconsin through his constituent services, while defending many of President Donald Trump’s actions that he has supported. 
Hosted by WFRV’s Tom Zalaski and Stacy Engebretson, the debate focused on the economy, the political environment, agricultural consolidation, data centers, healthcare, election integrity and the war in Iran. 
Economy
On the economy, Wied acknowledged that gas and diesel prices have risen because Trump started the war in Iran, but said that “decisive action” in Iran is what was needed. 
“Gas and diesel prices are too high, and we know that that comes from the president’s actions, and he took decisive action with a threat that we have in Iran,” Wied said. The threat posed by Iran is “something that every president has dealt with my entire lifetime, and through his intelligence briefings, he felt that there was an immediate threat with a nuclear weapon, and he took decisive action,” Weid said of Trump.  
“I think as soon as this conflict is over, and it has moved from kinetic warfare over to economic warfare, we’ll see those prices come down,” he added. “During the Biden administration, prices were extremely high as well. Gas and diesel prices were very high during the administration.”
When pressed about his votes to continue the war in Iran, Wied said he wouldn’t support a vote by Congress to end the war, calling it a “symbolic gesture.” 
Crosson responded that the people who create a mess don’t then get credit for cleaning it up. 
“You caused the instability. Congress acquiesced to the president, to the whims of the president, in kicking off this illegal and unwarranted war,” Crosson said. “This is one where you can’t blame sleepy Joe Biden for this situation and circumstance. We’ve got to end this war.” 
Polarization
The two men were also asked about the level of political polarization and tension in the country as voters are inundated with negative campaign advertising. 
Crosson said that if elected, he’d focus on “affordability, accountability and quantifiable results.” He argued that Wied, who hasn’t held any in-person town halls during his nearly two years in office, has ducked his responsibility to face his constituents. Wied argued that the telephone town halls he’s held help him reach more people across the district. 
“To me, a tele-town hall already communicates the message that there is a reluctance and there’s a fear of standing in front of people,” Crosson said. “Look, I’ve stood before heads of state, four-star military commanders, ambassadors, 3,000 irate, agitated truck drivers. I know what it means to be held accountable in person. There is nothing that substitutes an in-person exchange of information of concern. And yes, they can get spirited, but we should be leaning into that. That’s the nature of this role. If we don’t have the intestinal fortitude to go into that sort of thing, then we shouldn’t be in this role.” 
Wied said he’s met with more than 300 groups from the district, done news interviews and sends out a weekly email newsletter. He also said that holding town halls in person brings out a “left-wing mob.” 
“I’ve met with over 300 groups here just this year alone. The thing with an in-person town hall is you have this left-wing mob. You have people that work at the Brown County Democrat Party that threatened to kill me,” Wied said, referencing an incident last year in which an unpaid volunteer from the county Democratic party was investigated for making threatening phone calls to Wied’s D.C. office. “They come into these and they scream and they holler and they agitate, and you can’t even get a question. I have no problem meeting with people, and I do. I’ve met with, again, over 300 different groups in this area. I am in the community every single day. I’m the last one to leave to get to D.C. I’m the first one to come home, and we get in the car and we go to all 11 counties every single week. And I will answer any question from anyone.” 
Agriculture
Northeast Wisconsin is home to some of the state’s largest factory farms. As consolidation has pushed farmers to expand their operations while squeezing out smaller family farms, neither candidate offered many specifics on how Congress can help reverse that trend. 
Wied, who sits on the House Agriculture committee, pointed to his work to get schools serving whole milk again and the passage of a 2026 farm bill by the House of Representatives as actions that he’s taken to help area farmers. A full farm bill has not been enacted since the 2018 version of the law expired in 2023. 
“I’ll continue to meet with all of our farmers of all sizes and continue to do everything I can to help them succeed,” Wied said. “What I’m seeing, though, is a very big interest in the next generation to get into farming. There’s issues for sure, but I’m right there to help them, and I will continue to be an advocate and fight for them in Washington.” 
Crosson pointed to the tariffs that the Trump administration has imposed on imports from Canada and other major trade partners. He said he’d spoken with an area dairy farmer who can no longer afford to buy Canadian dairy cattle. 
“Congress has the responsibility for the imposition of tariffs, and if there is an imbalance of trade, then we look at it rationally,” Crosson said. “We don’t do it irrationally at the whims of the occupant of the White House. Here again is one of the things that Congress again has acquiesced in its mission and responsibility to be that watchdog, that check and balance on the excesses of the presidency, that’s one of the things that we have to do to get ourselves back in place.” 
Data centers
As local opposition to data centers has roiled campaigns across the country, the candidates both advocated for local control over the massive developments. 
Wied qualified his statement, adding  that the U.S. has to keep up in the race to develop artificial intelligence and data center deals can be beneficial to communities. 
“Well, I think this is an emerging technology that we need to be the leader in the world in, and there are other countries like China that are really growing in the artificial intelligence, or super intelligence as it’s now being called,” he said, referencing the term that Trump decreed should be used to describe the technology at a White House event late last month. “Some areas around the country are negotiating very good deals. You’re seeing data centers go in and teachers being rewarded with higher pay. There can be a deal, but it cannot be without the approval of the people here locally.” 
Wied went on to blame Gov. Tony Evers for forcing communities to construct “big solar farms.” 
Crosson said he doesn’t trust the big tech companies building the data centers to have the interests of communities at heart. 
“There has to be some level of state and federal laws, policies, procedures that protect our local communities,” he said. “We definitely have to have local control. We need to have the people involved in the decision-making process along the way.” 
Healthcare
Republicans across the country are running for reelection after voting to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut billions in federal healthcare spending. Wied argued that the Affordable Care Act is responsible for pushing up medical costs and that he and other Republicans fought to bring federal money to rural hospitals. 
Some money did get sent to fund Wisconsin’s rural hospitals, but it’s far less than the shortfall they will face because of  the broader cuts to Medicare and Medicaid. 
“Ultimately, we need to have a system where people can go directly to the doctor and not have to deal with these insurance companies,” Wied said. “As it relates to Medicaid, we had some of the most transformational reform, but here’s what it did: It basically says that you have to work if you are able-bodied and you do not have a dependent. The Affordable Care Act put people on the sidelines. If you’re a 29-year-old gamer sitting in mom’s basement, you’re going to have to work 20 hours a week, volunteer, or be going to school. That was significant savings, but what it’s going to do is put people onto payrolls and get them off the couch and actually to work.” 
Crosson noted that the OBBBA is set to kick millions of Americans off their health insurance and argued that healthcare should be a human right. 
“They keep saying that what was called Obamacare was not something that they wanted,” Crosson said. “They tried multiple times to nullify it, but there still hasn’t been anything that replaces this. I start with the premise that healthcare should be a fundamental human right, unequivocally. Once we do that, that’s the vision. We backward plan to where we are, and we move towards that objective. There’s enough dollars to do this. Everybody stops the conversation by saying how we’re going to afford it. There’s money there. We just have to have the national will to do that.” 
Election Integrity
Green Bay has been a hotbed of election conspiracy theories since the 2020 presidential election. When asked about trust in elections, Wied said that people have sincere concerns about the validity of the country’s elections — pointing to grant money Green Bay received from a Mark Zuckerberg-aligned non-profit to help fund the added cost of administering an election during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
He said that Congress should have passed the Save America Act, which would have instituted a strict national voter ID requirement, because states such as Illinois and Minnesota don’t require a photo ID to vote and therefore they  allow undocumented immigrants to cast ballots. 
It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in federal elections, and there’s no evidence that it happens in significant numbers. 
“One of the biggest issues that I hear as I continue to travel around all of our great 11 counties here in northeastern Wisconsin is that people are concerned with election integrity,” Wied said. “That’s why I proposed and we passed in the House the Save America Act. What that says is, look, you have to be a citizen and show ID in order to vote in federal elections. We have elections all across our country with states like Minnesota and Illinois that don’t do that. They don’t require you to show an ID or be a citizen, and that’s not OK. We need to ensure the integrity in our elections.”
Crosson said the federal government should have no say in how Wisconsin’s elections are run and that fearmongering about these issues only discourages people from voting. 
“This is a state requirement, a state responsibility, and we don’t need federal intervention that has the effect of disenfranchising voters,” Crosson said. “This is about making people afraid to come to vote because they know that we outnumber the crazy.” 
‘Communism’ and stock trading
Toward the end of the debate, the two candidates were allowed to ask each other one question. 
Crosson asked Wied about the large number of trades he’s made while in office. Wied’s net worth has increased by more than $3 million since he was elected and the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel previously reported that Wied has bought and sold stock in a number of companies that have business before the committees on which he serves. Wied has said all of these trades were made by his independent financial adviser. 
Wied said that the stock purchases happened because he and his wife had some savings to invest after selling their business. Then he pivoted to attacking prominent Democrats. 
“We sold our business in 2022, and we had some savings. We hired a financial advisor. My wife nor I have ever asked them to buy or sell anything, nor would we,” he said. “But let’s be real. I think the real issue is people don’t trust Congress. You have people like Ilhan Omar that all of a sudden made $30 million out of nowhere. You have career politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Joe Biden that are worth millions, and they’ve never had a real job. That’s why we need to have term limits. We cannot allow people to enrich themselves in Congress.”
Wied highlighted Crosson’s campaign appearances with “known Communist” Francesca Hong, the state representative and former Democratic candidate for governor, and asked if Crosson wants to abolish the police. 
Crosson said he “comes at everything from a law and order perspective” and noted his military career included postings in Europe during the Cold War and working with the Mexican government to prevent drug trafficking over the country’s southern border. 
“Whether or not Francesca Hong is a ‘communist’ is something that you and her would have to talk about,” Crosson said. “I fought communism in my 20 years of service. I fought against totalitarianism.” 
“Of course, I’m for law and order,” he continued. “This is more exploitative conversation to inflame the folks who are inclined to not dig deeper into the facts. So of course I’m for law and order. Who isn’t? But what I don’t want to see happen are people taking advantage of their power and authority and imposing that on our population. That’s not law and order. That’s terrorism, and I’m going to fight that hard.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier ramps up social media discourse as attorney general election approaches
text:
Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on June 15, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Uthmeier's office)Attorney General James Uthmeier is seeking further social media regulation for young Floridians after rejecting a national social-media settlement and following a court victory last week.
Appearing at a news conference Thursday, Uthmeier gave parameters of legislation he wants to pursue next regular legislative session. Those are restrictions for social media use by minors beyond a 2024 law that has been long tied up in court. That law bans social media use for Floridians younger than 14 and requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds.
The parameters, distributed absent official bill language, are in the same wheelhouse Uthmeier asked Instagram to comply with earlier this month as part of ongoing litigation with that social-media company.
Florida taking next step against Instagram after rejecting nationwide settlement

Uthmeier faces reelection in less than two weeks. His Democratic challenger, former state Sen. Jose Javier Rodriguez, criticized the incumbent’s handling of social media litigation, saying, “Florida families deserve an Attorney General who understands that protecting children matters more than political headlines.”
The legislative concept would require age determinations and parental consent for minors to download apps, according to the attorney general’s office. He’s also seeking to prohibit AI chatbots from giving minors companionship, encourage harm, or generate sexual content.
The app would require social media apps to offer a quiet mode from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. and during the school day when school is in session, as well as a two-hour daily use limit. 
Companies would face up to a $50,000 fine per violation. 
“These are the smartest data engineers in the world. If a pedophile is shut off their account, they’ve got to make sure that that person does not come back and if they fail they will face damages,” Uthmeier said.
Joining Uthmeier were Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd; Polk State College President Anastasios Kamoutsas, a former commissioner of education; parents; and state Rep. Jennifer Kincart Jonsson, a Republican from Lakeland.
“Technology is changing faster than ever and we have a responsibility to make sure our laws keep up,” Kincart Jonsson said.
The makeup of Florida’s next Legislature is still to be determined by voters, and no bills aside from claims bills have been formally filed for the 2027 session, which starts March 2.
Uthmeier cannot personally file a bill. Only a member of the Florida House or Senate may do that.
Settling
Florida and New Mexico rejected a near-nationwide settlement with Meta, the company that owns Instagram and Facebook, in a child-safety case. The settlement, worth about $18 billion, would’ve brought millions to Florida, but Uthmeier has refused to settle.
“We told them we’ll see them in court. We stand to make a lot more money in court than caving, settling, selling out our kids for pennies on the dollar,” Uthmeier said, then pointed to New Mexico’s Wednesday court-ordered payout. 
A state court there ordered Meta to pay the state $25 billion. The judge said the state was entitled to about $220 billion following a jury trial that determined Meta violated New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act 44 million times.
New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay state $25B

In a news release distributed about the same time as Uthmeier’s press conference, his Democratic opponent Rodriguez criticized Uthmeier’s approach to the Meta settlement.
“When Congress failed to act, attorneys general across the country stepped up and, after years of battle in court, secured historic protections for children on social media. James Uthmeier walked away from those protections for a cheap press conference promising a bigger payday without any plan to achieve it,” Rodriguez said. 
Last week a federal appeals court ruled that the social media ban for minors is likely constitutional, reversing and vacating a preliminary injunction against its enforcement.
Appeals court lifts block on Florida law restricting social media access for teens

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit wrote that the 2024 law operates “not as an outright prohibition of platform usage but rather as a ‘conditional ban’ of sorts — namely, on platforms’ use of addictive features and algorithms.”
As indicated by tech companies’ reaction to the ruling, they want to avoid identification requirements to use the internet. “In the name of curbing overuse, the decision risks imposing identity authentication on Floridian internet users of all ages,” Computer & Communications Industry Association President Matt Schruers said following the ruling. 
“We beat them in court. The 11th Circuit ruled just last week that our law is upheld so it is on the books and these companies are on notice if they don’t follow it, our office is going to take them to court, and they’re going to have to pay,” Uthmeier said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: New geological estimate puts Alaska North Slope gas resources at 96 trillion cubic feet
text:
Tundra in the northeastern area of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska is seen from the air on June 28, 2014. A new U.S. Geological Survey resource assessment estimates undiscovered natural gas resources across the entire North Slope, including hte 23 million-acre petroleum reserve. (Photo by Bob Wick/U.S. Bureau of Land Management)Alaska’s North Slope probably holds enough undiscovered natural gas to fuel the nation for nearly three years, according to a new federal report.
A resource assessment released Wednesday by the U.S. Geological Survey produced a mean estimate of 96 trillion cubic feet for undiscovered conventional natural gas reserves across the entire North Slope.
That is far more than the 35 trillion cubic feet of known reserves, most of which lie within the Greater Prudhoe Bay Unit, which has been producing oil since the 1970s.
The 96 trillion cubic feet estimate is “roughly three times the size of the known gas accumulations on the Alaska North Slope,” said Alicia Lindauer, coordinator of the USGS energy resources program, in a news briefing Wednesday.
“If you think about the total natural gas consumption across the country, it would be the equivalent of just under three years’ worth of U.S. natural gas consumption.” 
The new assessment also contains a mean estimate of 17 billion barrels of undiscovered oil on the North Slope.
It is the first North Slope-wide resource assessment for natural gas. Past USGS assessments have been for portions of the North Slope. Recent USGS assessments for different areas were released in 2021, 2020 and 2017.
The total was not surprising, given that it was a North Slope-wide assessment, said William Craddock, a USGS geologist who was one of the report’s authors.
“In a sense, we think this is fairly consistent with how the province has been viewed in the past,” Craddock said at the news briefing.
The report incorporates new knowledge and new technology, the USGS officials said. Like other geologic reports, it does not consider the economics of extracting that oil and gas, they said.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Big oil discoveries at Willow, the huge project that ConocoPhillips is developing on the western North Slope, and at Pikka, the nearby project where operator Santos started production this year, were among the factors considered, the report’s authors said.
“Those plays in particular are very prospective, are highly prospective, for undiscovered oil and gas resources,” Craddock said. “The geology that defines those fields extends across vast portions of the northern part of this province, and so that prospectivity is reflected in the undiscovered oil and gas resource numbers.”
Like other USGS resource assessments, the new report does not consider economic factors. The new report also considers only conventional oil and gas, whether associated with oil deposits or independent of those liquids. It does not consider unconventional resources like gas hydrates or coalbed methane.
And like other USGS resource assessments, it includes estimate ranges. For natural gas, the range is between 17.3 trillion and 276.6 trillion cubic feet.
The new assessment includes three general geologic layers below the North Slope’s surface: the Brookian sequence, which holds rocks 140 million years old and younger, covering most of the Cretaceous era; the Beaufortian sequence, which holds rocks from about 140 million to 200 million years old, including the Jurassic period; and the Ellsemerian sequence, which has rocks as old as about 350 million years, and includes the Triassic period.
The Brookian sequence is the one most relevant to current and future oil activities on the North Slope. It holds formations that are important to current North Slope oil production, including the Sagavanirktok formation, which provides oil produced at Prudhoe Bay and other fields, and the Nanushuk and the Torok formations, which underlie newer fields on the western side of the North Slope.
Trump administration touts report
USGS officials said the new resource estimate was not ordered for any specific reason but is part of the agency’s normal operations, which include periodic assessments every few years of energy resources on the North Slope and elsewhere.
“This assessment was conducted as part of our regular process. We’ve had ongoing work to really assess both oil and gas resources across the Alaska North Slope. This one wasn’t prompted by a specific request but was part of that overall plan to assess the entire Alaska North Slope,” Lindauer said.
However, Department of the Interior leaders said the new assessment is in line with President Donald Trump’s policies and an Inauguration Day executive order called “Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential.”
“Alaska is one of America’s greatest energy frontiers, and President Trump is committed to unlocking its extraordinary potential,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in a statement. “Alaska’s natural gas reserves can supply affordable, reliable, secure energy to Americans and our South Pacific allies for generations, and this assessment helps underscore the importance of understanding these vast resources beneath the North Slope and using world-class American science to turn that potential into opportunity. By advancing responsible energy development, we can strengthen American Energy Dominance, create jobs and deliver lasting economic benefits for Alaskans and the entire nation.”
For now, the 35 trillion cubic feet of known natural gas and the estimated 96 trillion feet of prospective natural gas remains stranded on the North Slope, hundreds of miles from any market. For that reason, energy companies have not explored for North Slope gas and have focused instead on oil, which has been shipped through the Trans Alaska Pipeline System since 1977.
Proposals to build a massive natural gas pipeline project to commercialize the North Slope’s gas — sending it either through Canada to Lower 48 markets or through an 800-mile pipeline to a liquefaction facility at tidewater for shipment to Asian markets — date back to the time even before oil production started at Prudhoe Bay in 1977.
None has been deemed economically viable.
Alaska natural gas pipeline dreams stretch over half a century

The Trump administration is the latest presidential administration to advocate for a massive natural gas pipeline project to ship North Slope reserves to markets.
Trump, his cabinet members, Alaska Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, said last month that the Republic of Korea had pledged to invest $54 billion in the current project, which proposes to ship LNG to Asia using an 800-mile pipeline and a liquefaction plant at Cook Inlet.
The claim was false. The Korean government said it has not made any such commitment, though it is evaluating possible participation in the Alaska LNG project.
During an Oct. 13 campaign rally in Wasilla, Trump said the government of Taiwan has committed to invest in the project. In response, the Taiwanese government said it, too, is considering participation but has not yet made a commitment.
