name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s health agency director to step down by end of year
text:
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron presents on the agency’s budget to the Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee on Jan. 27, 2026. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. 
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” 
“This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” 
Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. 
Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. 
“I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” 
Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” 
“The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. We will continue to focus on the work and provide quality, efficient, and effective services for the people of Idaho.” 
Before joining Idaho’s health agency, Charron held leadership positions in the Texas Medicaid program and with the Texas Office of Inspector General. She also worked in government programs and “compliance roles” for a community-based health plan in Arizona, according to her biography. 
 Charron leaves Idaho’s largest agency with the biggest budget 

The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare runs public assistance programs like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Women and Infant Children program. The health department also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, provides child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. 
As head of the agency, Charron oversaw some of the beginning stages of the state’s shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies, as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345. 
The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. 
Charron has also overseen the influx of federal funds from the Rural Health Transformation Grant. Idaho received $186 million for the first year of a five-year grant, meant to go toward improving access and quality of rural healthcare. 
Her tenure followed the previous director, Alex Adams, who served a little over a year in the position before President Donald Trump appointed him to lead the federal Administration for Children and Families under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 
Before Adams, Dave Jeppesen led the agency for five years before retiring in 2023.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: With time short, a modest ‘Super PAC’ speaks up for Ryan Fazio
text:
Hands Off Our Schools, an independent expenditure group backing Republican Ryan Fazio for governor, is winding down with a $164,000 expenditure to produce and place digital ads promoting Fazio in the campaign’s final days.
The expense booked Tuesday and reported Wednesday night to the State Elections Enforcement Commission is a pittance relative to the $8.4 million that Fazio had available in his own campaign account on Oct. 1.
But it is noteworthy as a reminder of what has been missing from the 2026 campaign for governor of Connecticut: Super PACs that spent millions in 2022, mostly on attack ads directed at Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat, or his Republican challenger, Bob Stefanowski.
With public polling consistently showing Lamont with a double-digit lead over Fazio, the race has not attracted significant outside money.
Neither the Republican Governors Association nor the Democratic Governors Association are playing in Connecticut this year — a departure from 2022, when the DGA spent $2.7 million and the RGA spent $3.7 million through PACs established in the state. Another GOP super PAC spent $1.65 million.
Hands Off Our Schools, mostly funded by Fazio supporters in Fairfield County, did some early direct mail and text messages attacking Erin Stewart, the former New Britain mayor expected to be Fazio’s rival for the GOP nomination. But the group went silent after Stewart quit the race in May.
Its new ads were not available Thursday, but the group’s filing stated they are limited to positive spots for Fazio and do not attack Lamont.
“It’s a pro Ryan message about lowering cost of living, increasing affordability in Connecticut,” said Darren Bruno, chair of Hands Off Our Schools. “It’s a pretty standard sort of spot, and just trying to ensure that as many people in Connecticut know who Ryan is and understand that he’s a good candidate.”
Bruno is a Connecticut-based lawyer with the Freedom Foundation, a conservative think tank. PACs like Hands Off Our Schools can accept six-figure contributions as long as they do not coordinate with a campaign or party.
Ben Proto, the Republican state chair, said he would have preferred to see ads directed at laying blame for Connecticut’s high cost of living at the feet of Lamont, not President Donald Trump.
“My position is very clear: It’s Ned Lamont and Democrats,” Proto said. “You can try to blame Donald Trump, but Connecticut did not become unaffordable on Jan. 20, 2025.”
But polling in Connecticut and elsewhere consistently shows voters blaming the president, his tariffs and his attack on Iran for the rising costs of heating oil and gasoline.
It’s a theme Fazio emphasized in Torrington Wednesday night in a town hall-style meeting, a staple of his campaign.
“My very first priority in office as governor will be to pass the largest middle-class tax cut in state history, saving the average middle-class family $2,500 per year in tax relief,” Fazio said. “That is not a ‘nice to have.’ That is not an option for Connecticut. It’s a necessity.”
The governor has countered he already has delivered the state’s largest cut to the income tax.
Lamont and Fazio debate for the first time tonight 7 p.m. on WFSB, Channel 3. They have a second and final debate Tuesday night on WTNH, Channel 8.
As of Wednesday night, 140,830 votes already had been cast by absentee ballot or in the early voting that began Monday.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Legislative District 18 race pits financial adviser against AI strategist
text:
The 2026 candidates for  Legislative District 18, from left: Jess Goldoni of Omaha and Taylor Royal of Bennington. State Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha declined to seek reelection. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)BENNINGTON — It was the crack of dawn when legislative candidate Jess Goldoni opened a listening session at a local cafe, fielding concerns ranging from data centers to technology overreach and tax-burdened startups.
Legislative candidate Jess Goldoni talks to people who dropped by a Bennington cafe for a listening session she hosted Friday, Oct. 16. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
To the visitors who showed up at her Friday “coffee hours,” Goldoni underscored her background that includes co-founding a small business that educates clients on artificial intelligence capabilities. She’s studied AI risks and opportunities. If elected, she’d push to create a “special tech committee” to help guide the state’s use of such rapidly growing technologies that are triggering debates nationwide.
“The bench of technology experience is very thin in government right now,” said Goldoni, 43, who is facing off with Taylor Royal, 36, to represent District 18 in the Nebraska Legislature. “The policies we’re going to have to make — to protect our workforce, protect our kids — require that technology. But we’re not even asking the right questions.”
Meanwhile, opponent Royal knocked on his 13,000th or so door, touting a financial prowess he believes positions him to help rightsize the state budget and determine where Nebraska should invest and grow. Royal is a certified public accountant, financial adviser and co-owner of Royal Wealth Partners.
Candidate Taylor Royal continues door-knocking in waning days of race. (Photo courtesy of Royal campaign)
Nebraska’s projected deficit is $208 million by the end of the current budget period that wraps up next June. An $846 million deficit is also projected for the next biennium, which ends in June 2029.
“If there was ever a time where you’d want a CPA in office, I think now is that time,” said Royal. 
Indeed, each of the District 18 candidates argues that their respective skill set and professional background they’d bring to the Nebraska Unicameral are more valuable to constituents and useful to growing the state’s economy.
 Hot contest 

The two contenders — she’s Democrat and he’s Republican — are in the final days of a hotly contested matchup, currently the third most expensive among legislative races on the Nov. 3 ballot. At last report, a total of about $600,000 had been raised, with Goldoni outpacing Royal by garnering about 61% of overall fundraising.
The winner will represent a north-central Douglas County legislative district that includes parts of northwest Omaha and Bennington. Viewed as among the most competitive and possible swing districts in the state, the gate flew open when incumbent state Sen. Christy Armendariz, a Republican, opted against running for a second four-year term.
Boundaries of Nebraska Legislative District 18 in Douglas County. (Courtesy of Nebraska Legislative Research Office)
Officially, the Nebraska Legislature is nonpartisan, and candidates’ political party affiliations won’t appear on the ballot.
Of roughly 41,000 people living in District 18, about 31,000 are eligible to vote, according to voter registration data from the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office. Republicans outnumber Democrats about 12,500 to 9,700. A large chunk of the district, more than 8,100 voters, is registered nonpartisan. 
 Appeal to nonpartisan voters 

Both Royal and Goldoni are seeking to appeal also to that independent voter pool.
Goldoni said she is “not afraid” to break rank with her political party. 
“I’ve been told that I’m not liberal enough, that I’m not progressive enough. My answer to that is I’m representative of the district … they care about, ‘Can I buy groceries, can I fill my gas tank.” 
Said Royal: “Hypothetically, I will likely agree with conservatives. At the same time, I’m not going to shoot down an idea because it didn’t come from a Republican, so to speak.” 
In Royal’s case, fellow Republican Armendariz was among those nudging him to run for office. He said he admired her tenacity and negotiation expertise on the budget-writing Appropriations Committee. 
The two diverge, however, on their approach to public education, he said. Armendariz championed state funding for the private education of kids in low-income households. Royal said his wife, Katie, is a public school educator who now stays at home to care for their two young children. He said he doesn’t support state funding for private education. 
“I want to make sure we are going to fully fund public schools and maintain the gem of great public education we have in our state,” he said.
Royal said he supports increased access to child care subsidies — which he considers more of a “Democrat idea” that would have placed him on “that side of the table.” 
 Goldoni’s ‘ultimate fix’

Goldoni graduated from the University of Nebraska at Omaha with a degree in journalism and public relations advertising. For the past 20 years as a marketer, the Omaha native helped clients build businesses in industries ranging from finance to law, healthcare and agriculture. The company she co-founded last year is Nebraska AI.
Jess Goldoni of Omaha, 2026 candidate for Nebraska Legislative District 18. (Photo courtesy of Goldoni campaign)
As a new lawmaker, she said, she’d hold coffee hours monthly in her district to hear concerns and ideas. Her priorities, she said, are to help find a structural fix to the state’s money woes and relieve taxpayer burden. 
“We have to have serious tax reform and that starts with a full audit of all incentives, exemptions, programs, everything,” Goldoni said during an interview at Hay Jay Cafe, where on the past few Fridays she hosted the early morning constituent conversations. 
She said she has personally knocked on roughly 12,000 doors, some of them twice. 
The “ultimate fix” for Nebraska’s economic health, Goldoni said, is growing Nebraska’s population and industries. She’s an advocate for an expanded homestead exemption to help retain retirees and opposes using public funds for private schools. 




Quotation







We have to have serious tax reform and that starts with a full audit of all incentives, exemptions, programs, everything.


– Jess Goldoni, District 18 candidate



Goldoni believes her experience in teaching how AI and new technology can impact students and workplaces is one of the assets that sets her apart. Of large data centers, she said, they’re already here — including a Google plant near her house. Rather than a ban, she supports “resetting Nebraska’s rules for a new era.”
Key to establishing statewide standards, she said, is “having somebody in government that knows what big tech is trying to do, and can see it and protect us,” including by demanding transparency and water and rate protection. 
This is Goldoni’s first run at a political office. She said she was encouraged by lawmakers including term-limited state Sen. Justin Wayne of neighboring District 13.  
 Boosting state allure

For Royal, his run for Legislature follows unsuccessful bids for Omaha mayor in 2017 and Nebraska treasurer in 2018.
Taylor Royal of Bennington, 2026 candidate for Nebraska Legislative District 18. (Photo courtesy of Royal campaign)
The UNL graduate said he returned to his home state in 2015 from Texas, where he earned a master’s degree and worked for an international tax firm. He said he watched Fortune 500 ConAgra Foods pull its headquarters from Omaha, despite having benefited from previous state tax and economic incentives — and contrasted that to Texas growth he said was propelled by outreach strategies from its elected officials. 
“It’s important that businesses here and outside know that Nebraska is open for business and that we have the best professionals willing to move at a pace that can … get that business through the door,” Royal said.
Asked about recent staff reductions within the Nebraska Department of Economic Development, and how he might respond as a lawmaker, Royal said he was not aware of all the dynamics but that it was “not a good look.” 




Quotation







It’s important that businesses here and outside know that Nebraska is open for business...


– Taylor Royal, District 18 candidate



As reported last month by the Examiner, in less than a year and a half, at least 61 employees left the state agency charged with boosting economic development, with only two of those involuntary terminations. DED at the time had 69 full-time workers left. 
If elected, Royal said, he’d work to make the state more affordable and alluring by focusing on property taxes, insurance costs, homestead exemption expansion as well as economic development tools. 
He’d like to see Nebraska implement a rate rollback, a budget mechanism where local governments automatically lower their property tax rates when overall property valuations increase. 
Royal recalled a campaign-trail comment that set the stage for a new lawmaker. He said a woman watching her grandkids told him: “Nebraska, it feels like it doesn’t want its old people and doesn’t have a place for its young people.”
“I was like, dang, that sounds spot-on, unfortunately.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC inmate has a chance to leave death row, but lawyers say it’s the safest place for him
text:
This shows the common area of the death row facility, where inmates eat and spend time, with their individual cells in the background. The facility is located on the prison agency's main Broad River campus in Columbia, S.C. The photo was taken in 2019 following a renovation before death row inmates moved in. (Photo courtesy of the S.C. Department of Corrections)COLUMBIA — An order from South Carolina’s high court created the possibility that Donnie Council could leave death row. But in the 18 years since that ruling, his lawyers haven’t tried to get him moved.
They think death row might be the best place for him.
Another condemned inmate, Ron Finklea, is similarly in resentencing limbo, though for not nearly as long. Neither his attorneys nor prosecutors have taken steps in the 2½ years since the state Supreme Court created the potential for him. It’s unclear why.
Donnie Council as of February 2023. (Photo courtesy of the S.C. Department of Corrections)
But for Council, the reason for his peculiar legal position is straightforward: his mental illness, schizophrenia.
“It’s safer for him and for the rest of the prison population at large for him to just be held where he is,” said Boyd Young, a state public defender who heads Council’s defense team.
Young also represents Finklea but declined to comment on his case.
Council, now 60, was sentenced to death in 1996 for suffocating Elizabeth Gatti, an elderly widow, at her home in Aiken County. In addition to murder, he was also convicted of kidnapping, poisoning, sexually assaulting and burglarizing the 72-year-old woman in 1992.
Gatti’s body was found hogtied in her basement, with layers of duct tape wrapped around her head, surrounded by bottles of cleaning fluid that investigators said she was forced to drink.
But in 2008, the state Supreme Court affirmed a lower court’s decision to toss Council’s death sentence and have him resentenced.
The high court found that Council’s lead trial attorney failed during his sentencing to obtain and present evidence that could have led the jury to decline capital punishment.
According to justices’ order, this potentially mitigating evidence included records that delved into Council’s significant mental health issues from childhood and his family history of alcoholism, domestic violence, mental illness, impoverished living conditions and criminal activity.
If Aiken County prosecutors again seek the death sentence in Gatti’s killing, they’ll have to go through another sentencing trial — which in a capital case is separate from the trial to determine guilt or innocence. But due to his mental illness, Council is not legally competent to be retried.
The state could instead ask for a sentence other than death. A judge can make that decision. It wouldn’t require a separate trial.
That’s what happened to former death row inmate Quincy Allen, who was resentenced in 2024 to life in prison without the possibility of parole after a federal court found the judge over his 2005 sentencing trial ignored his mental illness. After nearly two decades on death row, the convicted killer was moved to Perry Correctional Institution in Anderson County.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More restrictive but familiar
Death row is more restrictive than the facilities where people serve other prison sentences. But it represents stability for Council, helping regulate the symptoms of his schizophrenia, Young said. It keeps him and the people around him safe, added the defense attorney.
“After people are in certain conditions long enough, they get comfortable,” Young told the SC Daily Gazette. “Those conditions, even though possibly more restrictive, they feel more safe.”
Council’s documented symptoms include paranoid ideations and delusions of grandeur.
Young and co-counsel Robert Bank, both attorneys with the S.C. Commission on Indigent Defense, said they believe death row provides the best incarcerated housing situation for him. They explained why:
• Death row, at Broad River Secure Facility, is a familiar environment to Council.
• It currently holds 21 men. So, it’s not as noisy as other prisons with bigger populations.
• Death row inmates have a cell to themselves. In another state prison, Council could have a cellmate.
• The facility is self-contained with its own medical unit. If Council experienced a mental health crisis while housed elsewhere, his attorneys said, he would likely be taken to the Department of Corrections’ Gilliam Psychiatric Hospital, which is inside another prison at the sprawling Broad River campus, exposing him to more inmates in crisis situations.
• Council’s accustomed to the people around him: his fellow death row inmates, corrections officers and healthcare providers.

Broad River Secure Facility, the brick buildings on the right side of the photo, contains South Carolina’s death row unit. (Photo courtesy of the S.C. Department of Corrections)

“It’s not chaos for him right now,” Bank said. “We’re making our best-guess decision on what we think will happen.”
Not competent to be retried
Council was diagnosed with schizophrenia around 2001, five years after entering death row.
Council is getting treatment through the Department of Corrections, but it’s unclear when, or even if, he’ll become legally competent to assist in his defense for a resentencing trial.
State inmates with incompetency issues can’t be medicated against their will if they’re not a danger to themselves or to others, Young said. But they can be forcibly medicated if they become aggressive, he said.
The 2nd Circuit Solicitor’s Office, which covers Aiken County, has not responded to multiple phone calls and emails from the SC Daily gazette requesting an interview with prosecutors about Council’s case.
The S.C. attorney general’s office acknowledged that county prosecutors can either set another death penalty trial or withdraw their notice to seek capital punishment.
“The decision to continue to seek death rests with the solicitors,” said Robert Kittle, spokesman for the attorney general’s office.
In the three decades since Council was sentenced to death, 41 of South Carolina’s condemned prisoners have been executed.
When asked whether Council could remain on death row for safety reasons, even if he is resentenced to a non-death sentence, Corrections spokeswoman Chrysti Shain said the department’s score-based classification system determines an inmate’s custody level and housing assignment.
“We wouldn’t be able to speculate or give an opinion on any inmate’s future housing,” Shain said.
The other resentencing order
Ron Finklea as pictured in February 2023. (Photo courtesy of S.C. Department of Corrections)
Finklea, the other condemned inmate in limbo, was sentenced to death in 2007 for killing a security guard at a former manufacturing plant in Lexington.
Investigators said the now-53-year-old shot the victim, Walter Sykes, two times and burned him alive while trying to rob an ATM at the plant in 2003.
Then in 2019, a Lexington County judge threw out Finklea’s death sentence and ordered him resentenced.
The judge found that, because Finklea withheld information about his severe physical and psychological child abuse at the hands of his mom, his trial attorneys failed to present this mitigating evidence to the jury.
The state Supreme Court declined in July 2024 to review the case, paving the way for the lower court’s decision to be carried out.
It’s unclear why Lexington County prosecutors have not resentenced Finklea in the past two years. Rick Hubbard, solicitor for the 11th Circuit, which has jurisdiction over the case, said he could not comment on the matter because it’s ongoing.
Young and Bank also declined to discuss Finklea’s current situation.
Available court records don’t show that he has a competency issue.

name: Delaware
title: Coons, Katz offer competing visions for Washington at Wilmington Senate forum
text:
Photo taken by Delaware LIVE. Graphics added by on 10/22 using AI.
Federal spending, health care costs and foreign policy highlight differences as Delaware voters begin casting ballots.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
WILMINGTON, Del. — Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons and Republican challenger Dr. Mike Katz presented different approaches to controlling federal spending, reducing health care costs and addressing America’s foreign policy challenges Thursday during a U.S. Senate candidate forum at the Hotel du Pont.
The hourlong discussion, hosted by the Rotary Club of Wilmington and moderated by Jake Owens of Spotlight Delaware, gave voters an opportunity to compare the candidates as early voting began for the Nov. 3 general election.
Coons emphasized his 16 years in the Senate, bipartisan legislative experience and willingness to challenge President Donald Trump’s policies. He said his campaign is focused on three priorities, in this order: opportunity, security and justice. Coons described opportunity as helping Americans build better lives, security as protecting families and their futures, and justice as addressing political divisions and abuses of power.
Katz, a physician, former state senator and business executive, argued that after 16 years of Coons representing Delaware in Washington, it is time for a change. He characterized the election as a performance review of the incumbent and a job interview for the challenger, calling for new leadership focused on financial responsibility, government efficiency and solutions to longstanding problems.
While both candidates promised to work across party lines, their differences were evident in how they would address some of the nation’s most pressing challenges.
Photo: The Gold Ballroom at the Hotel duPont, the stie of the Candidate Forum on Thursday October 22,2026.
Federal spending and debt
With the national debt approaching $40 trillion, both candidates acknowledged that federal spending and borrowing have become serious problems.
Coons said Republicans and Democrats share responsibility for growing deficits. He advocated increasing taxes on wealthy Americans and highly profitable corporations while providing relief to working families.
Katz argued that Washington cannot continue increasing taxes without addressing the underlying cost of government.
He called for restructuring federal operations, eliminating waste, establishing balanced budgets and developing a plan to reduce the national debt.
Moderator Owens challenged both candidates to identify specific budget decisions they would make, including which constituencies they would be willing to disappoint.
Neither presented a comprehensive deficit-reduction plan identifying specific spending cuts and revenue increases.
Social Security and health care
The candidates also offered different approaches to preserving Social Security and controlling health care costs.
Coons supported raising the income cap subject to Social Security payroll taxes and working through a bipartisan process to consider additional changes necessary to strengthen the program.
Katz said Social Security represents a commitment to Americans who have contributed throughout their working lives. He advocated reviewing how the program operates before considering changes to benefits or retirement requirements.
On health care, Coons defended the Affordable Care Act as a means of expanding access to insurance and preventive treatment.
He argued that improving access to primary care could reduce expensive emergency treatment and improve long-term outcomes.
Katz, drawing on four decades in medicine and health care management, said the system requires more fundamental reform.
He argued that government subsidies and insurance changes primarily determine who pays rising medical bills without adequately addressing why care costs so much.
Katz acknowledged beneficial provisions of the Affordable Care Act, including protections for people with pre-existing conditions, but described the overall law as a failed approach to controlling health care costs.
Neither candidate provided a detailed legislative plan showing how his proposals would reduce costs for Delaware patients and employers.
Tariffs, energy and family expenses
The cost of living was another area of disagreement.
Coons criticized the Trump administration’s broad tariffs, arguing they increase prices for consumers and businesses, particularly those importing construction materials or exporting products to Canada.
He pointed to Delaware industries, including chemicals, agriculture and port operations, as examples of businesses affected by international trade policies.
Katz described tariffs as a legitimate economic tool when used selectively to protect American workers and businesses from unfair foreign competition.
He said tariffs should have clearly defined objectives, measurable results and congressional oversight.
Both recognized the importance of maintaining American competitiveness, but Coons placed greater emphasis on removing trade barriers while Katz focused on targeting unfair trade practices.
Iran war divides candidates
Foreign policy produced some of the forum’s clearest differences.
Coons strongly criticized the administration’s war with Iran, arguing that inadequate planning and insufficient consultation with Congress and American allies contributed to higher gasoline prices and instability in the Middle East.
He called for ending the conflict and restoring shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Katz said preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons remains essential to American and international security.
He criticized decades of foreign policy decisions, including the 2015 nuclear agreement supported by Coons, which Katz argued failed to resolve Iran’s long-term nuclear threat.
Both expressed concern about presidential military actions without sufficient congressional involvement, although they emphasized different responsibilities and policy failures.
On Ukraine, Coons strongly defended continued support for the country against Russia’s invasion. Katz criticized failures of American and international leadership but did not outline a detailed alternative strategy for ending the conflict.
Katz questions political process
One of the forum’s more pointed moments came when Katz departed from a question about Ukraine to raise concerns about the conduct of Delaware’s Senate campaign.
He alleged that campaign communications had been hacked, staff members had been threatened and supporters had experienced intimidation.
Katz also criticized the absence of a traditional public debate and what he described as insufficient scrutiny of the incumbent.
The allegations were not substantiated during the forum, and no evidence was presented establishing who might have been responsible.
The campaign has previously criticized Coons for declining other proposed debates, including a student-organized event at the University of Delaware. Thursday’s forum brought both candidates together, although the format did not allow direct exchanges or audience questions.
Bipartisanship and congressional accountability
Despite their disagreements, both candidates supported maintaining the Senate filibuster, which generally requires 60 votes to advance major legislation.
Katz said the rule protects minority-party interests and discourages either party from imposing sweeping changes without broader support.
Coons also defended the filibuster while expressing openness to certain reforms, particularly involving voting rights.
Asked when they would oppose their own parties, Katz pledged to evaluate legislation based on Delaware’s interests rather than party loyalty.
Coons cited examples of bipartisan legislation he had worked on with Republican colleagues, arguing that his record demonstrates an ability to deliver results even when party leaders disagree.
The discussion also touched on artificial intelligence, immigration and U.S. military assistance to Israel.
Both candidates supported responsible AI development, although Katz emphasized innovation and competitiveness while Coons stressed safeguards and the potential impacts of data centers on communities.
On immigration, Katz emphasized stronger border enforcement and legal immigration reform. Coons called for border security combined with greater accountability for federal immigration enforcement and legal pathways for qualifying immigrants.
Different approaches, shared challenges
Throughout the forum, Katz returned to his central argument that longstanding federal problems require changes in management, priorities and accountability.
Coons pointed to his relationships in Congress and legislative experience as reasons he could continue delivering results for Delaware.
Both identified rising costs, federal debt and political division as major concerns. Their disagreement centered largely on whether those problems are better addressed through changes to existing federal policies or more extensive restructuring of government programs.
The forum also left questions about specific spending reductions, long-term Social Security financing and measurable health care savings.
With early voting underway, Delaware voters now have a clearer comparison of the candidates’ priorities — and the decisions each would face in Washington.

name: Michigan Advance
title: DOJ to send election monitors to seven Michigan communities
text:
After sending federal monitors to three Michigan cities for the primary election, the U.S. Department of Justice will once again send monitors to observe elections on Nov. 3, according to state officials.After sending federal monitors to three Michigan cities for the primary election, the U.S. Department of Justice will once again send monitors to observe elections on Nov. 3, according to state officials.
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel on Thursday issued a news release stating that seven Michigan communities had received notices from the Department of Justice that federal monitors would be sent to their polling places on Election Day. 
Those communities include Detroit, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids, Hamtramck, Lansing and Warren.
“The law provides specific parameters that allow monitors, observers and challengers to witness elections at local polling places,” Nessel said in a statement. “It’s important for residents to know that DOJ monitors are a standard part of our election process, and we anticipate they will comport with state and federal law just as they did in this year’s August Primary. But make no mistake, my office stands ready to hold accountable those who attempt to unlawfully interfere with or intimidate Michigan voters or election workers, regardless of who they may be.”
Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie said Michigan has hosted federal election monitors before, and the state’s election clerks are well prepared.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“State and local election officials have been in regular contact with DOJ about their plans for this election,” Edevbie said. “As always, we will follow the law, and we expect all monitors, observers, and challengers to do the same. Voters can cast their ballots with confidence and know that our Department remains fully prepared to protect and defend their right to vote.”
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer also issued a statement ensuring that Michigan’s elections are secure and that the presence of federal election monitors is an expected part of the process. 
“Election officials here work year-round to ensure every eligible voter can cast a ballot and the same continues to be true ahead of Nov. 3rd,” Whitmer said.
Unless allowed further access by the local clerk, federal monitors will observe from 100 feet away from the entrance to a polling place, though clerks often have them come into the polling place. 
Election officials told Votebeat Michigan, the monitors overseeing Michigan’s primary election were “polite and unobtrusive.”
Congressional leadership can also send individuals to monitor locations where U.S. House or Senate candidates are on the ballot. Those individuals are selected by congressional leadership and approved by the president’s administration.
Unlike the DOJ’s monitors, these individuals are granted full access to observe the areas where ballots are cast, processed, tabulated, audited or certified before and after the election. However they cannot handle ballots or election equipment, interfere with voters and election administrators, or take any action that would reduce ballot security or voter privacy.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘Clear political stunt’: Beshear rejects Ball’s nominees for executive ethics commission
text:
Kentucky State Capitol in 2020 before construction project (Photo by Sarah Ladd)A day after submitting nominations for an appointment to the Executive Branch Ethics Commission, Republican Auditor Allison Ball says Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear rejected her list. A spokesperson for the governor said the list was “a clear political stunt.” 
Ball said in a Thursday statement she found it “deeply disappointing that the Governor would choose to abruptly reject, with no explanation, our slate of nominees for the Executive Branch Ethics Commission within hours of submission.” 
Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Beshear, told the Kentucky Lantern Ball’s nominations were “a clear political stunt focused more on partisanship and garnering news coverage than finding the most appropriate person to enforce the Executive Branch Code of Ethics.” 
“The Governor hopes the Auditor will take her next round of nominations more seriously for this independent state agency whose mission is to strengthen trust and uphold ethical standards,” Ellis added. 
The auditor had nominated three people on Wednesday with complicated histories with Beshear. They were: 

Christine Trout Van Tatenhove, who is special counsel to Republican House Speaker David Osborne and the wife of former Judge Gregory Van Tatenhove. He was appointed to the bench by President George W. Bush and recently became the dean of the University of Kentucky College of Law. Beshear was critical of the dean appointment over seemingly “partisan and undue outside influence.” 
Former Kentucky Supreme Court Chief Justice Laurance VanMeter, who is the husband of Fayette Circuit Judge Lucy VanMeter. She is currently running for a spot on the Court of Appeals against Judge Will Moynahan, a Beshear appointee. 
David Beck, the former president and CEO of Kentucky Venues who was removed from the role over the summer after the Supreme Court ruled a 2021 law that would have removed control of the board from the governor was unconstitutional. 

Ball said her list had “three highly qualified individuals with outstanding credentials.” Van Tatenhove is “a distinguished attorney with decades of dedicated public service and legal expertise,” VanMeter “spent a career upholding justice at the highest levels of our Commonwealth,” and Beck is “a widely respected agricultural leader and former Kentucky Farm Bureau and Kentucky Ventures executive,” she added. 
“Any one of these individuals would have served Kentucky with honor, independence, and distinction as they have throughout their careers,” Ball continued. “There is simply no valid basis for rejecting candidates of such undeniable integrity, and doing so undermines public trust in the ethics process while doing a profound disservice to the people of our Commonwealth.”
Beshear and Republicans have sparred over the authority of the ethics commission in the past. In June, the Kentucky Supreme Court ruled that 2022 law giving other executive branch officials besides the governor appointment power over the Executive Branch Ethics Commission was unconstitutional, along with the state fair board law. The Republican-controlled General Assembly had approved both laws during Beshear’s first term as governor. Republicans in the executive branch asked the high court to reconsider the decision. 
The auditor’s nominations were made under a previous process outlined in a 2020 executive order from Beshear, which says the attorney general and auditor may give the governor a list of three names for him to choose a commission member. State law says a governor can reject a list of nominees and ask for a new list. 
According to a copy of the letter from Beshear’s office to the auditor, Beshear requested a new list of nominees by Oct. 28. 
The Executive Branch Ethics Commission oversees ethics standards for all executive branch employees.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico workforce participation at prepandemic levels but lags behind nearby states, report says
text:
A new report from the New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions surveyed more than 1,200 unemployed New Mexicans and found that the top barrier to entering the workforce is a lack of nearby jobs. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico’s workforce participation rate has fully recovered to prepandemic levels but continues to lag behind neighboring states, according to a new report.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state Legislature last fiscal year awarded the New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions $750,000 to study the long-standing issue and identify practical solutions. The report, which Department of Workforce Solutions Secretary Sarita Nair presented to lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee Wednesday afternoon, distilled the department’s findings after surveying more than 1,200 unemployed New Mexicans.
“We tried to answer three questions,” Nair said. “Who is not participating in the labor force? How do New Mexicans experience the barriers to participation differently? And what could help people reengage with the labor force, how do we fix this?”
According to the survey, 58% of respondents said they are neither working nor seeking work. However, 60% reported participating in gig work, freelancing or cash-only work in the last year. 
A lack of nearby jobs ranked as the most commonly listed reason for unemployment, according to the report. Caring for family, low wages, lack of skills or training, health issues and disabilities and housing instability were also high-ranking barriers to entry.
While the statewide workforce participation rate of 58% trails behind that of neighboring states and the national average of 61.8%, the new report found that some regions in New Mexico are faring much better. Portions of Albuquerque, for example, reported workforce participation rates of 69%. Northwest New Mexico, particularly a piece of San Juan County, posted the lowest rate at 48%.
The report also found that people with lower levels of education, particularly those who did not complete a high school diploma, have a significantly lower workforce participation rate.
“Clearly, rural economic development and remote work are going to be a big piece of the answers to these questions,” Nair said.
The Department of Workforce Solutions on Tuesday announced that New Mexico’s unemployment rate for September was 4.7%, above the national rate of 4.2%. Luna County had the highest unemployment rate of any New Mexico county at 10.9%, according to the department.
State lawmakers have grappled this year with how to fill gaps in New Mexico’s workforce. A summer report found that New Mexico outspends most states on public assistance programs but struggles to place participants in jobs. Another legislative report earlier this year found that some 32,000 young New Mexicans are neither working nor going to school. Recently, an interim legislative committee looked at an agricultural program in southern New Mexico that offers jobs to at-risk youth and wondered if the program could be replicated across the state in areas with high unemployment rates.
During her presentation, Nair pointed to efforts underway in other states as potential models to emulate.
In 2023, Minnesota established an “Indigenous Workforce Initiative,” which created a database to connect employers and Native American workers who face acute economic and employment disparities, she said. Pennsylvania created a “clean slate” program, which automatically seals certain criminal records after a waiting period, reducing the amount of paperwork job applicants with criminal histories need to complete. 
State lawmakers asked Nair how state leaders can better address these problems. Sen. George Muñoz (D-Gallup) pointed to New Mexico’s historically high levels of reliance on social services like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
He asked Nair how the state can serve people caught in the middle, who might only be able to attain a low-paying job but don’t want to work too many hours as it could jeopardize losing their SNAP benefits.
“It’s kind of a worker’s conundrum,” he said.
Nair in response pointed to the state’s Transition Bonus Program, which temporarily awards money to people who lose their Temporary Assistance for Needy Families benefits because their wages are too high.
“It’s been really successful. It helps people do things like fix their car so that they can reliably get to work,” she said. “Programs like that are probably the answer to some of your questions.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma State Department of Education requests $4.4 billion budget
text:
The Oklahoma State Department of Education, pictured in Oklahoma City, has asked for a Fiscal Year 2028 budget of $4.4 billion. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A new literacy law and rising insurance costs drove a request for $123.3 million in additional funding for the Oklahoma State Department of Education.
The agency is asking the Oklahoma Legislature for a total of $4.4 billion in the 2028 fiscal year, a 2.88% increase, but the budget proposal could change.
The Education Department’s current leader, state Superintendent Lindel Fields, did not seek reelection. His elected successor, either Robert Franklin or Jennettie Marshall, will take office in January and could bring different budget priorities.
Fields’ administration presented its budget request to the Oklahoma State Board of Education on Thursday. The request now goes to the state Legislature for consideration during lawmakers’ 2027 session, which begins in February.
Most of the requested budget increase comes from the cost of school employees’ insurance benefits, which is projected to rise by $110 million next year, said Kristin Stephens, deputy superintendent of operations.
Kristin Stephens, deputy superintendent of operations at the Oklahoma State Department of Education, attends a news conference Oct. 2, 2025, at Eisenhower International School in Tulsa. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
As the state implements stricter laws on elementary reading instruction, the Education Department proposed bringing literacy training and services to districts’ local areas by opening regional service centers. Otherwise, educators and school leaders would have to drive to the agency’s headquarters in Oklahoma City, Stephens said.
Placing agency staff around the state would cost $7 million while partnering with local stakeholders, like CareerTech centers, to use existing facilities.
“Districts need for us to be more accessible to them,” she said. “We want to lean in and support as best we can. We also want to be able to deploy literacy training and the best methodologies that we can do. There is something about proximity. Proximity matters.”
The new literacy law also will require second graders to take the third-grade state reading test starting in the 2027-28 school year, giving students an early opportunity to pass it. Administering the extra tests will cost $2 million, according to the budget request.
The Education Department asked for another $3 million for improvements to its Oklahoma City building, particularly to improve the customer entry and experience, Stephens said. 
The agency also requested $1.3 million for its operational budget. Stephens said some of those funds would establish a research department within the agency.
“I think a lot of folks look to (the Education Department) as the expert on all things that are going on across the state,” she said. “What families are doing, where they’re going, all of those types of data points, and I think that’s what the emphasis would be for us — having a research department that would have those data points at the ready and not rely on outside stakeholders.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Durham, NC one of 30 cities chosen for Bloomberg Philanthropies’ new housing supply initiative
text:
An accessory dwelling unit in Durham. (Photo: City of Durham)The City of Durham is one of 30 cities recently selected to participate in a new Bloomberg Philanthropies housing initiative to bring funding and expertise to cities to help increase housing supply and expand options.
Participating cities will receive $450,000 to $750,000 to pilot technology that quickly clears construction approvals, engage architects to draft permit-ready plans, or hire staff to push stalled projects along. 
Durham Mayor Leonardo Williams {Photo: City of Durham)
Mayor Leo Williams said the amount Durham will receive from Bloomberg hasn’t been determined. 
The city will use its award to expand its Accessory Dwelling Units Pilot program, Williams said. It could be used to hire another staffer to focus solely on the ADU pilot program, he said.
The Bloomberg award “may not be enough money to really have an impact on building units, so we may be able to hire some manpower to help carry this out and execute those ADUs faster,” Williams said.
ADUs are self-contained housing units that are commonly referred to as granny flats, in-law suites or backyard cottages. The Durham program provides low-interest loans to eligible homeowners to build ADUs that will remain affordable for 30 years. The city has already invested $1.75 million in the pilot program.
Sarah Viñas (Photo: City of Durham)
Sarah Viñas, the city’s Housing & Neighborhood Services director, said meeting Durham’s housing needs will require bold ideas and more choices.
“We’re really excited to be one of the first cities elected to participate in the Bloomberg Housing Initiative,” Viñas said. “We’re going to focus on expanding housing options across the city and testing out expansion of accessory dwelling units and other creative housing types to address our affordability challenges.” 
Like other cities across the country, Durham is struggling with a housing affordability crisis, Viñas said.
“Our challenge has definitely increased over the last several years and through the pandemic as housing costs have increased significantly,” Viñas said. “The cost to build has increased and the cost of housing overall has increased, and that’s on the homeownership side and the rental housing side.” 
She said more housing is needed, especially housing that’s affordable for low-wage residents.
“We also know that there are a lot of displacement pressures that are impacting existing residents,” Viñas said, “so another key piece of our challenge is to preserve the housing that we do have, and to support longtime residents so they’ll be able to stay in the city that they’ve called home.”
Low-income renters in North Carolina far outnumber affordable housing units   

Cities chosen for the initiative will model programs in Atlanta, Austin, Texas and San Diego. Atlanta created a position to kickstart stalled projects. Austin increased options for accessory dwelling units to lower rents, and San Diego fast-tracked building application reviews to increase home construction.
Bloomberg Philanthropies noted in a press release that years of under-building has left America with housing shortages in every region of the country and at every income level. Roughy 8.1 million families now share a home with people outside their household because they cannot find another within their means, it said. 
A study commissioned by the North Carolina Chamber of Commerce found the state faces a total housing supply gap of 764,478 units through 2029. That includes 442,118 homes for sale and 322,360 rental units.
Bloomberg Philanthropies only announced the first 15 participants last week. Albuquerque, New Mexico, Alexandria, Virginia, Charleston, South Carolina, Chattanooga, Tennessee, Cleveland, Ohio, Columbia, South Carolina, Louisville, Kentucky, Miami, Florida, Nashville, Tennessee, Omaha, Nebraska, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, Providence, Rhode Island, and San Jose, California were chosen along with Durham to participate in the initiative.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Kanawha school official declines to discuss role of Hope Scholarship in enrollment drop
text:
Paula Potter, superintendent of Kanawha County Schools, addresses reporters during a news conference Thursday. (Henry Culvyhouse | West Virginia Watch)Despite losing more than 900 students this new school year, the superintendent of West Virginia’s largest school district is reluctant to blame the Hope Scholarship and school choice options for enrollment decline. 
At a press conference Thursday morning at the Kanawha County Schools central office, Superintendent Paula Potter told reporters the 4.2% drop in enrollment is a result of an aging population, declining birth rates and more options outside of public schools. 
“Our school system is a microcosm of our society,” she said. 
Potter did not directly answer questions from reporters about how the Hope Scholarship – a program that pays $5,400 per student for families to use in private education –  figures into the decline. 
Potter said the district has kept track of where the students went, but she did not disclose it. 
“I’m the superintendent of our public school system. I’m not focused on voucher programs or other programs,” Potter said. “We’re committed to seeing what’s working for our current students and welcoming anybody who wants to be a part of our school system, and again, we recognize that school choice is an opportunity for families to have that choice.” 
Kanawha County Schools educates 21,199 students, the most of any county school system in the state.
“I would like to talk about the 21,000 students that we do educate. We have a large number of students and families that we service, and I don’t want to discredit that,” Potter said. “We are focusing on student loss because we want students here, but I feel like we need to capitalize on the fact that we are educating over 21,000 students in Kanawha County.”
Meanwhile, other superintendents were more direct. 
Marion County Superintendent Donna Heston said the drop in enrollment “represents a reckoning in that many Legislators are speaking out of both sides of their mouths” by advocating for stronger classroom to workforce programs while simultaneously supporting school choice options. 
“Legislators are systemically dismantling one of the pillars of this country, widening the gaps between the haves and the have nots,” she said. 
Marion County saw an enrollment drop of 336 students. Heston confirmed Thursday that the district had 230 students leave for the Hope Scholarship between July and September. 
And over at Roane County Schools, the hardest hit in terms of percentage, Superintendent Michelle Stellato confirmed 100 out of 230 students lost had taken the Hope Scholarship. 
Potter said a key way to turn around the enrollment decline is with economic development, which leads to population growth. She deflected a question about  what else the district should do in light of Berkeley County losing students. Berkeley County is the state’s second-largest school district, and has had growth for decades.
Potter again turned to the 21,000 students her district teaches. 
“Students are enrolling, but we do have less students in Kanawha County, enrolling everywhere, there’s been a decline, even in some of our choice options as well. And so, again, the school system is a microcosm of our society,” she said. 
Berkeley County announced Thursday it had directed its attorneys to file notice of a lawsuit against the state on the grounds that the state’s school funding formula is inadequate.
Superintendent Ryan Saxe said the timing of the legal move is not related to the news of enrollment decline. 
“While declining enrollment adds another layer of financial pressure, it was not the reason for pursuing this action,” he said. “Our concerns are rooted in the longstanding gap between the resources provided and the actual costs of meeting our students’ needs. Ultimately, this effort is about ensuring that West Virginia’s public school funding system can support the thorough and efficient education guaranteed by our state constitution to each and every one of our students.”

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers propose $11M fix to restore school sports and activities funding
text:
Wyoming’s new school funding model added more than $250 million in state education funding, including for widely supported teacher raises, to be spread across Wyoming’s 48 districts over two years.
But school districts also encountered shortfalls and new constraints, particularly related to funding activities like sports and theater. The new model resulted in disparities — giving 26 districts an increase in funding for activities, and leaving 22 others with shortfalls. A statewide association projected funding for student activities would take a $3.9 million hit, and warned of cuts, consolidation or other belt-tightening for activities prized by many students and families. 
On Wednesday, the Wyoming Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration advanced a bill supporters see as a good fix for the activities conundrum. 
The concept is to give each district the base amount it takes to fund an essential activities program at the smallest level, and then adjust based on district size. It would cost almost $11 million in Wyoming’s school foundation program funds for one year.
Laramie Democratic Sen. Chris Rothfuss called it a sensible solution.
Natrona County, Kelly Walsh, Riverton and Rock Springs high school athletes celebrate atop the podium during the 2014 track and field Class 4A West Regional at Natrona County High School in Casper. (Ryan Dorgan/Casper Star-Tribune)
What the committee has learned is “that districts were effectively using teacher salaries to support activities because we were insufficiently funding activities,” he said. “The testimony that we’ve heard, the data that we’ve seen shows, in my opinion, that we were about $10 million short, and this ends up with a system that adds it back about $10 million. So I think this is a good approach to bridge that gap.”
The committee agreed to sponsor the bill by a slim margin, voting 6-5. The vote means it will go into the session with committee backing, which has historically lent gravitas to legislation. 
Golf, cheer, speech and debate
After the school funding bill passed the 2026 Legislature, Gov. Mark Gordon let it go into law without his signature, arguing it would strip local control and could impact noninstructional expenses related to things like activities and nutrition.
It wasn’t long before concerns bubbled up from the activities association and districts. Most districts indicated they could rely on carryover funds to support activities in 2026-2027, according to the association, an approach that is “widely viewed as a temporary, one-year solution rather than a sustainable path forward.”
Recalibration committee members worked over the summer to find an activities-funding fix. Jackson Democratic Rep. Mike Yin was the chief architect of the bill the committee passed Wednesday. He worked with education stakeholders to develop it. What he discovered was that the state has long underfunded activities, he said, which he attempted to rectify.

Rep. Mike Yin, D-Jackson, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“We heard from people saying we didn’t want to cut student activities,” Yin said, “and so what I tried to do as best as I could is just model towards our actual expenses for school districts on activities, so we don’t give them less than what they currently spend on activities.”
Yin and stakeholders referred to their bill as a “cost-based-plus” model that would be scalable from tiny districts to large ones. 
It wouldn’t benefit all districts. The formula would result in estimated funding increases for 34 school districts, estimated decreases for 13 school districts and no
estimated change for one, according to the Legislative Service Office. But, supporters said, it would “right-size” the funding.
The committee considered two other options: doing nothing, which would keep the status quo, or advancing a bill to revert the activities funding to the way it was before the 2026 school funding bill passed.
Even though Yin’s bill represents the most expensive option, Sheridan Republican Rep. Tom Kelly supports it. 
“I am typically very averse when I see the larger price tag,” Kelly said. But in this case, he said, the value of high school activities is large enough to warrant the cost. 
Funding mandates and court decisions
The Legislature is constitutionally required to fund Wyoming’s public schools and is tasked every five years with a “recalibration” process. The undertaking involves assessing the state’s school funding model and making necessary updates. 
The latest recalibration came in the wake of a 2025 court decision that Wyoming was violating the state’s constitution by underfunding its public schools and must remedy that. 
Wyoming appealed that decision. In September, months after the new funding bill passed, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled that the state has failed to adequately fund K-12 teacher salaries and properly account for inflation. But the court struck down other portions of a lower court’s finding that Wyoming has a constitutional obligation to pay for school resource officers, student nutrition and computers.
Lawmakers on the Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration listen to testimony June 17, 2025. (Claudia Chavez/Better Wyoming)
The recalibration committee discussed the ruling’s implications with an attorney in executive session on Wednesday morning. Members then voted against sponsoring a bill to fund technology needs, with critics like Kelly questioning the wisdom of adding screen time for young children. The committee also tabled bills concerning nutrition and school resource officers. 
Committee Co-Chairman Rep Scott Heiner, R-Green River, said lawmakers still want to explore funding school officers and nutrition programs, but not through recalibration.
The latest Supreme Court decision stemmed from a 2022 lawsuit against the state by the Wyoming Education Association, which represents more than 6,000 of the state’s public school employees. On Thursday, WEA President Kim Amen said the committee’s decision to table those bills was disappointing. 
“Ninety-three percent or more of our students go to public schools, and we should be funding them accordingly, not based on ‘well, we don’t have to fund food because the court said we don’t,’” she said.
The committee will meet again in December.

name: VTDigger
title: International and out-of-state students are an asset, not a threat
text:
Dear Editor,
I have spent more than 30 years working in information technology at four institutions of higher education, and I’ve consulted for many others. In my experience, the suggestion that admitting an international or out-of-state student takes away an educational opportunity from an in-state student misses many things, of which I will point out three.
First, most of the time, international and out-of-state students do not pay the same amount to attend an institution as do in-state students. In fact, they often subsidize some costs that would otherwise be met by in-state students. Vermonters would be better off discussing what
to charge international and out-of-state students and how many places to allocate to them. Vermonters could theoretically allot more funds to make up for any loss of revenue from international and out-of-state students, but I have not seen any indications the state would do this.
Second, as a small state, Vermont is not financially able to offer many programs of study.  Therefore, the state enters into reciprocity agreements with other states whereby Vermont students may attend a program of study not offered in Vermont but offered in the other state at a discounted rate well below the other state’s out-of-state tuition. I can only see this as a financial benefit to the state and the student.

READ MORE

Finally, there are the immeasurable financial savings brought about by exposing international students to our wonderful American way of life, principles, ideals and so on. I believe many international students have returned to their home country and applied them, which I think makes the world a better and safer place for Americans. 
Any arguments regarding international students staying in the U.S. after graduation from a U.S. institution of higher education conflate this issue with U.S. immigration laws and policies. Such immigration issues should be addressed separately from those related to international student attendance at U.S. institutions.  
Richard BlevinsReadsboro, Vt.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Swadley to serve no prison time, ordered to pay $1.2M for defrauding Oklahoma tourism department
text:
Brent Swadley, left, escorted by one of his attorneys and a police officer, enters a courtroom at the Oklahoma County Courthouse on Oct. 21, 2026, for his sentencing after being convicted for defrauding the state. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A restaurant owner convicted of defrauding the state will serve no prison time, but must pay $1.2 million in restitution, an Oklahoma County judge ordered.
Oklahoma County District Judge Cindy Truong on Thursday sentenced Brent Swadley to a suspended six-year sentence after a jury convicted him of inflating invoices related to the operation of Swadley’s Foggy Bottom restaurants at six state parks.
The jury that convicted Swadley in May of one count of conspiracy to defraud the state and five counts of giving fraudulent claims to the state had recommended he serve 10 years in prison and pay $75,000 in fines. 
The Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office, which prosecuted the case, had asked the court to impose the jury’s recommended prison sentence and had sought over $9 million in restitution.
But after listening to two days of arguments about the sentencing and restitution, Truong instead opted for the suspended sentences, meaning Swadley will serve no prison time, but his felony convictions will remain on his criminal record. Truong sentenced Swadley, who has denied wrongdoing, to five years for the conspiracy count to be served concurrently with four one-year sentences for fraudulent claim convictions. The fifth and final fraudulent claim conviction received a one-year sentence to be served after the first five years.
Brent Swadley speaks to his attorneys inside a courtroom at the Oklahoma County Courthouse on Oct. 21, 2026, for his sentencing after being convicted for defrauding the state. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Her ruling was met with audible crying from Swadley’s family and supporters who filled the courtroom. 
Truong said while she doesn’t excuse Swadley’s actions, it wouldn’t do the public “any good” to have him spend another day in the Grady County Jail. 
“I don’t want DOC or the county to be responsible for you anymore,” she said, referring to the Department of Corrections and the county jail where he was most recently held. 
Truong said Swadley faced the brunt of the scrutiny in this case, but the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Department also had failures that need to be held accountable.
Swadley was hired by the agency to renovate and operate Swadley’s Foggy Bottom restaurants at six state parks. He was accused of defrauding the state by at least $3.1 million through inflated invoices to the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Department. 
Two other defendants in the case previously pleaded guilty. Curtis Breuklander was sentenced to 10 years probation and Timothy Hooper received five years probation.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond said in a statement that Truong has “invited fraudsters like Brent Swadley to injure Oklahoma with impunity.”
“When a judge ignores years-long investigations by multiple state agencies and a jury of Oklahoma citizens who thoroughly reviewed all the evidence, public confidence in the justice system is undermined,” he said in a statement.
Leaving the Oklahoma County courtroom with his attorneys Thursday, Swadley, who had remained behind bars in county jail since the jury’s verdict, was visibly choked up as he thanked his legal team, his supporters and God. 
Robert Gifford, an attorney for Brent Swadley, spoke with members of the media after Swadley’s sentencing at the Oklahoma County Courthouse on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
“This wouldn’t have happened without Him,” he said, pointing up to the ceiling. 
Truong also ordered Swadley to pay $1.2 million in restitution by Dec. 1, 2028. Swadley must also pay a $50,000 fine and $14,400 in incarceration costs by Dec. 1. 
He must complete 160 community service hours, with the first 20 completed by Dec. 1, 2027. Truong said she prefers that he complete these hours with the Diversion Hub, an Oklahoma City nonprofit, to help people learn to cook and interview for jobs. 
Robert Gifford, an attorney representing Swadley, said the sentence handed down Thursday was “appropriate.”
“Justice was done,” he said. 
Swadley plans to appeal his conviction, Gifford said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Colorado is way behind on Waymo rules
text:
A view from inside a Waymo driving south on Broadway in downtown Denver on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Last month, as vendors were setting up booths at a farmers market on South Pearl Street in Denver, a car drove down the closed road. It evaded barricades, ignored signs and came precariously close to market participants, who eventually were able to guide it out of the danger zone.
The behavior would likely be considered a traffic violation had the car been driven by a human. But this was a Waymo, an autonomous passenger service vehicle. No people were inside it. There was no one to ticket.
The incident was not the only time since the beginning of September when Waymo started operating in Denver that its cars have performed in a way that might have earned a fine for a human driver. But Colorado law does not account for misbehaved autonomous vehicles, and local police have no way to issue tickets when the cars violate traffic laws.
That’s got to change.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At least one Colorado lawmaker is thinking about how to address this regulatory gap. Rep. Jenny Willford, a Democrat who represents Northglenn and north Thornton, plans to introduce a bill in the next legislative session, which starts in January, that would regulate autonomous vehicles and establish a way for police to enforce laws when Waymos run afoul of them.
One of the main provisions in the bill would create and define a new oversight category for autonomous vehicles within the state’s Public Utilities Commission. They’re licensed under the luxury limousine carrier type, Willford said.
“Obviously they’re not luxury limousines,” she said. Her bill would create a category that reflects Waymo’s business model, includes appropriate safety provisions and clarifies the commission’s oversight authority, such as its ability to investigate complaints. 
The bill would also establish how law enforcement could issue tickets when autonomous vehicles break the law.
A view from inside a Waymo driving south on Broadway in downtown Denver on Sept. 7, 2026. (Illustration by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)
Willford said she’s engaging with stakeholders about the bill, and these will include local law enforcement officials and representatives from Waymo. Asked whether she foresees the bill attracting bipartisan support, she expressed doubt.
“In the past, I’ve certainly recognized that my colleagues on the other side of the aisle have been opposed to establishing any sort of oversight or regulation on businesses. So my expectation is that will be consistent when we’re looking at this legislation, but who knows? Maybe they’ll surprise me.”
She previously told Westword that she had considered running a bill on autonomous vehicle regulations during the last legislative session, but Gov. Jared Polis, a fellow Democrat, stood in the way.
“The governor was very, very, very opposed to doing anything connected to Waymo,” Willford told the outlet.
Polis is term-limited and will leave office in January.
Willford’s law, were it to be enacted, would be similar to new regulations adopted in California, which took effect in July. They allow law enforcement to cite autonomous vehicle operators for moving violations and more generally ensure the operators comply with the state traffic code. The rules also ensure operators are responsive when their vehicles are involved in emergency situations.
Colorado regulations can’t arrive too soon, and state lawmakers should have anticipated the oversight gaps years ago. The farmers market incident was hardly the only time Waymos have gotten into trouble in Denver — it wasn’t even the only time they’ve threatened a local farmers market. They’ve been flummoxed by construction zones and pedestrians, and at least one has been involved in a crash (a human driver rear-ended it).
“Uncertainty is the kryptonite of all of AI, and especially self-driving cars,” Missy Cummings, a computer science professor at George Mason University, told 9News. “The instant that the environment changes in an unpredictable way, this confuses the car.” 
Nevertheless, early data indicates that Waymos are much safer than cars with human drivers, and their rapid, widespread adoption should be encouraged, not thwarted.
Willford has used Waymo. She’s a fan. This year she sponsored a successful ride-hailing bill that sets requirements for driver background checks, a measure that followed a case in which a man was charged with unlawful sexual contact against Willford during a Lyft ride in 2024. Waymo offered extra security.
“Honestly, as a survivor of sex assault, like you know, via a Lyft driver, it was really nice to be able to get into a vehicle and not have to worry about, you know, the person in the driver’s seat,” Willford said.
As she develops proposed regulations for autonomous vehicles, she doesn’t want her posture to be adversarial, she said, adding, “But they do need to be regulated. There does need to be appropriate oversight.”
