name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 would let voters reclaim their voice
text:
HOUSE SPEAKER Ron Mariano says Question 3, which would replace party nomination primaries with a single first round that includes all candidates, is “being targeted by a small group of individuals with a lot of money.” 
“They’re all investment bankers. They want a way to get more Republicans elected, and this is a much better way,” he said, echoing the No on 3 campaign’s claim that “billionaires are paying for this ballot question, which will make it easier for billionaires to buy our elections.”  
The professional politicians of both parties use this argument as a smokescreen because they really don’t want to change the undemocratic, noncompetitive system that keeps them in office for decades without fear of being voted out. 
The No on 3 campaign supports ranked-choice voting as a better alternative to all-party primaries. Left unsaid is the fact that the 2020 ballot question to bring ranked-choice voting to Massachusetts, which was defeated, also received six-figure contributions from wealthy  donors — for precisely the same reason today’s all-party primary has received such funding: because winning a ballot measure that the political establishment opposes requires financial support from anyone with deep pockets. 
The Speaker of the Massachusetts House rivals the governor as the most powerful elected official in the state, yet Speaker Mariano got into the Legislature by winning just 223 more votes than his opponent in a special primary election 35 years ago in the small sliver of the state made up by his Quincy-based district. 
Since then, he has never faced a significant opponent, and in almost all of his 36 elections he was completely unopposed, as is the case again this year. When the previous Speaker retired in 2020, Mariano, the loyal deputy, was rubber-stamped without opposition.  
With his control of committee assignments and the huge annual stipends they bring, the Speaker has unassailable control of members’ votes since he controls their pay. Like most Massachusetts incumbents, Mariano racks up huge donations year after year, building up his war chest, all while running unopposed.  
No wonder he wants things to stay the way they are.  
The premise of the No on Question 3 argument, that competing in both September and November is an unfair burden, treats the general electorate as an inconvenience to be avoided. In Massachusetts, you can count the legislative seats truly contested between Democrats and Republicans on one hand. While voters show up in November for marquee statewide races like governor, the vast majority skip low-turnout September primaries—the contests that actually decide who holds power on Beacon Hill for decades. Question 3 simply demands that lawmakers earn the votes of the entire electorate. 
Today, when challengers dare to take on an entrenched insider, they sometimes come close, only to hit a sudden-death wall: the partisan primary.  
This year, state Sen. Will Brownsberger had an opponent for the first time in 14 years. He drastically outspent his challenger, Daniel Lander, but survived the Democratic primary by only 35 votes.  
Lander would have been a highly competitive candidate in the higher-turnout November election, but he had no path forward. Instead, Brownsberger will now cruise to re-election in the general election, facing only token opposition from an unenrolled candidate. Under Question 3, a challenger doing unexpectedly well in the first round would advance to the general election, earning free media, new money, and volunteer energy. 
Opponents claim that Question 3 could prevent a favored party from having any candidates in the general election, but data from California and Washington show that “lockouts” (where a majority-party coalition is shut out entirely because of vote fragmentation) are rare.  
By contrast, we have the far more common problem of vote splitting in open seat elections. More than 40 percent of open seat elections for the Massachusetts Legislature result in a winner being elected who received a minority of votes in the crucial election. US Rep. Jake Auchincloss came to power via a 9-candidate primary, winning just 22.4 percent of the vote. Similarly, US Rep. Lori Trahan prevailed in a 10-candidate field in 2018 with just 21.7 percent.  
Question 3 addresses this minority winner problem by sending the top two candidates in an all-candidate primary to the higher-turnout election in November, rather than letting a 25 percent primary winner cruise to victory without significant opposition in November, build a war chest, and stay in office for decades.  
What about third parties? They don’t have a chance under the current rules. It was more than 100 years ago, in 1917, that a third-party candidate last won a seat in the Massachusetts Legislature. 
Yet Democratic Party operatives used a specious concern for Libertarian Party and Green Party candidates as a pretense in a challenge they filed that sought to prevent voters from even considering all-party primaries. The Supreme Judicial Court unanimously swatted down this argument aimed at keeping Question 3 off the ballot. The court ruled that the proposed law is a legitimate regulation of elections that treats candidates and parties fairly, referring to its 1908 decision that upheld the identical system used in municipal elections. 
Question 3 would actually benefit third parties by including their endorsement of a candidate on the first-round ballot—unlike the current system, where candidates in the primary can only list public offices held. Under Question 3, an endorsement requires the consent of both the party and the candidate. Third parties could develop a meaningful brand name that would provide voters cues to counteract the domination of the incumbents. 
Although incumbents would still dominate, the best evidence that Question 3 would make them more vulnerable is the steadfast opposition of almost all politicians who would be affected by the changes. 
Question 3 moves the final decision from the elections that most people ignore to the ones that have high participation, fixes the plurality winner problem of open-seat primaries, and empowers small parties by giving them a way to build a meaningful brand.  
Some progressives say that Question 3 is a plot to enable the right wing, while some MAGA supporters claim that it is designed to cement Democratic domination. Neither is true. By  moving the contest to the November election with vastly more participation, all-party primaries will help election outcomes better reflect the wishes of the citizens of each electoral district. After approving Question 3, we could improve the system by approving ranked-choice voting, which would also allow for consolidation of the current two stages into a single, high-turnout general election.  
On November 3, the current system ensures you almost certainly can’t vote out entrenched members of the Legislature or its leadership. But by voting yes on Question 3, voters can finally change the rules of the game and reclaim their voice.  
Paul Schimek is a transportation planner and data analyst based in Arlington. He is writing a book tracing America’s political dysfunction to its unusual regulation of political parties, starting with the 1888 Massachusetts ballot law.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 would bring California’s primary problems to Massachusetts
text:
QUESTION 3 on the November ballot is a matchup between the grass tops and the grassroots. The “yes” committee has raised $7.7 million (with the largest checks coming from private equity), and the “no” committee, with less than $200,000, is backed by a bipartisan coalition of unions, democracy groups, and working people.  
Much of the debate so far has been about the credible concerns of how healthy it is to have a small group of wealthy individuals bankroll a law that would make our elections look like the chaotic California elections. In fairness, many of Question 3’s mega-donors genuinely believe in this democracy reform, while it’s also true that some of them spent a lot of money trying to defeat the Fair Share Amendment, which funds our schools and transportation. 
Big money aside, less has been written about the merits and the track record of the election system the question would usher in, with all candidates competing in a single primary and the top two finishers advancing to the November final election. Here’s what the top-two election system produces in California and Washington.  
In Washington state’s 2016 race for state treasurer, a majority of primary voters in the five-candidate race picked a Democrat. Three Democrats split nearly 52 percent of the vote in the primary. Two Republicans, with 25 percent and 23 percent of the vote, finished first and second and took both spots on the November ballot. A majority of voters picked a Democrat in the primary yet there were no Democrats on the ballot in November.  
It cuts both ways. In 2022, six Republicans and two Democrats ran in California’s 4th State Senate District. The Republican candidates collectively won nearly 60 percent of the primary vote, but split it six ways, with the top Republican winning 17 percent. The two Democrats got 22 percent and 19 percent and took both spots on the final ballot. In that contest, nearly 60 percent of primary voters picked a Republican, but in November, they had to choose between two Democrats. 
This is the “top-two” system proposed by Question 3 in Massachusetts this year, and we should reject it.  
Supporters claim the top-two system boosts representation. The evidence, and conditions in Massachusetts, suggest otherwise. As chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, I take the representation argument seriously. Our communities are finally building a bench. More often now, two or three strong candidates of color run for the same open seat.  
Question 3 supporters should welcome that. Yet, under top-two, it’s a risk. In 2012, California’s 31st Congressional District was about 70 percent people of color and more than 40 percent Latino. The leading Democrat vying for the seat, Pete Aguilar, a Mexican-American politician, finished third in the “top-two” primary and was shut out because he split the vote with three other Democrats, while two Republicans finished first and second. In a district Barack Obama won with 57 percent of the vote, no Democrats were on the November ballot because of the top-two system. 
These are just a few examples where “top-two” delivered the opposite of what Question 3 backers claim. Proponents of the California system will say that lockouts like these, where vote splitting shuts a party out of November, are rare. While it’s true that it usually doesn’t happen, it happens enough that the threat of it happening is exactly how money becomes more influential in these races.  
If a party wants to avoid being locked out of November, significant pressure is placed on new candidates with less money and recognition to back out. We just saw this in California, where the state Democratic Party chair asked Democrats who “do not have a viable path” to drop out of the race for governor in order to reduce the real risk of only two Republicans appearing on the ballot in November.  
“Viable path” is often code for money. Gubernatorial candidate Tony Thurmond said party leaders were “essentially telling every candidate of color in the race for governor to drop out.”  
Pushing candidates out may be smart strategy for keeping at least one Democrat on California’s November ballot, but it shows the perverse incentives this system creates. How perverse? In 2022, the Republican leader of the California Senate spent about $50,000 on a mailer promoting a Democrat. The goal was to steer Democratic voters toward one Democrat and away from the other, dropping her below the leading Republican and opening second place for the GOP. We don’t need these perverse incentives in Massachusetts. Running is already hard enough for first-time and working-class candidates. 
Massachusetts wouldn’t be the first state to say no. Voters in Oregon (2014), Arizona (2012) and, in 2024, South Dakota rejected top-two primaries, mostly by about a two-to-one margin. That same year, similar all-party primary measures failed in Colorado, Idaho, Montana, and Nevada. Colorado’s fight looks a lot like ours: Backers led by a former health care CEO raised $19 million, the opposition, largely groups representing working people, raised less than $400,000 and still won via a grassroots effort.  
The promise of a turnout boost doesn’t hold up either. Two studies of top-two (here and here) found no boost in overall turnout. One found that up to 7 percent more voters skip the race when both finalists are from the same party. 
In Massachusetts, the election calendar makes this proposition particularly bad. Far fewer people vote in September. In 2024, 16.6 percent of registered voters cast a primary ballot. In November, about 68 percent voted. If you’re reading an op-ed about primaries, you’re probably a September voter. Thank you for being engaged! It’s true that a small September electorate already picks each party’s nominee. Question 3 wouldn’t fix that. It would give that small electorate a much bigger job: choosing the only two candidates anyone can vote for in November and leaving independents little chance of even making the ballot. Fewer than one in five voters would set the menu for everyone else. 
Finally, supporters say our current system shuts out unenrolled voters. But in Massachusetts, unenrolled voters can already vote in any party’s primary. Ironically, Question 3 would make it much harder for unenrolled and third-party candidates to make the November ballot. Today they can qualify for the November ballot by gathering signatures. Under Question 3, they’d first have to survive the September primary against major-party candidates. That has rarely happened in California and Washington.   
Democracy reform is personal for me. The first time I walked into the State House, I was a 16-year-old youth organizer advocating for our civics education bill with other Gateway City kids. Eight years later, I ran for state rep. and won a challenging primary and general election after fundraising less than $45,000 (California Assembly races can draw as much as $6 million in spending).  
That first session, we renewed our civics push and, thanks to a broad coalition, passed civics education legislation. Democracy is in a fragile spot right now. For too many people, democracy is not delivering, and we have to do better. Many are understandably ready to keep throwing any rock at the system, but we should be wary of big money trying to capitalize on that populist sentiment. The California system threatens to make things worse by further elevating the power of money in our politics and rewarding cynical electioneering.  
If the six- and seven-figure checks behind this campaign aren’t reason enough for concern, look at what the top-two system has produced in California and Washington: vote-splitting lockouts, perverse incentives to game the primary, and pressure on candidates without big money to drop out.  
The lesson is clear: Vote no on Question 3.  
Andy Vargas is a Democratic state representative from Haverhill. He is chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus and co-chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Business.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: All-party primaries would be a step backwards for Massachusetts
text:
THE ARGUMENT IN support of Question 3 on the Massachusetts ballot is that “all-party primaries”—in which all candidates appear on a single preliminary ballot in September, with the top two vote-getters advancing to the general election in November—will increase electoral competition in Massachusetts and thereby make elected officials more responsive to public opinion.  
As Tanisha Sullivan recently stated in CommonWealth Beacon, “[w]ith inherently more competition, elected officials are better incentivized to listen and deliver.”  
This assumption is not wrong so much as it is misdirected.  
Under the system Question 3 would bring to Massachusetts elections, political parties would no longer play any meaningful role in choosing the candidates who run as members of their parties in either the proposed “all-party” preliminary election or the general election. This would amount to the elimination of Bay State parties’ capacity to act as meaningful intermediary institutions and likely lead to an increase in the already alarming number of wealthy self-funded candidates running for public office, as well as the ability of well-financed special interests to leverage their resources to exert undue influence over both elections and public policymaking. Indeed, the list of Question 3 backers is a who’s who of putative plutocrats and special interest groups. 
While the stated intention behind Question 3 is to “empower” voters, more likely we would see a reduction in the quality of democratic deliberation and, in the long run, turnout declines. Allowing parties to provide voters a meaningful choice between candidates in November connects elections to policy decisions, regardless of how competitive those elections are. 
Question 3 advocates seem to believe that increasing the competitiveness of elections requires voters in the Commonwealth to discount party labels, to “vote the candidate, not the party.” 
While popular with average voters—at least in theory—the truth is that the most meaningful single piece of information about candidates for most voters is their party label. Question 3 would eliminate the ability of Bay State parties to police the use of their party labels by candidates in elections and sever the only meaningful accountability link between candidates/officeholders and party platforms.  
Question 3 would replace the present system with a bit of a free-for-all. Proponents believe competitiveness would somehow guarantee more meaningful choices at the polls for all voters, but it likely would do so only in a narrow way, and only for a narrow slice of the electorate. Proponents of Question 3 are, after all, activists with political and programmatic agendas who want to change the rules of elections to favor their interests.  
Average voters, on the other hand, who we know are disproportionately dependent on the information reflected in party labels, will gain little in real value. Question 3 proponents may be correct that more folks will turn out for a competitive race, but their proposal would sacrifice quality for quantity.  
If enacted, Question 3 would effectively eliminate partisan elections, and voters increasingly will see candidates whose party labels reveal no real commitment to a party’s principles or policy preferences. Elections in which party labels lack real meaning eventually will turn on candidate quality and produce what political scientists call “candidate-centric elections.” It’s notable that, even with meaningful party labels at present, far too much campaign and media focus is on candidates and not ideological and programmatic deliberation and debate. 
Proponents argue that political parties would still endorse candidates in all-party primaries. But the very nature of these races would undermine the value of any candidate’s partisan affiliation. 
Massachusetts political party organizations are already among the weakest in America—both of them. Candidate endorsement and party identification are not substitutes for the utility that partisanship provides to voters. For party labels to provide meaningful cues, there must be a tangible and enforceable accountability relationship between a party and its candidates and officeholders, especially for legislators whose individual outputs must complement collective outputs. This is the only way that partisan affiliation can have any meaning to voters.  
In the long run, the preliminary election in September would produce an unmediated and less meaningful choice for voters, while the November general election would produce personalized food fights between two candidates who would have to rely on policy-lite, candidate-centric campaigns that essentially give voters little they could use to hold the winner accountable for their performance in office. In other words, two non-partisan elections means two expensive races to the rhetorical bottom.  
As a practical matter, Question 3 would complicate the timing and increase the costs of running for office. If its proponents’ objectives include empowering marginalized voices and minor parties, then increasing the costs while reducing the time to organize and campaign seems particularly unwise.  
Supporters rarely mention the extra burden this system would impose on candidates. Instead, they emphasize the fact that this system is already used to elect many local officials in non-partisan local elections. But local elections are inherently different from district-wide contests. The successes and failures of local elected officials are easier for average voters to see and experience first-hand, which is simply not possible in a state legislative, congressional, or statewide race.  
It is worth noting that previous “democratic reforms” to party nomination processes in Massachusetts have done considerable damage to the accountability link between candidates and voters that partisanship promotes. Massachusetts has experienced a rapid decline of party registration since automatic voter registration became the norm. Further weakening the role and influence of political parties will not increase accountability.  
Consider that, if the national Republican Party had had firm control over its presidential nomination process in 2016, Donald Trump’s disastrous presidency could have been averted. Here in Massachusetts, Question 3 would usher in a Wild West of candidate-centric elections that would reward imagery and symbolism but leave voters few benchmarks with which to hold winning candidates accountable for their efforts once in office. 
At the end of the day, if Question 3 passes and is implemented as written, the job of Massachusetts voters will become more difficult and the problem the initiative was intended to mitigate (that is, public policymaking that is insufficiently responsive to the interests of average voters) likely would continue, albeit for different reasons.  
In the case of the Legislature, for example, which Question 3 proponents believe is insufficiently responsive because incumbents “toe the party line” dictated by legislative leaders in exchange for insulation from electoral competition, non-partisan preliminary elections would exchange unresponsiveness due to leadership control of rank-in-file legislators for the gridlock that cripples legislatures full of free agents whose re-elections turn on individual marketing, rather than any commitment to a coherent policy agenda. To the extent Question 3 weakens legislative leadership by enhancing candidate autonomy, we are likely to see increased polarization and culture war posturing, phenomena that, as compared to other parts of the country, Massachusetts has managed to avoid.  
At bottom, if enacted Question 3 likely will undermine the facilitation of accountability provided by partisan elections, a reality long documented by political scientists. The resulting candidate-centric elections, which will turn on the ability of individual candidates to “connect with voters” and not on competing policy preferences or ideological differences, will favor the best campaigners, not the best policymakers and not candidates committed to a coherent agenda or ideological perspective that voters can use to rationally judge winning candidates’ performance once in office.  
Question 3 will, at once, increase the degree of difficulty voters face when trying to distinguish candidates on substantive grounds, while freeing candidates themselves from the tactical inconvenience of clear accountability for meaningful and measurable results if elected.  
Jerold Duquette is a professor of political science at Central Connecticut State University, contributor at MassPoliticsProfs.org, and co-editor of The Politics of Massachusetts Exceptionalism: Reputation Meets Reality. Lawrence Friedman teaches constitutional law at New England Law | Boston and is the co-author of The Massachusetts State Constitution, published by Oxford University Press.

name: California
title: New Medi-Cal limits force hard choices for seniors
text:
Caretaker Lexi Marsh (left) helps Elizabette Guéçamburu eat her lunch in the kitchen of her home outside Patterson on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




Some low-income seniors and people with disabilities are being forced to draw down their savings to retain their healthcare coverage under a new Medi-Cal asset limit, writes CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang.
The new limit kicks certain groups off of Medi-Cal if they have more than $21,000 in savings as of July 2027. State lawmakers lowered the cap to help close a $12 billion budget shortfall in a compromise with Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Just two years ago Newsom set a policy that effectively eliminated the asset limit, allowing Medi-Cal recipients to hold on to savings. But when faced with a multibillion-dollar state spending gap, he proposed reinstating a cap at $2,000. The Legislature balked but agreed to lower the limit to $130,000 and then ratchet it down to $21,000 starting next summer.
About 600 people lost Medi-Cal when California imposed the $130,000 limit, according to state data. Senior and disability rights advocates say the cuts unfairly target vulnerable groups. They expect many more to lose Medi-Cal at the $21,000 limit. If the state returned to the initial $2,000 limit, an estimated 62,000 people would have lost Medi-Cal.
Elizabette Guéçamburu, a 44-year-old who has spinal muscular atrophy, requires a power wheelchair and daily caregiving. 
To remain eligible, she’ll likely have to give up financial independence and put some money into a trust controlled by a family member. She also had her family strike her from inheriting any portion of their 100-year-old farm.

Guéçamburu: “I have to surrender our legacy just to have medical security and have the ability to live my life.”

Read more.

Seen and heard at CA state worker strike


State workers represented by SEIU Local 1000 strike at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




Thousands of California government workers represented by SEIU Local 1000 walked off the job Wednesday to press Newsom for a better contract than he’s offered, and some of them came dressed to send a message. 
In Sacramento, prison analyst Don Chaddock wore a Santa costume and held a sign reading “Newsom + CalHR = Naughty List.” Chaddock said he is frustrated by the state’s in-office policy, which has him commuting to a suburb south of Sacramento.

Chaddock: “I don’t mind in-person if we’re actually doing something in-person. Right now, I drive to Elk Grove to sit in a cubicle.”

Here’s what CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe and I learned when we talked with striking workers in Sacramento and Oakland.



More cities want to stop data centers


An Amazon Web Services data center under construction in Gilroy on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Local elected officials in California are pumping the brakes on data centers, reports CalMatters’ Katherine Ortiz.
As public concern over their environmental impact and energy usage grows, at least 26 resolutions, moratoriums or bans on data center development across the state have been passed or proposed in the last four months. 
Los Angeles County’s Monterey Park became the first U.S. city to permanently ban data centers in June. Fast forward to October and Oakland’s city council approved a 45-day moratorium on new approvals; San Francisco approved a similar moratorium; leaders in L.A. and Santa Clara counties are considering limitations, too. 

Nicole Ghio, Food & Water Watch’s California director: “This is not a future that I think a lot of people want. I mean, it’s a great future if you’re a tech billionaire. It’s not a great future if you’re a regular American.”

Proponents, meanwhile, argue that developing data centers is a critical national interest.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaskans to vote on language change in voter eligibility law in midterm election
text:
Volunteers operate an in-person polling place for the special U.S. House primary election on Friday, May 27, 2022, in the atrium of the State Office Building at Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)This midterm election, Alaskan voters will decide whether to change state voter qualification language related to the citizenship requirement to vote. 
Only U.S. citizens are eligible to vote in national and state elections. Ballot Measure 3, which appears on the ballot as 25USCV, would not change any requirements to vote, but proposes adding the word “only” to state statute. 
In Alaska, the law states “a person may vote at any election who is a citizen of the United States.” Ballot Measure 3 asks voters whether to change language to add the word to read: “Only a person who is a citizen of the United States…may vote in any election.”
An eligible voter must also be at least 18 years of age, reside in the state and house district in which they seek to vote for at least 30 days just before the election, have registered to vote as required by law and not be registered to vote in another jurisdiction. Those eligibility requirements would remain unchanged. 
The ballot measure was sponsored by several former Republican state legislators, including former state senators John Coghill of Fairbanks and Josh Revak of Anchorage, and former House Speaker Mike Chenault of Nikiski, who currently serves on the board of the Alaska Gaseline Development Corp. 
Supporters of the measure, called Alaskans for Citizen Voting, argue the current law is unclear and should be updated to clarify only U.S. citizens may vote. The group has raised nearly $900,000 this election cycle, with more than $800,000 of that amount financed by major GOP donor and billionaire Richard Uihlein, according to reporting by the Anchorage Daily News. 
The Alaska Division of Elections held two public hearings on the proposed ballot measure in July and August. Coghill testified at a Jul. 27 hearing in support. 
“The current law says citizens may vote, but it does not specifically say that only citizens may vote, and this measure closes that gap, and it makes the law in Alaska unmistakably clear,” he said.
Coghill cited a proposal considered in Los Angeles, California earlier this year to allow noncitizens who have some form of legal permanent status — like Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, Temporary Protected Status holders or green card holders — to vote in city and school board elections. The city council rescinded the ballot measure in June. 
“This shows the issue is not hypothetical,” Coghill said. “So we should not wait for a similar fight here before clarifying our own law. The point of 25USCV is to close that door before it gets pushed open.”
The Alaska chapter is part of a national group, Americans for Citizen Voting, which works to pass citizen-only initiatives across the country. Five other states including Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia have proposed constitutional amendments this election to bar noncitizen voting.
Some elections watchdogs say the initiatives are a political stunt to turn conservative voters out at the polls this November, according to reporting by Stateline, particularly where Republicans are fighting for re-election and to maintain majority control in the U.S. House and Senate. 
In Alaska, no group officially formed to oppose Ballot Measure 3, but several current legislators gave personal testimony in opposition at the July hearing. 
Anchorage independent Rep. Alyse Galvin testified that Alaska already has a citizenship requirement, and the change would be redundant. She also pointed to increased scrutiny by the Alaska Division of Elections, which preemptively removed over 3,000 voters from the active voter list pending proof of citizenship and said the act instilled fear in her constituents with newly acquired U.S. citizenship in voting. 
“They’re afraid to go into the polls. That’s not okay. They’re afraid because of all of this rhetoric around what’s happening with ICE and everything else. They don’t know if now they’re on some special list. How do I get off the list? All of that. They don’t know how to navigate the system in a way that makes them feel comfortable enough to vote,” Galvin said. “And frankly, I don’t know how to help them do that. That is a concern of mine, a deep concern of mine.” 
“Our system somehow has created fear,” she continued. “And my worry is that this particular ballot measure is going to engender more of that, more of this sort of action, and more of this sort of fear.”
U.S. nationals excluded from Alaska elections
Anchorage Democratic Rep. Andrew Gray, who chairs the House Judiciary Committee, echoed the criticism that the ballot measure is unnecessary, and spoke to a recent case where he said U.S. nationals were prosecuted for voting in Alaska.     

Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, speaks Friday, April 26, 2024, on the floor of the Alaska House of Representatives. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
 

“I am not concerned about California. In Alaska, non-U.S. citizens are already forbidden from voting in local and state elections. This is what led to the arrest of voters in Whittier a couple of years ago,” he said.
Gray said the recent criminal prosecution of 11 American Samoan residents in Whittier — where some voted and a resident ran for school board  — was a failure of the Division of Elections, law enforcement and those residents in understanding the law. 
American Samoans are U.S. nationals, and have irrevocable rights to reside in the United States, but are not U.S. citizens and therefore do not have the right to vote in state or federal elections. In the Whittier case, 11 residents were charged with illegally voting, and the state dropped the charges after a court of appeals dismissed the case last month.
Gray said he opposes the ballot measure because it could eliminate the possibility of the Legislature or local jurisdictions changing the law to include U.S. nationals — like American Samoans — in the right to vote in Alaska elections.
“They should be able to vote. They should be able to run for local office like the school board, and they should be able to serve their local communities,” Gray said. 
“There is room at this particular moment without this ballot measure of expanding being able to vote and serve in the local school board, for example, if we were to expand it to American nationals in Alaska,” he said. “I think that’s the just thing to do. I think it’s the right thing to do. I think it’s the moral thing to do.”
A change to voter eligibility to include U.S. nationals would require a change in state law passed by the Alaska State Legislature and signed by the governor to allow voting in state and local elections. A change to the law barring U.S. nationals from federal elections would require action from the U.S. Congress. 
Early in-person voting has begun in Alaska, and continues through 8 p.m. on Nov. 3. 
In addition to Ballot Measure 3, voters will have a chance to weigh in on Ballot Measure 2, which would overhaul the state’s elections system by repealing ranked choice voting, reinstating closed primaries and repealing campaign disclosure rules established in 2020. 



Ballot Measure No. 3 25USCV – An Act Addressing Voter Qualification
Alaska law requires that someone must be a United States citizen and meet other
requirements to vote. This act would specify that only those who are United States
citizens and meet the other requirements may vote. This act would not change the
requirements to vote.
Should this initiative become law?

name: Delaware
title: Two Dover Men Arrested in September Home Robbery 10-22-26
text:
POLICE LOG – October 22, 2026Dover Police Charge Two Men In September Armed Home Invasion
DOVER, Del. — Dover Police have charged two 30-year-old Dover men in connection with an armed home invasion that occurred September 16 in the 100 block of Cherry Street.
Police said detectives identified both suspects during the investigation and obtained warrants for their arrests. One suspect was already being held at Sussex Community Corrections Center on unrelated charges dating back to September 17.
The second suspect was taken into custody October 21 with assistance from Probation and Parole. He was arraigned and committed to Sussex Correctional Institution on a $154,000 cash-only bond.
Both men were charged with second-degree conspiracy, first-degree robbery, first-degree burglary, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, and theft involving a victim age 62 or older.
The original investigation began after police responded to the Cherry Street residence shortly before midnight September 16. Police said a 15-year-old girl was sitting on a downstairs couch when a masked man entered through an unsecured rear door or window, pointed a handgun at her and demanded money.
The suspect allegedly took an iPad, iPhone, four bottles of medication and a Nintendo Switch charging dock before fleeing. Four family members were asleep upstairs at the time.
The suspects’ names were not released. Dover Police said Delaware House Bill 59, which took effect October 21, limits the release of names and photographs of adults charged with crimes under certain circumstances.

name: Michigan Advance
title: EGLE takes comments on wastewater permit for onsite water treatment at Saline Township data center
text:
Construction underway on Related Digital's hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceOn Wednesday, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy took questions and heard concerns from residents of Saline Township and communities across the state as it worked to finalize an environmental permit for an onsite wastewater facility proposed as part of the hyperscale data center under construction in the Washtenaw County community. 
Under development by ChatGPT creator OpenAI, along with Oracle and Related Digital, the 2.2-million-square-foot facility has served as the epicenter for backlash against data center development in Michigan.
While the Saline Township Board initially voted against rezoning the project site 4-1, Related Digital filed a lawsuit accusing the board of exclusionary zoning. The board ultimately voted 4-1 to settle the suit, allowing the developer to move forward with the project.
Rather than focusing on the water used by the data center itself or other concerns raised by data center opponents, Wednesday night’s hearing focused on the permits needed for an onsite wastewater treatment facility, which would be used to treat wastewater generated by the data center’s employees, including human waste.
The National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit under consideration would allow the facility to discharge the treated waste into the nearby Saline River, with daily monitoring requirements on multiple parameters, though EGLE staff clarified during the hearing’s question-and-answer session that they would be testing the treated wastewater, not the river.
Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy map of the proposed location for an on-site wastewater treatment plant at the OpenAI/Oracle data center in Saline Township. (Screenshot)
Tom Braum, a permit writer for the department’s Municipal Permits Unit, also explained that the responsibility for monitoring falls on the applicant, noting that Related Digital would be hiring a third-party consultant group to operate the treatment facility, leaving it to monitor and report sample data to EGLE.
While this permit would allow the facility to discharge its treated wastewater, it does not eliminate the need for permits from other units of government that may address cooling water, water withdrawals, permits concerning nearby bodies of water or zoning, Braum said.
“This permit itself is just one piece of the puzzle that focuses on their sanitary wastewater,” Braum said.
Braum also emphasized that the facility would not be allowed to treat industrial wastewater, including wastewater from the data center’s cooling system. The cooling water will be disposed of offsite when necessary, Braum said.
Responding to a question, Braum noted that the discharged waste would not be monitored for PFAS, as the department does not expect to find these kinds of chemicals in wastewater stemming from bathrooms and kitchens.
During the public comment period, residents from Saline Township, its surrounding communities and beyond called for stricter permitting conditions, questioned the safety of allowing the facility to self-monitor and raised concerns about how this additional discharge would affect the health of the river.
Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy map of the proposed discharge location for an on-site wastewater treatment plant at the OpenAI/Oracle data center in Saline Township. (Screenshot)
Sean Sutton, who lives downstream from the discharge site in the city of Saline, noted that the biologist report included in the permit documents recommended a monthly average phosphorus limit of 0.1 milligrams per liter, compared to the draft permit, which sets the limit at 0.2 milligrams per liter.
Excess nutrients like phosphorus can contribute to the growth of harmful algal blooms in waterways.
“I’m very concerned about downstream effects. The impoundment about six miles downstream here in Saline City is where nutrients and bacteria will settle and will accumulate,” Sutton said, noting that this is where residents, including his family, live and use the water.
Nichole Keway Biber, the Michigan water justice organizer with Clean Water Action, said the permit failed to account for the data center’s cumulative impact on the waterway, urging EGLE to reject the permit.
Nicki Rockentine, a Saline resident and environmental consultant, raised similar concerns, saying the permitting framework does not account for the cumulative impact of multiple discharge points along the waterway.
“While an individual permit may satisfy current standards, the cumulative effect of the multiple discharge sources deserves careful consideration,” Rockentine said, noting that the Friends of the Saline River had raised similar concerns.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Once a discharge is authorized, it often becomes a permanent feature in the landscape,” Rockentine said. “Environmental professionals such as myself spend much of their careers investigating contamination that originated from activities that were fully legally and widely accepted at the time. History has demonstrated that compliance with existing regulations does not always equate to environmental protection.”
Rockentine also noted that emerging contaminants are not limited to industrial waste and that PFAS, pharmaceuticals, personal care products and potentially even microplastics have been found in domestic waste.
Many of these substances are not comprehensively regulated and wastewater treatment systems are not designed to remove them, Rockentine said.
“The question before us is not simply whether discharge can meet today’s permit limits,” Rockentine said. “The question is whether establishing a new wastewater discharge in the Saline River is the best long-term decision for the watershed, especially when township zoning can be circumvented by lawsuits.”
Public comment on the permit will remain open until midnight Oct. 23, 2026. Those looking to submit comments can do so online through EGLE’s MiEnviro Portal, by emailing BraumT2@Michigan.gov or by sending a letter to Tom Braum, Water Resources Division, EGLE, P.O. Box 30458, Lansing, Michigan 48909-7958.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Population loss, Hope Scholarship driving enrollment losses in West Virginia, school districts say
text:
Inside a Kanawha County elementary classroom in West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/West Virginia Watch)West Virginia public school enrollment experienced one of the steepest drops since COVID, and local superintendents in the hardest hit counties are pointing to demographic loss and the Hope Scholarship as causes.
The West Virginia Department of Education announced Tuesday an enrollment decline of more than 8,200 students, representing a loss of 3.5% of the total public school population. All counties have experienced some degree of loss, although the Department of Education did note a few charter schools saw gains.
Roane County, less than 50 miles from the state’s capital, experienced the sharpest decline, at 14%, triple the loss it experiences in a typical year.
Michelle Stellato, the superintendent for Roane County Schools, said she anticipated a steep reduction because the county had to close two elementary schools.
She found that of the 230 students who left the system, 100 had taken the Hope Scholarship, a program that allows families to use public dollars for private education, regardless of their income.
“I think parents recognize that they have options when we are closing schools and they exercise their right to use those options,” she said.
Georgia Hughes-Webb, the director of data management at the West Virginia Department of Education, said population loss doesn’t completely account for the enrollment decline, during an interview on MetroNews Talkline Wednesday.
Hughes-Webb noted that U.S. Census statistics show a 4.6% decline in school-age children between 2020 and 2025. During that same time, Hughes-Webb said public school enrollment dropped by 7.9%.
“Because the school enrollment loss is outpacing that overall population loss, we have to look to other explanations,” she said. “It could be that more families are choosing non-public options. We don’t quite have all the data we need to fully answer that question. But certainly, given the comparison between enrollment loss and population loss, there are bigger factors at play.”
Earlier this year, state Treasurer Larry Pack, who oversees the Hope Scholarship program, announced more than 26,000 students had applied for it, an increase of 11,000 from the year prior.
Pack said in a statement that the Hope Scholarship isn’t to blame.
‘We are not aware of any significant increase in private school or homeschool enrollment in recent years that would account for the broader decline in public school enrollment. Rather than blaming the Hope Scholarship, we should be focused on addressing the underlying challenges facing our education system,” Pack said.
To be sure, the increase in Hope Scholarship participation can’t be completely attributed to public school students leaving the system. The 2026-27 academic year is the first in which students already attending private school or homeschool could apply for the program.
Demographic decline and more school choice options are challenging public schools in both rural and urban areas across the state.
David Oliverio, spokesman for Harrison County Schools, which lost 397 students, said there’s more competition in population centers like Clarksburg from private, parochial and charter schools and the Hope Scholarship contributes to that.
“But I think it’s really important to remember that families are still choosing public education overwhelmingly over the alternative here in Harrison County,” he said.
Calhoun County, with a total population of less than 6,000 residents, lost 59 students, amounting to 7% of the district’s school population. Superintendent Michael Fitzwater said the sparse, and largely older population, means there just aren’t many children going into the school system in the first place.
But non-public school options are exacerbating the situation, he said.
“In addition to the overall population decline, public school enrollment is affected by families choosing other educational options, including private school and homeschooling,” Fitzwater said. “Those choices can further reduce public school enrollment even when the students and their families continue to live in Calhoun County.”
Even counties with extenuating circumstances, like Lewis County where a summer flood washed away a school, school choice options are cited as a piece of the puzzle.
“Other factors such as a very large graduating class last year compared to the new enrollments, the Hope Scholarship and homeschool participants have also contributed to our lower numbers,” wrote Carolyn Long, superintendent of Lewis County schools, in an email response.
School officials in Cabell, Marion and Mingo offered similar responses — population is declining and students are being lost to private education due at least in part to the Hope Scholarship.
But not every county in West Virginia is in a population freefall.
Berkeley County, situated in the Eastern Panhandle less than 100 miles from the nation’s capital, has experienced a 14% growth in overall population between 2020 and 2025.
Yet, it lost nearly 400 students in its enrollment. Berkeley ranked second only to Kanawha in the number of students using the Hope Scholarship in the 2024-25 school year, the latest academic year with an annual report.
 Berkeley County Schools Superintendent Ryan Saxe said the district commissioned an independent study during the 2024-25 school year to determine why the enrollment was declining. 
Despite population growth, the district found changes in birth rates, aging population and “increased participation in educational alternatives such as homeschooling, private schools, charter schools,and the Hope Scholarship program” are contributing factors to the decline, Saxe said. 
“Of equal concern is the financial impact these changes have on public schools,” Saxe said.
School enrollment is the bedrock for the state’s school funding formula. During the 2026 legislative session, lawmakers tried to pass a bill to address the formula, which educators have said is outdated and inadequate.
That legislation died after being heavily watered down.
Late last month, the West Virginia chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union filed suit alleging the funding formula is shortchanging public schools so drastically that it’s unconstitutional. Then last week, the state board of education unveiled legislative proposals to fix the funding formula.
Del. Joe Statler, R-Monogalia County, is the chair of the House Education Committee. Since the Legislature gaveled out in March, he has led an effort to hear from stakeholders throughout the school system to figure out fixes for the school funding formula.
He said the committee will be digging into the numbers and looking over the proposal from the state board of education.
“I will tell you this is going to be the year of education,” Statler said. “Just hang in there.”
Stellato, the superintendent of Roane, said if there’s one thing lawmakers can do, it is to listen to the professionals, particularly the state school financial officer Uriah Cummings.
“Uriah Cummings has put forth an amended school finance formula, and he’s built it based off of our feedback and our struggles and the things that we know that are difficult to do and the way we run our schools,” Stellato said. “ I wish that the Legislature would give him an appropriate amount of their time and listen to the rationale behind it.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Dr. Daniel Edney named president of national public health organization
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney is becoming  president of a national nonprofit organization representing public health agencies across the United States, the group announced Wednesday. 
Edney will lead the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials for a one-year term while continuing to lead the Mississippi State Department of Health. He plans to focus his presidency on maternal and infant health, rural health and highlighting the important work of states and territories, according to a press release from the association. 
“Our nation’s public health leaders face increasingly complex challenges, but we also have tremendous opportunities to strengthen our public health system through collaboration, innovation and a shared commitment to improving the health of every community,” Edney said. “I am honored to serve as ASTHO president and look forward to working with my colleagues to advance policies and partnerships that support a healthier nation.”
ASTHO’s members are chief health officials from across the U.S. The organization works to develop public health leaders, support their agencies through training and technical assistance, and advocate for resources and policies that improve public health. 
Edney spent the past year serving as the organization’s president-elect. He succeeds Dr. Manisha Juthani, commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Public Health, as president. 
“It is a real privilege to welcome Dr. Edney as ASTHO’s next president,” said Dr. Joseph Kanter, the organization’s CEO. “He brings a remarkable depth of experience — not only as a visionary state health leader guiding Mississippi through critical public health milestones, but also as a frontline clinician deeply committed to tackling complex challenges like the opioid crisis.”
Edney has served as Mississippi’s state health officer since August 2022. He succeeded Dr. Thomas Dobbs. Edney previously served as the state agency’s deputy state health officer and chief medical officer and worked closely with Dobbs on the department’s COVID-19 response. 
He is also a former president of the Mississippi State Medical Association and former board member of the Mississippi State Board of Medical Licensure. He was in private practice in Vicksburg for more than 30 years, and is a board-certified general internist with a subspecialty board certification in addiction medicine.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Republican Kurt Alme leans into homegrown experience in case for Senate seat
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Kurt Alme speaks at a  President Donald Trump rally in Kalispell on Oct. 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)When President Donald Trump visited Kalispell for a rally last week supporting GOP candidates, it wasn’t Montana’s western congressional district — a race polling within the margin of error — that he spoke about first.
Instead, he gave a shout out to Montana’s Senate race, rated “Solid Republican” by political analysts, and shared the stage with the GOP nominee, Kurt Alme. 
Alme, a Harvard-trained lawyer, is known by colleagues as being the smartest guy in the room, but he has only worked in appointed roles — he’s a first-time politician. 
Alme was twice nominated as U.S. attorney for Montana by Trump, and he thanked the president “for being a job reference for me three times.”
“I’ve spent my entire career serving and protecting Montana families,” Alme said. “And now I’m ready to step up again to make our lives more affordable, make our communities safer, and protect our Montana way of life.”
Alme has run a subdued campaign this election cycle but is favored to succeed in a four-way race against Democrat Alani Bankhead, independent Seth Bodnar and Libertarian Kyle Austin. 
 Switcheroo

Montana’s U.S. Senate race has interested political observers this year for many reasons. The Democrat in the race has barely raised $110,000 and has splintered the state party. There’s a well-funded independent on the ballot with a military, corporate and educational resume and most of the state’s high-profile Democrats on board. And incumbent Republican Sen. Steve Daines was supposed to be on the ballot. 
Daines was elected in 2014, putting a Republican in a congressional seat held by Democrats for a century. Then a U.S. representative, he benefitted from longtime lawmaker Sen. Max Baucus’ resignation to become U.S. ambassador to China, and a plagiarism scandal involving his replacement, leaving the seat without a strong Democratic successor. 
In 2020, Daines was reelected over popular two-term Democratic Gov. Steve Bullock and has been a strong voice in the Senate on anti-abortion issues, as well as public lands.
In February, Daines was the first candidate to file for reelection with the Montana Secretary of State’s Office but withdrew in the final minutes of the March filing deadline, allowing just enough time for Alme to submit his paperwork. 
Daines told Semafor in an interview that he engineered his exit to prevent potential high-profile Democrats, such as Bullock, from entering and turning it into an expensive race. 
While Alme immediately garnered endorsements from the state’s elected Republicans, the move drew ire from within and outside the party. 
Al Olzsewski, former Flathead County Republican Central Committee chairman who lost a primary for the western congressional district, said the move “betrayed the trust of all Montanans,” and inserting Alme into the seat was a “deceptive maneuver.”
Alme, whose campaign declined requests for an interview with the Daily Montanan, captured more than 75% of the Republican primary vote. 
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally with U.S. Senate candidate Kurt Alme in Kalispell on Oct 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
 From Montana, for Montana

Alme was born in Great Falls and graduated from high school in Miles City, and he touts his Montana roots over two of his opponents — Bankhead and Bodnar — who moved here as adults. (Austin, who polls in fourth, was also born and raised in Montana.)
While he left the state for education — Colorado for undergrad and Harvard for law school — Alme has spent his professional career in the Treasure State. He has worked in two Republican gubernatorial administrations in budget and finance, been a lawyer in private practice, and was president and general counsel of the Yellowstone Boys and Girls Ranch Foundation, in addition to his stints as U.S. attorney. 
Under former Republican Gov. Judy Martz, Alme says he spearheaded one of the “largest tax cuts in state history,” with 2003 legislation that took Montana’s top income tax rate from 11% to 6.5%, and added a capital-gains tax credit. 
Under Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte, Alme served as budget director through the 2021 session, also working to secure another income tax cut. He has also said he worked to make Montana debt free, and Gianforte signed legislation doing so in 2023, two years after Alme had left his position. 
“That’s my record, and I’ll do it again in Washington,” Alme said during Trump’s visit to Kalispell. “Because we need to rein in Washington’s reckless spending to lower inflation, lower mortgage rates, so more Montana families can afford to buy a home. And we need to keep taxes low.”
Former Montana Attorney General Tim Fox, a Republican, said he was close with Martz and got to know many of her cabinet members, including Alme. 
“I was very favorably impressed with him. I mean, you talk about who’s the smartest person in the room — generally, it would be Kurt Alme, but he wouldn’t ever let you know that, or feel like he feels that way,” Fox said. “He’s a pretty humble guy, which I ascribe to probably his roots in places like Great Falls and Miles City, just being a small-town kid.”
Fox said when he was attorney general, he overlapped with Alme’s first term as U.S. attorney for about four years and got to know him more in a professional setting as both offices had similar responsibilities around crime prevention. 
Alme was a “real breath of fresh air” after previous U.S. attorneys Fox said didn’t communicate well with the state. 
“Kurt immediately reached out to me, and his people reached out to folks in my administration, and we built a lot of partnerships,” Fox said. “Kurt was the kind of guy that felt like, ‘Listen, we’re all on the same team, regardless of politics, and we all have a mission of keeping people safe and preventing crime and prosecuting criminals.’ And I thought he was just stellar in terms of how he worked across the aisle.”
Both times Alme was nominated to be U.S. attorney, dozens of colleagues and peers wrote letters of recommendation, many of whom spoke of his straightforward approach to solving problems and willingness to collaborate. 
His support crossed both sides of the political spectrum, including several Democratic state lawmakers, and spanned from local, state and federal offices. 
U.S. Senate candidate Kurt Alme celebrates early vote numbers with supporters at the Hilton Garden Inn in Billings during the primary election. Alme is favored to win the U.S. Senate contest that features a four-way race. (Photo by Larry Mayer of The Billings Gazette, used with permission)
Those who speak against Alme do so by denouncing the political party he represents and the president in the same breath. 
“Kurt Alme was installed on the ballot by D.C. party bosses in a backroom deal, and he’s been hiding from Montana voters like he’s in the witness protection program ever since,” Abigail Tracy, a Bodnar spokesperson, said earlier in the campaign. “Alme’s campaign strategy is simple: Say nothing, show up nowhere, and let party bosses and political elites in Washington, D.C., do the talking for him.”
Alme has largely aligned himself with the national Republican platform, including saying that while he would “push for a quick and successful” end to the conflict in Iran, “we can’t vote to stop allowing weapons use against Iran.”
“I’ll never support having our sons and daughters’ boots on the ground in another forever war, but we can’t allow that regime to have nuclear weapons,” Alme said in a candidate debate. “We need to support the president, our troops, and our diplomats as they work to set back Iran’s nuclear program and work to reopen their control of the straits.”
He has also said he was originally skeptical about the tariffs implemented by Trump, but said Canada has “gone with unfair trade for too long.”
“Somebody needed to stand up and push back for a level playing field,” Alme said. “I’ll work to be sure that any deal that comes out of this not only levels the playing field, but that it also provides more trade opportunities for Montana.”
 Not a two-party race

Incumbent officeholders enjoy an advantage in elections, and Alme doesn’t have one — though there is a little bit of a party advantage. 
“We do have the incumbent’s party, and Montana, I would probably characterize as like a reddish purple right now,” said Hope Dewell Gentry, a political scientist at Montana State University-Billings, who runs the school’s annual public opinion Mountain States Poll.
The last open Montana Senate seat was in 2014, when Daines flipped it from Democratic control. Before that? In 1978, when Democrat Max Baucus held the seat following the death of Sen. Lee Metcalf. 
Party advantage carries some weight, but Gentry added Alme is not “necessarily a known entity in Montana.”
“I don’t think he has the name recognition that he might hope for to give him an advantage,” she said. “Whereas Bodnar does have name advantage, but he also has name disadvantage because there are plenty of people who know him and don’t like him.”
With a four-candidate race that could splinter a large portion of the non-Republican vote, Gentry said, the winner of November’s election will only need a plurality of votes.
Alme has run a mostly quiet campaign, compared to the numerous public appearances, rallies and debates held by his opponents recently. Alme has only appeared on stage with the other candidates once — a debate held in mid-October. 
“He is campaigning as if he is in a safe place,” Gentry said. “If I was talking to him, I think I’d recommend to him to not feel that he is completely safe, especially with a lot of odd tension between the Democratic Party and the Democratic candidate.” 
Bankhead is polling third in the four-way race, with support among many traditionally Democratic-leaning groups and the majority of big-name Democrats in the state going to Bodnar.  
A fractured non-Republican voting block only helps Alme, Gentry said. 
One of the biggest things Gentry is watching for as ballots begin to trickle in is whether Trump’s recent visit to Kalispell will help turn out reliably Republican voters to boost Alme or could instead fuel a stronger protest turnout among those disapproving of the administration. 
“That’s a dangerous game when your popularity isn’t particularly high because people don’t tend to change their party affiliation,” she said. “What usually happens is if a Republican voter doesn’t feel into a Republican candidate, they’ll just stay home. But that works for the Democrats, too.”

name: Nevada Current
title: ‘No place easier’ to vote than Nevada, ‘unfortunately,’ Lombardo says
text:
Election workers deliver mail ballot drop boxes to the Clark County Election Center on June 9, 2026. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Republican candidates, such as Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, are walking a precarious tightrope by urging citizens to vote even while toeing the Republican party line that elections are not secure. 
In audio obtained by the Current from an October fundraiser, Lombardo, who faces a second-term challenge from Democrat Attorney General Aaron Ford, urged supporters to overcome voter apathy while simultaneously taking a shot at election integrity.
“If you are close to individuals and you ask ‘em ‘have you voted and they say ‘no,’ convince them. There’s no place easier to vote in the nation than Nevada. Unfortunately,” Lombardo added, his last-minute jab drawing laughter from the crowd.  
“Early voting starts the 17th. In-person voting is on the third. Then you can put your mail ballot in five days after the fact,” asserted Lombardo, who has a beef with a 2024 Nevada Supreme Court ruling that allows unpostmarked ballots to be counted for three days after the election.
The governor’s supporters roared at the suggestion that mail-in ballots are suspect. “What I’m driving at is there’s no excuse. No excuse,” he said.
Lombardo’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on how the governor balances the desire to turnout voters with messaging that calls integrity into question, or what he meant when he lamented that voting is easy in Nevada “unfortunately.” 
The episode is indicative of an electorate that has been whipsawed by President Donald Trump’s adherence to the notion that elections are rigged, even as he implores voters to get out to the polls and “pretend I’m on the ballot.”  
The president has made efforts to impose federal authority over state elections,  which dovetails with his persistent false claims of winning the 2020 election and his anti-immigrant agenda, a central tenet of his administration.  
The Trump-endorsed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which would impose a national voter identification requirement, is stalled in Congress, and last month, the Supreme Court blocked Trump’s executive order prohibiting mail-in voting. 
Like Trump, Lombardo has made election reform a focus in his first term. 
In 2023, lawmakers refused to take up legislation the governor sought to undo universal mail balloting. In 2025, Lombardo vetoed a voter identification bill he initially supported because mailed ballots would have still been verified via signature matching. The 2023 legislation the governor backed also would have required mail-in ballots to be received by the time polls close on Election Day, rather than 5 p.m. four days after the election, no matter how early the ballots were postmarked.
In November, Nevada voters are expected to approve a Lombardo-supported voter identification ballot measure for the second time and amend the state constitution. 
In the process, Lombardo has not shied away from election deniers. He has campaigned at Trump’s side, and in 2023 and 2025, vetoed measures that would have imposed prison terms on fake electors. 
Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo shakes hands with Nevada Republican Party chair and indicted 2020 fake elector Michael McDonald as Lombardo filed for reelection in March 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)
When Lombardo filed for election in March, supporters included Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald, one of the six fake electors who sent bogus electoral college certificates to Congress after Trump lost Nevada in 2020. 
Last week, Lombardo campaigned with election denier Joey Gilbert. 
Voter fraud is almost nonexistent in the United States, according to a variety of experts.
In July, Trump’s Dept. of Homeland Security asserted that Nevada may have as many as 15,903 “non-citizens” registered to vote. The government eventually whittled that number to 185. The state contends there is no proof any are undocumented.  
“The President has spent the better part of a decade attempting to manufacture a crisis around voting when there is none,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said in July, after Trump’s Department of Justice sent one of seven subpoenas to Aguilar, demanding personal voter data. 
The effect of questioning election integrity is unknown, however, eroding trust in the electoral process in an effort to mobilize the bases could prove risky “for Republican candidates and American democracy,” writes Christopher Miller, a visiting assistant professor of Philosophy, Economics, and Law at the University of Richmond. “That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can reduce motivation to vote – even if based on flawed information. But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November.”
“Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable,” Miller wrote. “Conventional wisdom suggests such discouraging numbers would depress turnout.”
He cited a study from Germany that indicated casual voters may be less motivated to vote when faced with the prospect of rigged elections, “because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm.”  Voters who are skeptical of “elite messaging” may be more motivated to vote. 
As of Wednesday afternoon, 16 million Americans had cast early ballots, according to NBC News. Of those, 50% were registered Democrats, 32% were Republicans, and 18% were something else.  In Nevada, Democrats had a slight lead over Republicans and others. 
Early voting in Nevada ends Friday, October 30. Election day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri child welfare workers say restructuring is putting children’s safety at risk
text:
A Sept. 1 restructuring of the state's child abuse and neglect response team put frontline workers on specialized teams organized by region (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).By late afternoon on Sept. 25, Missouri’s Children’s Division was struggling to find enough workers to respond to reports of suspected child abuse and neglect. According to an email obtained by The Independent, every available worker had been assigned at least three reports, yet 29 reports across 20 counties remained unassigned. 
Fifteen of those reports had been open longer than 24 hours — the deadline in Missouri law for division workers to locate the child and verify their safety in most cases.
“We have utilized all of our workforce and assigned at least three reports to everyone and still have many left to assign,” the email to division staff said. “I am asking that you all look for any supervisors who could possibly ensure safety on any of these reports please. Some of these are from yesterday that we have been unable to find coverage for.”
A Sept. 1 restructuring in the division assigned workers to specialized teams organized along regional lines. Instead of reporting to local supervisors and responding to reports in their county or circuit, workers answer to regional supervisors and are assigned cases spread across larger swaths of the state.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Twelve current and former division employees across seven circuits spoke with The Independent over the past month about their experiences since the restructuring began. All but two spoke on condition of anonymity because they didn’t have permission to speak publicly and feared retaliation. 
Workers said they are increasingly cutting their safety assessments short as they scramble to reach children within statutory timeframes. Their caseloads are rising as they postpone tasks needed to close outstanding cases and inherit cases from colleagues who quit.
And while division leaders promoted the restructuring as an opportunity for frontline workers to develop expertise in areas such as chronic neglect, sexual abuse or newborn assessments, workers said the changes haven’t narrowed the scope of reports they’re assigned.
Amy DeGraw, a former investigator on the chronic neglect team who resigned last month, described a day when she was asked to drive from the division’s Laclede County office in Lebanon to respond to a report in Rolla and then another in Nevada. That’s a round trip of about 340 miles.
DeGraw said it can take two or three hours to collect the information needed to ensure safety and close a case. 
Add a few hours of travel time, DeGraw said, and “one hotline call could take us anywhere from six hours to complete.” 
“They started making us do two or three of these a day,” she said.
Daniel Johnston, a former investigative supervisor in the southwest region who resigned last month, described running out of workers to assign reports. 
“One day, we got 40-plus reports that we had to assign in the region, and I ran out of staff,” Johnston said. “Everyone was getting three to four of them, and I was sending people two, three hours away. It was utter chaos.”
Daniel Johnston, a former Children’s Division supervisor in the southwest region, left his position in September, citing changes to division policy that he said prevent frontline workers from assessing children’s safety or developing trust with families (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Internal Children’s Division records show caseloads climbed in the weeks after the restructuring.
Between Sept. 30 and Oct. 13, the average number of open cases per worker on the child abuse and neglect response team increased from 33.1 to 38.5, according to photos of an internal data dashboard obtained by The Independent. The division’s goal is no more than 15 open cases per worker.
During those two weeks, the number of cases open longer than 45 days increased by 13.5%, from 10,171 to 11,544. State law generally requires investigations to be completed within 45 days, though extensions are permitted under certain circumstances.
Sara Smith, director of the Children’s Division, told The Independent the division has made adjustments to reduce workers’ travel time, including creating a centralized team to assign reports within a maximum 90-minute radius from workers’ base offices.
“We have a team that is helping make sure the assignment is within a certain radius, that we’re looking at the specialization, the workload that they have and the geographical space,” Smith said. “So just because I’m a supervisor and someone is next in the rotation and a report comes in to my specialized team, they might not be the one that we need to go.”
But current employees said that even with centralized assignments, they are still rushing their safety assessments and struggling to see children within statutory timeframes. 
Workers also said division leaders promised less time on call, but they are now required to cover longer and more frequent on-call shifts.
During an Aug. 26 legislative hearing, Smith told lawmakers the division was hiring workers for night and weekend shifts, saying “asking people to be available around the clock just isn’t sustainable.”
That week, division employees in some regions were told they would have to begin covering seven-day on-call shifts starting Sept. 1, fielding calls throughout the night and reporting for work as usual in the morning.  
Workers described sleeping in their cars, living off of gas station food and talking on the phone with relatives or colleagues to avoid falling asleep while driving through the night. 
Responding to calls far outside their home circuits also leaves workers unfamiliar with local resources that could help keep families together — and with the procedures of juvenile offices and courts when removing a child becomes necessary. On-call supervisors based hours away face the same problem, workers said.
One current division worker described fielding calls from four different supervisors during a recent on-call shift. The worker was pulled away from responding to a hotline report from the day before to work another case 90 minutes away. The first hotline report wasn’t reassigned, so the worker ended up responding during regular working hours. By that time, the report was four days old.
Johnston submitted his resignation letter during the last week of August, after learning about changes to assignments during on-call hours.
Before the restructuring, Johnston said, the division’s hotline unit routed reports directly to on-call workers based on where the report originated. He only stepped in if the hotline was having trouble reaching the on-call worker in his county or to provide backup.
Johnston didn’t cover an on-call shift during his last weeks on the job, but he explained how on-call responsibilities changed for supervisors.
“My time commitment went from me only touching a report every once in a while when they couldn’t get in touch with a worker,” Johnston said, “to me literally touching every report that comes in for southwest Missouri — notifying a worker, and if they can’t take it, finding someone who will — for a week straight.”
The division has advertised open positions for dedicated night and weekend workers, and Smith told The Independent she hopes to reduce the need for on-call shifts on top of workers’ usual hours.
“We’re working to hopefully over the next few weeks transition the number of team members on call to dedicated positions for nights and weekends to get that better work-life balance across the board for our teams,” Smith said.
In response to an emailed request for the current turnover rate and the number of child abuse and neglect staff who have resigned since Sept. 1, the Department of Social Services asked The Independent to file a formal request under the Missouri Sunshine Law.
 Ensuring safety

High caseloads and investigative backlogs are not new to the division. Neither is high staff turnover. 
Turnover of frontline division staff, including investigators, foster care case managers and hotline workers, reached 55% in fiscal year 2022, after former Gov. Mike Parson cut almost 100 jobs from the division in 2020. After the number of backlogged investigative cases surpassed 10,000 by September 2023, lawmakers approved funding to add back 100 positions. By September 2024, the backlog had decreased to fewer than 2,000 cases.
