Smith told lawmakers during the legislative hearing in August that frontline turnover was 40%, with about 90 vacant positions. The current state budget funds 1,781 field positions, which is the same as last year.
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith said the shift to specialized teams is intended to help frontline staff work more confidently and efficiently (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Current and former division staff interviewed by The Independent before the restructuring attributed growing caseloads to new rules and increasingly prescriptive policies that require more steps to move cases forward. 
A statement from the Missouri Department of Social Services in August said the restructuring was intended to address “longstanding nationwide workforce pressures, including high caseloads and staff turnover” and “create greater consistency in how we respond to children and families across Missouri.”
State law gives workers 24 hours from the time of a report of possible child abuse or neglect to assure the safety of each child who is an alleged victim. Division policy gives them three hours in emergencies. 
The tool the division uses to assess safety, called Structured Decision Making, or SDM, calls for  workers to attempt to interview parents, verify the safety of all other children in the household and document their findings and evidence within 72 hours of the hotline report.
But workers said they are increasingly doing only the bare minimum to document that they ensured a child’s immediate safety — locating the child, interviewing them, checking for visible injuries or signs of neglect and moving on. 
DeGraw said that in the first weeks of the restructuring, supervisors instructed workers to just “ensure safety.”
“If we don’t meet our contact time, we are going to fail ensuring their safety,” DeGraw said. “So that’s what they are requesting now: just drive, see the kid, verify they’re safe, and be done with it.”
A former division worker said the message came from multiple higher-ups.
“We would get told by our supervisors and even higher than them, ‘Go ensure safety. You can work everything out later,’” they said.
The worker said it wasn’t unusual to have to triage tasks before the changeover — to get an emergency call and have to drop work on another case. But because reports were limited to the county where they were based, it was easier for them to pick up where they left off.
“You can’t work four reports (a day) and also do a follow-up visit on a house that’s an hour and a half away,” they said.
Between Sept. 30 and Oct. 13, the number of open cases more than 72 hours old without documentation that a child’s safety had been assessed increased by more than a thousand, or 12.6%, from 8,104 to 9,128. That number rose faster than the total number of open cases, which increased from 18,063 to 20,324, or 12.5%.
A current division worker described pressure to get their “initial contacts” entered into the division’s database. If they don’t have time to do a home visit or interview parents, they said they just write, “Ensured safety.”
They said that while it’s “technically” possible to complete the SDM after those initial steps, “really what (safety) comes down to is about the parents and the home environment.”
“But they require you to have it in,” they said, “and they say you can change it at any time.”
Among other things, the SDM asks workers whether a child’s physical living conditions are hazardous and whether caregivers acknowledge and show a willingness to address safety threats.
 Sufficient information

The SDM is also one of the models being used by members of an 18-member child welfare task force established by Gov. Mike Kehoe in August.
Kehoe’s executive order directs members to propose “a statewide child welfare safety definition” and recommendations to incorporate that standard into the practices “of all child welfare partners, including Children’s Division frontline staff, juvenile offices, court systems and private providers.”
Members discussed draft legislation during an Oct. 19 meeting that would establish many of the steps the SDM requires division workers to take as part of the framework the division, juvenile offices and the courts must share when determining if children are unsafe.
During an Oct. 5 task force discussion of the SDM, members emphasized that the safety assessment depends on workers’ ability to collect sufficient information.
Emily van Schenkhof, executive director of the Children’s Trust Fund of Missouri, said “this whole safety assessment hinges on the child welfare worker having the capacity and training and tenure to be able to get sufficient information and to make these decisions.”
Missouri State Courts Administrator Kathy Lloyd said that “with the new process…we’ve had a couple of occasions where we’re running up against statutory timelines.”  
“Getting that sufficient information in the restricted amount of time is really a challenge,” Lloyd said.
Jessica Kruse, a circuit judge for the 38th Judicial Circuit in Christian County, said she had heard from emergency room nurses in Branson that workers had been sent from as far as St. Louis to respond to certain types of cases.
“That’s even less time to gather the information,” Kruse said. “It’s all travel time to get to the family.”
Smith said she had “heard about a few of these.”
“That should not be the case moving forward, especially as we get some more staffing,” Smith said.
Johnston said that unlike other members of a case’s multidisciplinary team — including juvenile officers, judges and guardians ad litem — division workers develop firsthand knowledge of how families are functioning by regularly visiting children and parents in their homes. 
But he said the restructuring, combined with the addition of policies that make cases harder to resolve, prevents workers from building that knowledge and earning families’ trust.
“This whole process is disempowering Children’s Division,” Johnston said, “who are the only people in the home of the child’s parents and of the placement, collecting the reports and talking to everyone.” 
If workers are too rushed to thoroughly evaluate reports of abuse and neglect, they can’t assess safety or link families with help, Johnston said.
DeGraw said she worries workers will miss something important.
“What if there is a severe emergency and these children are not being seen in a timely manner?”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Amy Klobuchar has already told us who she is.
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Two months after taking office as Hennepin County Attorney in 1999, Amy Klobuchar rearranged the furniture in the office’s reception area. The next day, the furniture had been moved back.
Klobuchar moved the furniture again. Someone moved it back. Klobuchar moved it again. One staffer told Klobuchar that the rest of the office liked the office’s original layout and many felt that Klobuchar’s new office arrangement caused a tripping hazard.
“I was immovable. The furniture would stay where it was. And for the record, I note that during my eight years as county attorney, no one tripped and fell due to the new furniture arrangement. Everyone got used to it,” Klobuchar said.
If you think this is an unflattering story told by anonymous sources, illustrating Klobuchar’s penchant for micromanaging and misplaced, obsessive priorities, you’d be wrong.
The story comes from Klobuchar’s own 2015 memoir, “The Senator Next Door: A Memoir from the Heartland.”
Rarely has a candidate for Minnesota governor spilled so many words about herself as Klobuchar, who is the author of two memoirs, the latest about her 2020 presidential run and governing during the pandemic. Klobuchar has also spent decades building her own brand to become one of the state’s most recognizable figures.
Time and again, Klobuchar — unlike her more private opponent, GOP nominee Lisa Demuth — is willing to share details that expose an almost perfect self-awareness. Her senior-year prom date ditched her because she refused to dance with him in the Ridgedale Mall fountain, lest she ruin her pink polyester dress. A boyfriend once broke up with her prior to a Halloween party while she was dressed as a Christmas tree — he may even be one of the exes who donated $17,000 to her first U.S. Senate campaign. She kept track.
Even when Klobuchar has sought to keep matters hidden, as in the case of reports of her tyrannical behavior toward her staff, the details are now well-known following the intense national scrutiny of her presidential campaign.
Despite her place as one of the most-talked-about and written-about Minnesotans in state history, voters will still have to decide if Klobuchar is a demanding boss who gets the best out of talented people, or a bully who will struggle to oversee 50,000 state employees; an ideologically malleable problem-solver, or an opportunist lacking any core principles; a model public servant, or a climber looking for one final bullet point on a resume that runs pages long.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her running mate Ben Schierer, mayor of Fergus Falls, lay out Klobuchar’s plan for housing policy if she wins the governorship alongside first-time homebuyers and housing advocates at a press conference in Columbia Heights Monday, June 8, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
A childhood steeped in politics
Klobuchar’s daughter, Abigail, was born in 1995 without the ability to swallow, and Klobuchar was discharged while Abigail stayed in the hospital to receive care. Disgusted by this treatment of a fragile new mom, Klobuchar organized fellow young mothers to lobby the Minnesota Legislature and got a bill passed to mandate a 48-hour hospital stay for mothers. President Bill Clinton later signed a similar federal mandate.
Although she has often presented this as a kind of political origin story, Klobuchar was actually steeped in politics growing up.
As a child, Klobuchar took messages from political leaders when they called the home phone hoping to talk to her dad, a reporter and columnist for the Star Tribune who often wrote about the downtrodden.
Klobuchar’s mother, a second-grade teacher and a member of the union, saved a message the 8-year-old Klobuchar took down for her dad: “Call callect, Jhon Heritage with the Vice Prestint. All they wanted to know if he’d be with VP in Detrit,” Klobuchar wrote in her 2015 memoir, explaining that her 2nd-grade self made a note to her dad that he was supposed to call John with the vice president’s office if he planned to join them in Detroit.
In junior high and high school, Klobuchar door-knocked for several state legislative races. After graduating as the valedictorian of Wayzata High School, her interest in politics took off at Yale and deepened when she wrote her 215-page senior-year thesis about the politics behind building the Metrodome, the predecessor to U.S. Bank Stadium. It was later turned into a book. Klobuchar spent hours interviewing legislators and business leaders about how the stadium was financed and built.
After her sophomore year in college, Klobuchar interned for Vice President Walter Mondale in 1980, the last year of the Carter-Mondale administration. Mondale would become a mentor to Klobuchar, working with her in the private sector. He attended her wedding and made a speech at the reception — held at the University of Minnesota’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs (of course).
Klobuchar went to a prestigious law school — the University of Chicago — because, she said, it was the route to politics for the Minnesota political figures she admired.
“I had seen inspirational public figures like Hubert Humphrey and Walter Mondale stand up for the people of our state and our country. I believed that becoming a lawyer would help me do the same thing,” Klobuchar wrote.
After graduating she started at the Minneapolis law firm Dorsey & Whitney, which would later become Mondale’s firm. Klobuchar carved a niche for herself representing telecommunications companies.
While moving up the ranks of Big Law, she organized events for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign. Mondale introduced her to Clinton.
It was a heady time for Democrats after the disastrous Reagan-Bush years. Sen. Paul Wellstone won a Senate race in 1990 with a folksy, grassroots campaign. Bill Clinton won two years later.
In retrospect, Klobuchar absorbed the lessons of Wellstone’s relentless campaigning across Minnesota. She hits all 87 counties every year.
But her politics seem to have been more influenced by Clinton, who sloughed off the old Democratic leftists, highlighted small but popular issues and made Republican themes his own, from tax cuts to welfare reform to a more aggressive posture toward crime, which soared during the 1980s and early 1990s.
It was never clear whether Clinton believed in what he was selling, but the point was that Democrats would never again lose 49 states as with Mondale in 1984.
In the past few weeks of her gubernatorial campaign alone, Klobuchar has said she’d avoid tax increases, form a regional anti-gang task force and root out fraud where fellow Democrat Gov. Tim Walz failed.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar greets supporters before speaking at the launch rally for Gov. Tim Walz’s third gubernatorial campaign at The Depot in Minneapolis Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Child of an alcoholic
This life of professional success and powerful friends may sound privileged, but she carried around baggage from her childhood.
Klobuchar often talks about her father, Jim Klobuchar, and to this day will bring him up in policy discussions.
In her first debate with Demuth earlier this week, Klobuchar evoked one of her father’s 23 books — “Will the Vikings Ever Win the Super Bowl?” — when asked about granting professional teams tax breaks for new arenas. (In typical Klobuchar-ian fashion, she managed to be on both sides of the issue: She wouldn’t want to lose our teams, but she doesn’t want taxpayers to get “hosed.”)
Klobuchar said she was largely unaware of her father’s alcohol use disorder until she was 12 years old. She and her father stopped at a bar in Minneapolis after a Vikings game. He drank with his friend upstairs, while the young Klobuchar sat at the bar drinking a 7 UP. On the way to their home in Plymouth, Klobuchar said her father weaved across Highway 55, and he crashed into a snowbank near their house.
“When the police came, they let him go home and that was the end of it. But I was scared. He told me he was sorry and that he would never do it again. I remember he cried,” Klobuchar wrote in her 2015 memoir.
Klobuchar’s parents got divorced when she was 15, and she was so upset she grabbed her coat and ran away from home for the first time to a nearby friend’s house. The divorce was amicable, but Klobuchar, who has a younger sister, took on the role of caretaker for her father.
“I was the oldest kid. I felt like I wanted to make it better, and so that was part of what I thought was my job because I wanted him to be able to not hurt himself or hurt someone else, but also so that he could get in a better place,” Klobuchar said in an interview with the Reformer.
Children of alcoholics often pick up on the fact their parents aren’t fully present, which can cause hypervigilance, i.e., the child is on high-alert and embraces perfectionism, said Brianna Hardcastle, a clinical director at a mental health treatment center in Florida whose own father died of alcohol use disorder.
Hardcastle said children of alcoholics can be high-achievers, so she wasn’t surprised to learn that Klobuchar, who served in the U.S. Senate for 20 years, is the child of an alcoholic.
That high-achieving perfectionism isn’t without cost, however, as legions of Klobuchar underlings would learn, sometimes viscerally.
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-MN, and Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-GA, (L) speak to the media following a U.S. Senate Rules Committee Georgia Field Hearing on the right to vote at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights on July 19, 2021 in Atlanta, Georgia. Photo by Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images.
Klobuchar the prosecutor
Klobuchar won her race for Hennepin County Attorney in 1998 and came into office with a 48-page leadership plan, which included aggressive enforcement of a new law imposing a five-year minimum sentence for felons who possess guns; lobbying the Minnesota Legislature to pass a law granting prosecutors the final word in closing arguments in criminal trials; and better coordination with the county’s more than 30 police chiefs.
Klobuchar’s tenure as county attorney was known for stiffer sentences, more criminal trials and more convictions.
That record came under scrutiny during her 2020 presidential campaign, when doubts were raised about the conviction of Myon Burrell in the killing of 11-year-old Tyesha Edwards, who was struck by a stray bullet while doing homework at her dining room table in 2002. At the time of the incident, Burrell was 16.
Klobuchar long touted Burrell’s conviction, and Edwards’ mother appeared in a campaign ad for Klobuchar’s first Senate run in 2006.
Klobuchar in her memoir called Edwards’ mother’s statement the “most touching”: “When our little girl Tyesha was murdered, Amy made sure that those gang members went away,” Edwards’ mother said.
But the prosecution was problematic: It relied substantially on jailhouse informants who had an incentive to lie and lacked physical evidence. Klobuchar eventually called for an independent investigation into Burrell’s conviction. The state commuted his life-sentence in 2020. A commutation does not affect a person’s conviction but only reduces their prison sentence.
While Hennepin County Attorney, Klobuchar’s poor treatment of staff began to leak, which would become a theme for the next quarter century.
Jim Appleby, an assistant Hennepin County attorney and president of the local union, wrote to AFSCME Council 5 leadership asking that they refrain from endorsing Klobuchar’s first Senate campaign because of how she treated her staff.
“Amy Klobuchar has demonstrated her disdain for the very employees that have placed her in the position to run for the office she now seeks. She has denigrated these lawyers both publicly and privately. She has refused to support their efforts to obtain a fair wage adjustment. She has taken credit for the hard work of her employees. She has severely damaged the morale of the office,” Appleby wrote.
But in the end, AFSCME Council 5 endorsed Klobuchar’s Senate campaign.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to audience members after the candidate forum for Minnesota governor at Farmfest in Morgan, Minnesota Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Klobuchar the senator
In 2005, Klobuchar began making moves to run for Minnesota attorney general. Then Mondale called and asked her to withhold from announcing her campaign for a few months. Weeks later, then-Sen. Mark Dayton announced he would not seek reelection to a second term. She decided to run for his seat during the Democratic wave of 2006.
Cynthia Bauerly, a Minnesotan who worked for Sen. Chuck Schumer, began tutoring Klobuchar early on in her first campaign while she was still county attorney. Bauerly would have multiple morning meetings per week with Klobuchar to talk about national policy issues, sometimes while Abigail was running around getting ready for school. Bauerly came away impressed with Klobuchar’s work ethic and interest in details.
Throughout her 20 years in the U.S. Senate, Klobuchar has mastered popular issues, often shrewdly working with Republican co-sponsors. She’s helped make America’s pool drains safer for children; expanded access to broadband for rural Americans; spearheaded an elections bill to ensure a smooth presidential transition following the Jan. 6 insurrection; and shoveled money into agriculture on big farm bills.
As a new senator, she worked quickly after the deadly I-35W bridge collapse in 2007 to secure federal funding for a replacement.
Even when Klobuchar has taken on powerful opponents, like the pharmaceutical industry or Big Tech, the foes tend to be deeply unpopular. Her antitrust book hit just as the issue had become a popular bipartisan cause, and she managed to avoid any discussion of local behemoth UnitedHealth, whose employees have been major financial contributors to her campaigns for two decades.
UnitedHealth was only referenced in passing twice, while Klobuchar mentioned Amazon and Google hundreds of times.
Klobuchar explained her legislative philosophy in a Reformer interview: “My approach to getting things done for people has been about just not leaving people behind.”
While Walz has earned a reputation for glossing over the details of governance, Minnesota can expect something very different if Klobuchar is elected: She is known as a policy wonk who puts in long hours.
“I have never gotten much sleep and am just one of those people who enjoys being awake,” Klobuchar wrote in her 2023 memoir “The Joy of Politics.”
She uses all that time to pore over details and inspect the work of her staff, following up with late-night and early morning emails.
This got her into trouble when she ran for president in 2020.
Klobuchar demeaned and berated her staff almost daily, Buzzfeed reported in 2019, sometimes throwing papers and office supplies in her staff’s direction. Some Klobuchar staffers said they cried “all the time” under her employ, and others described a work environment marked by “volatility, highhandedness and distrust.”
The senator has often responded by noting elite alums who have worked in her office: Jake Sullivan served as President Joe Biden’s national security adviser after working in the Obama administration; his brother, Tom Sullivan, served as counselor of the U.S. Department of State. Andrea Mokros worked in the White House and later helped put on the Super Bowl in Minneapolis. Sara Grewing is a district court judge. Franny Starkey served as Michelle Obama’s scheduler. Peter Cahill, who oversaw Derek Chauvin’s trial and is a retired Hennepin County judge, was Klobuchar’s deputy in the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office. Bauerly was appointed by Gov. Mark Dayton as Department of Revenue commissioner.
“I’m pretty good at spotting talent, and I have high expectations for the people who work for me,” Klobuchar wrote in her 2015 memoir. “I figure that if they work really hard and do a good job on one of my campaigns or in my office, that experience will serve them well later on. I’m proud of how often it’s worked that way: over the years we’ve helped a lot of people to launch their own successful careers.”
Klobuchar will need to make this rather charitable interpretation of her management style become reality if she’s elected governor. As senator, she’s managed a few dozen people. As county attorney, she managed hundreds. As governor, she would be responsible for an enterprise of thousands of people.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar gives a fifteen-minute pitch to delegates at the 2026 DFL State Convention before endorsing a candidate for governor Friday, May 29, 2026 in Rochester, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
The micromanager Minnesota needs? 
Klobuchar is well-aware of her reputation. During the 2020 campaign, she tried to spin it in her favor, once arguing it was a sign of how tough she could be with an American adversary like Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.
She’s making a similar argument in her run for governor.
Klobuchar told the Reformer that Minnesota needs a hands-on approach right now, especially in light of the hundreds of millions of dollars lost to fraud in the state’s social safety net programs.
“Right now in state government we need to make it more effective and accountable and that actually does include getting the details right and having higher expectations,” Klobuchar said.
Klobuchar has released a number of plans throughout her 10-month campaign, and she said she wants Minnesotans to hold her accountable for them.
“I really am going to create some high expectations,” Klobuchar said in the interview.
She said the Walz administration should have known taxpayer dollars were being lost to fraud, and hinted that she as governor will be keeping a watchful eye over Minnesota’s accounting books.
“People just should have noticed when you had a line item in the budget go from hundreds of thousands of dollars to millions and millions and millions of dollars — that should have been a red flag,” Klobuchar said.
Demuth has argued a governor Klobuchar would be no different than Walz. Demuth has said Klobuchar should have leveled these criticisms of Walz much sooner, like while it was happening. Klobuchar has responded that once the Feeding Our Future scandal became public in early 2022, she secured extra prosecutorial resources for then-U.S. Attorney Andy Luger, who is yet another close ally.
For some younger Minnesotans, Klobuchar’s name has long been in the state zeitgeist and is nearly synonymous with Minnesota itself. Asked what people might be surprised to learn about her that they don’t already know, Klobuchar gave a Klobuchar-ian answer of humble-bragging, box-checking and a sports reference:
“My husband and I are halfway done with hiking the Superior Hiking Trail,” she said, adding that they have done it in stints and noting that the trail is over 300 miles long. “Sometimes it involves him having to trek back to get the car and go pick me up at the end … But if anything, it shows I’m very goal-oriented, and I will get this done when I’m governor, as well as my lieutenant governor’s prediction that the Vikings will win the Super Bowl when I’m governor.”

name: California
title: California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough
text:
In summary
Despite seven new statewide laws regulating data centers, at least 26 resolutions, moratoriums, or bans on data centers have been passed or proposed in California since June.


Although California lawmakers recently passed a suite of laws intended to bring transparency to the development of new data centers, local communities across the state are signaling that disclosure isn’t enough.
California currently ranks third among U.S. states in overall data center density, according to independent trackers like the US Data Center Map, with the state home to 366 of such facilities that are either fully operational, under construction, or moving through the planning process. Local elected officials are proposing data center moratoriums to slow that momentum — if not stop it in its tracks.
“This is very much a unifying issue.”Nicole Ghio, Food & Water Watch
In the first half of October alone, Oakland’s city council unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on new approvals, making it the first city in Alameda County and the fourth in the Bay Area to adopt such a measure. San Francisco approved a similar moratorium this month, while the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors postponed a vote to permanently ban large-scale data centers, often called hyperscale facilities, on unincorporated land after receiving an overwhelming volume of public feedback. In Santa Clara, city officials considered a moratorium vote, and are moving forward with new rules to govern data center development, including more stringent water and air pollution regulations. Alhambra residents will vote on a moratorium measure in the November election.
Across California, at least 26 resolutions, moratoriums, or bans on data center development have been passed or proposed since June, according to the D.C.-based non-governmental organization Food & Water Watch, which tracks similar proposals nationwide. 
The escalating pushback underscores a widening gap between state-level regulation and municipal action. While Gov. Gavin Newsom last month signed into law seven new measures that focus primarily on disclosure requirements, environmental impact studies, and grid protection, grassroots groups and city councils are moving fast to halt construction entirely.
“I have a hard time remembering something that caught fire the way the opposition to data centers has,” said Nicole Ghio, California Director at Food & Water Watch. “Local municipalities have been able to respond quicker to the grassroots wave of opposition of people saying, ‘Hold on, let’s press pause. Let’s actually figure out what we’re doing before we commit to this huge change.'”
Opponents say these energy-hungry facilities strain power grids, potentially deplete water supplies and pollute the air, and contribute to broader economic anxieties around AI-driven job elimination. The anti-data-center movement cuts across party lines; conservative group Humans First, for example, finished its nationwide Data Center Revolt tour this month with three stops in California, joining a chorus of figures on the left who call for local control as well as additional  environmental and consumer protections.
“This is very much a unifying issue,” Ghio noted, adding that residents are alarmed by potential rate hikes and environmental degradation. “This is not a future that I think a lot of people want. I mean, it’s a great future if you’re a tech billionaire. It’s not a great future if you’re a regular American.”
Industry proponents, however, argue that halting infrastructure development risks eroding critical national interests. Doug Kelly, CEO of the policy advocacy coalition American Edge Project, framed the current buildout as an essential infrastructure race.
“Artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it, this is the next foundational block of infrastructure that America is building out,” Kelly said, comparing it to historical investments in railroads and highways. 
Kelly acknowledged that past developments lacked sufficient community input, leading to local friction. To address these fears without stopping construction, his organization promotes an “AI Community Compact” — an agreement offering local guarantees to protect ratepayers from cost spikes, safeguard resources, and promise early transparency.
“So, communities can decide whether they want data centers there or not, but they shouldn’t just blanket ban them because then you lose all your negotiating power,” Kelly said. “You’re literally saying ‘we want this billion dollar investment to go somewhere else, anywhere but here.’”
Yet for local advocates, piecemeal guarantees and disclosure laws fall short of addressing the underlying risk. Advocates point to a one-year pause on hyperscale data centers that New York’s governor ordered in July as a roadmap, hoping state legislators will eventually follow local leaders’ lead.
As cities continue to draft temporary freezes and outright bans, the tension between local community control and global technological dominance remains unresolved. State transparency laws may have opened the books on data center growth, but local opponents are making it clear that seeing the plans isn’t the same as approving them.

name: California
title: Medi-Cal cuts could push seniors and people with disabilities off of coverage
text:
Julia Feinberg feels like she’s living in a sinister version of Groundhog Day. For the second year in a row California lawmakers have made it tougher for seniors and people with disabilities to qualify for state-funded health benefits. 
Feinberg, 37, who has a degenerative neuromuscular disorder, said without Medi-Cal she would be confined to a nursing home rather than living and working as a therapist in Oakland.
“We keep having to have the same fight over and over and over again,” Feinberg said. She requires a power wheelchair and about 19 hours of caregiving each day, which Medi-Cal covers.
California is cutting Medi-Cal after a decade of expansion, part of sweeping federal and state cuts that experts estimate will kick more than 2.2 million Californians off coverage in the next four years, doubling the state’s uninsured rate. 
The latest cut came in June, when state leaders approved a budget that will lower the asset limit for low-income seniors and people with disabilities to $21,000 to qualify for Medi-Cal, starting in July 2027. Feinberg, who has built up emergency savings, will have to spend about $10,000 to get under the cap.


Medi-Cal: The Cut
Federal and state health care cuts will strip coverage from millions of Californians. CalMatters is tracking and reporting on these changes as they roll out.

Learn how to prepare for these changes and share your story with us
Watch our documentary in collaboration with Evident



In 2024, the state eliminated longstanding Medi-Cal asset limits, but since then lawmakers have chipped away at that policy. At the beginning of this year, state leaders reinstated an asset limit of $130,000, and the June budget lowered it further. 
A primary residence and one vehicle are exempt from the new limit, but people 65 and older as well as those with disabilities cannot own a second home or car, and they can’t have more than $21,000 in savings accounts, certain retirement accounts, life insurance policies or even burial plots. They must still meet Medi-Cal income eligibility limits of about $1,800 a month for a single person.
Advocates say the rules unfairly target older people and those with disabilities. 
“It’s really expensive to be disabled,” said Elizabette Guéçamburu, 44, who like Feinberg has spinal muscular atrophy and requires a power wheelchair as well as daily caregiving.
Guéçamburu said she’s saving up for a used wheelchair-accessible van, which costs about $75,000. Home modifications such as adding ramps and making bathrooms accessible also cost tens of thousands of dollars, none of which are covered by Medi-Cal. Guéçamburu said those expenses would be impossible to afford if she couldn’t save.
Guéçamburu lives on her family’s farm in Patterson where they grow walnuts, almonds and alfalfa. She works part time as the farm’s bookkeeper. In 2024, doctors diagnosed Guéçamburu’s father with prostate cancer, and he could no longer act as her caregiver. The same year, California eliminated asset limits for people with disabilities and seniors — Guéçamburu cried, able to qualify for Medi-Cal for the first time. 
“The timing was a godsend,” she said.




 Caretaker Lexi Marsh assists Elizabette Guéçamburu with various day-to-day tasks including guiding her through circulation exercises, helping her get inside her van and feeding Guéçamburu her lunch. Photos by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters
Now, her aging father is unable to take care of her should she lose Medi-Cal, and Guéçamburu is struggling to figure out what to do with money left to her by her grandmother. She’ll likely have to put it into a special needs trust controlled by a family member and give up financial independence. She also had her family strike her from inheriting any portion of their 100-year-old farm. Private home care costs thousands of dollars a month, making it hard for lower- and middle-income people to pay for it out-of-pocket.
“I have to surrender our legacy just to have medical security and have the ability to live my life,” Guéçamburu said. 
Asset limit flip-flop
Gov. Gavin Newsom eliminated Medi-Cal asset requirements in 2024 after a yearslong campaign by senior and disability rights advocates. In a statement before the elimination, Newsom said he was proud of the “bold investments” his administration was making to “protect life savings and homes.”
But two years later, faced with a $12 billion budget shortfall, Newsom proposed reinstating the former $2,000 limit, arguing that more than twice as many people enrolled as previously estimated. The Legislature opposed that proposal and compromised at the current higher limit of $130,000, lowering it again to $21,000 starting next July. 
Lindsay Imai Hong, California director for Hand In Hand, an advocacy group supporting families that need caregiving, said organizers are looking to the next governor for change.
“We would love to see the asset test permanently taken off of the chopping block,” Imai Hong said.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton said in a statement to CalMatters that he opposes asset limits. He criticized the state for extending other Medi-Cal benefits beyond what it could afford, including coverage for immigrants without legal status.
“Seniors and people with disabilities shouldn’t lose their coverage because they’ve managed to save some money. They’ve done the responsible thing. Why punish them for it?” he said.
Elizabette Guecamburu does her circulation exercises in the living room of her home outside of Patterson on Oct. 16, 2026. Guecamburu is afraid that recently passed state Medi-Cal cuts will disqualify her from benefits. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters
Democratic gubernatorial candidate and front-runner Xavier Becerra did not answer specific questions about the asset limit policy, but a campaign spokesperson blamed the Trump administration’s federal cuts for “squeezing” California’s Medi-Cal program.
Becerra will be “focused on protecting access to care and demand savings that are real, measurable and sustainable,” spokesperson Johnathan Underland said. On the campaign trail, Becerra has called himself California’s next “healthcare governor” and has previously floated raising taxes to reverse Medi-Cal cuts, but has not released detailed health policy plans.
Camille Nguyen, an attorney with the Legal Aid Society of San Mateo County, said most people who struggle to stay under the limit have little financial security.
“They have all of their life savings in cash savings instead of a house. That’s their retirement. That is the amount they are expecting to live off of for the rest of their life,” Nguyen said.
State data shows about 600 people lost Medi-Cal when California reinstated the $130,000 limit. Advocates expect many more to lose Medi-Cal at the lower limit, but the state never released budget estimates before lawmakers approved the $21,000 limit. If the state reinstated the much lower $2,000 limit, the Department of Finance estimated 62,000 seniors and people with disabilities would lose Medi-Cal over two years. 
Limit fuels anxiety, anger among people with disabilities
Feinberg said the prospect of losing Medi-Cal is especially scary because she would also lose access to a special disability program that pays for extra caregiving hours and has a multiyear waitlist. Caregivers help Feinberg get in and out of bed, dress and prepare her meals.
Before the limit was erased in 2024, Feinberg said she checked her bank account every day to make sure the balance was low. At the time, Feinberg was a graduate student and did not earn very much money. Now, as a licensed therapist Feinberg has been able to squirrel away some money.
“I don’t want to spend down that money. I want to save that for retirement, maybe buying a house in the future,” Feinberg said. “The prospect of not being able to have a nest egg is very unsettling.”
Guéçamburu said she’s angry and frustrated that the state views services for people with disabilities as expendable.
“It’s exhausting to have to justify your existence every legislative cycle,” she said.
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Are plug-in solar panels legal? Confusion abounds in CT
text:
Earlier this year, Connecticut joined a growing list of states easing restrictions on small, portable solar panels that can be plugged into a wall outlet to offset some residential electrical usage — and shave dollars off monthly bills.
The new law, passed as part of H.B. 5340, allows residents to purchase and install plug-in solar systems under 1,200 watts without notifying their utility company. It went into effect Oct. 1. Previously, anyone seeking to install any kind of solar device had to seek permission from their utility first, through an interconnection agreement.
But while the law exempts smaller systems from the interconnection process, it still requires the devices to meet the safety standards set by the state’s building and fire codes, as well as certification from UL Solutions, a national product-safety group.
That has led to confusion over whether plug-in panels are safe to own — or even legal.
Some of the hangup has to do with the lack of building codes that specifically address plug-in solar panels, which are a relatively new technology in the U.S.
In April, months before the new solar law took effect, lawmakers voted down revisions to the state’s building and fire codes over disagreements on an unrelated issue, road access for fire trucks. The codes, which are typically updated every four years by the state’s Department of Administrative Services, are now in limbo as officials and lawmakers seek to resolve the dispute.
Leigh Appleby, a spokesman for DAS, said there is no timeline for when the building and fire codes will be updated to specifically address plug-in solar panels.
“DAS is reviewing how the existing codes apply when a device is plugged into an existing outlet,” Appleby said in an emailed response to questions. “Adding or changing an outlet or circuit requires a permit and inspection. We can’t give a blanket assurance that every device or installation is safe or code-compliant. Local building officials and fire marshals enforce the codes in their municipalities and can assess specific installations.”
Without new state codes, however, local officials have no way to ensure that solar devices meet safety standards, according to Roger Nelson of the Connecticut Fire Marshals Association. (Nelson, who also serves as the fire marshal in Bloomfield, said he has not heard from any residents in his town about installing plug-in panels.)
“Until a code is passed, it’s not legal in Connecticut,” Nelson said.
Even Connor Yakaitis, a deputy director at the Connecticut League of Conservation Voters who was among the state’s early proponents of plug-in solar panels, said he was urging residents to be cautious. As more and more states pass laws similar to Connecticut’s, Yakaitis said officials around the country have been taking notice and working to resolve lingering safety and regulatory hurdles.
“Lot’s of people have been asking, ‘When can I go get these panels?” Yakaitis said. “We’ve been telling people not to buy panels until this is all ironed out.”
Regardless of the uncertainty, plug-in solar panels are widely available for sale online at prices ranging from a few hundred to several thousand dollars.
One online retailer, the California-based nonprofit Bright Saver, sells a 180-watt kit for $285, plus $29 for an annual membership. (Without a membership, the kits sell at retail for $499.)
Cofounder Cora Stryker said Bright Saver’s model is based on wholesale clubs such as Costco, which are able to offer lower prices by buying products in bulk. In addition, she said the group’s membership model helps to form a voting block that can advocate for removing existing barriers on plug-in solar. Bright Saver has 57 members in Connecticut and has shipped 49 kits to the state.
“Our whole goal is to build a massive membership that takes action to support clean energy… and make it dirt cheap,” Stryker said.
Stryker said Bright Saver’s plug-in kits meet the requirements under Connecticut’s law by having each of the component parts, such as the solar panel, plug and inverter, certified by UL Solutions. That definition, she said, is enough to cover most of the systems currently available on the market.
“I think it gives coverage for anyone in Connecticut who wants to buy one, even at the component level certification, and plug it in and not worry about the utility,” Stryker said. “It could be more explicit, but I think it’s OK.”
Other states, such as California and Vermont, have more stringent rules requiring that the entire system receive certification together as one device. UL Solutions launched a new full-system certification standard in January, but it has yet to approve any products for the U.S. market.
“That distinction is important,” Ken Boyce, UL Solutions vice president of principal engineering, said in an emailed statement. “A system assembled from individually certified components is not automatically certified. Component-level certifications may not address hazards arising from component interactions, including electric shock, circuit overload, compatibility with ground-fault protection, accidental contact with energized parts, and unsafe current flow. In other words, certified parts do not necessarily add up to a safe, certified whole.”
Stryker said Bright Saver plans to obtain UL certification on a fully-integrated system “in the very, very near future.” However, she said the requirements for that certification will necessitate rewiring by a licensed electrician and a special outlet, meaning the systems will not be available to most renters.
One of the authors of H.B. 5340, state Sen. Norm Needleman, D-Essex, said he is open to “refining” the law to add more clarity around plug-in solar, but he has yet to hear any specific concerns from constituents.
Connecticut’s law also requires that plug-in solar systems come equipped with a device that prevents electricity from being fed back onto the power grid during an outage. This rule was added in order to address concerns raised by utility officials that the devices could pose a threat to line workers who are working to restore power.
Additionally, anti-tampering features on many older electrical meters may fail to recognize any excess power sent onto the grid by unregistered solar panels, resulting in customers being charged extra for the power they produce. While this issue can be addressed with new, more advanced two-way meters, the rollout of those meters has been slowed in Connecticut due to disputes between regulators and Eversource, the state’s largest utility.
Eversource Spokeswoman Jamie Ratliff said in an email Monday that any devices sold in Connecticut must come with a warning about the potential for excess generation.
“It is important for the safety of our line workers and customers, as well as the reliability of the electric system, that only approved devices with built-in safety features are connected to the electric grid,” Ratliff said. “We understand that testing is taking place with certification agencies towards meeting these goals, which we believe is a necessary first step.”

name: California
title: Why the fate of California’s wealth tax could be decided well after the election
text:
The passage of Proposition 13 in 1978 was arguably the most significant political event in California during the last half of the 20th century.
While its primary purpose was limiting property tax increases, it also made raising other state and local taxes more difficult. It shifted public school support from local taxpayers to the state, profoundly impacted residential and commercial property markets, and spawned tax limitation campaigns in other states.
Prop. 13 also fuels a perpetual debate over how California’s public services should be financed that has spun off other ballot measures. One is Proposition 98, a 1988 measure that guarantees a certain level of state school support. And in 2020, voters rejected Proposition 15, which would have eliminated limits on taxing commercial property.
This year, Prop. 13’s advocates are pushing Proposition 43, which would require local tax increases to gain two-thirds voter approval. It would counteract a prior state Supreme Court decision exempting from that threshold taxes proposed via initiative.
Another measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 40, could have consequences that would rival Prop. 13’s life-altering effects if it were to pass. Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of about 200 California billionaires, with all but a small share of its proceeds used to shore up healthcare services that have seen declining federal and state support.
It’s sponsored by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West and draws support from left-leaning groups and politicians, such as U.S Sen. Bernie Sanders. Mainstream Democrats and other unions are divided. Gov. Gavin Newsom and his almost certain successor, Xavier Becerra, are opposed.
Billionaires such as Google co-founder Sergey Brin are spending hundreds of millions of dollars to oppose Prop. 40 and to pass Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, which would negate Prop. 40’s implementation if they gain more votes.
At the moment, Prop. 40 appears to be trailing. The most recent survey by the Citrin-POLITICO poll puts support at 46%, with 43% opposed.
If Prop. 40 fails, we’ll never know what its consequences would be, just as Prop. 13 was a shot in the dark and its history is still being written.
However one could make some educated guesses about what might occur should Prop. 40 enjoy a late-stage surge.
The first post-election factor would be whether Prop. 41, Prop. 42 or both also passed with more votes than Prop. 40. If Prop. 40 is not thwarted by either of those poison-pill measures, the next test would probably come in the courts, both state and federal.
Lawyers who helped draft the measure believe they have made it legally bulletproof. However, critics have laid out an array of potential legal challenges that would be novel because a wealth tax itself is unprecedented.
Assuming it survives the legal challenges, Prop. 40’s next hurdle would be logistic. The state Franchise Tax Board would devise ways to define, locate and value the taxable items of wealth. Cash and monetary investments would be fairly easy, but intangibles such as corporate ownerships and jewelry are trickier. Each of those procedural steps could also face legal hurdles.
There is also the question of residency. Prop. 40 says every billionaire who was a California resident on Jan. 1 must pay, but those who change residence after that date could contest the issue, and it could be years before their cases are settled.
Gilbert Hyatt, an inventor, moved from Southern California to Nevada before receiving royalty payments for one of his devices in the early 1990s. The Franchise Tax Board dinged him for income taxes in 1993, he resisted, and the case is still not completely settled after litigation in California, Nevada and federal courts that has gone as far as the U.S. Supreme Court.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: Your 2026 Nevada Republican marquee candidates: Lombardo and Flippo
text:
Quite a year for Nevada Republicans. (Photos: Lombardo's office; Flippo's campaign)The 2026 midterms have conjured up comparisons to the 2006 midterms, when a deeply and broadly disliked Republican president and his blundering warmongering prompted a blue wave in which Democrats won back control of both houses of Congress.
And in Nevada that year, a Republican who was sort of a doofus won the 2006 Nevada governor’s race anyway.
In 2026, the race for Nevada governor has gone about as expected. 
A core strategy of the Joe Lombardo campaign has involved ginning up that beloved staple of campaign professionals from coast to coast: micro-scandals that have nothing to do with real problems faced by households. To wit, the campaign’s opening gambit was Aaron Ford’s travel schedule. 
The Lombardo campaign also started by going back to the well and hauling up images of Lombardo the Lawman. Now in the stretch run, the campaign has accentuated the cop branding by tying Ford to the Black-people-are-criminals trope, which Republicans also deployed against Ford when he first ran for attorney general in 2018. 
Is that the campaign Nevada voters deserve? 
It doesn’t matter. It’s the one they were bound to get.
Affordability has never been a serious focus of the governor’s campaign, and it never was going to be. He and his people ride like they ride.
Perhaps the most surprising thing about this year’s race for governor is that neither Ford nor his allies have made a big buy for an ad starring a really quite self-important and haughty Joe Lombardo declaring “I’m Joe Lombardo” and “C’mon man.” It’s probably the one thing even the most casual of voters remember about Lombardo’s performance on the campaign trail. Oh well.
Prediction markets have been moving in Ford’s favor, for whatever that’s worth. Which may not be much — there’s a school of thought that says prediction markets are “informed by polls more than anything else,” and “downstream” of polling. And there’s been a dearth of public polling on the Nevada governor’s race.
Yes, Trump’s approval rating is pathetic. 
But then, so was George W. Bush’s on the eve of the 2006 midterms.
On the one hand, judging from polling over the years, inasmuch as casual voters think about governors, if they ever do, that thought tends to be “yeah, there should probably be one,” which usually works to an incumbent’s advantage.
On the other hand, the fundamentals — a catastrophic garbage fire of a Republican president, and during a midterm to boot — work in Ford’s favor.
In any case and no matter the outcome,  there’s one thing Nevada voters can count on: That winner, if asked, will tell them that now, clearly, is no time to raise the gaming tax.
Meanwhile, David Flippo continues to impress. One of the lies Trump’s minions were telling after Trump lost Nevada in 2020 was that a bunch of dead people had voted in Clark County. Like each, every, and all of Trump’s claims about election “fraud,” the Trump troops provided no proof. Because, to reiterate, it was all lies. It always has been. It still is.
But! Here we have not a dead person voting, but a dead person contributing to a campaign.
Ha ha no we don’t.
This week  the Wall Street Journal reported that Flippo’s campaign took a campaign contribution that was twice the maximum allowed amount, and then said whoopsy they meant to assign half of that money to another person altogether. 
Who turned to be dead. 
When asked, the crackerjack professionals at the Flippo campaign told the Journal dang, whoopsy again (or words to that effect) and rejiggered the donation a second time, into a categorization that maybe/who knows?/might approximate legality.
Campaign finance violations tend to make voters yawn. That said, trying to make your campaign contribution amounts look on the up and up by reattributing some of them to a dead person is, as campaign finance allegations go, not uninteresting.
Meanwhile, led by Mark Amodei, the Nevada Republican who Flippo would like to replace in Congress, a bunch of Northern Nevada Republicans are publicly sharing their disgust with Flippo. Even if it means having to suffer a Democrat in that congressional seat for a couple years, they hope to rid the Nevada political landscape of Flippo now they needn’t bother to primary a Republican incumbent in 2028.
Lombardo didn’t post his endorsement of Flippo on social media until seven weeks after the primary. Probably had to make sure Flippo was property vetted first.
The Washington Post this week reported that a long-ago Nevada Republican Party chair filed a Federal Elections Commission complaint because Flippo’s aforementioned financial filings are an omnishambles (except the Post phrases it differently). 
And of course all this comes after the Post reporting last month that Flippo lied in campaign materials about his military honors because … that’s just the kind of chap David Flippo is.
All of which raises the obvious question: When Flippo hauled his carpet bag up to CD2, who had “Washington Post and Wall Street Journal both do stories about Flippo” on their bingo cards? I didn’t.
To be clear: If enough Republican voters in Nevada’s 2nd congressional district hold their noses and elect Flippo, upon his swearing in they will be represented by an immediate lame duck and the most impotent and irrelevant person in the U.S. Congress.
So Flippo should take a moment to reflect on and relish this moment. He may not realize it now, but both the Journal and the Post (twice!) writing about him likely marks the zenith of his political “career.”
And whatever happens, Flippo will always be able to say that when the chips were down, not only has Trump stuck by his endorsement of Flippo. So has Lombardo.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Judge blocks DHS from conducting election-related sweeps in 9 states
text:
A federal judge on Wednesday night blocked the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens in nine states.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court in the Northern District of California, issued a preliminary injunction after voting rights advocates alleged that Homeland Security was sending armed agents to homes to question residents about their voter status. 
The injunction bars operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin until polls close on Election Day, though the administration may appeal in the coming days.
The decision marks a legal setback to the Trump administration’s intensifying campaign this fall against noncitizen voting ahead of Election Day. It comes as the Department of Justice is suing California to force state and local election officials to not count the ballots of some 20,000 voters the federal government says it suspects are noncitizens.
President Donald Trump has long decried the threat of noncitizen voting, which studies have shown rarely occurs. He now faces political peril, as Democrats appear increasingly likely to retake the U.S. House and possibly the Senate in the midterm elections.
Martínez-Olguín found that the importance of the public voting free of intimidation outweighed the Trump administration’s interest in rooting out noncitizen voting. But she paused her order until Friday, presumably to give the Trump administration time to appeal.
The evidence in the case, she wrote, leads to an “objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote.”
The lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. 
“Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them,” Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer at the legal advocacy group Protect Democracy, which represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement.
Martínez-Olguín wrote that the “ongoing intimidation that CNA/NNU members experience and the direct impediment it plays in their effort to engage voter outreach, education, and engagement efforts, are irreparable harms that are appropriately addressed by preliminary injunctive relief.”
A Homeland Security Investigations internal memo dated Aug. 31 describes a “surge initiative” beginning Sept. 1 that includes conducting field interviews. The memo, which was filed in court, identifies California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin as targets of the surge during September. Additional locations are redacted in the document.
Homeland Security didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision.
In a previous court filing, Department of Justice lawyers representing DHS have argued that the federal government has the authority to investigate potential voting by noncitizens. 
“Enjoining the government from even investigating such criminal violations would damage the public interest, not serve it,” they wrote.
Democratic groups and top Democrats in Congress filed a lawsuit Tuesday seeking to block Trump intimidating election officials.
This story was first published Oct. 21, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Counseling helps students thrive. Are CT community colleges meeting the need?
text:
On the Tunxis campus of Connecticut State Community College, a sign in front of a building reads, “Keep going. You’ve got this!”
Inside, some students quietly pour over books.
But in a more boisterous corner, with big windows facing some red-leaved trees, the Healthy Minds Club gathers in a classroom for its regular meeting. Faculty advisor Kelly O’Brien Mann talks to the group about the importance of setting goals in order to have a sense of purpose.
“If you don’t know what is it you’re working for, what’s meaningful to you, what does your life look like in the future?” she asks.
The club’s goal is to normalize talking about mental health. It’s a support group of sorts, where students share what they’re going through.
O’Brien Mann is a professor of psychology — but she wears more hats than that.
“In any given day, we might be doing counseling on the fly, and social work, and case management, and de-escalating, and helping students just problem solve with really complicated life issues,” she said.
Across the country, studies show many students struggle with mental health. In a recent survey by the Healthy Minds Network, an organization that conducts research to help guide campus policies, about one third of U.S. college students reported symptoms of moderate or severe anxiety, and roughly the same share reported symptoms of moderate or severe depression.
At Tunxis, there are usually two wellness counselors on staff to provide mental health services. O’Brien Mann would like to see more counselors there, including a nurse practitioner for medication management.
Short-term counseling services on campus are free, though O’Brien Mann said students who have more chronic mental health conditions and need consistent counseling have to look outside CT State.
“Trying to find a therapist who has availability, who takes your insurance, is a tricky thing,” O’Brien Mann said.
Other professors at Tunxis like Michael Hinton have concerns about crisis services being available.
“I’m walking this student down the hall trying to keep them calm and redirect them a little bit until we can get to mental health people,” Hinton explained. “And I walk into a room just, fingers crossed, hoping that there’s somebody here that can help.”
‘Mental health is a priority’
In Connecticut, mental health resources differ across state-funded schools. The University of Connecticut — the state’s flagship four-year school — employs nearly three dozen mental health professionals, who serve about 32,400 undergraduate and graduate students across its campuses.
A UConn spokesperson said the school appointed a task force in 2020 to focus on students’ mental health needs, and it has expanded services and personnel.
CT State offers one to two counselors at each of its 12 community college campuses. The system enrolled almost 38,000 full- and part-time students in fall 2026, a spokesperson said.
Like UConn, the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system has taken steps to enhance mental health services in recent years, including by joining JED Campus, a nationwide program of The Jed Foundation that helps schools evaluate and improve their support for students.
Nevertheless, this fall, CT State Tunxis started the semester with over 5,600 enrolled students and zero wellness counselors. The two counselors on campus left in the spring, and their positions weren’t filled by the start of this school year.
O’Brien Mann said it’s nobody’s fault — it’s just how things played out. But the lack of counselors speaks to a bigger problem for students in the community college system: an unmet need for more in-person mental health services.
“It would be great to say, ‘Here are the names of the two counselors, here’s how you get an appointment with them,'” O’Brien Mann said. “But I think understaffing for counseling has been a problem probably for every community college.”
The open jobs at Tunxis are being filled, according to Meredith Yuhas, director of mental health and wellness at CT State Community College. Staffing challenges are not a new issue, she said.
“This is the situation that we’ve faced continuously,” Yuhas said.
Yuhas said CT State is navigating a structural deficit and other financial pressures.
To help fill the gap for students, the college provides telehealth services with staff from a third-party contractor. The counseling and crisis support is free.
Yuhas acknowledged that having in-person counselors is important, and said the community college system is evaluating the needs on each campus.
“We have to be very intentional about staffing,” Yuhas said. “I think everybody agrees mental health is a priority.”
Ruth Pinto laughs as she talks with Eli Lund during the Healthy Minds Club meeting at CT State Community College Tunxis on Oct. 14, 2026. Pinto is studying to get a master’s in social work and attends the club with other students every week. Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
The mental health staffing at Tunxis has other people concerned, like psychology student Ruth Pinto.
Pinto helped a classmate get mental health support through the college’s CARE referral system, which connects students in distress with a multidisciplinary group of campus partners, such as faculty members, the accessibility and disability coordinator, the wellness counselor and the dean of students.
“All I wanted to do was the most important thing … to save his life and to save my friend who I love,” Pinto said.
Pinto also became her friend’s health proxy. But then she started struggling herself, and had a difficult time keeping up with schoolwork.
Pinto remembers walking into the former counselor’s office and breaking down when they asked a simple question: But how are you?
“And I was so stressed,” Pinto said. “And I didn’t realize, because I hadn’t paused to think about myself.”
The counselor helped Pinto get accommodations — support she didn’t realize she needed.
Community college students face more barriers
The state has studied the lack of college mental health support before. A 2021 law required Connecticut higher education institutions to assess resources on campus and identify areas of improvement.
Through its partnership with JED Campus, the state community college system launched a multi-year project to support student mental health, which included soliciting input and collecting data from students.
State Rep. Greg Haddad, a Democrat representing Mansfield who co-chairs the Higher Education Committee, said that in the last 20 years, college campuses have seen more need to provide mental health services.
“And so we see these, you know, growing budgets on college campuses to provide more services to students,” Haddad said. “But the legislature’s portion of the state subsidy has not been following suit.”
Haddad wants the state to do more. He said it’s tough because of tight controls imposed by Connecticut’s fiscal guardrails — budget laws that limit growth in spending.
But investment can be meaningful to students. In one recent survey by the Association for University and College Counseling Center Directors, respondents said counseling services helped academic performance and ability to stay in school for about three quarters of clients.
For community college students, completing a degree program can make a significant difference over the course of their life. Earning an associate degree is a pathway to more job stability. Associate degree holders also earn an average of $400,000 more during their working years than people with a high school diploma alone, according to a 2002 study of U.S. Census Bureau data.
However, research shows many community college students also face more barriers to completing their education compared with students in a four-year program, such as balancing school with work and family, and paying for transportation, housing and food.
These students need different kinds of support because many come from different backgrounds than traditional four-year students, said Amy Rusch, a doctoral student at the Department of Health Behavior and Health Equity at the University of Michigan’s School of Public Health.
“The really big difference is that community college students are experiencing the same mental health crisis with fewer resources to address it,” Rusch said.
Student Monika Rozsa-Horvath navigates some of those challenges. Rozsa-Horvath studies part-time in the Tunxis paralegal program. She also works at a daycare, and helps her brother, who uses a wheelchair, get to campus. Rozsa-Horvath said she sometimes sleeps only four or five hours a night to complete everything she needs to.
She said her stress levels are “through the roof.”
Receiving counseling outside of CT State has been a part of her life, but she said it’s been tricky to stay on top of.
“I just started up therapy again recently because school was a lot,” Rozsa-Horvath said. “I had lost my job a while back, so then I didn’t have the funds to be driving from Bristol to Hartford.”
Rusch said her team’s research showed community college students benefit from a coordinated continuum of care, such as teletherapy, crisis supports and in-person professional counseling.
Ruth Pinto, the psychology student who sought help, said some people need that in-person support in order to heal. Pinto said the friend she connected with campus resources recently marked six months of sobriety, a major milestone.
“I’m so proud I could cry,” she said. “But it’s of happiness.”
This story was first published Oct. 21, 2026 by Connecticut Public.
Connecticut Public is part of the Mental Health Parity Collaborative, a group of newsrooms that are covering stories on mental health care access and inequities in the U.S. The partners on this project include The Carter Center and newsrooms in select states across the country.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Legislature may take a look at accountability processes for tenured professors after audit
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Monday, May 6, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah lawmakers may soon evaluate how public universities hold tenured professors accountable after a legislative audit found the institutions struggle to correct instances in which faculty members are “persistently poor teachers.”
Auditors analyzed 666 performance reviews conducted in 2024 and 2025, which are required by law for all tenured faculty, and found that only eight of them were issued a teaching improvement plan. However, many had satisfactory scores despite having overwhelmingly low evaluations from students, the review showed. As a result, auditors said in a presentation to legislators this week that some students paid the price.
“Deans and department chairs described how much damage a single poor performer can inflict on a department when persistent underperformance is not corrected,” the audit says. “Poor instruction can contribute to students abandoning majors and academic programs, including in high-demand fields Utah needs. Even when students persisted through a course with poor instruction, they report being unprepared to succeed in their field.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In some cases of misconduct or violation of policy, universities avoided going through the established process for termination and instead negotiated separation agreements. That’s because apart from standards established in Utah law to terminate their employment, universities have their own sets of more complex policies that need to be followed, auditors said, which makes the termination process lengthy and expensive. 
But those agreements have also been pricey. A tenured faculty member who was found to have spent thousands of dollars on a university purchasing card for personal expenses bypassed the discipline protocol and was, instead, offered a separation agreement.
In exchange for leaving their post and not suing the university, the professor agreed to receive a $175,000 payment, a reference letter from the provost and the signature of a nondisclosure agreement to avoid discussing the circumstances of the separation case. 
That’s a case that left House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, with questions about why it is so difficult to fire professors in the state.
“In some cases it’s the Legislature’s fault that we’ve what put into statute things and then allowed the universities to add policies on top of that that make it very difficult to get rid of somebody, even to the point to where I have clear violations of the law and policies, and taking advantage of the taxpayer, and we still had to pay them to leave,” Schultz said. “That’s what’s created this problem.”



Let us know what you think...


 


Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, was also appalled by the practice.
“This is criminal, and I mean it’s also irresponsible of the institutions, if they think they can get away with this,” Escamilla said. “I mean, as a constituent, I’m very upset.”
The audit recommendation, Nick Varney, senior audit and operations supervisor said, is that the Legislature consider whether the minimum due process for removing tenured faculty specified in Utah code is excessive. Auditors also recommend the Utah Board of Higher Education consider requiring universities not establish processes for dismissing tenured faculty that go beyond what the law requires.
“As we looked at tenure as it’s been awarded throughout the institutions, we didn’t see any examples of academic freedom being harmed, where any faculty were terminated for academic freedom reasons, we didn’t see any of that,” Varney said. “Our primary concern is when it comes to an issue where faculty can and maybe should be terminated for cause.” 
The root cause for the lack of accountability among professors in less egregious cases, auditors said, is the traditional leadership model of academic departments, a rotating system that could undermine authority.
“Many of the department chairs that we spoke with described for us some structural barriers that limited their ability to lead effectively. Often, it was a matter of a lack of time, training, and authority,” Joe Hadfield, the supervisor of the audit told lawmakers. “But there were also some deeper issues where the incentives for performance for the leader were misaligned.”
Department chairs, for example, know that they are set to rotate back into the regular ranks of faculty after their leadership tenure, “so there’s an incentive to keep the peace” instead of making bold decisions to keep professors accountable, he said. Sometimes, a junior faculty member serving as department chair has to supervise the work of a higher ranked professor. 
“We recommend that the Board of Higher Education redefine department chair roles across institutions to position department chairs primarily as academic leaders, rather than faculty members with secondary leadership responsibilities,” the audit says. “Institutions should ensure that chairs have the time and support needed to carry out their leadership and supervisory responsibilities. This should enable chairs to provide stronger leadership and oversight within their departments.”
