name: Maryland Matters
title: Seeing double, seeing red: Moore demands Question 3 opponents halt lookalike ad
text:
Gov. Wes Moore's campaign sent a cease-and-desist letter Wednesday to Truth for Maryland, whose ads opposing Ballot Question 3 use logos similar to Moore's -- who supports Question 3. (Screengrab from Truth for Maryland ad)A new ad that urges residents to vote against a constitutional amendment that would loosen standards for congressional redistricting has drawn the attention of — and a cease and desist demand from — Gov. Wes Moore.
The ad, produced by the super PAC Truth for Maryland, uses fonts and colors similar to those used by the Moore campaign in an attempt to trick voters, lawyers for the governor said. The ad asks voters to oppose ballot Question 3 — which the governor supports.
“The website and advertisement are simply a cynical political ploy to try to trick Marylanders into misinterpreting the Governor’s position on Question 3, which he unequivocally supports,” lawyers for the Moore campaign wrote in a letter Wednesday.
“There is a substantial likelihood of confusion between your communications and the Governor’s campaign, which appears to be the point. A lay person watching the advertisement or going to the website would assume Governor Moore was involved with the committee,” the letter said.
Gov. Wes Moore’s campaign sent a cease-and-desist letter Wednesday to Truth for Maryland, whose ads against Ballot Question 3 use logos similar to Moore’s — who supports the question. (Photo from campaign websites)
Moore’s letter demands the PAC immediately remove the ad and stop using Moore’s likeness or his campaign font and colors. It also said the ad was referred to state elections officials for potential violations of laws regarding campaign misinformation.
Moore, in recent days, has appeared in ads backing the proposed amendment. For over a year, he has advocated for midcycle congressional redistricting, including a failed attempt to pass a bill and new maps earlier this year.
In a social media post Wednesday evening, Moore characterized the group behind the ad as “MAGA Republicans.”
But Andrew Brightwell, chair of the PAC, insisted in a text Wednesday that his is a “grassroots organization” that is “dedicated to re-electing Governor Wes Moore.” Brightwell, who was a spokesperson earlier this year for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ed Hale, said the group was “deeply disappointed to receive such a threatening letter from his [Moore’s] paid legal representation.”
“Sadly, it appears the weaponization of our legal system has expanded well beyond the walls of the White House and Congress and made its way to our very own State House. Nevertheless, we remain steadfast in our support of our great governor and our commitment to end extreme partisan gerrymandering,” Brightwell’s text said. “We will neither cease nor desist – we will persist.”


MAGA Republicans are running ads using pictures of me and copying my brand to lie to Maryland voters.
Let me be clear: Question 3 is how we fight back on Donald Trump. I will be voting YES on 3. https://t.co/tmKK7XiKvl
— Wes Moore (@iamwesmoore) October 21, 2026


The 30-second ad uses Moore’s image as well as fonts and the purple-and-gold color scheme of his reelection campaign. It also parrots slogans used by Moore, while not explicitly stating his position on the ballot question.
“Marylanders never follow blindly. We make up our own minds and protect our rights,” a narrator says in the commercial. “That’s why we know extreme gerrymandering is wrong. No politician should have unchecked power, but that’s what Question 3 does: Rewriting our constitution, ending fair elections and taking away our voice permanently. Governor Moore fights for every Marylander. Let’s do the same. Vote yes for Wes and against Question 3. Together, we’ll leave no one behind.”
The cease and desist letter demands the group “immediately remove” the video from the internet and that it also stop using the Moore’s name, likeness and image.
Jim Astrachan, a copyright and First Amendment lawyer in Columbia, said Moore’s cease and desist demand may run afoul of free speech protections.
“Political speech is the height of the First Amendment,” Astrachan said. “Speech that is generally regulated is going to be commercial speech. Commercial speech is a stepchild of the First Amendment, but political speech is the main event.”
Similarly, claims of misinformation in campaign ads could also run afoul of speech protections.
“People lie all the time in politics,” Astrachan said. “Can you imagine if the court had jurisdiction over lying and deception in political advertising? My God, they would never stop hearing cases. I’ll just say political speech is protected.”
He noted that Vice President JD Vance recently implied Texas Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico was a pedophile while offering no proof.
“They’re going to get away with it,” Astrachan said of Vance. “He can’t sue them for defamation. He can’t sue them to stop the conversation.”
But Astrachan said a copyright violation lawsuit could be possible if Moore’s campaign could show that images used in the ad were neither in the public domain nor owned by Truth For Maryland.
“You’d have to go to federal court,” he said. “That wouldn’t be election law.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Moore’s own campaign has used images of other candidates.
Earlier this year, Moore’s camp ran an ad during the Republican primary that criticized Dan Cox as too conservative for Maryland. The ad, which ran on Fox News, tied Cox to Trump.
Political observers said the ad was seen as a way to drive votes from Hale to Cox by solidifying Cox’s ultraconservative bonafides in a primary, where the most conservative tend to vote.
Cox won the primary.
The latest ad represents a new front in the battle over hyperpartisan redistricting and a proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that removes restrictions on how congressional districts are drawn in the state.
Moore has called for redrawing the state’s eight congressional districts. He has called it an attempt to ensure electoral competitiveness, but any redistricting would likely create a map that could eliminate the only district in the state held by a Republican.
Recent polling suggests that a plurality of Maryland voters oppose the amendment.
Truth for Maryland, which entered the fray Tuesday, became the second group campaigning against Question 3. The first was Protect Maryland Voters.
Truth for Maryland formed Oct. 14 and is registered to an address in Southern Maryland. A report filed with the Maryland State Board of Elections shows the PAC has no money. Brightwell said “the overwhelming majority of our donors are from Maryland.”
Another group, Fight Back Maryland, supports the amendment. That group is backed by Democrats, including Moore.
Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, said in a social media post that Moore’s attempt to remove the ad from public view may backfire.
“I suspect we’re going to see the Streisand effect play out here,” Eberly wrote, referring to a 2003 lawsuit the singer filed over an aerial photo of her home. The photo had been viewed a handful of times before the suit was filed, after which hundreds of thousands of people saw it.
Eberly said the ad Moore is “trying to stop will now be viewed by far more people as a result — and at no cost to Truth for Maryland.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: House Speaker makes case for unseating Democrat in WA’s heated congressional race
text:
Republican congressional candidate John Braun waves to supporters at a rally on Oct. 21, 2026 in  in Chehalis, Washington, as House Speaker Mike Johnson (center) extols attendees to get Republicans to vote. Braun, a Republican state senator, is running against Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in the 3rd Congressional District. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)House Speaker Mike Johnson returned to Washington state on Wednesday to campaign alongside Republican John Braun, a sign of how important the state senator’s bid to unseat Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is for the GOP’s hopes of keeping its majority.
Johnson came to Braun’s business in Chehalis to headline a rally attended by an estimated 550 people held outdoors. He was joined at Braun Northwest by four other Republican members of Congress including U.S. Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee.
Johnson, as he did earlier this year in Vancouver, framed the contest between Braun, the state Senate Republican leader, and Gluesenkamp Perez, the two-term incumbent, as “a contrast election between common sense and crazy.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana speaks at a rally for GOP congressional candidate John Braun in Chehals, Washington, on Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield)
He warned the crowd that Democrats in Congress, and many of those running for seats, are pushing a policy agenda to “abolish everything” achieved by the Republican majorities there now. He acknowledged that in nearly every midterm election sitting presidents lose seats, but insisted this year will be different if Republicans turn out.
“I’m absolutely convinced we’re going to defy history and hold the majority, “ he said.
Republicans outnumber Democrats 218-214 in the House and the Braun-Gluesenkamp Perez match-up is among a handful of competitive races nationwide.
Wednesday’s event marked Johnson’s second public event and third commute to western Washington this year as he seeks to maintain GOP control of the House and continue his reign as its leader. Johnson also made a brief stop in Olympia on Sept. 29 and met privately with Braun donors after a planned rally was canceled.
“The Speaker of the House doesn’t fly across the country twice for a seat he thinks is safe. He’s coming because he knows this race is close, and he wants a vote he can count on,” Gluesenkamp Perez told supporters in a fundraising email sent Wednesday morning.
Democrats’ grip on this seat frustrates Republicans because Donald Trump won in this district in each of his campaigns for president. GOP operatives were excited when results of a recent poll affirmed the race is close, with the candidates statistically deadlocked. 
In the months since Johnson’s Vancouver visit in August, the electoral climate has soured for GOP candidates due to high gas and diesel prices, growing enmity toward the Iran war and cratering public support for President Donald Trump.
Johnson roared past those political realities Wednesday, telling the crowd that House Republicans have delivered tangible tax cuts and more secure borders, and the president took steps to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
“We have a great record to run on,” he said.
Braun, until this campaign, sought to steer clear of the president and the political dramas of the other Washington. He’s focused instead on pushing back on a slate of taxes — including a new state income tax on high earners — and expansion of social programs enacted by Democratic majorities in the state Legislature and Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson.
After securing Trump’s endorsement, Braun has sought to distance himself from the president and his policies. On Wednesday, he didn’t mention the president and cast himself as a change agent for the district.
“This is an opportunity, an opportunity to change the direction for our state and our country,” he said. 
As he has throughout the campaign, he poked the congresswoman for passing a bill to name a post office. And then posed the rhetorical question: “Has Marie done a single thing for you or your family, a single tangible thing to make your life better?
Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington’s 3rd Congressional District.
Gluesenkamp Perez, meanwhile, has repeatedly sought to link Braun with the president.
“The senator has taken the endorsement of President Trump and the millions of dollars that come with it, and he will say yes to whatever this president wants him to do,” she said in their Oct. 13 debate.
Braun’s use of his business as a backdrop for Wednesday’s rally comes as the company’s safety record, and his interaction with workers, have been interjected into the campaign.
Gluesenkamp Perez is airing an ad in which the son of the man who died in a workplace accident in 2024 says that Braun “never called” him after the tragedy. The son worked for the company at the time but has since left. In a recent debate, she said her opponent owed the family an apology.
Braun has said he spoke with the man twice in person and his family delivered food to their home. “This was a terrible tragic accident,” he said in the debate. “We did everything we could to do this right. To say we didn’t try, it’s heartless.”
Following the rally, Braun said the business was chosen as the site because it “was a good location, given the number of people we had. Simple as that.”
“My opponent has been frankly ruthless in attacking me, my family, our company, and the people here, and I think frankly dishonest,” he said. “But we’re not going to let that cower us into not running the race and showing who we are.”
With voters casting ballots and the election a dozen days away, speakers hammered on how the outcome hinges on which candidate turns out their voters the best. 
It’s a message that Anthony Mixer of Chehalis, said he’s been telling people he meets while canvassing on behalf of Braun.
“This is a swing district. It will be very close,” said Mixer, a conservative political activist and former government affairs director for the Young Republicans of Washington. “The road to keeping the majority does run through Washington’s 3rd Congressional District.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: To avoid becoming roadkill, Florida panthers need critter crossings
text:
An endangered Florida panther emerges from a wildlife underpass built beneath a busy South Florida highway. (Photo by Carlton Ward Jr., used by permission)One of my favorite cartoons, drawn by a Pensacola artist named Jem Sullivan, shows a flock of sad-looking chickens gathered around a casket. The chicken minister delivering the eulogy says, “And though we’ll never know why Dave wanted to cross the road, we can rest assured that he is now, at last, on the Other Side.”
I think about this cartoon every time I see another story about a Florida panther that’s been run down by a car or truck. We lost two of the endangered cats last week, one in Hendry County and one in Collier, both of them apparently mowed down by vehicles.
That makes 14 flattened so far this year.
The panthers are far from alone. I took a long drive this weekend and encountered a wide variety of Florida roadkill — raccoons, possums, even a deer lying just off the shoulder.
Why are Florida panthers and other wildlife constantly trying to cross the road? Maybe because there’s no other way to get to the other side.
I’ve just finished reading a terrific book about roadkill by Ben Goldfarb. It’s called “Crossings: How Road Ecology Is Shaping the Future of Our Planet.” (No, RFK Jr., it is NOT a cookbook!)
The book talks about how we humans view roads as a path to freedom — as Bruce Springsteen sang in “Thunder Road,” two lanes that can take us anywhere. But for animals, roads are a prison wall, penning them in, separating them from mates, blocking them from their migration routes.
Any attempt to escape carries the strong likelihood of injury or death.
“Sometime during the twentieth century … roadkill surpassed hunting as the leading cause of vertebrate mortality on land,” Goldfarb wrote. “And it’s only getting worse as traffic swells.”
Yet it turns out — in between scurrying around to paint out every rainbow crosswalk and promoting flying cars instead of installing EV chargers — the Florida Department of Transportation has accomplished something worthwhile.
It has built a string of wildlife underpasses statewide, enabling us motorists to avoid crashing our cars into so many animals.
How, I wondered, is that effort going?
Cathy Salustri via Linkedin
I started calling people involved with Florida’s wildlife underpasses. One of the people I contacted was my friend and fellow author, Cathy Salustri, who actually walked through one of the panther underpasses that cross beneath Alligator Alley.
She remembered parking near the highway and walking down an embankment to a space that had been opened up under the busy road. The passage contained a small creek and lots of vegetation — and a subtle message for us humans.
“It was definitely a moment where I realized, once again, how close humans and wildlife exist in this state,” she told me. “I don’t remember it as visually remarkable, but the import of what it means for the future of Florida’s wildlife was massive.”
 Spotting the Skunk Ape
Wildlife underpasses began in the 1970s in England. At first, they focused on aiding amphibians in winning a real-life version of the arcade game “Frogger.” They were known as Toad Tunnels.
Reed Noss via Conservation Science
Scientists quickly saw how these tunnels could be adapted for larger animals. One such far-seeing advocate was Reed Noss, a University of Central Florida professor.
When the Florida DOT proposed expanding two-lane Alligator Alley into multi-lane I-75, “I suggested the entire Alligator Alley be elevated so the panthers could cross underneath,” Noss recalled this week. “Unfortunately, elevating the whole thing turned out to be cost prohibitive.”
The expense weighed heavily on the minds of DOT planners, who initially resisted the push to help panthers. At that point in the early 1990s, the big cats’ population had dwindled to fewer than 50 and they were suffering from genetic defects caused by inbreeding.
When the DOT at last agreed to try some passages, some critics openly questioned whether the panthers would use them. State biologists put up motion-sensor cameras that caught plenty of panthers crossing under Alligator Alley, according to the South Florida Sun-Sentinel.
“The radio trackings located the panther using the underpasses even before they were completed,” Audubon’s Charles Lee told the Sun-Sentinel.
The panthers weren’t alone, either.
The cameras snapped pictures of bobcats, white-tailed deer, bears, turkeys, raccoons, wading birds, and even alligators. Also appearing on camera: a guy in a gorilla suit, apparently cosplaying as the stinky Skunk Ape.
Elizabeth Fleming via Defenders of Wildlife
The DOT was convinced. “Twenty-four wildlife crossings and 12 other bridges modified for panther use were completed in the early 1990s within a 40-mile stretch of I-75,” the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission reported on its website.
The DOT boasted on X last year that it has now built more than 200 wildlife crossings statewide, with more than 50 specifically built for use by panthers. A dozen more are in the planning stages.
“Florida is now recognized as a pioneer in wildlife crossings across the country,” Elizabeth Fleming of Defenders of Wildlife’s Florida office told me. “And their Alligator Alley crossing is one of the largest in the country.”
 Turtle tunnels
While I was reading “Crossings,” I ran across a familiar name: Matt Aresco.
Aresco is director of the Nokuse Plantation, a 55,000-acre Panhandle preserve. It was launched by a dirt-road philanthropist named M.C. Davis, whose skills at poker playing and pool hustling made his fortune.
Matt Aresco via Nokuse Plantation
In 2000, while Aresco was just a grad student in Tallahassee, his girlfriend told him she’d seen a turtle massacre on U.S. 27. He hurried to the scene and found 90 dead turtles. It was easy to figure out why.
The highway bisected a wetland, leaving Lake Jackson on one side and Little Lake Jackson on the other. A drought was drying up the big lake, but the little lake still held water. The turtles in the big lake were trying to get to it. They didn’t make it far.
Softshells and snappers, cooters, and box turtles — they all attempted the exodus and they all failed. Sometimes, Goldfarb wrote, “car-struck turtles shot through the air like hockey pucks.”
Aresco, conscience-stricken, spent eight hours a day intercepting them, dropping them in a Rubbermaid bucket and toting them across between traffic.
Over the next four years, he saved more than 8,000 turtles. But he couldn’t save them all, nor the occasional alligator that wandered across the road.
A pile of road killed turtles on U.S. 27 in 2000. (Photo by Matt Aresco)
He begged the DOT for help but got only a tepid response. A maintenance worker brought him some fencing so he could direct the turtles to a small culvert under the road. Aresco soon found he was spending as much time fixing the tattered fence as he used to spend saving turtles.
He proposed building something called an ecopassage, modeled on a box-culvert-and-wall contraption that the DOT had built in Paynes Prairie. But there was no money for what he had in mind.
At last, in 2009, the Obama administration produced an economic stimulus package that sent billions to the auto industry and banks. Aresco’s little turtle ecopassage project got $3.4 million.
Some critics (looking at you, Sean Hannity!) mocked the expenditure of millions on mere turtles. But once the DOT built it, Goldfarb wrote, “The torrent of roadkill on Highway 27 shut off, neat as a turned spigot.”
I called Aresco and he verified the story. The ecopassage was completed in 2010, he said, giving turtles a safe way to get from one lake to the other.
“It’s working great,” he said. “There have been no road-killed turtles and alligators on that section of US 27 since the ecopassage was built 16 years ago.”
But he added, “There are lots of other places throughout Florida that have the same problem.”
 Both sides of the road
Noss told me that Florida wildlife underpasses have grown more sophisticated over the years.
There are ledges for smaller animals to cross above the larger ones, and ramps to make the crossing accessible to animals with shorter legs, he said.
The wildlife crossings are on more than just roads, too. Now there are pilings that let terrestrial animals find a dry-footed path across Florida’s many canals.
If you’d like to see where the crossings are, the Florida DOT even has an interactive map showing the locations.
An otter scampers under I-75 via Florida DOT.
Some points on the map link to photos and video of the animals using them. You can see an otter scampering along under I-75, a bear lumbering beneath State Road 20, a whole family of raccoons crowding the camera under U.S. 27 near Frostproof.
Carlton Ward Jr. via X
Speaking of cameras, one person I made sure to contact was Carlton Ward Jr., an eighth-generation Floridian and acclaimed wildlife photographer. He’s the person who accompanied Salustri on her visit. He’s seen the inside of more underpasses than anyone else who’s not a DOT employee.
Ward used lots of motion-activated cameras to snap pictures of passing panthers (try saying that three times real fast). His images wound up as both a handsome coffee table book and a National Geographic film, “The Path of the Panther.”
As befits one of the founders of the Florida Wildlife Corridor, Ward praised the Florida DOT’s dedication to installing underpasses at places that could be potential choke points.
When I asked if there shouldn’t be a lot more of them, he made a point that I hadn’t thought of.
“You can’t protect them on just one side of the road,” Ward said. “You have to be able to protect them on both sides.”
There’s no sense in building an underpass in a spot that leads wild animals into a new subdivision, he said. The state has to control both sides, either through outright purchase or a conservation easement. But lots of land is being gobbled up by new development before the state can save it.
“It’s a real race right now,” he said.
A family of raccoons crowds the camera at an underpass near Frostproof, via Florida DOT.
 Soaring through the sky
Over the past 30 years, Florida panthers have seen a dramatic revival.
Their recovery resulted from an unprecedented experiment that involved bringing in female Texas cougars to breed with male panthers. They produced healthy kittens, sparking a population boom. There were 20 in 1995, and now there are about 200.
Meanwhile, though, development continues wiping out panther habitat. Two new projects in Southwest Florida, new cities called Kingston and Bellmar, are projected to generate so much traffic that they will kill 25 panthers a year.
So much for that revival! Turn out the lights — church is over.
When I interviewed him in 2018, one of the developers of these projects insisted that holding them responsible for the deaths of so many panthers was wrong.
“I don’t control your driving, or your texting and driving, that might have caused you to run over a panther,” he contended, neatly sidestepping the fact that those drivers wouldn’t be there if not for the development.
If the agencies that regulate where and when development occurs won’t say no to these projects, then the only alternative is for the state to buy the land for preservation.
But Noss pointed out that our fine Florida Legislature this year cut all the funding for our popular Florida Forever land-buying program.
It’s a decision that stinks worse than any Skunk Ape. Instead of the $100 million they promised to spend every year, they gave it a big, fat zero.
“It’s one of the stupidest things I’ve ever seen in Florida politics,” Noss told me. Fleming said she hopes that, post-election, the Legislature will rediscover what’s important to the voters.
Meanwhile, the Florida DOT is now building the biggest wildlife crossing in Florida history on Interstate 4.
Unlike the others, it’s not an underpass. It’s an $18 million OVERPASS — 44 feet wide with 8-foot walls, soaring above the traffic. The goal: Link the Tenoroc Wildlife Management Area to the Green Swamp.
“This is the last thread in Polk County to be able to cross wildlife from south to north,” a DOT engineer said last year. “This is really our last chance.”
I sure hope that by the time that overpass opens next year, we still have panthers left to cross over to the other side.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Let CT’s minority school districts eat cake.
text:
For months, state officials suggested something was seriously about wrong with financial management in Connecticut’s largest urban school districts, painting a picture of local boards gorging themselves at the public trough. 
The State Department of Education called in independent forensic auditors CliftonLarsonAllen LLP to audit the books of both Bridgeport and Hartford Public Schools. By then, the narrative was already set. Local leaders had gorged themselves on public money, and the state was riding in as the white knight (pun intended) to restore order.

Joseph Sokolovic

Now the forensic audit results for the two largest districts in Connecticut both with a majority of Black and brown, students, both led by African American men, are in. The verdict? No stolen funds, no offshore accounts, non existent criminal schemes, and absolutely no systemic fraud.
Instead, the audits reveal a truth that state leaders seem desperate to cover up, our urban school districts are not gorging and purging funds behind closed doors. They are surviving on a strict sustenance diet, children’s futures left emaciated by a state funding system that for more than half a century has systematically starved our poor and minority children’s future.
Let’s look at the audacity of the state’s self serving narrative, look at the math. Connecticut still bases its Education Cost Sharing formula on a foundation of $11,525 per student, a ration frozen in time while the real cost of nourishing a child’s education, adjusted for inflation, is well over $16,500. While the state points to local shortfalls, it conveniently overlooks the nearly $1 billion racial funding gap separating wealthy, well-fed suburban districts from low-income, majority Black and brown urban district that are left to scrape for crumbs at the garbage dump.
Of course, the forensic reports identified operational flaws in both districts that should be acknowledged. It highlighted poor internal tracking and communication breakdowns between central offices and local boards. Those gaps warrant stronger internal controls and immediate remediation. But our districts are starving to death. The vultures are already overhead. We cannot afford to lose a single calorie.
Misclassifying line items does not create a multi-million-dollar structural deficit out of thin air. When districts are forced to stretch $11,525 to cover more than $16,500 in costs, the resulting deficit is not necessarily a sign of local waste. It is the predictable result of long-term starvation. When you starve a body of basic sustenance, its organs eventually begin to fail. Blaming a district for its emaciated budget is like blaming a starving person for being thin.
Rather than providing the necessary calories and fixing the broken ECS formula, the state offers bureaucracy as a substitute for bread. We see it in the creation of election year “Blue Ribbon” panel and in state oversight options like the Municipal Accountability Review Board (MARB).
While studies and commissions are framed as helpful partners, they share a central flaw, neither one guarantees a single crumb of additional revenue. Telling malnourished districts to practice “LEAN” austerity targets is like asking already emaciated group of students to tighten their belts even further. These panels shift focus away from state funding obligations and burden central office staff with endless red tape, while threatening the local autonomy of the boards elected to serve these communities.
The state’s political playbook is transparent: starve the district, point to its weakness, convene a panel to prescribe further austerity, and divert public attention from state-level funding failures in order to protect the food the ruling class hoards behind their precious guardrails.
This intentional neglect is not just a policy debate, it is a violation of civil rights. Article Eighth, Section 1 of the Connecticut Constitution guarantees a free, suitable, and equitable public education for every child in this state. By keeping urban districts on a starvation diet, the state is failing in its’ constitutional duty to Black, Latino, and low-income students.
We cannot wait for legislative goodwill that never arrives. It is time for civil rights and advocacy organizations, the NAACP, the ACLU of Connecticut, Hispanic Federation, Center for Children’s Advocacy, and others band together and draw a line in the sand.
We need a coalition of civil rights leaders, legal scholars, and courageous advocacy groups to step up and file a class-action lawsuit against the State of Connecticut for blatantly violating Article Eight of our constitution. To every public interest law firm, constitutional scholar, and legal aid organization in this region: I am begging you to take this fight to court pro bono.
Our urban students do not need another Blue Ribbon panel, MARB, or another lecture on how to manage their state-imposed starvation. They need an updated, fully funded Education Cost Sharing formula that provides real nourishment. Until state leaders stop pointing fingers at local school boards and start funding urban districts to meet actual student needs, the real fiscal mismanagement isn’t happening in Bridgeport or Hartford central offices, it’s happening under the golden State Capitol dome where the grain bins are already overloaded.
Our children need a revolution. And they need it now.
Joseph Sokolovic is Vice Chair of the Bridgeport Board of Education. The opinions expressed here are his alone.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley, Tiffany meet for gubernatorial campaign’s sole debate
text:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany met Wednesday evening in Milwaukee for the only debate in Wisconsin's race for governor. (Screenshot from WISN)Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany met at Marquette University Wednesday evening for the only scheduled debate in Wisconsin’s race for governor. 
Throughout the hourlong debate, hosted by WISN and moderated by Matt Smith and Gerron Jordan, Crowley worked to paint Tiffany as a yes-man for his billionaire donors and President Donald Trump, while Tiffany worked to cast Crowley as an extreme liberal focused only on raising taxes and distracted by his dislike of Trump. 
As Democrats hope that Trump’s record-low unpopularity can create a wave of support for them in races up and down the ticket across the country, polling has shown that Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race remains close, with Crowley so far maintaining a slight lead. 
If Crowley wins, he’d be the first Black man to be elected governor of Wisconsin and will represent an extension of Gov. Tony Evers’ eight years in office — especially if Democrats are able to fulfill their ambition to win majority control of both chambers of the Legislature for the first time in more than 15 years. 
A Tiffany victory would represent a return to the Gov. Scott Walker era of politics in the state, focused on deregulation and tax cuts and would mean Republicans gain control of a key swing state ahead of the 2028 presidential election. 
Taxes and the economy
The debate opened with an extended discussion about the economy, taxes and the state budget as affordability has become one of the main issues of concern to voters in this year’s midterm elections. 
Tiffany has built his campaign on the promise of massive tax cuts. He’s said he’ll cut property and income taxes while maintaining funding for government services. Since the early days of his campaign, Tiffany has argued that he can deliver massive tax cuts without significant cuts. 
“We are going to have sufficient money in this budget to be able to fund the things that are important to Wisconsinites: education, transportation, and infrastructure, healthcare, we’re going to have money there, and here’s why,” he said. “When you look at the last budget that was passed a year ago, it went up $15 billion, went from $99 billion to $114 billion, a 15% increase, the largest increase ever in a state budget. There is plenty of money in Madison to be able to provide more shared revenue, to give increased aid to our schools, there is enough money in Madison to be able to backfill those things that we need to.” 
The most recent state budget, passed by the Republican-controlled Legislature and signed by Evers, cut $1.3 billion in taxes while increasing funding for the University of Wisconsin system, childcare providers and special education. 
During a conversation about transportation funding, Crowley questioned how Tiffany will pay for his tax plans. 
“Congressman Tom Tiffany doesn’t have any plans,” Crowley said. “Congressman Tiffany literally just said that he would cut billionaire taxes to 0%. And how we’re going to fund transportation? He has no clue. How are you going to get the revenues when you continuously cut the amount of revenues coming into government? This is the reason why cities, towns, villages, and our school districts all across the state are struggling today, and that’s because he doesn’t work for the people. He’s working for the billionaires. He’s going to do anything and everything that they tell him to do because that’s who he’s been in the pockets of.”
Throughout the campaign, Tiffany has criticized Crowley for rising property taxes in Milwaukee County and the increase in the county sales tax included in a bipartisan 2023 deal to inject more money into local government budgets. 
The total property tax levy collected by Milwaukee County each year has increased, but the property tax rate actually paid by individual homeowners has increased less than the rate of inflation. The sales tax increase was included in the shared revenue bill passed by Republicans and has been seen as a policy move that helped stave off massive cuts to county services. 
Crowley said his record on taxes has been misrepresented by the Tiffany campaign and added that he wants to increase taxes on the state’s wealthiest people, take a holistic look at the total tax picture to find where people can get relief and better work with local governments. 
He also argued that Tiffany’s tax plans will only benefit his wealthy donors. Tiffany’s campaign has been largely funded by three billionaires, Beloit resident Diane Hendricks and Illinois residents Richard and Liz Uihlein. 
“He wants to do exactly what they did in Washington D.C.,” Crowley said. “They literally gave $80 billion in tax breaks to billionaires throughout the entire country on the backs of hardworking Wisconsinites who are losing their healthcare — 270,000 folks. Look, we cannot afford Congressman Tiffany as the next governor if we’re literally going to be balancing tax breaks for billionaires on the backs of hardworking Wisconsin family members. What we need to be focusing on is how do we make sure that we can get them access to better-paying jobs? How we can actually make sure that they can actually afford food on the table?.”
Billionaires and Donald Trump
Crowley repeatedly returned to the refrain that Tiffany will only serve the interests of Trump and his billionaire donors. 
“So while my opponent, you can see early on in the debate, is consistently focused on being against Donald Trump, I’m for Wisconsin,” Tiffany countered. “And rather than creating a bunch more programs that are going to end up taxing the people of Wisconsin more, I want to put more money in the taxpayers’ pockets.” 
Later in the evening, Tiffany said that Crowley is “ranting constantly” about billionaires.
“Have I ever said we’re going to cut taxes to zero? I have not,” he said. “He’s misrepresenting our positions, and he’s over there ranting constantly about billionaires. We need a governor that’s going to be focused on people here in Wisconsin to do what’s best for Wisconsin. Not worrying about others, not announcing what you are against, but telling people what you’re for.” 
Education
On education, Tiffany said he wants to provide more funding for public education while raising standards and accountability for struggling districts. He also said he would consider raising income limits on Wisconsin’s statewide private school voucher program through which families receive a tuition subsidy from the state government. 
“I just think people should have whatever choice that they make,” Tiffany said. “We made the choice of public schools, regardless of income. And if a child is trapped in a failing school, they should be able to choose the school that they want to go to.” 
Crowley responded by arguing that this position is the one held by the wealthy supporters of the voucher program. 
“This is a prime example of exactly who the congressman works for,” Crowley said. “I mean, when this program was started, it was to make sure that low-income students all across the state of Wisconsin got access to some type of option. At the end, and what ended up happening, they kept lifting the cap. And what they do next, they lifted the income limits. Those who were actually paying for private education then started utilizing public dollars to pay for their child’s education. I mean, Congressman Tom Tiffany, it doesn’t sound like you want to work for the small guys. Sounds like you want to work for those who have the money and have the means to continue to pay their way.”
Data centers
This year, public opposition to data centers has played a large role in campaigns across the country. In this race, both candidates have sent mixed signals on the issue while trying to cast the other as the pro-data center choice. 
Tiffany pointed to comments Crowley has made in which he celebrated the potential financial benefits data centers could have for local government budgets. As he’s said on the campaign trail, he tied his opposition to data centers with his opposition to solar and wind power developments and said he supports local control over development and would get rid of the sales tax exemptions for data centers currently in state law. 
“I’ve been against these subsidies,” Tiffany said. “Why would the wealthiest, some of the wealthiest companies in the world need subsidies from the taxpayers of Wisconsin? I’m opposed to them.” 
Crowley pointed to the $80 billion in tax breaks for data center developers Tiffany voted for in the One Big Beautiful Bill that was passed by Republicans last summer and said he’s going to do whatever he can to support local decisions around data centers. 
“We need to make sure we’re protecting our environment, protecting our land, protecting our farmland, protecting our waterways,” Crowley said. “But communities need to have a seat because if they don’t want a data center, they shouldn’t be forced to have a data center. There’s no ifs, ands, or buts about that. I’ve always sided with communities and the people when it comes down to data centers, Congressman Tom Tiffany, he’s done something different. I mean, he provided the tax breaks to the big tech companies who are steamrolling our communities today with these data centers.” 
In 2017, when Republicans in the Legislature, then-Gov. Walker and Trump were working to attract Foxconn to Wisconsin to build a manufacturing plant in Mount Pleasant, Tiffany voted in committee and the full Senate in favor of the $3 billion tax break the state gave the company. After Foxconn’s plans failed to fully materialize, Microsoft took over the site, where it is now building a data center campus. 
Elections
A chunk of the debate focused on questions about Tiffany’s vote to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, abortion and the tactics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — three areas in which Democrats have sought to tie Tiffany as closely as possible with Trump and the right flank of the Republican party. 
When asked why, after he voted to overturn the 2020 election results in Pennsylvania and Arizona, he said he would also have voted to overturn Wisconsin’s 2020 election of Biden, potentially nullifying the votes of hundreds of thousands of people, Tiffany said he did so because he had concerns about “Zuckerbucks” — the moniker Republicans gave to grant money given to municipal governments through a charity run by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to help them pay for the increased costs of administering an election during a pandemic. 
He also said he had concerns about the Madison city clerk posting online that voters concerned about going to the polls because of COVID-19 could use the state’s indefinitely confined voter provision. That comment was made in March 2020 ahead of the state’s April election that year and the state Supreme Court quickly issued an order blocking that guidance, so it had no bearing on how people voted seven months later. 
“Because of what happened there, when there was money coming in privately that should not have been, and the voters said that that should not be that way,” Tiffany said. “I mean, I can give you one other example of what happened there. There was the Dane County Clerk who declared that people who are indefinitely confined, they could just declare themselves to be indefinitely confined during the election. That clerk did not have the authority to do that. That requires an action by the state Senate and the governor to change that law. So there are a couple things like that that I thought should be addressed.”
Tiffany later said he would consider getting rid of the Wisconsin Elections Commission and changing how the state manages its elections. Tiffany and legislative Republicans voted to break up the state’s previous election agency, the Government Accountability Board, after it investigated allegations of campaign finance violations by Walker. 
“I think we need to sit down and have that discussion about do we make changes to the Wisconsin Elections Commission. I mean, I’m one of the people that voted for it a decade ago,” he said. “We thought that we hit on the answer to be able to have an effective body, but we need to make sure that there’s accountability by the Wisconsin Elections Commission, and they’re carrying out their job.” 
He continued, saying “there should be a simple principle in regards to our elections. It should be easy to vote and hard to cheat. We need to make sure that the Wisconsin Elections Commission is going to carry out that mandate for the voters of Wisconsin, because they’ve proven over the last number of years they want election integrity. Voters have voted consistently for election integrity.”
Crowley said that Tiffany’s election comments show he’ll sell out Wisconsinites for Trump, including in 2028 when the next governor will be responsible for certifying the results of the presidential race. 
Abortion
In this race, abortion has not been one of the campaign’s main issues, but Tiffany has a history of anti-abortion actions in the state Legislature and in Congress and has been endorsed by anti-abortion groups. He said that in the Legislature he voted for the state’s current ban on abortions after 20 weeks and that’s where he would continue to draw the line. 
“When I talked to my constituents, they said, ‘We want you to find a middle ground on this. We want you to compromise,’ and that’s exactly what we did,” he said. “I stand by that vote of a decade ago, and I will uphold it as the governor of Wisconsin.”
Crowley pointed out that while in Congress, Tiffany supported a bill that would have enacted a total federal abortion ban with no exceptions for rape, incest or the health of the mother. 
Tiffany said his position on the issue has “been consistent ever since I announced for governor,” while trying to cast Crowley as a pro-abortion extremist who would allow abortions for the full duration of a pregnancy. Crowley said that abortions after 20 weeks are nearly always serious situations that involve life-threatening medical questions and the decision should be made between a patient and her doctor. 
Crowley has argued on the campaign trail for an amendment to the state Constitution enshrining the right to have an abortion and he also said he didn’t believe the Legislature would pass a bill lifting all restrictions on abortion. 
In their closing statements, both candidates reiterated the arguments they’d been making all night. 
Crowley again argued that Wisconsinites can’t trust Tiffany to choose regular citizens over billionaires and Trump. Tiffany discussed the plane crash he was in while campaigning earlier this summer and the “best of Wisconsin” he saw from first responders — saying he wanted everyone in the state to see that, too. 
The Wisconsin Examiner previously reported that the pilot of that plane was a frequent Republican donor and an election denier who associates with some of the state’s most prominent election conspiracy theorists. On Wednesday, MeidasTouch reported that Tiffany’s campaign spent $70,000 on private flights in the past two months. 
After the debate, Republicans said that Tiffany “laid out his vision.” 
“Tom Tiffany laid out a vision to lower taxes and put Wisconsin families first, while David Crowley could not defend his failed record in Milwaukee County,” Republican Governors Association spokesperson Kollin Crompton said. “Crowley’s higher taxes and soft-on-crime policies are a warning, not a blueprint for Wisconsin. Tiffany knows Wisconsin, understands its people, and is running to put them first.”
Democrats and Crowley claimed a debate victory. 
“There was only one governor on stage tonight, and it wasn’t the guy who went to Washington to vote with Donald Trump 100% of the time,” Crowley campaign manager Garren Randolph said. “Congressman Tom Tiffany spent an hour offering Wisconsinites excuse after excuse for the role he played in jacking up costs on families across the state. Gas prices, healthcare premiums, and utility bills are all up because of Congressman Tom Tiffany’s loyalty to Donald Trump over the people of Wisconsin. On the other side of the stage, David Crowley showed Wisconsinites a leader who will actually work for them if elected governor. David laid out how he’ll lower taxes for working families instead of billionaires and lower the cost of gas, groceries, housing, and healthcare.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Takeaways from the final gubernatorial debate between Demuth, Klobuchar
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Minnesota State Fair. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar each focused on  guilt by association during their final gubernatorial debate Wednesday.
Repeating a theme on display up and down the ballot this year, Demuth argued that Klobuchar is aligned with Gov. Tim Walz and would govern similarly, while Klobuchar argued that Demuth would not stand up to President Donald Trump to do what’s best for Minnesota.
Wednesday’s debate, which was televised statewide and co-hosted by FOX 9 and Gray Media,  was the second this week between the two candidates for governor and their final face-to-face meeting before the Nov. 3 election.
Here are some takeaways from Wednesday’s debate:
Gloves off
Demuth repeatedly argued Klobuchar is no different from Walz, an unpopular governor who oversaw state government when fraudsters grabbed a foothold in Minnesota’s social safety net programs. Klobuchar has long stated that when she first learned of the fraud, she worked to hire more prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney’s office, which then went on to prosecute fraudsters.
“Even if she made a phone call on fraud, where was she? There was no press release. There was nothing to say that she was protecting our federal taxpayer dollars,” Demuth said. “She was silent on fraud until Tim Walz asked her to run for governor here in the state of Minnesota.”
Klobuchar called the attack “absurd” and threw Walz overboard, as she did in their first debate.
“How do I differ (from) Tim Walz? You have not come up with one way you differ from Donald Trump,” Klobuchar told Demuth. “I have been clear. I wouldn’t have pardoned the sex offender. I would have put more of the surplus money into infrastructure and technology. And yes, I would have caught the fraud earlier.”
Klobuchar threw out attacks more frequently than Demuth, noting that the House speaker lacks comprehensive governing plans on housing and child care and authored an anti-abortion bill in the Legislature that would criminally punish doctors. She also said Demuth’s campaign is being bolstered by millions from a Wisconsin billionaire and frequent Trump donor, Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. (Klobuchar is being helped by wealthy DFL donors, including Rockefeller heiress Alida Messinger.) 
What’s driving up costs? 
Costs have exploded in Minnesota was due to the regulations and tax increases passed by Democratic-Farmer-Labor lawmakers in recent years, Demuth argued. She argued that housing is more expensive because of stricter building regulations than other states; childcare is more expensive and there are fewer providers because fraudsters have infiltrated the industry; and gas prices are rising because Democrats increased the gas tax, while Klobuchar voted against extending the Keystone XL pipeline to increase fuel supply to Minnesota.
“You have to ask yourself, why are things so expensive here in Minnesota? They were expensive because of overspending by one-party control in 2023 and 2024,” Demuth said. “I will bring down prices. I will right-size our state budget and make sure that you can afford your lives.”
(Minnesota has the 18th lowest cost of living in the nation, according to SoFi.)
Klobuchar argued that Trump and his administration are largely to blame for rising prices, noting that the war in Iran caused an immediate jump in fuel prices; millions have been kicked off of their health insurance because of the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act; and Trump’s tariffs are increasing the price of goods.
“I can tell you the fastest way to bring down your gas prices, and that is to stop this war in Iran. That is it, beginning, middle, and end,” Klobuchar said. “And when you look at what my opponent brings up … she actually brought up and blamed it on the Keystone Pipeline. Then she blamed the health care costs on Barack Obama. I don’t know what will be next. Maybe Thomas Jefferson. But what I know is that Minnesotans understand what’s happened at the pump.”
Both worked to distance themselves from unpopular men
Demuth noted a number of ways she disagreed with Trump.
“As far as the war in Iran, I’ve been very clear about talking about that it needs to come to an end soon. I have also separated when it comes to bringing foreign beef and some of the other tariffs,” Demuth said. “What we have not yet heard is from Sen. Klobuchar, where she differs on a policy or a bill that Gov. Walz has put into place. She still calls him an incredible governor.”
Klobuchar responded that Demuth did not speak out against the war in Iran until last month and she praised then-Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem during Operation Metro Surge.
“We need someone who’s wiling to work with people, but also stand up when he does some really bad stuff,” Klobuchar said.
Demuth repeatedly said that Klobuchar would not name one policy with which she disagreed with Walz.
“I would love to hear if she has separated herself specifically from Tim Walz. Tim Walz allowed the childcare fraud and other fraud here in the state of Minnesota to explode to $9 billion, never firing any of his commissioners or agency employees, but yet you have someone standing here tonight that is supporting everything from the incredible governor, as she has said he is,” Demuth said.
Klobuchar, appearing exasperated, told viewers to “rewind the tape on this debate, please, and you will see exactly how I said I differed from Tim Walz.”

name: Delaware
title: Two Arrested in Fatal Off-Campus Shooting Following Homecoming Event 10-21-26
text:
POLICE LOG – October 21, 2026
Dover Police Arrest Two in Fatal Shopping Center Shooting
DOVER, Del. — Dover Police have arrested two men in connection with an October 10 shooting at the Dover Commons shopping center that killed a 22-year-old Philadelphia man and injured another man.
Police said detectives identified a 22-year-old Dover man as one of the suspected shooters. He was arrested October 16 at a residence in the 500 block of Crawford Avenue after police obtained arrest and search warrants. Investigators said they recovered a 9mm handgun, ammunition and clothing and accessories believed to match items worn during the shooting.
A second suspect, an 18-year-old male, was located October 21 at a residence in Snow Hill, Maryland, by members of the U.S. Marshals Service Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force–Salisbury. He was taken into custody without incident and was being held in Maryland pending extradition to Delaware.
Both suspects are charged with first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, three counts of possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, four counts of first-degree reckless endangering and carrying a concealed deadly weapon.
The shooting occurred at about 9:19 p.m. October 10 in the Dover Commons parking lot in the 1200 block of North DuPont Highway. Police found two gunshot victims, including Nasir Cox, 22, of Philadelphia. Officers transported both victims to Bayhealth Kent Campus in police vehicles because heavy traffic in the area was expected to delay emergency medical response.
Cox later died from his injuries. The second victim, a 21-year-old man, was reported in stable condition.
The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information, photographs or video from the area is asked to contact the Dover Police Department Criminal Investigations Unit at 302-736-7111.
All defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

title: Judge blocks Homeland Security from conducting election-related sweeps in 9 states
text: A federal judge on Wednesday night blocked the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens in nine states.Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court in the Northern District of California, issued a preliminary injunction after voting rights advocates alleged that Homeland Security was sending armed agents to homes to question residents about their voter status. The injunction bars operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin until polls close on Election Day, though the administration may appeal in the coming days.The decision marks a legal setback to the Trump administration’s intensifying campaign this fall against noncitizen voting ahead of Election Day. It comes as the Department of Justice is suing California to force state and local election officials to not count the ballots of some 20,000 voters the federal government says it suspects are noncitizens.President Donald Trump has long decried the threat of noncitizen voting, which studies have shown rarely occurs. He now faces political peril, as Democrats appear increasingly likely to retake the U.S. House and possibly the Senate in the midterm elections.Martínez-Olguín found that the importance of the public voting free of intimidation outweighed the Trump administration’s interest in rooting out noncitizen voting. But she paused her order until Friday, presumably to give the Trump administration time to appeal.The evidence in the case, she wrote, leads to an “objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote.”The lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. "Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them,” Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer at the legal advocacy group Protect Democracy, which represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement.Martínez-Olguín wrote that the “ongoing intimidation that CNA/NNU members experience and the direct impediment it plays in their effort to engage voter outreach, education, and engagement efforts, are irreparable harms that are appropriately addressed by preliminary injunctive relief.”A Homeland Security Investigations internal memo dated Aug. 31 describes a “surge initiative” beginning Sept. 1 that includes conducting field interviews. The memo, which was filed in court, identifies California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin as targets of the surge during September. Additional locations are redacted in the document.Homeland Security didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision.In a previous court filing, Department of Justice lawyers representing DHS have argued that the federal government has the authority to investigate potential voting by noncitizens. “Enjoining the government from even investigating such criminal violations would damage the public interest, not serve it,” they wrote.Democratic groups and top Democrats in Congress filed a lawsuit Tuesday seeking to block Trump intimidating election officials.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Healthcare, small business advocates urge reversing healthcare cuts, boost Democrats
text:
Business owner Kyle LaFond speaks at an event Wednesday organized by Protect Our Care and Main Street Action to call attention to healthcare  costs. With them are, from left, childcare center owner Macy Buhler, Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul, Joe Zepecki of Protect Our Care, and Laura Packard, a healthcare advocate. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Healthcare and small business advocates crossed Wisconsin Wednesday to call on the federal government to reverse policies they said were thwarting healthcare access and support Democrats running for Congress and other offices in the Nov. 3 election.
Protect Our Care is sending a bus across Wisconsin and other Midwestern states to call attention to the importance of healthcare in this year’s election, said Joe Zepecki, Wisconsin director for the advocacy group. Main Street Action, representing small business owners, has joined the campaign. In Wisconsin it includes stops to highlight Democratic congressional candidates in the 1st and 3rd Congressional Districts.
At a stop in Madison, several speakers criticized Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is running for governor, particularly for his vote in favor of the 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that included cuts estimated at nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid over the next 10 years while making tax cuts that heavily favored the wealthy.
While that law was enacted, Congressional Republicans several times rejected attempts to extend enhanced subsidies for health insurance purchased at the federal healthcare marketplace under the Affordable Care Act.
Zepecki said advocates have three demands: restoring the enhanced ACA premium subsidies to lower the cost of health insurance; reversing the Medicaid cuts in the 2025 law; and passing legislation that would expand the authorization for Medicare to negotiate prices with drug companies.
Kyle LaFond, the owner of a manufacturing company and a member of Main Street Alliance, said his ACA coverage now costs him $2,600 more per year. But for other families who include people with disabilities or who are otherwise vulnerable, “these costs are devastating,” LaFond said.
“We can’t be complacent,” he said. “None of this should be considered normal. Healthcare is a fundamental human right.”
Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul, who is running for reelection this year, recalled that when he ran for office in 2018, Wisconsin was among a group of states that joined a lawsuit to overturn the 2011 Affordable Care Act. Kaul’s predecessor as attorney general, Republican Brad Schimel, had signed on to the lawsuit on behalf of the state.
“One of the issues in our race was whether Wisconsin should be part of that suit,” said Kaul, a Democrat. After Kaul was elected, he withdrew Wisconsin from the lawsuit, which subsequently lost at the U.S. Supreme Court.
While that attack on affordable health insurance coverage failed, in the current administration of President Donald Trump “access to affordable healthcare remains under attack,” Kaul said.
The 2025 bill that cut Medicaid is just one example, he said. “But beyond that, the Trump administration has acted on its own without Congress to unilaterally make cuts designed to undermine access to affordable health insurance coverage or to make access to quality care less available,” Kaul added — citing the administration’s retreat from an evidence-based childhood vaccine schedule, cuts in funding for school mental health and public health and cuts to medical research.
Joining attorneys general in other states — all Democrats — Wisconsin has sued to block such actions and have won “significant victories,” he said, including the preservation of $200 million in public health funding for Wisconsin that had been threatened.

name: VTDigger
title: Emergency medicine responders meet with Becca Balint to talk rural health bottlenecks
text:
U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., speaks during a discussion the challenges faced by first responders at Milton Rescue in Milton on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
MILTON — U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., wanted to see how heavy a stretcher is. She got some help lifting it out of the back of one of Milton’s retired ambulances as part of her Wednesday visit with the Chittenden County town’s emergency medicine providers.
The ambulance was old and without the now-standard hydraulic lift that lowers stretchers out of the back of the truck. Milton had just retired the old ambulance after waiting three years — and paying nearly half a million dollars — for the new, state-of-the-art replacement, according to Town Manager Chris Taylor. A tour inside the old and new trucks closed out her hour-long visit with the rural emergency medicine squad.
Nearly a dozen Milton EMTs and paramedics joined Balint, her staff and Milton town executives to discuss the biggest challenges emergency medicine providers in Vermont face. With her visit, Balint aimed to underscore and understand the unique challenges rural emergency medicine providers are facing and what the federal government can do to support these municipal efforts. 
Chief among the providers’ concerns were all the ways that people turn to 911 as a way to address social problems such as mental health crises, food insecurity and housing issues. 
“I think the overwhelming theme was that EMS providers in these rural areas are responding, certainly to medical emergencies, but they are basically the people who are filling the gaps for community services that aren’t adequate enough,” Balint said in a subsequent interview with VTDigger. 
“Are (patients) starting to view you all as their primary care provider?” Balint asked paramedics during the afternoon roundtable. The room pulsed with nods and paramedics’ eyes lit up. 
Balint said she suspects more Vermonters are forgoing preventative care and relying on emergency responders as Medicaid tightens its eligibility and federal support for marketplace insurance plans shrink. Milton’s first responders confirmed that they often are the primary point of contact people in rural parts of the state have with the healthcare system. 
Patients know that they will be able to speak to a provider within minutes rather than waiting weeks or more for a primary care appointment, said Sean McCann, chief of the Milton medical response team.
The team also often responds to health emergencies that primary care could have prevented, they said. One Milton Rescue team member mentioned caring for patients who forgo prescriptions in order to pay their taxes and bills first. Others mentioned rural patients who simply can’t get to the pharmacy or the clinic for preventative care. 
“We do a lot more than clinical care,” McCann told Balint. 
But treating an ambulance and the emergency department as the first line of defense can introduce undue costs for the patient — many of whom are elderly and on fixed incomes — and for the healthcare system as a whole, where in-hospital care is some of the most expensive.
“For our state, you can’t talk about pre-hospital without talking about the hospital,” Katie Escobedo, a full-time paramedic in Milton, said, referring to the one trauma center in the state, UVM Medical Center. As the hospital tries to shrink its staff and number of beds, the emergency department cannot admit patients into the hospital as quickly, Escobedo said. When the emergency department gets backed up, people leave and call 911. She cited a misconception that arriving at the hospital in an ambulance might fasttrack a patient to seeing a provider.  
“There’s just a huge backup, especially in our lovely little state of Vermont, because we do have that one big University of Vermont (Medical Center), and everything is branched off of that,” Escobedo said.

U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., left, listens as Samuel Hayford, standing, speaks about the challenges first responders face at Milton Rescue in Milton on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

One way of addressing that would be to deploy more EMS providers into the community to treat patients where they are — whether that’s at home or on the street. It’s something that the Brattleboro Rescue Inc. emergency responders have put in practice and Milton is evaluating ways to implement too, according to Taylor, the town manager. 
Medicare, however, only reimburses emergency responders for transporting the patient to the hospital, not for treatment. It’s an issue Balint is trying to address through a bill she and U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., have jointly reintroduced. The bill would shift payment models to reimburse for treatment, instead of transportation.
Balint also hopes she can use her seat on a House anti-trust committee to address the expense and wait times that towns like Milton endure when purchasing an ambulance. In the meantime, Balint said she is focusing on securing federal funding for even smaller towns — Pownal and Hardwick — with tighter budgets to replace their own ambulances.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Cook Inlet’s gas shortage has become Fairbanks’ diesel bill
text:
Golden Valley Electric Association’s Eva Creek wind project is near Healy. (Alaska Energy Authority photo)On October 12, Golden Valley Electric Association asked its cooperative members to conserve electricity and prepare for possible controlled power outages. Scheduled maintenance, compounded by an unexpected shutdown of a unit at its North Pole Power Plant, had left the utility running all remaining available generation with very little reserve.
Coming just before winter, after a summer when residential electricity rates climbed above 37 cents per kilowatt-hour, the warning spooked many Interior residents. Paying high bills is one thing. Wondering whether the lights and heat will stay on as temperatures fall is another.
But the warning also raised a question: Aren’t we connected to a larger, regional transmission system called the Railbelt Grid? Then why does a shortage of available generation in Fairbanks leave us feeling like an electrical island?
The Alaska Intertie was built in the 1980s to connect the Interior to Southcentral utilities. Public money funded that connection so utilities could share lower-cost electricity, including power from the state-owned Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project and gas-fired generation from Cook Inlet. But the intertie also serves another function—it helps stabilize the entire grid and allows utilities to support one another in an emergency. It was called the Alaska Intertie for a reason. Its benefits were meant to extend beyond any one utility’s territory.
So when a potential shortfall emerges, as it did last week, shouldn’t we be able to draw on available power elsewhere on the system? And when we can’t, what stands in the way?
Cook Inlet’s gas shortage has become Fairbanks’ diesel bill
That question reaches beyond a few days of strained operations. Cook Inlet’s gas shortage has sharply curtailed the amount of electricity moving north. In 2014, the intertie carried roughly 540,000 megawatt-hours—an amount equivalent to more than 40% of GVEA’s annual electricity sales. Most was gas-fired economy power purchased from Southcentral utilities. But since early 2025, those economy-power purchases have fallen to essentially zero. 
Source: GVEA annual reports to RCA and GVEA Cost-of-Power Adjustment (COPA) filings
That leaves GVEA meeting its everyday electricity needs largely with local generation, supplemented by its share of Bradley Lake hydropower. Coal supplies about 40% of its electricity, while wind contributes a small share. Much of the rest comes from two liquid petroleum fuels, both produced at Petro Star’s refinery in North Pole: lower-cost naphtha, burned in GVEA’s more efficient LM6000 combined-cycle plant, and more expensive diesel, used in its older turbines and generators.
GVEA has been trying to kick its expensive diesel habit for years. For a while, it was making real progress: in 2014, the older diesel-fired turbines at North Pole supplied only about 3% of its electricity. Lower-cost imports and the addition of the LM6000 helped keep those units largely in reserve. But when gas-fired economy power from Southcentral dried up, GVEA relapsed. By 2025, those diesel turbines were supplying 15% of its electricity.
New turbine rotor waits to be installed at GVEA’s North Pole power plant during an overhaul of one of its diesel-fired units. Photo courtesy of GVEA.
This has left us more exposed to diesel prices just as prices have spiked due to the war in Iran. That double whammy—the loss of lower-cost imports and rising diesel prices—largely explains the steep increase in Fairbanks’ residential rates. Today, residents pay about 50% more per kilowatt-hour than Southcentral customers and more than three times as much as those in largely hydropower-based Juneau. 
GVEA members are even paying more than most residential customers in rural Alaska, where diesel dependence has traditionally made electricity especially expensive. The state’s Power Cost Equalization program was created decades ago to bring electricity costs for eligible rural household usage closer to those in Anchorage, Fairbanks and Juneau. The irony is that Fairbanks, one of those benchmarks for affordability, now has a residential rate about 10 cents per kilowatt-hour, or 40%, above the average PCE-adjusted rate reported for 2025. This is perhaps less surprising when one considers the scale of GVEA’s diesel dependence: last winter, its daily diesel consumption for power generation averaged more than three times that of all of rural Alaska combined.
Cook Inlet’s gas shortage has become Fairbanks’ diesel bill. But is that really fair?
Who benefits from publicly supported gas?
We don’t often think of Cook Inlet gas as a state-supported energy resource. That’s because private companies produce the basin’s oil and gas. However, the State of Alaska has consistently helped keep that resource flowing through cashable tax credits, favorable production tax treatment, royalty relief and public financing.
This support amounts to no small potatoes. The Department of Revenue reported Alaska paid $1.3 billion in cash to purchase tax credits for “non-North-Slope oil and gas activities” through 2021.                   
The Interior used to share in the benefits of these state investments through economy power purchases sent up the intertie. But with gas now scarce, the spigot to Fairbanks has been cut off. Southcentral utilities are understandably putting their own customers first. That is their responsibility. But an understandable outcome is not necessarily an equitable one, given the public investments that helped make those resources available. We cannot expect individual utilities alone to resolve complex policy questions about how publicly supported resources should be shared. That will require political leadership. Without it, meaningful near-term rate relief for the Interior is difficult to see. In the meantime, prolonged high energy costs threaten not only household budgets, but the broader Interior economy.                       
Fill the line
There are no quick or simple answers to these issues, but there are actionable steps we can take. GVEA’s precarious position means it stands to gain significantly from greater resource sharing and a stronger regional system. GVEA should be the utility that keeps knocking on doors—of other utilities, legislators, suppliers and a new governor—to bring everyone to the table. With so much at stake for its members, it should be both the most persistent advocate for regional solutions and a leader in making them happen.
Source: Energy Information Administration, GVEA annual reports to RCA
A big part of that is figuring out how to put the intertie back to work, both now and over the longer term. GVEA should adopt a new mantra: fill the line. The nice thing about a transmission line is that it doesn’t care how the electricity is generated. Whether the power comes from imported gas, gas delivered through a North Slope pipeline, coal, new hydro projects, the waste-to-energy project Anchorage has been pursuing, or even advanced nuclear, a stronger regional grid would help us develop the best resources wherever they are located and share the benefits across the Railbelt. No one has a crystal ball, but today’s scarcity should not define the limits of our ambition or our imagination.
In the meantime, GVEA can begin taking some practical steps toward regional solutions. One would be pursuing membership in the tight power pool through which Matanuska Electric Association and Chugach Electric Association coordinate their generation. Operating since April 2021, the pool allows the two utilities to select the least costly combination of available generation to meet their combined demand, rather than each relying on its own plants first. They retain their separate identities while sharing the benefits of operating more efficiently together. According to a recent presentation by MEA’s Julie Estey, that cooperation saves their customers approximately $6 million to $7 million a year—a substantial benefit from working together.
The published pooling agreement already anticipates GVEA joining someday, but its protections for existing participants mean that GVEA membership would need to benefit them, too. That may be difficult to demonstrate under current conditions. Yet GVEA’s plight, coupled with the broader question of equitable access to publicly supported energy resources, makes a case for negotiating beyond those existing terms. It will be a difficult conversation, but GVEA should be identifying the barriers, proposing solutions and seeking the political support needed to move forward now.
A stronger regional system would give all of us more options, greater reliability and access to affordable power. Today, Fairbanks is struggling; tomorrow, another part of the Railbelt could need help. Every utility has something to gain from making better use of our shared resources. Our market is too small to keep planning and investing as though each utility were an electrical island. We built the intertie to connect us. Now we need to make that connection work for all of us.
