name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Restoration projects underway at Idaho’s Minidoka National Historic Site
text:
Crews work on historic renovation projects at Minidoka National Historic Site near Jerome on Oct. 21, 2026. Officials hope the restoration projects and new interpretive exhibits will be complete in 2028. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)JEROME – More than $5 million worth restoration projects and forthcoming interpretive exhibits  are being designed to preserve the history and lessons from southern Idaho’s Minidoka National Historic Site. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Wednesday, U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, joined National Park Service personnel, local elected officials and the Friends of Minidoka to highlight three historic restoration projects at Minidoka that are being funded by $5 million from the federal Great American Outdoors Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law in 2020. 
Funding will help restore a root cellar, a mess hall and a barracks from the camp.
In alignment with those projects, leaders of the nonprofit organization Friends of Minidoka announced Wednesday that they had secured $650,000 in grants to develop and install interpretative exhibits at the buildings that are being restored and complete a digital mapping project that will map Minidoka’s historic barracks and individual living units. 
Friends of Minidoka officials announced they are launching a fundraiser to generate the final $100,000 for those projects. 
Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka, said the goal is for the restoration projects and new exhibits to be finished in the spring of 2028. 
During World War II, from 1942 to 1945, more than 13,000 Japanese Americans were incarcerated – after being forcibly removed from their homes without due process and without being charged with a crime – at the Minidoka War Relocation Center. 
To commemorate the people who were incarcerated there, Minidoka has been a part of the U.S. National Park Service for 25 years. 
 Minidoka survivor urges public to learn the history of camp

Karen Hirai Olen, a Minidoka survivor who was born at the camp in 1943, attended Wednesday’s ceremonies.

Olen called the restoration project amazing and said she hopes many people will visit Minidoka National Historic Site when the projects are complete. 
“My wish would be that they come out here and experience Minidoka,” Olen said. “Spend a day out here. Understand what people went through.”
“One, I want people to remember what happened here and two, that it should not happen to anybody else,” Olen said. 
Minidoka survivor Karen Hirai Olen tours the historic restoration sites at Minidoka National Historic Site. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)
Olen, who spent the first year and a half of her life incarcerated with her parents, grandparents and other family members at Minidoka, said she didn’t understand what Minidoka was until she was an adult. 
When she grew up and went to school in nearby Twin Falls, Olen said she didn’t know Minidoka was an camp and neither did any of the other students in her classes. 
“My parents never talked about it,” Olen said. “My mother called it the lost years.”
As an adult, Olen learned the history from her family and other, older Minidoka survivors. Olen has also participated in about 15 organized pilgrimages with other survivors to return Minidoka.
Olen said she began talking with other people incarcerated at the site and realized “this is what the camp really was that mother never told us.”
 Idaho congressman calls for reauthorization of Legacy Restoration Fund

During interviews and public remarks at Minidoka on Wednesday, Simpson said Congress needs to reauthorize funding from the Legacy Restoration Fund from the Great American Outdoors Act, which just expired. 
Simpson said funding from the Legacy Restoration Fund is paying for restoration projects at Minidoka and rehabilitation work at Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve and the Hagerman Fossil Beds National Monument. 
Overall, Simpson said the purpose of the funding is to address a backlog of maintenance projects at National Park Service sites across the county. 
“We have a huge backlog of maintenance, and that’s what the Legacy Restoration Fund was meant to address and start doing,” Simpson told the Idaho Capital Sun. “Because both the good news and the bad news is that Americans love our national parks.”

name: California
title: Thousands of California state workers walk off the job in contract dispute with Newsom
text:
In summary
The largest union in California state government held a one-day strike, drawing thousands of workers off the job. It’s pressing Gov. Gavin Newsom for raises and more flexibility to work from home.


Garbed in purple and holding signs that read “Fair contracts now!” and “Here to serve, not to starve,” thousands of state workers rallied at government buildings across California Wednesday to protest what they describe as unfair labor practices by Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration.
SEIU Local 1000’s first strike in its 44-year history unfolded in several cities including Sacramento, San Francisco and Los Angeles. The union — which represents about 100,000 workers, nearly half the state workforce — has been in contentious labor talks with the Newsom administration since its latest contract expired in late June. 
Its members want a better raise than Newsom has offered as well as more flexibility to work from home. Newsom just a year ago demanded wage reductions from the union to help shore up a budget crisis. State workers have accepted pay cuts in three of the eight years Newsmom led the state. 
“The budget is balanced on state employees’ backs,” said Local 1000 President Anica Walls. “It’s just showing how frustrated employees are with the lack of prioritizing us as people who really help California remain the fourth largest economy in the world,” she said.
Angela Musallam, a spokesperson for the California Department of Human Resources, which handles labor negotiations on behalf of the administration, said the department “remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table.” Both parties are scheduled to resume mediation talks on Oct. 30
In anticipation of the strike, operations at some state departments have been modified or limited, including at DMV offices and parks. Outside the Elihu M. Harris State Office Building in downtown Oakland, workers marched outside chanting “No contract, no peace.” They played drums, snacked on muffins and Little Caesar pizzas and cheered as cars honked along Clay St. in solidarity.
Amy Dickinson, an information technology associate at California Department of Industrial Relations’ Office of Information Systems, said she was striking “because the state has decided that we are not worth even bargaining with.”
“They have done nothing but say ‘no’ all this time. They won’t even give any counteroffers — that’s not bargaining, that’s a maximalist position,” said the San Leandro resident.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Lateefah Simon, who represents the East Bay Area,, spoke to the crowd in Oakland before joining them briefly in marching.
“Nothing happens without the workers,” said Simon. “For anyone to say that you don’t deserve wage justice, they haven’t looked at the rates of rent … at grocery prices.”
“There is enough for everything that you’re asking for. But the floor is respect.”
Unions, including Local 1000, traditionally are Newsom’s allies. They contributed to his campaigns and helped him defeat Republican opponents. But the Local 1000 strike is the second state worker walkout to occur on his watch. Previously, the California Association of Professional Scientists held a three-day strike in 2023. 
Besides pay boosts, Local 1000 members are pushing for higher state contributions for healthcare coverage, and changes to Newsom’s four-day-a-week in-office mandate, which they argue costs workers and taxpayers money and increases traffic and pollution. 
In Sacramento, Don Chaddock, a longtime analyst for the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, wore a Santa costume and held a sign reading “Newsom + CalHR = Naughty List.” Chaddock, who volunteers as Santa during the holidays for rural schools in his foothills area, said he is frustrated by the state’s in-office policy, which has him commuting to a suburb south of Sacramento.
“I don’t mind in-person if we’re actually doing something in-person,” he said. “Right now, I drive to Elk Grove to sit in a cubicle.”
State workers represented by SEIU Local 1000 strike outside the CalHR building in Sacramento on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Rebecca Bean, another employee who is against the return-to-office mandate, put it even more bluntly: “We’re not asking for stupid sh—.”
Bean commutes three hours a day by public transportation to Oakland as an analyst at the industrial relations’ office. She said the policy has made it more difficult to take care of her ailing mother who is in her seventies.
“Every time she has an emergency, I have to run all the way home. She won’t go to any medical appointments without me,” Bean said. Before the policy took effect in July, Bean scheduled appointments at the end or beginning of the day and was out only a few hours.
“Whereas here I have to schedule at least four hours to do something,” she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Reeves awards $32 million in federal funds to develop healthcare workforce and psychiatric services
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Gov. Tate Reeves on Wednesday awarded $32 million for healthcare workforce development and psychiatric emergency services as a part of a federal program to improve rural healthcare.
The 60 awards will support earn-while-you-learn programs for healthcare workers, workforce recruitment efforts, clinical mentorship projects and bolster interest in healthcare careers among middle and high school students. 
“These projects address different healthcare professions, but they share a common goal: removing the training bottlenecks that limit how many qualified professionals we can prepare to serve Mississippi,” Reeves said at a Wednesday press conference. 
The funds will also help establish three therapeutic units at hospital emergency departments to improve crisis mental healthcare.
Reeves was flanked by State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney and Courtney Taylor, executive director of AccelerateMS, the state’s workforce development agency. Both agencies are collaborating with the governor’s office to distribute and oversee the funding awards. 
This is the second round of funding announced by Reeves as a part of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program. Mississippi was awarded nearly $206 million in December as a part of the national $50 billion program. States will receive payments over five years for initiatives designed to bolster rural healthcare and offset the disproportionate impact that federal spending cuts President Donald Trump signed into law in July 2025 are expected to have on rural hospitals.
In September, the governor announced 167 awards worth $104 million for projects aimed at helping rural providers make facility improvements, expand service offerings, upgrade technology systems, bolster cybersecurity defenses and increase telehealth capacity.
Nearly 400 applicants requested roughly $241 million in funding for the four workforce grants awarded. In total, state officials awarded roughly $19.2 million to these projects. 
Reeves said the programs will help to address Mississippi’s healthcare provider shortage. Programs he highlighted Wednesday include those to help licensed practical nurses become registered nurses while continuing to work, train experienced practitioners to mentor students and strengthen the rural pharmacy workforce. 
“We have Mississippians who want to work in healthcare, and we have communities that need healthcare professionals,” he said. “We’re bringing those two things together by making training more accessible, by helping people advance their careers and by building a workforce that can serve their own communities for years to come.”
University of Mississippi Medical Center Greenwood, Merit Health Central in Jackson and Memorial Hospital Gulfport will establish psychiatric emergency service units to expand access to specialized care for people experiencing mental health crises.
“Far too often, families in our state and others find themselves waiting in emergency rooms for far too long, before their loved ones receive appropriate psychiatric care,” said Reeves. “That’s really not the way it should be, and we’re going to work hard to change that.”
Applications are also open for small, rural providers to adopt or upgrade electronic health records, and for innovative pilot programs that aim to improve healthcare. The state is also seeking proposals for a statewide health information exchange to allow health care providers to securely share patient information and coordinate care.
“The frustrations of our rural providers in not having the patient information they need in real time will be eliminated,” Edney said. 
He said the exchange will also be a source of data that can help the Mississippi State Department of Health better understand health problems and propose solutions. 
Reeves previously said Mississippi has submitted its request for second-year funding as part of the Rural Health Transformation Program to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and expects to receive word by November on the amount of federal funding allocated to the state.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Judge dismisses last-ditch attempt to block Colorado graduated income tax ballot measure
text:
Canvassers in Denver received petition packets as they prepared to gather signatures in support of a graduated income tax measure that will appear on the Colorado ballot in November. Colorado is one of at least nine states that will decide whether to cut, cap or raise taxes this fall. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A judge in Denver has dismissed a last-minute attempt by conservative opponents of a graduated income tax proposal to invalidate the measure on the ballots already in Colorado voters’ hands.
In an 18-page order issued Wednesday, Judge Heidi L. Kutcher of the Denver District Court rejected opponents’ argument that votes on Amendment 87 shouldn’t be counted because of paperwork issues with some of the entities that circulated petitions for the measure. The failure by some circulators to comply with an administrative rule established by the Colorado secretary of state’s office, Kutcher said, doesn’t outweigh Coloradans’ “fundamental right” to the initiative process as enshrined in the state constitution.
“To invalidate a signature that is otherwise a valid Registered Elector’s signature because a paid circulator was not registered by a licensed Petition Entity or registered for a specific initiative would place significant restrictions on the Registered Electors’ right to participate in the initiative process,” Kutcher wrote.

Amendment 87, which would raise income taxes on the top 3% of Colorado earners and slightly cut them for everyone else, qualified for the ballot last month after the secretary of state’s office determined proponents had submitted 130,938 valid signatures, more than the required threshold of 124,238 valid signatures, including from at least 2% of the registered voters in each of Colorado’s 35 state Senate districts, as required for constitutional measures. A long list of Colorado progressive groups is backing the Amendment 87 campaign, which relied on a combination of volunteers and paid signature gatherers.
Represented by attorneys from the powerful law and lobbying firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, plaintiff Michael A. Hancock, a conservative activist from Arapahoe County, sued proponents and Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold on Sept. 16, seeking to have thousands of signatures invalidated and the measure barred from the 2026 ballot, which was already certified.
The lawsuit was initially based on the allegation that 69 of the measure’s petition circulators lacked a training certificate required by the secretary of state’s rules. After the secretary of state’s office provided “updated information” showing that 66 of those circulators had, in fact, received training, the plaintiff subsequently argued the signatures should still be invalidated because those 66 circulators hadn’t to compled with a secretary of state rule requiring entities circulating petitions to submit “a signed form that includes a list of the proposed initiatives … the petition entity will circulate.”
In her ruling, Kutcher noted testimony from secretary of state’s office employees that the form in question “primarily provides an additional data gathering tool,” rather than aiming to prevent fraud, and that the plaintiff had “not asserted any fraudulent conduct by any Petition Entity or Paid Circulator.” Invalidating signatures over the issue “would violate the supremacy of the constitutional provision for initiatives,” she wrote.
“We appreciate the Court’s careful consideration of this matter, and look forward to voters making their voices heard on this question,” Griswold said in a statement Wednesday. “My office will continue to uphold Colorado law and ensure Coloradans can cast their vote on any measure that is qualified to the ballot.”

title: Scott Twito of Yellowstone County will become interim US Attorney for Montana
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Scott Twito, Yellowstone County Attorney for 16 years, will be interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana.
Twito’s last day with the county will be Oct. 25, and he steps into the new role on Oct. 26, he said in a letter of resignation last week. The U.S. Attorney’s Office confirmed Twito was tapped for the role.
Typically, the U.S. Attorney General appoints interim U.S. Attorneys to serve for 120 days, and a district court may reappoint or appoint a new interim until a permanent U.S. Attorney is in place.
U.S. Attorneys are nominated by the president and confirmed by the U.S. Senate.
The U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana conducts federal prosecutions in this state including of white collar crimes and public corruption.
Former U.S. Attorney Kurt Alme, nominated by President Donald Trump, stepped down in March to run for the U.S. Senate.
The White House did not respond to an email about whether Trump plans to nominate Twito for the permanent post, and the press office did not answer when called.
Twito did not respond to an email or voicemails in time for this story.
His letter of resignation said he was leaving the county because “a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity presented itself to me.”
In the letter, Twito said he worked for Yellowstone County for nearly 30 years, and he tried to serve with humility, “aware that each day of my job I answered to the residents of this community.
“They were my supervisors,” Twito said. “I am proud of my service and forever grateful to those who helped me along the way.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: Utah, you have done this 3 times. Now help us stop it.
text:
The chair used for firing squad executions is shown in the execution chamber at the Utah State Correctional Facility. A judge has signed a death warrant to execute death row inmate Ralph Menzies on Sept. 5, 2025. (Courtesy of the Utah State Department of Corrections)Utah, you have done this three times since 1977.
Gary Gilmore. John Albert Taylor. Ronnie Lee Gardner. Five rifles. A chair. A hood. A white target pinned over the heart. Sandbags stacked behind the chair so the bullets would not ricochet off the cinderblock. For 48 years, every firing squad execution in America was yours.
You know what the rifle does because you let reporters watch. When you shot Gardner in 2010, his arm jerked back with the impact. His fist clenched. It let go. It clenched again. His hand kept moving for two minutes. Some of the witnesses wondered whether you would have to shoot him again. Blood gathered in his lap. When the reporters toured the room, it smelled of bleach. Four bullet holes sat in the paneling behind the chair, all within four inches. Your medical examiner photographed the body. His brother Randy keeps those photographs in a manila envelope.
You have not fired since. Taberon Honie died by pentobarbital in 2024. In 2004, you stopped letting new prisoners choose the rifle. In 2015, you wrote it back into law for the day the drugs run out. Last year, you signed a warrant to shoot Ralph Menzies, a man with dementia. Your own Supreme Court stopped it. He died last November. You could have closed the door.
The country walked through the door you left open. South Carolina shot three men in 2025. Idaho made the rifle its first choice. Indiana tried to adopt the firing squad earlier this year. On Dec. 3, at Fort Hood, the military plans to shoot Nidal Hasan: the first military firing squad since the second World War. President Donald Trump approved it. Hasan is paralyzed. He uses a wheelchair. Seven weeks from now, the military intends to shoot a man who cannot even stand up.
I do not write this to shame you. I write because you are the one state that already knows the cost of the bullet. Every execution comes wrapped in four promises: certainty, humanity, honesty and free choice. Other states believe them. You found out with your own rifles.
Certainty. You never trusted one gun. You needed five. Five gave you two minutes of a moving hand. In South Carolina last year, Mikal Mahdi’s lawyers said the bullets missed his heart. A state can write a protocol. It cannot make a body obey a bullet.
Humanity. You built the chair. You built the wall with the gunport. You know what the bleach is for. Your own Legislature took the choice off the table in 2004. Something in you has always known that there is nothing humane about shooting someone.
Honesty. You load one of the five rifles with a blank so no officer has to know he fired the shot. That blank is a confession. You knew the weight was too much for one man to carry. Washington is learning the same thing.
Free choice. Gilmore chose the rifle. Taylor chose it. Gardner chose it. Menzies chose it. The choice was never theirs. Horrific choices always birth a horrific choice.
Here is what I believe. A state has a conscience. Yours has been stirring since 2004. When you shot Gardner, the family of the man he killed, Michael Burdell, asked you not to. They said he would not have wanted it. Religious leaders from across your faiths said the same. In 2016, a Republican senator who once supported executions carried a repeal bill through your Senate. In 2018, another tried. Something is stirring within you.
Now, it is your turn to lead. You were the first state to kill after the U.S. Supreme Court let the killing resume. Be the state that ends it. Repeal the firing squad before another state joins the symphony of gunshots. Say to Idaho, to Indiana, to the military, to the president: We tried this. We have the pictures. We know that nothing was gained. Put the gun down.
Do not wait for another body. Do not wait for Nidal Hasan to be obliterated on Dec. 3. Lead us out of this moral insanity. The nation needs your help to put down the gun.

name: WyoFile
title: Three years after gas drillers caused a stir leasing a ‘Path of the Pronghorn’ bottleneck, it’s been protected
text:
When an oil and gas company bid $19 per acre to drill a pinchpoint where the Sublette Pronghorn Herd migrates across the New Fork River, the 2023 lease sale turned into one of the largest fights in Wyoming wildlife circles. 
At the time, pronghorn were recovering from a devastating winter and a long delay in the state designating the famous migration route left the river crossing bottleneck vulnerable to drilling and disruption. Adjacent ranchland used by the fleet-footed ungulates, meanwhile, was equally at risk: The state’s policy, permissive of development, has no teeth on private land. 

A rutting buck pronghorn herds his harem of does on Antelope Flats in Grand Teton National Park.  (Mark Gocke for WyoFile)

Wildlife advocates pulled out all the stops to safeguard the ancient crossing, even unsuccessfully bidding on a state oil and gas lease — a move that led to a change in state law, prohibiting them from trying it again. 
Three short years later, almost all of the acreage where New Fork-crossing pronghorn pass through the bottleneck has been protected. A combination of public and private actions — Wyoming eventually designated the migration corridor and a conservation easement enabled, in part, by an oil and gas company — should deter development for the long haul.
“This private parcel and this state parcel, to go from being so vulnerable to so secure, is just such a win,” said Kerry Schultz, who directs the Jackson Hole Land Trust’s Green River Valley Program. 
“It’s just so cool to me how this landowner stepped up and made the decision to exercise their property rights in such an interesting and beneficial way,” she added. “And state parcel 194 went from being really vulnerable and really at risk, and it has also turned around.” 
The private land
The private land part of the story concerns the Wild Horse Ranch, 233 acres of riverside pastureland that Daniel resident Mike Looney’s father bought in the 1970s with the intent of subdividing and selling. 
“That’s just how he operated,” Looney told WyoFile. “He had to do that to pay for it.” 
Some of that subdivision occurred, but Looney had a different plan for the land after inheriting it when his father passed away in the 1980s. The Sublette County construction worker is “all about the wildlife,” and he wanted to see the “beautiful little place down on the river” stay the way it was. 




The vast majority of Mike and Catherine Looney’s Wild Horse Ranch, outlined in orange center-right, are now protected in perpetuity by a conservation easement. Future development of the state parcel, in blue on the left, would also be inhibited by Wyoming’s migration policy. (Sublette County GIS screenshot)
A conservation easement was compelling for Looney, who’s near retirement, partly because of dollars and cents.
“The big motivator, to be honest with you, was the appraised value of the conservation easement,” he said. “It finally became pretty attractive.”
But there were major impediments. PureWest Energy, for one, has had a surface lease agreement with the Looney family since 2005 entitling the Denver-based natural gas producer to develop up to three well pads on the property. One already exists. To enroll the rest of the property in a conservation easement that would prohibit development for perpetuity, Looney and the Land Trust needed to convince PureWest to waive some of its development rights. 
“I was shocked that we got that pulled off,” Looney said. “It’s great that we did.” 
PureWest Energy’s vice president of land, Lindsay Dick, fielded the inquiry. She told Looney that she couldn’t make any promises but would look into his request.
“We were like, ‘OK, we have a pad on there currently,’” Dick told WyoFile. “We can make this work if and when we want to drill other wells.” 





The Wild Horse Ranch, in green, has a new conservation easement protecting all of its acreage except for an existing well pad and future home site. (Jackson Hole Land Trust)

Directional drilling, she said, would enable PureWest to get at gas deposits on the rest of the ranch without any additional disturbance on the surface, where the pronghorn pass over. 
“That’s the beauty of the technology,” Dick said. “We’ve come a long way since 2008.” 
The Looneys and Schultz, with PureWest Energy’s cooperation, were able to come to terms on a deal.
“I’m thrilled about it,” Dick said. 
Funds for the easement on the Looney’s Wild Horse Ranch came from the Jackson Hole Land Trust, Wyoming Wildlife and Natural Resource Trust, The WYldlife Fund and 10 other groups and partners. 
The permanent protections safeguard 1.3 miles of the New Fork River, 104 acres of wetlands and 60 acres of sage grouse core area. The entirety of the ranch is within the designated pronghorn migration route and the easement protects 169 of the 183 acres — 92% — within the private land portion of the corridor’s bottleneck. 
And the public land
The June designation of the Sublette Pronghorn corridor, culminating a quarter century of effort, also tilted circumstances in the migratory herd’s favor on federal and state land. 
The Office of State Lands and Investments and Wyoming Game and Fish Department tried unsuccessfully to add a special stipulation to the state parcel that caused a ruckus when Kirkwood Oil and Gas leased it in 2023. There hasn’t yet been any new development since. (The parcel is bisected by some development that is grandfathered in, such as Paradise Road and some Ultra Resources tanks.)
Existing development, including a battery of Ultra Resources tanks, are located on a section of school trust land where the state of Wyoming auctioned off an energy lease for $19 an acre. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
“These wells, especially exploratory wells, are supposed to cost $13, $14 million, and so it is not something that you typically do quickly,” said Steve Degenfelder, a landman for Casper-based Kirkwood Oil and Gas. 
Degenfelder didn’t want to speculate on what would happen in the next two years. Because Kirkwood acquired the parcel, No. 194, in 2023, the company has until 2028 before its 5-year lease expires. There are no firm plans to try to build a new well pad, but Degenfelder also didn’t preclude the possibility. 
“I don’t want to say we wouldn’t,” he said, “and I don’t want to say that we will.”  
The standard ungulate migration stipulation isn’t affixed to Parcel 194 because the lease predated the corridor’s designation. But that doesn’t mean that the state’s migration regulations won’t come into play. 
Kirkwood would still need to submit an “application to drill” to advance its play. That process is handled by the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission. If an application were to happen, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department would be consulted and the state would “apply appropriate stipulations” respecting the migration policy, said Joe Scott, the commission’s natural resources program manager.  
Scott quoted Wyoming’s migration policy in an email. It states: “New development within pre-existing oil and gas units inside bottlenecks should not be allowed.”
The bottleneck portion of the migration path on Parcel 194, in other words, would be off-limits to new development for Kirkwood Oil and Gas and any other company down the road. That’s not to say there couldn’t be any development at all. “Medium-use” and “high-use” portions of the migration corridor also fall within the leased state section. 
The New Fork bottleneck’s protections have caused conservationists to cherish the moment. Meghan Riley, Wyoming Outdoor Council’s wildlife program manager, said that the importance of the newly protected crossing cannot be understated. 
“Many of the pronghorn that survived the bad winter of 2022-23 were only able to do so because this bottleneck provided the lifeline they needed to flee south,” Riley told WyoFile in a text message. “Seeing this habitat shift from being pretty vulnerable a few years ago to having this level of protection today is, frankly, inspiring.”

name: VTDigger
title: Another approval, another appeal in long-running fight over private airstrip in Lincoln
text:
A 900-foot airstrip at the home of BETA founder Kyle Clark in Lincoln seen on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
LINCOLN — A controversial private airstrip got the stamp of approval from the Vermont Transportation Board this month in what could have been one of the final steps in a years-long process.
But two Lincoln residents are pushing back — as they have for years. 
Residents Marilyn Ganahl and Sarah Laird filed an appeal Monday to the Vermont Supreme Court, asking the body to review the Vermont Transportation Board’s approval of a personal landing strip on Beta Technologies CEO Kyle Clark’s property on Orchard Road North in Lincoln. 
“The Clarks are disappointed, but unsurprised by new attempts by a small group of opponents to sue, appeal and usurp the official processes to take away the Clarks’ rights to enjoy their private property as allowed by the town, state and FAA,” a spokesperson for the Clark family wrote Wednesday. 
The transportation board’s approval, dated Oct. 8, follows four years of opposition from Lincoln residents who are concerned about aesthetics, noise and safety, according to Ganahl and Laird’s lawyer Roy Goldberg. 
The airstrip opponents are also asking a federal circuit court to review the Federal Aviation Administration’s July 28 denial of an appeal they had submitted opposing a conditional determination the FAA granted Clark in June 2025, according to court documents. 
The determination concluded that the airstrip is safe to operate, so long as Clark abides by the agency’s specified conditions. The conditions limited the airstrip to daytime private use that doesn’t conflict with “neighboring flight paths, municipal structures, or existing visual flight rules,” according to the documents. 
The FAA’s appeal denial said that concerns raised by Ganahl and Laird were “assessed” in its 2025 determination, but Goldberg said he and his clients still believe that the FAA did not consider a safety assessment filed by national aviation consultant Lee Moak, which was submitted to the agency with the June appeal. 
Moak said in an interview Tuesday that his assessment observed the topography of the area and the 900-foot runway. He found that the runway “may be incompatible” with surrounding land and roads, and recommended nine further steps by the FAA before approval. 
“I pretty much have done all flying, and this particular runway, I wouldn’t fly into or out of,” Moak said, noting over 50 years of commercial, personal and military aviation experience. “It doesn’t mean somebody else couldn’t. But if you look at my report and the science behind it, you would understand it really comes down to safety.”
Ganahl and Laird are asking the Vermont Transportation Board not to grant Clark a certificate of operation while they await a decision from the state’s Supreme Court, according to a motion for stay filed Monday. 
The town zoning administrator initially approved Clark’s 2022 proposal, but Ganahl appealed it. The town’s zoning board of adjustment then denied the application following several public hearings. Lincoln’s Development Review Board also voted against the proposal in 2023. 
Clark then challenged the zoning board’s decision in Vermont’s environmental court, which approved the land-use portion of his application, referring noise, safety and public interest concerns to the FAA and the Vermont Transportation Board in 2025.
The FAA granted its conditional determination in June 2025.
The transportation board found that public hearings were not necessary, per state law, and used email communications from residents, including Ganahl, as public comment during its decision-making process, according to its Oct. 8 approval. 
The lack of a public hearing remains a concern for the project’s opponents.
“There’s a lot of interested parties,” Goldberg said. “Most have been completely, you know, closed off for getting their views provided.”
The Clark family’s spokesperson maintains that the landing strip is “a permissible use of their private land,” she wrote, which is why the family has found success “at every step of the way.” 
“Unfortunately, as long as Vermont land use laws allow for individuals and groups with unlimited time and financial resources opposed to a project to engage in endless appeals and lawsuits, this will continue on,” the spokesperson wrote.
The airstrip is not yet operational, as Clark still awaits a Certificate of Operation from the Transportation Board, Goldberg said. Clark must complete conditions set out by the FAA and Agency of Transportation before the board will award him the certificate. 
“For the sake of landowners across Vermont who have experienced similar opposition to legally permissible private land use, the Clarks hope there will be resolution soon,” the Clark family’s spokesperson wrote.
The Vermont Transportation Board declined to comment.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Vice President JD Vance of Ohio backs Vivek Ramaswamy amid attack ad blowback
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference at the White House on June 18, 2026. Vance is expected to travel to Lucerne, Switzerland, Friday for follow-up talks after President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an agreement to end the countries' war. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)Vice President JD Vance is backing Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy over an attack ad against Democratic opponent Amy Acton featuring her mother, estranged since a rape charge by Acton against her stepfather when she was a child. Vance said he is disgusted by other Republicans whining about it.
In a swing of his own home town Cincinnati Wednesday, Vance touted dozens of indictments for food assistance fraud and pumped up Ohio’s GOP supporters at a campaign rally. But the comments on the ad garnered the most attention. The ad has drawn sharp criticism across the political spectrum.
“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance told the campaign rally crowd.
Ramaswamy takes responsibility for controversial ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother

“Politics is a tough business,” he added, “and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is: if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.”
The attack ad controversy
In the ad, Acton’s mother Donna Arthur repeatedly calls Acton a liar. Acton was removed from Arthur’s custody in the late 1970s, after her husband Cledith Arthur was charged with raping Acton, who was 12 years old at the time. After being released on bond, the Arthurs fled the state.
Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign initially issued a statement insisting “Vivek wants the election to focus on how to solve (rising costs),” and called Acton a “serial fabulist” but didn’t take credit for the ad’s production. Later that day, Ramaswamy again said he would “love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues” but acknowledged his campaign produced the ad.
Ramaswamy’s campaign told Axios it plans to spend $4 million running it statewide.


Vivek Ramaswamy is not fit to lead. Watch our new ad. pic.twitter.com/EhWNMdFjjH
— Dr. Amy Acton (@amyactonoh) October 20, 2026


Acton’s campaign quickly released an ad featuring her younger brother Phil Stearns criticizing Ramaswamy for trying to score political points off the abuse they both suffered as children.
“Shame on Vivek,” he says, “It’s the contempt he has for Amy it’s the contempt he has for Ohio. He’s not fit to lead.”
In the Ramaswamy campaign’s initial statement and later speaking to reporters, he’s justified the ad by blaming Acton for refusing to debate him. Vance went a step further.
“People have called Vivek Ramaswamy a murderer in some of the advertisements ran against him,” Vance claimed at the food assistance fraud event.
It’s not clear to which advertisement Vance was referring, and an email to his press contact seeking clarification got no answer.
Ramasmway’s campaign didn’t respond to similar requests either. But on social media, Ramaswamy shared two clips of Vance making the claim describing it as “hard facts” and “a strong message to Republicans & a strong reminder to everyone.”
Advertisements produced by Acton’s campaign, and by the Democratic Governors Association Super PAC backing her, criticize Ramaswamy’s tenure as a pharmaceutical executive for publicly lauding an Alzheimer’s drug that eventually proved ineffective. But Ohio Capital Journal was unable to identify any ads which suggest Ramaswamy is a murderer.
Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother calls her liar in ad; court documents say otherwise

SNAP fraud
Wednesday morning, Vance joined several Department of Justice officials in Cincinnati to announce indictments against 40 people who have allegedly defrauded SNAP, the program formerly known as food stamps. Those defendants allegedly stole $42 million from the program.
The biggest share of that total came from charges against Jorag Yaseen and Rami Kanaan who allegedly stole $29.7 million from the program. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, they used stolen account information from Ohio and other states to run false transactions at their Illinois stores.
Vance, however focused on a case out of Atlanta against Merecedes Reshard New, who goes by Shawty Dred on social media. They brought out a tv to show a clip of Reshard with a private jet.
“You broke, mother——,” New says in the clip, “Get you a jet. Get you a jet.”
“The simple fact is,” Vance said, “this is a man that we have connected to $4.4 million dollars in fraud against the SNAP program. A guy who is quite literally taking food from the mouths of children, so that he can enrich himself.”
According to a DOJ press release, New was able to operate for six years and allegedly controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts. He was arrested last week.
“SNAP exists to help hungry children eat,” Vance said. “It does not exist to provide private jets to a guy like Shawty Dred.”
But while the administration is tackling fraud in the program it has also made significant changes that will lead to reduced payments, primarily in Ohio’s urban counties.
As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, states have to shoulder a greater share of the burden based on error rates.
In a July 2025 statement, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins praised the changes for “tackl(ing) the fraud and waste that has run rampant” in the program.
Ohio lawmakers agreed to cover some of the shortfall, but the way they chose to divvy up the dollars leaves multi-million dollar shortfalls in Cuyahoga, Franklin, and Hamilton counties.

title: New visitor center in Vicksburg breaks ground, highlighting area’s role in Civil War
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
VICKSBURG – Mississippi officials broke ground Wednesday on a $114 million Civil War museum and visitor center next to Vicksburg National Military Park, one day after President Donald Trump signed legislation clearing the way for a new facility that will recount one of the war’s most consequential military campaigns.
This combination of images, released Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, shows the planned development of a Vicksburg Civil War Visitor Center and Museum at the Vicksburg National Military Park. Credit: Courtesy of the Mississippi Department of Archives and History
The expansive new building, set on nearly 13 acres adjacent to the national park, already one of the state’s largest tourist attractions, is expected to be completed by 2030.
A study cited by project supporters estimates the visitor center will help draw an additional 200,000 visitors to the region, pump $231 million into the local economy and create 1,630 jobs during its first seven years.
“What you have here today is an opportunity to continue to expand the real story about who actually fought here and saved this country of ours, and ultimately put it back together,” U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson said during the groundbreaking.
Thompson, who introduced the Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act on March 16, 2026, said many Black Mississippians believe their stories have been overlooked at historic sites across the state. He expressed hope the Vicksburg center will be different by including exhibits that recognize Black soldiers who died during the war.
Historians consider the Siege of Vicksburg a key turning point in the Civil War. The Confederate surrender to Union Gen. Ulysses S. Grant on July 4, 1863, helped Union forces take control of the Mississippi River and effectively cleave the Confederacy into two.
The planned 60,000-square-foot facility will include a museum exploring Vicksburg’s history from the prewar era through the siege, Union occupation and Reconstruction.
The space will also feature an event space, gift shop and cafe. Outdoor areas, officials said, will be used for educational programming such as living history demonstrations.
Wednesday’s groundbreaking featured a rare bipartisan appearance between Thompson, Mississippi’s lone Democrat in Congress, and Republican U.S. Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is campaigning for reelection.
Wicker called the project a lesson about the “complicated history” in Mississippi and across the country.
“We’re here today as an exercise in bipartisanship,” Wicker said. “Today is a nod to persistence. This is a day to be remembered.”
The legislation signed into law Tuesday transfers a small piece of the park to the state of Mississippi, which has pledged at least $40 million to fund the visitor center and its operations, according to the state Department of Archives and History. The state will also be responsible for carving a road that connects the park to the new facility.
The state will own the new facility, with the National Park Service serving as its long-term tenant and interpretive partner, while the Friends of Vicksburg National Military Park and Campaign is leading private fundraising and marketing.
Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann, a Vicksburg native, helped secure the state money to get the project off the ground. He said his great, great grandfather fought for the Confederacy about half a mile from the patch of grass where the visitor center will be constructed.
“It’s fair to say the Hosemanns haven’t moved very far,” he said.
Spence Flatgard, who presides over the state archives and history board, said the visitor center will give ample space to “tell many, many stories.”
“Mississippi has the most compelling history of any state in America,” Flatgard said. “We’ve got it all. Civil War, civil rights, Native American history, birthplace of American music. We have a lot to be proud of.” 
The federal government established a national park in 1899 to commemorate the battle.
The new facility, which has been under design for the past three years, will modernize the park’s aging visitor center, which officials said was prone to flooding. 
Mississippi Today Senior Editor Bobby Caina Calvan contributed to this report.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘All of us have a role in prevention,’ health official says as South Dakota suicide numbers rise
text:
Material from a new suicide prevention toolkit says "Be strong enough to ask for help." South Dakota men are most at risk for suicide, especially American Indian men and people working within construction and manufacturing, according to a new report on suicides in the state. (Courtesy of South Dakota Behavioral Health)EDITOR’S NOTE: If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org. 
The number of South Dakotans who died by suicide increased to 214 in 2025, according to new state data.
That’s “the highest South Dakota has ever seen,” said Vanessa Barnes, assistant director of the department’s Division of Behavioral Health. It’s an 8% increase from 198 suicide deaths in 2024, and the rate of suicide deaths per 100,000 people also increased from 21.4 to 22.9.
Barnes presented some of the data virtually on Wednesday to members of the South Dakota Behavioral Health Advisory Council.
“Behind all of these numbers are real people, real families, real communities,” Barnes said. “So we do use these numbers as a reminder that we have a lot of work to do in the realm of prevention. All of us have a role in prevention.”

A chart from the 2026 Suicide Surveillance Report shows South Dakota’s recent data. (Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Health)

More than three-fourths of the 2025 suicide deaths were among men, and construction and manufacturing workers were the industries most at risk for suicide in the state, Barnes said.
In response, the division created a toolkit to target “blue collar workers,” Barnes said.
The toolkits include gun locks, flyers for break rooms and bathroom stalls, fact sheets, hard hat stickers promoting 988 — the national mental health and suicide crisis hotline — Spanish-language materials and information on Naloxone, which is a medication that reverses opioid overdoses.
The free toolkits can be ordered through the state behavioral health website.
Firearms were involved in nearly 60% of South Dakota suicide deaths in 2025, most commonly among white men. 
The American Indian suicide rate was 2.5 times higher than the suicide rate among white South Dakotans in 2025. Barnes said the updated 988 campaign will also feature Native American men. No toolkit specifically focused on Native Americans is currently available on the division’s website.
The division has also placed 115 signs promoting the 988 crisis hotline in parking lots at universities and healthcare facilities across the state, with 200 more planned in the coming months.

title: More Mississippi county health departments could lose clinical services
text:

As funding challenges persist, Mississippi health officials may cut clinical services at more county health departments. 
If taken, this step would continue changes the Mississippi State Department of Health made after the Legislature in 2023 denied the department’s request for $9 million to hire the nurses needed to fully staff county health departments and send nurses into the homes of low-income women with high-risk pregnancies. 
“Our goal is not to retreat from anywhere, just restructure and reorganize,” State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney told Board of Health members at a meeting Oct. 14. 
Greg Flynn, a spokesperson for the health department, told Mississippi Today on Monday he could not say which counties are being considered for changes because the adjustments are still a “work in progress.” 
Edney said several county health departments with nurses on staff are seeing patient volumes too low to sustain that level of care. Other clinics, he said, may be able to support a physician or nurse practitioner and be upgraded to a higher level of service. 
During legislative budget hearings earlier this month, the health department requested level funding from lawmakers for the upcoming fiscal year, the third consecutive year the agency has not asked for a major increase. 
County health departments currently offer three levels of care as part of a reorganization Edney previously called a “pathway for survival.” 

Level 3 clinics, or “super clinics,” have a doctor or nurse practitioner on staff and offer a full range of services.
Level 2 clinics have a nurse on staff and offer limited clinical services and telehealth appointments with providers. 
Level 1 clinics do not have a clinician on staff, but offer federal programming for women and children. They serve as “access points” to other locations and may host occasional immunization events with nurses.

County health departments’ levels are not listed on the department’s website. Mississippi Today published a map in 2025 of department levels.
Edney said it is less costly to transport patients to a higher-level clinic than to provide a full range of services in every county. He said the state agency aims to be strategic in its planning to ensure that patients are close to a level 2 or level 3 clinic. 
All of the counties operating at a lower level of service have federally qualified health center partners providing access to low-cost healthcare, Edney said. 
“Our job is filling gaps, closing access loops and partnering with our community partners, and not competing,” he said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: UPDATED: 2 individuals come forward in Valley County train shooting case
text:
A railroad train crossing sign is pictured on Aug. 12, 2025. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)After a BNSF train crew reported they had been shot at near Glasgow Tuesday night, two individuals have come forward, “identifying themselves as present during the incident,” according to the Valley County Sheriff’s Office, which is handling the investigation along with BNSF Police. 
Earlier on Wednesday the department said the train crew witnessed someone shoot at the locomotive they were operating and notified law enforcement. No one was injured, but a shell casing was found by officers at the scene as well as “additional evidence” that will be sent to the Montana Crime Lab, a Wednesday morning press release said. 
Prior to the shooting, train crews described a four-door pickup truck with overhead lighting illuminating their train with a spotlight.
According to the Sheriff’s Office, the train was stopped and crew members saw a muzzle flash and smoke.
“We can’t provide specific details, but we appreciate the sheriff’s office investigating this matter as a serious threat to the safety of our employees and the public,” BNSF spokesperson Kendall Sloan wrote in an email.
The two people who came forward have been cooperating with the authorities, the Valley County Sheriff’s Office said later Wednesday afternoon. 
“Both stated their actions were not malicious or criminal in nature,” a Wednesday afternoon release from Valley County stated.
The incident happened near the intersection of Tampico Road and North Tampico Road about 12 miles from Glasgow. A train line runs along Tampico Road, and BNSF has a facility in Glasgow.
Valley County Sheriff Tom Boyer said in an email whether the round was fired at the locomotive or a train car was still under investigation. When it’s dark, a muzzle flash can look like it’s “at you” Boyer wrote, and law enforcement is still investigating that question.
Additionally, Boyer said that while shooting at trains is not something that’s common in Valley County, it has been an issue elsewhere. 
“Historically, people have shot at train cars across the county. The number, volume and data on that is obscure,” Boyer wrote. “One of the reasons they stopped transporting ‘new cars’ open air and protected them with an enclosure was because people shot the windows out.”
Also, Boyer added in a press release that while law enforcement appreciates “those who care about the safety of our train crews” that the public needs to let the investigative process work as designed.
“The facts of this case are still being gathered, and every person involved is entitled to due process,” the Wednesday afternoon press release said. “Any threats directed at individuals connected to this incident are taken seriously and will be addressed by law enforcement.”


4:35 pmThis story has been updated to include information about two people who have turned themselves into Valley County authorities, saying they were present during the incident. The Valley County Sheriff's Office and BNSF Police are conducting investigations. The headline on this story was also updated to reflect the changes.

name: VTDigger
title: Budget cuts are hurting patients
text:
Dear Editor, 
We are practicing clinicians, trainees and recently retired doctors who serve on the Vermont Medical Society’s board and are deeply concerned about healthcare affordability and access in the state. Despite sharing these goals with state regulators and lawmakers, we believe many current strategies unwittingly threaten the very access they seek to improve. 
As hospitals are required to quickly and dramatically reduce costs without increasing income, they have limited tools to balance their budgets other than cutting staff and services. At the same time, clinicians across the state are being asked to see more patients, often with fewer supports and in shorter appointments. Access is not improved when services are shuttered and the workforce responsible for delivering care is stretched beyond its limits.
So, what can be done? First, acknowledging that any cost-cutting measures have repercussions, we ask the Legislature and Vermont’s primary hospital regulator, the Green Mountain Care Board, to closely monitor the impact of recent decisions on employee retention, patient outcomes and access to services. 
Second, we urge the board to work with hospitals to implement regulatory parameters that more directly address the cost of care, instead of relying so heavily on net patient revenue. This metric includes volume and cost, which restricts the amount of care hospitals can provide, even if there is a need for services. 
Finally, we ask the board to consider a multiyear budget process to give hospitals enough time to invest in operational improvements, rather than expecting significant cost reductions within a year. 
To illustrate some of the consequences of recent budget constraints on patient care and clinician well-being, we gathered input from our members working at over half of the state’s hospitals, including critical access and midsize hospitals, and the academic medical center. We submitted it in our recent letter to the Green Mountain Care Board. Over a dozen clinicians shared their experiences.
One physician reported discharging more patients who are struggling or unable to care for themselves at home but do not have an acute medical condition — patients the hospital would have historically kept. The physician said their hospital can no longer afford to be a safety net for people living on the margins, adding, “It increases the moral injury of delivering care.”
Multiple physicians shared examples where staffing reductions, caused by budget constraints, led to limited capacity to accept transfers for specialist care, procedures or critical care, and forced small hospitals to transfer patients far from home or out of state, putting rural patients at a disadvantage.
One hospital cut its team of social workers, who had connected patients with substance use disorder treatment, housing support and other community resources, and helped schedule follow-up appointments. One clinician said, “Now we have a packet of phone numbers that we give to patients.”
A surgeon at a critical access hospital said budget cuts have limited the hospital’s ability to hire support staff and backfill positions that help patients manage their care. Without these resources, “many patients will have worsening chronic conditions and likely higher ED (emergency department) visits and admissions,” they said. “This is not hyperbole. I see this with my patients.”
A primary care clinician recently retired from their practice five to 10 years early because of the movement away from value-based care and a lack of support staff, saying, “I gave up my patients of 30 years. … I am a casualty of the system.”

READ MORE

At another primary care office, the medical director said clinicians in their practice routinely see more than 20 patients in a day and expressed concern about shorter patient visits, saying, “Patients are already upset with less time with their PCP and take it out on us, which in turn detracts from actual patient care and erodes our ability to effectively manage it all.”
A physician described how the culture of their workplace has changed to focus on cost, to the exclusion of clinical care, saying, “I have been in meetings where we’ve talked about improving mortality, and I’ve been told we don’t have time to talk about that, we really just need to talk about how we’re going to meet our budget targets. And those are mortality and quality committees.” 
Dr. Naiim AliWinooski, Vt., and Chapel Hill, N.C.
And members of the Vermont Medical Society board: Dr. Lauren MacAfee, president-elect, obstetrics and gynecology; Dr. Kimberley Sampson, vice president, obstetrics and gynecology; Dr. Mark Fung, treasurer, pathology; Dr. Katie Marvin, past president, family medicine; Dr. Aida Avdic, internal medicine; Dr. Alexandra Bannach, pediatrics; Dr. Becca Bell, pediatrics; Sarah Bushweller, physician assistant, internal medicine; Dr. Alison Davis, emergency medicine; Dr. Trey Dobson, emergency medicine; Dr. Donald Dupuis, general surgery; Dr. Joshua Cole, emergency medicine; Dr. Lydia Grondin, anesthesiology; Dr. Brian Irwin, urology; Rainhan Kabir, medical student; Dr. Jessie Leyse, infectious disease; Dr. Julie Lin, dermatology; Ryan Marawala, medical student; Dr. Bryan Monier, orthopedics; Lee Morissette, physician assistant, emergency medicine; Dr. Katelin Morrissette, critical care; Dr. Keith Nagle, neurology; Dr. Simha Raaven, psychiatry; Dr. Tamara Rimash, otolaryngology; Dr. Elly Riser, internal medicine; Dr. Catherine Schneider, general surgery; Dr. Ryan Sexton, emergency medicine; Dr. Robert Tortolani, family medicine; and Dr. Norman Ward, family medicine.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico health councils seek recurring funds from lawmakers
text:
New Mexico health council officials urged lawmakers on Oct. 20, 2026, to provide recurring funds to sustain health councils’ public health efforts throughout the state. Above: Volunteers for the Rio Arriba Community Health Council's Food Action Team pack food into bags at a community center in Dixon on Feb. 22, 2025. (Photo courtesy of Rio Arriba Community Health Council)New Mexico health council officials this week asked state lawmakers for recurring funds ahead of the next legislative session in order to sustain community public health efforts throughout the state. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico’s county and tribal health councils, established by the Legislature, provide frontline health and coordination in communities spread throughout the state, particularly in rural areas. Currently, 33 county health councils and 10 tribal health councils operate across New Mexico.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the health councils served nearly 400,000 New Mexicans by providing masks and tests, Valeria Alarcón, executive director of New Mexico Alliance of Health Councils, told lawmakers on the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee on Tuesday. Health councils have stepped up with emergency responses to extreme weather events throughout the state as well.
“Whether it’s fires, heavy rains or floods, counties have relied on their health councils to support evacuations and to get necessary supplies to shelters,” Alarcón said. She added that health councils play an important role in New Mexico’s efforts to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure as well. 
But funding uncertainty hinders health councils’ efforts every year, Alarcón told Source NM. The health councils have had to secure one-time funding allocations every year since 2024, with the Legislature appropriating $4 million last legislative session. As a result, the councils also experience staffing instability. On average, she said, the councils experience a 20% turnover annually.
“People get nervous around January and February, like, ‘Am I going to have a job come July?’” she said.
State Rep. Jenifer Jones (R-Deming) said she understands the need for recurring funding and added the health councils do “great work” in her district by providing transportation for medical appointments and administering vaccines through the council’s mobile units. “Being unsure if you’re going to have a job affects everything you do, all the decisions you make,” she said.
Maryanne Miceli, secretary and treasurer for the Alliance of Health Councils, told lawmakers she works directly with New Mexicans facing substance use and mental health challenges, housing instability and barriers to healthcare. 
“I see firsthand how important community-based resources are. I also see what happens when those resources are unavailable,” Miceli said, adding that the state “cannot build healthier communities when the resources supporting them remain uncertain.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis City Council asks ICE, National Guard to leave
text:
Members of the Tennessee National Guard on Nov. 21, 2025, patrol Memphis as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Memphis City Council on Tuesday voted in favor of a nonbinding resolution calling for the removal of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Tennessee National Guard from the city. 
The resolution drew dozens of speakers who urged its adoption during a public comment period. It takes aim at the presence of hundreds of agents assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, a multi-agency law enforcement effort dispatched to Memphis via an executive order by President Trump last September. No member of the public spoke against the resolution.
The resolution said an Aug. 30 raid on a Memphis nightclub that resulted in the detention of more than 120 immigrants raised “concerns about due process and the impact of federal immigration enforcement on local communities, including the disruption and separation of Memphis families.”
The resolution also cited the deaths of six individuals “as a result of incidents involving Memphis Safe Task Force operations.” Four Black men were fatally shot by members of the task force over a two-month span earlier this year; two other individuals died in vehicle pursuits during task force enforcement activities. No member of the task force has been criminally charged in the deaths. 
Attorney General touts success of Trump task force in Memphis

“We’ve seen raids, we’ve seen disruption, we’ve seen scare tactics and we’ve seen killing by these parts of the task force,” Council member Michalyn Easter Thomas, a cosponsor of the resolution said. “It’s time for them to leave.”
The resolution, which carries no enforcement powers, stands in stark contrast to the praise national and state Republican leaders directed at the Memphis Safe Task Force last week. U.S. Attorney Todd Blanche credited the presence of task force members from state and federal agencies, which include the Tennessee Highway Patrol, Homeland Security, IRS and others, with bringing Memphis crime to a 25-year low.
Blanche said the task force would remain in the city “as long as it takes.”
The resolution approved Tuesday cites the Memphis Police Department reporting that crime in Memphis during the months before the task force deployment had already reached a 25-year low.
The resolution urges the city to partner with residents and community-based organizations to address “sustainable public safety strategies that reflect community priorities and needs,” echoing longstanding criticisms that the task force is focused on punitive policing rather than addressing root causes of crime, such as lack of economic opportunity.
The resolution was enacted with a 9-0 vote with one council member, Ford Canale, abstaining.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s ties to the transgender-rights mailer controversy in Texas
text:
Wyoming’s lax business regulations are helping to obscure the source of political mailers in Texas this week that have stirred significant controversy ahead of the midterm elections.
The pamphlets, which purport to come from a transgender rights organization, were mailed to families across Texas, where a highly competitive Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton will partly determine the balance of power in Congress, according to The Texas Tribune. 
Addressed to the “student” of the household, the mailers purport that parents need not be involved with a student’s transgender identity and include a section about emancipation, or when a minor becomes legally recognized as an adult. The messaging also implicates the Transgender Education Network of Texas — an advocacy group that says it has nothing to do with the mailers. 
According to the return address, the Texas Transgender Student Union is responsible for the mailers. State records, however, include no such business registered in Texas. Meanwhile, Wyoming filings show a company by that name registered here last month, where state law does not require businesses to disclose their members or managers. The Wyoming connection was first reported by a Texas Observer journalist. 
Democrats and others have criticized the pamphlets as an obvious ploy to rally conservative voters in a midterm election with Texas Democratic candidates polling stronger than they have in decades, The Texas Tribune reported. Republicans, meanwhile, have focused on support for transgender Texans as a sign that Democrats are out of touch with most Texas voters and described the information in the pamphlet as predatory.  
The Texas pamphlets are only the latest example of controversial political mailers to spring from the high degree of privacy provided by Wyoming’s business regulations. Because state law does not require a company to disclose its members or managers, it effectively allows the owner to remain anonymous to the public. The privacy that stems from Wyoming’s lax business regulation laws is sometimes referred to as the “Cowboy Cocktail.” One office building in Sheridan serves as the address for thousands of businesses — including the Texas Transgender Student Union.
In May, as WyoFile previously reported, a super PAC suspected of backing long-shot Democrats in Nebraska, Pennsylvania and Texas, thought to be easier targets for Republicans in November, relied on a newly formed Wyoming company for some of its $3 million in advertisements. 
Earlier this month, Republicans and undeclared voters in Alaska received mailers alleging their elections “are ripe for fraud” and encouraging them to leave most of their ranked-choice ballot blank, according to The Alaska Story. The mailers list a Cheyenne address and purport to be paid for by The Center for Honest Voting, a company registered in Wyoming on Oct. 6, according to state records. Otherwise, the source of the mailers is unknown to the public. 
In recent years, Wyoming lawmakers have focused their election reform efforts on how and when voters may cast their ballots, and paid less attention to campaign finance. However, the incoming Legislature is expected to turn more attention toward dark money, or political spending where the source of funds is not publicly disclosed.
