name: Kansas Reflector
title: Republicans attempt to tie Kansas Democrats to extremism with spurious claims at Trump rally
text:
U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann speaks ahead of President Donald Trump's rally Oct. 19, 2026, at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)PARK CITY — President Donald Trump’s campaign rally Monday in Kansas provided a platform for his misleading and hyperbolic claims, including the disputed assertion that protesters were being paid to interrupt him.
He also used an antisemitic slur to defend U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall.
Some of the Kansas Republicans who took the stage before Trump similarly used exaggerated or misleading claims while urging Republicans to vote in the Nov. 3 election.
Trump appeared in an arena outside Wichita alongside Marshall; Kansas U.S. Reps. Ron Estes, Tracey Mann and Derek Schmidt; Republican gubernatorial candidate and state Sen. Ty Masterson; Attorney General Kris Kobach, who is running for reelection; state Rep. Pat Proctor, who is running for Secretary of State; and Treasurer Steven Johnson, who is running for reelection and led the rally’s attendees in prayer.
Protesters interrupted Trump’s speech multiple times throughout. The first few outbursts elicited from Trump claims that the protesters were paid to be there.
“Oh, here’s another one. Listen to that one,” Trump said. “I can tell by the voice they get paid. They get paid.”
The Wichita Eagle reported 11 people were escorted from the arena through the night, and talked to several who disputed that they were paid.
While defending Marshall’s history of suing former patients — and in some cases having them arrested — for failing to pay medical debt during his time as an OB-GYN, Trump used an antisemitic slur to describe the backlash that ensued after the New York Times reported Marshall’s collection practices.
According to court records, Marshall sued more than 700 patients for varying amounts of medical debt, and roughly 80 of them were arrested as a result. Marshall charged some of his former patients 18% interest on their debts, which is higher than state statute permits without written agreement. 
“And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy. And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability. And he didn’t do it. He has a law firm that did it.”
“Shylock” is an insulting and contemptuous term for a Jewish person, derived from the name of a character from the William Shakespeare play “The Merchant of Venice.”
Trump said Marshall got “a bum rap.”
“So I don’t know if I should be saying it, but that’s the way it is, Roger. I have to tell it like it is. You got screwed with that stuff,” Trump said.
Trump also made derogatory remarks toward Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Michigan U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib. All three are Muslim.
 
Claiming socialist ties
The Trump rally came 15 days before Election Day, and Trump encouraged attendees to “please pretend I’m on the ballot.”
Republicans throughout the rally sought to tie Democrats to socialism, communism and extremism. Trump said at one point the Democrats’ agenda is “a plan to extinguish Western civilization.”
Mann, who represents Kansas’ 1st District, said the Democratic Socialists of America “has completely taken over the Democrat Party.” 
The DSA is a 100,000-member group that has endorsed fewer than 50 candidates this year in municipal, county, state and federal races. No one running for statewide or federal office in Kansas has been endorsed by the DSA. One candidate for state representative in southeast Kansas was endorsed by the DSA this year. 
In order to usher in Republican victories on Election Day, Mann said, “we need to tie every Democrat up and down the ballot to this insanity.”
Marshall said his Democratic opponent, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, who has never held public office, supported Obama-era open border policies and pushed for “benefits for illegals.” Hamilton held an appointed advisory council position under the Obama administration, which evaluated how best faith-based groups and community organizations could bolster social services and public policies across the U.S.
Marshall also said Hamilton was “the reason the Methodist church split.” Hamilton, who leads one of the largest United Methodist congregations in the country, has been a pastor for roughly 30 years. The United Methodist Church underwent a schism between 2019 and 2024 with more than 7,000 churches leaving because of their opposition to same-sex marriage and gay clergy. Hamilton’s church, Resurrection, remained a part of the United Methodist Church.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: After successive damaging ex-typhoons, Western Alaska considers future storms
text:
Alaska Air National Guard rescue personnel, assigned conduct a search and rescue mission in support of storm response operations over Western Alaska on Oct. 13, 2025., The villages of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok were evacuated in the aftermath of ex-Typhoon Halong, and other communities suffered damages as well. The region's residents worry more storms like ex-Typhoon Halong in 2025 and ex-Typhoon Merbok in 2022. (Photo provided by the Alaska AIr National Guard)A year after a Pacific storm largely destroyed villages in Alaska’s Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and prompted the biggest air evacuation in state history, people in the region are bracing for repeat occurrences.
Among them is Johnny Andrew Jr. of Kwigillingok, a Yup’ik village of about 400 people, most of whom were evacuated when the storm hit. Calling into a special radio program aired by Bethel-based public broadcasting station KYUK last week, Andrew said in the past, people assumed that massive storms like ex-Typhoon Halong would be rare, separated by several years.
That is no longer a safe assumption, said Andrew, who is one of the small number of residents still in Kwigillingok and trying to clean and restore the village.
“Our world is changing, so not the same as what it used to be back then,” he said in his call to KYUK.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Three years before Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and other Yukon-Kuskokwim villages were wracked by ex-Typhoon Halong, a previous storm, ex-Typhoon Merbok, slammed into Alaska. It affected almost all of Western Alaska, but its track was a little farther north, with particularly dire impacts to the Norton Sound and Bering Strait region,
Monica Price, a member of a Yup’ik dance group that performed at last week’s Indigenous Peoples Day celebration at Alaska Pacific University in Anchorage, said people around the region are worried.
“How do we prepare for something like this? Because if it’s not Kipnuk or Kwig, it’s going to be someplace else,” said Price, who is from Bethel. 
Ex-typhoon defined
The term “ex-typhoon” is specific to a type of Pacific storm. Although the official meteorological name may seem benign, ex-typhoons can be more consequential in certain circumstances than the typhoons that spawn them.
Typhoons are cyclones caused by heat and water evaporation. They become ex-typhoons when they leave the tropics — and when they do so, they expand dramatically.
Typhoons and hurricanes have very strong winds that are concentrated in relatively small geographic areas. Ex-typhoons tend to have winds with peak levels that are not quite as strong, but they are spread over much farther distances. While typhoons draw their energy from warm ocean waters, ex-typhoons get their energy from the differences in air temperatures in the atmospheric layers. The contrast between warm and cold air causes the transition to broad-ranging ex-typhoons.
 

Alaska Air National Guard rescue personnel conduct a search and rescue mission on Oct. 13, 2025, in support of storm response operations over Western Alaska.(Photo provided by the Alaska Air National Guard)
 

	Whether ex-typhoons will become more frequent or more powerful is a complicated question, said Brian Brettschneider, a climate scientist with the National Weather Service.
Ex-typhoons in the Pacific waters west of Alaska are actually plentiful, though the vast majority do not reach past the Aleutians to the Western Alaska mainland, much less cause damage there. In the last 50 to 75 years, there have probably been 100 former typhoons that have had an impact in Alaska, Brettschneider said.
Just this month, ex-Typhoon Choi-wan prompted an alert about higher winds and water levels in the Bering Strait’s Seward Peninsula.
“The disasters unleashed by ex-Typhoon Merbok in 2022 and ex-Typhoon Halong last year involved “a lot of moving parts,” Brettschneider said.
“You need a confluence of events to happen simultaneously to have a Halong or a Merbok to impact Alaska,” he said.
Those events converged for both of those two ex-typhoons, said Rick Thoman, a scientist with the Alaska Center for Climate Assessment and Preparation at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
In the case of Merbok, the typhoon formed far east of the normal spot, and was fueled by much-warmer-than-normal waters.
In the case of Halong, the ex-typhoon became especially strong before it slammed into Western Alaska. It took an unusual track, and as it moved, “everywhere was warmer than normal, and that increased the intensity,” Thoman said.
A changed environment
The statistical record does not show a pattern of an increasing number of fall storms or of increasing storm intensity, Thoman and Brettschneider said.
Researchers in the future might be able to look back and see a pattern that hasn’t emerged yet, Thoman said.
“The environment that these storms are occurring in is different,” he said.
Higher North Pacific temperatures that have persisted since about 2020, even discounting effects from El Niño cycles, he said.
Meanwhile, permafrost thaw has softened coasts and riverbanks, making them erode more easily. Permafrost thaw has also caused the ground to sink — at the same time that ocean levels are rising, adding volume to storm surges. Delayed sea ice formation leaves coastal areas more exposed to wave action.
 

Alaska Air National Guard rescue personnel conduct search and rescue operations over Kipnuk on Oct. 12, 2025, following ex-Typhoon Halong.(Photo provided by the Alaska Air National Guard)
 

	Those climate change effects make Western Alaska, including the Yukon-Kuskokwim region, more vulnerable to fall storm damage, whether from an ex-typhoon or from a more typical Bering Sea storm.
“What really matters is that we’re going to have more events that produce catastrophic damage,” Thoman said.
El Niño questions
This year, there is a curveball in the storm picture: an ultra-strong El Niño cycle, with record-high sea surface temperatures in the central Pacific Ocean and associated amplification of tropical Pacific storms.
Both Thoman and Brettschneider have been fielding frequent questions about what to expect this season in Alaska from El Niño.
It is hard to say whether this year’s El Niño will cause ramp up storm damage risks in Western Alaska because the cyclical phenomenon has some contradictory features, the scientists said.
During strong El Niños, tropical cyclones tend to be farther north and east, thus closer to Alaska, Brettschneider said. At the same time, there isn’t as much cold air coming from Siberia during a strong El Niño, meaning a lack of one of the ex-typhoon ingredients. The temperature and density difference between warm tropical air and colder continental air is the factor that will “supercharge” a decaying typhoon into a powerful ex-typhoon, he said.
For Thoman, who recently traveled to Bethel to participate in the KYUK call-in program and make other local presentations — including one specifically about El Niño — said worries about effects in that region are understandable.
“People are very sensitive to big storms,” he said. So when they read or hear about “the super-duper-duper El Niño, it’s perfectly reasonable to be like, ‘Well, how is this going to affect me? Do I have to be worried about yet another terrible storm?’”
 

Pollution response teams from the U.S. Coast Guard conduct post-storm assessments in Kipnuk on Oct. 22, 2025, after the community was impacted by severe flooding from ex-Typhoon Halong. Cleanup and recovery is expected to take years. (Photo by Petty Officer 1st Class Shannon Kearney/U.S. Coast Guard)
 

	Based on past history with strong El Niño cycles, Alaskans across the state can expect a warmer late fall and winter, with precipitation falling as rain rather than snow, according to Brettschneider’s analysis.
On the ground
Whatever the current season holds, big changes in the landscape in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region are already evident.
Burt Paul, one of the Kipnuk residents who has stayed in the damaged village of about 700 people to help with the cleanup and recovery work, said storm-driven mud and clumps of terrain remain spread widely.
“The surface of the land, it’s like a fresh crust on the land,” he said.
The region’s hydrology had changed, too, Paul said.
Major lakes have drained a lot of their water, leaving them shallow, difficult and probably worse for fish. “All summer, the level is low, like bathwater,” he said.
Chunks of land loosened by the ex-typhoon have also drastically altered river flows, he said. “Some rivers are so clogged with these patches of surface material, they’re unable to receive water,” he said.
For those still in the village, regular routines are now altered, as he described it. People who tried to use the rivers and lakes for traditional subsistence food-gathering ran into problems, he said, and usual practices may have to be adjusted in the future — for example, switching nets for hooks.
“We might have to change some strategies to fish,” he said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Despite earlier hesitation to campaign, DeSantis hosts event supporting Amendment 3
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking in Tampa on July 1, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Gov. Ron DeSantis for more than an hour Wednesday sat at a table with Miami leaders in front of TV cameras and advocated for the proposed constitutional amendment to increase homestead property tax exemptions.
In June, having spent months proposing some form of property tax reductions, the governor said he didn’t think he would campaign for the amendment.

If approved by 60% of the voters on Nov. 3, Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for all non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would create a process for the Florida Legislature to allow counties and cities to expand the exemption further, potentially eliminating all non-school homestead property taxes over time.

Now, with the election less than two weeks away, DeSantis assembled a group of locally elected Miami officials to talk in support of the amendment — reminiscent of the news conferences he hosted in advance of the 2024 election when he advocated against amendments to legalize recreational marijuana and enshrine the right to abortion in the Florida Constitution.
“You’re seeing a lot of local governments basically coming out of it and try to tell people that the sky is going to fall. ‘You’re not going to have any services, you can’t do this, it’s just the worst thing ever,’” DeSantis said at the event billed as a “roundtable” at the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office Wednesday. 
“And I really want to commend folks here who work in local government who are saying just the opposite. They’re saying, ‘We reject fear-mongering, we reject some of these fake narratives.’”
The governor insisted that local governments’ budgets have ballooned faster than population growth and inflation would justify.
DeSantis had said he likely would refrain from campaigning for the amendment, although still vote for it, in part because it wasn’t the version he’d asked for. The amendment was written by the House of Representatives and the Senate went along.
DeSantis won’t formally campaign for property tax amendment 

A University of North Florida poll released Wednesday found 50% of likely Florida voters would support the amendment, falling short of the 60% threshold required to pass it. 
A September UNF poll compared voters’ main concerns from 2022 to early 2025. Last year, “property insurance, specifically, has been consistently listed among voters’ top issues, along with housing costs and property taxes,” it reads. In 2022, “housing costs” were the top issue for 2% of surveyed voters.
“I wish we could snap our fingers and say next time you go to Publix you’re going to pay what you were paying back in 2019,” DeSantis said. “We don’t set those prices at the state level or any government level but this tax is one thing that we do control.”
DeSantis said he “would encourage” Floridians to vote against Amendment 1, which would increase the capacity of the state’s budget stabilization fund — a rainy day account.
Savings and avoided costs
Flanking DeSantis were Miami officials including Rep. Alex Rizo, a Republican running for Florida Senate, and Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz.
Senate President Ben Albritton says he’ll vote ‘no’ on property tax cuts

“Before asking taxpayers for more, we have a responsibility to examine what we are spending, what we are paying for, and where we can do better,” Cordero-Stutz said. 
Cordero-Stutz listed off more than $30 million in “savings and avoided costs” during her time as sheriff.
To the contrary, on Tuesday outgoing Senate President Ben Albritton issued a statement of opposition to Amendment 3 via social media accounts of the Florida Sheriffs Association, which also opposes the amendment, as do the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police and the Florida Association of Professional Firefighters. 
In June, Albritton celebrated when Senate voted to place the amendment on the ballot.
Opponents have warned that loss of tax revenue could put damaging pressure on local budgets for public safety and other community services. State economists estimate that, if passed, Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Dems eye the Yakima Valley legislative district as one to flip in WA. Turnout is the challenge.
text:
Just east of the Cascades, Washington’s Yakima Valley is at the center of a lengthy court battle over the region’s legislative boundaries. This year, the district is entering its second election since the it's map was redrawn and Latino voters became the majority. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard) 
Washington state’s 14th Legislative District is coming up on its second House election since a redistricting order put Latino voters in the majority. 
Democrats are vying to flip two of the district’s state House seats long held by Republicans, but low voter turnout could be a problem. 
Reps. Gloria Mendoza, R-Grandview, and Deb Manjarrez, R-Wapato, represent the district with both taking office in 2025. 
Mendoza, who serves as the assistant ranking minority member of the transportation committee, is facing off against Democrat Chelsea Dimas. Dimas is the daughter of farmworkers and serves on the state’s Commission on Hispanic Affairs. 
Manjarrez serves as the assistant ranking minority member of the housing committee. She’s running against Democrat Ezequiel Morfin, an electrician who’s advocated for farmworker protections for years. 
In the 2024 general election, the district had the lowest voter turnout in Washington with 56.5% of registered voters casting ballots. 
In 2023, U.S. District Court Judge Robert Lasnik ruled that Washington’s legislative map violated the federal Voting Rights Act by diluting Latino voting power in the Yakima Valley. A new map was adopted the following year creating a Latino-majority 14th District stretching from East Yakima to Pasco. It includes Wapato, Toppenish, Grainger and Sunnyside, as well as the Yakama Nation Reservation. 
Redistricting opened up an opportunity for Democratic candidates in the historically Republican-held district. But turning that possibility into electoral victories has proved challenging. 
Community organizers are trying to change that. 
Poder LatinX, a nonprofit organization, hosted events this election season to encourage voting and educate residents about district boundaries. In August, the group hosted a Poderosas Summit where local Latina leaders spoke about their experiences in politics and urged residents to turnout. Earlier this month, the League of Women Voters of Yakima County walked the 14th District’s boundary line and provided residents with information on how to vote. 
When the new map was adopted ahead of the 2024 election, it was “the first time in a long time, community-rooted candidates actually had a shot at flipping these districts blue,” said Sunnyside Mayor Vicky Frausto.
In October, the League of Women Voters of Yakima County walked the line where the 14th District’s boundary ends and provided community members with information on how to vote. (Photo courtesy of the League of Women Voters of Yakima County)
In the months leading up to that election, Democratic candidate Maria Beltran went door-to-door in the Lower Yakima Valley, campaigning for a seat in the state Senate. The first-time candidate said that canvassing turned into teaching voters how government works. Many people didn’t know what district they lived in nor who represented them, she said. 
“I came in with the aspiration of giving people hope,” Beltran said. “Folks like us can step up and run for office, and we could run strong campaigns.”
Beltran narrowly lost to her opponent, Sen. Curtis King, R-Yakima, by 1,219 votes, but it was the closest a Democrat had ever come to unseating King.
“Sometimes it is really challenging for elected officials to understand how we struggle,” Beltran said. “I’m a native Spanish speaker, and that’s what the campaign was about. It was about our future and what folks wanted to see.”
Progressive Democratic leaders say this year the political environment might work in their favor. Cuts to Medicaid and other social services by the federal government could motivate voters to turnout, they say. District 14 is among several that would have to flip to create a state Democratic legislative supermajority. 
“As Trump’s approval ratings continue to plummet and voters realize that Republican policies are making their lives harder, we have a great opportunity to build Democratic strength, organize new communities, and build support for the Democratic values and policies that will empower the Yakima Valley to thrive,” said Shasti Conrad, chair of Washington’s Democratic Party. 
Republicans aren’t buying it. 
“This idea that Lasnik’s gerrymander is suddenly going to work where it has already failed is wishful thinking,” said Jim Walsh, chair of Washington’s GOP. “I would say the chances of impeaching and disbarring Lasnik are probably greater than the chances of flipping the 14th.”
Dimas may be closing in. In 2024, she lost to Mendoza by around 3,000 votes. In this year’s primary, she took the lead for the first House position by 200 votes. 
In this year’s primary, Manjarrez led with 45% of votes while Morfin received 34% and Tony Sandoval, another Democrat, received nearly 20%. 
The legislators have outraised their Democratic opponents. Mendoza pulled in more than $164,000 while Dimas has raised $113,000 as of Oct. 21.
Manjarrez has outraised Morfin by more than $100,000. Morfin raised $57,000, while Manjarrez has over $194,000. 
Manjarrez said she’s not worried about the possibility of the district flipping. 
“If you look at the quality of the candidates in both Gloria and myself and how we represented the 14th, we’re very good representatives,” she said. 
It’s not guaranteed that the new legislative boundaries will stay in place. The redrawn map remains the subject of a lengthy legal battle. 
On Oct. 5, the U.S. Supreme Court accepted a legal challenge to Washington’s new boundaries, then remanded it to a lower court to determine if the 2024 redistricting complies with this year’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais that made it harder to challenge voting maps on the basis of race.
A decision will not affect this year’s election, but it could lead to the boundaries changing again before they’re next scheduled to be redrawn in 2031.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico hunting outfitters group says it ‘strongly rejects’ AG opinion that carveout is illegal
text:
The New Mexico Council of Outfitters and Guides in a social media post Oct. 19, 2026, said it disagrees with Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s determination that state policy reserving tags for hunters who contract with outfitters violates the state constitution. (Elk photo courtesy NM Department of Wildlife)A coalition of New Mexico professional outfitters earlier this week pushed back against a recent opinion from Attorney General Raúl Torrez that concludes a state policy reserving 10% of tags for hunters who contract with outfitters is unconstitutional.
The New Mexico Council of Outfitters and Guides issued a statement on social media Monday on behalf of professional outfitters, who regularly charge out-of-state hunters thousands of dollars for a guided hunting tour along with promises of better odds of bagging an elk, deer, bighorn sheep or other game.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The council said it “strongly rejects” Torrez’s opinion his office released earlier this month that determined the “outfitter set-aside” both violates the Public Trust Doctrine of the state constitution and also unfairly benefits wealthy, out-of-state sportsmen over local residents.
The group’s post says Torrez misinterpreted case law and relied too heavily on an interest group’s analysis, which found that nonresidents received more than 90% of the elk licenses the state issued to those who contracted with outfitters in the hunting season that ran between late 2022 and early 2023. 
“The opinion fundamentally misinterprets federal jurisprudence, conflates private market values with public draw allocations, and ignores the strict regulatory requirements New Mexico outfitters are required to meet,” the coalition wrote. “NMCOG calls on state leadership to reject this flawed advisory opinion and stand with the small businesses, rural communities, and working families that depend on New Mexico’s outdoor recreation.”
Kerrie Cox Romero, the council’s executive director, told Source NM on Wednesday that her board is “considering” whether to sue Torrez over the opinion and also intends to lobby the Legislature against adopting his recommendations at the upcoming session. 
She said Torrez’s conclusions, in addition to being based on faulty legal basis, ignore the impact outfitting has on rural economies and state revenues. The outfitting industry contributes millions of dollars through gross receipts tax, as well as fees to the Department of Wildlife and other payments to federal and state land management agencies like the United States Forest Service and State Land Office, she noted.
“It’s so tone deaf,” she said. “The outfitting industry is a core industry for rural New Mexico.”
John Blair, senior counsel and communications director for the New Mexico Department of Justice, did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Wednesday on the group’s criticism. 
While Torrez’s opinion is not binding, it came in response to a letter from 21 Democrats in the state Legislature who wrote they were concerned out-of-state hunters were buying their way into hunts for New Mexico game. Their letter came shortly after the Department of Wildlife announced results from its annual big game draw, which angered some New Mexico residents who didn’t receive a hunting tag. 
Lawmakers including state Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces) announced shortly after Torrez released his opinion that they would take up major reforms to the law governing the allocation of hunting tags at the next legislative session, which begins Jan. 19 and runs for 60 days.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Hemp businesses don’t have to destroy their stock after federal ban starts. They just can’t sell it.
text:
Mike Simpson, cofounder and director of marketing for Lovewell Farms in Hopkinton, displays the company's THC sparkling lemonade at the Broadway Street Fair in Newport on Oct. 10,  2026. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s hemp businesses can keep all of their intoxicating products after a new federal THC potency limit takes effect in less than two months — they just can’t sell them if Congress doesn’t change course.
An Oct. 8 bulletin from the state’s Cannabis Control Commission gives hemp businesses the option to quarantine existing inventory containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. These products are set to become illegal nationwide come Dec. 11. The policy was included in an email the commission sent to all 201 of the state’s hemp licensees on Oct. 9. 
“They are not permitted to be further processed, moved, distributed and/or be offered for sale unless explicitly authorized by the federal government and/or the Cannabis Control Commission,” the notice states. 
Hemp licensees will have to submit an inventory report to the commission by Dec. 4, according to the bulletin. After Dec. 11, hemp businesses cannot add or remove products from their quarantined inventory. They can request to destroy those products at any time, but the state’s Cannabis Office must supervise the destruction. Regulators may also conduct inspections and inventory audits.
State regulators warned the hemp industry in a Sept. 11 bulletin that products exceeding the new limit “must be removed” prior to the federal deadline or else they faced fines. 
The new federal potency limit was originally set to take effect Nov. 12, but lawmakers delayed the effective date one month as part of a short-term government funding bill signed by President Donald Trump in September.
Charon Rose, spokesperson for the Cannabis Control Commission, said state regulators updated the guidance to avoid forcing businesses to destroy inventory amid uncertainty over whether Congress might change course again before the deadline.
“We just want to be mindful,” Rose said in an interview Wednesday.
Some hemp growers and distributors objected to the commission’s September guidance, arguing the rules would force them to destroy products that complied with regulations adopted by the state in 2024.
The end is near for US hemp THC market. But uncertainty continues for Rhode Island growers.

Workers from Lovewell Farms, the state’s only outdoor hemp farm, repeatedly raised concerns with regulators, including at a Sept. 18 commission meeting where they suggested updating the state’s guidance. 
Mike Simpson, co-founder of Lovewell Farms, said the updated guidance, while helpful, ultimately does little to clarify what growers like him are supposed to do with their inventory.
“Essentially they say we’re allowed to grow, and none of that is going to be affected… but then I can’t sell any of it,” he said in an interview. “It really makes no sense.”
Craft Collective Homegrown, a Massachusetts-based beverage distributor and wholesaler, also challenged the September guidance in an Oct. 7 letter to the commission, advocating for businesses to hold on to high potency THC products for up to six months, with the inventory tracked and inspected and no sales permitted.
Adam Oliveri, CEO of Craft Collective Homegrown, called the commission’s latest guidance a “meaningful step forward” in preserving Rhode Island’s budding hemp industry, which generated $2.85 million in sales in 2025.
Oliveri and Simpson still questioned whether hemp businesses would need separate approval from the commission to resume testing, processing and selling quarantined products if federal law changes after Dec. 11.
Simpson also wanted to know whether the commission must update its own hemp regulations to align with the new federal definition, which would require a public comment period.
Rose said regulators are continuing to assess how evolving federal requirements could affect quarantined hemp products and the state’s existing regulations.
“Any changes to federal law or guidance could affect the requirements applicable to these products and the steps necessary for licensees to resume activities that are currently restricted,” she wrote in an email.

name: VTDigger
title: Essex failed to warn voters about a tax vote. Now the November result might not count.
text:
Poll workers await the next voters at the Essex Town polls on Town Meeting Day in March 2023. File photo by Auditi Guha/VTDigger

Essex residents will vote on whether to add new local taxes this November — but the matter is far from settled. 
A yes vote in a few days would need another sign-off by voters in March, due to a missed deadline for alerting the town. A no vote, on the other hand, means the measure fails.
“In this case, ignorance is not bliss,” Bruce Post, a former Essex selectboard member, wrote on a Front Porch Forum post which he shared with VTDigger. “It could end up costing you a lot of pennies.”
Essex is proposing that residents and visitors pay a penny more on every dollar of meals, drinks, rooms and retail sales, with half the money going to help lower property taxes. 
The math is the easy part. The harder question is whether voters will trust the town that put this on the ballot. 
The local option tax is proposed as a way to offset property taxes and generate revenue for the town. The taxes would add one penny per dollar to meals and alcohol, rooms or sales, with each component of the tax being voted on three separate ballot options. 
According to Vermont tax policy, 75% of all local option tax revenue goes directly to the municipality, while 25% goes to the state.
When residents of Essex received their ballots this year, there was a section on the ballot that listed three questions for local option tax implementation. But residents did not receive an official warning of the ballot measure from the city 30 to 40 days before the election, which is the time frame required by Vermont state law. 
The late notification was caused by an oversight among town officials, according to Shannon Jackson, chair of the Essex selectboard. They thought an official warning of the ballot measure would be included in the state elections notices, but they found out last Friday that the warning was not included.
The town immediately consulted legal experts, Jackson said, who advised the town to go forward with the vote.
Jackson said he was “disappointed” that the mistake occurred but emphasized it was not an intentional action. He added that he will be appearing on Town Meeting TV along with Duggan and Ethan Lawrence, the selectboard vice chair, at 5:25 p.m. on Wednesday to explain further.
“This was an honest mistake made by our town,” Jackson said. “And since it occurred, we have done everything possible to ensure transparency and honesty with the public to ensure that this vote can properly occur and be ratified should anything pass.”
Post, who was on the selectboard from 2009 to 2012, expressed in an interview with VTDigger his frustration with the selectboard, saying it had months before now that this issue could have been addressed. 
The taxes are hard to find on the ballot, Post wrote in a Front Porch Forum post, adding, “some people never turn the ballot over; others don’t even know they’re there.”
The late-stage warning leaves Essex residents in a tricky situation, very close to the upcoming election, Post said. In a conversation with a friend of his before the warning was issued, Post found that his friend had received his ballot but still had no idea that the local option taxes were part of the vote.
“And how many hundreds of ballots will already have been cast?” Post added.
The town of Essex issued a statement on Oct. 12, announcing the error and the town’s plan for proceeding. They decided with the advice of their legal counsel to go forward with the November vote, but emphasized that the vote will be non-binding until a second vote occurs at another town meeting, which is the procedure lined out in Vermont law for situations such as this one. If the vote fails this November, town manager Greg Duggan said, that will be the final vote.
“If any of the local option tax questions pass, we anticipate having the ratification vote(s) at Town Meeting in March 2027, and will ensure plenty of voter education happens prior to that vote,” the town’s statement said.
If the tax measures pass in November, a second vote will be held at a town meeting on March 2, according to Duggan. The vote will be decided on a simple majority, he added.
According to a FAQ sheet from the town of Essex, which analyzed revenue from 2025, the taxes could bring in over $1 million in net revenue. The total tax revenue generated in 2025 from meals sales added up to $136,634, while the revenue from alcohol sales added up to $15,962. The tax revenue from local retail sales added up to $1,006,489 and tax revenue from online retail and short-term rental sales added up to $251,622.
Once they subtracted the state’s share of the tax — which added up to $352,677 — the net proceeds were $1,058,030.
Rachael Lizotte, a travel agent in Essex, shared a Front Porch Forum post with VTDigger in which she argued that the tax could be a valuable source of revenue for the town.
“Essex — you’ve seen how this has gone in the past,” Lizotte said. “A vocal group of community members rallies together to take on an ‘issue campaign’ — and then the misinformation starts.”
“It’s often really really hard to keep up.”
Essex is in severe need of revenue, Lizotte wrote.
“There really is nothing left to cut — I’m sure we all feel this acutely in our own lives too,” Lizotte said. “But still things need to operate.”
Still, pennies add up, said Post, the former Essex selectboard member. He added that the town’s mistake served to erode his trust in town leadership. It was a serious misstep on a high-impact vote, he added, and town leadership, particularly the town manager, needed to be making sure things were in order.
In this case, Post said, the town failed to do so.
“So it leaves a bad taste in my mouth and the mouths of other people,” Post said.

name: VTDigger
title: Children who witness domestic violence are victims too
text:
This commentary is by Meghan Masterson, executive director of KidSafe Collaborative, and Lauren Porell, director of program services for Steps to End Domestic Violence, who are writing on behalf of the Chittenden County Children Exposed to Domestic Violence Committee.
Domestic and intimate partner violence doesn’t just affect the adults directly involved, as became tragically evident recently when a Burlington man was accused of killing his wife with a flashlight in front of three children. Nationally, an estimated 1 in 4 children live in a household where domestic violence is present sometime during their lifetime. In Vermont, a 2025 survey found that domestic violence was part of the reason 430 children were not safe in their homes. For 75% of those children and youth, domestic violence was identified as a factor that had prevented or was preventing them from returning to live with their parents.
Children who see, hear or live with violence between caregivers can be profoundly affected, even when they are not physically injured or directly targeted.  Children may experience fear, confusion, grief and the loss of their sense of safety. It impacts the very core of who they are and how they see the world.

READ MORE

Children depend on the adults around them for security and care. That is compromised when domestic violence is present. This reality reminds us that the impact extends beyond the immediate incident. They carry the sometimes invisible effects of what happened long after the immediate danger has passed and may experience ongoing fear, confusion and grief.
These experiences matter. The absence of physical injury does not mean the absence of harm.  During October, Domestic Violence Awareness Month, it is important to recognize and respond to the impacts on children too. Every child deserves to grow up in an environment where they feel safe. 
Children are not simply bystanders to domestic violence. They deserve to be believed and protected in the same way adult victims are. Their safety and well-being must be part of how we understand, prevent and respond to domestic and intimate partner violence. That requires awareness, collaboration and a shared commitment across our communities and the systems and organizations that support children and families. 
We must recognize children’s experiences, take their needs seriously and ensure the impact on them is never overlooked.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT to make healthcare subsidy available to childcare workers
text:
Connecticut officials on Wednesday announced that eligible staff in the early childhood sector can now apply for a subsidy toward health insurance plan premiums, a benefit connected to the ambitious endowment created to expand and make affordable the state’s childcare and preschool network.
The subsidy will provide educators and staff employed by licensed child care centers or operating licensed family child care homes with $1,000 to $1,200 annually toward insurance premiums for plans through the state’s healthcare insurance exchange, Access Health CT. An estimated 7,200 to 8,800 early childcare workers are eligible for the program.
Access Health enrollment will begin Friday and end on Jan. 15, 2027. Coverage starts after Jan. 1.
The $10 million in funding for the healthcare benefit will draw from the Early Childhood Education Endowment, which this year received a more than $400 million infusion. According to the Office of Early Childhood, the fund now contains $735.6 million.
To achieve its vision of affordable, accessible early childhood education, the state is trying to bolster and grow a workforce that’s currently struggling to stay in the profession at all, given low wages.
“We have known for years that our childcare system and especially our childcare educators and staff are really undervalued and that comes to bear when it comes to what their pay is and their benefits,” said Rep. Kate Farrar, D-West Hartford, at a press conference to announce the subsidy. “But our childcare system cannot work without dedicated workers like our childcare educators are, and unfortunately too many of them are not valued with the pay and benefits that they deserve, and that’s why through the endowment we continue to increase provider rates. But this insurance subsidy offers one other way that we can support our educators and staff to access the health insurance that they deserve.”
Sen. Ceci Maher, D-Wilton, said that the subsidy has been a long time coming for providers who are on the frontline of illness.
“Every cold, every flu, and they are on the floor with our children playing, taking care of them, feeding them. How can we not provide this care for them, when if they’re not available to take care our children we lose our entire work infrastructure?” Maher said. “This is so important that we roll this out, that we offer insurance, that we meet the promises that we made to our childcare providers across the state of Connecticut.”
Maria Amado, union president of the Family Childcare Council of Connecticut and owner of Green World Family Childcare Home in Hartford, also said that working in childcare is intrinsically tied to health challenges. 
“It is not fair to expect that, because of the work that we do — being prone to get sick — it should be part of our work and that we would need to financially destroy ourselves to be able to seek healthcare,” she said at the press conference. “Over the last 10 years as providers and educators, we have been fighting to obtain healthcare that is an affordable cost. And during those 10 years, we’ve received many excuses. There’s not enough money. Not this year. Just wait another. Wait your turn.”
The subsidy will provide up to $100 a month to subsidize health premiums. But officials say that it’s part of a bigger picture of supports.
Susan Rich-Bye, the director of legal and government affairs for Access Health CT, said that the benefit comes “at a really wonderful time” as a new state tax credit will also be helping some small business offer health insurance. That means some employees may simultaneously receive help from both programs, making the cost savings more significant.
“We encourage customers to take advantage of free enrollment help that we offer online, in person, and over the phone,” Rich-Bye said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Wasatch County sheriff offers to go on paid leave ahead of council vote on call for his resignation
text:
A portrait of Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby hangs in the sheriff's office in December 2021. (Photo by Adam Herbets/Utah Investigative Journalism Project)Embattled Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby sent a letter to County Council members Tuesday night offering to go on paid administrative leave until his term ends at the end of the year. 
The letter, obtained by Utah News Dispatch, came ahead of the Wasatch County Council’s 4 p.m. meeting Wednesday, when council members were expected to vote on a resolution calling for Rigby to resign before his current term ends in January. 
Rigby — and former Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds — were charged about a month ago with obstruction of justice in a case tied to the high-profile prosecution of Kouri Richins, the realtor convicted of poisoning her husband with a fentanyl-laced cocktail and then writing a children’s book about grief. 
2 Utah sheriffs are charged with obstruction in case tied to Kouri Richins prosecution 

Court records unsealed in Utah’s 3rd District Court earlier this month show Rigby and Edmunds were charged by grand jury on Sept. 24, a rare move in Utah. They have pleaded not guilty.
“It is with the best interests of the Wasatch County Sheriff’s Office and the citizens of Wasatch County foremost in my mind that I will step back from my day-to-day duties and take voluntary administrative leave while my case is pending,” Rigby wrote in the letter to the council. 
“My position on the charges has not changed and I will address them in court,” the sheriff added. “The work of protecting this community deserves the County’s full attention and I do not want my case to distract from it.”
The charges follow coverage of the investigation by the Utah Investigative Journalism Project for Utah News Dispatch, which reported that in January of this year, Rigby “allegedly presented an anonymous letter to Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates” containing severe allegations about a Summit County sheriff’s deputy. The specifics of those allegations have not been released.
That deputy, Eric Mainord, was challenging Rigby in the race for Wasatch County sheriff and was also a detective on the Richins case, the Utah Investigative Journalism Project reported. 
Rigby lost the June Republican primary election to Jeremy Hales, the county’s emergency manager. Mainord withdrew from the race before the primary. 
Wasatch County sheriff under criminal investigation for actions tied to Kouri Richins trial

Rigby’s offer to go on paid leave came the day before the Wasatch County Council was slated to consider a resolution that would have upped the pressure on him to resign from his position rather than continuing to serve in the role through the end of the year. 
The resolution notes that because of the felony charges against him, Rigby’s access to the Utah Criminal Justice Information System (a network used by the Utah Bureau of Criminal Identification that contains criminal records, driver’s licenses and other records) had been disabled, disqualifying him from accessing that information. 
The Wasatch County manager is also cited in the resolution as saying Rigby would have to be “100% escorted” around areas in the sheriff’s office that would have access to that network’s data and he’d “need to sign the visitor’s log any time he came in or out.” 
The resolution also notes that county officials suggested he work remotely to “mitigate the risk of UCJIS violations, and Sheriff Rigby has refused that suggestion.” Additionally, county officials “offered to pay out Sheriff Rigby for any compensation that he would accrue the remaining time of his term” if he resigned. 
Rigby refused that offer too, the resolution says. 
While also pointing to “at least 50 news articles” or social media posts about the charges against Rigby, the resolution expresses concern that the pending felony charges against him, “combined with the media coverage are hurting the public faith in the office, and negatively impact the Wasatch County Sheriff’s Office, even if Sheriff Rigby were to be found not guilty at some future date.” 
It’s possible that Rigby’s offer to go on paid leave could change the outcome of the council’s vote on the resolution later Wednesday, but that remains to be seen.  
“I believe voluntary administrative leave offers a measured path forward, with stability and continuity for the Office,” Rigby wrote in the letter. “I will work cooperatively with the County to make the transition a smooth one.”
This story is breaking and will be updated.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump ties NC Camp Lejeune settlements to GOP win, angering survivors
text:
An entry sign at North Carolina's Camp Lejeune. (Photo: https://www.marines.mil/)GREENVILLE, N.C. — President Donald Trump told a crowd of supporters Tuesday that his administration would direct the U.S. Department of Justice to settle remaining claims from veterans and family members sickened by contaminated drinking water at Camp Lejeune, but would do so only if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. 
“I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible and get it off the books and get it finished,” Trump said at the rally at the Pitt-Greenville Airport. 
“If we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said. “If we do win, you’re getting it.” 
This isn’t the first time Trump has tied the resolution of outstanding claims to the outcome of the upcoming midterm elections. He also tied outstanding Helene aid to a Republican win at a recent event in Gastonia, North Carolina, although he later said he was joking.
The Camp Lejeune Justice Act, enacted in 2022, established a process for people exposed to contaminated water at the Jacksonville base between 1953 and 1987 to seek compensation for resulting illnesses. 
Trump said his administration had delivered $1 billion in cash settlements to veterans and their families, most of whom he said were based in North Carolina. The Justice Department reported last month that it has already released more than $879 million in payouts through the claims process overall. 
However, that’s only a small part of the funding that’s been earmarked for survivors. The money has been the subject of a long-running legal battle between the federal government and survivors, who say it has been too slow to pay claims.
Jill Steen Dilgard lost her father to cancer, as well as an uncle and two cousins. All four served at Camp Lejeune. She began advocating for affected families in 2017, when she first learned about the contamination. 
She filed a claim with the government in August 2022, and has been waiting for a payment ever since. 
Dilgard told NC Newsline she was “furious and sickened” when she heard Trump’s remarks. She said the people affected by the contamination should never become part of a political fight. 
“I don’t care what side of the political aisle you come from,” she said. “ You’re making derogatory remarks toward people who went through a horrible, horrible experience and many still fight in that battle.”
She also said Trump could have done more in his first term to resolve the claims. 
“If he has all the authority he says he does to make this happen, why didn’t he do the right thing from the get-go?” she said. 
Federal study finds high rates of eight cancers in former Camp Lejeune troops, families, workers

Democratic Gov. Josh Stein also criticized Trump’s comments in a social media post Tuesday after the rally. 
“Real leaders fight for the people, not for power,” he said. “To condition doing the right thing by sick North Carolinians on who wins the election is foul.”
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, a Raleigh Democrat, has worked on legislation intended to address delays in the Camp Lejeune claims process. She said a backlog of claims in the federal court system has slowed the process.
Ross co-sponsored the bipartisan Ensuring Justice for Camp Lejeune Victims Act of 2025, which would update the 2022 law to help claimants receive timely payouts by capping attorney fees and speeding up when claims go to trial. But the bill hasn’t moved. 
“There are people dying before they get justice,” she told NC Newsline. 
Ross criticized Trump for promising to resolve claims if Republicans win Congress while the legislation is stalled. She said the issue should not depend on which party controls Congress. 
“It’s wrong, unethical and un-American,” she said. “If he had that power, why is he making sick and grieving families wait today?”
Trump also told supporters he wanted the settlements to go directly to the families affected at Camp Lejeune. 
“We don’t want to give any to the trial lawyers,” he said. “We want it to go to the families, not the lawyers.” 
It’s not clear whether that’s possible. But Dilgard said that doesn’t matter if the claims aren’t paid to the families at all. 
“How can you play political games with people’s lives?” she said. “It’s just not something you ever want to see or hear.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Supreme Court justices ask why they should upend voters’ will in candidacy dispute
text:
North Dakota Citizens Alliance Executive Director and law student Brandon Prichard, at left of center, speaks during oral arguments in front of the North Dakota Supreme Court via videoconference on Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo screenshot via North Dakota Supreme Court YouTube page)Justices of North Dakota’s Supreme Court appeared skeptical during arguments Wednesday over why they should overturn the will of the voters in a case that asks them to basically void the election results if any of four challenged Republican House nominees is elected this fall.
Three Republican officials are asking the court to declare the seats vacant and order them filled by appointment, a process that would favor the challengers. Two of them lost their primaries to three of the candidates they allege are ineligible due to primary petition errors they said Secretary of State Michael Howe’s office wrongly allowed to be corrected without the original signers’ consent.
Lawsuit challenges legality of 4 North Dakota legislative candidates

The challengers are District 25 GOP Chair Matt Evans, Rep. Jeff Hoverson, R-Minot, and District 7 GOP executive committee member Douglas Pearson. They are challenging the eligibility of candidates Blaine DesLauriers and Tim Mihalick of Minot-area District 3, Steve Sauter in Bismarck-area District 7 and Terry Goerger in Richland County’s District 25. Evans and Hoverson lost their primaries to Goerger, DesLauriers and Mihalick. 
The justices asked Citizens Alliance of North Dakota Executive Director and law student Brandon Prichard about the timing of the court case so close to the general election and what basis the court has to do what the challengers ask.
“There’s nothing in the North Dakota Constitution, North Dakota statutes or North Dakota decisional law that authorizes this extraordinary remedy that the petitioners are seeking,” Justice Mark Friese said. 
Prichard said the court should keep the candidates on the ballot but state they were improperly listed and, should they win, go to the process in state law for filling vacant legislative seats by appointment of the local legislative district party committee.
Friese said, “But our elections have, throughout the history of our state, been decided by votes of the voters, not local committees.” 
Voters can’t vote for someone who was “not properly listed on the ballot,” Prichard said. He cited a 2020 case of a House nominee who died about a month before the general election and subsequently won a seat that was ultimately filled by appointment of the district party.
“That gives the political party the final say if the candidates are invalid and the remedy as a matter of law would go back to that local Republican committee,” said Prichard, who was a Republican state lawmaker from 2022-2024.
Arguments set in court case challenging 4 North Dakota legislative candidates

Chief Justice Lisa Fair McEvers said the challengers knew about the issues for at least a couple of months before filing their court petition about a month after the general election filing deadline. She wondered why that shouldn’t be a reason for the court to deny the case. 
Prichard said there is still a way to “correct this without causing extreme burden,” and it took the challengers time to gather evidence and go through a process to petition the court. The challengers moved “as quickly as we possibly could” to bring the case, he said.
The chief justice asked why that same type of work could not have been done before the June 9 primary. 
“If you’re looking for some technical error of your opponent, you can look at any time, can you not?” McEvers said.
Prichard said the open records request that found the alleged errors was not a “gotcha” but an “information-gathering process.” The challengers did their best to bring their case in time, he added. 
North Dakota Solicitor General Phil Axt, arguing on behalf of the secretary of state, said what the challengers want the court to do is improper and unprecedented in the U.S. Presumably, the district parties would fill the vacant seats with the same people the voters rejected in June, he said. 
6 incumbent North Dakota lawmakers ousted in GOP primary

The court has long applied a rule that the will of the voters won’t be undone based on technicalities unless specific allegations arise, none of which the challengers have alleged, Axt said. 
Prichard cited laws requiring specific information from petition signers, including a complete residential address, and a 1970 court case he said means corrections are only valid if done or directed by the signer.
Signers could have given consent for petition corrections when they signed or when reached by phone sometime later, he said. And it’s reasonable that petition signers wanted their signatures counted and implicitly consented to additions to the forms, he said. 
“Even if the court concludes the secretary made errors in accepting any of these petitions, those errors, to the extent they were errors, provide no basis for undoing the will of the voters,” Axt said.
McEvers said the court took the case under advisement. It’s unclear when the court will act.
Justices Douglas Bahr and Jerod Tufte recused themselves from the case, replaced by former Justice William Neumann and former state district judge David Reich.
The case centers on a flash point in North Dakota’s dominant but divided Republican Party: how candidates get on the primary ballot, either with the GOP endorsement or by petition signatures. Ultraconservatives who control much of the party say candidates should be endorsed. Longtime and traditional Republicans have increasingly gathered petition signatures, arguing it’s better to let voters decide than party activists. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: WyoFile
title: Uinta County coroner arrested, accused of ‘systemic, multi-year fraudulent billing scheme’
text:
EVANSTON—State agents arrested Uinta County Coroner Greg Crandall on Wednesday and accused him of funneling more than $40,000 in public money into his private accounts while serving as both an elected official and funeral home operator.
Crandall appeared in an Evanston courtroom to face 11 charges — five felonies and six misdemeanors — tied to accusations of misconduct in his official duties. Crandall has been coroner since 2003 and is seeking reelection in two weeks. He denied the allegations during his first court appearance Wednesday.
Crandall, 66, faces up to 35 years in prison, $35,000 in fines or both if convicted of felony charges of aggregate theft, issuing a false certificate and three counts of making a false written statement to obtain property or credit, court documents show.
He also faces up to three years in jail, $13,500 in fines or both if convicted of misdemeanor charges of official misconduct; constructive possession of a controlled substance in pill or capsule form; issuing a false certificate; neglect of a ministerial officer to perform duty in a criminal case; confidentiality of reports, photos and recordings; and conflict of interest.
The investigation into Crandall and two deputy coroners began in April 2025 after the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation received a letter of request from Uinta County Attorney Loretta Howieson Kallas, who had “outlined severe operational and evidentiary failures,” according to Crandall’s arrest affidavit. As of press time, no charges had been filed against the deputy coroners.
The alleged misconduct occurred between July 2021 and September 2025. According to the affidavit, Crandall, while serving the dual roles of coroner and funeral home operator, “funneled $41,389.62 in public funds directly into his private business accounts.” Prosecutors also accused him of submitting an “officially altered death certificate containing statements he knew to be false or unverified.”
Authorities further allege he failed to protect and secure confidential coroner records and evidence such as prescription pills.
The aggregate theft charge, which combines several separate smaller thefts into a single felony charge, stems from a “systemic, multi-year fraudulent billing scheme executed by Coroner Crandall to deprive Uinta County of public funds exceeding $1,000 through deception, internal control bypasses and intentional rate manipulation,” the court document states.
Investigators pored over evidence, conducted interviews and performed a comprehensive audit of the Uinta County Clerk’s Office budget, expenditures and voucher records, including a 26-year review of Uinta County Board of County Commissioners meeting minutes. That review found that Crandall conducted county coroner business at Crandall Funeral Home “without any authorized lease, rental agreement, fee schedule or formal board resolution,” according to the affidavit.
The filings come more than three months after Crandall’s political opponent in the primary election and son-in-law, Allen Kopp, publicly stated during a candidate forum that “what has happened in the coroner’s office, for years, is criminal.”
Kopp purchased Crandall Funeral Home from his father-in-law in 2024.
“We need some transparency,” Kopp said during the July 9 forum. “I removed the coroner’s office from my building for a number of reasons.”
Circuit Court Judge Thayne Peterson referenced the election during Crandall’s court appearance on Wednesday.
“I understand we’re 12 days away from an election in which your name is on the ballot,” Peterson said during an expedited court appearance shortly after Crandall’s arrest that morning. Peterson read Crandall his constitutional rights and outlined the charges against him.
“I understand the elements,” Crandall said of several of the charges. “I adamantly deny it.”
Crandall, who appeared via video, told the judge that due to an “adversarial” relationship with Kopp, he “depended on [my] deputies to take care of stuff,” and he is now “accused of neglect for trying to cooperate.”
Peterson deviated from the $5,000 cash bond recommendation presented by Fremont County Attorney Micah Wyatt, who is serving as special prosecutor in the case, and set a $10,000 personal recognizance bond for Crandall. That means Crandall won’t have to put up any money to get out of jail ahead of court proceedings.
A preliminary hearing for Crandall is scheduled for Oct. 30. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
