name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Judge grants protections to Bloomington man confronted over ‘86 Todd Rokita’ post
text:
A federal judge granted preliminary protections to a Bloomington man who was warned he could be indicted over an “86 Todd Rokita” Facebook comment. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A federal judge ordered preliminary protections Tuesday for a Bloomington man who was confronted at his home by an investigator for Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita over an “86 Todd Rokita” Facebook comment.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker found Lee Lawmaster likely to succeed on his claim that investigations director Kurt Spivey used his government authority to coerce him into silence by warning he could be indicted.
The Oct. 20 order grants Lawmaster’s request for a preliminary injunction and rejects Spivey’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana.
The injunction is narrow — prohibiting Spivey from coercing or threatening Lawmaster with legal sanctions intended to suppress or punish his past and future social media posts containing “86” or related political rhetoric.
Story continues below.
59880afd-f308-4a51-acc7-2253d1bb030b
 
Spivey’s home visit came May 1 after Lawmaster posted the comment on Rokita’s official Facebook page. Lawmaster said his posts expressed opposition to elected officials and solidarity with former FBI Director James Comey following his indictment over a social media image depicting “8647.”
Lawmaster maintained that “86” meant removing officials from office.

During the encounter — captured by Lawmaster’s home security camera and Spivey’s audio recorder — Spivey displayed a badge and warned the Bloomington man he could face indictment.

“Listen, if Comey was indicted, we could easily indict you over this today,” Spivey said, according to court documents. “Now, hopefully, we don’t have to come back? Cool?”
Spivey offered to “let this one slide” if Lawmaster agreed to “tone it down a little bit.” Lawmaster subsequently stopped posting “86” comments, curtailed his political commentary and made his personal blog inaccessible to the public.
In court filings, Spivey characterized the encounter as a courteous threat assessment during which he affirmed Lawmaster’s speech rights and closed the matter. He also argued an injunction would hinder the office’s ability to assess threats against elected officials.
Barker rejected those arguments, however, saying Spivey likely used the investigation to silence Lawmaster by “threatening the imposition of legal sanctions unless there was compliance with his demands.”
“Thus, that the parties’ interaction was by both accounts relatively polite and civil does not detract from the conclusion that Director Spivey coerced Mr. Lawmaster by stating that if Mr. Lawmaster ceased posting his ‘86’ comments, Director Spivey would ignore the ‘easily indict[able]’ incident altogether,” Barker wrote. “That is coercion by any reasonable measure.”
The judge also rejected Spivey’s immunity defense, allowing Lawmaster’s damages claim against him personally to proceed.
The ruling grants preliminary relief only while the lawsuit continues.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma board plans revote on Jewish charter school
text:
The Statewide Charter School Board meets Oct. 12 at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — An Oklahoma state board has scheduled an uncommon third vote on a first-in-the-nation Jewish charter school.
The Statewide Charter School Board will meet at noon Friday at the state Capitol to reconsider Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School’s application to open, according to a meeting agenda released Wednesday. Ben Gamla applied to become the first state-funded religious charter school in the country.
The school failed to earn board approval last week in a 4-3 vote. It fell one vote short of the five needed to pass. One member of the nine-seat board was absent, and another position is vacant.
“The rule for the board is that they have to have five votes for any final action,” the board’s attorney A.J. Ferate said. “There was no final action in a 4-3 vote either way. The function is that the board will make another attempt to meet five votes one way or the other at its meeting.”
Oklahoma law requires “an affirmative vote of at least five members” for the board to take any final action.
Ben Gamla would operate as an online school teaching both Jewish religious beliefs and secular school subjects.
“We are hopeful that the board’s reconsideration will result in approval of our application,” said Brett Farley, a member of Ben Gamla’s founding group.
Ben Gamla Charter Schools founder and former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, right, speaks with Brett Farley, executive director of the Catholic Conference of Oklahoma, left, before a Jan. 12 meeting of the Statewide Charter School Board in Oklahoma City. The board considered an application from Deutsch and Farley to found an online Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Taking a third vote on a charter application is unusual.
State law outlines a two-vote process for reviewing applications for new online charter schools. If rejected by the board after an initial review, the application can be revised and submitted within 30 days for reconsideration. 
Typically, the second rejection is considered final. The board’s chairperson, Brian Shellem, initially told reporters Ben Gamla’s second vote was no different, and the school’s founders would have to submit a new application to be reconsidered.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond came to the same conclusion that the school was rejected and “any new application from Ben Gamla would have to start over and could only apply to a later school year,” according to a statement from his office last week.
But, the process for Ben Gamla has been anything but typical.
The state board first voted in March to reject the school, whose founders then sued in Oklahoma City federal court. The board backed Ben Gamla’s legal case, as it did for a prior attempt to open a Catholic charter school in the state. That previous effort failed before the Oklahoma Supreme Court and U.S. Supreme Court.
A federal district judge ruled in Ben Gamla’s favor in September, deciding a charter school cannot be denied solely because of its religious character.
That prompted a second board vote last week on Ben Gamla’s application, but it lacked the support it needed to pass.
Friday’s meeting agenda includes not only a revote but also a potential appeal of the federal court decision, which Ben Gamla founders reportedly have demanded to resolve the conflicting judicial rulings.
Board member William Pearson, one of three who voted against the school, said the vocal opposition from Oklahoma’s Jewish community against Ben Gamla weighed heavily in his decision.
Although the school’s application projected hundreds of students to enroll in its first year, Ben Gamla’s leading founder, former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, of Florida, told local Jewish leaders that he expects only 10 students in year one.
Shellem, who leads the state board, called Ben Gamla’s application “strong and thorough” and said it “would have been a great addition to our charter school network” by giving more families a quality educational option.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Startup proposes massive nuclear power plant campus in Lewis County
text:
A rendering of the proposed nuclear power plant units in Lewis County, Kentucky. (Courtesy the Nuclear Company)A Lexington-based nuclear energy startup is proposing to build a massive nuclear power plant complex along the Ohio River in Lewis County, which, if fully realized, would be the largest nuclear power plant site in the country and the first nuclear power plant in Kentucky.
In a Wednesday press release, the Nuclear Company stated it is proposing to build six Westinghouse AP1000 reactors along Lewis County land next to the Ohio River owned by Sam Howard, the CEO of Trace Creek Construction in Vanceburg that is partnering on the proposal. 
The six nuclear power plant units, the entire campus called “Prosperity One”, could generate a combined 6.6 gigawatts of electricity; for comparison, Kentucky’s largest electric utility’s entire power plant fleet can generate more than 7.2 gigawatts of electricity. 
In a provided statement, the company’s chief nuclear officer Joe Klecha said that communities along the Ohio River have formed America’s industrial backbone.” 
“We are proud to partner with the community to apply our team’s collective experience to deliver lasting jobs, a stronger tax base, and reliable power for Kentucky.”
The release states the project “answers President Trump’s call to accelerate American energy production and represents a major step toward restoring America’s ability to build nuclear power at scale.” 
The company is beginning “site development activities”, including geotechnical and environmental assessments and electricity transmission planning and is seeking federal approvals to begin site construction by 2028, according to the release. 
The startup launched in 2023 to speed up the deployment of nuclear power plants that have been stymied by years-long permitting delays and cost overruns. The last two nuclear reactors built in the United States — located at the Alvin W. Vogtle Generating Station in Georgia becoming operational in 2023 and 2024 — saw seven years of delays and $17 billion in overbudgeted costs, according to the Associated Press. Klecha held “construction and operational readiness leadership roles” for those two nuclear reactors, according to the Nuclear Company release. 
The Nuclear Company’s CEO is Jonathan Webb, who was also the CEO of the former Eastern Kentucky greenhouse produce startup AppHarvest. In 2023, the nonprofit newsroom Grist reported that Webb was fired after the company faced mounting revenue losses, with the company filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The online newsroom also reported former AppHarvest employees said they worked in unsafe conditions and had little training for their greenhouse operations. 
Joseph Billman, the mayor of the Lewis County seat of Vanceberg, told the Lantern he believed the project would “do nothing but help the economy and help our town grow.” 
“This will not only bring jobs. It will bring people here,” Billman said. “It’s going to do nothing but grow the economy for Vanceburg and Lewis County.” 
During an Oct. 10 special meeting, the Vanceburg city council passed a resolution as a final step for the county to submit an application for the county to be designated as a “nuclear ready community” through the Kentucky Nuclear Energy Development Authority. The GOP-controlled Kentucky legislature created the application process for the designation as part of encouraging local education and awareness of nuclear power and the energy industry. The application process included educational public forums on nuclear energy held in Lewis County earlier this summer. 
Kevin Cornette, the executive director of the Buffalo Trace Area Development District, told the Lantern that community leaders had sought the “nuclear ready” designation because of interest shown by developers looking at land along the Ohio River, mentioning proposed gas-fired power and hyperscale data center developments taking place across the river in Ohio. 
Cornette said his area development district was not aware of the Nuclear Company’s power plant proposal when community leaders began to seek the certification earlier this year. Billman said he was personally not aware of the Nuclear Company’s proposal before the Wednesday announcement. 
Some local residents are expressing concerns about the pace of the proposal’s development, safety concerns surrounding nuclear power generation, and whether the public should have been notified of the power plant proposal sooner. 
Carey Highfield, a Lewis County resident who lives on land miles away from the proposed site, said he was concerned about the proposed project being near local schools. 
The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires emergency planning zones to have safety planning around a nuclear power plant “if extremely unlikely events unfold.” Accidents at nuclear power plants are generally very rare, according to the World Nuclear Association, a nonprofit representing the global nuclear energy industry. Earlier this month, federal authorities renewed the certification for the design of the power plant units being proposed in Lewis County, the same units used at the new reactors in Georgia.
Vanceberg city council member Richard Walje was the only vote against the resolution for the “nuclear ready” designation application. Walje told the Lantern he believes the public hasn’t had adequate time to understand and debate the potential of nuclear energy in the community.
“I think most of the county doesn’t realize it’s happening at all,” Walje said about the power plant proposal. “It needs to be slowed drastically, in my view, and the counterargument needs to be heard.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: McMorrow says fake polling ‘experiment’ hurt campaign, eroded voter trust
text:
Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow participates in a U.S. Senate candidate debate during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Wedgewood Polls was among several firms that released data during the 2026 Democratic primary race for the U.S. Senate showing state Sen. Mallory McMorrow trailing her opponents by a wide margin and Abdul El-Sayed — the eventual nominee — well ahead of his chief rival, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham. But Wedgewood now says the poll’s data was fake and was an “experiment” designed to be a “wake-up call” to voters about the vulnerabilities of modern polling.
Wedgewood made the admission after election analysis website FiftyPlusOne said Tuesday that it had launched an investigation into how the firm had conducted their survey research.
A poll released by Wedgewood Polls on June 24 showed El-Sayed ahead of the pact by 46%, Stevens at 39% and McMorrow with a low 9% potential vote share. That same poll showed McMorrow as the only candidate unable to beat Republican nominee Mike Rogers in the fall.
McMorrow, who eventually bowed out of the primary race July 5, addressed the controversy on X Tuesday, saying that the Wedgewood “experiment” had a real impact on her campaign and its endgame decision to leave the race.
“Donations dried up. Volunteers were devastated and pleading for guidance on what to do,” McMorrow wrote. “Reporters hounded me with calls to drop out. Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken. But tens of thousands of people poured their hearts, time, energy, hard-earned money into something they believed in — for a year-and-a-half, and it was treated like a game. Our volunteers gave their all. And then some. I felt like I had let so many of them down.”
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, left, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, center, and former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, right, participate in a U.S. Senate candidate debate during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
For its part, Wedgewood Polls said its fake polling was “to test whether media outlets, aggregators, and commentators would report on data without verifying the source, methodology, or underlying firm legitimacy.”
“Despite having no history, formal credentials, or real data behind the vast majority of our releases, Wedgewood Polls was added to major polling aggregators, including The New York Times, FiftyPlusOne and VoteHub, and repeatedly treated as a legitimate data source,” the firm said in a news release.
FiftyPlusOne wrote that Wedgewood did not respond to a request for information, and followed up with its public statement instead, adding that any assertion that the aggregator hadn’t vetted the polling firm before was false.
“We reached out to them to ask who they were and confirm the methodology statement on their website. We were given two names, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater.” the blog post said. “We were able to independently confirm that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry and reviewed their methodology statement in detail. It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different. Wedgewood operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm, including collecting money from donors to conduct crowd-funded polls, and sharing raw survey data (which we now have confirmed was fraudulent) with FiftyPlusOne on Oct. 15, 2026.”
In making her statement Tuesday, McMorrow said she wanted to be clear that commenting on the controversy was in no way meant to detract from her support of El-Sayed and that “Michigan Democrats are locked in to beat Mike Rogers. We WILL send @AbdulElSayed to the US Senate.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“But between crap like this, endless fundraising texts that drive supporters away with spammy fake deadlines and trash ‘match’ claims, scam PACs run rampant for firms to grift without actually supporting candidates, undisclosed content creators pushing content out either misrepresenting themselves as residents of states they don’t live in or hiding whether they were paid and by who so they could make a buck, and the tidal wave of dark money ads – I hope Democrats are ready to blow up the system with campaign finance and transparency reforms,” McMorrow wrote.
She added that “trust is already at an all-time low.”
“We don’t get out of this mess without rebuilding trust,” McMorrow wrote. “And media — who loves to ride the drama of a pollercoaster — needs to take a hard look at what’s legitimate and what’s not. If this teaches us anything — don’t get complacent and don’t trust the polls. 
McMorrow also touched on the fact that another polling firm, Mitchell Research and Communications Inc., also had her in single districts during the primary.
The senator from Royal Oak said “that poll was bull**it — and our team proved it.”
“It was an open SurveyMonkey link that people were able to send around to friends and take multiple times. We expended a lot of capital (and took a serious risk) – calling it out as bull**it. MIRS ultimately declined to publish it because of shoddy methodology,” McMorrow wrote. “But then this one hit immediately after. It was a one-two punch. Then all of the sudden it was a pattern –- and people believed it had to be true. It killed us.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri media organizations sue highway patrol over redacted crash reports
text:
(Getty Images)Four media organizations, including the Missouri Broadcasters Association and the Missouri Press Association, have filed a lawsuit against the Missouri State Highway Patrol alleging the patrol’s redacted crash reports violate the state’s open records law.
The MBA and MPA, alongside Gray Media and Warden Publishing Company Managing Editor Roxie Murphy, are asking the Highway Patrol to restore full public access to crash records.
The MBA and MPA are news membership organizations that represent hundreds of local media organizations across the state. KOMU 8 News is a member of the MBA. Gray Media is a television ownership group that owns multiple stations in Missouri and Warden Publishing Company owns several local newspapers in the state.
In a petition filed on Friday, the organizations allege that the Highway Patrol’s withholding of information in crash reports violates the Missouri Sunshine Law.
The petition states that, beginning in 2024, the patrol has redacted names, addresses, phone numbers and other identifiable information in crash reports received through Sunshine Law requests.
The Highway Patrol began redacting personal information in online crash reports on Nov. 1, 2024, citing concerns that making the information public could lead scammers to target family members of victims. KOMU 8 News reported at the time that the Highway Patrol said the change would only apply to online preliminary crash reports.
Before 2024, the Highway Patrol posted crash reports with identifiable information, stating on its website that all information in reports is considered an “open record” that must be made publicly available, according to a statement from MPA and MBA.
“People have been calling our member stations upset that they didn’t know that their neighbors or prominent community members were in a crash,” said Chad Mahoney, president and CEO of the broadcasters association.
The petition outlined several instances in 2026 of news outlets submitting a Sunshine Law request for unredacted reports and allegedly being denied that information.
In the petition, the news organizations are asking for restored access to unredacted crash reports, between $1,000 and $5,000 awarded to each plaintiff, their attorneys’ fees and all other relief they may be entitled to.
This story was originally published by KOMU. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear asks KY universities review policies against sexual assault after Cornell lawsuit
text:
Gov. Andy Beshear asked Kentucky colleges and universities to review sexual assault policies.(Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is calling on universities within the commonwealth to rigorously review their policies against sexual assault and harassment within 90 days. 
Beshear is asking university officials to consider if campus policies against sexual violence ensure students are protected and feel safe. As part of the review, universities should at a minimum review awareness campaigns, access to resources, reporting steps and more. 
“My request is not suggesting any Kentucky institution has failed in this area,” Beshear said in a Wednesday press conference. “We should always be looking for ways to improve and to do better. We must be proactive and intentional when it comes to sexual violence. This is how we ensure Kentucky students are safe and that they feel safe.” 
Beshear said his office reached out to universities and colleges in Kentucky before making the announcement. 
“The responses have been encouraging, understanding that this moment requires more and the willingness to do that rigorous review to make sure if there is anything else we can and should be doing to protect our college students, that those policies are put into place,” he added. 
The move comes after a former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit in September alleging she was gang raped after being coerced into consuming drugs in 2024 by men in a fraternity house. 
Beshear said he also requests that the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education, which oversees the state’s public universities, ensure that university board members are educated on policies and procedures against sexual harassment. That includes best practices on reporting and conducting investigations. 
Last week, Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore asked a state agency there to review policies against sexual assault on campuses.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Democratic South Dakota secretary of state candidate draws contributions from Republicans
text:
The South Dakota Secretary of State's Office in Pierre. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)A Democrat’s campaign finance report shows some of his contributions coming from across the political divide as he campaigns for South Dakota secretary of state, after the Republican incumbent endorsed him. 
A report filed this week shows Democratic nominee Terrence Davis, of Sioux Falls, raised about $53,500 since May and spent about $18,400. He reported about $57,600 remaining in his campaign fund, including money from a prior reporting period.

Democratic nominee for South Dakota secretary of state, Terrence Davis. (Courtesy of Davis for South Dakota)

Some of his contributions came from Republicans. That includes $1,000 from Joe Kirby, who helped lead an unsuccessful ballot question campaign two years ago to implement open primaries, and Kirby’s wife, Jennifer. David Knudson, a Republican who formerly served in the Legislature and ran for governor, and De Knudson, a former Sioux Falls City Council member, gave $1,000. Harry Christianson, who served in the administration of Republican former Gov. Bill Janklow, gave $250 to Davis’ campaign.
De Knudson said she doesn’t like what she’s heard from the Republican nominee for secretary of state, Rep. Heather Baxter of Rapid City, about Baxter’s support for hand-counting of election results and criticism of vote-counting machines. 
“I find all that to be ludicrous,” Knudson said. 
The secretary of state’s duties include overseeing elections. Activists who support hand-counting have said vote tabulation machines could be hacked or tampered with, but vote-counting machines in South Dakota are not connected to the internet, and post-election audits have shown the machines to be accurate.
The Republican support for Davis comes after Republican Secretary of State Monae Johnson’s September endorsement of Davis over Baxter. Johnson lost the Republican nomination to Baxter at the state Republican convention during the summer. The general election is Nov. 3, and advance voting is underway.

Heather Baxter addresses the state Republican convention on June 27, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City just prior to winning the party’s nomination for secretary of state. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)

Knudson said she knows Johnson, and Johnson’s endorsement played a role in Knudson’s decision to support Davis. 
Davis called the support he has received from Republicans “amazing.”  
“People are looking at what makes sense moving forward,” Davis said. 
Baxter reported raising about $80,000 since May and spending about $86,000, including money her campaign had on hand from the prior reporting period. She had $1,900 remaining. Individual contributions exceeding $100 accounted for about $59,000 of her fundraising. Her largest individual donors included Republican state Rep. Tony Kayser, R-Sioux Falls, and his wife, Kathryn, who contributed a combined $8,000. 
Kayser sponsored and Baxter co-sponsored failed legislation earlier this year that would have changed laws governing vote-counting equipment. They both co-sponsored a failed bill to prohibit the use of automatic vote tabulating equipment. 

Tamara Lesnar is the 2026 Libertarian nominee for South Dakota secretary of state. (Photo courtesy of Tamara Lesnar campaign)

Baxter said in a statement that she supported that legislation because “I saw issues with the certification process and some of the equipment not being in compliance with state and federal law.”
“As the next secretary of state, I will work to make sure South Dakota is 100% federally compliant and aim to provide transparency on all aspects of election administration,” she wrote.
Baxter’s campaign finance report shows she received $1,700 worth of yard signs from Rick Weible. He has promoted hand-counting across the state and testified in favor of the bill that would have banned tabulation machines. 
Meanwhile, Libertarian candidate Tamara Lesnar’s report shows $420 raised, $270 spent and $150 left. 



Other state offices
Candidates running for other state offices also filed campaign finance reports this week, covering their fundraising and spending since May.

Public Utilities Commission: Republican Don Haggar’s campaign took in $40,000, spent $33,000 and had $11,000 remaining, including money from a prior reporting period. Democrat Frank Kloucek brought in $38,000, spent $24,000 and had $14,000 remaining. 
State Auditor: Republican Catherine Barranco took in $52,000 and spent nearly all of it. Democrat Tom Cool took in $4,350 and spent all but about $500.
State Treasurer: Republican Melissa Hull took in $25,000, spent $23,000 and has $6,000 left, including money from a prior reporting period. Democrat Margaret Kuipers took in about $9,000 and spent nearly all of it. 
Commissioner of School and Public Lands: Republican Brock Greenfield took in about $9,000, spent about $9,000 and had $1,000 remaining, including money from a prior reporting period. Democrat Raeann Mettler took in about $11,500, spent $10,000 and had about $1,400 remaining.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Feds announce release of reserve heating oil, after letter from Maine’s senators
text:
The Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve has only released heating oil twice in its 26-year history, and this is the first time it will be used to lower prices. (Photo by U.S. Department of Energy)The U.S. Department of Energy will release 315,000 barrels of reserve heating oil amid high prices, after U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King called for action last month. 
According to a press release from the senators Wednesday, the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve will release roughly a third of its supply to help reduce the price of heating oil. The reserve has only released heating oil twice in its 26-year history, and this is the first time it will be used to lower prices. The reserve holds approximately one million barrels, 200,000 of which are located in South Portland.
“Maine has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil,” King, an independent, said. “Maine is one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help.” 
King said that while this is good news, “we also want to keep pressuring the Administration to bring those prices down before winter really sets in.”
Collins and King sent a letter to President Donald Trump last month, urging him to release heating oil from the reserve. 
“After receiving Senators Collins’ and King’s letter and extensive discussions with Senator Collins, I have directed the department to exchange barrels from our Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate heightened home heating oil costs during the upcoming winter,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “Of course, this is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption.”
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
According to data from the department, the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.97 per gallon on Oct. 13, up roughly 79% from last year. That is down slightly from Sept. 21, when the average price reached a record high of $6.02. 
“The (U.S. Department of Energy) anticipates this release will put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter,” Collins said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Westinghouse investing $1B to make a new kind of uranium at SC nuclear fuel factory
text:
A rendering of Westinghouse's proposed new $1 billion nuclear fuel factory in Lower Richland. (Photo courtesy of Westinghouse)COLUMBIA — Westinghouse Electric Company plans to expand its nuclear fuel campus south of Columbia to make a new type of uranium for power plants.
The nuclear power giant announced Wednesday it would invest $1 billion in a new factory, alongside its existing plant in southern Richland County, to make what it calls low enriched uranium plus.
USC, Westinghouse sign agreement for nuclear workforce training center

Westinghouse said the investment marks the first fleet-scale nuclear fuel factory built in the United States in more than 50 years. Construction is underway and operations are expected to begin in 2030.
It’s unclear whether the investment involves new jobs. Officials did not immediately provide answers to the SC Daily Gazette’s questions about the workforce.
“South Carolina is already leading America’s nuclear renaissance, and our state has been producing the nuclear fuel that powers approximately 10% of the United States from Westinghouse’s fuel operations in Richland County,” Gov. Henry McMaster said in a statement.
This expansion has been in the works since at least 2024, when Westinghouse began meeting with federal nuclear regulators about the plant’s design.
Low enriched uranium plus, or LEU+, has a higher level of uranium enrichment — 5% to 8% compared to the usual 3% to 5% — and allows nuclear power plants to run longer before needing to refuel, according to Westinghouse.
The fuel was used for the first time in the United States last year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“By expanding our domestic nuclear fuel production capabilities, we are creating economic opportunities, supporting good-paying jobs and positioning South Carolina as a leader in the nation’s energy sector,” U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn said in a statement. The plant is located in the 6th Congressional District he represents.
Westinghouse also said the production process for the new fuel “reduces chemical use and lowers the potential for environmental impacts.”
The existing fuel plant has long struggled with environmental issues, including groundwater contamination that dates back decades, uranium buildup in air pollution controls in 2016 and a uranium leak in the plant’s floor 2018, according to reports by The State newspaper.
Built in 1968, the existing Columbia Fuel Fabrication Facility is one of the largest nuclear fuel plants in the world, producing fuel pellets, fuel rods, fuel assemblies and fuel components. More than 1,200 people work there, according to Westinghouse.
“Our workforce has supported this facility for generations, and this expansion ensures that we’ll continue to see high-paying jobs and economic stability for years to come,” Richland County Council Chairwoman Jesica Mackey said in a statement.
An aerial view of Westinghouse’s Columbia Fuel Fabrication Facility in Lower Richland. (Photo courtesy of Westinghouse)
In exchange for its investment, Richland County approved Westinghouse for ongoing property tax breaks.
Laws passed in 2017 and 2021 effectively lowered the property tax rate on manufacturers from 10.5% to 6%. This proposed deal takes the rate even lower — to 4% — over 40 years.
Westinghouse CEO Dan Sumner also said the company is “grateful for (U.S. Department of Energy’s) tax credit program,” but did not go into detail about how it would apply to this project.
The announcement of the new factory plays into federal efforts to increase nuclear power production nationwide.
In June, the U.S. Energy Department also announced $17.5 billion in loans to speed the construction of 10 other Westinghouse nuclear reactors, to be built in pairs at five undisclosed sites across the U.S. by 2030.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Minot pig iron permit public comment period opens
text:
A site rendering shows the proposed North American Iron pig iron plant planned for northeast of Minot. (Courtesy of North American Iron)The North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality has opened a public comment period on a new heavy industry proposed northeast of Minot. 
North American Iron is proposing to transport mine waste from Minnesota to Minot where it can be refined into small iron pellets known as pig iron, which then can be used to make steel.
The department says its preliminary evaluations show that the pig iron plant will comply with air pollution rules and air quality will not be harmed. 
Proposed North Dakota pig iron plant to turn Minnesota mine waste into steel, a first for US 

North American Iron’s construction permit application and the Department of Environmental Quality’s proposed permit documents are available for review at http://deq.nd.gov/AQ/PublicCom.aspx.
Comments can be emailed to AirQuality@nd.gov or mailed to North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality, Division of Air Quality, 4201 Normandy St., 2nd Floor, Bismarck, ND 58503-1324.
The comment period closes Nov. 20.
The department also has scheduled a public hearing if it determines that there is enough interest. The hearing is planned for 5:30 p.m. Dec. 2 at Minot City Hall.
If the department does not receive a formal request for a public hearing during the comment period, or if it determines that there is not a significant degree of public interest, the department may cancel the hearing. 
North American Iron plans to develop a 2,400-acre site northeast of Minot. A related company, Calumet Reclamation Co., would provide the iron-rich mine waste from a site in northern Minnesota.  
One potential source of greenhouse gas emissions from the facility would be from burning natural gas. 
Jim Bougalis, CEO and founder of North American Iron, has said a 300-megawatt natural gas-fired power generation facility will be built at the site.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ‘Not an easy decision’ — CT Arts Alliance closes, moves mission to CT Humanities
text:
The Connecticut Arts Alliance, a statewide organization that has focused on legislative advocacy in the arts and culture sector for the last 21 years, has closed its doors due to increasing financial strain.  
The work of the nonprofit continues, however, as its executive director, Rufus de Rham, moves the organization’s assets and mission into CT Humanities, and shifts his focus to the legislative session ahead. 
Earlier this month, de Rham confirmed that CAA has formally dissolved, and moved its mission and remaining $60,000 in financial assets to CT Humanities. He cited significant federal cuts to the arts and humanities, as well as a rapidly shifting legislative landscape and shrinking pot of funding for nonprofit arts organizations, as the reason for CAA’s closure.      
De Rham was the second paid executive director of the organization; prior to 2020, CAA operated as an all-volunteer board. He will now serve as CT Humanities’ inaugural director of cultural advocacy and community engagement. Two of CAA’s former board members, Connecticut Main Street Center Executive Director Michelle McCabe and Northwest Connecticut Arts Council Director Stephanie Burr, have also moved over to CT Humanities to serve on its board. 
“It’s not an easy decision to dissolve an arts organization, but our primary concern was continuing the work,” de Rham said in a phone call last week. “This will, I think, allow us to make a stronger advocacy push for the greater cultural sector. We have a federal administration that is fully dismantling arts and culture funding in this country, and we’re going to keep doing the same work we’ve been doing.”
“We saw an opportunity to really reimagine the cultural sector,” said CT Humanities Executive Director Jason Mancini. “Rufus is a really delightful human being, a wonderful partner and a total policy wonk. We wanted to see how we could co-create something.” 
De Rham said that the decision to move beneath CT Humanities’ umbrella was one of both practicality and survival — if not of CAA’s formal 501c3 itself, than of its mission. For just over five years now, CAA and CT Humanities have been working closely together, during the tenure of CAA’s first two paid executive directors. 
De Rham took over at the organization in January 2025, around the same time that President Donald Trump took office and announced a freeze on federal funding that the administration later rescinded. Like former CAA Director Brett Thompson before him, he worked closely with CT Humanities from the beginning of his tenure, as well as with the Connecticut Office of the Arts (CoA), a state agency that lives within the Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD). 
He was one of the first to hear when the administration’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) slashed National Endowment for the Humanities funding through a series of rapid-fire grant cancellations and significant staff reductions in April 2025 (a judge later ruled that those cuts were unconstitutional, but much of the money has not yet been reinstated, or taken over a year and an arduous request process for organizations to get back). Even before similar cuts came for the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) the following month, impacting hundreds of organizations across Connecticut, de Rham knew it was only a matter of time.  
It was clear to him immediately that CAA would have to change its operating structure to stay alive (at CT Humanities, Mancini was having the same kind of discussions; he described the DOGE cuts as “existential” and “catastrophic” in a phone call last week). And it was also clear to him, in a budget year that included a proposed 17.5 percent cut to the Connecticut Tourism Fund, that the advocacy work CAA was doing was vital to the sector.
“We were like, ‘How do we restructure and reorganize?’” remembered de Rham, whose $65,000 salary was the organization’s most significant expense. By that time, federal pandemic relief funds were gone, and individual and foundation grants were few and far between. 
“We tried to think through multiple ways, including returning to an all-volunteer board and fundraising for advocacy work and a lobbyist, which CAA used through the firm Gallo-Robinson. 
Then they looked at how aligned the mission was with the work CT Humanities was already doing. 
A period of transition  
De Rham and members of the board navigated that decision during a legislative session that was already feeling the strain of federal cuts. In addition to the proposed cut to the state’s Tourism Fund, proposed reductions to dedicated line item funding added up to a total of slightly over $2.2 million for the sector, he told members in an email in February 2025. 
De Rham, working closely with Mancini, was able to activate people from across the sector, from small educational nonprofits to large theaters that reliably receive line item funding in the governor’s budget each year. On CAA’s website and in frequent email updates to members, he provided tutorials on how to write public testimony, with anecdotes about workforce development, statewide economic impact, and the cultural vitality of a city or town that has a thriving arts landscape. 
CAA, rallying support around the issue, successfully fought that 17.5 percent reduction, and the Tourism Fund received a $16.1 million allocation in 2025. Likewise, DECD’s line item funding remained even. 
Hope Chávez, executive director at the Arts Council of Greater New Haven, remembered how grateful she felt to have someone walking her through the process after she stepped into her first regional leadership role in 2023. 
“Rufus and I have had a very fluid line of communication about advocacy in the last two and a half years. Just quick calls to say, ‘I’m tracking this bill, are you tracking this bill?’” she said. She remembered the number of times in the last two years that she’s come to Hartford to testify, or tapped 10 fellow arts workers to do the same, specifically because de Rham made the ask. “It’s so nice to have someone who can credibly answer those questions.”
“I’m very happy that someone with Rufus’s skill set in particular and existing legislative relationships is the one, at least for now, to build this machine inside CT Humanities,” she added. “There are so many people in our sector that want to burn it all down, and I would offer as a provocation back to that, composting. It [CAA] didn’t go away. It’s being composted back into the soil.”
In the 2026 legislative session, CAA and CT Humanities — still collaborating informally — focused their efforts on items including House Bill 5443, which if passed would have allocated half a percent of the state’s meals tax to the Connecticut Tourism Fund (the two organizations also supported Senate Bills 02 and 55, which also would have allocated portions of the same tax to the Tourism Fund). 
Together, they prompted over 200 arts leaders, as well as working artists, educators, and cultural conveners to present verbal and written testimony in support of the bill. While the bill ultimately did not move forward, it was the closest the sector had ever gotten to that allocation from the meals tax, de Rham said. 
In many ways, it was also proof of concept that their collaboration, which included coordinated outreach efforts and step-by-step guides on how to write testimony, worked. In August, CAA’s board voted to dissolve the 501c3, and move a remaining $60,000 in assets over to CT Humanities. The organization formally dissolved in September of this year. 
Over multiple conversations last week, both de Rham and Mancini framed it as a transition that will benefit both the sector and the cultural workers within it. If the arts and humanities don’t change how they are talking about their work, they said, they risk losing funding as the dollars available continue to shrink. Meanwhile, both agreed that arts policy often intersects with housing, healthcare, and public education in ways that they have not yet broached during the legislative session.
As CT Humanities’ first director of cultural advocacy and community engagement, de Rham will be responsible for talking to legislators, tracking proposals, spearheading advocacy efforts, and breaking down policy decisions in a way that people across the sector can understand them. He said he’s excited to start having conversations about the basic needs that artists have, including affordable housing and healthcare benefits for artists at a time when both have become prohibitively expensive.  
“The primary focus will be state funding,” de Rham said. “This will allow us to have a much broader advocacy base because there’s different support and connections [across the arts and humanities]. The concept is it’s all a huge tent and umbrella.” 
He added that CT Humanities is on comparatively stable financial footing. Currently, the organization’s annual budget is about $5.6 million, a number that includes $2.4 million from the State of Connecticut, $600,000 from America 250, and $675,000 from the NEH — only about half of the funding that Mancini would have expected over a year ago. 
In addition to its work regranting many of those dollars, it’s able to afford a lobbyist in Hartford, which gives the organization a larger advocacy footprint.  
An evolving arts landscape
The move to bring together the work of both organizations represents yet another chapter for CAA, which had been in flux for just over two decades. For the first 15 years of its existence, CAA existed as an all-volunteer board comprising arts leaders and administrators from across the sector, from representatives from the state’s regional theaters and large presenting houses to those running midsize ballet companies and small after-school arts programs. 
In those first years, “it was more of a roundtable and working group,” de Rham said, adding that he wasn’t part of that early work, but has heard about it through the organization’s board members and institutional history. In 2005, CAA incorporated as a 501c4, which it remained until 2020 (that 501c4 still exists; it underwent a name change and is now the largely-dormant Connecticut Arts Advocacy Network).  
Its advocacy work remained limited, largely because its board members were all working to keep their own arts organizations, including several of the state’s eight Direct Regional Service Organizations, or DRSOs, financially afloat. Then around 2018, the board launched a strategic planning process, with the goal of hiring a paid executive director and forming a 501c3. 
In 2018, as several new gubernatorial candidates emerged from the woodwork, CAA piloted “Create The Vote,” an initiative with the Connecticut Alliance for Arts Education (CAAE), designed to get political candidates talking about the arts. The advocacy push worked: Create The Vote held a candidate forum on arts and culture in New Haven that July, and then-incoming Gov. Ned Lamont included sector professionals on a gubernatorial transition committee focused on arts, culture and tourism that winter. 
Create The Vote, with CAA, gave arts advocates a framework to start talking critically about the sector’s significant impact on Connecticut’s economy and the cultural health of its towns and cities, still a talking point that advocates reach for in their testimonies. Currently, teh sector brings in $13.9 billion dollars and supported 53,000 jobs, according to research from the National Association of State Arts Agencies
In 2020, Brett Thompson became its inaugural executive director, a transition that also prompted CAA to incorporate as a 501c3 for the first time, just as members had discussed in those strategic planning meetings . Thompson was already familiar with the organization: he had served on the board for several years during his tenure as chief operating officer at the Greater Hartford Arts Council. 
In a legislative landscape transformed by the Covid-19 pandemic, from remote public hearings to an infusion of pandemic relief funding for the sector, Thompson started communicating with both arts workers and legislators around specific policy items, from proposed legislation to specific funding proposals on behalf of the sector to a continuation of Create The Vote that braved the remote pivot.   
In 2022, he began working with CT Humanities and the Connecticut Tourism Coalition to build a “Funding Roadmap” inspired by a $30.7 million CT Cultural Fund that CT Humanities had launched the year prior, through an infusion of pandemic relief funding and partnership with the Connecticut Office of the Arts (CoA), a state agency that lives within the Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD). 
“Most people understand what the arts are, but most people don’t understand what the humanities are,” said CoA Director of Arts, Preservation and Museums Elizabeth Shapiro. For her, the Cultural Fund was the beginning of a collaborative chapter that she now thinks of as crucial to the health and growth of the sector. 
The roadmap, which proposed a historic $58.5 million boost to arts, culture, and tourism, became a cornerstone of CAA’s policy work, helping to shape what became House Bill 6692 during the 2023 legislative session. That overall figure — which did not ultimately pass — included $17.5 million for the CT Cultural Fund, that number included $8 million for arts, culture and tourism line items, $5 million for CT Humanities and the Connecticut Office of the Arts, and $3 million for sector-wide workforce development.   
“Brett really grew the organization and set all the infrastructure in place,” said de Rham, who served on CAA’s board during his tenure leading the Northwest Connecticut Arts Council and later the Warner Theatre in Torrington. Each year, for instance, Thompson created a guide to which bills CAA supported, and communicated that information to member organizations who used it as fuel to testify in Hartford. 
A path forward 
Reached for comment, several CAA and CT Humanities supporters praised the decision to combine the work of the two organizations. McCabe, who first got to know CAA as a political candidate in the state’s 28th Senate District (that’s Bethel, Easton, Fairfield, and Newtown), and joined its board for the first time in 2021, called it a collaboration that will ultimately both benefit and unify the sector. At the time of the vote to dissolve, she was serving as CAA’s board chair. 
“This sector has been so devastated by the change in administration at the federal level,” she said. “Recognizing the realities of the situation [we’re in], it just made sense to pull all of those efforts together rather than to figure out how to do it alone.”
“I think it’s really honoring the spirit in which the organization was founded,” she added. “We are enlarging the tent through this. I see this as part of an evolution.”
CT Humanities Board President Frank Mitchell, who served for years as the executive director of the Amistad Center for Art & Culture, also pointed to the decision as one that benefits the sector when it is itself in transition. In the past six years, he’s watched organizations struggle as they receive pandemic relief funds, spend those funds, and then brace for federal cuts as they realize that they are suddenly cash-strapped. 
Or, in his words, “it’s starting to rain and there are not a lot of umbrellas.” Mixing metaphors, he framed it as getting in a bigger, necessary-to-survive vessel at a time when a shark is headed toward the boat. 
“Given the economy and given what’s happening in D.C., it’s a great time to be thinking about advocacy and to have this redoubled effort,” he said. “We’re at a point where we really do need advocacy across the board, and we need to be giving people a reason to be their own best advocates as well.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana K-12 chronic absenteeism rate declines for fourth year
text:
Indiana Education Secretary Katie Jenner speaks to the State Board of Education on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of the State of Indiana)Hoosier students are slowly returning to their pre-pandemic attendance patterns: Indiana’s K-12 chronic absenteeism rate declined for the fourth consecutive year to just shy of 15% in 2026, the State Board of Education learned Wednesday.
Students are considered chronically absent if they miss 10% or more of the school year, the equivalent of 18 school days or three weeks of classes.
Excused and unexcused absences are both counted toward this rate.
Chronic absenteeism peaked in Indiana K-12 schools at 21% in 2022 — twice the pre-pandemic rate.
Excessive absences are most acute in high school, with 30% of seniors missing at least 10% of days for the 2025-26 school year.
One likely reason for their absence: apathy.
Student focus groups conducted by the Indiana Department of Education found the most common explanation for poor attendance was a belief that school wasn’t relevant, Education Secretary Katie Jenner said.
“They didn’t see the value,” she said. “They could miss (school) and still make it through.”
Ron Sandlin, chief innovation officer for the department, said poor attendance at Indiana high schools “underscores the critical work we’re doing around our diploma seals and rethinking high school.”
Story continues below.
2025-2026-Chronic-Absenteeism-Data
 
The purpose of the new diploma seals, he said, is to connect each student to an educational pathway they deem relevant to their lives beyond high school.
“As we engage more students and give more opportunities in their high school career, we will start to see those rates reduce at a disproportionate rate relative to the other grades,” Sandlin said.
Data shows chronic absenteeism is declining among at-risk student populations, including Black, Hispanic and multi-racial students, English learners and students who qualify for free or reduced-price lunches.
Springs Valley Community School Corporation reported a dramatic turnaround in its chronic absenteeism rate, which fell from 21% in the 2024-25 school year to just 1.7% last school year.
State officials attributed the improvement to consistent communication with parents about district attendance policies.
Lawrence County Independent Schools saw its absenteeism rate decline from 31.4% to 16.3% in a single year through targeted outreach to students who repeatedly missed school.
The Indiana Department of Education tracks chronic absenteeism because attendance is strongly correlated with academic performance.
Sandlin said 74% of students marked chronically absent last school year passed the state IREAD exam — an improvement from prior years, yet it still trails the 90% pass rate for students who maintained good attendance that year.
Just shy of 19% of chronically absent students earned proficient math scores last school year, compared to 45% of their peers with good attendance records.
A similar pattern is evident in English language arts proficiency and college readiness, with only 21% of chronically absent students meeting college-ready benchmarks compared to 42% of their peers who didn’t miss a lot of school.
State officials are urging school districts to report absences quickly, issue reminder letters to families and lower the threshold for intervention to improve student attendance.
Pat Maples, the former superintendent of Hamilton Southeastern Schools and current State Board of Education member, asked if county judicial systems are getting involved to remind parents of the consequences of excessive absences.
“I think that’s a partnership that makes a difference for the school when juvenile probation gets involved, and all of a sudden it gets people’s attention,” he said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico medical malpractice reform leading to lower rates, but full impact years off, experts say
text:
New Mexico Office of the Superintendent of Insurance Chief Actuary Christian Myers, left, and New Mexico Hospital Association President and CEO Troy Clark, right, speak before the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee in Santa Fe on Oct. 20, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Medical malpractice insurance rates are set to decrease for hospitals and providers across New Mexico, but the full impact of the state’s recent legislative reform won’t take hold for another three to four years, experts told a panel of state lawmakers Tuesday.
Reforming New Mexico’s medical malpractice laws emerged as a key issue of this year’s legislative session. House Bill 99, which Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed into law in March, capped the amount of damages juries can award in medical malpractice cases. It also specified that one injury counts as one malpractice claim — previously, patients could file separate claims against each provider who was present at an operation gone wrong.
A trio of healthcare and insurance experts told lawmakers on the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee that malpractice insurance rates are set to decrease for hospitals and independent providers, thanks to the new law.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We anticipate (House Bill 99) will lower prices for providers and hospitals for medical malpractice in the long-term,” New Mexico Office of the Superintendent of Insurance Chief Actuary Christian Myers told lawmakers.
However, panel members said the state’s healthcare industry still faces several outstanding challenges. The annual number of medical malpractice settlements statewide continues to increase; only a handful of malpractice insurance providers will write policies in New Mexico; and specific data on how many physicians practice in the state is difficult to come by, they said.
“We hope that as HB99 continues to be in place longer; it’ll draw more insurance companies back to the marketplace so we get more competition and further lower the price of our medical malpractice insurance,” New Mexico Hospital Association President and CEO Troy Clark said at the Tuesday hearing.
Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) questioned the panel of experts about whether the reform passed in this year’s legislative session has been successful in courting out-of-state physicians to move to New Mexico.
During the session, advocates for malpractice reform and interstate medical compacts often credited New Mexico’s outdated laws for a mass exodus of providers.
However, Roybal Caballero cited a report presented to the interim Legislative Health and Human Services Committee earlier this year that indicated that from fiscal year 2023 to fiscal year 2026, the number of medical doctors’ licenses increased statewide by nearly 4,000. She questioned whether that contradicted the “mass exodus” arguments made in favor of reform.
Clark responded that licensure numbers don’t accurately represent how many physicians practice in the state. Doctors who retire or leave the state often do not cancel their licenses, he said, meaning the figures are often an overcount.
He said that he has heard from leaders in the hospitals he works with that fewer doctors are leaving the state after the passage of medical malpractice reform, but believes that it will take “three to four years” to build up a healthy medical workforce.
“We actually have seen the exodus start to slow down,” he said. “Before, our success was trying to replace the ones that were leaving as quick as they were leaving. Now, I think we’re starting to see growth.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rep. Jenni Furtado to lead state Democratic party
text:
Rep. Jenni Furtado, an East Providence Democrat, has been chosen as the next chairwoman of the Rhode Island Democratic Party. (Courtesy of the Rhode Island General Assembly)A freshman state representative from East Providence will be the next leader of the Rhode Island Democratic Party, House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski announced Wednesday.
Rep. Jenni Furtado will replace former party chair Liz Beretta-Perik, who resigned Tuesday, following her husband’s indictment on federal fraud charges related to his former education firm in Ohio.
Furtado, 33, was first elected to House District 64, spanning parts of Pawtucket and East Providence, in 2024. She is unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.
Blazejewski, a Providence Democrat, praised Furtado for her work ethic, first on the East Providence School Committee and then at the State House.
“These are difficult times, and Democrats need a chair who knows what working families are up against. Jenni does, and I’m grateful she’s willing to take this on,” Blazejewski said in a statement.
Historically, the House speaker has played a prominent role in selecting party leaders, including in 2014, when then-speaker Nicholas Mattiello backed Rep. Joe McNamara as party chair following the resignation of former leader, Rep. David Caprio. McNamara, a Warwick Democrat, chose not to seek reelection in 2023, leading to Beretta-Perik’s election as the first woman to chair the state party.
The 150-member Democratic State Central Committee is expected to meet to ratify Furtado as the new party chairwoman in the “coming days,” although the date and time have not been set.
The daughter of first-generation Peruvian immigrants, Furtado’s story is one of firsts. The Roger Williams University School of Law graduate was the first in her family to graduate college. Her election to the East Providence School Committee in 2020 made her the first Peruvian-American official to win elected office across the state. She served as school committee president in her second term, in 2022, before running for the open House District 64 seat in 2024, easily defeating her primary challenger.
In her first term in state office, she cosponsored state legislation to cap interest on medical debt and ease local zoning restrictions to promote development of single-family homes, including townhouses. 
“I’m honored by the opportunity to serve as chairwoman of the Rhode Island Democratic Party, and I’m grateful to Speaker Blazejewski for his support,” Furtado said in a statement. “These are difficult political times, and people want to know that Democrats are listening and working on the things that affect their everyday lives. “I look forward to working with Democrats in every city and town across the state to do just that.”
Furtado did not immediately respond to calls for comment Wednesday.
Furtado grew up in Mamaroneck, New York, where her family immigrated to escape guerrilla warfare in Peru, according to biographical information provided by the legislature. Her mom worked as a house cleaner, and her dad as a handyman, both juggling multiple jobs while Furtado and her brother learned English in public schools.
Furtado graduated with a bachelor’s degree from St. John’s University in New York City before moving to Rhode Island for law school.
She is married to Marc Furtado, an East Providence native who is active in city Democratic politics and works as a project manager for the federal General Services Administration, according to his LinkedIn page.
