name: Maine Morning Star
title: The outcome of Maine’s US Senate race may not be known for weeks. Here’s why.
text:
Maine's November 2026 ballot for U.S. Senate lists Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, along with space for a write-in candidate. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)The winner of Maine’s U.S. Senate seat might not be known for days or weeks after the Nov. 3 election. That’s because the odds favor a ranked-choice runoff.  
“We think there’s a huge likelihood that it’s going to happen,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows told Maine Morning Star. 
While only two candidates, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, will appear on the ballot, the six declared write-ins prompt ranked-choice voting, meaning voters can rank three names on their ballot. 
That’s also the case for the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District between former Gov. Paul LePage and State Auditor Matt Dunlap, as there is one declared write-in. 
If a voter writes in the name of someone who isn’t a declared write-in candidate — such as former Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out in July — their vote will not be counted for any candidate. Counted as blanks, those votes, along with ballots where the first choice is left blank, still matter in determining whether the race goes to a runoff. That has been a tipping point in the past. 
The primary elections for state and federal offices in Maine can use ranked-choice voting, but the method only applies to federal races in the general election, so the three-way gubernatorial election will not be ranked. 
Maine and Alaska, the only two states to use the method for statewide elections, have U.S. Senate races that could determine the balance of power in U.S. Congress. Some worry the possibility of delayed outcomes due to runoffs open an opportunity for President Donald Trump to cast doubt or interfere in the results. 
“Any time between an election and the call in the race, any of that sort of purgatory, basically, I think conspiracy theories end up filling the gap,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, the University of Virginia Center for Politics’ nonpartisan newsletter on American elections. “I mean the president is very irresponsible about what he says about election integrity and so I’m sure he would allege foul play even if there was no real evidence of it.”
So far, the Trump administration has attempted to restrict voting by mail, purge voter rolls and send sensitive personal information to the Department of Homeland Security, among other efforts to influence voting ahead of the midterms, which have largely failed. 
“We are mindful that all eyes of the nation will be on Maine should the U.S. Senate race go to ranked choice voting,” Bellows said. “For that reason, we’ve been preparing for weeks inside the office to discuss staffing levels and what measures we could take to make the processes as efficient as possible.” 
A look back 
A look back to 2024 shows why Bellows thinks a ranked-choice runoff is likely. Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, who currently serves the 2nd District, had been challenged by Republican Austin Theriault, a state legislator at the time. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.After the count of first-choice votes, Golden received 196,388, while Theriault received 194,130. There were 421 first-choice votes for declared write-in Diana Merenda. Meanwhile, 11,997 people left their first-choice blank (or wrote in someone who was not a declared write-in).
A race goes to a ranked-choice runoff if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes on Election Day. That calculation is based on total ballots cast, including blanks. 
In this race, there were 402,936 total ballots cast. So, while Golden won a plurality of first-choice votes, he received just under 49% of total votes.
“A very small number of voters has a big impact because the law is total ballots cast,” Bellows said. 
Golden eventually won the runoff, which was completed in four days, by Nov. 15, 2024. Last-place candidates (in this case, Merenda) are eliminated first and votes are then redistributed to a voter’s next choice. That’s repeated until one candidate receives more than 50% of votes.
However, the official outcome was delayed longer. Theriault requested a recount, which in Maine is a hand count done by representatives from each campaign. Theriault’s campaign ended the recount after a handful of counties and cities had been completed, saying those counts answered their outstanding questions. The race was officially called for Golden on Dec. 4, 2024. 
A similar sequence of events could occur in determining the official results of Maine’s U.S. Senate race, which polls have as a virtual toss-up. 
“If the race actually reflects the polling, it seems pretty plausible that one of the two candidates actually won’t get to 50%, that neither of them would,” Kondik said. 
Another possibility could be that Collins wins the most first-choice votes, but that there are more write-ins than blanks this year, and Jackson ends up winning after second choices are factored in, or vice versa. 
That’s what happened in 2018, when Golden was initially elected in the nation’s first use of ranked-choice voting for a congressional race. 
Former Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin received the most first-choice votes, however the second-choice votes for the third party candidate that year overwhelmingly went to Golden, handing him the victory after the runoff.  
Poliquin filed multiple lawsuits to try to block the tabulations, but federal courts affirmed the method’s constitutionality for general elections for federal races. 
Maine voters passed ranked choice voting by referendum in 2016. After that, the justices of the Maine Supreme Judicial Court issued a unanimous advisory opinion concluding that the parts of the law that apply to general elections for state offices were unconstitutional under the Maine Constitution, which requires the winners of those offices in a general election to be decided by a “plurality.” Primary elections and elections for federal offices are governed by state statute and not by the Maine Constitution. 
The court more recently weighed in this year, again determining that expanding the method to general elections for state office would violate the Maine Constitution.
Noting all the prior cases, Bellows said, “We are prepared for anything, whether that is litigation or other types of federal interference.”
But critics of ranked-choice voting, including Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine, caution that the method opens up more questions from people who have ulterior motives, particularly in light of declining trust in elections.  
“Voters are increasingly questioning the integrity of American elections,” Brewer said, “not that there’s any evidence that should lead them to do so, but primarily because we’ve had a chief executive who’s for the last 10 and a half years, or however long he’s been doing it, questioning the integrity of American elections.” 
Officials with the Maine Secretary of State’s Office prepare ballots for ranked-choice tabulations for three primary elections in Augusta on June 12, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)
Tabulation timelines 
While municipalities informally report results to the state and media on election night, under Maine law, they have two days to report official counts to the Secretary of State’s Office. That means it may not be clear on election night whether ranked-choice tabulations are needed. 
“We’ll make it as quickly as we can,” Bellows said of that determination. “If it is obvious that neither contender has received 50% plus one, then we’ll make that announcement even before all the clerks have officially filed. We want to give the public and the candidates as much notice as possible. We also want to be sure that we’re correct.” 
State law does not stipulate when the runoff would need to begin or end, though there are other statutory deadlines that must be met, such as submitting results to the governor by Nov. 23. The law is also silent on the order, if there are multiple runoffs and recounts that need to occur. 
In 2024, for example, the runoff and multiple legislative recounts occurred at the same time. This year, Bellows said, “We will most likely start ranked choice voting first, and then move into recounts as that capacity allows.”
Based on how long ranked-choice tabulations have taken in the past, Bellows said she expects a runoff would likely go until at least the Friday of the week following Election Day. During the primary in June, the ranked-choice runoffs for the Democratic and Republican primaries for governor, as well as the Democratic primary for the 2nd District, took a week and concluded well past midnight. 
The bulk of that time is the Secretary of State’s staff logging results from every ballot, checking multiple times to ensure the totals line up. The tedious process has in the past been livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s Facebook page. Actually running the ranked-choice tabulation formula produces results in a matter of minutes.
“We think it’s better to be accurate than fast,” Bellows said, “although we certainly are going to try to be as fast and accurate as possible.” 
While not a requirement, the results from the counties farthest away are typically logged first, so there is adequate time in case any missing materials need to be retrieved, Bellows said. 
When it comes to recounts, the candidates get to choose which areas of the state get recounted first. 
There are no automatic recounts in Maine. (That was almost an issue in 2024, when no candidate initially requested a recount after preliminary results had shown a tie between Rep. Lucas Lanigan and his challenger, Democrat Patricia Kidder.) 
Any candidate other than the apparent winner can request a recount with the Secretary of State within five business days after the election — except for races that use ranked-choice voting, when only a candidate who received one of the top three rankings at the end of the second to last round can request a recount. 
Candidates do not have to pay a deposit for the recount if the races are very close — 1% or less of the apparent margin of victory. Beyond that, state law outlines the cost, which is paid by the requester.
Forecasters such as Kondik already anticipated not knowing the result of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race on Election Day, since that race has four candidates on the ranked ballot. But the possibility of having to wait for Maine as well could further delay the overall ability to call the balance of power in the U.S. Senate, with Maine seen as one of the four seats Democrats would need to flip to gain control. 
“Maine is one of the most difficult to forecast races on the board,” Kondik said, “and it’s hugely consequential for the outcome of the Senate.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge denies Trump administration request to dismiss NAACP lawsuit against xAI
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can intervene in the NAACP lawsuit against Elon Musk’s xAI, but blocked the federal government’s attempt to dismiss the case. 
“We are pleased the Court saw through the Department of Justice’s deeply flawed arguments, which aimed to block communities from holding xAI accountable for the harmful air pollution being pumped out by its illegal power plant,” Patrick Anderson, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, one of the organizations representing the NAACP in court, said Tuesday.
The NAACP is suing the company, now known as SpaceXAI, over its use of 69 gas turbines to power its data center in Southaven. In the suit, the organization alleges that SpaceXAI is polluting the air and violating the federal Clean Air Act. It has asked U.S. District Judge Debra Brown to prohibit the company from operating the turbines unless they go through the state permitting process. 
In June, the Department of Justice filed a motion to join the lawsuit with SpaceXAI. The DOJ said it could intervene because the suit deals with a federal law, and that the company’s data center is “a matter of paramount national security.” The company’s artificial intelligence chatbot, Grok, has helped launch missiles during the conflict with Iran.   
When the company first set up the turbines last year, the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality told the company that it would not need air permits to operate because the turbines are “temporary” and “mobile.” 
The turbines are mounted on top of trailers and can operate for up to 12 months. However, MDEQ recently allowed the company to continue operating some of the generators for an additional five months due to a delay of the permanent turbines, which have air permits.
MDEQ maintains that the temporary turbines are operating in compliance with state regulations.
The Trump administration argued that it could dismiss the case because a federal agency, the Environmental Protection Agency, enforces the Clean Air Act. Brown denied the request to dismiss the case.
“The EPA’s role as a primary enforcer of the Clean Air Act does not mean that the federal government retains complete control over all Clean Air Act litigation,” Brown wrote in court filings.
“Congress intended to allow individuals to sue even when federal and state governments may, for whatever reason, decline to enforce the Clean Air Act,” Brown wrote.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Commentary: Why shouldn’t New Mexico invest in its largest electricity provider?
text:
Workers repair power lines in Albuquerque on Feb. 25, 2026. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)Every month, New Mexicans pay their PNM bill to keep the lights on. Right now, decisions about who profits from that bill, and who has a say in how the utility is run, are being made in corporate boardrooms hundreds of miles away.
With Blackstone still seeking to acquire TXNM, PNM’s parent company, the question of who should own our state’s largest electric utility is far from settled.
Last year, a Blackstone affiliate bought $400 million in TXNM Energy stock without getting the approval New Mexico law requires first. In July, state regulators ruled the sale illegal and ordered it undone. The companies subsequently unwound the transaction, and TXNM sold new shares to repay the loan it used to return Blackstone’s money. Now Blackstone is trying to sweeten its offer, increasing rate credits and proposing changes to the company’s board. But PNM customers are already paying more for electricity, including a $6.23 monthly increase that took effect in April, more than the roughly $3 a month in rate credits Blackstone is proposing.
That particular opportunity has passed, but the larger question remains: Why shouldn’t New Mexico explore becoming an investor in its own largest electric utility?
New Mexico should evaluate whether acquiring a meaningful minority stake and board representation at TXNM Energy could be a sound long-term investment that also gives the state a greater voice in the future of its largest electric utility, and a say in decisions about wildfire prevention, reliability, affordability, clean energy, economic development, and major new industrial loads.
This approach also protects the workers who keep the lights on. Because it is a minority investment, not a takeover, PNM would remain privately operated and its employees remain employees of a private company. Their existing collective bargaining agreements stay intact.
This isn’t a new idea. More than 1,500 New Mexicans have already signed a petition from groups like Organized Power in Numbers (OPIN), YUCCA, and United Academics UNM calling on state leaders to explore state investment in TXNM. There’s also a strong financial case for investing in PNM.
Utilities are attractive long-term investments precisely because they operate regulated monopolies and earn PRC-approved returns on prudent capital expenditures. Instead of those returns flowing to Wall Street, why shouldn’t New Mexico evaluate whether they could strengthen our permanent funds and benefit generations of New Mexicans?
State Investment Council (SIC) officials have argued that investing in TXNM could put the interests of ratepayers at odds with the Council’s responsibility to earn strong returns. But why should we accept that as a given fact? Utilities make money while operating under regulations that are supposed to protect consumers every day. New Mexico should be able to ask whether it can earn a responsible return on an investment in its largest electric utility while also having a greater stake in keeping power affordable and reliable.
There are legitimate legal and financial questions to work through. But those are questions for state leaders to answer, not reasons to dismiss the idea before they have seriously explored it.
New Mexico’s permanent funds hold more than $75 billion, and the SIC already invests in infrastructure, private equity, real estate, and other businesses throughout the United States and around the world in pursuit of long-term returns.
The question is simple: if New Mexico’s money can be invested in infrastructure and companies across the country and across the globe, why shouldn’t we consider investing it here at home—in an essential state utility that New Mexicans depend upon every day?
PNM is not an ordinary corporation. It holds a monopoly on power for hundreds of thousands of New Mexicans. Its infrastructure, rates and investment decisions affect virtually every aspect of our economy.
Yet its future is still tied up in Blackstone’s proposed acquisition of TXNM.
There is another path. We are asking our elected officials to seriously explore whether New Mexico, not wealthy private equity investors, should benefit from our state’s resources and ratepayer dollars.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump vowed to stop an ‘energy emergency.’ Then he created a real one.
text:
“This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.”

On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump declared that the United States was experiencing a “national energy emergency.” The “harmful and shortsighted policies of the previous administration,” he wrote in an executive order, had left the nation’s energy resources “far too inadequate,” a situation that “causes and makes worse the high energy prices that devastate Americans.” Since then, Trump has attempted to use the emergency declaration to speed up permits for fossil fuel development and bolster the nation’s power grid with more fossil fuel resources.
Almost two years later, as Trump stares down a midterm election, his claim of an emergency has an ironic ring. The United States is experiencing a kind of energy emergency characterized by high fuel prices, but it is not the one he described when he took office. Not only that, but the executive powers he unlocked with his emergency order have proven useless for mitigating the current crisis and for lowering the high prices he decried upon taking office.
“The genesis of the problem is the war in Iran,” said Gbenga Ajilore, the chief economist at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan economic think tank, who has analyzed Trump’s energy policy. Trump’s attack on the country has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the destruction of refineries and oil fields, which has reduced the global supply of refined fuels like gasoline and diesel. The supply crunch for these refined fuels has been even worse than for crude oil, and has hit wallets harder.
This irony points to a hard truth about how the fossil fuel system works. Even with all the powers available to the executive branch, Trump has not been able to tamp down prices either for petroleum fuels or for electricity. He has been able to muscle through specific oil projects and keep certain power plants open, but the markets for oil and power are so large and complex that these interventions have made no difference in consumer prices. Whether these high prices constitute an emergency or not, there isn’t much he can do about it — short of ending the war in Iran. 
“If you reverse that, it may not drop like a rock, but it’s going to start going down,” said Ajilore. “Outside of that, there really isn’t much to do.”
Electricity: Keeping coal plants running
The practical impacts of Trump’s energy emergency declaration have affected two key parts of the energy system, the areas where the president had the biggest disagreements with the Biden administration. The first was the power grid, where former president Joe Biden sought to deploy large new amounts of solar and wind power even as data centers drove up electricity demand. Trump promised on the campaign trail that he would cut energy bills in half, and he directed federal agencies to “identify and exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them” to facilitate power generation. 
The Energy Department took the order and ran with it. Secretary Chris Wright, a noted champion of fossil fuels, has issued several emergency orders to prevent the scheduled retirement of coal plants around the country. The secretary argued in these orders that strained grid conditions made it necessary to preserve all available power capacity, even though the utilities that ran the plants were trying to shut them down. 
Instead of reducing energy prices, these orders have come at significant costs. In Michigan, keeping the J.H. Campbell plant open has cost ratepayers in the Midwest almost $300 million on net, even though the plant is generating far less power than it did before the order. In Colorado, a utility has had to continue operating a coal plant it was about to retire even though the plant is broken and needs serious maintenance. In many cases, the retiring plants were among the oldest and least efficient facilities in their regions, so keeping them on doesn’t save consumers money even if they do add power to the grid.
It took a while, but the courts have started to question these interventions. In September, after Michigan sued over the coal plant mandate at Campbell, an appellate court blocked the Department of Energy’s order, rejecting the administration’s reading of federal law. The judge in the case also took issue with the administration’s claims of an energy emergency in the region’s grid, writing that Wright’s assertion of an emergency was “unpersuasive” and that his policy “invites frequent federal interventions that … threaten the stability of the energy market.”
“We saw in the Michigan case that the facts just don’t match up with the claims and with the law, and I suspect that in some of these other cases, if not all of them, we’ll see similar decisions,” said Melissa Birchard, the mitigation program director at the Georgetown Climate Center, a research institute based at Georgetown Law School. The state’s utility commission and the regional grid operator both rejected the idea that there was an energy shortage in the region around the Campbell plant.
Crude oil: Drill, baby, drill
The other area where the administration used the emergency declaration to reverse Biden-era policy was in the oil and gas sector. Here, too, there was no critical shortage, as U.S. oil and natural gas production were both near all-time highs. While Biden approved some large drilling projects such as the Willow effort in Alaska, he attempted to block oil leases in the Gulf of Mexico and canceled the Keystone XL oil pipeline. Trump’s executive order attempts to steamroll the environmental and procedural permits that have slowed down energy development in the past — the order directs agencies to use “all relevant lawful emergency and other authorities” to “expedite” the construction of oil wells, pipelines, and other energy facilities. It also seeks to waive the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act wherever possible.
The order has produced a few notable wins for the fossil fuel industry. Earlier this year the Trump administration convened what is known as the “God Squad,” a committee of Cabinet secretaries with the power to override the Endangered Species Act. In a meeting that lasted only a few minutes, the committee waived all species protections for oil and gas drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, a measure that will enable BP to pursue a deepwater rig project known as Kaskida. 
The order also directed the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to speed through permitting for pipelines and other infrastructure under the Clean Water Act, and the Corps last year identified a list of around 600 projects eligible for fast-tracking. It later withdrew that list, but some projects on its permitting database are still tagged with “energy emergency,” such as Enbridge’s Line 5 oil pipeline replacement, a mineral sands mine owned by Chemours, and a natural gas pipeline in Florida. It’s unclear whether and when these projects would have moved forward absent the order, but expediting them won’t do anything to bring down the high prices Trump mentioned in his emergency declaration. The largest of them, Kaskida, is years away from producing oil, and would only produce a small fraction of the oil that moves through the Strait of Hormuz in a normal month.
In addition to Michigan’s Campbell lawsuit, around a dozen states have sued the Trump administration over his original executive order, arguing that there is no energy emergency in the United States. The oral argument in that case is scheduled for October 20, and Birchard expects that the courts will view the “emergency” declaration with the same skepticism as in the Campbell case.
“We see this accumulated effort to declare emergencies,” Birchard said. The question is “whether the courts are going to start saying, ‘Hey, one emergency we might have believed, two emergencies we might’ve believed, but now we’re seeing a pattern of many, many emergencies. How do we set up, you know, a set of facts that really supports that many emergencies?”
Refineries: The weak link
Meanwhile, a separate crisis has unfolded in a segment of the energy system where Trump’s order has had almost no effect. The United States and the rest of the world are experiencing a shortage of refined fuels like gasoline and diesel, which has driven up prices not only at the gas pump but also for major goods that are hauled on diesel trucks. The price of gasoline remains well above $4 a gallon, and the price of diesel is at a historic high of over $6 a gallon. The so-called “crack spread,” or difference in price between refined and crude oil, reached a multiyear high over the summer as well.
The primary cause of this shortage is the war in Iran, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz and destroyed numerous Middle Eastern refineries, but Ukraine’s attacks on Russia have also destroyed several oil refineries. The flow of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz has recovered over the eight months of the war thanks in part to American military escorts for tankers, and countries like Saudi Arabia have also managed to export their oil through other channels, which has prevented a global crude shortage. The problem is that consumers don’t buy crude oil. They buy gasoline and diesel, products that are produced at massive refineries. 
There is little Trump can do to mitigate this rise in prices. Refineries in the U.S. are already operating at maximum capacity to take advantage of high profit margins, and many large refineries have delayed scheduled maintenance so they can keep producing as much fuel as possible while high prices last.
“Refiners are running close to flat out,” said Abhi Rajendran, the head of research at Energy Intelligence, a firm that analyzes developments in the oil and gas sector. “They’re making money, but there’s not really any kind of slack to ramp things up.”
The only solution to high prices would be to produce more gasoline and diesel, but the refinery system isn’t flexible enough to do that. There are only a few dozen major refineries in the country, as opposed to many thousands of oil wells, and each refinery can only produce so much before it needs maintenance. Refineries cost many billions of dollars to build, they break or shut down all the time, and companies like Marathon and Chevron see no reason to construct new ones in the United States. Overall demand for refined products has declined over the past few years as cars grow more fuel-efficient and consumers embrace electric vehicles.“Refined product demand has actually been in decline for a long time,” said Rajendran. “In normal times, [refinery capacity] is more than adequate. There’s no real economic case for new refineries, because if these wars end, then it’s just wasted money.”
Trump’s original executive order mentions refining, but it did not do anything to expand refinery capacity, which has left the president with few good options. He considered a diesel export ban, which would prevent companies from selling American diesel overseas, but backed off after opposition from the oil and gas industry. In any case, it would only have caused a marginal decrease in prices, and might have caused prices to rise further as refiners cut back their production. 
The president’s other efforts, like buying Russian diesel and encouraging states to expand diesel subsidies, will likely have an even smaller impact. The total amount of diesel that Russia has promised to deliver “immediately” as part of Trump’s recent deal is equivalent to less than one day of U.S. diesel consumption.
The upshot is that, absent a breakthrough in Iran, high fuel prices will likely last through the year. While the states that sued Trump over the emergency order argue that steep energy prices themselves don’t constitute an emergency, it seems clear that many Americans feel strained by their gasoline and power bills. A recent Fox News poll found that more than 8 in 10 Americans are concerned about gas prices, while the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index fell this summer to its lowest level on record. Another recent poll, from the Associated Press, found that two-thirds of Americans blame Trump for high costs, while only one-third blamed “factors outside Trump’s control.”

Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Receiver leading the Hinds County jail says officials give him too little money and information
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Hinds County Board of Supervisors President Robert Graham leaned over the wooden barrier dividing the courtroom from the sparse audience inside the federal courthouse in downtown Jackson. 
“This is a waste of time,” Graham said of Tuesday’s hearing about the troubled Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond. 
Technical difficulties with a projector had just led U.S. District Judge Carlton Reeves to pause the proceedings. Reeves had been in the midst of unpacking a thorny dispute over the jail’s budget between his appointed receiver, Maryland-based public safety consultant Wendell France Sr., and Hinds County.
France contended the county was providing him with too little information about the jail’s budget, impeding his efforts to improve unconstitutional conditions at the Raymond Detention Center, the county’s most troubled facility and the one under his direct control. 
“My only recourse was to come to court and say we didn’t approve a budget,” France told the judge. “I’m not sure what else I’m supposed to do as the receiver.” 
Through Nick Morisani, a private attorney hired to fight the federal consent decree, the county claimed it had, in fact, provided France with adequate information and resources. 
But when the court finally got its projector working, Morisani presented Reeves with a spreadsheet showing France had received significantly less money than he requested for salaries and capital improvements. 
The back-and-forth ultimately concluded with Reeves suggesting he would order the county to move detainees out of the Raymond Detention Center if it continues to obstruct France’s efforts to improve the unconstitutional conditions. 
“I’m not sure that anybody needs to be in the RDC period right now,” Reeves said. 
Morisani defended the county, asserting that France had $2 million left over from last year’s budget that he hadn’t spent. To this, France said he had overspent the jail’s budget, citing a line-item for professional services the county spent $3 million on last year despite originally allocating $150,000. 
France said he did not know what caused the overspending. “Tell me what the money is for,” he said. 
The path forward, Morisani said, could be clearer if the receiver would spend the money the county already gave him. 
“Maybe cooler heads can prevail that way,” Morisani said. 
“I don’t know if there are uncool heads around, Mr. Morisani,” Reeves responded. 
A Hinds County Sheriff’s Office van passes by the entrance to the Hinds County Detention Facility in Raymond, Miss., Monday, Aug. 1, 2022. On Friday, July 29, U.S. District Judge Carlton Reeves, placed the center into receivership after citing “severely deficient” conditions at the facility.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Reeves, the county, and Christopher Cheng, an attorney with the U.S Department of Justice, also haggled over how to interpret a 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals order limiting the receivership’s scope. 
At one point, Morisani suggested the county would appeal if Reeves tried to direct its budget – an argument that drew a sharp response from the judge. 
“Well, I know we stayed at the 5th Circuit for over a year, and conditions got far worse,” Reeves said. “We can go back down that path again if that’s where Hinds County is going to drag the court.” 
The contentious hearing came more than a year after France finally assumed operational control of the Raymond Detention Center, a rare move that has occurred in a handful of jails and prisons around the country. 
In that time, the jail has continued to be crowded and deadly. 
“We should not get so tied up in the abstract budget issue that we miss the whole point,” Cheng said. 
In April, three men charged in a shooting at a south Jackson apartment complex were attacked within 24 hours of each other. Two of the suspects were housed in Raymond and a third suspect was housed at the Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility in the Mississippi Delta. 
Over the summer, an 18-year-old was stomped to death in the Raymond jail, just days after he was booked and arrested in connection to a killing at the same south Jackson apartment complex. A video of the beating circulated on social media. 
The county also admitted to Reeves that it was going to miss yet another self-imposed deadline on its main solution to the problems at its Raymond jail: Finishing construction on a new detention center just south of downtown Jackson. 
Reeves asked the county if it was going to hire enough people to staff the new facility. The county admitted it did not have a plan. 
“It’s a national problem, but it seems like when it comes to Hinds County that it’s only a Hinds County problem,” John Hall, an attorney representing Sheriff Tyree Jones, said of staffing at jails and prisons. 
In 2016, the U.S. Department of Justice sued the county alleging a pattern or practice of unconstitutional conditions in its detention facilities. The county and DOJ entered a consent decree with a list of changes to address jail conditions.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Greenwich voters cast ballots and donate food at the polls
text:
Greenwich resident Sandra Walker cast her ballot during early voting Tuesday, where she noticed a food donation bin inside Town Hall.
Walker runs an annual food drive for City Harvest in New York City, but said she didn’t have anything to give at the moment.
“I was sorry about that,” Walker said. “But I will bring food to our local food bank.”
The donation bin is part of a food drive by Neighbor to Neighbor, a local nonprofit which also operates a food pantry in Greenwich.
Neighbor to Neighbor and Republican Registrar of Voters, Fred DeCaro III, say the bin meets potential donors where they are. Thousands of voters are expected to vote during the midterms as food insecurity, they say, has only continued to increase over the last few years.
Residents wishing to make a donation of non-perishable food, can do so at Town Hall during early voting hours through Nov. 1.
DeCaro says 560 people voted on Monday. Putting the bin at Town Hall, he says, just makes sense.
“We realize that we are going to have between six and 8,000 people who are going to come here to vote, and we know we have a very generous electorate,” DeCaro said.
DeCaro said this is the first time the town has held a food drive during early voting, and said he was inspired by a similar effort in Bristol. But he said the town last held a food drive during a special election in 2020, when it sent out postcards to residents. The results, he said, were positive.
DeCaro said they’re now relying on social media to drum up awareness. But a few residents interviewed by Connecticut Public, including a Roman Catholic priest, were not aware of the donation bin.
DeCaro said he’s not sure how many people will end up donating, but so far, he’s excited.
“We don’t know that we’ll have quite the level of participation,” DeCaro said. “But we did fill up the first bin at the beginning after day one, and if I get 14 bins worth of food for Neighbor to Neighbor, I’ll be really happy.”
K. Brent Hill, executive director for Neighbor to Neighbor, said the bin raises awareness of ongoing food insecurity challenges in town. Greenwich, he said, is wealthy, but many residents are unable to afford food.
“We served over 900 households, and that’s approximately 2,200 individuals, and last year we saw a 14% increase in clients that we serve,” Hill said. “So the need is definitely there.”
Hill said changes to eligibility requirements for the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) have also had an impact.
A recent report by Connecticut Voices for Children stated poverty levels across Connecticut have now surpassed pre-pandemic levels. The report stated much of the increase was related to the federal government failing to maintain COVID era benefit increases and projected long term funding cuts.
While some residents like Walker didn’t know about the donation bin, she along with the Rev. Michael Murphy, of St. Michael’s church (which is also hosting an upcoming food drive on Nov. 7) said he knows more people are struggling to get by.
“Maybe not in the immediate area around St. Michael, but certainly in the general area for sure it is, especially with the economy the way it is, it’s gotten very expensive to buy gas and food,” Murphy said.
This story was first published Oct. 20, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. spent nearly $400K on an energy study. Three years after its completion, the state hasn’t released the results.
text:
FIVE YEARS AGO, Massachusetts officials hired the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), a leading global energy firm, to help navigate a complicated problem quickly coming to the fore: how the state’s ambitious climate commitments would impact its electrical grid.  
The expected growth in intermittent energy sources like solar and wind and rising demand for electricity for transportation and heating threatened to strain the state’s ability to deliver power reliably. 
So the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center, a quasi-public state agency, set out to find innovative approaches to improve the electric distribution system. 
The agency inked a $379,000 deal with EPRI in 2021 to host three workshops with the utilities, state officials, and other stakeholders, and submit a white paper to the agency outlining barriers and opportunities for meeting the climate targets. Samantha Gilman, a spokesperson for EPRI, confirmed that the organization submitted the required white paper to MassCEC in 2023 — and was paid the full amount of money for the work.   
That report identified between $27 billion and $46 billion in investments that need to be made through 2050 in electric system infrastructure upgrades alone to connect more solar power, meet increased demand, respond to shifting electric generation patterns, and maintain overall reliability.  
And it noted that the utilities were falling short of the average annual spending required to boost the distribution system by up to $800 million per year to modernize their vast network of substations, circuits, transformers, and other pieces of infrastructure. 
Yet the study has not been publicly released. It’s one of at least three the state has commissioned but delayed or shelved on how it will reach net-zero emissions by 2050 and adapt to the impacts of a warming world.  
The other cases involve a second MassCEC-led report and a high-profile analysis of the net-zero transition sought by Melissa Hoffer, the state’s climate chief. Those studies cost up to $200,000 and $650,000, respectively, putting the total cost of these delayed or buried reports in addition to the EPRI study at roughly $1.23 million. 
CommonWealth Beacon independently obtained a copy of the 2023 EPRI report that MassCEC didn’t make publicly available. When presented with the report, the agency didn’t dispute its authenticity and legitimacy. 
When asked why the report hasn’t been released in the last three years, MassCEC spokesperson Victoria King said in a written statement that “other state processes kicked off shortly thereafter on electric distribution investments, and the focus shifted to more concrete planning efforts being undertaken by the utilities.”  
King didn’t elaborate on what other state processes she is referring to that would render the need for the EPRI report moot, given that the state had already paid for it.   
Evan Horowitz, executive director at Tufts’ Center for State Policy Analysis, said in an interview that reports like these, commissioned with public money and dealing with substantive decision-making around policy choices of this magnitude, “as a matter of law, have to be publicly available, as a matter of principle, should be made public.” 
“Why are you commissioning the reports and then hiding them? One possibility is content-neutral: Different people care about different things,” he said. “The other possibility is it’s not content-neutral, and the findings are somehow concerning or worrisome, and you don’t want the findings to be shared. But then the question is: What are the reports for in the first place if not to provide crucial information?” 
What’s more, all three studies were set to be completed in 2023, 2024, and spring 2025, respectively, the latter of which was some 18 months before this year’s general election.  
Even before Gov. Maura Healey entered the heart of campaign season — one that has been defined by skyrocketing energy costs and affordability issues — her administration has seemed sensitive to the price tag attached to the tens or hundreds of billions of dollars likely needed to support a sweeping green transition.  
Gov. Maura Healey speaks at a press conference related to heating assistance. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon) Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon
Larry Chretien, executive director of the Green Energy Consumers Alliance, said that while he didn’t know about the study or the reason it hasn’t been published, he hopes it’s not being held because the Healey administration is concerned with how the large dollar signs within reports will be perceived.   
Infusing the electrical system with more clean energy and doubling down on energy efficiency would result in savings from reduced fossil fuel use and lower overall demand, resulting in less money spent on the distribution system in the first place, he added. 
“If you run around just telling people it’s too complicated, we can’t deal with it, then you get the ‘don’t look up’ approach, which is when people run away from the tough conversation,” Chretien said. “There are ways of making this understandable. It’s not an excuse that it’s complicated or that the numbers are big.” 
Peak demand in Massachusetts is projected to more than double by 2050, according to the unreleased ERPI report. Without addressing capacity constraints across the distribution system, a doubling of electricity would result in “overloading” distribution feeders, the conductors that transport power, that serve three-fourths of customers in the state, the study found — potentially leading to power outages and equipment damage.  
The steep price tag included in the report lands among a volatile energy landscape in the state. Healey has sought to shield ratepayers from rate hikes and cast the utilities as greedy, but the EPRI study makes the case that there are legitimate significant new investments that the utilities will need to make.  
Burying these findings doesn’t make the problem go away, Horowitz said. 
“If you’re going to spend that much money on reports,” he added, “you better care about what they tell you.” 
In another case, MassCEC hired Somerville-based consulting firm NMR Group, Inc. to study the upfront costs of electrifying and increasing the energy efficiency of existing buildings in Massachusetts.  
“Our plan is to disseminate the findings broadly,” reads a description of the project on MassCEC’s website. 
According to screenshots of an archived version of the webpage that show the project timeline, the report was due in spring 2025, with future updates to come in early 2026 and early 2027. 
Yet in June, the webpage was changed to simply say: “The study started in September 2024 and is expected to be completed early 2027.” 
King, with MassCEC, didn’t dispute the changes on the website, saying that the new timeline reflects “project delays as well as changes in scope” but didn’t provide any explanation for the delays. The request for proposals released by MassCEC in February 2024 allocated $200,000 to this project, though the agency didn’t comment on whether the final total was more or less than that amount. 
NMR didn’t respond to multiple emails and calls seeking comment. 
These two examples follow another previously reported case of the Healey administration seeking to slow-walk or outright avoid the release of reports that would put a large dollar figure on the cost of the green transition. 
Hoffer, the nation’s first cabinet-level climate chief who was appointed by Healey on her first day in office, laid out an 87-page agenda in 2023 detailing her priorities. The first item on that list was an economic analysis of the cost of the state’s net-zero policy and the financial investments required for state officials to consider to meet that cost and dramatically cut pollution.  
Hoffer wanted the report done by the end of 2024. Yet after receiving five bids to conduct this work and selecting Boston-based AECOM to embark on the sprawling study at a cost of up to $650,000, the contents of the report remain unknown to the public nearly two years after Hoffer’s due date.  
In an interview earlier this year as part of a wide-ranging profile, Hoffer indicated that the report has in fact been submitted and she has seen it. The net-zero analysis is “largely informing policy,” she said, but “is still under review.” 
Robert Rio, a former senior vice president at the Associated Industries of Massachusetts who now lobbies on energy issues through his own firm, said that businesses and residents are already at a “breaking point” when it comes to energy costs. 
“Any initiatives from here on,” Rio said, “need full cost transparency to regain the trust of the ratepayer.”

name: National
title: City, state employees are proud of their work but face burnout, harassment
text:
Justin Hubly, executive director of the Nebraska Association of Public Employees, leads a news conference in December 2023 in Lincoln. New national research found high levels of job satisfaction among public employees, but high levels of burnout and harassment at work. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)State and local government employees report high levels of job satisfaction across the country, but face significant rates of burnout and on-the-job harassment.
That’s according to a new national survey of nearly 5,000 public servants across all 50 states released today by The People Lab at Harvard University’s Kennedy School. Researchers say the survey, which includes respondents from hundreds of local governments, provides the nation’s most comprehensive analysis of workplace conditions in local governments.
Most employees reported high levels of job satisfaction: 82% said they were at least somewhat satisfied with their job, while 60% said they were satisfied or very satisfied. 
“That’s good news that people are still kind of proud to say they work for the government,” said Elizabeth Linos, faculty director of The People Lab.
But 40% of employees also reported experiencing at least one symptom of burnout. And 27% said they intended to leave their jobs in the next 12 months.
“You have such a big portion of your public sector workforce that are burnt out on any given day,” Linos said. “…And it’s not the pandemic and it’s not a particular crisis, so to me that says a lot about how much work we have to do to support our public servants.”
States face more budget pressures amid rising costs, slow growth

State employees consistently reported less favorable workforce conditions than their city and county counterparts, with lower satisfaction, lower engagement and a substantially higher intent to leave.
The study initially aimed to survey local government employees, so it includes results from only about 320 state employees, compared with more than 4,400 employees in city, county and other local governments. 
Linos said future analyses would include more state employees to better understand the distinctions between levels of government. She expects the research may mirror polling on public perception of government, which finds people report more faith in their local governments than the federal government. 
“You could imagine a world where being able to see the impact of your work more directly leads to more workplace satisfaction than if you have to kind of make the case for how your work has impact, if you work at higher levels of government,” she said.
In the survey, 35% of employees reported experiencing harassment at work over the past year, defined as being bullied, threatened, attacked or harassed. That included 22% who reported harassment from internal sources such as coworkers or supervisors, while 17% reported harassment from external sources such as residents or the media. Those who reported harassment were far more likely to report emotional exhaustion at work and intentions to leave their jobs. 
Harassment levels were higher among local government employees and employees who identified as female, non-binary or other gender. 
Among those who shared their political party affiliation, Republican and Democratic public servants reported more favorable workforce conditions than independents across nearly every measure. 
Linos said the results should inform policymakers and government leaders alike. Every societal challenge — from transportation to climate change to housing — relies on a functioning public sector, she said. 
“The people of government, to me, are the central component of that capacity,” she said. “So if we don’t understand and appreciate the work that the people of government do, we’re not going to be able to solve the bigger public policy challenges that we’re trying to solve, and oftentimes that work is hidden from the public.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: Delaware
title: Minicucci returns, leads Blue Hens to 23-point victory over Missouri State
text:
Delaware quarterback Nick Minicucci dives into the endzone for his lone rushing touchdown against Missouri State. Photo credit: Dave Reeder
Senior quarterback, Nick Minicucci, returned from a two game absence to lead the Fightin’ Blue Hens (3-4, 1-2 CUSA) to a 61-38 win over the Missouri State Bears (2-5, 1-2 CUSA) at home on October 20.
 
NEWARK, DE — Senior quarterback Nick Minicucci stood behind center Steven Demboski along the numbers near the Blue Hen sideline. Minicucci practiced receiving the snap from the Blue Hens’ starting center while the offense waited for the media timeout to end. A typical pre-drive exercise for a quarterback getting ready to take the field. Minicucci was set to return.
Minicucci led the offense out to the field for their first drive and officially returned after a two game absence. The Blue Hens’ explosive offense returned with him.
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens defeated the Missouri State Bears, 61-38, Tuesday night, earning their first Conference USA (CUSA) win of the season in dominant fashion against their fellow sophomore CUSA member.
“Personally, I was not going to let anyone tell me I couldn’t play, so I was going to do anything possible to get back,” Minicucci said. “I mean I was waking up at 3:30 in the morning to go head over to Star Campus for an hour every morning … I lived in the training room.” 
UD’s signal caller had a slow start in his first on-field reps since leaving Delaware’s final non-conference game against Virginia in the second quarter. 
Minicucci attempted only two passes on the Blue Hens’ first drive and threw a pick-six on the Blue Hens’ second that resulted in a touchdown for Bears safety J.J. O’Neal. Missouri State led 14-7 after the interception late in the first quarter, but Minicucci was spectacular from then on.
Minicucci and the Delaware offense bounced back from the turnover to score on their next drive via a six-yard touchdown pass to Bryson Graves. UD’s defense forced a three and out on Missouri State’s ensuing possession — the only three and out of the half — and returned possession back to the Delaware offense. Minicucci connected with sophomore tight end Scott Moore for a 26-yard score over the middle of the field putting UD ahead in the middle of the second quarter.
“After the first drive, I think Nick really settled in and it was, you know, one of his better games to be honest,” head coach Ryan Carty said postgame. 
The Bears tied the score on a 11-yard pitch and catch between starting quarterback Henry Belin IV and CUSA’s leading receiver, Isaiah Myers, but lost the lead on UD’s next offensive possession which ended in a 33-yard field goal by Tucker Smack. 
Missouri State regained possession with a little over two minutes left in the first half and drove 78 yards down the field in eight plays to score before halftime. Belin and Myers connected once more for the go-ahead score, this time on a six-yard throw and catch. 
The Bears led, 28-24, at halftime and Myers finished the first half with 148 receiving yards on nine catches. Myers finished the game with 11 catches and an FBS season high 242 receiving yards.
The game seemed poised to continue its back-and-forth nature after both teams scored on their opening possession of the second half. Minicucci found tight end Elijah Sessoms in the back of the endzone for a go-ahead score on UD’s second offensive drive and it seemed as though Missouri State would answer after driving into Delaware territory on the following possession.
Belin took the snap on second down and dropped back to pass. The fifth-year quarterback had little time to survey the field before he realized Delaware linebacker Jawarren Corbin was bearing down on him and, while trying to escape the sack, Belin fumbled the football. Sophomore defensive end Brandon Gorham scooped the ball up and returned it to the Bears’ four yard line before being tackled. 
“[Defensive Coordinator Manny Rojas] knew they [were] gonna cut, and the A-gap would be wide open so we called an A-gap blitz and my luck, it came wide open,” Corbin said about the game changing play. 
Minicucci ran the ball in for the score and UD earned its first double-digit lead of the night, 45-35, in the final five minutes of the third quarter. 
Corbin’s play swung the momentum to the Blue Hen sideline and broke the shootout game flow both teams settled into. George Mullins continued the momentum shift with an interception on the Bears’ next drive which led to a Jo Silver three-yard touchdown run. 
Sophomore safety George Mullins celebrates after earning his third interception of the season. Photo credit: Dave Reeder
Corbin earned an interception of his own on the Bears next drive wrapping up a career best day. Corbin finished the game with his first career interception, first career sack, first career forced fumble and a career high six tackles. Corbin started in place of the injured Colin Gallagher.
“It felt great,” Corbin said about his performance. “You never know when your name’s gonna get called and when my name got called, I just prayed that I’ll make the best of the opportunity.”
Corbin’s interception led to Minicucci’s fifth passing touchdown — a three-yard pass to senior Donovan Lewis — and completed Minicucci’s return to play. Freshman Tyler Bell relieved Minicucci with nine minutes remaining in the game and Delaware ahead, 58-35.
Minicucci finished the game with 225 passing yards, five passing touchdowns and a 69 percent completion percentage. Minicucci’s five passing touchdowns tied the program’s single game high — the last to throw five passing touchdowns in a game was Nolan Henderson in 2022 — and tied his personal career high with six total scores. 
Minicucci also etched his name in the Blue Hen history books passing Rich Gannon on the program’s career passing yards list for sixth place all-time and moved into third place all-time in career passing touchdowns.  
In addition to Minicucci’s prowess through the air, Delaware finished with a season high 232 rushing yards. Fifth year runner Jo Silver led the team with 101 rushing yards followed by 58 from fellow fifth year, Kaderris Roberts. Both players scored a touchdown in the game and helped take some of the pressure off Minicucci in his return.
“We have to be able to run the ball when we need to,” Carty said. “We’ve got to be able to set up those plays that we can get big ones on later on, and then we got to take some heat off of Nick, in particular when, you know, he’s coming back from injury. … And so it was really great to lean on those guys, and you know coach Rogers does a great job with those guys. The O-line, you know, blocked their butts off today and really worked together in unison.”
Fifth year running back Kaderris Roberts runs into the endzone scoring Delaware’s first touchdown of the game. Photo credit: Dave Reeder
UD finished the game with 482 total yards of offense and generated 13 explosive plays (passes of more than 15 yards and runs of more than ten) in CUSA’s highest scoring game since 2017.
“Really proud of the execution that we had today. We were so much more disciplined, so much more detail oriented. We were intent. Our sideline was better. Our passion was better. We played more connected. We believed in each other so much better than we did in the past couple weeks, and I think that’s hopefully the start of something that can give us some confidence going into next week,” Carty said. 
The Blue Hens’ will play their next two conference games on the road starting with a game against Western Kentucky on Tuesday, October 27. They’ll follow that with a trip to Kennesaw, Georgia, to take on Kennesaw State before returning home on November 14, to play the FIU Panthers. 
UD is two games behind Liberty for first place in the CUSA standings and have five conference games remaining. Delaware needs three more wins to be eligible for a bowl game.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: New controversies bring fresh disagreements to final RI gubernatorial debate
text:
WPRI's Tim White, left, and Ted Nesi, right, seen from behind, moderate the last gubernatorial debate before the Nov. 3 general election on Tuesday night, Oct. 20, 2026, at Rhode Island College. The three gubernatorial candidates on stage from left to right are independent Ken Block, Republican Aaron Guckian and Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)
The Washington Bridge got only a fleeting mention during Rhode Island’s final gubernatorial debate Tuesday, eclipsed by fresh controversies over tax returns, public polling and federal lawsuits.
But familiar tensions carried through the hourlong event at Rhode Island College, hosted by WPRI-TV 12, as candidates bickered over who was best suited to lead the state.
The latest public poll, released by The Pell Center at Salve Regina University on Tuesday morning, shows Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes with an 11-point lead over independent Ken Block, with Republican Aaron Guckian a distant third. 
Guckian, who has just $7,000 in his campaign finance account, has faced pressure to drop out, including from his GOP primary opponent, Elaine Pelino, who is urging her supporters to vote for Block.
Guckian vehemently rejected a question from debate moderators that his presence in the race was “helping Helena Foulkes win.” 
“That question leads the voters and the public down a road I don’t respect,” Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, said.
He noted his 17% support among likely voters, per the Pell Center poll, was similar to pre-election support for 2010 Republican candidate John Robataille, who narrowly lost to independent Lincoln Chafee.
Guckian turned the tables on Block, calling him a spoiler multiple times throughout the debate, including when he pointed out that Block brought typed notes to the podium. Candidates were told in advance they could not bring notes. 
Block put his papers away after being singled out. But he did not give up other battles so easily, including his insistence that his tax returns were not for public view.
Foulkes repeated her calls for Block to release his 2025 tax information Monday, citing a Rhode Island Current profile piece in which Block refused to share the documents. Foulkes’ campaign shared summary documents from her tax filings with media outlets, including Rhode Island Current, on Monday. Foulkes and her husband reported nearly $3 million in taxable income, before deductions, paying more than $176,000 in state taxes and nearly $713,000 in federal taxes.
“It’s fair for the people of Rhode Island to know what is the financial status of these two men who are running for this office,” Foulkes, 62, of Providence, said of her opponents. 
Guckian has also not released his tax returns, but promised to do so, having just submitted his filings by the Oct. 15 extension deadline. 
Block maintained his stance to not share his tax returns. As a small business owner with multiple pass-through organizations reflected on his personal income statements, Block said sharing the documents could help his business competitors.
“I’ve been plenty transparent,” Block, 61, of Barrington, said when pressed by moderator Ted Nesi why he could not share even top-line summaries of his tax flings without exposing proprietary business information.



Quotation







It’s fair for the people of Rhode Island to know what is the financial status of these two men who are running for this office.


– Helena Buonanno Foulkes, Democratic nominee for governor


WPRI moderators Tim White, left, and Ted Nesi, right, face the three gubernatorial candidates on stage on Tuesday night, Oct. 20, 2026, at Rhode Island College. From left to right are Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, Republican Aaron Guckian and independent Ken Block. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)
Foulkes also faced questions about transparency after a $315 million settlement reached last week between the Department of Justice and her former employer, CVS Health. She served as president of CVS Pharmacy for part of the time covered by a 2024 lawsuit alleging the pharmaceutical giant filled unnecessary prescriptions for opioids. Under the settlement, CVS did not admit any wrongdoing.
Foulkes did not answer directly when asked if she agreed with that statement by CVS. Instead, she reiterated her campaign’s refrain about efforts to cut off pill mill doctors and other drug abatement measures.
“Of course, there’s always more you want to do,” she said. “At the same time that we were cutting off doctors, we were being sued by doctors. We were also being sued by patient advocate groups that we weren’t filling enough of those prescriptions. So it was complicated.”
Gov. Dan McKee hammered Foulkes over her ties to CVS and the opioid crisis during the Democratic primary. 
But Block and Guckian have criticized the Democratic nominee more on policy and ideology than her resume.
Guckian called Foulkes’ housing plan “a con job,” blasting her proposal to use the state millionaire’s tax to set up a low-interest loan program to incentivize developers to build affordable units. Foulkes says the proposal will create 20,000 new homes by 2034.
Yet Guckian and Block both evaded questions about how many new housing units their own housing proposals would generate. Guckian said his proposed “veterans village,” a veteran-specific affordable housing community located near Quonset, would grow like a crescendo, from 5,000 to 10,000 then 15,000 units.
Block offered a range of 10,000 to 30,000 while emphasizing the importance of streamlining permitting and regulation for developers, with buy-in from municipalities.
“Difficult problems often require a lot of prep work before you can actually bring forward an answer that’s going to work,” he said. “There’s a lot of ‘ready, aim, fire,’ I’m hearing over there. But what we really need to do is take our time, lay the groundwork, and we’ll have a much more successful outcome.”
Squabbles over housing plan details, as well as energy and education policies, have surfaced in previous debates.



Quotation







I’ve been plenty transparent.


– Ken Block, independent candidate for governor


But the final debate offered new insight on other key issues, including the controversial 2011 pension reforms led by then-General Treasurer Gina Raimondo. Retired state workers and teachers have denounced the pension cuts, routinely pressing lawmakers to restore the cost-of-living increases that were frozen to shore up the state’s pension system.
Granting that wish comes at a major cost for the state, and it risks some of the progress made toward reducing the unfunded pension liability, according to a 2024 analysis by a panel overseen by the general treasurer’s office.
Block said he would restore cost-of-living increases for those who retired before 2012, and have diminished ability to replace lost pension benefits. He proposed using excess earnings from pension fund investments, not state tax revenue, to fund the COLA benefits.
Foulkes also expressed empathy for the retirees on fixed incomes, grappling with rising costs, but said she could not commit to any pension changes without a better understanding of the financial implications.
“I’m not going to do what politicians too often do, which is stand up here and make a promise I can’t commit to,” she said.
Guckian, who has pledged to cut 10% from the state’s $15.2 billion budget, maintained that savings pulled from government efficiency and incentive measures could be used to help retirees.
“If I don’t do it, I won’t run again in four years,” Guckian said of his proposed cost-savings measures.
Yet Block, whose software engineering firm helps state governments and private governments reduce unnecessary spending, dubbed Guckian’s pledge to cut $1.5 billion in state spending a “fantasy.”
The pair relayed contradictory accounts of a phone call between them in January. Block said Guckian called to ask for his support and advice in how to save money in the state budget. Guckian said he called Block only to ask if he was going to run, at which point Block said it was unlikely because of his business.
“He quit on moderates, he quit on Republicans, and he’s going to quit on you,” Guckian said, alluding to Block’s two prior runs for governor under two different parties.
Block’s response: “I’ll let the voters figure out which one of us is more believable here.”



Quotation







He quit on moderates, he quit on Republicans, and he’s going to quit on you.


– Aaron Guckian, Republican nominee for governor on Ken Block


What the candidates did agree on
There were brief moments of agreement among the three.
Each answered yes when asked if the state should reexamine its sports betting laws, given the potentially harmful and addictive implications, especially for young people. 
They shared openness to demolishing the “Superman” building in downtown Providence if the redevelopment plan to turn the vacant office building into apartments does not come to fruition. All supported holding back third-grade students who aren’t proficient in reading, based on a model started in Mississippi. 
Each enthusiastically supported subjecting magistrate judges to the same independent, merit-based review by the Judicial Nominating Commission already used for Superior and Supreme Court judges. And none wanted to give law enforcement agencies free rein to use of Flock cameras, though they differed in how much regulation is necessary for automated license-plate readers.
Block and Foulkes both supported a line-item veto, which would empower the executive branch to influence specific items in the state budget, while Guckian said he did not think the effort would be successful.
Block and Guckian both expressed support — Block’s more reserved – for a natural gas pipeline expansion project that would widen pipelines in Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Foulkes was opposed, emphasizing the importance of renewable energy sources instead.
Asked who they would support in the lieutenant governor’s race, Foulkes backed Democrat Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos while Guckian named Republican challenger John Loughlin.
Block refused to answer.
Early voting runs through Nov. 2, ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: VTDigger
title: Picture future you: How young teens can explore their potential at VSAC’s career and STEM fairs
text:
Think back to middle school. Maybe you hadn’t thought much about life beyond high school, or maybe you hadn’t spent much time outside of your community or home state. What if someone encouraged you to think bigger and more broadly about your possibilities? What if you could find a way to reach out of your comfort zone and into your curiosities? 
That’s the experience LaKysha Patnode had when she was a student, and exactly what she’s hoping to pay forward for other Vermont kids when she spends a day at VSAC’s Career and STEM Fair.
LaKysha Patnode and her colleague, Ryan Gillen of Champlain College, at their booth at the career fair.
LaKysha says she didn’t know what she wanted to do and she definitely wasn’t thinking about college when she was at Colchester Middle School and the Center for Technology in Essex. But her experience with VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, and her VSAC outreach counselor (who, in LaKysha’s words, “believed in me 100% at a time in my life when I didn’t know what I wanted to do or how to get there”) encouraged her to explore and try. 
With help, LaKysha went to Champlain College, graduated with a bachelor’s degree in computer networking and cybersecurity, and went on to get her master’s degree, also from Champlain, in information security operations. 
Now, LaKysha is an information assurance advisor at nuHarbor in Burlington. In plain terms, that means she works in cybersecurity, on data security and privacy. When she presented at VSAC’s Career and STEM Fair in Lyndon earlier this month, LaKysha was excited to see so many students engaged in her session, where she provided hands-on demonstrations about cybersecurity hygiene and how to protect their privacy when, for example, they download a new app to their phone. “Most kids don’t think about checking the permissions associated with that,” she said. “Does every app need access to your microphone, camera, and all your contacts? No!” 
LaKysha says it’s meaningful to her to have the opportunity to help broaden horizons for the next generation. “I feel like my journey is a testament to what can happen when people see potential in you at a young age,” she added. “Because of VSAC’s GEAR UP, I was thinking bigger about my own possibilities. Then, Champlain and nuHarbor’s partnership is why and how I ended up here. All along the way, I was encouraged to make connections and reach out of my comfort zone. Opportunities like these career fairs really help. Even if the students don’t realize it, these are the building blocks for how you move forward professionally.” 
A day of hands-on experimentation nudges students along
Courtney Skar is a school counselor at Montgomery Elementary School, which serves children through 8th grade. She says that participating in the fair helps her students relate things they are learning at school to real life examples and picture themselves as adults. Everything at the event is a conversation-starter, helping kids think about the connection between their interests, the skills they notice about themselves, and potential future careers. 
“I had to pull students away from the hands-on parts,” she laughed. “There were robotics and coding opportunities, where kids could steer robots, medical exhibits where students were able to wear a team vest and go through a scenario, a LEGO racetrack where they could understand the dynamics that made cars go faster or slower, and a science area where they were building cells and talking about how things work. At this point in the year, we’ve started some conversations about their future that get them thinking, but the career fair is a real catalyst that escalates ideas and reinforces where they can go and what they can do.” 
Courtney, like LaKysha, benefited from VSAC’s support when she was in school. As a participant in VSAC’s Talent Search for first-generation students motivated to attend postsecondary education, Courtney leaned on the support the program provided to navigate the college search process and to visualize her own career. “That experience is what led me to work in schools, and it’s such a neat experience to help realize those connections for the next generation,” she said. 
“When your students come back feeling a little more like they can see themselves as their future adult selves, that’s a win,” she added. 
Self-designed bikes propel students to think about engineering careers
A little over a week later, VSAC hosted nearly 400 students on the Castleton campus of Vermont State University for a fair of similar format in the Rutland area. 
James Holden is an engineering instructor at Stafford Technical Center. He brought four students with him to the event to showcase their mechanical engineering projects, which are unusually engineered bicycles. 
Each Stafford student succeeded in creating their own design and translating it into a machine shop project and then a final product. The students were motivated to finish their projects for the fair and excited to showcase them there. 
About 170 middle schoolers donned helmets and rode the bikes, which ranged from one with caster wheels to encourage rotation and drift, one with hand pedals and feet steering, and one with handlebars similar to a zero-turn mower and a treadle pedal. These unique engineering creations were a hit at the event, with middle schoolers able to ride them and learn about why they were engineered the way they are. They were also able to see Stafford students—not much older than they are—take pride in their projects. 
“Not everyone feels successful in every subject or in every learning environment,” James said. “When we show the STEM fair attendees that we can offer learning in a different way and with projects kids can really see themselves in, they start to see how they succeed.”
All told, nearly 1,200 students from 27 middle schools across Vermont explored STEM identities and future career pathways at two Career and STEM fairs, in the Northeast Kingdom and Rutland. VSAC’s Career and STEM Fairs are held annually and produced in partnership with Vermont State University, Careers CLiC, the Vermont Department of Labor, and the J. Warren and Lois McClure Foundation, as well as the many local employers and organizations who gave their time to engage and inspire students. 
Looking ahead, VSAC will host a virtual career panel for middle school students across the state in November. If the Career and STEM Fairs are any indication, Vermont’s extraordinary students will bring curiosity, energy, and enthusiasm from start to finish!

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults.
