name: California
title: Big California state worker strike set to begin today
text:
A tablet at the counter of the Department of Motor Vehicles in Fresno on Oct. 2, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela for CalMatters




Perhaps today is not the best day to go to the DMV.
California state workers are planning a one-day strike today in multiple cities including Sacramento, San Francisco and Los Angeles. They’re protesting what they say are unfair labor practices by Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration. The work stoppage could affect services at the DMV, unemployment offices and other departments. 
SEIU Local 1000 represents about 100,000 workers employed in dozens of agencies across the state. They’re accountants, government analysts, nurses, IT workers, custodians and more.
The union has been negotiating a new labor agreement since its contract expired on June 30, and is demanding better pay, more affordable healthcare coverage and more flexibility to work from home. 
CalHR, the state agency that handles state labor negotiations, said it “remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table.”
With as many as 95,000 union members eligible to strike, you may experience some delays in government services. DMV offices might close early, according to a department spokesperson. State parks could be affected, too, though rangers are not represented by Local 1000. Hearst Castle in San Luis Obispo County, for example, adjusted its tour schedule to accommodate people who already have reservations.
This may not be ideal from a customer service standpoint, but union president Anica Walls urges Californians “to give our employees some grace.”
The union is taking a risk with the strike, noted former state Senate President pro Tem Don Perata. He supports labor and wants the union to get a good deal. 

Perata: “Somebody ought to pay attention to them. The strike costs those people a lot more than anyone else.”

Read more.
More on the labor fight: Local 1000 was once in Newsom’s corner, kicking in $1 million to help him fight a recall campaign. CalMatters’ Adam Ashton has more on what led to today’s strike, including the wage cuts that Newsom demanded to get out of a budget jam. 



Join CalMatters, AAJA Sac, ABC 10 and The Sacramento Observer for a free VotingMatters event today in Sacramento. The event enables attendees to learn and discuss the upcoming election and focuses on the ballot propositions and insurance commissioner race. Register here to attend in person.
Other Stories You Should Know


Taxing the rich, but not just billionaires


Students at an eighth-grade science class at Lawson Middle School in Cupertino on Aug. 26, 2025. Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters




The billionaire tax may be drawing the most attention on the ballot, but another tax-the-rich proposal will face voters in November too, reports CalMatters’ Carolyn Jones.
Proposition 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. Voters first approved the tax in 2012, when it was first touted as a temporary measure, and then renewed it again in 2016. Now, supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
The tax generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year. In flush years, it makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers, according to the California Teachers Association.
But at 13.3%, California already has the highest personal income tax rate of any state. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, an anti-tax advocacy group, questioned whether schools need more money given their declining enrollment.

Susan Shelley, the association’s vice president: “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does.”

Read more.



Where lives depend on levees


A repaired section of the levee near Isleton on the Sacramento River on April 1, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




A state audit has found that California water officials aren’t doing enough to make sure levees in the Central Valley are adequately maintained to protect against flooding. But water managers argue that stepping in to oversee more than a thousand miles of levees and flood control structures isn’t so simple, writes CalMatters’ Rachel Becker. 
The audit warns that nearly a third of agencies maintaining flood control levees on the tributaries of the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers have been carrying out “unacceptable routine maintenance.” It also said the state’s Department of Water Resources has not taken over levee maintenance when local agencies fail to do so, despite it being required under state law.
But state water managers said it would take at least $165 million more per year than they or local agencies currently spend to fully address the issue. The department also told the auditor that levee risk depends on the threat, the levee’s performance, and what it protects — not just its maintenance.
Read more.



And lastly: Tell us your car crash story


Loren Chow holds a photo of his wife, Jenny, who died in a 2022 semitruck collision, at the home they shared in Los Altos on Aug. 19, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




This week, we brought you the latest installment in License to Kill, a series investigating the staggering rise of deaths on California’s roads. 
Our reporters are now hard at work on their next story, and they could use your help. 
If you have a story about someone being killed or badly hurt by a driver who wasn’t prosecuted, we want to hear from you.

The state’s mandate forcing a California school district to leave a Nevada high school athletic program because of Nevada’s exclusion of transgender athletes is loaded with logistical challenges, writes Xavier Jimenez, who helps manage a ski shop and lives in Truckee.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Proposed Kansas nuclear reactor stock drops 50% after critical report calls it a ‘money pit’
text:
California-based Deep Fission began drilling bore holes in Parsons, shown here as of March 2026, as part of the company's pilot project to put a nuclear reactor one mile underground. A recent report from Iceberg Research cast doubts, which the company denies, on Deep Fission's viability. (Photo by Deep Fission)TOPEKA — The company behind a pilot nuclear project near Parsons is under fire after a report said it is underestimating costs, overestimating the project’s energy efficiency and promoting an unrealistic timeline.
The report by Iceberg Research, which assesses publicly available financial information to look for irregularities, called Deep Fission a “money pit.”
Deep Fission said in a news release that the report is “highly misleading” and contains “numerous distortions, inaccuracies and mischaracterizations.”
The stock market took note, however, and the California-based company’s stock, listed on NASDAQ as FISN, has dropped more than 50% since the report came out Sept. 24.
The report deepened concerns of members of Prairie Dog Alliance, an activist organization demanding more information about the nuclear project and raising concerns that it is untested technology.
“Given how speculative and novel their approach is, we are alarmed by the state of Kansas and their acceptance of Deep Fission’s activities,” said spokesperson Marjorie Reynolds. “The local county commission should be demanding a more open, inclusive public participation process.”
Reynolds said her organization wants Kansas governmental entities to develop a set of rules that specifically addresses Deep Fission activities. In addition, they are calling on Deep Fission to “halt its Gravity micro-reactor siting pending resolution of all allegations.”
Central to the report was Iceberg’s analysis that Deep Fission misrepresented the cost of energy that would be produced by its reactor. Before the company made its initial public offering in June, Deep Fission said its levelized cost of energy, or LCOE, would be $50 to $70 per MWh, Iceberg reported.
After that, Deep Fission dropped the reference, according to the report. Using figures in the prospectus, Iceberg calculated the cost of energy would be between $148 to $289 per MWh.
Such a cost to provide energy wouldn’t be competitive with other energy options, Iceberg said, pointing out that most data centers being built are choosing to use natural gas for power.
Reynolds said in an email to Kansas Reflector that the report and subsequent stock price fall, as well as possible legal actions, raise concerns the company won’t be able to complete the project.
“As a direct result of the Iceberg Research report, there are now five different law firms conducting investigations on behalf of alarmed Deep Fission stockholders alleging that Deep Fission employees have possibly engaged in securities violations,” she said. “Will this lead to a further investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission?”
Iceberg’s report also questioned the proposed timeline for the Deep Fission reactor to be online. 
“FISN claims it can secure Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approval in less than a year,” the report said. “Yet it has already struggled with the less demanding Department of Energy (DOE) process, missing the program deadline while at least four peers have already completed it.”
The report criticized Deep Fission’s statements that it has a large customer pipeline, pointing to the undeveloped industrial park in Parsons as having “doubtful demand” for a nuclear reactor.
In its response to the report, Deep Fission said it stands behind information it has publicly disclosed.
“The Company has been consistently transparent with its shareholders, its regulators and the public about what its technology can do, the progress it has made and the work that remains, including the risks and uncertainties inherent in developing and commercializing nuclear energy,” the company statement said.
The company said it is reviewing the report and evaluating options, including potential legal remedies.
Iceberg Research said in a disclaimer statement that readers should assume it has a short position in the securities and “therefore stands to realize gains in the event that the price of the covered securities declines.”
Also in the disclaimer, Iceberg said its reports are opinions, “which we have based upon generally available public information, field research, inferences and deductions through our due diligence and analytical process.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Yellowstone receives record $105 million gift for infrastructure, conservation, access
text:
Crystal Heter, president and CEO of Tallgrass; Gov. Mark Gordon; Interior Secretary Doug Burgum; Sean Klimczak of Blackstone and Lisa Diekmann, president and CEO of Yellowstone Forever, sign an agreement Oct.17 establishing the conservation and stewardship fund at the Old Faithful Inn at Yellowstone National Park. (Yellowstone National Park photo)Yellowstone National Park and Tallgrass, a Colorado company building an AI power hub near Cheyenne, Wyoming, have launched a $105 million conservation and stewardship fund for the country’s first national park, calling it the largest single private gift in the agency’s history.
The park announced creation of the fund this morning in conjunction with its nonprofit conservation partner, Yellowstone Forever, and Tallgrass, a Blackstone Infrastructure portfolio company. The fund will establish a permanent source of support for long-term stewardship, the groups said.
Among the projects the effort will fund is a $35 million visitor center at Norris Geyser Basin, Steven Davidson, senior vice president at Tallgrass said in an interview with WyoFile.
“There’s no place for you to sit and engage with a ranger directly,” he said of the sprawling basin. The center will offer opportunities for experiences that are “a bit more interactive,” he said.
The fund will advance conservation and research, invest in infrastructure and expand opportunities for Wyoming residents and students to visit the 2.2 million-acre reserve. The groups said the donation will establish the Tallgrass WYld Yellowstone Initiative, named for the company that’s been operating in Wyoming for more than a decade.
“The focus is for Wyoming,” Davidson said. “If you are a Wyoming kid, family, we are going to target these programs for you. Let’s be proud and selfish for Wyoming kids.”
Gov. Gordon called the gift “extraordinary” and said it will help Wyoming students better connect with Yellowstone.
“Ninety-three percent of the park is in Wyoming, and so few of our school kids in Wyoming really know what a remarkable place that is,” he said in an interview. That’s because people in Wyoming who love the outdoors “already all have favorite places. We’re blessed with beautiful mountains almost everywhere, and so unless you have a sort of a sense of the history and (of) some of the remarkable stuff about Yellowstone, why would you skip over the Winds or the Absarokas?”
Learning about the migration routes of Yellowstone wildlife puts the park in context with the rest of the state, he said. The education and access elements of the initiative “gives us an opportunity to really talk about the connectivity with all the other great parts of Wyoming,” he said.
At Norris, more interpretation provided at a visitor center would allow visitors to talk about “more than just: You came and saw,” he said. “Talking about the uniqueness of that area is a valuable thing for visitors at the park generally.”
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called the investment “historic,” and said in a statement it brings together “the best of American enterprise and conservation.”
“We’re grateful to Blackstone, Tallgrass and Yellowstone Forever for their partnership and extraordinary commitment,” his statement reads.
For Blackstone, the gift “reflects our belief that infrastructure investment can and should be a force for good, helping us invest in Yellowstone’s future and the growth of the communities that surround it,” Sean Klimczak, the company’s global head of infrastructure said in a statement.
Lisa Diekmann, president and CEO of Yellowstone Forever, called the gift a transformational investment.
“It gives us the ability to meet urgent needs today while building enduring support for the research, education, stewardship and visitor infrastructure that will protect this park for generations to come,” she said.
The gift comes at a time of change and challenge for Yellowstone, the country’s first national park. The Park Service estimates $1.2 billion in deferred maintenance and repairs. Barclay Trimble just assumed duties as Acting Superintendent of Yellowstone National Park. He replaced Cam Sholly, who left his post after eight years.
Tallgrass, a “multi-commodity infrastructure” company based in Colorado, operates more than 10,000 miles of pipelines. Early this year it received approval to build an AI data center south of Cheyenne. Google will be Tallgrass’ partner, according to Measured AI, a recent switch from original partner Cruso.
Tallgrass is building the gas-fired Cheyenne Power Hub for the 1.8 gigawatt project. Tallgrass’ $7 billion project is located on more than 1,000 acres in the Switchgrass industrial park south of Cheyenne. The data center will occupy more than 700 acres, according to plans. The data center has faced pushback from rural neighbors in Laramie County concerned about lost views and potential water contamination.
On Monday, Tallgrass President and CEO Crystal Heter said, in a statement announcing the donation to Yellowstone, that the company is proud to strengthen the park’s connection with the next generation.

name: Nevada Current
title: NV voter fraud is shockingly rare, bears scant resemblance to Trump’s portrayal, analysis shows
text:
Led by President Donald Trump, Republicans for years have relentlessly alleged mass voter fraud without producing any evidence of its existence. (Screenshot from Trump campaign's video of Minden, Nevada rally in September 2020)There have only been 11 instances of election fraud in Nevada – out of nearly 9 million votes cast –  over the last decade, according to a new report from UNLV. Most have those resulted in criminal convictions.
Led by President Donald Trump, Republicans for years have relentlessly alleged mass voter fraud without producing any evidence of its existence. 
Jim Marchant, the Republican candidate for Nevada Secretary of State, has repeatedly claimed that the state has “had fraudulent elections since 2008.”
Using data compiled from the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, Brookings Mountain West and Lincy Institute at UNLV published a report last week analyzing election fraud that showed 85 cases since 1998 in Mountain West States, which includes Nevada, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah. 
Election fraud includes buying votes, duplicating votes, false registration, fraudulent use of absentee ballots, illegal ‘assistance’ at the polls, impersonation fraud at the polls, and ineligible voting.
A separate Brookings Institute analysis of the Heritage data two years ago noted that in order to create an election fraud database the “Heritage staff had to go back decades in time where there have been hundreds of millions of votes cast and a very small number of cases of election fraud have been found, none of which affected election outcomes.”
The analysis of the Heritage data also noted that during the 10-year period where 11 instances were found in Nevada that there were 14 elections and 8.5 million votes cast.
Of the 11 cases identified between 2012 and 2021 in Nevada, 10 resulted in criminal convictions.
The analysis found that in over nearly three decades in the Mountain West Region there have been 30 cases across the region of duplicative voting, which is the highest type of election fraud cases among the five states. 
Four cases in Nevada involved duplicate voting and five involved false registration – one case used both. 
Among the duplicate voting cases included Donald Kirk Hartle, a Clark County man Republicans showcased in attempts to spread misinformation and unfounded claims about massive voter fraud. 
The Nevada Republican Party had promoted Kirk’s story that his wife Rosemarie, who died in 2017, had cast a ballot in the 2020 election. But it was Hartle who voted under his late wife’s name.
Hartle pleaded guilty in 2021.
Two Nevada cases over nearly three decades involved a “non-citizen.”
One was a Las Vegas resident named Biqui Diana Parra Rodriguez who “illegally obtained personal information” of a person and “registered to vote under her name in 2011 and in 2012,” according to a 2014 press release from the Nevada Secretary of State. 
The Las Vegas Review-Journal reported at the time that she had registered as a Republican and a Democrat. 
The other case involved Hortencia Segura-Munoz, who registered Republican, cast ballots in the 2008 and 2010 elections, and was convicted in 2014.
The report found two cases of ballot petition fraud in Nevada with one criminally convicted and another sent to a diversion program. 
There was one case in all five states that had a conviction for buying votes, and it was in Nevada. 
Stephen Gregory Zority was charged in 2017 for illegally paying a woman “with gift cards and cash for registering Republican voters in Clark County.”  He was convicted in 2021.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: House members took a big step to boost recycling. It’s the Senate’s turn.
text:
Jon King50 years ago, Michigan changed the way it handles empty beverage containers, but over the years we’ve fallen behind. We’ve fallen behind on the technology. We’ve fallen behind on the policy. We’ve fallen behind on the long trail of evidence that points to better, more effective solutions.
Michigan’s bottle bill adds a 10-cent deposit on canned and bottled carbonated beverages sold in the state, but we rarely think about what happens to the containers after we return them to the supermarket. We empty them, we bag them, we let them pile up and eventually we slowly feed them into a machine and get a refund.
But what happens to the bottles after they’ve gone down that conveyor belt? Believe it or not, that’s just the beginning of the process, and every step of the journey carries costs.
The Bottle Bill requires distributors to collect and process returned containers. For the first 13 years of the Bottle Bill, unclaimed deposits were used by distributors to build and operate the program on behalf of the State.
That made sense, because container recycling is worth the effort, but it isn’t cheap. It requires cleaning, sorting, trucking, storage, and processing. It requires logistics coordinators,  mechanics, drivers and warehouse staff.
Unfortunately, in 1989, the Legislature changed the Bottle Bill into an unfunded government mandate on distributors, withdrawing investment in the infrastructure and operating expenses needed to make the Bottle Bill work.
Beverage container return area at Meijer in Howell. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
In other words, the state withdrew support for investment in only this specific recycling program.
Instead, state government hit Michigan employers with a giant and costly mandated requirement – and for almost 40 years it hasn’t paid for it.
That’s a problem worth addressing, because over the course of those nearly four-decades, the technology, the knowledge, and the best practices when it comes to container recycling have all developed by leaps and bounds. It’s tough, though, to capitalize on new technologies and approaches without investment.
That’s why Michigan lawmakers deserve credit this year. They’ve recognized the need to invest, and they’re taking steps to make it happen.
Republicans and Democrats in the Michigan House of Representatives worked together earlier this year to pass a bill that will pump desperately needed investment into state-mandated recycling programs.
House Bill 5517 provides a small, targeted tax credit to help distributors maintain and modernize the infrastructure needed to pick up, store, clean, sort, crush, transport and  remake containers returned for the 10-cent deposit.
The legislation provides Michigan’s beverage distributors with a tax credit equal to ½ cent per returnable container sold – a modest responsible fix that addresses a decades-old funding imbalance within the current deposit system.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Michigan’s beverage makers and distributors have invested significantly in deposit return program infrastructure, including new processing lines in metro Detroit and Grand Rapids, purchasing lower emission transportation vehicles, and much more. Throughout the decades, and despite disinvestment by the state, they’ve kept up their end of the bargain. Thousands of local employees, including union labor at facilities across Michigan work hard at recycling.
This legislation ensures these Michigan recyclers can continue to make the investments needed to carry out the costly state-imposed system of bottle deposit returns.
 It’ll fund more efficient programs and cleaner systems and operations. It’ll pay Michigan workers who are keeping our state and our neighborhoods clean.
The bill passed with an overwhelming bipartisan 94 to 12 majority. Now it’s gone to the Senate where it’ll need approval before heading to Governor Gretchen Whitmer for a signature.
We’re committed to recycling and urge the Michigan Senate to take swift action too.

name: California
title: Why are California state workers so mad at Gavin Newsom? Spoiler alert: Pay cuts
text:
In summary
California state workers say they’re tired of governors balancing the budget “on their backs” and are beginning a statewide state strike today.


The state workers who are planning the first-ever statewide walkout in 44 years this week once were on much better terms with their boss, Gov. Gavin Newsom.
SEIU Local 1000, state government’s largest union, kicked in one of the single biggest  checks to Newsom’s 2018 campaign, a $500,000 contribution. It followed up with $1 million more to help Newsom fend off a recall in 2021. 
That alliance made sense for the union, especially considering that Newsom’s Republican opponents were much less friendly to labor.
But today the two sides are far apart with Local 1000 preparing its first statewide strike since signing its first collective bargaining agreement in 1982 as it accuses Newsom of bad-faith bargaining. Its members are trolling Newsom online with memes likening him to infamous Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, caricaturing him as a sci-fi villain and mocking his presidential ambitions. 
What happened to the labor love fest?
At the bottom line, Newsom was stingier with public employees than voters who think of him as a labor-aligned Democrat might assume. He demanded wage reductions from state workers over three years of his tenure and limited raises to 3% in financially flush times. He also took a hard line in calling employees back to the office four days a week after many grew accustomed to working from home during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
“The fact the state has refused to bargain in good faith is what got so many members active,” said Anica Walls, president of Local 1000. The union represents about 100,000 workers. “They’re just kind of tired of always feeling the budget is balanced on state employees’ backs.”
That feeling goes back more than 20 years for some California public employees. Like many workers, they accepted furloughs and wage reductions during the Great Recession. That period lasted from 2008 to 2013 under former governors Arnold Schwarzenegger and Jerry Brown. But Brown then pressed for more concessions, including an additional paycheck deduction to fund retiree healthcare and higher worker contributions toward pensions.
Union leaders had high hopes Newsom would end the trend of temporary pay cuts and givebacks, as shown by the campaign contributions he gained in 2018.  
It didn’t work out that way.
Here’s a look at some of the issues that led the state’s largest public employee union to break with Newsom and put him on the spot with its first statewide strike.
Money, money, money
California state government spending surged during the Newsom administration, climbing from $201.4 billion in the 2018-19 financial year to $321 billion in Newsom’s 2025-26 budget. That’s a 59% increase.
Payroll is up, too, but at a slower rate. Compensation for state workers hit $25.2 billion in 2025, about 32% more than 2019.
To be sure, Newsom gave bonuses to many public employees — especially prison staff — when the state was flush with money just after the pandemic. But he’s been thriftier with wage increases. They topped out 3% in most contracts.
Meanwhile, Newsom at two key moments pressed public employees to accept pay cuts. The first happened in the panic of the early pandemic when the governor braced for a severe recession. Unions agreed to wage cuts of roughly 9% and in exchange workers received days off that they could save and bank for later. 
The second wage cut happened in 2025 when the governor sought to close a severe budget deficit. Most unions, including Local 1000, again accepted deals for two years of wage reductions in exchange for days off. They also agreed to defer raises until next year. 
One union did not accept those terms, the California Association of Professional Scientists. The scientist union was the first to strike against Newsom, holding a three-day walkout in 2023. It viewed the contract it negotiated in 2024 as critical, and it didn’t want to give up its raises when Newsom asked.
But, just before an agreed-upon raise was supposed to take effect last summer, it learned that the state budget didn’t include money for the wage increase.
The conflict again angered public employees who expected a pay boost. The union appealed to state lawmakers, who funded the raises in a follow-on spending bill.
“We negotiated that collective bargaining agreement in good faith and believe a deal is a deal,” said the union’s vice president, Justin Garcia. 
Working from home
California government changed overnight during the pandemic, when Newsom ordered employees to work from home unless the nature of their job required them to report to a prison or state hospital. That was a major cultural adjustment for a bureaucracy known for time cards, rigid schedules and a refusal to pay for workers’ office parking.
The Newsom administration commended workers for making the change and it publicized a dashboard that showed state employees were just as efficient at home as they were in the office.
But as time passed Newsom said he grew concerned that remote work stifled the in-person collaboration that he argued was important for a successful organization. He called employees back to the office two days a week in 2024, and four days a week beginning last summer. 
Many state workers want more flexibility. They point to a 2025 state audit that found the state could save $225 million a year by allowing more remote work. 
Retirement plans diverge
State workers hired before 2013 have a better retirement deal than public employees who joined since then. That issue is not front-and-center in the Local 1000 strike, but it’s bubbling up as newer workers learn about their colleagues’ benefits. 
Former Gov. Brown championed the law that trimmed pension benefits. It came out of the Great Recession, which caused California’s major pension funds to hemorrhage billions of dollars and highlighted a generous pension enhancement that former Gov. Gray Davis had signed into law a dozen years earlier. 
Now, public employees work longer and pay more of their own income toward their pensions. Newsom last month vetoed a bill that would have sweetened retirement formulas for police and firefighters, a proposal that likely will return to Newsom’s successor in the near future. 
“What people thought before was a cush state job because we had good retirement, the ability to retire with a pension, that does not look the same to people who came after 2013,” said Walls, the Local 1000 president.
Where else can they go?
Local 1000 and other state government unions might be frustrated with Newsom, but they tend to get a better hearing from Democrats than Republicans. Schwarzenegger, after all, championed four failed ballot measures that would have stripped them of their power and influence. 
“They (unions) have to make converts in the church in which they worship,” said Don Perata, a union-aligned Democrat and former Senate president pro tem who battled with Schwarzenegger. 
He praised Local 1000 members for carrying state government through the pandemic and for taking on difficult jobs to serve Californians. He recognized governors and lawmakers have to pass balanced budgets, and said that means they should be more careful in running up the cost of programs that might eat away at funding that could be used to pay public employees better. 
“It’s past time to show there’s recognition and not just by blowing smoke at them,” Perata said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Tax reform group to offer plan despite request to delay release
text:
The citizens group hoping to reform Connecticut’s oppressive property tax system will release its recommendations Monday, hoping to force candidates for state offices to take positions during the final push toward Election Day.
The Connecticut Citizens Assembly on Property Taxes declined a request from state Comptroller Sean Scanlon to withhold its proposals, which members teased would require bold action and political courage, until after the election.
“Bringing out ideas like this now is a good vehicle for conversation,” assembly member Bob Bailey of Vernon, a finance director, said Tuesday, adding that voter concern about Connecticut’s affordability makes the report particularly timely.
Organized by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, Yale University and the University of Connecticut, the 100-member assembly has been working since early July to better understand the only major levy cities and towns can raise.
Cities and towns here generated $12.5 billion via property taxes in 2022, about $400 million more than state government raised through its largest revenue engine, the income tax, according to the Department of Revenue Services’ last major tax analysis.
But state government also leans on many other taxes. It generates billions annually from levies on retail sales, business earnings, real estate transactions, utilities, cigarettes, inheritances and certain cash gifts.
Unlike the income tax, though, the property tax is regressive, meaning its rate is not adjusted to reflect a payer’s earnings or wealth. Critics say it disproportionately burdens middle-class families and small businesses, stifling economic growth and creating wide disparities in the quality of schools and other services communities provide.
According to the Tax Policy Center at the Urban Institute and Brookings Institution, only New Hampshire and New Jersey relied more heavily on property taxes than did Connecticut in 2021.
Assembly members were tight-lipped in early September about specific reforms under consideration. But they warned the group was eyeing bold proposals, not small reforms unlikely to make much impact.
How candidates react to these ideas could tell voters a lot, said James Farrell, an East Haven accountant and assembly member. 
“Their input is valuable on how they’re going to address it,” he added.
Comptroller says tax reform ideas should wait until after elections
But state Comptroller Sean Scanlon said there’s a downside, as well, to rolling out bold reform ideas now.
“I just am not sure it’ll get a fair hearing” in the final two weeks before an election, he said, adding that home stretch of many campaigns generates heavy rhetoric, distortions and exaggerations.
The assembly had planned to report in late September, but a Nor’easter that struck the state Sept. 26 forced the group to cancel a key meeting and push its schedule back.
Still, the citizens’ group has spent months crafting solutions, the comptroller added. “I want what’s best for them and for their ideas to be taken seriously.”
But the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, in cooperation with Yale and UConn, organized the assembly and its schedule specifically so members could use their ideas to challenge political candidates if they chose, CCM Executive Director Joe DeLong said Monday.
Scanlon, who is seeking reelection and supporting fellow Democrat Ned Lamont’s bid for a third term, said he did not have discussions with gubernatorial campaigns about delaying the assembly’s proposals.
Lamont holds double-digit leads in recent polls over GOP gubernatorial challenger Ryan Fazio, who has centered his campaign on charges the governor has allowed Connecticut to unaffordable for many households.
A spokeswoman for the Fazio campaign, Hannah Lemek, said the Republican nominee would welcome a chance to discuss the assembly’s new property tax reform proposals.
Taxpayers “are pleading for help,” Lemek said. “They’re telling us what they need, and so we need to listen to them.”
Lauren Gray, spokeswoman for the Lamont campaign, also said it didn’t seek to delay the assembly’s report.
“The governor looks forward to reviewing proposals from Citizens’ Assembly once they are released,” she said.
Created using lotteries to assemble a broad, cross-section of residents, the panel was allowed to govern itself completely, DeLong said, adding he nonetheless agrees with the assembly’s decision to release proposals soon.
The state’s heavy reliance on property taxes “has befuddled elected policymakers in Connecticut for generations,” DeLong said. “We owe it to these [assembly members] to give them a reaction, a response. I think it actually helps democracy.”

name: California
title: What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3
text:
In summary
Voters first passed the tax in 2012, then renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.


If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.
Prop. 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”
Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. 
Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.
The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. 
Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.
In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.
Union’s big push
The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”
The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.
The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.
Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. 
“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.
The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.
‘Not sustainable’
Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments and declining enrollment. 
“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”
In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. 
California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.
Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.
That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. 
“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”
He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.
“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

name: California
title: Trump’s crackdown on immigrant voting in California is a ploy to influence election
text:
The federal crackdown on voting by non-citizens in California is obviously aimed more at having a political impact than combating serious crime.
It bolsters President Donald Trump’s repetitive, but unproven, claims that Democrats have stacked the political deck by allowing non-citizens to vote. It singles out California, a deeply blue state and a whipping boy in elections across the nation.
Finally, it occurs as Californians are marking mail-in ballots for the Nov. 3 midterm election and deciding the fate of Proposition 39, which would require voters to show eligibility credentials.
Last week, Trump’s Justice Department sued California and Los Angeles County, after demanding that state officials set aside ballots from 20,000 registered voters it says may not be eligible to vote.
The demand was rejected, and on Monday the Justice Department filed charges against 28 immigrants who are lawful permanent residents, alleging they were either illegally registered to vote or had voted in an election.
“Today’s charges demonstrate why that lawsuit is so important,” Acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters. “It’s about preventing voter fraud that cancels out the votes of U.S. citizens. Enforcing federal law increases the integrity of elections.”
California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said those who vote illegally should be prosecuted but added, “28 out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically. It’s 0.0001% of all the registered voters, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Meanwhile, in a courtroom in Oakland, opponents of the federal demands were arguing that the Trump administration’s actions violate the federal Voting Rights Act by discouraging legitimate voters from casting ballots.
It has been obvious for months that the White House was planning some sort of intervention as voting began in California. The state’s size, its blue politics, its large immigrant population — both legal and undocumented — and its ultra-convenient voting procedures make it a target.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who manages the Justice Department’s Los Angeles office, said it’s possible state officials will face federal charges.
“They are being complicit in non-citizens voting in our elections,” Essayli said. “And as they were warned last week, not only is it a civil violation, but they could also face criminal consequences for that conduct if they knowingly process ballots from non-citizens once we’ve informed them who the non-citizens are.”
The roots of this conflict were planted in 1978, when then-Gov. Jerry Brown and a Legislature controlled by Democrats removed restrictions on absentee ballots. For decades, voters had to persuade election officials they needed such ballots because they were unable to vote in person.
Democrats believed making absentee voting much easier would increase turnout and help them win elections. However Democrats failed to exploit the change in the 1982 elections, while Republicans used it to elect George Deukmejian governor and Pete Wilson as a U.S. senator.
Nevertheless, Democrats continued to incrementally loosen voting laws, including automatic registration through the Department of Motor Vehicles, same-day voter registration and mailing ballots to all registered voters.
Election officials say they take pains to ensure that only eligible voters cast ballots. It’s a system that could be manipulated, but there’s absolutely no evidence of any organized effort to do so.
That may be why Prop. 39, which would require voters to show proof of eligibility — and probably end the state’s all-mail system — is not doing well. Drafted by Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a political gadfly, Prop. 39 has been failing in all major pre-election polls, most recently drawing just 42% in a Citrin-POLITICO survey.
DeMaio and other Republicans may hope that the Trump administration crackdown will help Prop. 39 prevail, but it’s unlikely.

name: California
title: California decision to pull Tahoe schools from Nevada athletics imperils more than trans athletes
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Xavier Jimenez
Xavier Jimenez helps manage a ski shop and lives in Truckee. He previously led a team of software engineers in the Bay Area.


Most winter mornings in Truckee begin the same way. The house is cold, coffee warms my hands, and the Caltrans cameras glow on my phone. Kingvale, Donner Lake, the Summit — one by one. I’m looking for the same things every parent up here looks for: how fast the snow is stacking up, whether trucks are sliding, whether the road still looks like a road.
Living in the Sierra teaches you to pay attention. As a former ski instructor responsible for kids on the mountain in every kind of storm, I learned early that the map is not the territory. Conditions change fast. A morning that looks manageable can turn into a whiteout by lunch. You don’t guess. You prepare. 
That’s why the state’s mandate forcing Tahoe-Truckee Unified School District to leave the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association and join the California Interscholastic Federation has landed with such a thud. 
It started in April 2025 when the NIAA adopted a new rule requiring eligibility in sex-segregated sports to be based on the gender assigned at birth. That didn’t line up with California law, which lets students compete according to their gender identity.
After public outcry, Tahoe-Truckee Unified’s school board ultimately voted to stay in the NIAA anyway — mostly because it’s the only athletic conference that doesn’t force kids over Donner Pass all winter. After that, a former student filed a discrimination complaint. Even though no transgender athlete was competing in the district at the time, the state said the board’s decision violated California protections and ordered Tahoe-Truckee Unified to leave the NIAA by the 2026–27 school year.
It’s not that families oppose inclusion — California’s protections for transgender students matter deeply, and every student deserves dignity and a chance to belong. And yet, the conflict created by the NIAA’s eligibility rule is real.
For decades, Truckee and North Tahoe teams have traveled east into Nevada, away from the Sierra crest. CIF competition sends them west over Donner Summit — one of the most volatile mountain passes in the country — sometimes before dawn, in months when chain controls, zero visibility and sudden closures are routine. CHP’s own social media posts show cars in ditches, jackknifed trucks and warnings not to underestimate conditions.
A meteorologist recently described the summit as “a mess” and urged people not to travel unless necessary. That was in April. 
January is worse.
Through a public records request, our community obtained correspondence showing how the state’s decision took shape. On July 3, 2025, the California Department of Education encouraged the district and the former student to resolve the matter locally — even noting that a successful resolution could end the investigation. Later that month, the department asked the student for specific examples of harm caused by NIAA participation. They did not identify any documented incidents, records show.
What’s apparently missing is any sign that the state examined how suddenly changing athletic conferences would affect the rest of the student body: the hundreds of rural athletes who rely on sports for stability, connection and opportunity. The very students who would be asked to travel over a high‑elevation pass in winter, sometimes multiple times a week.
The investigation feels thin because it is thin. And thin investigations make bad policy.
The consequences extend beyond transportation. Under CIF’s standard calendar, soccer moves into winter. In Truckee and North Tahoe, winter isn’t a mild inconvenience — it buries fields under several feet of Sierra cement. Indoor space is already limited. Moonshine Ink reported that 90% of North Tahoe’s girls soccer players also play another winter sport.
This switch doesn’t just shuffle schedules. It could wipe out an entire program. 
Tahoe-Truckee Unified has formally requested a two‑year transition, citing hazardous winter travel, the need to purchase winter‑capable athletic vans, and the need to secure overnight safety plans for teams stranded when the pass closes. The district also warns that entering CIF mid‑cycle will likely result in “independent status,” leaving teams without consistent league schedules or postseason opportunities. 
For seniors, there is no do‑over. They don’t get the season back.
For my son Rio and his classmates, these next two years should be about growing as athletes and teammates — not becoming test cases for a plan that doesn’t fit the place they live. 
Our community remains committed to keeping Tahoe-Truckee Unified in the NIAA until the state can show it has a plan that protects every student — transgender students seeking fair participation, and rural students whose safety depends on transportation decisions grounded in Sierra reality.
Every parent here has already accepted a deeper truth: Of course we’re not sending our kids over Donner Pass in the teeth of winter. Not until the adults responsible for this mandate can show us how they intend to keep them safe. 
That’s not defiance. That’s responsibility.

name: California
title: Vital Central Valley flood control levees are poorly maintained, state watchdog finds
text:
With California bracing for a wet winter, the state auditor warns that nearly a third of local agencies maintaining vital flood control levees in parts of the Central Valley have been performing “unacceptable routine maintenance” — some of them, for years. 
The audit says the state’s Department of Water Resources “has not followed state law requiring it to take over the maintenance of levees” when local agencies fail to do so — and urged it to start. 
But state water managers at the department pushed back, saying the audit “portrays a fundamental lack of understanding of the complexities of flood management” and draws too direct a link between routine maintenance and flood risk. 
Taking over maintenance can cost tens of millions of dollars up front “that must be weighed against other investments that may yield greater risk-reduction benefits,” the department said in a letter responding to the audit. 
Others question whether the state is up to the job. “They can’t even take care of what they have now, and they want them to take over everybody else?” said Tom Engler with MBK Engineers, who works as the district engineer for a dozen Northern California reclamation districts responsible for levee systems. 
The audit warns that inadequate maintenance increases the risk that these aging, earthen embankments fail, endangering more than a quarter-million people, 133,000 buildings worth nearly $40 billion dollars, as well as hundreds of thousands of acres of farmland. Historically underserved communities and socially vulnerable people are especially at risk. 
Is the state up to the job?
California oversees 1,600 miles of levees and other flood control structures on the main stems and certain tributaries of the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers, as part of the State Plan of Flood Control. 
But that responsibility is layered, built on federal requirements and topped by state oversight. Sandwiched in between are the levee and reclamation districts, private landowners and local governments that conduct maintenance under agreements with the state. 
Some note that, in fact, the state already manages some of the levee systems in Butte and Sutter counties that are on the auditor’s list of local agencies performing unacceptable levels of maintenance.
“Tell me how that makes sense,” said Engler. “[I]t would take a lot more people, manpower and equipment to get it all done.”
Department of Water Resources spokesman Jason Ince said this highlights the audit’s overreliance on maintenance inspections to assess risk. According to Ince, of the three levee systems under the responsibility of DWR’s Sutter Maintenance Yard on the list: 

One standalone levee within the floodplain of the Feather River channel “is entirely surrounded by water when the Sutter Bypass experiences high flows,” and doesn’t function as a critical flood control structure. 
Another includes a segment likely made redundant by the 1968 construction of the Thermalito Afterbay near Lake Oroville. The state began petitioning the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to de-authorize it in 1984, Ince said. 
Problems with the third, along the Wadsworth Canal, stem from its original construction and require working through environmental regulations protecting the threatened giant garter snake, California’s official state snake. 

The department told the state auditor that levee risk depends on the threat, the levee’s performance, and what it protects. It also disputes the auditor’s count of people and properties at risk because it “misses critical context on other flood infrastructure in the region and that location’s hydrology,” Ince said.
“Maintenance contributes to performance,” the department said in its letter, “but it is not the only or always the most effective action for reducing risk.” 
Engler, whose districts include some on the list, had mixed reactions to the audit, which he said he was still reviewing. 
“It has some things that I would definitely agree with, and it has a lot of things that I just go, ‘Who did they talk to about that? That’s totally off base,’” he said.
He echoed state water managers that most threatening issues for levees aren’t maintenance deficiencies, but long-term structural problems dating back to their construction generations ago. 
He also said some of the agencies on the “unacceptable” list shouldn’t be there. Many, the audit reported, were listed because of chronic problems with burrowing rodents and overgrown vegetation — which can obscure serious issues, or cause dangerous erosion when trees fall in storms. 
But some, he said, were named simply because of timing: the livestock the local agencies enlist to graze down plants and brush hadn’t finished before the inspection, and the levee managers didn’t update the state after they were done. 
“We know our levees are in good shape. We know the maintenance has been done,” he said. “Our rating never goes from unacceptable back to acceptable, just because we forget to report.”
Dwindling funds, deteriorating levees 
Maintaining levees built generations ago — clawed at by ground squirrels and buffeted by water — is pricey. 
State water managers said that they have provided $400 million to local agencies for levee maintenance over the last 10 years. But they told the auditor it would take at least $165 million more per year than they or local agencies currently spend to fully address levee maintenance in Central Valley areas over the coming decades.
Maintenance matters, the auditor said, “because it reduces the likelihood that levees will fail and cause flooding that would damage property and endanger lives.” 
Instead of rising, the audit reports, state funding is dwindling. 
Gov. Gavin Newsom earlier this fall vetoed a bill to create an annual repair fund for 1,100 miles of aging levees in the Delta, about a third of which fall under the State Plan of Flood Control, according to the Legislative Analyst. The rest are privately or locally owned. 
In his veto message, Newsom said that funding in this year’s budget made the measure redundant. But the money comes nowhere close to the audit’s recommendations. 
The state’s program to help local agencies pay for levee repairs isn’t keeping up either. 
The audit reported that since 2012, state water managers have “been unable to complete repair projects as of August 2026 for 14 of the 48 critical sites,” meaning these issues could reasonably cause a levee to fail during a flood or high-water event. Most of those sites had been on the repair list since 2023, the audit said. 
The program’s money is running out, and the department “does not have additional funding available to repair projects for new critical sites that it will inevitably identify,” the audit said.
Lawmakers also in recent years failed to provide the funding needed to continue a state-run Flood Maintenance Assistance Program. Without it, Meegan Nagy, general manager of Knights Landing Ridge Drainage District said, local agencies “now lack funds to work on deferred maintenance and execute larger projects.”
Nagy said the district was counting on the Flood Maintenance Assistance Program to help repair erosion that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had identified over long stretches. Now, without that money, the district has only the funds to continue repairs through next year. 
Failing to fix these issues puts federal disaster recovery funds at risk. 
“Sites that we have been proactively repairing under this erosion program can quickly become critical during high water,” Nagy said. That, she added, “could quickly lead to potential levee failure during a flood event.” 
Adam Borchard, executive director of the California Central Valley Flood Control Association
urged lawmakers to take the audit “seriously and earnestly invest in our critical flood control infrastructure in the Central Valley.”
Engler said the fault of inadequate funding lies squarely with the California Legislature. 
“Nobody cares about flood control because it’s not that big, hot, sexy topic,” Engler said. 
That could change this winter. “Hopefully, it doesn’t pan out like it could,” he said. “But we’ll see.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: How Nevada working families get stuck with the tab when politicians pledge ‘no new taxes’
text:
Under Nevada's tax structure, the lowest-income families pay 11.9% of their income in state and local taxes. Meanwhile, the wealthiest 1% pay just 2.8%. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)The 1980s called. It wants its tax policy back.
The One Big Beautiful Bill delivered tax cuts favoring the wealthy while slashing billions in Medicaid spending, threatening healthcare access for millions of Americans. A year later, everyone’s costs are up except the top 1%. 
In Nevada, 31,000 enrollees are expected to lose care in the next 3 years. Forecasters anticipate $100 million in lost hospital revenue, likely driving up healthcare prices. Henderson Hospital, already struggling, just closed its neonatal intensive care unit.
With the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies, Nevada Health Link plans face another 17% increase. 
Meanwhile, Joe Lombardo has pitched his reelection campaign on promises to expand high-quality health care for families, fund our education system, and raise no new taxes.
Which begs the question: who’s going to pay for it? In Nevada, working families are the ones footing the bill.
According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy’s Who Pays? study, Nevada’s lowest-income families pay 11.9% of their income in state and local taxes. Meanwhile, the wealthiest 1%, who benefited greatly from the One Big Beautiful Bill, pay just 2.8%.
Our state continues to struggle with education and childhood poverty, problems made harder to address by a system that asks the least from those with the most.
But to Lombardo’s credit, he’s pulling from a proven playbook. The only problem is that history has exposed its flaws.
After Ronald Reagan cut the top marginal income-tax rate by 42%, his successor, George H.W. Bush carried the anti-tax message onto the campaign trail.
In one of the most infamous moments of his political career, Bush uttered five words: “Read my lips: no new taxes.” His economic advisors warned this would make governing impossible. 
Surely enough, the bill for a decade of tax cuts came due. Wealth soared under the Reagan years, but the benefits were far from equal.
Wages for many workers were backsliding, the federal debt ballooned, and in 1990 the country entered a recession. Meanwhile, the Balanced Budget Act threatened mandatory budget cuts to programs like Social Security and Medicaid if Congress failed to address the newly created deficit.
In the end, he helped pass the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990. Taxes were raised, the base was furious, and Grover Norquist, patron saint of the no new taxes pledge sworn to by Republicans from coast to coast, endured many sleepless nights.
While the headlines were incessant, Bush hadn’t actually raised taxes for the majority of Americans. He raised the top individual income tax rate by 3%, which touches households earning $621,000 or more, an unimaginable sum for most Nevadans.
At the same time, he preserved life-saving programs and expanded the earned income tax credit. Today, Lombardo faces a familiar dilemma.
No-new-taxes pledges leave elected officials with fewer options to fund public services, even as strains on those services grow. So when harm comes to the dinner table, we’re told the pantry is empty.
This is especially troublesome, because Nevadans need investment now more than ever. Working families haven’t gotten a moment of peace since foreign and trade wars launched a full-scale invasion into our monthly budgets.
Tariffs have turned everyday necessities into a luxury. Healthcare costs have gone up while care goes down. Homes sit on the market because they’re just too expensive. Gas prices skyrocket while billionaires launch real rockets into the sky, funded by taxpayers.
At the heart of this conversation is a simple question: Who pays, and what do they get in return? Families paying into the system are told there’s not enough money to keep hospitals open, while corporations and wealthy investors continue benefiting from generous tax subsidies.
If you own a starter home in Henderson, you’re asked to play by a different set of rules than someone with a hillside view of Lake Tahoe. Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Despite possessing a fortune approaching $300 billion, Brin paid no federal income tax in 2019, 2020, or 2023. That doesn’t mean he paid no taxes, but it does mean he’s held to a different standard than a doctor or nurse.
At the same time, Brin is pouring unimaginable sums of money into opposing nurses’ efforts to fund healthcare in California. Meanwhile, Nevada happily hands Google hundreds of millions in generous tax breaks for data centers, and Brin inherits depreciated tax breaks on his $42 million home.
As Nevada approaches the next legislative session, lawmakers can reimagine how the state raises revenue and what it chooses to fund.
That includes closing tax loopholes for big tech companies, ending property tax depreciation carveouts for wealthy residents like Brin, ending LET exemptions for ticket sellers who rob our children trying to affordably see Olivia Rodrigo in concert and their schools, and implementing sustainable revenue sources that can support education, housing, and jobs. 
Washington State offers a roadmap. Facing similar funding challenges without an income tax, lawmakers enacted a capital gains excise tax to help fund early-childhood care.
Parents across the state already contribute their sweat equity to raising the next generation of Nevadans. It’s time we ensure private equity contributes equally. 
As a proud parent, I want my boys to grow up on a playground where everyone gets their turn on the swingset. 
President Barack Obama has weighed in recently, saying Lombardo’s opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, will hold the line on taxes. 
But holding the line doesn’t mean that billionaires get to turn Nevada into another Delaware or victim of Citizens United. It means holding them accountable to contributing equally to the public services that made their fortunes possible. 
Public attitudes towards revenue are more nuanced than the slogans suggest.
Recent polling by the State Revenue Alliance found that more than three in five voters believe paying taxes is important because it funds their communities’ needs and gives everyone a better shot in life. And an even larger share, 79%, believe Big Tech companies like Google should pay more in taxes.
Bush acknowledged something that Lombardo is trying to obscure: Governing requires paying for the supports families rely on.
So when Governor Lombardo promises no new taxes, what does that promise actually mean for the bartender, nurse, or school teacher already paying a greater share of their income than Nevada’s wealthiest residents?
It doesn’t mean their costs stop rising.
It means families continue paying some of the highest childcare costs in the country, access to quality education remains out of reach, and mothers drive hours away for life-saving medical care.
The 1980s called. Don’t pick up the phone.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah energy providers have ‘mature’ cybersecurity protocols, but there are gaps, audit says
text:
Transmission lines lead away from the coal-fired Intermountain Power Plant near Delta, Utah on Monday, Feb. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah’s largest electricity provider has “mature” cybersecurity tools, but the Utah Legislature may consider additional oversight for it and municipal utilities after legislative auditors determined that direct federal and state supervision on the protocols is limited.
The only state agency that oversees cybersecurity for Rocky Mountain Power — which sells about 78% of the state’s electricity — is the Utah Public Service Commission, legislative auditors said in a report presented to lawmakers on Tuesday. But, that governance is limited to commissioners’ rate-setting processes. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Multiple levels of government have jurisdiction for ensuring adequate electricity cybersecurity. The federal government regulates cybersecurity for large portions of the electrical grid, including large scale generation and transmission,” auditors wrote. “States can provide oversight of cybersecurity for electricity distribution, the stage where power is delivered to customers at lower voltages.”
Rocky Mountain Power didn’t have much to say in its audit response, saying that the company “takes cybersecurity extremely seriously and remains committed to maintaining a strong, resilient, and continuously evolving cybersecurity program designed to protect critical electric infrastructure and support the reliable delivery of electric service to customers.”
“We believe the report provides a fair and balanced assessment of the company’s cybersecurity program and accurately reflects our commitment to protecting critical infrastructure, managing evolving cyber threats, and maintaining reliable electric service for the communities we serve,” the company wrote.
However, unlike large-scale electricity providers, municipal power systems — which provide about 16% of Utah’s electricity — have opportunities for improvement in issues, auditors wrote.
“This finding is concerning because cyberattacks have the potential to disrupt the delivery of electricity such as that seen in Ukraine in 2015,” the audit says, referring to the 2015 Russian cyberattacks on Ukraine power which impacted 225,000 customers. “Cyberattacks can also affect related systems and open the door to future attacks on power systems.”



Let us know what you think...


 


None of the five municipal power systems auditors interviewed used independent third-party assessments to evaluate their cybersecurity controls. They didn’t develop, document or regularly practice incident response plans either, auditors wrote. 
“While attacks can be disruptive, the impact on municipal power systems is generally limited to individual power systems unless simultaneous attacks occur,” according to the audit. 
Lacking plans for incident response could contribute to longer lasting power outages if a cyberattack were to occur. Those extended disruptions could affect critical infrastructure like hospitals, drinking water and sewage treatment systems, the audit says, as well as schools and transportation. 
But, because utilities administered by municipalities cover the service of limited areas, they may be able to recover faster if they have manual controls available at substations.
Amid those gaps, legislative auditors recommend looking into whether state involvement is necessary “to encourage municipal power systems to improve cybersecurity practices.”
“This could include such things as having the Cybersecurity Commission or Cyber Center help develop model incident response plans, requiring municipalities to adopt baseline cybersecurity controls, or encouraging adoption of best practices by reducing potential liability for those that do adopt best practices,” the audit says.
