name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s Amendment 3 would allow some abortions. Whether women could get them is unclear.
text:
An abortion procedure room pictured on March 3, 2025, at Planned Parenthood in Columbia (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).After Missouri banned nearly all abortions in 2022, Valerie Weaver began noticing a troubling change in some of the pregnant patients she cared for in Kansas City.
They were arriving to her sicker. Some had developed infections, blood clots or other complications while waiting for treatment. Some were so ill they required general anesthesia rather than an epidural or spinal, increasing the risks of their care.
Weaver, a certified registered nurse anesthetist with a doctorate in nursing practice who cares for high-risk obstetric patients, said the problem was particularly acute in situations such as a woman’s water breaking before her fetus could survive outside the womb. 
“That law made it so where we couldn’t care for the mother until she had an active threat against her life,” she said.
In 2024, Missouri became the first state to overturn an abortion ban at the ballot box. Weaver said her patients now have a choice they lacked under the ban: End a pregnancy before an emergency develops, even if there is still a fetal heartbeat, or continue the pregnancy.
But Weaver fears those conditions could return after the Nov. 3 election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amendment 3 would repeal the reproductive rights amendment Missouri voters approved in 2024 and reinstate an abortion ban with exceptions for medical emergencies, as well as certain fetal anomalies and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest within the first 12 weeks. It would also enact a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors, which is already banned in state statute. 
Supporters insist those exceptions would protect women who need abortions.
But some physicians, attorneys and patients who experienced Missouri’s previous ban say the exceptions could prove difficult to implement in practice, leaving doctors uncertain about when they can intervene.
 Medical emergencies and fetal anomalies

The first TV ad for Stop the Ban, the campaign to defeat Amendment 3, features a Missouri mother who faced a dangerous pregnancy complication. 
“I needed an abortion to save my life,” she said. “And now politicians are trying to take that right away from us.” 
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway in a recent interview hosted by the Family Research Council, a conservative nonprofit, called the No on 3 campaign messaging “a flat out lie.”
Dr. Sarah Florence, a board-certified family medicine physician from Fenton who spoke in support of the amendment at the Midwest March for Life in April, said the language isn’t written to sacrifice women’s health.
“Sometimes the mother must be separated from the baby in order for her life to be saved, and sometimes for the baby’s life to be saved as well,” she told The Independent this week. “ But that never, ever, in medicine, requires the additional step of intentionally killing the child first.”
Stickers saying “repeal and replace Amendment 3,” referencing the 2024 abortion rights amendment, are distributed during Missouri Right to Life advocacy day at the Missouri State Capitol on March 26, 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Molly Duane, litigation director at Amplify Legal, the litigation arm of Abortion in America, said cases in other states show why exceptions likely not work as supporters intend. Duane represents women in several states who she said were denied or delayed lifesaving pregnancy care because of an abortion ban.
The proposed language in Amendment 3, Duane said, “is an absolute disaster zone.”
“It has all of the problems that the abortion bans in other states where I have litigated have that have caused people to be denied care for ectopic pregnancy, miscarriages, fatal fetal diagnoses, conditions like pre-eclampsia, water breaking prematurely, bleeding and septic infections,” she said. “It has all of those problems, plus more.” 
For example, she said, Amendment 3 defines a fetal anomaly as a “structural or functional abnormality in the unborn child’s gestational development that would make life outside the womb impossible.” The use of the word “impossible,” Duane believes, would exclude many devastating anomalies, because in most cases the infant could be born alive, but die soon after. 
Florence, when asked about this language, said doctors can’t see into the future to know how a pregnancy will progress.
“I am confident that there are doctors that don’t hesitate to talk about a congenital abnormality being incompatible with life,” she said. “And that’s used to justify abortion.”
 ‘Cruel and inhumane barriers to healthcare’

Erika found out she was pregnant with her second child in November 2022, months into Missouri’s near-total abortion ban. She agreed to speak to The Independent on the condition that she be identified by her first name, citing concerns for her privacy and the charged political climate around abortion in Missouri. 
On a trip to Disneyland, Erika, her husband and her toddler posed with the ultrasound photos next to Lightning McQueen. She thought up the perfect caption for a post about her pregnancy: “Ka-Chow! Not all kicks come from Route 66.” 
But she never made the announcement. 
A few days later, at Erika’s 20-week anatomy scan, she learned her son, who she named Easton, had a rare fetal anomaly. 
“I’m going to be honest, it’s not good,” she recalls her doctor saying. “But I’m going to take care of you.” 
But her doctor later determined she could not provide an abortion in Missouri without risking prosecution. Erika and her husband eventually flew to a hospital in Washington, D.C.
There, she had an abortion. After she delivered her son’s body, she held him.
“I didn’t have to watch him suffer and suffocate to death,” Erika said. “He was able to be given the compassion and the dignity that I believe he deserved.”
After Missouri passed the reproductive rights amendment, Erika and her husband decided to try again. Her doctor reassured her that if anything went wrong this time, she could get care without leaving the state.
“Amendment 3 is incredibly personal to me,” she said from her Kansas City home, where she recently brought home her infant daughter. “Stopping this abortion ban means that future families won’t experience the cruel and inhumane barriers to healthcare that I did.”
 Rape and incest exceptions

Amendment 3 would allow abortions in cases of rape or incest for survivors who end their pregnancy within 12 weeks. 
Lawmakers removed a proposed police-reporting requirement before placing the measure on the ballot.
Julie Donelon, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Organization to Counter Sexual Assault, has concerns with the 12-week deadline. It often isn’t long enough for survivors to discover they’re pregnant, process the trauma of the assault, and then seek out care, she said.
“We know that providers won’t be readily available,” Donelon said. “That could really push that deadline of the 12 weeks exception for rape and incest survivors.” 
Right now, Donelon said MOCSA points any survivors who are pregnant and want information on options to Planned Parenthood, not hospitals. 
Last year, all 46 abortions performed in Missouri hospitals were listed as medical emergencies, meaning none were elective, according to data from the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. 
Susan Frelich Appleton, a professor at Washington University School of Law who also serves as a member emerita of the board of directors of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, believes abortion would become virtually non-existent under Amendment 3, including for survivors. 
“How does a provider determine that the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest? As we see from recent news stories, it’s often not a clear-cut matter,” she said. “It’s such a judgment call that it would be very risky to hang your hat on the rape and incest exception.”
Amanda Sanders, a spokeswoman with the Yes on 3 campaign, said Amendment 3 explicitly carves out protections for survivors while also regulating the providers who would care for them.
“None of this is about delay,” Sanders said. “This is about what happens to a woman if something goes wrong.” 
Subhead: Would abortion providers remain open?
By May 2022, the month before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Missouri enacted an abortion ban, only one Planned Parenthood clinic in the state was still offering abortion. The rest stopped providing the procedure following decades of regulations enacted by the legislature that they said made it impossible to do their jobs.
Sanders said the 2024 amendment left Missouri as the “wild west of abortions,” pointing to dozens of abortion regulations that were struck down as unconstitutional under the  reproductive rights amendment.
“An abortion clinic that has no oversight is a back alley abortion,” she said. “And so that’s what we have right now under the status quo.” 
Amendment 3, she said, restores “common sense” regulations. 
After the 2024 reproductive rights amendment passed, Planned Parenthood and the ACLU of Missouri sued the state, arguing that about 40 of these statutes and regulations on the books in Missouri were unconstitutional because they created obstacles to care without making procedures safer.
In June, Jackson County Judge Jerri Zhang struck down dozens of regulations, including a 72-hour waiting period, special licensing requirements for abortion providers and hospital admitting privileges. She upheld a requirement that medication abortion be administered in person, and that only doctors can perform abortions or prescribe medication abortion.
Zhang wrote in her order that several safeguards remain in place even absent of all the regulations set by the legislature. 
The ruling is under appeal. If Amendment 3 passes, it would take effect 30 days after the election. 
Michael Wolff, a former chief justice of the Missouri Supreme Court and dean emeritus at Saint Louis University School of Law who was featured in a TV ad opposing Amendment 3, expects the court orders blocking the old abortion restrictions to fall away. That could leave Planned Parenthood providers unable to offer even abortions allowed under the exceptions.
The Missouri Attorney Generals Office in a statement said Amendment 3 would affect the ongoing litigation between Planned Parenthood and the state, “likely to the benefit of Missouri’s existing health and safety regulations.”
Dr. Jennifer Smith, an OB-GYN in St. Louis, addresses abortion rights advocates gather for a canvassing kick-off event on Aug. 29 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
Dr. Jennifer Smith, a St. Louis OB-GYN who is campaigning with Stop the Ban, said patients who qualify for an exception could still struggle to get care at hospitals, especially if the procedure isn’t covered by insurance. Planned Parenthood clinics have partnerships with abortion funds that help cover costs for patients. 
“We need Planned Parenthood to be functioning, because people can’t get this care in their hospital,” Smith said.
It’s unclear what services Planned Parenthood could provide under Amendment 3. In a brief statement, Missouri’s Planned Parenthood affiliates said Amendment 3 would “force women to leave the state to receive basic care.” 
“As a practical matter,” Wolff said, “if I were advising the abortion providers, they would have to stop.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Spending tops $20M in Washington state’s hottest congressional race
text:
(Photo illustration by Getty images)Candidates in Washington state’s most closely watched congressional race have spent more than $10 million entering the final weeks of the campaign.
Meanwhile, outside forces are shelling out nearly twice as much to sway voters in the 3rd Congressional District contest that will help decide which political party controls the U.S. House in 2027.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who is pursuing a third term, has raised $8.8 million and began October with roughly $640,000 on hand, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission.
Her opponent, Republican state Sen. John Braun, has hauled in $3.2 million and started October with $1.1 million available.
Large sums are getting poured into the race by Democratic and Republican organizations, and an array of political committees, at least one tied to President Donald Trump. 
Collectively they have committed in excess of $15 million on advertising, mailers, text messages, phone calls and direct outreach to voters in Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Wahkiakum and Skamania counties, and a touch of Thurston County. 
Though much of that sum has been spent, groups on both sides of this electoral battle are reserving air time for television ads leading up to the Nov. 3 election.
They’re dumping money into this one race in the southwest corner of the state because of the stakes. With Republicans outnumbering Democrats in the U.S. House by a slim margin, 218-214, the two parties are competing hard in close races, and recent polling shows the two candidates deadlocked.
As evidence of the importance, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Lousiana, will be in Washington on Wednesday to join Braun at a campaign rally.
This is viewed as a Republican-leaning district as Trump won it in all three of his campaigns for president. But the GOP lost the congressional seat in 2022 when Gluesenkamp Perez, co-owner of an auto repair and machine shop and a Democratic newcomer, beat Republican Joe Kent, a former Army Special Forces soldier who Trump backed.
She defeated Kent in a rematch in 2024 even with Trump on the ballot.
As of early October, Gluesenkamp Perez has been the target of around $11 million in direct opposition spending based on a review of federal election records.
Of the total, the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC dedicated exclusively to electing Republicans to the U.S. House of Representatives, expended $4.8 million.
No Going Back, a political action committee aligned with Trump’s MAGA Inc., had spent roughly $3.9 million opposing Gluesenkamp Perez, plus about half-a-million dollars boosting Braun’s candidacy.
The American Action Network has shelled out $1 million. And the National Republican Congressional Committee and Braun campaign have jointly spent roughly $2.6 million, most of it taking aim at the incumbent.
“The level of outside spending in this race has been obscene,” said Tim Gowen, Gluesenkamp Perez’s campaign manager. “Republican groups, including Trump’s own super PAC, have spent more than $10 million on deceptive negative ads — more than double what groups supporting Democrats have spent.”
Records show Braun has been the target of $4.3 million in spending by the House Majority PAC, the super PAC focused on electing Democrats to the House. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and Gluesenkamp Perez campaign have jointly spent $2.6 million in opposition ads. 
A Braun campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Minnesota must act on what fosters know about homelessness
text:
About four in 10 young people ages 24 and younger interviewed while experiencing homelessness had lived in a foster or group home. Among that group, the average age of first homelessness was 13. (Photo by Getty Images)We need to stop treating homelessness among people raised in the foster care system as a problem that begins when they leave the state’s care. By then, we may already be years late.
At Foster Advocates, a foster-founded and foster-led organization, we have been telling Minnesota about the instability that can follow repeated moves, disrupted relationships, and support that arrives too late. 
A new report gives the state more evidence. What matters now is what we do with it.
Wilder Research’s new report, developed with Foster Advocates, draws on the 2023 Minnesota Homeless Study. About four in 10 young people ages 24 and younger interviewed while experiencing homelessness had lived in a foster or group home. Among that group, the average age of first homelessness was 13.
That is not an average for all fosters, and it does not establish that every young person first became homeless while in care. But it makes clear why a response focused only on when fosters leave care is not enough. For a child who is already homeless, help is overdue.
Foster leaders helped interpret these findings, bringing their knowledge to questions the numbers alone could not answer. They explained that identifying a single “first time” can be complicated: For some, the loss of home began with removal or repeated moves, even when a placement did not meet an official definition of homelessness.
A bed and an address do not tell us whether a young person feels safe, knows how long they can stay, or has someone they trust. Those are questions we need to ask early and often, and the young person’s answers need to matter to ensure every child has a safe, stable place to live and people they can count on.
Minnesota’s response to the new findings should start with taking fosters seriously when they say something is wrong. When a young person says they feel unsafe, or do not know where they will sleep, or cannot stay where they are — that should be enough to begin helping. We should not require a shelter stay before offering support or punish a young person for trying to get safe.
State and county agencies should be able to answer three questions: 

Does this young person have somewhere safe to live now? 
Who is responsible for helping when that changes? 
When will that help arrive? Recording a concern is not the same as resolving it. 

 Agencies must then take responsibility for connecting their work rather than making a foster manage every handoff. A support referral should not count as success if the young person still has nowhere safe to stay. Coordination needs to lead to housing they can afford, support they can actually access, and someone responsible for following through.
That means addressing the barriers between a program on paper and help in a person’s life. Ask fosters about bureaucratic boundaries —  applications, eligibility rules, referrals and county boundaries. Then, assign responsibility for eliminating those barriers and provide the resources to do it. Better communication is important, but it cannot substitute for an affordable home or money for a deposit.
Preparation for adulthood for the 10,000 or so fosters in Minnesota should build on the relationships a foster wants to keep and provide practical help with housing, income, transportation and benefits. That support cannot end on a foster’s 18th birthday or with a referral. A missed paycheck or medical bill should not cost a young person their home. They should have people they trust and flexible help when something goes wrong.
Finally, fosters must hold real authority in designing and evaluating this response. Pay people for their expertise and involve them before priorities, budgets and measures of success are set. Fosters should help decide what needs to change and assess whether those changes are making life more stable. “Nothing about fosters without fosters” has to mean more than an invitation to share a story.
We should judge Minnesota’s response by whether fosters are safely housed, connected to people they trust, and able to get help when they need it. Fosters should not have to keep proving that this is happening before something changes.
The report is here, and so is the knowledge of the people who helped make sense of it. State and county leaders need to work with fosters to turn that knowledge into changes people can feel in their lives. For a young person who needs somewhere safe to sleep tonight, that work cannot wait.

name: Mississippi Today
title: One year after Leland mass shooting, no indictments, only questions
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Leland has marked a year since a homecoming block party in the heart of downtown erupted in gunfire, claiming the lives of eight people and leaving grieving families and the community to process the tragedy. 
Families of the victims and residents returned to Main and Fourth Streets on the Oct. 11 anniversary of the nation’s deadliest mass shooting of 2025. Instead of chaos and people seeking cover from gunfire, the memorial offered music, prayer, candlelight and a balloon release. 
More people flock into town this week for Leland High School’s Friday homecoming festivities. Meanwhile, court records and statements from officials offer little indication of progress in the shooting investigation. No one’s been indicted, few have been charged and no motives have been established.
Leland Mayor John Lee Credit: Leland website
Leland Mayor John Lee said families and the community are still wondering why the tragedy happened and lacking the closure that only trials and convictions can begin to provide. 
“That’s going to be delayed,” Lee told Mississippi Today, noting that few cases have been brought forward in court. 
The eight who died are remembered: 

William Sexton, 37, of Leland; Calvin Plant, 19, of Greenville; Kaslyn Johnson, 18, of Greenville; Amos Brantley Jr., 18; of Greenville; and JaMichael Jones, 34; all buried in Greenville. 


Oreshama Johnson, 41, was a Leland High School alum who enjoyed working with children. Shelbyona Powell, 25, of Greenville, liked to sing, dance and spend time with family.  Ebanee Williams, 25, graduated fourth in her class from South Delta High School in Rolling Fork and was called a fearless, artistic free spirit. 

Sixteen other people were wounded.
Authorities have charged and publicly identified five people they say were involved. But state and federal court records show none has been indicted for murder, while one has pleaded guilty to a potentially related gun possession charge and is now in federal prison. 
Local, county, state and federal agencies have investigated the case, which remains active and open. It is a complex case with no established timeline to complete the investigation, said Alex Gibert, a spokesperson for the Department of Public Safety. DPS oversees the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, the Office of Homeland Security and the Bureau of Narcotics, which are among agencies involved in the investigation. 
“We recognize the tremendous impact this tragedy has had on the victims’ families, the Leland community, and the state of Mississippi. We understand the desire for answers and appreciate the patience of those affected as investigators continue their work,” the department said in an statement to Mississippi Today. 
“Our priority remains conducting a thorough investigation and ensuring that any findings are supported by the evidence.”
An early theory the FBI gave for motive was that the shooting may have been “sparked by a disagreement among several individuals.”
Gibert, though, would not comment about a potential motive, any firearms evidence collected, whether any evidence has been tested or other details “that could compromise the integrity of the case.” 
A bullet casing near the curb of North Main Street in Leland, Monday, Oct. 13, 2025, where a shooting resulted in multiple fatalities during a homecoming celebration days earlier. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
FBI Jackson Field Office spokesperson Marshay Lawson referred comment to the Leland Police Department, which she said was the primary investigator who invited the bureau to assist. 
Leland Police Chief Isaac Morris Sr. reiterated that the investigation is ongoing. Morris, who became chief in August, said much of that investigation had already been done under the previous administration. Jimmy Myrick was the chief when last year’s shooting happened and he was the department’s leader until his termination in the spring.  
The FBI released five names of people allegedly linked to the mass shooting. Terrogernal S. Martin, 33; Morgan Lattimore, 25; Teviyon L. Powell, 29 and William Bryant, 29 were charged with capital murder. Latoya A. Powell, 44, was charged with attempted murder.  
Investigators contacted in the past two weeks did not say whether additional people have been charged in connection to the shooting. 
Five suspects have been held at the Washington County Regional Correctional Facility in Greenville since last year, according to court records. 
Meanwhile, grand juries have met four times in Washington County to consider cases for indictment. Grand jury proceedings are secret, so it isn’t known if anyone has been indicted in the case. But indictments are typically public once suspects are served, which is something that could be done in this case with most of the known suspects in jail. 
Detainee awaits indictment a year later
Among those arrested in the mass shooting is Morgan Lattimore, whom authorities identified as being 25, although arrest records show his date of birth in 2008 would have made him 16 at the time of the arrest. He was charged with eight counts of capital murder and one count of attempted murder.
The high school student has had no prior convictions, according to his attorney. Lattimore missed his entire junior year and what currently would be his senior year. 
Lattimore’s bond was initially set at a $3.05 million cash bond – a figure he cannot afford and his attorney asked to be reduced. 
It took until at least June for his bond to be brought down to a $500,000 surety bond and for him to be housed separately from adults at the jail, according to a bond motion filed by his attorney, Stephen Edwards Jr., the Washington County public defender. 
On Oct. 12, Lattimore had a second bond hearing in Washington County Circuit Court, which led to a second reduction of $250,000. 
A surety bond enables his family to use a bondsman who can pay the full amount while the family pays 10%. Lattimore’s initial cash bond meant his family would have had to pay the entire amount without help. 
Edwards declined to comment on his client’s case. But in a Sept. 28 motion for bond reduction, the attorney argued that a lower bond would help his family make the payment and bring him home to Leland to await trial should he ultimately be indicted. 
Other suspects from the shooting have also had bond hearings this year, resulting in bond reductions from the million-dollar cash amounts to surety bonds ranging from $50,000 to $250,000, according to court records. 
Edwards has questioned since last December what evidence exists to establish probable cause that Lattimore shot and killed eight people and attempted to kill another at the homecoming block party. 
The attorney wrote that the only evidence presented at a December 2025 preliminary hearing for Lattimore and five co-defendants was testimony from an MBI agent who saw video of the incident.
Edwards said the video wasn’t provided to him or the court. According to the agent’s testimony, the video showed shots were fired from north of the crowd and some returned fire. The agent testified that Lattimore ran, took cover and returned shots, firing off “less than five shots,” according to court records.
Crime scene tape remains at the scene on North Main Street in Leland, Monday, Oct. 13, 2025, where a shooting resulted in multiple fatalities during a homecoming celebration days earlier. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
But Lattimore did not fire the initial shot, nor was he in the area where the initial shot took place, Edwards wrote. Testimony didn’t indicate who or what Lattimore shot at and if his bullets struck anyone. Lattimore also cooperated with the FBI, giving them a statement and his gun, according to his attorney. 
“The MBI essentially testified that Mr. Lattimore and others were charged because they chose not to keep running and taking cover, instead choosing to shoot back,” Edwards wrote in a December 2025 petition for writ of habeas corpus, a civil legal filing that allows people to challenge their detention. 
Washington County Circuit Judge Ashley Hines held a hearing in February at which a portion of surveillance video was played in court.  
The video showed Latimore in a crowd of people running after gunfire went off and how he fired fewer than five shots, court records state. That video also showed him among a group that took cover behind a vehicle and then running inside a building for safety. 
In April, Hines found probable cause to charge Lattimore with eight counts of capital murder. 
“Although he was not the only shooter or initial shooter, Lattimore had a gun which he shot multiple times,” Hines wrote in a March 12 order. “Eight people died and numerous people were injured during the shoot-out.”
Again, the video was not given to defense counsel, Edwards wrote in the September motion to reduce Lattimore’s bond.  
District Attorney Dewayne Richardson, whose district includes Washington County, did not respond to a request for comment about whether the Leland suspects have been indicted or if their cases are expected to be presented to a grand jury. 
Suspect convicted of federal gun charge
Court records show that William Bryant, one of the five the FBI identified was indicted on a federal gun possession charge and took a plea deal in exchange for the government agreeing not to charge him with related offenses, according to court records
The indictment states that he possessed a gun in Leland the day of the mass shooting, but it does not mention a location or time of day that Bryant had the weapon. 
A spokesperson from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District declined to comment because of an active investigation. Gregory Park, the federal public defender who represented Bryant, did not respond to a request for comment. 
To help determine how much prison time he should serve, the federal government submitted one exhibit: Video of the Oct. 11, 2025, mass shooting. Mississippi Today has not been able to obtain a copy of the video or view it, and it is unclear whether it’s the same video Lattimore’s attorney has referenced. 
By July, he was sentenced to serve three years.
Undercurrent of public mistrust
Joshua Jackson, special agent in charge of the Bureau of the ATF division overseeing Mississippi, announces his agents’ takedown of a trafficking ring in the Delta and Tupelo at the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Oxford on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Local police, state officers and federal agents banded together to execute the operations. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
Two weeks after the mass shooting, the FBI arrested more than a dozen law enforcement officers accused of public corruption for accepting bribes and helping to move drugs from the Delta and Tennessee – the culmination of a years-long investigation. 
Those charged include Milton Gaston, the former sheriff of Washington County whose department has been involved in investigating the Leland shooting. 
Since the arrests, at least seven officers have pleaded guilty and one was acquitted. 
At an October 2025 news conference announcing the arrests, Robert Eikhoff, special agent in charge of the FBI Jackson Field Office, said his agents faced initial impediments responding to the Leland shooting because of broken trust in law enforcement. 
“We learned of the community’s distrust of select law enforcement officers due to concerns of corruption,” Eikhoff said. “Law enforcement is only effective when the communities they protect can trust that law enforcement officers are honest in serving the community’s interest. Mississippians deserve and rightfully expect officers to obey their oath.”
Leland to return for homecoming
Across the Delta, homecoming traditions such as pageantry, football, music and tailgating continued despite homecoming-related shootings last year in Leland and Rolling Fork. 
For Leland, homecoming celebrations this year will look different than years before, local leaders said. 
The parade was moved to 10 a.m. from the afternoon on Friday, and the football game will start at 2 p.m. Leland police officers and Washington County sheriff’s deputies plan to provide security at the game, said Mayor Lee. 
Lee said some of the most noticeable changes will be no more tailgating and large gatherings on school or city property. He said people can still celebrate at home, saying it’s a right the city can’t “(take) away from them.” 
Chief Morris said his department has worked with the school district on safety, and he credited the district for safety measures such as bag checks and metal detectors that have resulted in no issues at games this season. 
“This is the one year anniversary of the mass shooting and we want to make sure everyone feels safe and comfortable coming to the game,” he said. 
“We’ll be happy for them to come back,” Morris said, “and celebrate our homecoming, as always.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Insured patients struggle to schedule mental healthcare, study shows
text:
New data from five states including New Jersey shows patients with Blue Cross Blue Shield healthcare plans still struggle to schedule visits with mental health providers. (Getty Images)Problems with the doctor directories created by commercial health insurance plans leave many patients struggling to schedule mental health appointments, according to a new study of Blue Cross Blue Shield plans in New Jersey and four other states.
An analysis of secret shopper data published Friday in the Journal of the American Medical Association showed that fewer than a quarter of answered calls resulted in an appointment with a psychiatrist or psychologist. More than half of the inquiries identified a doctor who was no longer in the network, had retired, or was not at that address, or revealed another directory error, researchers found, and 22% found providers who were too busy to see another patient.
“In this study, access barriers previously documented in public insurance programs extend to the privately insured population, undermining the assumption that commercial coverage automatically translates into meaningful access to mental health care,” said the authors, researchers from the public health school at The Ohio State University and Stanford University School of Medicine’s psychology department.
Studies have long shown it can be hard for people with public insurance plans like Medicaid to schedule certain appointments without a long wait or other complications. The new data is focused on commercial Blue Cross Blue Shield networks, not public insurance.
The new analysis indicates appointments were easier to schedule through Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey, which insures more than 3.5 million state residents, than with doctors in networks run by its commercial cousins in the other states surveyed, Delaware, Montana, Rhode Island, and Virginia. In all, researchers posing as patients made nearly 6,000 calls, including almost 1,100 to doctors in New Jersey.
One-third of the calls to Horizon resulted in an appointment and just over 45% identified a directory error, the best performance in both categories for any state, according to the findings. But the first available appointments were three weeks away on average, a bit longer than the national average.
Horizon spokesman Tom Wilson said the company’s provider network had more than doubled since 2020, to include some 20,000 clinicians, including specialists and services the analysis failed to include. In 2025, he said, nearly 700,000 Horizon members filed some 8 million behavioral healthcare claims with the company.
“The secret shopper analysis provides an inaccurate, incomplete, and unfair picture of Horizon’s behavioral health network, which substantially exceeds New Jersey’s network adequacy standards,” Wilson told the New Jersey Monitor.
Those standards are state requirements that insurance companies must include enough doctors and other clinicians in their networks to properly serve their members, and that those providers are not too far from those members’ homes.
Linda Schwimmer is president and CEO of the New Jersey Health Care Quality Institute, which conducted a similar secret-shopper survey last spring focused on children’s mental health.
“Insurance coverage does not reliably mean access. Directories can be inaccurate, in-network providers may not take new patients, and waits can be long,” Schwimmer said.
Schwimmer said the study published Friday echoes the Quality Institute’s findings in March, which showed that fewer than 15% of mental health providers listed in Horizon’s Omnia network, a widely used plan with a robust directory, could offer a young teen an in-person appointment within two weeks.
“Two independent studies reached the same conclusion: Even New Jersey families with good commercial coverage cannot count on their insurance to connect them to timely mental health care,” Schwimmer told the New Jersey Monitor in an email.
Federal funding cuts to Medicaid, which covers 1-in-3 children here, will increase pressure on the system, she said.
The Horizon spokesman said the state is facing the same shortages of clinical providers — particularly for behavioral health — that have been reported nationwide. New Jersey has just over half the psychiatrists it currently needs and faces a “catastrophic” mental health workforce shortage going forward, a national nonprofit advocacy group reported in March.
Wilson said Horizon is working with other insurers on a national effort to improve the reliability of provider directories. But they still depend on doctors to inform them when they are moving or changing hours, he said.
New Jersey lawmakers proposed several bills in the wake of the Quality Institute report, including a measure that would strengthen the state’s oversight of health insurance companies and require them to maintain up-to-date directories. A version passed the Senate health committee in June and a companion bill was scheduled for a hearing Monday, but the meeting was canceled.
“We believe that network adequacy, network directory accuracy, the credentialing process, and enforcement all need to be revamped given the changes in technology capability, telehealth, health system mergers, and provider aggregator platforms,” Schwimmer said.
The group plans to gather experts in early November to discuss a range of policy solutions, she said.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill has prioritized youth mental health, including nearly $50 million in the current budget to expand school-based services for kids, and taking steps to reduce the negative impacts of social media on children. At least 1 in 5 children have been diagnosed with a mental health condition, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and 40% of high school students said they felt hopeless or depressed at some point in the last year.
In recent years New Jersey has also built out its crisis-response system for adults facing mental health or addiction issues, but it has struggled to fund the last piece of this puzzle, five drop-in centers that advocates say are desperately needed.
More than 700 people died by suicide in New Jersey last year, an increase from 2024, according to state data, and more than 80,000 were screened for serious psychiatric issues.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: Be careful what you wish for
text:
Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026. (Getty images)The latest fad in American politics is candidates who claim to be independent of political parties.
Conjuring images of potbellied, cigar-smoking party bosses from the late 19th century, these candidates proclaim that their only interest is in the welfare of the “average, everyday voter.” In truth, their only accountability is to the donors who pay their bills.
On the national level, more than 200 independents are running for the U.S. House and Senate, a record number. Even those of us who have been engaged in politics for years are sick of the bickering and badgering that have taken over our political system. The toxic influence of money has turned our political system into a hotbed of crony capitalism and cynical manipulation of public opinion.
While it appears that this surge of independent candidates is spontaneous, plenty of people in politics understand the potential power of a bloc of votes in Congress that does not align itself with either major political party. Many of those people are working to advance what has become known as the “fulcrum strategy.” The idea is that a small, disciplined bloc of independent or third-party legislators can control policy outcomes by tipping the balance of power between the political parties. It’s simple and potentially effective.
Probably the most prominent group supporting this strategy has been the Forward Party, founded in 2021 by former presidential candidate Andrew Yang, former New Jersey Governor Christine Todd Whitman, and businessman Michael Willner.  On Sept. 23 to 25, the Independent National Convention was held in Washington D.C. Montana’s two independent candidates, Seth Bodnar and Micheal Eisenhauer attended.
In this election cycle, others have joined the movement to promote independent candidates.
Among those is former Senator Joe Manchin and the Independent Leadership Council which has been pouring money into Bodnar’s race.
Before jumping on the independent bandwagon there are a few things to consider. First among them is this: How accountable to the “average, everyday voter” is an independent candidate?
The truth is that running for office, particularly federal office, is extremely expensive. The unprecedented maneuvering in our Senate race has been driven by money from political action committees and other “dark money” groups. Some of these groups are aligned with traditional partisan interests, while others represent players who are relatively new to politics. But all of these donors expect something in return for their investment in candidates. That is true of independents, Republicans, and Democrats alike.
No matter what you think about our major political parties, they provide mechanisms for holding candidates and officeholders accountable beyond the cold, hard cash. Both parties have local central committees populated by volunteers who live in the communities they represent. These local organizations often provide many of the volunteers who form the backbone of local and statewide campaigns.
Both parties have written rules and by-laws which govern their activities. They hold conventions to elect officers and develop positions on issues they care about. These conventions are open to party members. Both parties also develop platforms of positions on various issues at member conventions that are available to the public. None of this exists for independent candidates or officeholders.
It’s worth noting that the current controversy within the Montana Democratic Party is not unique to Democrats. Republicans are mired in an internal blood feud that has been going on for years and virtually paralyzed the last legislature. Despite Republicans’ electoral success in Montana, they are failing to govern effectively.
I’m not blind to the problems with our two-party system. The United States Supreme Court dealt a death blow to our political system with the Citizens United decision, which opened the floodgates to a torrent of dirty money flowing into elections. The reality is that we now do our political work under an authoritarian regime run for and by oligarchs.
The next two elections may be our last chance to change what looks like a very dark future.
And our Democratic leaders, people rank and file Montana Democrats have supported for years, blew it in this election.
Hopefully, the rest of the country can do better.
The solution is not to create a cabal of nonaligned “independent” players who broker political deals with relatively little public engagement. Far better to strengthen and unify the traditional system, which has worked imperfectly for decades, and to get the massive amounts of money out of our political process.
Ken Toole served in the Montana Senate with Jon Tester.  He worked for Nancy Keenan when she was Superintendent of Public Instruction.   He was the Vice Chair and Chair of the Lewis and Clark Central Committee. He was elected as the Western District Chair’s Representative on the State Democratic Party Executive Board. He was elected twice to the Montana Senate and once to the Montana Public Service Commission.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Grow what you know: Nebraska’s economic opportunity
text:
Norm Crain displays an ear of corn and a beaker of 200 proof ethanol produced at the Adkins Energy ethanol production facility October 4, 2004 near Lena, Illinois. (Photo Illustration by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Nebraska has the ingredients to build a stronger bioeconomy. The opportunity now is to turn those assets into a focused strategy for growth.
Across Nebraska, the biosciences are already at work in human and animal health, agriculture, renewable fuels, biomanufacturing, medical technology and research. The University of Nebraska Medical Center anchors a nationally significant medical and research ecosystem. Nebraska’s corn and soybeans can become higher-value products, from biobased plastics to enzymes and Omega-3. Blair is home to major industrial biomanufacturing operations. Five of the world’s 12 largest animal health companies have facilities here.
These are Nebraska assets that offer nationally important capabilities in industries that will shape how America produces food, improves health, manufactures materials and competes globally.
The question is how Nebraska turns these strengths into more companies, investment and high-quality jobs.
Bio Nebraska, the state’s bioscience trade association, represents more than 125 companies and institutions working across this ecosystem. Earlier this year, we partnered with the Nebraska Corn Board on an assessment of Nebraska’s bioeconomy. We want to move the conversation from what Nebraska has to a more practical question: What does Nebraska need to do next to grow its bioeconomy?
The study began by asking whether Nebraska needs an industrial biomanufacturing pilot facility. Its conclusion is instructive. A new general-purpose facility is not the first move Nebraska should make. Existing national capacity is underused, and Nebraska can gain more by strengthening industry relationships, better using existing facilities and directing investment toward areas where the state has a genuine competitive advantage.
That finding points toward a larger opportunity: Nebraska needs a statewide bioscience and bioeconomy strategy.
States that have built nationally recognized bioscience sectors have been deliberate about it. They identify their strongest clusters, connect research to commercialization, develop specialized talent, attract capital and companies, and make sustained policy and infrastructure investments around areas where they can compete.
Nebraska should study those models and build one suited to our own strengths. That starts with identifying the sectors where Nebraska has the greatest potential to lead and the barriers standing in their way. It means mapping existing facilities and capabilities before building new ones; strengthening connections among universities, industry and entrepreneurs; aligning community college and university programs with workforce demand; examining incentives and access to capital; and determining where targeted public investment can unlock private growth.
Some of that infrastructure is already producing results. Nebraska’s bioscience industry employs nearly 19,000 people, with an average annual wage of roughly $90,000. Our research universities conducted nearly $435 million in bioscience-related research and development in 2023. Programs created through the Business Innovation Act have helped Nebraska startups and small businesses attract additional investment and generate revenue.
Workforce development is moving as well. Metropolitan Community College just launched a biotechnology program, while Southeast Community College’s biotechnology and Central Community College’s mechatronics programs are well-established. These efforts matter because companies need a reliable pipeline of workers, and Nebraskans need visible pathways into the high-quality careers those companies create.
The next step is to connect these pieces around a common economic strategy and protect the investments that make growth possible. That includes commercialization programs such as the Business Innovation Act, workforce development, research capacity and initiatives that expand Nebraska’s STEM talent pipeline.
Nebraska has assets that other states would like to have: agricultural resources, research institutions, global companies, manufacturing capacity, entrepreneurs and a growing skilled workforce. The opportunity is to organize around them.
Nebraska should be more competitive by being disciplined about where we have an advantage, learning from states that have successfully built bioscience economies and making sustained investments in the people, companies and infrastructure most likely to produce growth.
We know what Nebraska is good at. Now we need the strategy to grow it.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Missouri faces growing North American trade uncertainty
text:
President Donald Trump points into the crowd after headlining a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, with thousands in attendance (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner).Just as hopes grew for a breakthrough in United States–Mexico trade talks, an Oct. 15 report by The Wall Street Journal, subsequently reported by Reuters, revealed another roadblock.
The two countries were reportedly close to an agreement to lower U.S. tariffs on Mexican automobiles, steel and aluminum. But disagreements within the Trump administration slowed progress. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly opposed significant reductions in the 25% tariff on Mexican automobiles and the 50% tariffs on steel and aluminum.
The setback follows the breakdown of similar negotiations with Canada, the United States’ other major North American trading partner. Although discussions with Mexico continue, these developments raise concerns about the future of North American trade and the stability of the United States–Mexico–Canada (USMCA) trade agreement.
For Missouri, this is more than a disagreement in Washington. Mexico is Missouri’s second-largest export market, buying billions of dollars’ worth of the state’s farm and manufactured goods each year. From the corn, soybean and rice fields of the Missouri Bootheel to automotive assembly plants in Kansas City and Wentzville, the state’s economy is deeply entwined with North American supply chains. Further deterioration in relations could have significant consequences for Missouri farmers, manufacturers, workers, and consumers.
In 2025, Missouri sold about $4.3 billion worth of goods to Mexico, according to the Missouri Economic Research and Information Center. Together, Canada and Mexico purchased approximately $10.1 billion in Missouri goods, accounting for more than half of the state’s merchandise exports.
Mexico is also Missouri’s leading agricultural export destination, with crops such as corn and soybeans playing an important role in that relationship. For Missouri farmers, the stakes include access to a major foreign market, competitive prices, and the risk that future trade restrictions or retaliation could encourage Mexican buyers to seek alternative suppliers.
Manufacturing faces a different but equally important challenge. Missouri companies export goods to Mexico while importing vehicles, electrical equipment, and manufacturing components. Because production networks often cross international borders, tariffs can increase costs for American manufacturers that depend on Mexican inputs, even when those policies are intended to protect domestic industries.
The consequences extend beyond exporters and manufacturers. Transportation companies, warehouses, equipment suppliers, and local businesses serving agricultural and industrial communities all benefit from cross-border economic activity. Trade disruptions could affect investment, hiring, and household purchasing power. Smaller businesses may be especially vulnerable because they often lack the financial resources to absorb higher costs or quickly identify alternative suppliers and markets.
The latest setback does not mean a broader trade confrontation is inevitable. Negotiations continue and their eventual outcome remains uncertain. Nevertheless, three scenarios illustrate what could be at stake.
The first is a negotiated agreement that addresses both countries’ concerns while preserving North American economic integration. Washington could secure concessions on trade, investment, or market access, while Mexico could obtain relief from some U.S. tariffs on automobiles, steel, and aluminum.
For Missouri, such an agreement could reduce uncertainty for exporters, preserve agricultural market access, and provide manufacturers with greater confidence to invest and expand. Although some trade restrictions might remain, more predictable rules would help businesses make long-term decisions.
A second scenario is prolonged uncertainty. Talks could drag on for months without a comprehensive agreement, leaving existing tariffs and unresolved disputes in place. Even without additional restrictions, uncertainty can impose economic costs. Missouri manufacturers might delay expansion or equipment purchases, while agricultural exporters could hesitate to enter long-term contracts. Such decisions could gradually affect investment, employment, and economic activity across the state.
The most disruptive scenario would involve new U.S. tariffs or restrictions, followed by Mexican retaliation against U.S. exports. If Mexico imposed tariffs on American agricultural products, Missouri farmers could face declining competitiveness and increased pressure on commodity prices.
Manufacturers importing Mexican components could experience higher costs, while exporters might encounter additional barriers. Some domestic producers could benefit from reduced foreign competition, but businesses relying on imported materials could face the opposite effect. Consumers could also pay higher prices for affected vehicles and other products.
Over time, persistent trade barriers could encourage companies to relocate production, diversify suppliers, or develop relationships with alternative markets. Once these adjustments occur, restoring previous trade relationships may prove difficult, even after negotiations succeed.
These risks are particularly significant given the deterioration in United States–Canada trade relations, which I examined in an earlier column. Canada and Mexico are not simply two separate export markets. Together, they form part of an interconnected production and distribution system developed over decades.
This standoff comes at a critical moment for USMCA. During the July 2026 joint review, the United States declined to extend the agreement in its current form for another 16 years, leaving its future subject to annual reviews. Although the agreement remains in force, uncertainty over its long-term direction adds another layer of risk for businesses that depend on stable North American trade relations.
Missouri businesses, however, need not remain passive observers. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative has opened a public comment period ahead of the 2027 USMCA review, with submissions due January 12, 2027.
Missouri’s agricultural organizations, manufacturers, chambers of commerce, and other business representatives have an opportunity to document the consequences of trade uncertainty and communicate their priorities to federal negotiators.
For a state whose economic future is closely tied to its North American neighbors, remaining silent while the rules of trade are rewritten is a risk Missouri cannot afford to ignore.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: Collapse of NJ’s health plan for public workers could raise costs for all residents
text:
Hundreds of public workers rallied outside the Statehouse in Trenton on June 18, 2026, to demand lawmakers rein in rising healthcare costs. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)What happens when a state allows its public health plan, which covers hundreds of thousands of workers and retirees, to collapse? We’re about to find out in New Jersey unless Gov. Mikie Sherrill and the Legislature take decisive action to reform the State Health Benefits Plan.
Here is where things stand: open enrollment in New Jersey’s State Health Benefits Program is just wrapping up, and the annual cost of family health insurance for some local government workers now exceeds $68,000. That’s more than the starting salary of many of the public employees who depend on that coverage. Yes, you read that right. In some cases, insuring a worker and their family costs more than the worker earns in an entire year.
If that isn’t bad enough, another double-digit premium increase was just approved in August and will take effect in January. Towns and counties are responding the only way they can: dropping out of the plan, shifting more costs onto workers, or passing costs to the taxpayers through property tax increases. 
Without any real efforts to bring down costs, the local government side of the plan withers, towns leave, and private insurers are there to pick up the pieces. Put bluntly, that is not a solution. It is a demolition plan.
When public plans shrink, everyone pays more. The State Health Benefits Plan sets the benchmark for New Jersey’s private market. Kill the benchmark, and watch what happens to prices for the small business owner in Camden, the freelancer in Montclair, the family buying on the exchange in Toms River. For retired public employees, the stakes are even higher: the healthcare benefits they spent their entire careers earning could simply disappear.
That is why the state’s largest local government labor and management organizations, groups that agree on almost nothing else, have united behind a reform package. We are fighting for sound policy reforms that improve the plan menu and implement reference-based pricing, claims auditing, and pharmacy benefit manager reform. These common-sense fixes would save taxpayers, local governments, and workers millions. They should have been adopted years ago.​ But stabilizing the plan is the floor, not the ceiling. If New Jersey is serious about healthcare affordability, the answer is not less public coverage. It is more.
Other states have shown that healthcare costs can be brought under control without cutting benefits. Oregon capped hospital payments under its public employee health plans and saved over $100 million in just over two years. Connecticut removed private managed care companies from Medicaid and replaced them with a publicly run system, with significantly lower administrative costs. Montana saved nearly $48 million over three years by linking hospital payments to Medicare rates. Washington has also introduced Cascade Select, a public option that caps provider payments at Medicare levels. Under that model, premiums rose by just 3% in 2024, compared with 9% under the other plans.
New Jersey should consider those approaches to reducing healthcare prices and administrative costs rather than simply passing the cost on to workers and taxpayers.
As federal Medicaid cuts and reduced Affordable Care Act subsidies threaten coverage, New Jersey should be expanding coverage to ensure working families keep their health insurance.
Why is this more than just a healthcare issue? Because voters have made the affordability crisis unmistakable. In Elizabeth, nearly 800 residents petitioned to place a rent cap on the November ballot, and a judge just cleared it for the ballot over landlords’ objections. People are done waiting for markets to fix what markets broke. Housing and healthcare are the same fight: The cost of living is crushing working families, and they are demanding that the government act like it.
The State Health Benefits Plan crisis tests whether Trenton has understood that. One path leads to a shrinking public plan, a fragmenting insurance market, higher prices for everyone, and broken promises to retirees. The other leads to a stabilized public employee plan and a state that uses public purchasing power to drive costs down for all of us.​
New Jersey can be a national model for public healthcare that delivers on its promise. Or it can preside over a collapse that everyone, insured and uninsured, public and private, will pay for. We have to choose now, not kick it down the road. It’s time to make choices that prioritize working New Jerseyans over corporatized healthcare.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Democratic gubernatorial nominee talks Trump, money
text:
From right, Cyndi Munson and Mike Mazzei are pictured at public appearances. (Photo of Munson by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice. Photo of Mazzei by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Cyndi Munson acknowledges she has less money to spend and a lot of Republican voters to sway, but said she has one thing her leading opponent doesn’t: momentum.
Even as Republican Mike Mazzei has pumped millions of his own money into his campaign for governor, Munson, 41, said she senses a bipartisan swell of support behind her Democratic candidacy for governor heading into the Nov. 3 general election.
The Oklahoma City resident faces Mazzei, 61, and independent candidates Jerry Griffin, 82, of Tulsa, Robert E. Brooks Sr., 47, of Moore, and Orlando Lynn Bush, 61, of Edmond.
“I have felt the momentum for quite a bit of time and it’s obviously increased since the Republican primary and Republican primary runoff,” said Munson, House Democratic minority leader.
Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, who has held the state’s top role for the past eight years, cannot run again due to term limits. The last Democrat to hold the state’s top office was Brad Henry, whose term ended in 2011. Every statewide and federal office is currently held by Republicans.
Mazzei, 61, of Tulsa, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, initially agreed to an interview with Oklahoma Voice to discuss his campaign and priorities, but then canceled, saying he had a scheduling problem. He said he could not reschedule. 
Mazzei edged out Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the statewide Aug. 25 runoff by a little more than 2,000 votes.
A former state senator who later served as Stitt’s budget secretary, Mazzei works as a financial adviser for the company he founded, Trinity Strategic Wealth.
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, during his watch party in Tulsa, Okla. Mazzei secured the Republican nomination for Governor of Oklahoma by defeating Gentner Drummond.Photo by Ace Cuervo/Oklahoma Voice
He wants to eliminate the income tax, end property taxes for seniors and veterans, stop foreign entities and out-of-state investors from buying property, and reform Oklahoma’s education system, according to his campaign website.   
Mazzei has put $11 million in bank-backed loans into his campaign.
“I do think he is trying to buy the governor’s office,” Munson said, who has raised about $1.7 million.
While all 77 Oklahoma counties voted for Trump the three times he was on the ballot, Munson believes Trump’s overwhelming disapproval rating nationwide due to inflation and the war with Iran could help her win.
She said her events are becoming more bipartisan, with some Republican voters telling her they are voting this election cycle for the candidate, not the party.
She said it is not just the war and inflation, but decisions have been made that impact farmers and ranchers and also hinder access to healthcare and food stamps. She said she will not be a rubber stamp for Trump’s policies.
“They may share the party registration of the president, or maybe even voted for him, but they see how these policies are impacting their own lives and their communities, and so I think that is where a lot of the frustration really is and why people are ready for change,” Munson said.
Cyndi Munson greets supporters at her campaign watch party on June 16, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
As of Sept. 30, Oklahoma had slightly more than 1.3 million registered Republican voters compared to just under 622,000 Democrats, about 23,600 Libertarians and nearly 498,000 independents, according to the Oklahoma Election Board.
Munson has been to all 77 counties campaigning on affordability, education, healthcare and repealing the state’s abortion ban.
She holds a degree from the University of Central Oklahoma and worked in nonprofits before being elected in 2015 to the Oklahoma House.
“You can just see financial backing, the difference between me being backed by people every day working Oklahomans and him just writing a check to himself,” Munson said. “And that disconnect is very, very clear.”

name: WyoFile
title: Natrona County and Prometheus Hyperscale consider bypassing state review for new AI complex
text:
Natrona County officials are drafting a list of potential conditions, permits and expectations they will require of Prometheus Hyperscale, the company proposing a 1,250-megawatt artificial intelligence computing complex east of Casper.
Top of mind, according to county commissioners who spoke to WyoFile, are assurances that the data center’s water consumption and electricity needs don’t harm residents, as well as measures to keep noise and light pollution in check and a yet-to-be-determined sense of whether the data center would be a net benefit for the community.
“This process is just barely even kicking off,” Natrona County Commission Chairman Jim Milne said. “It’s going to be a long, long haul, and we have ample opportunity to talk to them and adjust.”
Prometheus Hyperscale began publicly floating its Natrona County project last spring, and then addressed commissioners during a packed meeting in September. Prometheus founder Trenton Thornock listed his bona fides as a sixth-generation Uinta County rancher with close ties to Wyoming’s natural resources and its residents. 

A worker tests a natural gas-fueled electric generating engine at Mesa Power Solutions’ manufacturing shop in Casper. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

His company’s data center here — with an initial investment of about $500 million and potential to expand — is designed to use a closed-loop cooling system to limit water usage, as well as injection wells to sequester carbon dioxide emissions from a fleet of natural gas-fueled electric generators to power the operation separately from the public grid.
In addition to creating new jobs and injecting a new stream of tax revenue into the county, Thornock’s pitch included bypassing a one-shop-stop state industrial permitting process to tailor-fit the project to Natrona County parameters. While the Wyoming Industrial Siting Council is “cumbersome and time-consuming,” working directly with the county would not forgo “any applicable environmental or regulatory requirements,” Oil City News reported Thornock saying at a September commission meeting.
The idea has its appeal, Milne and other commissioners have said. And Prometheus is already several phases into a very similar process in Uinta County, where the company is building another data center complex.
“They’re still going to have to go through the same stuff that they would have to go through with [the Industrial Siting Council],” Commissioner Dave North told WyoFile, noting the project must still undergo reviews to comply with state wildlife, water and myriad other state statutes. “They’re not getting out of anything. It just expedites the whole process.”
State versus county review
Typically, industrial projects of a certain scale must undergo a Wyoming Industrial Siting Act review and obtain a permit from the Industrial Siting Council, which requires some 19 different state and federal agencies to analyze and weigh in on projects.
But a handful of prospective data center developers have favored opting out of the  Industrial Siting Act. The “industrial park exemption” allows developers to approach counties that have robust zoning to, essentially, take on the task, if they’re willing. This is a potentially attractive option for counties with expert staff and means, like Natrona County, according to North.
A view from Hat Six Road east of Casper, a region where a developer proposes to build a data center complex. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“We can tell them exactly what we want,” North said. “If you don’t have zoning, and you don’t have a development department, this would be a wreck.”
Though it adds work for county officials who may not have industrial permitting expertise, commissioners still get to consider project-specific reviews from state and federal agencies, he said. Plus, unlike the appointed members of the Industrial Siting Council, Natrona County officials are beholden to their constituents and can ask developers to invest in the community beyond its scope of work and regulations they’re held to — like ponying up donations for parks and other services.

Residents who packed a Sept. 1, 2026, Natrona County Board of Commissioners meeting were asked to raise their hands if they support a proposal by Prometheus Hyperscale to build a data center. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

“We’ve got to keep an open mind on both sides,” Milne said. “We need to be fair to the developer and to the public.”
North noted that the county’s review and negotiations with Prometheus won’t be directly decided by residents, but he noted that residents will have the opportunity to quiz both company and county officials and weigh in.
“I will tell you, we’re listening,” North said. “Not only are we listening to the concerns of the citizens, but I’m passing that information on to Prometheus and saying, ‘You’re going to have to address this.'”
Caution signs ahead
Though some counties might have the resources and wherewithal to take on such a task, there are potential pitfalls and the Industrial Siting Council process has merits, local environmental watchdog groups told WyoFile.
Those detailed reviews from 19 state and federal agencies that the council requires are not necessarily wholly transferable in developer-county negotiations, according to Lander-based Wyoming Outdoor Council Data Center Campaign Manager Jocelyn Wulf.

Prometheus Hyperscale founder Trenton Thornock. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

Unless county officials press for specifics, “they’re not being reviewed as extensively and comprehensively by these agencies,” Wulf said. “They have to consider that they need to cover every possible eventuality on their own. So, in theory, these counties could have far fewer regulations than the [Industrial Siting Act requirements], or they could also have far more. It could go a lot of ways, really.”
Also, not every county with an industrial park exemption is equipped to get what they expect from shrewd, well-monied corporations.
“We’re afraid it could become kind of a race to the bottom,” Outdoor Council Energy and Climate Policy Director John Burrows said. “That’s a good reason, I think, to have more of a state focus on the regulation of data centers.”
There are no applications now before Natrona County officials, according to North and Milne. Both stress there will be public forums and opportunities to ask questions and weigh in.
For its part, Prometheus said it also plans to conduct public meetings in Natrona County.
“We want them to be useful, and plan to schedule them once we have more concrete information to share,” Prometheus Chief of Staff Abby Pick told WyoFile via email. “We are committed to moving through that process transparently, working alongside local officials and the community every step of the way.”
