name: Florida Phoenix
title: Senate President Ben Albritton says he’ll vote ‘no’ on property tax cuts
text:
Senate President Ben Albritton talks to reporters following the 2026 session Sine Die on March 13, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Less than five months after Florida Senate President Ben Albritton hailed his chamber for voting to put a measure on the Nov. 3 ballot seeking a major expansion of the homestead property tax exemption for non-school taxes, he now says he opposes the proposal.
“As a native of Florida’s heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart. It’s who I am,” Albritton says in a statement posted on the Florida Sherriff’s Association social media page. “Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida’s rural counties, gutting essential services for law enforcement, emergency response services, and critical infrastructure.”
Albritton goes to say the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission is scheduled to meet in 2027 and suggests that is a better venue to vet such a major proposal. Both the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Florida TaxWatch have made similar remarks.
If approved by 60% of the voters on Nov. 3, Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for all non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It creates a process for the Florida Legislature to allow counties and cities to expand the exemption further, potentially eliminating all non-school homestead property taxes over time.
Opponents have warned that loss of tax revenue could put damaging pressure on local budgets, public safety, and other community services. State economists have estimated that, if passed, Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.
That’s why it’s opposed by organizations throughout the state, including the Florida Sheriffs Association, the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, and the Florida Association of Professional Firefighters.
Albritton has previously said he “stands with law enforcement” regarding issues such as firearms regulations, and he repeated that in his statement, saying, “I proudly stand with the Florida Sheriffs, first responders and my neighbors across rural Florida.”
Albritton’s announcement is a bit of an about-face. After the Florida Senate this June voted to put the property tax cut plan on the ballot, Albritton hailed the decision.
“Owning your own home has been the American dream since our nation was founded 250 years ago. What better way to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary than a massive property tax cut through a $250,000 homestead exemption for Floridians,” Albritton said on June 2 in a written statement.
“I’m grateful to Governor DeSantis for leading the conversation on cutting property taxes and putting forward this robust proposal for the consideration of Florida voters this fall. For our part, the Senate has consistently advocated for an amendment that is significant and straightforward — a $250,000 homestead exemption in honor of America’s 250th birthday achieves that goal and then some.”
Albritton represents all of Charlotte, DeSoto, and Hardee counties and parts of Lee and Polk counties in the Florida Senate. Although his tenure as president of the Senate ends next month, he won’t be term-limited out of his seat until 2028.
Florida’s previous Senate President, Kathleen Passidomo, also recently announced that she, too, will vote against Amendment 3.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Costs and permitting are barriers to nuclear-powered electricity in Idaho, utilities say
text:
Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios, but high costs to build such projects can create barriers. (Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA)High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. 
However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate.
“When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.”
Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power)
“On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. 
For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. 
The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit.
The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor.
None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. 
But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project.
The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. 
“The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Alaskans should decide the future of Alaska seabed mining
text:
Gulls on the Nome beach, Oct. 2, 2020. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)What happens when an experimental industry tears up vast swaths of the seabed and everything that lives on it? What happens when it dumps everything back into the water except a few minerals that are immediately taken out of our state? What happens when we don’t know what technology will be used, when there’s scarce environmental analysis, when the financing is unclear and when there’s no chance to engage? This is the future of offshore seabed mining that the federal administration and industry interests want to force on Alaska. All under a regulatory framework that has hardly been updated since its creation before Alaskan statehood. 
As people who eat from the ocean, as people whose communities rely on both commercial and subsistence fisheries and as Alaska Native leaders, we say that the process is too fast, the potential impacts too risky and the unknowns too large. We are Presidents of Kawerak Inc, a nonprofit tribal consortium, and Sealaska, an Alaska Native Corporation, and the people we serve depend on healthy oceans and fisheries and live on the coasts where seabed mining is being considered. 
We want a moratorium on the exploration, leasing and extraction of seabed mineral resources in Alaska federal waters and on the Alaska Outer Continental Shelf. We want to see the Department of the Interior suspend further consideration of seabed mineral lease sales during this moratorium. And we want this moratorium to hold at least until environmental, socioeconomic, subsistence, cultural and cumulative impacts are evaluated and understood and affected Alaska Native Tribes have been fully and meaningfully consulted. 
Seabed mining could wreck parts of our ocean — and our culture and food security are connected to it. In January 2026, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management put over 113 million acres of Alaskan seafloor under consideration for this risky industry, including Norton Sound, Goodnews Bay, Aleutian Arc, Gulf of Alaska seamounts, Chukchi Borderlands and Canada Basin. Over 80% of those acres are already under restrictions that limit bottom trawling or all commercial fishing to safeguard critical seafloor habitat and the fisheries and ecosystems they support. Why should those areas then be opened to mining? 
And if these areas aren’t near where you fish, hunt or live, the federal government could add new areas, as they did near the U.S. Pacific Territories under this same process. 
As Alaskans, we depend on a healthy ocean. Tens of thousands of Alaskans rely on our multi-billion-dollar seafood industry for their livelihoods. For many of us, our seafood is a primary food source. We refuse to jeopardize our sustainable, renewable fisheries and subsistence harvests with experimental, nonrenewable, speculative mining. 
Commercial mineral extraction has never occurred on U.S. federal seabeds, and most types of mining being considered have never occurred anywhere in the world. Yet, the federal administration wants to hold Alaska offshore lease sales for this unproven industry as soon as next year. Leases would last a minimum of 20 years, and our oceans could take centuries to recover from mining operations. And the federal government continues streamlining the process. No environmental impact statement is required before leasing, and the opportunity for public comment closed in April with no guarantee of another before leases are sold. 
How do you as an Alaskan benefit from this rushed, reckless and restricted federal process? Why should we as Alaskans trust that others know enough about Alaska’s oceans, culture, socioeconomics, subsistence and fisheries to make these decisions without us? Alaskans must be the ones to decide whether seabed mining should occur here. Not DC. Not the industry.   
Proponents of seabed mining would suggest the most valuable parts of our ocean are a few minerals of unproven worth. We Alaskans know that the most valuable parts are everything else.  
Alaskans deserve the time and information it will take to figure out if we want this industry in our waters.

name: VTDigger
title: Layoffs announced at Vermont Information Processing in Colchester
text:
Vermont Information Processing in Colchester seen in August 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Vermont Information Processing, a beverage industry software firm based in Colchester, announced layoffs to employees Tuesday. 
The cuts come less than two years after the previously employee-owned company was acquired by private equity firm Warburg Pincus for roughly $1 billion. Last month, Vermont Information Processing, or VIP, announced it had purchased the Colorado-based firm Encompass Technologies. 
At the time, VIP said “AI will be a key part” of the company’s — and the industry’s — evolution. 
The company also unveiled a new suite of artificial intelligence features for its customers this summer.
Internal communications to employees obtained Tuesday by VTDigger called the cuts a “permanent reduction in force” at the company’s Colchester facility. The Vermont site will remain open, the communications said, and “remaining staff” will not be impacted. The company also has a footprint outside the state, including in India.
The company declined to confirm how many people had been laid off.
One primary reason for the layoffs, the internal documents said, was that certain technology has “reduced the manual workload required for specific functions in the company.”
The company is also implementing what a spokesperson called a “product-led” organizational model.
“Following a review of our organizational structure and business priorities to support this product-led transition, VIP made the difficult decision to reduce the size of certain teams,” the spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement to VTDigger Tuesday afternoon. 
The Vermont Department of Labor said it was aware of the layoffs and also declined to confirm the scale of the job losses.
“The Department is always concerned to hear about layoffs, and our top priority is to support affected individuals,” said Rachel Dumeny, a spokesperson for the Labor Department. In general, Vermont requires companies planning to lay off more than 50 employees in a three-month period to notify state officials in advance.  
Communications to employees referenced financial severance packages.
“We are grateful for the contributions of our impacted colleagues and are supporting them through this transition,” said the company’s statement Tuesday.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democratic Governors Association investing $1 million to support David Jolly
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly speaking at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club in Ybor City's Cuban Club on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)Weeks after he virtually begged for national financial support for his campaign, the Democratic Governors Association (DGA) announced Tuesday that it is investing $1 million to David Jolly’s campaign for Florida governor.
It comes less than two full weeks before Election Day, as Jolly attempts to become the first Democrat to lead Florida in the 21st century against Republican Byron Donalds.
“David Jolly has the clear momentum in this race because unlike Byron Donalds, he’s focused on what Floridians care about: making the state affordable to working families,” DGA spokesperson Kevin Donohoe said. “DGA is proud to support Jolly who has run an aggressive, grassroots campaign that has given him a clear path to victory.”
Donalds has blown Jolly away in fundraising. The Naples Republican has raised nearly $149 million and already spent more than $110 million. Jolly has raised less than $22 million.
The Jolly campaign did announce Tuesday that a fundraiser with former President Bill Clinton in Miami brought in more than $3 million.
And with just 13 days left to go, Donalds holds $33 million more in cash on hand, according to the campaign finance watchdog group Open Secrets.

name: Daily Montanan
title: LA man sentenced to prison after fraud that used ‘Montana-registered shell companies’
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images..A Los Angeles man who used “Montana-registered shell companies” in a multimillion dollar fraud was sentenced this week to 63 months in federal prison and ordered to pay $1.9 million in restitution, according to the IRS Criminal Investigation division.
Lamont McCarthy pleaded guilty in July to wire fraud and also will serve three years of supervised release in addition to prison time, a news release said.
IRS Criminal Investigation, the law enforcement arm of the IRS, described the scheme in its news release, citing court records from the Central District of California:
McCarthy purchased and controlled shell corporations listed as Cal Construction and India Towing. The companies “existed only on paper” and didn’t have legitimate operations.
“He then used these companies to submit fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan applications, falsely claiming they had substantial revenue, active operations, 15 employees, and significant payroll expenses,” the news release said.
But it said the companies didn’t have any employees, and they didn’t generate any revenue.
In an email, IRS Criminal Investigation public affairs officer Joe Simms said McCarthy applied for those loans in 2021.
“Once approved, more than $1.9 million in PPP funds were wired to accounts McCarthy controlled,” the news release said. “Instead of using the money for payroll or other authorized business expenses, McCarthy diverted the funds for his personal use.”
Simms said the investigation was launched in 2023 and a criminal complaint was filed in June 2026.
In a statement, Scott Brown, acting special agent in charge of the IRS Criminal Investigations field office in Phoenix, said the case demonstrates the IRS Criminal Investigation’s commitment to ensuring those who abuse pandemic relief programs are held accountable.
“While Montana business owners and families were struggling during the Covid pandemic, McCarthy was scheming to defraud the government relief program for personal gain,” Brown said in a statement.
It wasn’t clear whether McCarthy had a connection to Montana.
IRS Criminal Investigation conducted the investigation with the U.S. Small Business Administration, the news release said.
It said U.S. District Judge Percy Anderson presided over the sentencing, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Monica Tait of California handled the prosecution.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: The slime machine in Ohio politics has reached a despicable new low in the 2026 election
text:
A voter voting. (Photo by Jim Neuger/States Newsroom)I knew 11 years ago that our public discourse would be degraded down into unfathomable levels. The 2026 campaign in Ohio has now confirmed it beyond anything I could’ve imagined.
Every time I look at a screen, politicians and political operatives are showing a sickness of heart and mind that’s truly horrifying.
So-called “news influencers” fester like open wounds of viral rot on America’s body politic, necrosis setting in, poisoning the lifeblood of our Republic with sepsis, throwing hallucinations, derangement of the senses, loss of orientation, and delirium into our collective public experience.
Cynical politicians wielded an axe of unprecedented mid-decade gerrymandering across the country in naked abuse of political power and flagrant betrayal of the public trust.
Obscene amounts of money are being dumped into our elections by a Second Gilded Age Who’s Who Directory of the most monstrously malfunctioning human egoists imaginable.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The most expensive elections in American history are bombarding Ohio families with the stupidest, most despicable campaign ads I’ve ever seen, vomited forth as stinking detritus from the dark, depraved insides of political operatives and the “consultant” class.
They’ll spend three-quarters of a billion dollars torturing all of us in Ohio with these ads this year, AdImpact projects.
It’s worse than that, though. The dark money special interests are getting a hell of a deal, you see.
To them, it’s only three-quarters of a billion, but on the back end, through regulatory capture, sweetheart lawmaking, government contracts, and a whole galaxy of other mechanisms, they’ll receive hundreds of billions in public goods and resources. It’s pennies on the dollar.
The public is reportedly very concerned about public corruption. They should be. I have not known an Ohio in my adult life without a staggering amount of public corruption.
Now that kind of public corruption is being normalized on the national level, with the most venomous, adolescent politics possible to go alongside it.
I don’t really understand this morally and ethically barren hellscape era of American politics we are in, but I do know normal Ohioans pretty well.
Normal Ohioans are horrified and sick of the madness.
No decent, well-balanced person I know thinks things are going well — absolutely not in our political discourse, but also not in the general American or Ohio experience.
It seems glaringly obvious to normal Ohioans that the political class has abandoned representation of their constituents for the representation of themselves, their friends, and their preferred private and special interests.
Everywhere we turn, families get squeezed, at the grocery store, at the gas pump, for school supplies, for toiletries, for everything from a haircut to our healthcare.
I don’t think the 50-year relentless upward redistribution of wealth in America is doing the trick for Ohio families.
I think Ohio families feel that they’re getting ripped off. I think Ohio families are incredibly frustrated by it.
They turn one way, they get ripped off; they turn the other, they get ripped off again.
Here’s what frustrates me as a crusty old journalist of 20 years: This whole game is so old and so boring, and if only the people of this state and this country could realize the true power they have, they can still fix it. We can demand the best of our public servants and we do not have to settle for anything less.
We do it by standing up for ourselves. We do it by turning away from the screens and toward each other as human beings.
The screwheads and the depraved hucksters of political provocateurs, operatives, and influencers want us to dehumanize each other.
They want us to play in their game, but it’s a bloodsport — it costs human lives and robs humans of their humanity.
It robs the screwheads of their humanity too. Resentful over their lost heart, they try to drag the rest of us into losing ours.
They try to make Americans believe that other Americans are our enemies. They try to convince us that our neighbors want to destroy us, destroy our families, destroy our way of life, and destroy the country.
This is all nonsense and demagoguery. Most people just want to live their lives decently and be left well enough alone.
They try to example us to be our worst selves, to narrow our minds, to live in paranoia and resentment, to shut out and reject and dominate and victimize other human beings.
This is a bunch of crap. Anybody who follows that mindset will find themselves and their lives, in time, as soulless and friendless and barren as the ancient fables warned.
The solutions are simple and small but could cascade into something much larger, if humanity in 21st Century America is ever able to regain its grasp.
We stop providing a market for hate and start giving our attention to each other as full human beings, in our homes, in our neighborhoods, in our communities, in our states, and in our country.
We be honest with ourselves, with each other, and about each other.
We demand honesty of those who seek to represent us in our self-government.
We demand honesty from those who demand our attention.
We demand a fair system to represent our interests and give us equal opportunity to earn our own way.
We recognize that every human being and every human life is different, and we give each other decency and grace.
We cooperate with each other in good faith to build extraordinary and beautiful things that benefit not only ourselves and our communities now but future generations, so they too may continue to cooperate and build extraordinary and beautiful things together.
We’ve gotten into this pit collectively. We can get out of it that way too.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Panel studies ways to make Oklahoma more attractive
text:
Downtown Tulsa pictured April 9, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A legislative panel was told Tuesday to look past tax policy and to invest in education and other areas to make the state a more attractive place to live and work.
Oklahoma’s overall tax burden, which includes corporate, income, property and unemployment insurance taxes, has gone from 29th to 19th in the last four years, said Chad Warmington, State Chamber CEO and president.
“So, from a tax competitive standpoint, Oklahoma is in really good shape,” he said.
Oklahoma is also doing well in the area of infrastructure, he said.
But Oklahoma’s low rankings in the areas of health and education need to be addressed, Warmington said.
Warmington was among nearly a dozen speakers who spoke at a legislative interim study at the Capitol about what policies and priorities lawmakers must focus on moving forward to make Oklahoma a more attractive place to live and to recruit and retain businesses. 
Sean Burrage speaks to the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education after he was named the next chancellor for higher education with a unanimous vote on Oct. 9, 2024 at the regents’ offices in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma lags behind the rest of the nation in educational attainment, said Sean Burrage, Oklahoma’s chancellor of higher education.
Just 29.3% of Oklahoma adults have a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared to a national average of 36.8%, he said.
“If we want Oklahoma to compete for opportunities in aerospace, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, engineering technology, and other growing industries, we have to increase the number of Oklahomans earning post-secondary degrees and credentials, and our challenges begin well before students arrive at college,” Burrage said.
This year, Williams Companies, the largest natural gas midstream company in America, will hire 1,500 new employees, but will struggle to hire 150 of them from its home state, said Chad Zamarin, president and CEO of the Tulsa-based business.
“The talent we need is not being adequately developed locally and not choosing to move here,” Zamarin said.
While the state’s cost of living is affordable and commutes are shorter, education and workforce development are critical, he said.
Public safety is also a factor, Zamarin said. Homelessness and mental health must be treated aggressively and outcomes must be funded, he said.
“You will note that I do not list corporate tax cuts, corporate incentives, personal income tax cuts as top priorities,” Zamarin said. “Quality of life advantages far outweigh tax and incentive strategies in Oklahoma.”
Oklahoma is not losing talent to Texas due to tax policy, he said.
“We are losing on the basic conditions that determine whether talent says yes to our state,” he said.
Justin Harlan is the managing director of Tulsa Remote, which offered out-of-state remote workers $10,000 to move to Tulsa for a year.
Some 85% are still living in Tulsa two years after. He said 75% have continued to live there since coming in 2019, he said.
The top applications were from Austin, New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and San Diego, he said.
Parks, the outdoors, cultural offerings, safety, food and music were ranked as the top reasons for staying, Harlan said.
“People in expensive cities are actively looking for somewhere more livable and affordable to live and Oklahoma can be that place,” he said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Bill to legalize, regulate and restrict who can ride e-scooters passes state House
text:
A person rides an electric scooter on a city street. (Photo by Getty Images)Love them or hate them, electric scooters are one step closer to being a legal and regulated means of transportation in Pennsylvania.
The state House on Tuesday approved legislation that would place restrictions, including an age limit, on the use of the two-wheeled micro-mobility devices. It would also allow Pittsburgh, Scranton and more than 50 other cities to establish e-scooter sharing programs.  It passed by a 176-27 vote and heads to the Senate for consideration.
E-scooters are currently illegal in the commonwealth. That hasn’t slowed their widespread adoption as children’s toys and as a way for commuters to get to work and back.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Rep. Emily Kinkead (D-Allegheny) introduced the bill after a pilot micro-mobility program in Pittsburgh expired. Its abrupt end left many who relied on the scooters to get around the city’s hilly neighborhoods stranded and about 40 people unemployed.
Kinkead said the measure would give cities the option of allowing scooter sharing programs, giving people “access to a micro mobility option that is available across the country.”
It would also address common criticism of the devices, she said. 
“What it also does is puts reasonable restrictions on private e-scooters, so people are no longer riding them on sidewalks, so that children are no longer riding them,” Kinkead said.
Legislation pending in the state House would renew an e-scooter mobility program in Pittsburgh and put private users elsewhere on the right side of the law. (Capital-Star photo).
The bill would require e-scooter riders to be at least 16 and limit the vehicles’ speed to 25 mph. It would also require riders under 18 to wear helmets, among other provisions. 
A violation of the proposed law would carry a $10 fine, although municipalities would be free to adopt their own ordinances with enhanced penalties.
Safety concerns surrounding the use of e-scooters by children were the impetus for a companion bill in the Senate sponsored by Sen. Tim Kearney (D-Delaware). Senate Bill 1008 did not advance out of the chamber’s Transportation Committee.
Rep. Jennifer O’Mara, a fellow Delaware County Democrat, said the community there was devastated by the death of 12-year-old Abby Gillon, who was struck by a car while riding an e-scooter with a friend in Aston Township. Both girls, neither of whom was wearing a helmet, were critically injured and Abby died of her injuries two days after the crash.
“I know my office heard from so many parents reaching out to us, asking for the guidelines and the rules, and they were astounded when I told them these aren’t even legal,” said O’Mara, who authored an amendment adding restrictions for young riders.
The bill requires sellers of e-scooters to provide notice of the proposed law and allows a vendor who violates the provision to be fined up to $1,000.
It also tasks PennDOT with developing educational materials on e-scooter use and assisting municipalities and police departments with enforcement of the law.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri education chief resigns amid controversy over A-F ratings for public schools
authors: Steph Quinn, Annelise Hanshaw, Rudi Keller
text:
Stacey Preis, former interim commissioner of education, speaks to reporters on Tuesday after submitting her resignation to the Missouri State Board of Education (Rudii Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri interim Commissioner of Education Stacey Preis resigned Tuesday after just four months on the job amid speculation she was about to be fired.
Speaking to reporters while the State Board of Education met in a closed session, Preis didn’t deny her situation but said no one had “directly” told her to resign to avoid being removed.
Preis said she resigned “after much consideration” because she thinks “the board’s agenda is better served by a different commissioner.”
Her departure comes amid weeks of speculation that Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, could be named the state’s next education commissioner. O’Laughlin, whose legislative career has focused heavily on education policy, has expressed interest in working with the state’s education establishment.
The possibility of O’Laughlin taking over the department was a topic of conversation among school administrators attending Tuesday’s meeting, though the board has not publicly identified her as a candidate.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Preis’ resignation comes a month after she and officials from the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education recommended delaying the release of A-F grades for public schools during the board’s September meeting. Gov. Mike Kehoe’s executive order requesting the grade cards had called for a public rollout by Sept. 30.
The delay responded to school administrators’ appeals to the board to withhold the grades until districts had an opportunity to review their preliminary ratings and the methods used to calculate them.
Preis emphasized at the time that the board was committed to ensuring the grading system accurately reflected schools’ performance.
“A lot of people have been putting a lot of time and effort into this,” Preis said. “And we just are really trying hard to do it right.”
On Tuesday, Preis questioned the value of adding another grading system to the state’s existing measures of school performance, calling it “one additional system laid on top of another and another.”
“It was something that we were given, and we will make the best of it,” she said. “Or they will make the best of it.”
After the board concluded its closed session, board President Brooks Miller of Sunrise Beach said he could not address why Preis chose to resign. He said he had not intended to fire her.
“I wouldn’t say I know that much about it,” Miller said.
The Missouri State Board of Education convenes on Tuesday in Jefferson City (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Preis took over as interim commissioner after the sudden retirement of Karla Eslinger in May. She said in June she was not interested in seeking the permanent position but wanted to help “continue advancing department priorities,” including implementing an A-F grade card system for public schools.
The grade cards, which were requested by Kehoe in January, have faced financial and staffing constraints that have prevented full implementation this year, along with resistance from school officials who question whether the ratings will accurately reflect student performance.
After announcing her resignation, Preis told reporters the primary challenge facing Missouri schools is a lack of support, “both financial and otherwise.”
“We do the best that we can to support them,” Preis said. “Schools need resources. They need to know that people care about them, that they’re looking at them, that they’re not just judging them and grading them.”
Asked whether her resignation was prompted by the possibility of being fired, Preis said no one on the board had suggested that she would be voted out of her position during the closed session if she didn’t resign.
Asked if anyone else had suggested that to her, Preis responded, “No, not directly.”
 O’Laughlin speculation

O’Laughlin has not publicly announced that she is seeking the commissioner position, but she addressed speculation about her future in June during an event in Macon endorsing Chris Stigall for Congress.
“I know that some of you, maybe several of you, thought we would be talking about education, which has always been my primary passion,” she told a gathering of supporters. “And I’m always available if the education establishment wants to take advantage of my willingness to work with them to make education better.”
O’Laughlin did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. 
The Independent asked Kehoe for his assessment of Preis’s performance and whether he supported O’Laughlin becoming commissioner. 
Kehoe did not directly answer either question. Instead, his communications director, Gabby Picard, pointed to the state board’s authority to hire a commissioner.
Kehoe has appointed a majority of the board’s members and “has confidence in their judgment,” Gabby Picard, the governor’s spokeswoman, said in a statement. The governor wants a commissioner focused on improving reading and math performance who also understands Missouri’s budget constraints, she said.
State law requires the commissioner to “possess an educational attainment and breadth of experience in the administration of public education.”
O’Laughlin’s Senate biography says she has experience “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.” She chaired the Senate Education Committee from 2020 to 2022, advocating for policies that shifted public funding toward private education.
Senate Minority Leader Doug Beck, an Affton Democrat, has questioned whether that background is sufficient. Last month, he told the St. Louis Post-Dispatch she is “completely unqualified.”
In 1970, the State Board of Education sought an attorney general’s opinion on a candidate “who is not a certified teacher” but had led the House Education Committee and worked as a part-time professor at Missouri Valley College.
Then-Attorney General John Danforth wrote that the candidate was not qualified, since he lacked experience in administration.
“Executive experience in the field of public education would be invaluable, if not essential, in the performance of (the commissioner’s) duties,” Danforth wrote.
Miller, the board president, declined to address whether O’Laughlin was being considered for commissioner.
“That’s personnel issues,” he said.
 Commissioner search

The board took no action Tuesday to name a new commissioner. Instead, it unanimously adopted the recommendation of its commissioner search committee to hire The K12 Search Group to lead its nationwide search.
The firm was one of two options the board was considering during a meeting that was inadvertently livestreamed for a few minutes on Sept. 22. Subsequent commissioner search committee meetings have been closed from the public.
During the meeting, Kerry Casey, who chairs the search committee, said that while the firm hadn’t conducted a commissioner-level search, it had recently “worked in states that were going in the direction that we in Missouri are wanting to go also.”
They are “strong in our, let’s call it reform, approach,” she said.
According to its website, The K12 Search Group has “focused almost exclusively on CEO and senior leadership searches for charter schools and mission-driven K-12 education organizations.”
In September, the board signed a memorandum of understanding with the National Association of State Boards of Education to assist in its search.
The search is being funded by outside organizations. On Tuesday, the department identified the donors as the Ewing Marion Kauffman Foundation, Greater Kansas City Community Foundation, Regional Business Council, The DeBruce Foundation and Town Branch Foundation.
 A-F grade cards

During the public portion of the meeting, board members discussed adjustments to the grading framework and gave the department the go-ahead to share a technical guide reflecting the changes and preliminary scores with school districts.
Mark Penny, executive director of the Missouri Association of School Administrators, told The Independent that districts should have received the guidance sooner.
“It’s disappointing that the state board has seen the technical guide and 555 LEAs haven’t seen the document,” Penny said.
Discussion of grade cards at times gave way to expressions of discontentment from school administrators and others in the audience.  
Board member Vince Schoemehl of St. Louis expressed skepticism about grade cards more broadly, saying some schools could see public grades as a threat.
“(The department)’s got a whole lot of sticks,” Schoemehl said. “We don’t have a lot of carrots. This whole thing strikes me as another stick…. I believe, as a matter of reference to this board, people respond better to inspiration than threats.”
Public school administrators and others pack a meeting of the Missouri State Board of Education Tuesday amid speculation about the appointment of a new education commissioner (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Casey said the framework is not intended as a punishment. 
“The action that will come of this is support, is good things, is resources,” she said. 
Several audience members, including school administrators from across Missouri, responded with a loud “No!” Others laughed when Casey suggested the ratings could help direct more funding to public schools.
“Now, I will be the first to acknowledge the action on our budget makes it a little bit harder, Casey said.
The skepticism comes as the state faces budget constraints that could limit its ability to provide additional support to schools receiving low grades.
The board in its September meeting declined to request the roughly $300 million increase needed to fully fund the state’s public school formula next year. It instead requested the same amount of funding allotted to schools in the current state budget.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Alani Bankhead wants to be ‘the fighter in DC’
text:
Democratic candidate Alani Bankhead speaks to Montana Democrats during a gathering at the Northern Hotel in Billings during the summer of 2026. She is running for the U.S. Senate in the 2026 Election as the Democratic nominee, facing off against three other candidates (Photo by Jenna Martin for the Daily Montanan).Alani Bankhead’s quest to win a U.S. Senate seat as a newcomer to politics doesn’t sound like an impossible task to former Gov. Brian Schweitzer.
Schweitzer, a Democrat who won a race for governor in Montana in 2004 with a Republican lieutenant governor, endorsed Bankhead after the primary.
He said he doesn’t buy the claim that a Democrat can no longer win in the state, and he doesn’t fault Bankhead for seeking statewide office as a political unknown.
“I’d never been elected to anything when I ran for governor. Nothing,” said Schweitzer, who lost a Senate election in 2000, but was elected as governor again in 2008.
Nonetheless, Bankhead faces fierce headwinds, from the pipeline of money flowing to her independent opponent, Seth Bodnar, to the dysfunction of the Montana Democratic Party, to the support Republican Kurt Alme has by virtue of his political party.
Bankhead, who lives in the Helena area, came swinging out of the gate. Her aggressive stance turns off some Democrats, but the military veteran argues it’s a spirit Montanans need in Washington, D.C.
“We are in a fight for our democracy right now, and it’s important for people to understand who’s going to be the fighter in D.C.,” Bankhead said to the Daily Montanan.
 Progressive candidates clashing

Bankhead, who is the third generation of her family to serve in the military, was a bodyguard to the secretary of the U.S. Air Force when a review of nuclear sites was ordered, and she visited Malmstrom Air Force Base, she said.
“I remember tooling around Great Falls, and people would wave on side roads,” Bankhead said.
She said she and her husband decided that’s what they wanted.
They landed in the Helena area five years ago after her husband retired from active military duty and became a U.S. Environmental Protection Agency agent investigating clean air and clean water violations.
The couple intended to recover from a couple of decades of military service, with Bankhead retiring as a U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel and special agent.
But she said one reason she decided to run for office is they encountered neighbors who were struggling to put food on the table.
“We did not sacrifice and deploy and get shot at and bombed so that this could be happening in the richest country in the world,” Bankhead said.
In December 2025, Republican U.S. Sen. Steve Daines of Montana failed to appear for a vote to extend the Affordable Care Act subsidy.
A spokesperson told MTN News at the time that Daines was traveling, but Bankhead figured it should be curtains for Montana’s senior senator.
“Your whole job is to meet with people and vote on their behalf,” Bankhead said. 
She decided to try to take his job. 
“You’re getting fired,” she recalled thinking. 
 Daines maneuvers, Dems misfire

Daines had his own plans.
With two terms under his belt in the Senate, he would have been the tough-to-beat Republican incumbent, but at the last minute, he withdrew and endorsed Alme — who filed eight minutes before the deadline on the last possible day.
Daines’ sudden exit left some Montanans, including members of his own political party, miffed because it closed the field to candidates who may have been interested if only they had been given notice.
At least a couple of powerful Democrats tried to convince Bodnar to file as a Democrat too, but he filed as an independent. He has said he feels “politically homeless.”
Democratic political consultants pitched a strategy to boost Bankhead in the primary election and back the independent in the general election, said political scientist Jessi Bennion, of Montana State University and the University of Montana.
It’s a roadmap playing out in other conservative states, but Bankhead meant to campaign to the finish.
“They (Democrats) boosted her not even asking her if she would actually get out,” Bennion said to the Daily Montanan.
 Bankhead holds on

Bankhead never intended to back out, said so repeatedly and said Bodnar was the “last person” for whom she’d drop out.
She’s been stumping on a message of connecting her military service to her ethic as a future senator — she worked around the world to protect vulnerable people, she said, and she would work in D.C. to protect the powerless.
She has said she has the connections in D.C. and understanding of the political landscape to be effective.
On the campaign trail, Bankhead talks about stopping child exploitation around the world. Her campaign site quotes Brig. Gen. Amy Bumgarner, who signed her meritorious service medal award.
Bumgarner said Bankhead’s leadership in training agents, prosecutors and intelligence analysts led to 120 arrests in child sex abuse cases and a 96% conviction rate, according to a copy of the medal commendation on her website.
“When I talk about who I serve, it’s always been the vulnerable and the forgotten, right?” Bankhead said in an interview with the Daily Montanan. “And you can see that in my career trajectory. I hate bullies. I hate people who use power against weaker folks. I think if you have power and money, you should use that to create a better community for everybody.”
On paper, Bankhead and Bodnar appear similar in some ways. They both served in the military, moved to Montana within the last decade, espouse an ethic of public service and have criticisms of both political parties.
Healthcare, a top election issue for Montana voters, is one area where they part ways. Bankhead supports universal healthcare, and she said the country already has a model that works. 
She points to TRICARE for military families, a program funded with public dollars but provided by private doctors and hospitals.
Bankhead said the path is to extend Medicaid and Medicare until everyone is covered. She said the state and federal government already pay the cost of universal healthcare, but people are not getting the coverage.
“It’s a phenomenal system,” Bankhead said of TRICARE. “I mean, it’s not perfect, right?”
But Bankhead said it would have benefits for Montana’s rural healthcare needs, such as housing and pay incentives for providers who step into hard-to-fill vacancies.
“We have those solutions already in place,” Bankhead said.
She and Bodnar differ in style as well. Bodnar is personable in front of an audience, and Bankhead is punchy.
She’s comfortable on the attack, and one Missoula supporter said “she has fire and purpose in her attitude.” 
“I thought that Alani ate Bodnar’s lunch in their debate appearances,” said Dan Jensen in an email. “She is twice the fighter he is.”
 Fighting within

Bankhead has had to fight on some unexpected fronts in the campaign.
On Oct. 12, right after ballots went out, Shannon O’Brien, chairperson of the Montana Democratic Party, resigned to endorse Bodnar, but Bankhead said O’Brien had been working against her all along.
Her campaign gave an example: Bankhead had asked O’Brien after the primary when the Democratic party “would push back on Bodnar the way it had on Republican candidates,” her spokesperson said.
“She never got an answer,” said spokesperson Kaight Meyers, with the Bankhead campaign, in an email.
Only nine days later, when Bankhead followed up with the entire executive board, did O’Brien respond, Meyers said: “We continue to stand with you!”
O’Brien did not respond to a text message from the Daily Montanan that outlined that narrative.
In stepping down from the party and endorsing Bodnar, O’Brien said Bankhead didn’t have the momentum or resources to win.
But the Bankhead campaign said the lack of resources falls on the party; the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee sent $0 to Montana Democratic Party this cycle, but $2.8 million by the same time in 2024.
“The national party starved its own nominee, then cited the starvation,” Bankhead’s campaign said in an email.
 Trends for GOP

Schweitzer said the people who argue a Democrat can’t win in Montana anymore “apparently don’t own a calculator.”
He rattles off presidential election years and the percent of voters in Montana who supported the Republican, generally 49.5% to 59.1% since 2000.
In 2004, 59.1% of Montana voters supported the GOP president, the same year Schweitzer won.
In 2016, 56.2% supported Republican Donald Trump for president, the same year Democrat Steve Bullock won re-election as governor.
Schweitzer said Democratic insiders talked to each other and decided it was impossible to elect a Democrat for governor the first year he ran too.
“I consider myself fortunate that I didn’t know any of those people and fortunate that I wouldn’t have listened to any of their advice anyway,” Schweitzer said.
More liberal Montanans wanted the state to show its purple roots again with one choice on the ballot.
But Bodnar registered as an independent. His supporters tried to push Bankhead out of the race, and Bankhead called for Bodnar to step down. Both were unsuccessful.
So on the ballot, left-of-center voters and anti-MAGA Republicans have options, and political analysts have Alme leading the pack.
Bennion, the political scientist, said it’s hard for average Democrats to feel like they have a voice in politics with such maneuvering behind the scenes.
“That right there is the big mistake, as far as the political gamesmanship of it all,” Bennion said.
Editor’s note: Reporter Jordan Hansen contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Attorneys seek spring trial for man facing murder charge in Rutland deadly police chase
text:
Supporters of Rutland City police officer Jessica Ebbighausen attend a hearing for Tate Rheaume in Rutland County Superior criminal court in April 2024. Rheaume is charged in the crash that killed Ebbighausen in 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The driver accused of crashing his pickup truck and killing a Rutland police officer during a motor-vehicle pursuit more than three years ago is expected to stand trial next spring with the case to be heard in Rutland County.
Attorney David Sleigh, representing Tate Rheaume as he faces several charges, including a count of aggravated murder, told a judge Monday during a hearing that he was withdrawing a motion filed earlier this year seeking to move the trial out of Rutland County.
Sleigh had contended in that earlier filing that the media attention the case garnered would make it difficult to seat a fair and impartial jury in Rutland County. 
The prosecution had opposed moving the case out of Rutland County.
Both Sleigh and Ian Sullivan, the Rutland County state’s attorney, told Judge Susan McManus at the hearing Monday in Rutland Superior criminal court that they were working on putting together a questionnaire to help screen potential jurors as part of the jury selection process.
Sleigh had raised the possibility of withdrawing the change of venue motion at a hearing earlier this month, adding that as an alternative he would be seeking to screen potential jurors through a written questionnaire.
“I think it’s an efficient way to address the enormous amount of publicity this case has generated, and the strong feelings that appear to exist in a large number of people in Rutland County,” Sleigh told the judge at the hearing last month. 

READ MORE

Rheaume, 23, of Salisbury, has pleaded not guilty to the charges leveled against him stemming from the July 7, 2023 pursuit that led to the death of 19-year-old Jessica Ebbighausen, a Rutland City police trainee.
That pursuit ended on Woodstock Avenue when police said Rheaume, fleeing an officer in his pickup, crashed nearly head-on into a cruiser driven by Ebbighausen.
“It looks like we would be asking the court to look for two weeks for trial, late April or early May of 2027,” Sullivan told McManus during Monday’s hearing.
“That’s correct, your honor,” Sleigh added. 
The judge said she anticipated an “expanded jury pool,” especially with the trial expected to run two weeks.
McManus said she would set another hearing in the case in about four weeks to talk about setting the dates for the trial. 
“At least we’ll have time to solidify what that juror questionnaire will look like,” the judge said. “I don’t want to delay this any further.”
Rheaume did not attend Monday’s hearing and has been held without bail at the Southern State Correctional Facility in Springfield.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Protecting students starts outside the classroom, SC leaders say
text:
U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling talks about threats facing students during a school safety conference at Lexington 2 Performing Arts Center in West Columbia, S.C., on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)WEST COLUMBIA — As online threats rise, law enforcement officers and education officials in South Carolina are looking for ways to protect students both at school and at home.
Around 300 law enforcement officers, teachers and school administrators spent Tuesday learning about the threats that face students both inside and outside classrooms. The inaugural, day-long conference was meant to supplement laws and programs passed by the Legislature in recent years to help keep children safe.
Some of that work involves what people traditionally think about when considering school safety, such as keeping weapons and drugs out of schools, state leaders said Tuesday.
Legislators have spent tens of millions of dollars on improving safety inside schools.
This year, for the fourth time, legislators put $20 million toward grants for school safety improvements. Those can include improved door locks, increased security, metal detectors and other weapons detection systems, or storage for cellphones.
In 2024, legislators spent $5 million on a school mapping program meant to give law enforcement officers a better idea of a school’s layout if they need to respond to a shooting or other emergency. And since 2018, legislators have also spent roughly $160 million to help schools pay and retain armed officers, which resulted in every public school in the state having the money to hire a full-time “school resource officer” last year.
Physical safety in the classroom remains a constant priority, said state Superintendent Ellen Weaver. In her upcoming budget request, Weaver will ask legislators next year to fund a pilot program putting support staff in schools who can help out school resource officers but aren’t certified law enforcement. She did not say how much the program would cost.
But more and more of the threat students face comes from the internet, she said.
“We know the threats that are facing our children today are real, and they are constantly evolving,” Weaver said.
Under a 2024 law, students are not allowed to use their cellphones during the school day. But teachers and law enforcement officers want to make sure students are protected at home as well as in the classroom, Weaver said.
Interventions at school might save a child’s life, said U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling. Training sessions Tuesday included learning about online groups that target children and the warning signs of a child involved in those groups.
The FBI has seen a significant rise in cases involving predatory groups of adults, known as “nihilistic violent extremists,” manipulating children on video game platforms or messaging sites into harming themselves or others, said Anish Shukla, the special agent overseeing the FBI’s Columbia office.
Other online threats include extortionists, who attempt to blackmail people, often using incriminating or sexual images they’ve sent, into sending large sums of money. Those cases can drive children to suicide.
“It used to be that staying on top of the latest trend, studying for a big exam or winning a Friday night game were the biggest things on a kid’s mind,” Stirling said. “Now, they face a new frontier of dangers and threats that we must all be aware of across the country and right here in South Carolina.”
Legislators have tried to address those problems, too.
A law passed earlier this year put restrictions on social media accounts for people under the age of 18, though major technology companies immediately challenged that law in court. That case is ongoing.
Policy changes can help, but people will continue to target children regardless of the law, Weaver said.
“Not everything can be solved with a piece of legislation or with a budget request,” she said. “Parents have to step up and take responsibility for educating themselves about these dangers and educating their children about what they need to be on the lookout for.”
Trusted adults are essential in keeping children safe, Stirling said. Children need to know they can talk to someone without judgment if they need help, he said.
When those sorts of cases are reported, law enforcement also needs to know how to handle it, Stirling said.
Like the FBI, Stirling’s office saw an uptick in cases involving threats to students, he said. Some cases that spanned the state might have ended sooner if local law enforcement officers were aware of the sorts of issues other jurisdictions were dealing with, he said.
Along with the training sessions, the symposium gave law enforcement officers a chance to talk about what they’re seeing in their areas and share ideas for solutions or potentially connect the dots on similar cases, Stirling said.
“I guarantee you that someone’s life will be saved — someone’s life that potentially could have forever been altered — will be saved today,” Stirling said.

title: Brattleboro shelter resident pleads guilty in 2023 killing
text:
Zaaina Mahvish-Jammeh, 42, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder during a hearing at Windham Superior Court, Criminal Division, on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Mahvish-Jammeh admitted to killing Leah Rosin-Pritchard, a shelter coordinator with Groundworks Collaborative, on April 3, 2023. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 20, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — The shelter resident accused of killing shelter coordinator Leah Rosin-Pritchard on April 3, 2023, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. 
Zaaina Mahvish-Jammeh, 42, made the plea during a hearing Tuesday morning in Windham Superior criminal court. Judge Heather Gray said attorneys are proposing a sentence of 20 years to life, split to serve 10 years with probation for life. 
Gray ordered a pre-sentence investigation. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled later, with victim impact statements anticipated. 
Mahvish-Jammeh was a resident of Morningside House and asked to meet with Rosin-Pritchard, 37, then proceeded to strike her with an ax that had been hidden under a sheet, according to the plea agreement. Mahvish-Jammeh struck Rosin-Pritchard “all over her face and body, causing life-threatening injuries,” the agreement states. 

Judge Heather Gray said attorneys proposed a sentence of 20 years to life, with 10 years to serve and lifetime probation. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

Attorney James Valente of Costello Valente Group, who is not involved in the criminal case, called the sentence “complicated,” as Mahvish-Jammeh could be “released” on the criminal sentence but held as an involuntary inpatient if it is determined that she poses an immediate risk to the public due to her mental health. 
Mahvish-Jammeh has been described by a judge as suffering from mania and psychosis. She was ordered to be hospitalized in 2023 and was deemed mentally unfit to proceed with trial. The following year, she was deemed competent to stand trial. The case was scheduled to go to trial in January. 
Rosin-Pritchard’s family is suing Groundworks for wrongful death and intentional negligence in Windham Superior civil court. Groundworks previously paid an approximately $10,000 fine issued by the Vermont Occupational Safety and Health Administration that was reduced by half after certain safety recommendations were instituted.
Rosin-Pritchard’s parents, the plaintiffs Paula Rosin and David Pritchard, represented by Valente, serve as administrators of her estate. A motion by Groundworks to dismiss their claims, arguing that the matter is a workers compensation issue, was denied. 

READ MORE

“The court declined to rule on that motion to dismiss before discovery could be conducted to get a better sense of what facts everybody agrees on and what facts everybody disagrees about,” Valente said. “That’s the process that is currently ongoing.”
A new shelter called Hope’s House, constructed at the site of Morningside House on Royal Road, opened earlier this month. With the new shelter, leaders at Groundworks described wanting to increase safety and improve programming. 
“What happened at our former shelter was a tragedy, and we don’t diminish its impact,” Groundworks Executive Director Libby Bennett and Groundworks board of directors Chair Peter Elwell said in a statement ahead of the new shelter opening. “We cannot change the past, but we have a responsibility to learn from it. Those lessons are reflected in how we’ve designed and programmed our new shelter, our approach to safety, and how we support our guests and staff. We’re carrying those lessons forward as Groundworks enters this next chapter.”
