name: Washington State Standard
title: WA hospitals anticipate losing billions in revenue from Medicaid cuts
text:
U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, left, talks to doctors and healthcare leaders after a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, at Harborview Medical Center in Seattle. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)SEATTLE — Washington’s hospitals anticipate losing nearly $6 billion in revenue through 2033 due to steep Medicaid cuts in the coming months.
That’s according to a new report from the state hospital and community health associations. It comes as Democrats play up high healthcare costs and coverage losses in the runup to next month’s midterm elections. Voting has already begun.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell and local healthcare leaders discussed the expected woes for hospitals in a Tuesday news conference at Harborview Medical Center in Seattle. They emphasized that the hefty drop in federal funding for the insurance program serving low-income Americans from the tax break and spending cut bill congressional Republicans approved last year will affect all patients, as wait times in emergency rooms rise and premiums for those still insured increase to account for the lost revenue. Staff could be cut and clinics face closure.
Fewer people enrolled in Medicaid means more people going to ERs for care instead of being able to access primary care, and more costs that hospitals have to cover without being reimbursed, advocates say. Hospitals are required to serve patients in emergency departments whether they’ll be paid or not. 
“When you drive down the cost of uncompensated care, you help keep healthcare costs in check,” Cantwell said. “When you don’t do that, you are literally driving up the cost on all of us.”
Republicans believe the funding cuts, amounting to over $900 billion over the next decade across the country, were necessary to protect the program from waste, fraud and abuse.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Around 200,000 Washingtonians are expected to lose coverage by the end of next year due to the cuts. Many could meet newly enacted work requirements but won’t be able to surpass constant new paperwork barriers to maintain their insurance, officials expect. About 600,000 enrollees are expected to be subject to these requirements.
The work requirements, which begin Jan. 1, will require enrollees to prove every six months that they’re working, volunteering or attending classes at least 80 hours per month or show they qualify for an exemption. The mandate would apply to healthy adults up to age 64 without dependent children under 13 years old.
Roughly 10,000 in Washington have already lost coverage on Oct. 1, as the law stripped Medicaid coverage for refugees, asylees and other lawfully present immigrants, including people who fled the war in Ukraine and trafficking victims, for example.
Tens of thousands of people have also dropped the health plans they had through the Affordable Care Act when insurance became less affordable as federal subsidies expired. The debate over this issue in Congress led to a lengthy federal government shutdown last year. Coverage through the state’s exchange will cost an average of 22.2% more in 2027.
Rural healthcare
Medicaid cuts will hit hospitals hardest in some of Washington’s more rural areas, like in the 6th Congressional District on the Olympic Peninsula, projected to lose $1 billion. The 2nd Congressional District in northwest Washington and the 5th Congressional District in eastern Washington are next on the list.
Jefferson Healthcare in Port Townsend is bracing for millions in lost revenue and over $1 million in new uncompensated care to account for. CEO Mike Glenn says many rural hospitals are considering layoffs, clinic closures and other service reductions.
“Small rural hospitals will be harmed disproportionately because rural communities tend to be older and poorer than urban communities, and more dependent on public payers like Medicare and Medicaid,” Glenn said.
This map shows the impact on hospitals in each congressional district from federal Medicaid cuts, according to the Washington State Hospital Association. (Graphic courtesy of U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell’s office.)
Republicans in Congress embedded $50 billion in the bill for rural healthcare. From this, Washington is expected to get hundreds of millions of dollars over the next five years for an array of initiatives to boost health systems in less populous areas.
The lost revenue for Washington hospitals is projected to get worse each year, starting with $339 million in 2027 to $1 billion per year in the 2030s.
“When you take hundreds of millions of dollars away from safety-net hospitals like Harborview, you are not just putting care for Medicaid patients and uninsured patients at risk,” said hospital CEO Sommer Kleweno Walley. “You are putting Harborview’s ability to serve our entire community at risk.”
Meanwhile, clinics across Washington that primarily serve low-income patients anticipate losing between $98 million and $118 million in Medicaid reimbursements next year, according to the report. These federally qualified health centers serve as the safety net in many communities since they don’t turn away residents without insurance. The clinics estimate at least 82,000 of their patients across the state will lose health coverage, leading to over 200,000 fewer visits per year.
Consequences in the ER
Doctors laid bare the consequences for patients of the Medicaid cuts to come.
Dr. Lauren Whiteside recently cared for a homeless young man at Harborview’s ER after he overdosed on fentanyl. It was his second overdose in a week, she said. She connected him to an outpatient treatment program based at Harborview, and he was stable on medication a month later. Six months later, he was no longer homeless.
“This is what access to care can do,” Whiteside said. “The decisions we make about Medicaid and healthcare access are not abstract policy decisions. They shape when and how people get treatment, and they shape what kind of healthcare system we want for our community.”
Facilities are already seeing the effects of more people seeking care in emergency rooms.
Dr. Marie Vrablik, the medical director of the emergency department at the University of Washington Medical Center’s Montlake campus, told the story of a man on a medication drip in the ER. He was waiting for a bed when his drip ran out. He went into shock. They were able to rush him into a room to save his life.
“But because of crowding and folks waiting for care that, in a better situation, they could have gotten in primary care offices, we couldn’t get him in in a timely manner,” Vrablik told reporters Tuesday. “And as a physician, I worry that we will only see these situations increase.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees approves board to replace faculty senate
text:
A sign at Jacksonville State University as seen on October 19, 2026. The JSU Board of Trustees voted Tuesday to approve the Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable, an alternate to the dissolved faculty senate. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees voted Tuesday to approve the Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable, a replacement for its now-abolished faculty senate.
In a statement released by JSU Tuesday afternoon, JSU President Don Killingsworth said “faculty have always played an important role in shaping the direction of Jacksonville State University, and that will continue.”
“We made a commitment that faculty would continue to have a meaningful voice in university decisions, and the President’s Faculty Academic Roundtable is an important part of fulfilling that commitment,” the statement said. “I look forward to working directly with these representatives, hearing their perspectives and ensuring that faculty input remains an important part of our decision-making process.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Board of Trustees dissolved JSU’s faculity senate in August, citing a need to comply with HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April. 
The law has been interpreted differently by higher education institutions across the state. Auburn University’s Board of Trustees dissolved its faculty senate in June, prompting backlash from faculty members. Troy University and the University of Alabama System Board of Trustees opted to maintain their faculty senates.
The Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable consists of 13 members, including David Dempsey, the former president of the now-dissolved faculty senate.
Lance Ingwersen, a history professor at JSU, said in a statement after the Board of Trustees’ meeting on Monday afternoon, the board was less representative than the faculty senate and could limit faculty expression.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Rogers, El-Sayed outline differing approaches to tariffs and AI during Detroit Economic Club forum
text:
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, left, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed. (Photos by Katherine Dailey and Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, during a forum hosted Tuesday by the Detroit Economic Club, both agreed that international tariffs could be sound economic tools — if used correctly — and that AI could be dangerous without federal guardrails.
With just two weeks until the Nov. 3 general election. El-Sayed and Rogers are battling it out in a race that is currently rated as a tossup, according to Cook Political Report. A recent debate between the two candidates ended up turning contentious, with few opportunities to talk policy in a calm setting.
As El-Sayed and Rogers are set to take the debate stage again on Wednesday evening, the forum hosted Tuesday by the Detroit Economic Club allowed each candidate to answer more complex questions about policies affecting Michigan.
On tariffs, one of the primary economic tools used by President Donald Trump during his second term in the White House, both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed that they could be used in a positive way that might not hurt Michigan’s economy in the way that Trump’s tariffs reportedly have.
El-Sayed said he was not against using them, but not in the way Trump has, while Rogers said he would advocate for the president to make adjustments.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Like all the things that Donald Trump does, they are chaotic, they are ham-fisted, and they are self-serving,” El-Sayed said. “His version of tariffs is about accruing power either over corporations or over trading partners. That’s exactly why he’s doing this, and this version has been terrible for the American auto industry. It has been terrible for workers.”
Using an analogy that he’s espoused during campaign rallies, El-Sayed likened Trump’s tariff policy to an oncologist giving too much life-saving chemo to a cancer patient, which could be deadly, instead of a little at a time to fight the disease. El-Sayed said he believes in a tariff policy that is tied to an industrial policy “that actually makes sense.” 
“I think we need to continue to be the world’s leader in internal combustion engines, and I think we should build a $25,000, 300-mile range EV over the next seven years,” El-Sayed said. “We should subsidize so that we can do that off the top in the next two years, and then slowly pull those subsidies. And as we do that, we should be tariffing the EV market so that we can use our own market to incubate that product, so that we can sell it on the global market and compete with Chinese low-cost EVs.”
El-Sayed clarified that he believes that the U.S. will continue to be the world’s leader in internal combustion engines, but he also doesn’t “want us to cede the global EV market, which is growing every single day.”
“You cannot do tariffs without hooking it to a smart policy that actually makes sense around your industrial viewpoint,” he said. “And there has to be some subsidies because the whole point of a tariff is to protect and use your market to incubate something that you’d like to grow in your domestic market.”
Rogers, who had been a champion of Trump’s tariff regime when it was first rolled out, has since softened that tone. He has more recently said, in campaign ads and on the trail, that Trump should end his tariffs against Canada, and did so again Tuesday.
“When they went to Canada, I thought that was not the right direction,” Rogers said. “Mainly because they didn’t account for how integrated we are in the automotive business, and content providers here sell into Canada for cars that actually come back to be finalized in an American plant. I just don’t think they factored all of that, so having that conversation, to me, is important.”
Rogers noted information he said was relayed to him by Detroit Diesel, and said that the company was adding a third shift because of Trump’s tariff policies.
“We talk to small fabrication shops, they haven’t added shifts in decades,” he said. “They’re adding second shifts. That’s good for us in the long run. We just have got to get this thing right.”
In that vein, Rogers did praise Trump’s tariffs that he claimed have been helpful.
“The very fact that cars are coming back to the United States, including Michigan, from Mexico and China, are because of the tariffs that were applied to help us, I think, correct about 40 years of bad trade policy,” Rogers said. “So you see that the Silverados are coming to the Orion plant. That’s huge. It’ll be a multi-billion-dollar investment. General Motors is actually bringing about 500,000 new cars to be built in the United States, and we’ll have some of that up here in Michigan.”
Although the forum was not a debate, and both men were not in the room at the same time, El-Sayed noted that policies Rogers supported when he was a congressman led to the economy needing to be saved from past trade deals and economic strategies.
“The guy you just heard from said that NAFTA in the long run would be a good thing for Michigan,” El-Sayed said. “If you’re an auto worker, it has not been a good thing for Michigan. We’ve hemorrhaged jobs.”
Nominees agree on strict guardrails for AI
Rogers and El-Sayed both agree that AI research needs stronger federal guardrails, but their approaches differ.
Rogers said that guardrails were needed because he’s seen “personally” how intelligent systems can go haywire quickly, recalling his time chairing the U.S. House Intelligence Committee and was briefed on an early AI-guided missile that appeared to make its own decisions during a test. 
“It gave you a little bead of sweat on your forehead. This was back when I left Congress in 2014. Think about what happened and how fast this stuff has advanced,” Rogers said.
It was that experience that led Rogers to call for stronger guardrails under the guise of a national security framework, which is already in the works, and he said he would support it if he is elected to the U.S. Senate.
“I still need to go through the details of the bill, and see if it can be improved,” Rogers said, who added that it may be time to rewrite the federal government’s anti-trust laws to craft a narrow exemption allowing AI companies to cooperate on safety issues, which they currently cannot do. “One of these companies is going to see something that they know is not going to work. If the other company doesn’t see it, they plow through it. My argument is: let’s have that narrowly crafted anti-trust exemption so you can talk to each other on safety, not on anything else in the business, but on safety.”
El-Sayed, a noted AI skeptic, said he was deeply worried about the fact that AI companies, with the help of the federal government, were “about to open Pandora’s Box and nobody knows what’s about to happen.” He brought up an analogy from the Disney film “Fantasia,” likening AI systems getting out of hand, much like Mickey Mouse’s sorcery leading mere broomsticks to come to life and self-multiply.
“That’s what recursive self improvement looks like. The CEOs of both OpenAI and Anthropic don’t agree on everything, but they agree that this could take 50% of the white collar jobs in America, and the problem with that is that transition is not going to happen over a 25 to 50 year time horizon. It’s going to happen over a five to 10 year time horizon,” El-Sayed said. “Beyond the question of what these technologies are able to do to slip human control, or empower the worst actors — terrorists or rogue states — to create bio weapons we can’t even imagine, that’s where we sit right now.”
El-Sayed added that the situation compounds when those real-world dangers are coupled with the physical footprint and potential environmental dangers of AI support facilities. He has called for democratic control of AI systems to avoid systems being built that could fundamentally alter everyday life for Americans.
“AI should not be able to do certain things like fire weapons or fire you or deny your healthcare. We need an SEC or FDA-style regulatory agency that can oversee the development of these models to make sure we don’t open Pandora’s box only to hate it at the very end,” El-Sayed said. “I think that the legacy AI corporations right now need to be rebuilt as public interest corporations, shorn of traditional big tech.”
El-Sayed also called for “democratically appointed leadership of at least 50% of their boards.”
“I think the government should hold about 50% of the value,” El-Sayed said. “Why? Because if in fact this is going to sweep through the economy and take 50% of our jobs. We’re going to have to figure out what people do after that.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island Hospital resident physicians ratify first union contract
text:
Resident physicians and fellows represented by the Committee of Interns and Residents (CIR/SEIU) rally outside Rhode Island Hospital in Providence on June 5, 2026, calling for their first union contract. The physicians ratified a three-year agreement in October. (Photo by arewefreelance/courtesy of CIR/SEIU)Union officials announced Tuesday that almost 700 resident physicians and fellows ratified their first contract with Rhode Island Hospital.
The contract includes pay increases, better retirement benefits and other improvements for the early career doctors working at Rhode Island’s largest hospital in Providence, also the flagship facility of Brown University Health.
The contract follows months of negotiations and was approved last week by 95% of physicians who participated in the vote, according to a news release by the union which represents the doctors, the Committee of Interns and Residents (CIR/SEIU).
The agreement outlines a 12% increase in base pay, lower health insurance premiums, more workplace accommodations for lactating mothers and a 401(k) employer match of up to 6%, according to the union.
Dr. Samantha Palacios, a second-year emergency medicine resident at Rhode Island Hospital, said in a phone interview Tuesday that she’s grateful the negotiations didn’t escalate to a strike. Although she sees room for future improvement, Palacios said the unionized residents are pleased with their progress.
“I think overall the sentiment from everybody is just excitement that this fight, at least for the time being, is over,” Palacios said.
Rhode Island Hospital spokesperson Kelly Brennan confirmed Tuesday that the contract runs through June 30, 2029, and called the agreement “the result of productive discussions and the dedication of both negotiating teams.”
“We are grateful to our residents and fellows for their ongoing commitment to patient care and are proud to move forward together in support of our mission to deliver high-quality care, advance medical education, and serve our community,” Brennan wrote over email.
The newly ratified contract concludes a lengthy organizing and bargaining process which began in 2024, when the doctors now represented by CIR/SEIU initially shared their plans to unionize. They formally joined the union after a union election in January 2025, becoming the first resident physician group in the state to do so.
Rhode Island Hospital residents’ organizing efforts ramped up in recent months. More than 100 unionized resident physicians rallied outside the hospital on June 5, citing their wages as inadequate given their sizable workloads as well as the high cost of living in the region. 
Immediately after the rally, resident doctors delivered a petition to the hospital’s chief medical officer. The petition, signed by more than 70% of the hospital’s residents, noted support for the union at the state level and called for compensation more in line with the pay offered by other institutions. The union claimed at the time that many residents were living from paycheck to paycheck and making salaries that amounted to about $16 to $18 an hour. 
“We have received majority support from the RI state legislature, who recognize the essential work that we do, and how the Hospital needs to come to the table with offers that reflect the value of our labor and our dedication to our patients,” the petition’s signatories wrote in their letter.
Amid bleak financial forecast, Brown Health announces buyouts, executive layoffs

The union picketed earlier this month on Oct. 2, following the union’s rejection of hospital management’s then-latest offer.
Palacios said Tuesday the successful organizing effort demonstrates how important residents are to the hospital.
“The hospital truly does run off of our labor,” she said, noting that residents’ wages have not always reflected the “very laborious week[s]” they work. 
“We weren’t asking for mountains to be moved,” she added. “We were asking for the bare minimum.”
Residents at three other Rhode Island hospitals — Women & Infants, Butler and Kent hospitals — also unionized with CIR/SEIU in 2025. Those contract campaigns are still underway, according to the union. All three of those hospitals belong to the Care New England network. 
Palacios said the union’s success at Rhode Island Hospital has “moved the needle” for negotiating efforts at these other hospitals — efforts with which the Rhode Island Hospital residents can now assist.
“We’re grateful that we can now turn our efforts toward getting their contracts ratified as well,” she said.

title: What do foul-mouthed candidates think they’re gaining?
text:
Dear Editor,
What the heck do the few people running for office who use bad language in public think they gain? I know two things they don’t gain: the admiration of Vermont’s older voters who see that language as shocking or, at the very least, in bad taste. And they don’t gain the admiration of younger voters because even though, unfortunately, they are used to hearing bad language, they don’t say, “Wow, I’d like that person a lot more if they used the F-word.”
Craig TomkinsonMount Holly, Vt.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Dominion-NextEra merger hits turbulence, faces opposition from Va. leaders, SCC staff
text:
Dominion Energy offices in Richmond, Va. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce/ For the Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday warned that Virginia regulators should reject the proposed $67 billion merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy unless the companies agree to freeze residential base-rate increases for six years and nearly triple their promised monthly customer credits. 
Her demands came after State Corporation Commission staff recommended Monday that the deal as proposed be rejected, citing financial risks and inadequate protections for Dominion’s Virginia customers. Attorney General Jay Jones also spoke out against the merger Tuesday, joining Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi’s opposition to the deal.
After statewide tour, Virginia Lt. Gov. Hashmi officially opposes Dominion-NextEra merger

“The deal in its current form is not nearly good enough for Virginia or for Virginians,” Spanberger told reporters in a Zoom call. 
The governor said the conditions her administration filed with the SCC on Monday were aggressive but achievable. She wants commitments that regulators can enforce rather than promises of benefits that may never materialize. 
“These are very real requirements that I am putting forward because they have very real tangible benefits for Virginians,” Spanberger said. 
Dominion defended the transaction, which would create the nation’s largest utility if approved by state and federal regulators. 
Spokesman Rayhan Daudani said the merger would provide more than $2.1 billion in near-term customer and community benefits, including bill credits, payment assistance, workforce development and charitable investments. 
The companies say the deal would create 1,000 new direct jobs in Virginia and maintain current employee headcount in the state for five years. 
“The combination will also strengthen our ability to invest in reliability and critical infrastructure while helping keep energy affordable for Virginia families and businesses,” Daudani said. “Dominion Energy Virginia will remain locally led, separately regulated and fully accountable to the State Corporation Commission.”
 Spanberger seeks six-year rate protections

Expert testimony filed Monday on behalf of Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond calls for freezing residential base-rate increases for three rate-review cycles, or six years, and providing monthly customer credits of $29 for four years. 
The companies’ revised proposal offers a $10 monthly credit for residential customers using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity. 
Base rates account for only part of a customer’s electric bill, meaning a freeze would not prevent other charges from increasing. 
Spanberger clarified Tuesday that the SCC would still be able to lower rates under her proposal.
“While rate freeze is a pretty straightforward way to talk about it, it’s actually a rate-hike freeze,” she said. 
She argued that bill credits would offer little relief if customers faced simultaneous rate increases that consumed the savings. The administration also wants clear performance standards and consequences if the companies fail to meet their commitments. 
Asked whether rates could jump once the six-year period ends, Spanberger said future SCC proceedings would determine appropriate charges. She acknowledged that regulators must also consider the long-term consequences of combining the two companies. 
Spanberger became the first Virginia governor to formally intervene in an SCC proceeding when she joined the merger case in August. 
Her intervention allows the administration to request documents, question the companies and submit testimony. The final decision rests with the SCC’s three commissioners, who are not bound by recommendations from their staff. 
 SCC cites financial risks

In a 201-page filing Monday, SCC staff concluded that Dominion and NextEra had not demonstrated the merger would preserve adequate utility service at just and reasonable rates, as required under Virginia’s Utility Transfers Act. 
The filing warned that Dominion could face additional financial and business risks because of NextEra’s unregulated operations. 
Among the safeguards staff proposed are an independent board for the Virginia utility, limits in dividend payments and a holding-company structure intended to protect Dominion if its parent company enters bankruptcy. 
The recommendations also call for maintaining the company’s employment levels for Virginia for 10 years and preventing the consolidation of generating facilities or local district offices during that period. 
SCC staff proposed another review seven to eight years after the merger closes. The recommendation leaves open the possibility of approval if the companies accept additional standards, but the final decision rests with the commissioners. 
Hashmi endorsed the staff recommendation and supported Spanberger’s position.
“Virginians deserve meaningful protections and accountability, not a deal that puts corporate interests ahead of the people we serve,” Hashmi said in a statement Tuesday.
The staff filing also raised questions about financial information withheld during the review. 
According to staff, projections for the combined companies were largely redacted from the documents provided during discovery, even under confidentiality protections. The companies said some of the withheld material involved market-sensitive projections concerning NextEra’s unregulated operations. 
Asked whether regulators could adequately assess the merger’s benefits without that information, Spanberger said: “In short, I don’t believe that they can.” 
Dominion and NextEra executives have argued that combining their operations would improve purchasing power, expand supply-chain resources and strengthen access to credit, helping control costs. 
The SCC’s determination comes weeks after regulators agreed to admit documents related to NextEra’s failed acquisition of a Florida utility to the case, details advocacy group Clean Virginia — also an intervenor in the case — said were necessary to gain a full picture of the proceedings.
State regulators to allow part of NextEra’s political past to be examined in Dominion merger case

 Data centers, clean energy and jobs

Spanberger’s proposed conditions extend beyond rate protections and utility bill credits.
Her administration also wants stronger safeguards against utility disconnections and changes to how electricity costs are divided among customer groups. 
It also proposes creating a separate Virginia-based subsidiary to develop zero-carbon power generation for large data centers. The subsidiary would be financially insulated from other customers to prevent those projects from shifting costs onto households and businesses. 
Another proposal would increase the share of debt in Dominion’s financing structure from 48% to 60%, with the aim of reducing the company’s overall cost of capital.
Additionally, the administration wants to revise how certain electricity costs are allocated, reducing the share paid for residential customers. 
Some of Spanberger’s proposals would require legislation rather than SCC approval. Those include creating an independent energy efficiency utility and eliminating the cap on Virginia’s rooftop solar program. 
Spanberger said those changes could benefit customers whether or not the merger proceeds. 
She also emphasized the importance of continuing Dominion’s offshore wind project, arguing that customers who have helped finance it should not see their investment jeopardized by decisions made after the merger. 
Jones, in a video statement Tuesday, said the merger would do little to solve the problems already facing Virginia’s electric grid, including growing demand, aging infrastructure and high costs.
‘A different deal on the table’: AG Jay Jones asks SCC to reset the clock on Dominion-NextEra merger

“That’s exactly why we have opposed this merger in front of the SCC, because the transaction won’t do anything to address those fundamental issues,” Jones said. 
He has also requested the merger review timeline be extended, proposing the 180-day period start on Sept. 14, when the companies filed additional measures in the merger proposal.
Dominion and NextEra filed their original application July 15. Under the all-stock agreement, NextEra shareholders would own 74.5% of the combined company, with Dominion shareholders holding the remaining 25.5%. 
The merger also requires regulatory approvals outside of Virginia. 
The SCC will hold in-person public hearings in Newport News on Oct. 7, Fairfax County on Oct. 9, and Richmond on Nov. 5. Written comments will be accepted through Nov. 12. An evidentiary hearing begins Nov. 17. 
Virginia regulators face a Jan. 11, 2027, deadline to act on the application under the state’s six-month review period, unless regulators agree with Jones’ request to extend it. That deadline does not guarantee the merger will close.

title: Nebraska medical cannabis cultivators call for changes to lab testing, fees, physician protections
text:
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission listens to a representative of one of the commission's four licensed cultivators during a meeting on Oct. 19, 2026, at the State Office Building in Lincoln. Commissioners seated, from left: Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and former District Judge J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s four licensed medical cannabis cultivators are pushing for changes to testing, fees and legal protections for healthcare providers as questions loom over when the fledgling program will provide for legal sales.
Representatives for the four licensed cultivators sent a joint letter to the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission on Oct. 15 urging the commission to consider the licensing and availability of cannabis testing laboratories and the assessment of fees before the cultivators even have a “viable path to revenue.”
Dustin Krajewski of Meadowlark Medicinals LLC, former state Sen. Kent Rogert of KRL Med LLC, Pat Thomas of MahāMotā Cultivation Co. and Robert Wagner of Midwest Cultivators Group signed the letter.
Under the commission’s regulations, only four cultivators can be licensed.
An uncertain supply chain
MahāMotā, near Raymond, moved ahead with planting despite delays from the commission. 
The Legislature did not authorize the commission to assess fees until April, and the commission had already been working to finalize a prior set of regulations. The commission is refusing to grant more licenses until it can assess fees for future licenses. 
A MahāMotā representative said Monday that the company is still on track to harvest this year but sees no path to how testing facilities could legally receive, possess or test their plant.
“We request an update to the current proposed regulations that provide clarification of the licensing or authorization process, who may transport samples to a laboratory, how transportation and manifest requirements apply to those transfers and whether out-of-state laboratories may be used,” the cultivators said in their letter.
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Commissioner Lorelle Mueting, interim commission chair, said the regulatory process has been the commission’s “primary concern,” so she couldn’t speak to the testing concerns. She instead flipped the onus on MahāMotā and said they were warned the supply chain wouldn’t be fully up and running by the time the first harvest came.
“Every cultivator assured us that they could store product and that wasn’t a problem, and there was no reason to delay planting because storage was a viable option,” Mueting said.
The MahāMotā representative said the company assumed a smaller time frame, maybe three to six months. Mueting said the commission never gave that estimate and had questioned whether the product could be stored for up to two years before issuing licenses.
“I understand that it may degrade and all those things,” Mueting continued, “but I feel like those were things that possibly you knew or the owner of the company knew going in.”
Nebraska voters overwhelmingly approved legalizing and regulating medical cannabis almost two years ago, in November 2024.
‘Safe, accountable and sustainable program’
In their letter, the cultivators also expressed concern that the proposed fee structure calls for $36,500 in annual costs, before required bond premiums and other compliance costs — $23,500 to renew the license each year and $13,000 to use the commission-authorized seed-to-sale inventory tracking system. 
Advocates for medical cannabis join together before a public hearing at the Nebraska State Office Building in Lincoln, Nebraska, on state-drafted regulations for the new medicine approved by Nebraska voters in November 2024. Oct. 15, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The companies said the fees should reflect the program’s “operational readiness” and licensees’ ability to “lawfully bring products to market.”

“We ask the Commission to consider the time current operators will need to reach revenue, accounting for any necessary laboratory licensing or authorization and the issuance of manufacturer and dispensary licenses,” the letter states.
The cultivators are also making a call to the Nebraska Legislature to provide clear legal protections for physicians who recommend the medicine, calling the law “essential to encouraging practitioner participation, supporting patient access and sustaining Nebraska’s medical cannabis industry.” Bills to do so failed to pass in 2025 and 2026.
The cultivators urged commissioners to defer substantial recurring charges until such “essential components” are in place. If not, the companies suggested reduced fees or a payment schedule, such as for the $13,000 annual fee to integrate with the state’s seed-to-sale tracking.
If not, the cultivators warned, the delays could risk the viability of licensed establishments, potentially requiring repeat licensing or facility development and delays for patients.
Said the cultivators: “We share an opportunity, and a responsibility, to support one another’s success and build a safe, accountable and sustainable program that carries out the will of Nebraska voters.”
The commission is set to consider comments on its regulations on Nov. 16. If approved, the proposal would head to the Attorney General’s Office for review and then to the governor.

title: Vermont experts say bats need our help. How do we get over our fear of them?
text:
Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department staff and TNC partners conduct an annual hibernaculum bat count for a partner university’s white-nose research in 2024. Photo courtesy of Vermont Fish & Wildlife Dept.

“There’s some bats in the freezer over there.”
That’s what Alyssa Bennett remembers her boss saying to her when she was starting her job as a small-mammal biologist at the Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department 15 years ago.
Bats are elusive creatures, so whenever officials found a dead one out in the field, Bennett says, they’d often bring it back to the office and store it.
Bennett had some taxidermy experience when she started the job. So she took an eastern red bat from the freezer and made a taxidermied specimen so realistic that one of her co-workers asked how it would be able to breathe in the glass box she’d staged it in, perched on a branch with one wing outstretched.
People most often associated bats with the terrifying night monsters of Halloween: blood-sucking, rabid vampires. But, Bennett said, when people started seeing the effects of white-nose syndrome — a contagious fungal infection that has killed nearly 6 million bats in the Northeastern U.S. since 2006 — people’s fear toward bats started to shift.
“People started to see pictures of these struggling, dying bats crawling in the snow in the middle of winter, starved, with shredded wings,” Bennett said. “People who were like, ‘Bats are gross and scary,’ said, ‘I still think they’re gross and scary, but I know they’re in trouble, and I don’t want to hurt them.’”
She said International Bat Week, which takes place during the last week of October, is an opportunity for people to learn more about these species that are rarely encountered otherwise.
Nine species of bats call Vermont home, and five of these are listed by the state or federal government as threatened or endangered. Northern long-eared bats were classified as federally endangered in 2022 in response to the devastation of their population from white-nose syndrome. Various conservation efforts are underway, but experts say there’s a long way to go.
White-nose syndrome
When Barry Genzlinger, a state-licensed bat rehabilitator based in Milton, receives a bat that’s afflicted with white-nose syndrome, it can be a long road to recovery. Even once he’s treated the infection, he said, he still has to keep a close eye on the bat.
“Be on top of that every minute until we see that they are out of the woods, and that takes weeks,” he said.
The fungus that causes white-nose syndrome is not native to North America. It spreads through contact, so bats can catch it from one another or from surfaces like cave walls. It looks like it turns their noses white, but it can spread to the rest of the body, especially during hibernation when their immune systems slow way down.

Alyssa Bennett displays information about white-nose syndrome with some of her taxidermy bats. Photo courtesy of Bev Briggs

Experts think it makes bats’ skin itchy, so when the creatures are supposed to be resting, they will wake up irritated. Waking up repeatedly through the winter uses up their precious fat stores. When they emerge in the spring and their immune system starts to ramp up to fight the infection, they don’t have enough energy and die.
The fungus also eats away at bats’ wings, causing holes that, in combination with their immune response, can be fatal.
Vermont’s bat populations were hit hard in 2008 and 2009. 
Bennett, who started the job in 2011 and saw Fish & Wildlife’s pictures from that time, described “carpets of dead bats” at some sites. When she visited those sites in more recent years, she said, they were like graveyards littered with bat bones.
The syndrome is now endemic, which means it’s established and here to stay. The initial decline of bats has slowed. Bennett said some bats that remain may hold the key to surviving the syndrome, describing the survival of little brown bat populations, in particular, as a potential example of rapid natural selection. She said there’s an evolutionary process happening right before our eyes.
Conservation efforts
Bennett said that before white-nose syndrome, positions like hers didn’t really exist.
“There was a handful of bat biologists working for government agencies before white-nose syndrome came along, and then this introduced fungus that our bats were really naive to just swept through like wildfire,” she said. 
Now, she said, most states have someone on staff who does bat work.
Bennett has applied for several grants in recent years that support bat conservation work. She said the availability of these grants is typically announced in the spring, but she is still waiting for those announcements this year.

Three little brown bats with no signs of white nose disease. Photo courtesy of Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department

Vermont is eligible to apply for certain federal funds that can help Fish & Wildlife acquire tracts of land with critical habitat for two species of endangered bats: the Indiana bat and the northern long-eared bat. Will Duane, the land acquisition coordinator for the department, said it’s exciting to be able to do conservation work in western Vermont that’s focused specifically on bat habitat.
Through that funding source, officially named the Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund, Fish & Wildlife has already received grant money to acquire land in Addison County by the Lemon Fair River in 2024 and on Snake Mountain in 2025. Duane called Snake Mountain an “island of protected biodiversity” surrounded by farmland.
Applications are open for this year’s grants from the conservation fund. Duane said he’s submitting Vermont’s application next month for a project in Dorset in collaboration with The Nature Conservancy and the Trust for Public Land.
Efforts closer to home
This time of year is when bats start looking for a place to hibernate for the winter. That means it’s also a good time for homeowners to take steps to prevent the animals from roosting in their attic. Fish & Wildlife provides guidance for safely removing bats during this season, when they don’t have vulnerable young.
Barry the Bat Guy, as Genzlinger has come to be known, estimates he’s rehabilitated at least 1,000 bats. Many of them arrive to him — or to either of the other two licensed bat rehabilitators in the state — with white-nose syndrome, mites or ticks, or a broken wing. Genzlinger also houses bats that people discover in their homes during the winter. He keeps them safe while they hibernate until the spring, and then releases them.
“It’s the middle of winter,” he said. “You can’t catch a bat and throw them outside. That’s certainly a death sentence. So instead, you call the Bat Center.”
The Vermont Bat Center is a nonprofit organization that provides educational opportunities about bats and supports the state’s three bat rehabilitators.
The center’s website features pictures of the rehabilitation process, including photos of Rusty and Spike, little brown bats who were rescued from a bucket of nails, resisting their checkups and feasting on their first mealworms.

A bat with white nose disease hangs from a cave wall. Photo courtesy of Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department

Bats are not easy to encounter up close. The best shot at getting a glimpse is usually after twilight, when they can be seen swooping around to eat mosquitoes and other common insect pests.
Bennett said their mystery might have contributed to humans’ fear factor, which is why it’s important to her — and Genzlinger — to share what they know about bats and demystify them.
They say it’s hard to be scared of a creature that’s about the size of your thumb and weighs less than three pennies.
There’s still a lot to learn about — and from — bats. Researchers from the University of Vermont are studying bats to see if their genetic code holds secrets to cancer treatment and living longer. And the National Wildlife Health Center has been testing a vaccine for white-nose syndrome in the western U.S. Researchers across the country are developing experimental treatments, as well.
Bennett said there’s also a box to check on the Vermont income tax return that would add a contribution to the department’s nongame wildlife fund, which supports the conservation of little brown bats and four other non-bat species in Vermont.
Genzlinger, who would like to see more bat rehabilitators become licensed, particularly in the southern part of the state, emphasized how important it is to protect Vermont’s bat species, especially the endangered and threatened ones.
“If you were to throw one of those out in the snow,” he said, “you might as well be killing a bald eagle or a peregrine falcon.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Advocates call for unity in face of attacks on homeless in CT
text:
Ever since the night that rocks came hurtling through the woods into his camp, Mark Greenawalt wakes at every sound, no matter how small.
A rock left a dent in the side of Greenawalt’s house, but no one was hurt. His neighbor, Isaiah Peck spends hours sitting at the camp entrance, standing guard over the Milford encampment near the Lowe’s Home Improvement Store. 
They are two of the three permanent residents of a homeless encampment that’s been built over decades into a village of sorts, complete with a television, decks built in the woods, and designated spots where they feed some of the animals that approach the camp from the surrounding forest. It’s also been the site of recent harassment, in which multiple people threw rocks and fireworks, yelled insults and painted swastikas on the trees outside the encampment.
Greenawalt has lived there the longest; over the last 20 years, he’s helped build it into what it is today, and is the de-facto mayor of the collection of sheds and buildings nestled among the trees. The residents of the encampment cook dinner together each night and have set up a spot to play music.

Swastikas are seen painted on trees outside a homeless encampment in Milford on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. The encampment has been the subject of recent attacks and harassment in the last few weeks. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“It was nice and peaceful until this happened,” Greenawalt said. He’s planning to move soon, after successfully getting a housing choice voucher that will help him pay rent in a private apartment in the New Haven area.
The attack at the Milford encampment occurred at the end of September. Milford police have identified three suspects but haven’t made any arrests. They’ve also reported the incident as a hate crime, according to a statement from Police Chief Keith Mello.
The attacks are not limited to Milford. Late last week, a 22-year-old man sleeping outside was also hit in the head with a rock in a Bridgeport park. Bridgeport Police Chief Roderick Porter said officers have a person of interest in the case and are close to an arrest, and the victim is in critical but stable condition.
The incidents have left homeless service providers and the unhoused population shaken.
Advocates on Tuesday held a press conference in Bridgeport to call attention to the issue.
“At the federal level, we are seeing increased attacks on people experiencing homelessness, both through words and policies that criminalize poverty and treat people without housing as problems to be removed, rather than neighbors who need our care, love, and support,” said Sarah Fox, chief executive of the Connecticut Coalition to End Homelessness. “Even here in Connecticut, a state that prides ourselves on looking out for one another, we are not immune to the harm caused by this very dehumanizing rhetoric.”
This year, the National Coalition for the Homeless recorded a significant rise in serial attacks on people experiencing homelessness, including what the organization referred to as “shocking levels” of law enforcement involvement in attacks on people experiencing homelessness.
The coalition attributes the rise in violence to a corresponding increase in legislation and court rulings they say criminalize homelessness, leading to more “vigilantism and hatred directed towards people who are forced to live outdoors.” In addition to some state-level laws passed in states such as Kentucky, Florida and Missouri, the U.S. Supreme Court in 2024 ruled that it was legal for people to be arrested for activities such as sleeping outside.
Connecticut lawmakers for the past two legislative sessions have tried to pass a law that would prohibit arrests or fines for these activities, but the measures haven’t moved on the House or Senate floor. Local officials have opposed the bills, saying they need to be able to clear camps for health and safety reasons.
Homelessness in Connecticut and nationwide has also been rising since the COVID-19 pandemic, albeit more slowly over the last year than in the years prior.
President Donald Trump’s administration has also said it wants to shift to a practice of putting people experiencing homelessness in institutions for mental health or drug addiction, rather than the housing first approach that’s been used over the past decade.
“When those in power at the highest level demonize our homeless neighbors, they sanction society and institutions to act based on harmful beliefs, stoking the flames of the anti-homeless violence we see in our own communities,” said Sadia Rahman, of the National Homelessness Law Center, at Tuesday’s press conference.
State lawmakers on Tuesday said they want to focus on increasing funding or trying again to prohibit arrests and fines for sleeping outside to help the unhoused population. Republicans and Democrats also called for unity and kindness.
Outreach worker Jason Blakeman walks through a homeless encampment in Milford on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. The encampment has been the subject of recent attacks and harassment, including people throwing rocks and painting swastikas on the trees. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
“Hate has a cost, and we are seeing that now here in the city of Bridgeport and in Milford,” said Housing Committee co-chair Rep. Antonio Felipe, D-Bridgeport.
Several speakers pointed to rhetoric and actions from the Trump administration and far right as roots of violence. Housing Committee ranking member Rep. Tony Scott, R-Monroe, steered clear of critiquing the Trump administration but said Connecticut’s politics aren’t as divisive as national politics, and that they’ll work on a bipartisan basis to help the homeless in the state. 
“Screw D.C.,” Scott said. “We can do this ourselves.”
The people living at the Milford encampment attribute the attacks on their homes not to politics, but to hate and boredom. The people who attacked the encampment yelled at Greenawalt and his neighbors about not paying taxes, Greenawalt said.
Just last year, the Milford encampment was also the site of an intentionally set fire that killed one of its long-term residents, a man Greenawalt said was his best friend. Greenawalt bears scars on his arms and scalp from trying to pull Joe Kane out of the fire. Kane’s absence is felt deeply at the encampment. Greenawalt still says good morning and good night to his burned-out home each day.
Greenawalt said that given the attacks, he’s excited to be moving to an apartment where he can feel at peace and secure. It took a long time to secure all the documents and get him a voucher, he said.

Outreach worker Jason Blakeman says goodbye Longtime resident Troy Gosbin after a morning check-in at a homeless encampment in Milford on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. The encampment has been the subject of recent attacks and harassment, including people throwing rocks and painting swastikas on the trees. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

He’ll return to the encampment, though. He has a groundhog he’s named Freddy who he feeds daily. The animal likes to scamper across Greenawalt’s front porch, sometimes sniffs at the man’s foot, then heads over to the spot where Greenawalt generally keeps some of Freddy’s favorites — apples, celery, and the occasional chicken nugget.
“It’s none of their business how I live,” he said, of the attackers.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: K-12 scholarships through federal tax credits start in January. Nonprofits will oversee spending.
text:
A federal funding program will give students money for private school tuition, tutoring and textbooks, with no set limit on how much they can receive. (File photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Starting in January, nonprofits can dole out scholarships to South Carolina students for K-12 private tuition and other education expenses, thanks to a federal tax credit program.
The program, approved as part of last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has similarities to a state tax credit approved over a decade ago that legislators ultimately revised because of concerns about how one nonprofit handled the money.
That same nonprofit, Palmetto Kids FIRST, plans to participate in the federal program, said its president, Jeff Davis, who is also chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. While critics have concerns about the program’s accountability, Davis pointed to federal oversight to keep the program in check.
The nonprofit’s participation is ultimately up to the state Department of Revenue. Last week, Gov. Henry McMaster instructed the agency to begin evaluating applicants.
So far, 30 states, including South Carolina, have opted in. Each state must decide annually whether it wants to continue, meaning the next governor will get to decide if South Carolina remains in the program.
A proposed federal rule laying out the specifics of how it will work, issued earlier this month, still needs final approval before going into effect. Public comments are open until Dec. 1.
How does the federal program work?
Starting Jan. 1, taxpayers can give approved nonprofits up to $1,700 annually for a dollar-for-dollar reduction in the federal taxes they owe. A married couple filing jointly can donate up to $3,400 for a corresponding reduction in their tax liability.
Unlike similar state-run programs, there’s no cap on how much nonprofits can collect in donations or award as scholarships. They just can’t spend more than they collect.
They also don’t have to give equal amounts to students. So, some students could get their entire tuition covered while others get partial scholarships through the same nonprofit. That’s entirely up to the nonprofit.
Scholarships through the federal program can stack on top of state funds. So, a student whose parents receive scholarships through South Carolina’s voucher or tax-credit programs can also get money through the federal program. For some students, that will allow private tuition to be fully paid. It could also allow additional expenses to be covered.
Expenses that qualify for a scholarship are broad. They include tuition, tutoring, books, computers, internet fees, transportation and uniforms.
The only eligibility limitation for students is that their parents’ income can’t be more than triple the local median.
That means families in Richland County, for example, can’t make more than $277,200. In Greenville County, the cap rises to $319,200, and in Charleston County, it’s $352,500.
Nationwide, as many as 90% of children qualify, according to a study by public policy think tank Urban Institute.
Although states are responsible for overseeing the program and approving nonprofits for participation, South Carolina can’t add any rules beyond what’s in the federal law.
Under those rules, each nonprofit must award scholarships to more than 10 students attending more than one school. That’s meant to prevent schools or parents from setting up nonprofits for their own students. And nonprofits can keep up to 10% of what they receive; 90% of donations must go toward children’s education.
It’s not yet known how many nonprofits could be collecting money in South Carolina. The state Department of Revenue has until Feb. 1 to report a full list of qualifying nonprofits.
How is the federal tax credit similar to SC’s programs?
In 2013, South Carolina legislators adopted a similar, though much more limited, program to help pay for educational expenses.
The tax credit allowed children with documented disabilities to receive up to $11,000 each to pay for education expenses, such as tuition at specialized schools. Like the federal program, nonprofits registered as “scholarship granting organizations” to raise and distribute funds.
Palmetto Kids FIRST, one of five registered nonprofits, far outraised all the others during the initial years of the program.
But after complaints from parents and school officials, a Department of Revenue investigation found Palmetto Kids FIRST was soliciting donations from parents in exchange for money for their child. Every parent who donated later received money from the program, while parents who didn’t donate were less likely to get funds, according to the report.
Davis, whose wife was listed as the nonprofit’s president at the time, denied the claims of offering parents a quid pro quo. Although he sent letters asking parents for donations, and many of those same parents later received money for their own children, he said he never promised anything.
Concerns over Davis’ handling of the money ultimately led legislators to overhaul the program, renamed the Educational Credit for Exceptional Needs Children, in 2018.
Legislators created a single nonprofit, Exceptional SC, to dole out the scholarships. Changes in the program’s structure, combined with changes to federal tax law that reduced the benefit for donating, tanked the amount the program raises and donates each year, said Edward Earwood, chair of the Exceptional SC board.
During the 2023-24 school year, the program distributed $5.8 million to 1,322 students, according to the most recent data from the Department of Revenue. The nonprofit is allowed to collect up to $12 million under the law.
On average, each student received $4,500, according to agency data.
The federal program, by design, will have a much larger reach than the state tax credit, Earwood said. The credit will be easier to claim than the state version, giving people more of a benefit for participating, and the rules will allow more children to qualify, he said.
“It’s pretty distinctively different,” he said.
The limited “exceptional needs” tax credit remained the state’s only private school choice program until 2023, when the Legislature passed its first broad K-12 scholarship program using state taxes.
Advocates have fought since to expand that Education Scholarship Trust Fund, which provides qualifying students money for educational expenses. The scholarship amount is adjusted annually, as a percentage of how much the state spends on public schools, and awarded on a first-come, first-served basis.
This school year, 15,000 students whose parents make up to 500% of the federal poverty level are receiving about $7,600 each.
That scholarship program could be dwarfed by the federal one.
What might the federal tax credit look like in SC?
For Miracle Academy in Bamberg County, scholarships through the federal program could help recruit more students, as well as pay tuition for parents who are barely scraping by, said Principal Teresa Middleton.
“We definitely want to start with the parents who are really making the sacrifice,” Middleton said.
She also wants the money to help students who are already enrolled pay their $12,000 annual tuition. About 25 of the school’s 40 students are already receiving state funding, but that doesn’t cover the full amount, Middleton said.
“We’re hoping the federal system will be better for parents, better for children, better for schools and better for people who are looking for educational options,” she said.
If Palmetto Kids FIRST is approved to distribute funds under the federal program, the nonprofit’s loftiest goal is to raise $300 million, Davis said. That’s his guess for what it would take to cover private school tuition for all interested parents in South Carolina.
Around 70 schools have already signed up to receive money through the nonprofit, he said.
The nonprofit will ask parents and families at those schools to donate, Davis said. He emphasized that donors can designate a specific school to get the money but not a certain child.
“There are a lot of people that would just like to know where their federal tax dollars are going,” Davis said. “Instead of a big black hole in D.C., they at least want to know that it’s going to support a child.”
Davis pointed to federal oversight measures as a way of keeping the program on track. Nonprofits are subject to annual third-party audits under the federal guidelines, which will look at the organization’s eligibility, as well as whether students were selected based on their need for services.

What are critics’ concerns?
That didn’t stop Dena Crews’ concerns. The use of nonprofits to oversee the funds worried the president of the South Carolina Education Association, who said those oversight practices likely won’t be enough to decide if the money is spent as intended.
“There’s no accountability,” Crews said. “You’re just handing over money.”
Crews pointed to the state’s scholarship program as an example. During the first year, the Department of Education removed 1,005 ineligible students after some had already spent $64,000, a problem that did not repeat.
Legislators have yet to receive test scores for students using the money after the state Education Oversight Committee decided the first year didn’t have enough usable results. A report of test scores for the first two years is expected before the end of the year.
The federal program could run into similar issues monitoring student progress, Crews said. She suggested it would be better for the taxes to be collected and spent addressing needs in public education.
Middleton called the program bittersweet.
While she’s glad to see students receiving educational choice, she also sees how families are affected by federal cuts.
The private school also operates a daycare, and while she expects her private school enrollment to soar with the help of the federal tax credit, daycare enrollment has plunged, she said.
Other families are losing access to healthcare and grocery assistance because of policy changes, she added.
“We’re picking up one group and leaving another group behind,” she said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Trump affirms endorsement of Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race, belittles Cindy Holscher
text:
Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee for governor, speaks alongside President Donald Trump during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. Masterson's opponent in the Nov. 3 election is Democrat Cindy Holscher. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — President Donald Trump renewed his endorsement of Republican Ty Masterson in the Kansas governor’s race, while repeatedly heckling Democrat Cindy Holscher during a political rally near Wichita.
Trump, speaking Monday night in Park City, said his blessing of Masterson before the August primary was significant. Masterson prevailed with 43% of the vote in the seven-candidate GOP field. Former Gov. Jeff Colyer’s exit from the Republican race at the June filing deadline coincided with Trump’s backing of Masterson.
“All I know is he was doing good, but then I endorsed him, and he becomes a rocket ship, right? Right, Ty?” the president said. “I think if you lost, it would be the single biggest upset in the United States, maybe in the history of our country.”
Trump, who has sought to be the face of the 2026 midterm election despite weakening approval ratings, told the partisan crowd that it was important for Kansas voters to “defeat crazy Cindy Holscher” on Nov. 3. He mentioned Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly endorsed state Sen. Ethan Corson — not Holscher — in the Democratic primary. The president didn’t add that Kelly endorsed Holscher after she won the primary.
“Cindy Holscher is the most radical candidate ever to run for Kansas governor,” Trump said. “I would call her a radical lunatic.”
Holscher, a state senator from Overland Park who won the three-candidate Democratic primary, responded to the president’s rhetoric by suggesting name-calling didn’t benefit Kansans laboring with the escalating cost of living, high fuel and grocery prices, and challenges securing health and child care.
“Thanks for shouting me out at your rally, Mr. President,” Holscher said. “You can call me whatever names you want, but I’m here fighting for the everyday Kansans who are struggling and are sick of politics as usual.”
“While you’re in town,” she added, “I hope you’ll take time to listen to the farmers who are suffering because of your tariffs, your beef imports and the Iran war that caused diesel to skyrocket. Or, the everyday folks who are anxious about their grocery bills, the cost of their health care and the price of gas.”
Holscher, who won the Democratic Party’s nomination for governor with 48.6% of the primary vote, said she wasn’t beholden to “one political party or partisan agenda” and would continue to serve interests of Kansas families as governor.
Holscher has sought during the campaign to link Masterson to Gov. Sam Brownback’s decision in 2012 to sign a bill slashing state income tax revenue. Brownback and GOP lawmakers chose not to reduce spending, which resulted in significant budget problems. A coalition of Republicans and Democrats in the Legislature repealed much of the Brownback tax program in 2017 over objections of Masterson and Brownback.
Masterson, an Andover Republican and president of the Kansas Senate, said Trump understood Kansans believed in freedom, hard work and the American dream. Masterson said Kansans essentially had no option but to elect him to replace Kelly, the second-term Democrat who cannot seek reelection.
“I don’t think you have a choice,” Masterson said. “You can’t go out and vote for socialists. You must vote Republican.”
In an interview, Holscher she she had never considered herself a socialist despite Masterson’s attempt to label her as such.
During the Trump rally, Masterson said he longed for the days when the U.S. House had a Blue Dog Coalition composed of fiscally conservative Democrats. The current Democratic Party was “unrecognizable,” he said.
“The insane are running that party and running it into the ground,” Masterson said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New State Lab opens on North Dakota Capitol grounds with expanded capabilities
text:
Christie Massen, left, lab services section director for the Department of Health and Human Services, speaks during a tour of the new State Laboratory next to Lt. Gov. Michelle Strinden on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s new State Lab officially opened Tuesday with public health and environmental quality officials praising the enhanced safety equipment and testing capabilities.
Construction began in April 2024 on the $70 million federally funded facility under then-Gov. Doug Burgum, who said at the time the new lab would be the first new building on the Bismarck Capitol grounds in 43 years.
The new lab will house about 50 staff of the Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Environmental Quality with room to expand if needed. 
“With the expanded space, we no longer have to test in hallways and have equipment sitting in our hallways, and not enough workspace,” said Christie Massen, lab services section director for the Department of Health and Human Services. “This is much more efficient and safer.”
The new 104,000-square-foot building will have expanded capabilities, such as testing for forever chemicals, PFAS, in the near future, and testing substances found in near-fatal overdose cases, she said. 
Jim Quarnstrom, right, chemistry division director for the Department of Environmental Quality, speaks to Lt. Gov. Michelle Strinden during a guided tour of the new State Laboratory on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“At the old lab, we didn’t have the proper materials in the construction of that lab because they (PFAS) are everywhere and they contaminate,” said Jim Quarnstrom, chemistry division director for DEQ. “Hopefully within a year or two, we’ll get the equipment we need and get a program going.”
To continue testing drinking water from cities and towns across the state, the Environmental Protection Agency will need to certify the department’s testing procedure, which could take about a month, Quarnstrom said. 
The new building has safety enhancements such as designated rooms for workers to don protective gear and separate emergency showers if lab technicians are ever exposed to dangerous substances, Massen said.
Some labs in the new facility require negative air pressure to keep dangerous substances, such as anthrax, plague, ricin toxin, tuberculosis and different types of fungi, contained.
The new lab will also be able to test substances involved in non-fatal overdoses in North Dakota, Massen said. Fatal overdose substances are processed by the medical examiner’s office at the state’s Crime Lab on East Main Avenue or sent out of state.
“Now, we’ll be able to screen and see what’s happening in our public for those who survive the incident,” she said. 
The new lab also has a permanent spot for the North Dakota National Guard 81st Civil Support Team’s mobile laboratory, which provides on-site emergency response for terror threats involving nuclear, biological and toxic materials, said Capt. Tom Hansen, nuclear medical science officer for the National Guard.
Massen said having the State Lab on the Capitol grounds makes their work more “on display.” 
“Laboratory science has a tendency to be hidden,” she said. “We’re usually behind the scenes and people don’t really know what we do. So it’s nice to be able to showcase what we do and help recruit students and laboratory professionals into the public health world.”
Lt. Gov. Michelle Strinden said replacing the old State Lab, built in 1974, was long overdue. She said the opening reinforces the state’s goal of becoming the healthiest state in the nation.
“Our lab staff here deserve to have quality workspaces that reflect the vitally important work that they do,” Strinden said. “The work happening inside this building will touch the lives of people living in every corner of North Dakota.”
The State Laboratory sits on the Capitol grounds in Bismarck on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine judge greenlights state’s initial approval of Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion
text:
Trucks bring waste to Cell 16 at Juniper Ridge Landfill, a plot of land where trash is actively being landfilled. Just over half of Maine’s landfill waste ends up in Juniper Ridge, which is expected to reach capacity in 2028. (Photo by AnnMarie Hilton/ Maine Morning Star)A Penobscot County Superior Court justice has backed the state’s finding that expanding Juniper Ridge Landfill is in the public interest, according to a release from the challengers, clearing the way for the project to move forward. 
“This ruling is a setback, but it can’t bury the truth that the Penobscot Nation and local residents have brought into the open — that this landfill is part of a broken system that puts polluters’ wallets over people’s health,” Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement. “The knowledge, persistence and power of these communities have already shifted the conversation — and that momentum will carry forward until justice is served.”
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection first issued a positive public benefit determination for the expansion in October 2024, but the Penobscot Nation and Conservation Law Foundation appealed the decision. 
In January, Justice Bruce Mallonee struck down that determination, and in March the department again found that the expansion was in the public interest. The groups returned to court in July, where opponents argued the state has continued to fail to meet environmental justice standards. 
But in a statement Tuesday, the Penobscot Nation and Conservation Law Foundation said Mallonee ruled in favor of the department.
“We have fought pollution, injustice and decades of harm to heal the Penobscot River, a relative that has sustained our people since time immemorial and continues to sustain communities across Maine,” said Penobscot Nation Tribal Chief Kirk Francis. “We are not asking the state to undo generations of harm overnight. We are asking it not to take us backward. Our cultural survival is tied to the health of the Penobscot River, and there is too much at stake to keep adding to the harms it already carries.”
More than half of Maine’s landfill waste ends up at Juniper Ridge. It is owned by the state through the Bureau of General Services, which has an operating contract with NEWSME Landfill Operations, a subsidiary of waste management company Casella.
The landfill is expected to reach capacity in 2028, and in order for Casella to apply for a license to expand, the DEP must determine the expansion would benefit the public.
