name: California
title: ¿Es esta la contienda congresional más normal de EEUU? Los candidatos de San Diego se presentan con plataformas clásicas
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Socialistas democráticos. Agricultores vestidos con ropa Carhartt. Médicos populistas.
 La izquierda insurgente se ha manifestado de diversas formas en California y en todo el país durante este ciclo electoral.
 Pero la situación es muy diferente en el distrito congresional número 48, que abarca los condados de San Diego y Riverside.
 La demócrata Marni von Wilpert, concejala de la ciudad de San Diego, se presenta como una candidata tradicional y conservadora en una de las contiendas más reñidas de California para la Cámara de Representantes. Se enfrenta al republicano Jim Desmond, quien se postula como un conservador partidario de la austeridad fiscal.
 Un ejemplo de ello: la ex vicepresidenta demócrata Kamala Harris hizo campaña a favor de von Wilpert el mes pasado, mientras que otros demócratas temían que ella alejara a los votantes indecisos que aún estaban resentidos por las elecciones anteriores.
 Desmond, supervisor del condado de San Diego, ha hecho de la reducción de impuestos y la bajada de los precios de la energía su principal propuesta, manteniendo al mismo tiempo una sana distancia del presidente Donald Trump para evitar alienar a los votantes indecisos.
 La verdadera pregunta es si las políticas liberales convencionales o el conservadurismo fiscal serán suficientes para movilizar a la base y captar a los votantes independientes en ese distrito indeciso, aunque de tendencia demócrata.
Según encuestas internas de las campañas, la contienda está muy reñida. Von Wilpert lidera la recaudación de fondos con 4.5 millones de dólares. Desmond ha recaudado 3 millones de dólares.
La concejala Marni von Wilpert durante una reunión del Ayuntamiento de San Diego el 14 de abril de 2026. Foto de Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters.
Se han invertido más de 6 millones de dólares externos, más que en prácticamente todas las demás contiendas para la Cámara de Representantes en California, casi la totalidad para Von Wilpert. Esto incluye más de 4 millones de dólares del Comité de Acción Política (PAC) de la mayoría demócrata en la Cámara de Representantes y 2 millones de dólares de Democratic Majority for Israel, un PAC proisraelí que apoya a los candidatos demócratas. El PAC No Going Back, recientemente formado por Trump, ha donado más de 330,000 dólares hasta el momento para apoyar a Desmond.
 El gasto en campañas independientes ocupa el tercer lugar en California, por detrás del muy seguido distrito congresional número 22 en el Valle de San Joaquín, entre el actual representante republicano David Valadao y el demócrata Randy Villegas, que ha atraído 19 millones de dólares de grupos externos, y la contienda por un escaño en la Cámara de Representantes en el área de Stockton entre el representante demócrata Adam Gray y el republicano Kevin Lincoln, que ha recaudado 7 millones de dólares, según California Target Book.
 El dinero probablemente será un factor decisivo entre dos candidatos que están igualados, dijo Paul Mitchell, un estratega político demócrata que diseñó los nuevos mapas de tendencia demócrata que remodelaron el distrito.
 Es una de las pocas contiendas congresionales reñidas en California después de que la redistribución de distritos electorales de 2025, impulsada por los demócratas, convirtiera el escaño, tradicionalmente republicano, del representante Darrell Issa en un campo de batalla de tendencia izquierdista. A los votantes adinerados y conservadores de Temecula y Fallbrook se unieron los votantes de Oceanside y Palm Springs, donde Harris ganó las últimas elecciones presidenciales por amplios márgenes.
 Issa, quien ha representado a la zona durante más de dos décadas, consideró brevemente la idea de postularse en Texas antes de abandonar su candidatura a la reelección.
 Al no haber un titular que defienda el escaño, los demócratas lo ven como una oportunidad propicia para un cambio de rumbo en un año electoral en el que se espera que recuperen la Cámara de Representantes de manos de los republicanos.
 “El distrito 48 es un verdadero enfrentamiento entre dos candidatos con posiciones bastante similares, y el desafío será que Desmond tendrá que ganar contra este enorme viento en contra de una inminente ola azul”, dijo Mitchell. 
 Corriendo con el sistema
 Von Wilpert se mantiene fiel a su trayectoria como demócrata moderada y proisraelí, y destaca su capacidad para recuperar su escaño en el consejo municipal, que entonces era republicano, como un argumento convincente tanto para liberales como para conservadores del distrito. Para ello, ha recurrido a figuras demócratas tradicionales como Harris y el senador californiano Adam Schiff.
 En un mitin celebrado en Escondido la semana pasada, Schiff afirmó que el elevado coste de vida en el condado de San Diego hace que los votantes del distrito 48 sean receptivos a la postura antibelicista y a los argumentos fiscales de von Wilpert, en los que ella se ha presentado como una opositora a Trump, deseosa de votar a favor de resoluciones para poner fin a la guerra en Irán y repudiar sus políticas arancelarias.
 “Este es un distrito donde la gente es muy consciente del alto costo de vida, del alto costo de los alimentos y los medicamentos, y también está muy involucrada con las familias de militares y preocupada por la guerra en Irán”, dijo Schiff a CalMatters en una entrevista.
 Von Wilpert es solo uno de los pocos demócratas que aceptaron la ayuda de Harris en un momento en que su impopularidad todavía es vista como tóxica por algunos, incluidos candidatos en Texas, Kansas y Alaska que rechazaron el apoyo de la exvicepresidenta durante la campaña. Ambos aparecieron juntos en otro mitin en Escondido el mes pasado.
 “Es muy popular en nuestro distrito, y la gente está harta de la Casa Blanca de Trump”, dijo von Wilpert.
 La estrategia es diferente a unos cientos de kilómetros al norte, en el disputado distrito del Valle Central, donde el recién llegado demócrata Villegas ha adoptado un mensaje populista y antimultimillonario junto al senador de Vermont, Bernie Sanders, en un intento por desbancar a Valadao. Sin embargo, la estrategia de von Wilpert de llevar a cabo una campaña demócrata segura y rutinaria en un distrito clave es cuestionable.
 La presencia de Harris en la campaña electoral puede ser arriesgada en las zonas del país donde perdió, pero ese no es el caso en San Diego, según el consultor político Evan McClaughlin. Los demócratas obtuvieron una ventaja de tres puntos porcentuales en el registro de votantes al rediseñar el distrito.
 “He visto a gente escribir artículos que dicen: ‘¡Dios mío, nadie la quiere en el distrito!’”, dijo McClaughlin. “Puede que sea cierto en algunos lugares donde no ganó, pero ganó en este distrito”. 
 Manteniéndolo hiperlocal
 Desmond, exalcalde de San Marcos, ha hecho campaña como un conservador fiscal de manual, preocupado por las regulaciones onerosas y los impuestos elevados. Es uno de los dos votos republicanos en la junta de supervisores del condado, y a menudo evita expresar opiniones disidentes sobre temas culturales, pero sí se pronuncia sobre inmigración, como cuando se opuso al plan del condado de prohibir que los agentes federales usaran sus campos de tiro.
 Se ha esforzado al máximo por distanciarse de Trump, a pesar de contar con el respaldo del presidente. En cambio, se centra en asuntos locales, como su oposición a un proyecto de línea eléctrica en Temecula.
 El portavoz Sam Oh lo recalcó, afirmando que Desmond apoya a Trump, pero que actuará de forma independiente del presidente en el Congreso. Añadió que la reprimenda de Desmond a las declaraciones de Trump a principios de este mes, en las que afirmaba que Irán podría “destruir” San Diego y Los Ángeles, era un ejemplo de ello. 
 El supervisor del condado de San Diego, Jim Desmond, escucha a los oradores durante un foro sobre la Ley de la Verdad en el Centro de Administración del Condado de San Diego el 24 de marzo de 2026. Foto de Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters.
 «Discrepo vehementemente con los comentarios del presidente Trump», publicó en las redes sociales . «Ninguna ciudad estadounidense es prescindible, y ninguna familia estadounidense debería ser tratada como daño colateral».
 “Estamos hablando con los votantes sobre los temas que les importan. Si quieren que hablemos sobre el presidente, con gusto lo haremos”, dijo Oh.
 Oh no permitió que Desmond concediera una entrevista a CalMatters a pesar de las repetidas solicitudes realizadas por correo electrónico, llamadas telefónicas y mensajes de texto.
 Pero las campañas solo pueden controlar la narrativa hasta cierto punto, y aunque Desmond desea centrarse en los problemas locales, será difícil superar la impopularidad de Trump, dijo Thad Kousser, profesor de ciencias políticas de la UC San Diego.
 “Parece que haría falta algo extraordinario para movilizar a suficientes republicanos o convencer a suficientes votantes independientes para superar las dificultades geográficas del distrito, pero sobre todo el panorama nacional de estas elecciones de mitad de mandato”, dijo Kousser.

name: Missouri Independent
title: State says Missouri’s marijuana market is competitive. But who owns it?
text:
Illicit Gardens employees sort dried marijuana buds at the company's manufacturing and cultivation facility in Kansas City (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).Missouri regulators say the state doesn’t need to issue more licenses to grow, manufacture or sell marijuana because the legal cannabis market is meeting consumer demand.
But the statewide study behind that conclusion couldn’t answer a key question: whether a small number of companies controls a substantial share of Missouri’s marijuana businesses.
The study, released last week, examined cannabis purchasing habits, monthly consumer spending and sales in both regulated and unregulated markets. New York-based Cannabis Public Policy Consulting LLC found no evidence that Missouri’s statewide or regional cannabis markets are overconcentrated based on how sales are distributed among licensed facilities.
The researchers could not determine how concentrated ownership was among cannabis businesses because they lacked usable data on who owns the licenses and whether multiple dispensaries operating under different licenses belong to the same company. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“…ownership-based analyses would provide a more comprehensive assessment of market structure by evaluating concentration across common ownership groups,” the report states.
Division Director Amy Moore acknowledged that limitation in a statement following the study’s release, saying the agency plans to incorporate ownership data into future analyses.
“While this study did not include all factors related to market evaluations, such as ownership data,” Moore said, “DCR intends to include this information as recommended by CPPC in future studies to assist with more comprehensive market monitoring.”
The report comes just months after at least two lawsuits were filed, alleging some cannabis companies have violated Missouri’s antitrust laws.
Missouri’s Constitution establishes minimum numbers of cannabis licenses but allows regulators to issue additional licenses to meet demand and maintain competition. The study’s findings will help guide those decisions as the state considers whether to expand its existing market.
The study found that Missouri’s regulated market captures the vast majority of cannabis purchases. About 93% of purchases occur at licensed dispensaries, which account for more than 90% of purchases in every congressional district.
Consumers spend about half their monthly cannabis budgets on flower — the dried marijuana buds commonly sold in containers — followed by vape products and edibles.
Annual dispensary sales rose from about $1.30 billion in 2023 to $1.51 billion in 2025. Over the same period, the number of active dispensary licenses increased from 201 to 220.
Average annual sales per dispensary remained relatively stable at $6.5 million to $6.9 million, the report found, suggesting consumer demand largely kept pace as more dispensaries opened.
The report concluded that Missouri’s regulated cannabis market is “effectively meeting demand and has successfully transitioned into a mature, competitive marketplace.”
It recommended that future policy decisions focus less on expanding consumer participation and more on maintaining competition, improving market efficiency and ensuring supply keeps pace with changing consumer demand.
The report also recommended monitoring ownership concentration by using “de-identified” information. Although ownership concentration alone does not necessarily mean competition is limited, the report said, combining ownership and sales data would give regulators a more complete picture of the market and help inform future licensing decisions.
“While ownership information is collected as part of Missouri’s licensing and regulatory processes, these data are complex and subject to legal and confidentiality considerations that may limit external use,” the report states.
Arkansas marijuana company tied to more than a quarter of Missouri dispensaries

Earlier this month, cannabis regulators filed proposed rules that would require every licensee to submit a report annually that outlines the ownership percentage for each entity or individual. However, those reports “would be subject to the same confidentiality analysis as any other information received from a licensee,” under state law, said Lisa Cox, spokeswoman for the division.
Missouri’s Constitution requires at least 24 dispensary licenses in each of the state’s eight congressional districts. The state is also expected to issue a total of 144 microbusiness licenses, which are limited in size and scope and intended to benefit disadvantaged business owners.
The state has approved 222 dispensary licenses, 63 manufacturing licenses and 85 cultivation licenses to operate, according to July figures in the report. 
Another 20 microbusinesses had been approved to operate.
Moore said the division would continue monitoring the market and reassess when another study would be useful, citing changes in the cannabis industry and the planned rollout of additional microbusiness licenses.

name: California
title: Los trabajadores estatales de California están a punto de ir a la huelga. ¿Qué significa esto para el DMV, el EDD, los parques y más?
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Se espera que decenas de miles de empleados del gobierno estatal abandonen sus puestos de trabajo el miércoles en una huelga de un día que podría afectar los servicios del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados, las oficinas de desempleo y otros.
 Los miembros del sindicato SEIU Local 1000 protestan contra lo que consideran prácticas de negociación de mala fe por parte de la administración del gobernador Gavin Newsom . El sindicato ha estado negociando un nuevo convenio laboral desde que expiró su último contrato de tres años el 30 de junio, y la huelga sería el primer paro laboral a nivel estatal del Local 1000 en sus 44 años de historia.
El sindicato representa a unos 100,000 empleados públicos, cuyos miembros trabajan en decenas de agencias en todo California. Entre ellos se encuentran contadores, analistas gubernamentales, enfermeros, técnicos informáticos, personal de limpieza y otros.
 El sindicato Local 1000 podría cancelar el paro laboral en cualquier momento hasta el miércoles. Pero si lo hace, así es como la huelga podría afectarle. 
 ¿Todavía puedo ir al DMV?
 Sí, puede hacerlo, pero los servicios podrían sufrir retrasos dependiendo de quién participe en la huelga. Las oficinas del DMV también podrían cerrar antes de lo habitual, según un portavoz del departamento. Lo mismo ocurre con otros servicios de atención al público, como las prestaciones por desempleo en el Departamento de Desarrollo del Empleo y la asistencia alimentaria en CalFresh.
 Los parques estatales también podrían verse afectados, aunque los guardaparques no estén representados por el Sindicato Local 1000. El Castillo Hearst, en el condado de San Luis Obispo, por ejemplo, ajustó su horario de visitas para dar cabida a las personas que ya habían reservado plazas para visitar la finca del magnate de la prensa.
 Puede que esto no sea lo ideal desde el punto de vista del servicio al cliente, pero la presidenta del sindicato, Anica Walls, insta a los californianos a “tener un poco de comprensión con nuestros empleados”.
“Si acuden a la oficina del DMV y los servicios son limitados, pidan cita para otro día”, dijo Walls. “Tengan en cuenta que estamos defendiendo a 100,000 trabajadores estatales que no han tenido un salario digno. … No se trata solo de los empleados estatales. Se trata de la clase trabajadora en general”.
 ¿Qué trabajadores estatales no pueden declararse en huelga?
El sindicato Local 1000 representa a casi la mitad de la fuerza laboral del estado, y 95,000 trabajadores podrían participar en la huelga . Los 5000 trabajadores restantes están legalmente excluidos de la huelga, ya que su ausencia “crearía una amenaza inminente y sustancial para la salud o la seguridad pública”, según el sindicato. En general, trabajan en el sector de la salud o la seguridad pública.
 Ocho agencias y divisiones estatales emplean a trabajadores considerados esenciales. Entre ellos se incluyen trabajadores como enfermeros en residencias de veteranos, cocineros en prisiones estatales, operadores de Caltrans y otros:

 Departamento de Asuntos de Veteranos
 Servicios de atención médica penitenciaria
 Departamento de Correcciones y Rehabilitación
 Departamento de Correcciones y Rehabilitación, División de Operaciones de Libertad Condicional para Adultos
 Departamento de Educación
 Departamento de Servicios para el Desarrollo
 Departamento de Hospitales Estatales
 Caltrans

Para ver qué empleados en qué centros de trabajo se consideran esenciales, consulta esta lista .
 ¿Cómo llegamos hasta aquí?
 Muchos empleados estatales están frustrados con Newsom, quien ha exigido recortes salariales para equilibrar el presupuesto en tres de los ocho años que ha estado al frente del estado. Estos recortes prácticamente anularon el último aumento salarial del 3% que otorgó a los miembros del Sindicato Local 1000.
Tras señalar un aumento de 20,000 millones de dólares en el gasto del fondo general durante los últimos dos años, el sindicato exige mejores salarios y una cobertura sanitaria más asequible que la que ha ofrecido la administración. También reclama mayor flexibilidad para trabajar desde casa , oponiéndose a la orden del gobernador de que los empleados estatales regresen a la oficina.
 Pero las negociaciones han sido polémicas. En julio, el sindicato presentó una queja ante la Junta de Relaciones Laborales del Estado, acusando a CalHR, la agencia estatal encargada de las negociaciones laborales, de retrasar las negociaciones y rechazar las propuestas de plano. El mes pasado, la junta laboral falló a favor del sindicato y concluyó que CalHR “se negó a reunirse y dialogar de buena fe”.
 A principios de este mes, los miembros del sindicato autorizaron la huelga. Los miembros del Local 1000 realizarán manifestaciones en más de una docena de ciudades, incluidas Oakland, San Francisco, Los Ángeles, San Diego y Sacramento, donde también marcharán hacia las oficinas de los legisladores cerca del Capitolio. 
 ¿Cómo ha respondido la administración de Newsom?
 En respuesta a las conclusiones de la junta laboral, Angela Musallam, subdirectora de comunicaciones de CalHR, declaró en un correo electrónico a CalMatters que “el estado ha estado y sigue estando abierto a la negociación”. Añadió que el estado “está preparado para recurrir a la mediación para ayudar a las partes a llegar a un acuerdo”.
 CalHR también presentó una queja por prácticas desleales ante la junta para intentar detener la huelga. CalHR alegó que la huelga era ilegal porque el sindicato no había identificado inicialmente a los trabajadores esenciales que quedarían excluidos del paro. El sindicato discrepó de la interpretación de CalHR, argumentando que sí había identificado a dichos empleados. La semana pasada, la junta falló a favor del sindicato, rechazando la solicitud de CalHR de una orden judicial. 
 ¿Podría haber otra huelga?
 Ambas partes tienen previsto reunirse para mediar el 30 de octubre. Por ahora, el sindicato planea ir a la huelga solo el miércoles, pero Walls afirmó que si la administración de Newsom continúa con sus negociaciones de mala fe, el sindicato intensificará sus acciones. Esto podría incluir presentar otra queja ante la junta laboral y, posiblemente, convocar otra huelga.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: USDA offering $8B in farmer relief payments
text:
A farmer fills up a tractor with diesel. (Photo by Preston Keres/USDA)Farmers will be eligible to receive one-time payments from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to provide relief for high fuel and input costs. 
USDA and President Donald Trump announced Monday night at a rally in Kansas that farmers would have $8 billion made available in the Harvest Fuel Relief program. Farm groups expressed appreciation Tuesday for the relief program, but said they also hope to see long-term policy solutions that will support the farm economy. 
The relief announcement comes as farmers are in the thick of harvest and filling up with diesel fuel at historically high prices — more than $6 per gallon nationally — due to global trade disruptions. The announcement was also made two weeks ahead of a competitive midterm election that has sent Trump and members of his Cabinet across the country to support Republicans on the ticket. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Speaking at a rally in Park City, Kansas, while supporting Republican candidates U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and Ty Masterson, Trump reminded farmers of his efforts to support biofuels and of a recent move to suspend penalties for on-road use of dyed diesel fuel. 
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
“When the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers,” Trump said in Kansas after announcing the USDA relief program. “We love our farmers.” 
A news release from USDA said the Harvest Fuel Relief program will “provide simple, proportional support to producers” and use a uniform formula for modeled losses during the 2026 crop year. USDA said the program would be similar to the $12 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance program announced at the end of 2025 and distributed this year. 
Both programs were authorized through the Commodity Credit Corporation, the USDA-led and congressionally funded corporation that supports many of the department’s programs. 
Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said the Harvest Fuel Relief program would “help bring certainty” to farmers so that they can “continue to feed our nation.” 
“President Trump is the most pro-farmer president of my lifetime and he is continuing to put Farmers First every day,” Rollins said in a news release. 
According to USDA, commodity-specific payment rates for Title I crops — major row crops including barley, corn, wheat, soybeans and sorghum — will be released in November. The payment methods for “other eligible commodities” will be announced at a later date. USDA said the program will not be linked to crop insurance. 
National Corn Growers Association President Matt Frostic said corn growers are “eager to learn more details” about the fuel relief program. 
“As we work to tackle the many economic challenges facing growers and rural communities, we urge Washington to focus on durable, bipartisan, long-term solutions that will result in lasting improvements to the farm and national economy,” Frostic said in a statement.
He said actions to pass legislation for the year-round, nationwide sale of E15 fuel, renewed trade agreements between the U.S., Mexico and Canada, and to pass a farm bill would support farmers long term. 
A post on X from USDA said farmers can apply for the program online via Login.gov. Pre-filled applications for the assistance program will be available for row crop farmers in January. 
USDA said it will accept data showing increased fuel costs from specialty crop producers and other non-Title I commodity producers, as the department works to determine payment rates for these commodities. Producers are encouraged to send information to HarvestFuel@usda.gov. 
Farmers Union leaders call for long-term assistance
National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said the organization was questioning how the relief program would help specialty crop producers who were asked to “submit their own cost data” but had “no clarity yet on whether or how they’ll be covered.” 
Larew said the assistance will be “helpful for some farmers” but that rising fuel costs have put family farmers in a “difficult position.” 
“One-time payments can’t provide the stability they need to plan for the future,” Larew said in a statement. “ … We need to provide long-term certainty and investment in diversifying our fuel sources with renewable options, not a cycle of ad hoc relief.” 
In Iowa, the farmers union president was more pointed against the Trump administration and said the “Band-Aid response” would not fix the problems caused by “trade wars and a military war that have put farmers on the front line of the consequences of those policy choices.” Iowa Farmers Union has endorsed Iowa’s Democratic candidates in the upcoming election. 
“We need genuine efforts to help farmers now while fixing the real causes of our current situation,” Aaron Lehman, Iowa Farmers Union president, said. “We need to conclude the war without sacrificing our farmers’ bottom lines. We need to end the monopoly stranglehold on agricultural inputs. We need to become more energy independent by developing sustainable domestic alternatives.” 
USDA and Republican lawmakers are also touting their work passing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act which included provisions to boost reference prices for farmers and expand the farm safety net, among other initiatives. USDA said the harvest fuel relief program ” builds upon the Trump administration’s unprecedented support for America’s farmers.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Audit finds flaws with Colorado’s marijuana testing framework
text:
(Photo by Faith Miller/Colorado Newsline)Colorado’s regulatory framework to test marijuana for contamination and warn consumers about risks has significant gaps, a state audit found.
The recently-released audit focused on problems with product testing and inconsistent monitoring from the Marijuana Enforcement Division. Auditors did not find evidence of widespread health and safety risks, but the framework is not airtight.
Colorado voters approved recreational marijuana in 2012. MED, within the state’s Department of Revenue, licenses businesses and oversees compliance with marijuana rules and laws.
“It’s really a combination of factors that impacts MED’s ability to identify public safety risks and to ensure that businesses comply with safety requirements,” audit supervisor Catherine Friday told members of the Legislative Audit Committee on Monday. “As a result, there’s an increased risk that marijuana products sold in Colorado may have contaminants or may inaccurately list potency.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Businesses select their own samples, for example, and send them to private labs for potency and contaminant testing. Twenty-four other states with legalized marijuana do not allow self-selected samples and instead rely on a third party.
“Is that something that’s going to be addressed?” Sen. Rod Pelton, a Cheyenne Wells Republican, asked. “Because if I’m a shady character, I know which products I’m going to sample and which ones I’m not. That’s a pretty gray area to me.”
Kyle Lambert, deputy director of the marijuana division, said it’s a topic the division has researched extensively but ultimately decided against changing this year. One of the reasons is the logistics and cost challenge of getting to rural businesses around the state, he said. Third-party collections also do not guarantee samples are representative of a business’s entire batch.
The division also does not have the resources to conduct on-site inspections for every business every year, though it has improved the percentage of inspected businesses in the past three years. The division’s own goal is to inspect every two years.
The audit also found that the division sometimes does not issue timely safety advisories for products that could cause health concerns, and affected products could remain on shelves for months. Auditors found that between 2023 and 2025, potentially harmful marijuana products were on the market for over seven months on average before the division issued an advisory. The average timeline improved in 2025 when regulators revised advisory guidelines.
Auditors recommended that the division work to make sure consumers and businesses know how to report safety concerns and continue streamlining the advisory process.
The division agreed with all of the audit’s recommendations.
“We recognize there are clear opportunities to improve through the audit’s recommendations, and we also appreciate the state auditor’s acknowledgment that it found no evidence to support claims of widespread health and safety issues with regulated marijuana products,” Dominique Mendiola, the division’s senior director, said. “The state auditor’s office recommendations will inform a constructive roadmap to further enhance how we build on these initiatives that we’ve taken and continue to carry out our mission.”
The audit included one legislative recommendation to strengthen the state’s reference lab’s role to support marijuana enforcement operations. The lab, operated by the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, cannot test for pesticides, residual solvents and mycotoxins, and lab officials estimate they’d need about $13 million to increase its capacity.
Lawmakers on the audit committee could vote on whether to introduce a bill related to the issue next legislative session.

name: California
title: Te explicamos la Prop 37: ¿Puede un bono de 25 mil millones de dólares hacer posible la compra de viviendas en California?
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Es un bono, pero no como cualquier otro bono que se someta a votación.
 Promete ofrecer hipotecas a los compradores de vivienda, pero no las hipotecas típicas.
 Se crearía un programa de ayuda para el pago inicial, pero uno diferente a cualquier otro en el país.
 Este año, en la boleta electoral de California hay muchas propuestas importantes y controvertidas , pero ninguna tan extraña como la Proposición 37.
 Sus defensores la consideran una solución “elegante” al problema de que tantos californianos no pueden permitirse comprar una vivienda. Sus detractores la califican de artimaña ingeniosa y poco rebuscada. Prácticamente todo el mundo, incluso algunos expertos contratados para analizar la propuesta, tiene dudas.
 Aquí tienes algunas de las preguntas más importantes, con las mejores respuestas disponibles.
 P: ¿Qué efecto tendría la Proposición 37?
 R: Si se aprueba, el estado podría obtener préstamos de hasta 25 mil millones de dólares para establecer un nuevo programa de préstamos que ayude a las personas a afrontar los pagos iniciales de la compra de viviendas nuevas.
¿25 mil millones de dólares ? Eso es mucho dinero, incluso para un estado con un presupuesto de 352 mil millones de dólares .
 Así es. Pero a diferencia de otros bonos que se someten a votación, se supone que este no le costará nada al estado.
 Cuando el estado vende bonos, está pidiendo dinero prestado. La mayoría de los bonos, como las Proposiciones 1 y 38 , se pagarían directamente con los impuestos.
Con la Proposición 37, el estado actuaría más como un intermediario de préstamos. La Agencia de Financiamiento de Vivienda de California obtendría el dinero de prestamistas privados (mediante la venta de bonos) y luego lo volvería a prestar a los compradores de vivienda. Cuando los compradores de vivienda paguen esos préstamos, el dinero regresaría a los tenedores de bonos con intereses.
 Si los compradores de vivienda no cumplen con sus pagos, los prestamistas privados serían quienes asumirían el costo, no los contribuyentes estatales. Eso es lo que estipula el texto de la medida, aunque algunos analistas han expresado dudas de que los legisladores estatales puedan resistir la presión política para rescatar a los compradores de vivienda en caso de una ola de impagos.
 ¿Estos préstamos son simplemente hipotecas para viviendas?
 Segundas hipotecas, específicamente.
 Los compradores aún tendrían que adquirir una casa a la antigua usanza, acudiendo a un banco o agente inmobiliario y solicitando una hipoteca que cubra la mayor parte del precio de la vivienda. Sin embargo, aún queda un pago inicial. El pago inicial promedio en California es del 20%, según la Asociación de Agentes Inmobiliarios de California, aunque suele ser menor para quienes compran por primera vez. Para una casa de $800,000, eso equivale a $160,000.
 ¡Eso es muchísimo! ¿Esta segunda hipoteca está destinada a cubrir la totalidad del pago inicial?
 Casi todo.
El programa permitiría que estos préstamos cubrieran hasta el 17% del valor de una vivienda, reduciendo los 160,000 dólares a 24,000 dólares.
 ¿Es positivo ayudar a las personas a endeudarse más al comprar una vivienda?
 Para muchos californianos, ser propietario de una vivienda es prácticamente inalcanzable, incluso para aquellos que podrían considerarse de clase media acomodada. California tiene la segunda tasa de propiedad de vivienda más baja o la más baja de todos los estados, según cómo se mida.
 Para muchos californianos que viven de alquiler, las elevadas cuotas hipotecarias mensuales —que suelen ser más altas que el alquiler promedio en gran parte del estado— hacen que comprar una vivienda sea inviable. Para quienes se encuentran en esta situación, añadir una segunda hipoteca con otro pago mensual no les ayudará.
 Pero para algunos, es el monto del pago inicial lo que les impide acceder a la vivienda propia. Aproximadamente el 40% de los compradores recientes recurrieron a amigos o familiares para superar esta brecha financiera, según una encuesta nacional . Esta brecha es especialmente grande en California, donde los precios de las viviendas son muy altos.
 Pedirle a una familia que ahorre tanto dinero es como pedirles que “viajen a la luna en un cohete de cartón”, dijo Bob Hertzberg en una entrevista.
 Es una metáfora curiosa, pero ¿quién es Bob Hertzberg?
 Es el expresidente de la Asamblea estatal, el exlíder de la mayoría del Senado, un negociador activo en una amplia variedad de debates políticos contemporáneos de California y el autor y promotor singularmente enérgico de la Proposición 37.
 Hertzberg lleva años trabajando en esta idea, junto con la Asociación de Agentes Inmobiliarios de California, y afirma haber dado con una solución, si bien inusual, muy “elegante” para los inquilinos de clase media que no pueden reunir el dinero para el pago inicial.
 Si esto se aprueba, ¿podría obtener uno de estos préstamos?
 Si eres un californiano típico, es muy probable que al menos cumplas con los requisitos.
 Bajo este programa, cualquier persona que gane menos del doble del ingreso promedio de su condado califica, que oscila entre aproximadamente $116,000 en Imperial y poco más de $410,000 en San Mateo para una familia de tres. Esto cubre aproximadamente al 90% de todos los inquilinos , según un análisis reciente del Instituto de Políticas Públicas de California.
 Hertzberg y otros partidarios creen que es positivo que una zona tan extensa de California cumpla los requisitos. 



 Existen numerosos programas de ayuda para el pago inicial dirigidos a compradores de vivienda de bajos ingresos , compradores de primera generación o veteranos , pero Hertzberg argumenta que la clase media, en un sentido amplio, también necesita ayuda. Además, según él, los requisitos mínimos simplificarán considerablemente los trámites burocráticos.
 Pero algunos opositores, como la Liga de Mujeres Votantes de California , temen que ofrecer un posible impulso a tantos compradores potenciales signifique que quienes menos necesitan ayuda —personas con ingresos inferiores al límite, dotadas de una riqueza considerable o que pueden pedir préstamos a sus familiares— sean las más propensas a obtener los préstamos.
 Eso, advierten, solo reforzará las desigualdades económicas y raciales ya existentes en el estado.
 ¿Qué tipo de vivienda podría adquirir un prestatario con una de estas segundas hipotecas?
 Se aplican tres condiciones.
En primer lugar, hay un límite de precio. Esto se vuelve un poco técnico , pero básicamente la vivienda debe costar menos de 1 millón de dólares en el interior de California y hasta 1.5 millones de dólares en Los Ángeles, el condado de Orange y el Área de la Bahía.
 En segundo lugar, la vivienda debe ser construida por un “constructor cualificado”.
 Se trata de una constructora que se compromete a respetar el límite de precio, construir dentro de las ciudades ya existentes y aceptar la responsabilidad legal en caso de incumplir algunos requisitos laborales básicos.
 A cambio, podrían construir las segundas viviendas que cumplan los requisitos para obtener una hipoteca. Además, quedarían exentos de demandas por defectos de construcción si reparan un error a satisfacción del propietario. En caso de que las disputas lleguen a los tribunales, los honorarios legales estarían limitados.
 Según Dan Dunmoyer, presidente de la Asociación de la Industria de la Construcción de California, el programa probablemente tendría más sentido comercial en las zonas del estado donde los precios de las viviendas son más bajos y donde hay muchos prestatarios de ingresos medios. Es probable que se trate de ciudades en lugares como el Inland Empire y el Valle Central.
 La tercera condición es que la vivienda sea de nueva construcción o haya sido recientemente reformada. En otras palabras, el prestatario debe ser su primer ocupante. No se admiten viviendas de segunda mano.
 ¿Por qué solo viviendas nuevas?
 Esto pone de manifiesto una crítica común a los programas de ayuda para el pago inicial.
 Darles una ventaja financiera a algunos compradores sin cambiar la cantidad de viviendas en circulación simplemente cambia quién consigue una casa y quién no. Es como reservar un asiento para alguien en un juego de sillas musicales. Puede que tu amigo consiga un sitio, pero la misma cantidad de personas terminarán en el suelo cuando la música se detenga.
 En el peor de los casos, la nueva inyección de dinero no hará más que elevar aún más los precios.
 La idea es que, al reservar estos préstamos para nuevas viviendas, se garantice que la nueva oferta se ajuste a la nueva demanda, lo que resultaría en un aumento neto del número de viviendas y de propietarios de viviendas en California.
 ¿Cuántas viviendas se construirían realmente gracias a este programa?
Según un análisis encargado por la campaña del “Sí a la Proposición 37”, esto podría resultar en la construcción de hasta 190,000 viviendas. Sin embargo, el autor reconoce que esa cifra es una estimación optimista.
 La cifra real depende de cuántos constructores decidan que vale la pena obtener la certificación, cuántas de estas viviendas se habrían construido de todos modos, el precio de cada vivienda y qué parte del pago inicial desea cubrir cada prestatario con el préstamo, además de un montón de otras incógnitas.
 ¿Qué otras incógnitas?
 Hay bastantes, pero la Oficina del Analista Legislativo, un organismo no partidista, destacó dos importantes en su análisis de la medida.
 Desconocemos si los inversores comprarían realmente estos bonos y, de ser así, a qué precio. Tampoco sabemos cuántos compradores querrán solicitar estos préstamos.
 ¿Por qué los compradores de bonos podrían no estar dispuestos a prestar el dinero?
 Financiar segundas hipotecas se considera más arriesgado que financiar las tradicionales, ya que estos préstamos aumentan la deuda del prestatario, el primer préstamo tiene prioridad de pago y el segundo no cuenta con la garantía implícita del estado de California ni de las entidades hipotecarias federales Fannie Mae o Freddie Mac. Si el prestatario quiebra, el inversor es el responsable.
 Los inversores típicos querrían ser compensados por todo ese riesgo adicional. Eso significa tipos de interés elevados.
 En estos momentos, los tipos de interés hipotecarios tradicionales superan con creces el 7% . Los inversores comunes “van a querer bastante más que eso” para una inversión no probada y más arriesgada, afirmó Edward Pinto, codirector del Centro de Vivienda del American Enterprise Institute, un centro de estudios de tendencia conservadora.
 ¿Es por eso que los compradores podrían no querer utilizar estos préstamos?
 Esa es la razón principal.
 Incluso si la segunda hipoteca tuviera una tasa del 7%, podría añadir 1000 dólares a los pagos mensuales de la deuda de un nuevo propietario, dependiendo del precio de la vivienda. Es un precio muy alto a pagar por un pago inicial menor. Menos del 40% de los inquilinos que cumplen los requisitos de la Propuesta 37 podrían afrontar estos pagos mensuales más altos para una vivienda de nivel básico, según el análisis del PPIC.
Para una vivienda cuyo precio se encuentre en el límite superior del rango de elegibilidad, menos del 0.5% de los inquilinos que cumplen los requisitos podrían permitírsela.
 ¿Hay algo que el estado pueda hacer para reducir estos tipos de interés?
 Se supone que el dinero público no debe subvencionar ni respaldar estos préstamos, así que no directamente.
 Pero Hertzberg dijo que tiene un plan.
 Es posible que se convenza a grupos filantrópicos y fundaciones benéficas —«la gente de Giving Pledge», en sus propias palabras— de comprar los bonos a tasas inferiores a las del mercado, incluso tan bajas como el 3 %. Esto estaría en consonancia con el espíritu cívico de la compra de bonos de guerra durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial, afirmó Hertzberg. Pero también podría cumplir con ciertos requisitos de impacto social corporativo, las declaraciones de misión de las organizaciones sin fines de lucro e incluso las normas federales de préstamos comunitarios.
 Dijo que ya había hablado con algunos posibles donantes al respecto, pero se negó a dar nombres.
 ¿Qué ocurre si los inversores no compran los bonos, los compradores no solicitan los préstamos, o ambas cosas?
 Potencialmente nada.
 En un reciente panel de discusión , Chris Hoene, director ejecutivo del California Budget & Policy Center, una organización de tendencia izquierdista, expresó su escepticismo sobre el éxito de la Proposición 37. Sin embargo, también afirmó que sus desventajas son limitadas.
 “Aún podría funcionar, y si no funciona, el estado no tiene realmente ninguna responsabilidad”, dijo.
 ¿Así que en realidad no le gusta, pero dice que no puede hacer daño? Qué raro.
 Te dije.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Proposed school, daycare vaccine changes are challenged in administrative court
text:
A health care worker places a bandage on a child after giving a vaccination shot. New federal guidance to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 comes as states including Florida are already charting their own course on vaccine policy. (Photo by Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)The administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis didn’t follow rulemaking procedures and overstepped its authority when it proposed eliminating four required vaccines for school and daycare entry, a rule challenge filed in state administrative court alleges.
“K.O.,” a school nurse with three young children; “T.F.,” a 70-year old individual with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia; and Jacksonville family physician Danielle Carter filed the challenge in administrative court on Friday along with the Florida Academy of Family Physicians.
The plaintiffs seek an administrative hearing and determination that the Department of Health lacks authorization to eliminate requirements that schoolchildren and children attending child care or daycare be vaccinated against Haemophilus influenzae type b (“Hib”), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
The plaintiffs also are asking to recover their attorney fees.
Florida law requires children at a minimum to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, and tetanus to attend school but allows exemptions for valid medical and religious reasons.
The DOH holds authority under statute to also require vaccinations for “other communicable diseases as determined.” 
Under that authority, and in accordance with “recognized standards of medical practice,” the plaintiffs argue, the DOH has long required the four additional vaccines. That mandate, according to the challenge, is in line with DOH’s statutory mission to “ensure that all children in this state are immunized against vaccine-preventable diseases.”
The proposed new rule, the plaintiffs argue, runs afoul of the DOH’s authority and isn’t supported by science.
“Yet, despite no new medical or scientific evidence or data calling into question the necessity, safety, or efficacy of these vaccines, the Department now proposes to eliminate them from Florida’s mandatory school-entry immunization requirements, abandoning longstanding public health protections without conforming to recognized standards of medical practice, without corresponding medical or scientific justification, and in direct violation of the Department’s statutory duty to ‘ensure that all children in this state are immunized against vaccine-preventable diseases,’ ” the challenge notes.
During a recent hearing on the proposed rule, DOH Secretary Joseph Ladapo said the changes weren’t based on the effectiveness or safety of vaccines but were about protecting parental rights.
Ladapo: Eliminating vaccine mandates isn’t about science, it’s about parents’ rights

Florida has a  statute that protects parental rights and within that law is “the right to make health care decisions for minor children.” 
But those challenging the rule argue the statute makes clear those decisions cannot conflict with other statutes. Additionally, the plaintiffs contend the DOH lacks authority to enforce the statute.
“The State Surgeon General has repeatedly invoked his own purported “moral” and “ethical” justifications for eliminating Florida’s “vaccine mandates”while framing these beliefs as legitimate public health considerations. 
“But neither the State Surgeon General’s personal convictions nor the Department’s policy preferences, irrespective of whether they legitimately fall under the umbrella of ‘public health,’ confer authority for this Proposed Rule modification that the Legislature has not granted,” the challenge states.
“In fact, the Legislature has specifically permitted parents to exempt their children from school entry vaccine mandates based on religious beliefs, establishing the outer limits of the State of Florida’s public health policy when it comes to exemptions,” it adds.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Improper procedure alleged
The challenge argues that DeSantis administration failed to comply with Florida’s Administrative Procedures Act, which requires an agency to publish notice of a proposed rule within 180 days after publishing the most recent notice of rule development. 
The APA allows an agency to exceed the 180-day window so long as it submits a concise statement every three months explaining the delay to JAPC.
The plaintiffs argue that the “department did nothing to advance the rulemaking for 255 days.”
The DOH first published notice of proposed rulemaking on Sept. 10, 2025. On Nov. 26 that year, it announced it would hold a public meeting on the proposal in Panama City Beach and published the proposed rule language.
The DOH held the meeting in Panama City Beach on that Dec. 12. The DOH subsequently received more than 1,000 public comments, the record shows. But there was no follow up on the administrative front as the DeSantis administration turned its efforts to lobbying the Legislature to pass the policy instead.
And although the DOH did send two letters to JAPC (on Feb. 26 and June 30 this year) the notes didn’t explain the delay, the plaintiffs allege.
DeSantis vowed to make his vaccine policy a top priority before leaving office in January 2027 and the DOH returned its focus to changing the rules administratively.
On Aug. 24, the agency published a notice of a new proposed rule, the language of which nearly tracked the initial rule published eight months earlier. On Sept. 30, DOH announced it was dropping language to establish parents’ ability to object to vaccines based on morals or conscience, and also announced it would hold a workshop on the proposed rule on Oct. 8 in Lake Mary.
Exemption for moral, ethical beliefs zapped from DeSantis administration’s proposed vax rule

The plaintiffs
Parties must hold standing to challenge rules, and the legal challenge lays out why those involved can pursue the litigation.
The suit notes that Dr. Carter is a family physician whose patients includes infants, school-aged children, and expectant mothers and newborns, and that the proposed changes would “directly implicate her professional responsibilities, the delivery of preventive and primary medical care, and the health and safety of her patients.”
T.F. lives with chronic malignancy of her blood and bone marrow, and has received a bone marrow transplant. “T.F.’s health depends on the community immunity maintained by requiring schoolchildren to be vaccinated against communicable disease,” the challenge says. “The diseases related to the vaccines that the Department proposes removing are especially dangerous and frequently life-threatening to an immunocompromised elderly patient.”
K.O. is a registered nurse who works at a charter school and the parent of a 2-year-old child who attends a licensed child care facility. K.O. is responsible for reviewing immunization records, administering care, and responding to communicable-disease conditions among students,” the complaint says.
“[R]emoving the vaccines from school attendance requirements would increase the presence of unimmunized children in her workplace, heightening her occupational exposure to vaccine preventable disease and enlarging the compliance, screening, and outbreak-response duties she must discharge.”
The FAFP is a not-for-profit association “with a substantial number of members” who are regulated by the rule. Approximately 95% of active physician membership of FAFP are Board Certified in Family Medicine, requiring expertise in treating patients from child birth through palliative care.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: During brain drain research, New Yorker finds reasons to remember Mississippi
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

Before I moved to Jackson for the summer, a New Yorker living in Montgomery, Alabama, told me to pay close attention to people’s reactions when I shared my summer plans.
I had just recently received nearly unanimous encouragement for my decision to study abroad in Madrid, so I was curious what she meant; this potential for contrast became a little game for me. I was a double agent, watching closely for the reactions I predicted: coastal elitism and disparagement.
What I noticed instead was more damning. A pause, a curious tilt, an eye squint. The subtle signs of drawing a blank. My friends and family in New York City and Boston didn’t condemn Mississippi. To have such strong opinions, they would have needed to observe, judge and then reject Mississippi. Instead, Mississippi sits outside their scope of consideration altogether.
I grew up in New York City, where a heavy dose of civic pride taught me that I hail from the center of the universe. College in Boston marked a departure down a well-blazed path for New Yorkers looking to expand their world, but only just so. In this universe, Mississippi is an abstraction, rarely registered beyond a childhood memory of spelling practice: MI-SS-I-SS-I-PP-I! It is scarcely acknowledged as a place to go, let alone stay or build a life.
It wasn’t until I talked with my professor, Gene Corbin, about his years living and working in Mississippi in the 90s that its inclusion in this universe—as much more than a thing to spell—became obvious and necessary.
Professor Corbin sent me to Jackson to work for Jake McGraw at Working Together Mississippi. My task was to join in their effort to research why Mississippi struggles to attract and retain college-educated people, a phenomenon known as “brain drain.”
Mississippi Today, in conjunction with Rethink Mississippi and the University of Mississippi Center for Population Studies, created a first-of-its-kind study dedicated to the state’s brain drain crisis. I began my job this summer by reading through the thousands of survey responses they had collected, placing myself at the “stay vs. leave” crossroads that many Mississippians perennially consider. Immersed in these fraught considerations, I found that most respondents reckoned with a home state where they don’t feel they have sufficient opportunities to stay, but they would, and they want to.
Ella Caplan Credit: Courtesy photo
Ironically, I was analyzing an instinct that I recognize in myself and my friends: glancing toward the coasts, assuming that real life, real opportunity, happens there. The difference is that Mississippians must weigh the cost of outsourcing opportunity with what it costs to stay. Having started on this note, I was primed to spend the rest of my time in Jackson open to experiencing the full weight of either conclusion. Paradoxically, the more I studied leaving the state, the more I felt the value of staying. I was swimming against the current.
As the summer progressed, my understanding of Jackson grew beyond what I read in my research and rested instead on the experience of building a routine and community in this city. I listened to Blues at Hal & Mals on Mondays, learned about community organizing for a weekend in Louisville and wandered through the “L.V. Hull: Love Is a Sensation” exhibit at the Mississippi Museum of Art on rainy weekdays. I felt deep affection for a culture that I also recognized—one I had seen fragments of in New York City and pop culture my whole life.
Multiculturalism is a core part of New York’s identity, and most New Yorkers would balk at being called insular. But my time in one of New York’s great cultural wellsprings revealed just this: a blind spot in New York’s identity and proof that some constituent cultures are celebrated while others are forgotten.
So, let’s celebrate. You all know this better than I do, so forgive me for stating the obvious: Elvis Presley is from Mississippi, and so is Oprah. Robert Johnson, raised primarily in the Mississippi Delta, is the blues giant who inspired the 2025 film “Sinners.” And civil rights legend Medgar Evers is the namesake of a City of New York public college in Brooklyn, a fact I would fairly confidently state many Brooklynites could not explain. What happens in Mississippi does not stay contained behind a state line; it ripples throughout the rest of the country. The case for staying in this cultural wellspring is easily made.
Yet Mississippi is a real place, one whose challenges are concentrated and in their rawest forms – the brain drain didn’t come out of nowhere. And still the state remains unconsidered, even by those who claim to care passionately about social and racial justice. The instinct to engage injustice when it is exotic and geographically or historically distant keeps places like Jackson invisible. We should refuse to tolerate this hypocrisy.
Mississippians, the problem isn’t that coastal “elites” are judging you; it is that we ignore you. The message I will bring back with me is that if you, like me, desire a full understanding of the country you live in, and not just its wealthiest cities, come to Mississippi. If you don’t come, read; and if you won’t, at the very least, consider with curiosity.

Ella Caplan is a senior at Tufts University, studying sociology and Spanish. She grew up in New York City.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmaker questions industry group leaders over homeowners’ insurance non-renewals
text:
New Mexico state Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas), whose House District 70 includes many homes burned in the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire, questioned an insurance industry expert Oct. 20, 2026, on an uptick in homeowners' insurance policy non-renewals. (Source NM file photo and Gonzales photo courtesy NM Legislature)A New Mexico state lawmaker whose district continues reeling from the largest wildfire in state history questioned industry leaders Tuesday about the increasing rate at which insurers refuse to renew homeowners’ policies, particularly in fire-prone areas. 
State Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas), whose House District 70 includes much of the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire burn scar, asked a panel of insurance industry leaders speaking before the interim legislative Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee about recent insurance trends in the state, including the highest-ever rate of insurance companies opting not to renew policies. 
National insurers opted not to renew more than 6,200 homeowners’ insurance policies in New Mexico in 2025, according to recent figures the state’s Office of the Superintendent of Insurance provided. That marks the highest annual number of non-renewals in state history, and represents a near-tripling of non-renewals since 2021. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If you have a total exodus of the industry in some of these communities, how are we able to then rebuild?” Gonzales asked.
Julie A. Rochman, a former CEO of an insurance industry research organization, told Gonzales national insurance companies may “back away” from high-risk properties as they grapple with global economic forces, including increasing construction costs for fire-damaged properties and rising premiums insurance companies themselves face from global reinsurance companies. 
Federal regulations on property and casualty insurers also limit how companies can invest premium dollars, Rochman noted, which reduces the funds insurers have to cover widespread losses. And the insurance companies could run afoul of state regulations if they irresponsibly underwrite insurance policies in areas that are on the cusp of a natural disaster. 
“Carriers will back away because they may have so much risk already on their books in New Mexico that they cannot take more and still support the ability to pay any and all claims as needed,” Rochman said. “I think the industry is constantly looking for that balancing act, but we can’t overextend ourselves to write property that we shouldn’t be writing.”
New Mexico insurers refused to renew policies for record number of homes in 2025, official says

In response, Gonzales urged insurance companies to “find some middle ground to work towards” due to the “very troubling” increase in non-renewals. 
Rochman also chairs the state’s Fair Access to Insurance Requirement Plan board, which offers insurance to those who cannot find insurance on the private market. 
In 2025, the Legislature gave $10 million to the OSI to help homeowners with FAIR Plan coverage mitigate their homes against wildfire risk, including measures like clearing trees from near structures, installing screens on vents and making roofs more flame resistant.
Rochman said Tuesday that homeowners’ “sweat equity” in mitigating against wildfire risk, particularly creating a 5-foot buffer around homes of flammable materials, remains the single most important step they can take to improve the insurance market statewide and also protect their homes.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: 5 members of Colorado’s congressional delegation report suspicious letters
text:
U.S. Rep. Jason Crow speaks alongside, from left, U.S. Reps. Brittany Pettersen, Joe Neguse and Diana DeGette in Aurora last year. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)All four of Colorado’s Democratic members of the U.S. House of Representatives and one U.S. senator received letters with a suspicious substance Monday, the lawmakers said. 
The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to officials in several states, including Nebraska, Minnesota, Arizona, Mississippi and Oregon. In a statement, the FBI said it is not confirming specific cases, but it confirmed it is investigating a “series of suspicious mailings” sent to offices nationwide and seeking to identify individuals responsible for the letters.
Several letters in other states were sent to election officials. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold’s office has not received any similar mailings, her office said Tuesday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette said in a statement that her staff members are unharmed after her Denver office received a letter with a “suspicious substance.” She condemned the “shameful act of intimidation” that targeted her and other officials. 
Federal authorities are investigating a letter House Assistant Minority Leader Joe Neguse’s Boulder office received containing a white powder, his office said. He said there is no continued threat to public safety but that there is a “palpable sense of fear” in communities across the country.
“The nature of this mailing, and others like it being received by elected officials across the country, whether to cause physical harm or provoke unease among public servants, will not prevent me and my team from working day in and day out to serve the people of Colorado’s 2nd District,” Neguse said in a statement. 
U.S. Rep. Jason Crow’s Aurora office also received a letter that contained an unknown substance. He said his staff is safe and his office remains open. 
The FBI took for testing an envelope that U.S. Rep. Brittany Pettersen’s Lakewood office received Monday. 
“This is a deeply disturbing effort to intimidate sitting Members of Congress,” Pettersen said in a statement. “I’m grateful for the safety of my staff – who are hardworking public servants, and should not have to fear for their lives while doing their jobs.”
Postal investigators intercepted a letter addressed to U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper’s Denver office before it was delivered. The Denver office of Colorado’s other U.S. senator, Michael Bennet, has not received any letters similar to those sent to other offices, his office said Tuesday. Hickenlooper is running for reelection this year, Bennet is not.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania elections chief highlights voter rights two weeks ahead of Election Day
text:
Voter rights include asking for language or literacy assistance as well as casting a ballot privately without harassment. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)With just two weeks until Election Day, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt focused on the rights of voters in a weekly media briefing — whether they choose to vote by mail, provisional ballot or in-person.
Voters can request language and literacy assistance at their polling place from anyone who isn’t their employer, union representative or the judge of elections at that location. They also have a right to privacy without being subject to intimidation, harassment or discriminatory conduct. 
“It’s important that every voter be informed about how to exercise their right to vote and make their voices heard,” said Schmidt. “A voter who experiences any of these should report it to the county board of elections or the district attorney’s office.”
What is on-demand mail ballot voting?

People can also call the year-round voter hotline at 1-877-VOTESPA (1-877-868-3772). Every polling place in the commonwealth must have at least one accessible voting system for people with disabilities. 
As of Monday’s deadline to register to cast a ballot on Nov. 3, Pennsylvania has more than 9 million registered voters, including 3.8 million Democrats, 3.6 million Republicans and 1.5 million independent voters. 
More than 634,000 Pennsylvanians have already returned their mail-in ballots. The deadline to apply for a mail-in ballot is Oct. 27 and completed ballots must be received by election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
Schmidt noted that polls open at 7 a.m. on Nov. 3 and close at 8 p.m., but emphasized that any voter in line at 8 p.m. will be allowed to cast a ballot. Voters who requested a mail-in ballot can decide to vote in person by bringing their ballots — including the outer envelope — to their local precinct. 
Those who requested a mail-in ballot but didn’t receive one can cast a provisional ballot at their polling place on Election Day.
Provisional ballots are also an option for voters who are told by their county elections office that their mail-in ballots can’t be counted, meaning they might be missing a signature or secrecy envelope. 
“In an emergency situation, such as an unexpected illness, a disability or a last-minute absence from the municipality, a voter can request something called an emergency absentee ballot,” Schmidt added. “The deadline to submit that application and ballot at their county elections office is 8 p.m. on Election Day.”
Following the election, a county election board will review each ballot to determine if it will count. 
Pennsylvania law requires first-time voters to use a form of identification to vote, but allows voters who recently moved in-state another chance to vote at their previous address — so long as they update their registration with their new address after casting their ballot.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming student test scores uniformly reach or exceed prepandemic levels for first time
text:
Six years after the COVID-19 pandemic upended education and led to nationwide learning loss, Wyoming’s standardized testing scores have rebounded.
Student scores increased across science, math and language arts in both the 2025-26 Wyoming Test of Proficiency and Progress, commonly known as WY-TOPP, and Wyoming Alternate Assessment, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Education Megan Degenfelder announced in a Friday press conference. 
It’s the first time that scores have reached or exceeded prepandemic levels across all three areas of testing. Degenfelder recalled participating in a similar press conference in the past, where she delivered less thrilling results. 
“Three years ago, at this very press conference, I stated that we must do better,” Degenfelder said, “and Wyoming, together we have delivered.”
Superintendent of Public Instruction and candidate for governor Megan Degenfelder chats with Landon Bowman, 14, on Aug. 13, 2026, in Riverton during a town hall hosted by Wyoming Boys and Girls Clubs Alliance. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
She credited a “laser-focused” effort that has involved policymakers, school administrators, classroom teachers and others. “These results show us that our statewide priority around literacy reform and efforts to raise the bar are working,” she said.
Degenfelder also trumpeted gains made in school performance rankings, which rely on indicators such as student achievement and graduation rates. For the 2025-26 school year, 75% of schools serving students in grades 3-8 met or exceeded the achievement standards, a 5% gain. 
Results breakdown
Launched in 2017-18, WY-TOPP measures student mastery of Wyoming’s content and performance standards. Students take the computer-based assessment every year from third through 10th grade; it covers math, English language arts and science. 
The assessment has been tweaked during its lifetime, with officials altering the science portion and removing writing from the third grade assessment, for example. 




After several years of declining or stagnating scores on Wyoming’s statewide standardized assessment, known as WY-TOPP, students made notable gains in 2026. (Wyoming Department of Education)
In the 2025-26 results, student proficiency increased 1.6% in English language arts, 4.1% in math and 1.3% in science over the previous year, according to the education department. Overall scores in all content areas have inched up since 2020, but this marked the first time they uniformly reached or exceeded prepandemic levels.
The 2021-22 school year represented a nadir in proficiency results for Wyoming, with overall student proficiency dipping to 53.1% in English language arts, 48.3% in math and 47.3% in science. The newest results grew to 57.3%, 54.9% and 52.5%, respectively. 
A statewide standout is Washakie School District 2, home to Ten Sleep School, which had proficiency rates of 70% or better in all three content areas. Other high-performers include Sheridan School Districts 1 and 2. 
So what fueled the improvements? Degenfelder credited a matrix of efforts, including strategic literacy instruction, teacher support and strong parental involvement.  
“Marking solid math gains and building steady progress in reading doesn’t happen by accident — it is the direct result of dedicated teachers, strong instruction in the classroom, statewide priorities and unwavering family and community support,” she said. 
School performance
In tandem with test scores, the department also released 2025-26 school performance results. That measures how well individual schools are meeting state and national standards. When schools don’t meet standards, it triggers state intervention to help map out, support and implement improvement plans.
The 75% of schools that met or exceeded the achievement standards in 2025-26 reflects both an increase in the percentage of schools that met expectations and a decrease in the percentage of schools that only partially or did not meet them.
Degenfelder lauded an effort stretching back to the late 2000s, when a legislative committee spent six years creating a statewide accountability system that factors in not just standardized test performance, but also growth, postsecondary readiness and graduation rates.
Sen. Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, sat on that committee. 

Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, during the 2026 Wyomning Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“I think this is one of the most important pieces of legislation that I’ve worked on in my career in the Legislature, and probably one of the most important pieces of legislation that we’ve passed in the past 20 years,” he said during the press conference. “Now it’s been 10 years since the system was fully implemented in its current form, and we’re seeing the results.”
In this area, Degenfelder also highlighted schools with major gains, such as Carey Middle School in Cheyenne, which jumped two categories when it met expectations after six years of falling short. The state’s largest middle school embarked on what Principal Matt Schlagel called a “redesign” to meet the academic and social needs of students. 
“We’re not done,” he added. “We want to be back up here next year as an exceeding-expectation school. Now that we’ve felt how good it is to meet expectations.”
