name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Democrats outnumber Republicans in first day of early voting in CT
text:
Democrats outnumbered Republicans by nearly a 4-1 margin at the polls Monday in the first of 14 days of early voting in Connecticut, the secretary of the state’s office reported Tuesday.
With polls open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., 42,241 cast votes in person and another 23,170 cast absentee ballots by mail or at drop boxes. Early voting continues through Nov. 1, the Sunday before the Nov. 3 election.
By not quite a 3-1 margin, Democratic voters also dominated the first absentee ballots received.
The top line race in Connecticut features Gov. Ned Lamont, a 72-year-old Democrat seeking a third term, against Ryan Fazio, a 36-year-old Republican state senator from Greenwich. Other statewide constitutional offices, all five U.S. House seats and all 187 General Assembly seats are on the ballot.
Fazio, the 287th voter at Greenwich town hall on Monday, slid his ballot into one of the state’s new generation of tabulators that scan the paper ballots. His fiancée, Amy Orser, was the 286th voter in the wealthy hometown they share with the Democratic governor and his wife.
“I think I got 100% right,” Fazio said, smiling as he likened the ballot to an exam.
Lamont’s plan is to vote on Election Day.
Like every other state except Louisiana, all votes in Connecticut are cast on paper ballots that are preserved for any necessary recount. The tabulators are not online, a protection against hacking.
Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas and local lawmakers encouraged early voting at press conference Monday outside the Miller Memorial Library, the early voting polling site in Hamden.
“Emergencies happen every single day — sick children, accidents, flat tires, a family situation, a work situation — and early voting is how you ensure that one emergency doesn’t deprive you of the right to vote,” Thomas said.
Polls are open for early voting most days from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with extended hours of 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Oct. 27 and 29. Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3.

From left, Gov. Ned Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz and Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas encouraging early voting outside a polling place in Hamden. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

Early votes were cast Monday by 24,862 Democrats, 6,506 Republicans, 10,356 unaffiliated and 517 minor-party voters; absentee ballots by 12,019 Democrats, 4,396 Republicans, 6,455 unaffiliated and 300 minor-party members, according to Thomas’ office.
There also were 182 early votes cast by residents using same-day registration.
The most first-day votes were cast in West Hartford, 981; Milford, 846; Stratford, 841; Fairfield, 812; Norwalk, 756; Stamford, 689; Manchester, 671; Glastonbury, 646; East Lyme, 611; and Trumbull, 596.
Connecticut was the among the last states to offer early in-person voting, beginning in in 2024. It was quickly embraced, with 837,233 voting early in the 2024 presidential election.
“Imagine that over 800,000 of our just under 2 million voters voted early and safely and securely cast their ballots,” said Bysiewicz, a former secretary of the state. “So today, all of us want to encourage you to do the same. You can avoid long lines that occur on election day.”
For the first time, the state this year also offers voting by mail with absentee ballots that are available to any registered voter. Previously, absentee ballots could only be used under limited circumstances, such as illness and being out of town during hours of voting on Election Day.
“Take advantage of it,” Lamont said.
Thomas confirmed that her office was among four involved in elections to be targeted with mail containing a suspicious white powder that has not been publicly identified. They were intercepted by postal inspectors, she said.
Similar letters have gone to members of Congress across the country.
Fazio used his early vote, which attracted a handful of reporters, as an opportunity to reiterate his case against the governor, which focused on the impact of inflation and high taxes on Connecticut voters. 
“They’re suffering under the weight of the third-highest taxes and the highest unemployment rate in the country after eight years of the Lamont administration, and they want new leadership, and they want Democrats and Republicans to work together in our state rather than move to their corners and constantly fight,” he said.
The consensus of public polling is that voters’ top concern is, indeed, affordability, but they are more inclined to blame President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war on Iran, which has driven up fuel prices. Three recent polls have Lamont leading by 20 percentage points, something Fazio downplayed.
“Well, you certainly don’t like complacency,” Lamont said. “What we’re trying to do is remind people that your vote matters and elections matter. I think we’ve learned that a lot, especially over the last few election cycles.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Push for tighter trucking company oversight sees Statehouse support
text:
Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling, right, speaks with Rep. Jim Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie, before an Indiana Statehouse news conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A key state legislator says he’s ready to push a crackdown on so-called chameleon trucking companies that’s been championed by Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling.
The issue has been a lead talking point of Engling’s campaign in which he’s raised concerns about trucking businesses that register with the secretary of state’s office but later shut down and reregister under new names when they face safety investigations.
House Roads and Transportation Committee Chair Jim Pressel joined Engling at a Statehouse news conference Tuesday, saying such businesses organize as limited liability corporations and exist “for a moment in time” until safety officials start closing in.


Engling set for Bayh ad suit
The Indiana secretary of state’s race could soon be moving into the courtroom.
Republican candidate Max Engling’s campaign said Tuesday that it expected a defamation lawsuit would be filed this week against Democrat Beau Bayh’s campaign over references in a TV ad saying that Engling had been convicted of reckless driving.
Engling acknowledges several speeding tickets on his driving record but labels as “a lie” claims of a reckless driving conviction.
Bayh’s campaign says the ad is accurate and that Engling’s “threats of frivolous lawsuits are reckless.”
An Engling spokeswoman said prominent conservative attorney Jim Bopp was preparing the lawsuit.


“We’ve got great logistics companies. We’ve got great motor carriers,” said Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie. “But what we don’t have is a mechanism to identify these chameleon carriers.”
Crashes involving semis driven by foreign-born drivers have often drawn attention, leading to Indiana and other states adopting tougher commercial driver licensing requirements.
Pressel authored legislation approved earlier this year that imposes felonies and fines on improperly credentialed truck drivers and tightens employer and training‑school penalties. That bill cleared the Legislature with nearly unanimous approval.
Engling said the secretary of state’s office needs to implement systems to detect suspicious business filings, such as multiple registrations from the same home address.
“We know that there are problems like that that need to be further investigated and potentially prosecuted,” Engling said. “But part of the issue is that we don’t have a clear idea to the magnitude of the issue.”
The other secretary of state candidates haven’t emphasized the fraudulent business filings crackdown as Engling has. 
The campaign of Democratic candidate Beau Bayh did not immediately reply Tuesday for a request for comment.
Bayh said during a recent candidates debate that the secretary of state’s securities division needed to become better prepared for fraudsters using artificial intelligence tools.
“The secretary of state needs to move into the new age of fraud,” Bayh said. “One of the very important responsibilities of the secretary of state is rooting out securities fraud in our state, making sure particularly our seniors are not taken advantage of.”
Pressel said the secretary of state’s business registry should be connected with the state Department of Revenue, the Bureau of Motor Vehicles and the state police to spot fraudulent trucking companies.
Another step Pressel mentioned was possibly requiring those companies to have physical operations in the state rather than just a mailing address.
Pressel said he was glad Engling was emphasizing the issue.
“I think he’s on the same page with me as we need to identify those folks and then create that portal to where it goes straight to the Department of Revenue that handles mobile carrier services,” Pressel said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: SJC upholds Mass. law restricting firearms for people under 21
text:
MASSACHUSETTS’S LAW PREVENTING people under 21-years-old from obtaining a license to carry handguns or large capacity firearms is constitutional, the state’s highest court ruled on Tuesday. But two justices dissented, arguing the matter should have been sent back down to a lower court for more detailed expert testimony and briefs.


Mikai Thomson, who was a passenger in a car that ran a red light, was arrested in December 2021 after he fled police and discarded a semiautomatic handgun. Because the 20-year-old Thomson had no license to carry, he was charged with and convicted of carrying a firearm without a license.
Despite never applying for a license, Thomson challenged the age restriction in his specific case and on broader grounds. It would have been futile for him to apply, since the law prevented him from being licensed, and the regulation unconstitutionally diminished the Second Amendment to a “second-class right” by depriving adults under 21 from carrying, Thomson’s lawyers argued.



COMMONWEALTH vs. MIKAI THOMSON




Download the decision




Thomson did not have standing to challenge the law as it applied to him, Justice Gabrielle Wolohojian wrote in a 49-page opinion for the court’s majority, because Thomson was never actually denied a license. But he did have standing to challenge the law as unconstitutional on its face, the full court agreed. 
“Because restriction of firearm possession by those deemed too young to handle them safely outside of supervised settings is consistent with the nation’s regulatory tradition,” Wolohojian wrote, the majority upheld the lower court’s conviction. 
The decision comes as Bay State voters are deciding whether to keep or scrap a sprawling firearms law passed in 2024, which includes the same age restriction. 
In its analysis, the SJC noted that rulings from the US Supreme Court have found that the Second Amendment established a right to have and use arms for self-preservation and self-defense, but that right is “not unlimited.”  
A 2022 US Supreme Court decision created a new test for how states must defend their gun restrictions: whether the law has a relevant historical analogue from the Founding era.  
The licensing system in Massachusetts “gives progressively greater unsupervised access to the possession and use of firearms by young people as they mature in age,” Wolohojian said. This was the result of “calibrated legislative determinations” on when and where young people can be entrusted with deadly weapons.  
Young people can carry firearms under an array of circumstances in the Bay State, the court noted, such as under the supervision of a licensed gun owner. Minors from 15- to 17-years-old can apply for a Firearms Identification Card (FID) with parental consent to carry rifles or shotguns that are not large capacity, as can anyone 18 or older without needing a parent’s permission.  
But, under Massachusetts law, they have to wait until they are 21 for a license to carry rifles and shotguns including large capacity and semiautomatic firearms and all handguns. 
Age-based restrictions are common in the United States and in Massachusetts, the court’s majority noted. Exactly what the cut-offs are for any specific right — like voting on a jury or drinking alcohol — is a matter for the Legislature to determine, Wolohojian wrote.  
The licensing age restriction works by relaxing over time “as young people mature” to protect them “from the consequences of firearm possession –- to themselves and others — stemming from their own immaturity.” 
Wolohojian wrote that this is analogous to laws from the founding era in Massachusetts in which minors, even those enrolled in military service, were not expected to supply their own arms. Supervising officers were tasked with overseeing the use of firearms to preserve public safety, she wrote.  
She also noted that a federal judge upheld the Massachusetts age restriction against an NRA-backed challenge in August, using similar logic.  
Justice Scott Kafker dissented, joined by Justice Dalila Wendlandt. In the 28-page dissent, Kafker took issue with the majority’s analysis, especially when three appeals courts decisions struck down policies in other states that restricted carrying firearms by those between 18- and 21-years old.  
The briefing was too thin on this extremely complicated question of which historical analogues are most informative, he wrote, and the case should have been sent down to the lower court for deeper scrutiny.  
“I believe further briefing and expert historical analysis are required to draw the appropriate analogy reliably and correctly,” he wrote. “Lamentably, as a result of the court’s chosen course, the first time the defendant will see much of the history undergirding the court’s legal conclusion will be when the court’s opinion issues.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire’s SCOTUS appeal puts student voter ID law in flux
text:
A voter shows a photo ID at the Warner polls on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)Whether high school and college students in New Hampshire can use their student identification cards to vote on Nov. 3 remains up in the air, after the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office took the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court last week. 
The request, filed by the state Attorney General’s Office Thursday, asks the Supreme Court to reverse an Oct. 2 order by Judge Joseph Laplante of the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire to halt the new law. 
House Bill 323, signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte in April, removed high school, college and university identification cards from the list of acceptable ways for voters to prove their identity when casting a ballot. 
Under the law, voters are allowed to use a driver’s license (issued by any state), a U.S. passport, a U.S. armed services ID card or any other form of government-issued identification, including a state-issued non-driver’s-license ID card available from a Division of Motor Vehicles location. 
The restriction on student ID cards was in effect for the Sept. 8 primary. However, after the voter advocacy groups Coalition for Open Democracy, League of Women Voters of New Hampshire, and the Forward Foundation sued, Laplante issued a mixed ruling that temporarily allows student IDs to be used in the Nov. 3 election as the case continues. 
The state’s request to the U.S. Supreme Court is an emergency application for stay; if granted, Laplante’s order would be lifted and the student ID ban would take effect on Nov. 3 while the Open Democracy lawsuit continued in the District Court over the next year. 
A day after the New Hampshire Attorney General filed its request, the Republican National Committee filed an amicus brief in support of the state’s effort.
Here’s what to know ahead of the Supreme Court ruling, which had not been issued as of Tuesday afternoon. 
Why did plaintiffs bring the lawsuit?
Open Democracy, the lead plaintiff in the lawsuit, argues the law is an unconstitutional and unnecessary restriction on a commonly used method of proving identity for high school and college students. 
Some students in New Hampshire may not have easy access to a government ID, the plaintiffs argue; they may not have driver’s licenses or own passports, and college students living on campus may have left their passports at home, the plaintiffs argue. 
Plaintiffs also say the alternative option allowed under the new law — a $20 non-driver’s ID available at the DMV — is a headache for students to obtain. DMV offices require appointments, are located more than 30 minutes away from New Hampshire college campuses, such as the University of New Hampshire in Durham or Dartmouth College, and are often open only during class time hours. 
And plaintiffs argue the new law does not provide enhanced security requirements for identification, because students can use their existing student ID card as proof of identification to obtain the non-driver’s ID from the DMV. 
In their lawsuit, lawyers for the plaintiffs say the new law violates the 26th Amendment, which lowered the voting age to 18, the First Amendment, and the 14th Amendment, which the courts have interpreted to establish voting rights.
Specifically, plaintiffs argue the state’s reasons for enforcing the law are not strong enough to justify the burden the law will impose on voting — a test known as the Anderson-Burdick framework. 
That balancing test is a popular tool for plaintiffs fighting more restrictive voting laws. It was used by U.S. District Judge Samantha Elliott to strike down another New Hampshire voting law in May, House Bill 1569, which required strict proof of citizenship in order to vote. The state has appealed that decision. 
However, when it comes to voter ID laws, the Anderson-Burdick test could face an uphill battle. The Supreme Court ruled in 2008 that Indiana’s voter ID requirements did not violate the balancing test, in the landmark 6-3 decision in Crawford v. Marion County Election Board. That case did not explore prohibitions on student ID cards. 
What is the state’s defense of the law?
The state argues HB 323 is a legitimate attempt by the Legislature and governor to maintain secure and efficient elections. 
They argue that student identification cards are less reliable and less secure than government-issued ID cards because they don’t have expiration dates and could allow students to use them years after they have already graduated. 
Attorneys for the state also noted that many school ID cards lack anti-counterfeiting features like holograms and ultraviolet markings. 
The state also challenged the standing of Open Democracy to bring the lawsuit, arguing that they were not likely to suffer a legally sufficient “concrete injury” as a result of the lawsuit. 
How did Judge Laplante rule?
In his Oct. 2 order, Laplante gave plaintiffs a mixed result. He did not appear to agree with the plaintiffs’ constitutional arguments — at least not enough to issue a preliminary injunction.
“HB 323 did one specific thing: it removed student ID cards from the forms of identification that are expressly valid to obtain a ballot,” Laplante wrote. “The legislature made that choice, and the court upholds it at this preliminary stage because the plaintiff has not demonstrated a likelihood of proving that it is unconstitutional.”
However, Laplante agreed with plaintiffs on a different issue. In April, the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office issued guidance to election officials stating that they should not allow New Hampshire residents to register to vote using a high school or college ID card. That guidance was wrong, Laplante noted; the new law signed by Ayotte that month barred student ID cards only for identity when casting a ballot, not when registering. 
Thus, Laplante wrote, even though the plaintiffs had not established that the law is unconstitutional, the confusion caused by that incorrect guidance justifies a pause on full enforcement of the new law on Election Day next month. 
“The Secretary of State is therefore ordered to issue, as soon as practicable, revised guidance for the November 2026 general election clarifying that, although student identification cards are no longer expressly valid to establish voter identity under RSA 659:13, election officials may consider them, along with other available evidence, when determining voter identity under RSA 654:12(d)(4) and RSA 659:13(c)(1) and (3),” Laplante wrote.
What is the state’s emergency argument to the Supreme Court? 
In short, the Attorney General’s Office argues Laplante’s order came too close to Election Day, and that freezing the new law at this point will cause voter confusion and disrupt management of the elections next month.
To make that argument, the state is invoking the “Purcell principle,” a rule-of-thumb established in a 2006 Supreme Court case that federal courts should not issue decisions that change election rules too close to an election.
In this case, the Secretary of State’s Office has already updated and distributed its Election Procedure Manual to local officials, and Laplante’s order requires the office to inform all election officials to ignore portions of that manual as they prepare for Election Day, the state argues. 
The state is also arguing to the Supreme Court that it will likely prevail on the merits when the lawsuit gets a full hearing in U.S. District Court, and that the state would face “irreparable harm” should the law not go into effect Nov. 3, two requirements to obtain any emergency stay of this nature.
“Re-educating local election officials and the public in a short time is practically impossible and risks voter confusion and inconsistent application of law, if not voter disenfranchisement,” the Attorney General’s Office argued Thursday. 
In a reply to the Supreme Court filed Monday, attorneys for Open Democracy say the Purcell principle supports leaving the ruling in place, not overturning it. They noted that Secretary of State Dave Scanlan already issued updated guidance the day after Laplante’s ruling this month to reflect that election officials may accept a student ID alongside other evidence at the polls. 
“The Secretary’s revised guidance is now the status quo,” the plaintiffs argued Monday. “A stay wouldn’t preserve it. It would reverse the rules for a second time in a month.”
How have federal courts handled challenges to student ID bans in other states?
This case is untested territory – New Hampshire’s case is the first involving a ban on student identification to vote to reach the U.S. Supreme Court. And though the court is acting on an emergency request for stay — and will thus not issue a binding decision — its decision could provide a window into further rulings. 
New Hampshire is one of 36 states that require voters to provide identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Granite State adopted a voter-ID law in 2012, after the Legislature overrode Democratic Gov. John Lynch’s veto. 
And with its law this year, New Hampshire became one of 11 states not to allow student identification to be used to prove identity. Other states include Arizona, Idaho, Indiana, Missouri, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Caroline, Tennessee and Texas. The Florida Legislature has also passed a law repealing student ID use, but it will not take effect until January 2027.
But there are some recent cases to keep in mind. 
Outside of New Hampshire, three states have been sued over their laws barring student identification for voter identification, and plaintiffs have so far been unsuccessful. 
In Idaho, the League of Women Voters and the advocacy group BABE VOTE attempted to overturn that state’s ban on student IDs for voting, but the Idaho Supreme Court upheld the laws in April 2024.
In Tennessee, a federal district court dismissed a lawsuit in 2015 brought by the Nashville Student Organizing Committee and other organizations against its law; the court found that students are not a protected class under the 14th Amendment and that the requirement that non-drivers obtain an alternative identification was not a substantial burden on voting.
Today, the only ongoing federal lawsuit similar to New Hampshire’s is in Indiana. In May 2025, an Indiana University student and two advocacy groups, Count US IN and Women4Change Indiana, sued in federal court to challenge the state’s 2025 student ID ban, arguing it amounted to a “surgical attack on young voters,” and violates the First, 14th, and 26th Amendments. 
Yet despite the lawsuit, Indiana’s law is set to take effect Nov. 3. A federal district court blocked the law in April, but the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals reversed that block that same month. The case is scheduled for oral argument Oct. 27.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Tioga County man charged with sending death threat to state lawmaker
text:
The Indiana Station of the Pennsylvania State Police in Indiana County, on  Jan. 21, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)A Tioga County man is charged with sending death threats to the office of a state representative.
Timothy D. Geisler of Mansfield was being held Tuesday in Tioga County Prison on a misdemeanor charge of making terroristic threats with the intent to intimidate. 
His arrest stems from a series of rambling, politically charged emails state police say he sent since June to the district office of Rep. Jamie Walsh, a Luzerne County Republican, according to court documents.
They culminated with an Oct. 1 message in which Geisler allegedly made specific threats against Walsh and his family, a criminal complaint charging Geisler says. 
The complaint notes the Pennsylvania State Police Political Violence Threat Unit also received notifications that Geisler left voicemails at Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office containing non-specific threats.
Walsh issued a statement Monday expressing gratitude to law enforcement for efforts to ensure his safety and that of his family and legislative staff. 
“Threats and intimidation have no place in our democracy. No public servant, family member or staff member should have to fear for their safety for serving their community,” Walsh said. “Political disagreements are to be expected but must never escalate into threats of violence or attempts to intimidate those who serve the public.”
The Pennsylvania Capitol in downtown Harrisburg on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
According to the complaint against Geisler, a member of Walsh’s staff began receiving “rambling, somewhat unhinged and political based” emails in June. The staff member initially replied with advice to contact his federal representatives for help with the issues raised.
After subsequent emails, the office of counsel for the House Republican Caucus contacted Mansfield borough police and requested a welfare check and for Geisler to stop emailing.
On Oct. 1, Walsh’s staff received an email from Geisler that accused Walsh “rigging another election,” and warning “now you’re gonna f****** die.”
Geisler is being held in lieu of $100,000 bail, according to court documents.
The charge is the latest criminal case stemming from a series of threats against Pennsylvania elected officials. 
In May, Adam G. Berryhill, 43, of Lebanon was charged with making terroristic threats targeting state House Speaker Joanna McClinton of Philadelphia, House Judiciary Committee Chairman Tim Briggs of Montgomery County, Government Oversight Committee Chairwoman Morgan Cephas of Philadelphia and Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta of Philadelphia, all of whom are Democrats. 
Last October, a Harrisburg man pleaded guilty to attempted murder, arson and dozens of other charges, admitting he firebombed the governor’s official residence as Shapiro and his family slept inside. 
Cody Balmer, 38, who confessed to police when he was arrested hours after starting the fire on April 13, 2025, said that he disagreed with Shapiro’s position on the Israeli response to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by the Palestinian militant group Hamas. Balmer is serving a 25 to 50 year prison sentence.
Last year, former Pennsylvania House Speaker Mark Rozzi (D-Berks) told the Capital-Star he resorted to wearing a bulletproof vest for several months after facing a stalker with a history of unusual behavior, including a statement that he was willing to “die in combat.” Rozzi said the incident contributed to his decision to retire from politics. 
The Exeter Township man who faced misdemeanor charges for harassing Rozzi and his then-girlfriend died before the case was set to go to trial last year, Berks County District Attorney John Adams said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: This midterm election, 21 Alaska judges are on the ballot for retention
text:
Alaska Supreme Court Justice Jude Pate, right, asks a question during oral arguments in a case concerning correspondence education allotments, on June 27, 2024, in the Boney Courthouse in Anchorage. (Photo by Andrew Kitchenman/Alaska Beacon)Early in-person voting opened Monday across the state, and in addition to high-stakes races for governor and U.S. Congress voters also have a chance to weigh in on whether or not to allow 21 judges to remain on the bench.
Under the Alaska Constitution, judges are up for retention in elections that take place on even-numbered years to allow voters to decide whether they should be allowed to stay in office. Judges do not run against each other, and are not allowed to campaign. Judges are vetted and nominated on a merit-based system by the nonpartisan Alaska Judicial Council, which advances a list of nominees to the governor who makes appointments.
Not all judges appear on every ballot. Voters are asked to consider only their district judges.
This year, one justice of the five-member Alaska Supreme Court, Jude Pate, is up for a ten year term. Pate was appointed to the state’s highest court by Gov. Mike Dunleavy in January of 2023, and this is his first retention election. Prior to the Supreme Court, he served as a Superior Court judge in Sitka. 
In the 45-member Superior Court, 16 judges are up for retention to serve six-year terms. There are four judges of the 20-member District Court standing for retention for four-year terms. 
In an unusual move, the Alaska Judicial Council — which issues performance evaluations and recommendations for retention of judges ahead of elections — published recommendations not to retain Kelly J. Lawson to the Kenai Superior Court and Martin Fallon for the Kenai District Court, and issued no recommendation for Marianna Carpeneti for the Juneau Superior Court. 
It’s the first time in 12 years the council has recommended a “no” vote on retaining judges, according to Alaska Public Media. 
The council recommended voters retain the other 18 judges. 
The council is made up of three attorney members of the Alaska Bar Association, and three public members appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Legislature. Recommendations were based on a variety of performance factors including surveys with attorneys, court employees and analyses of the judge’s financial disclosures, caseloads and whether the judge’s decisions were affirmed or appealed. 
In the First Judicial District, which covers Southeast Alaska from Ketchikan to Yakutat, Carpeneti is up for a retention vote in Juneau and Daniel E. Doty and Katherine H. Lybrand are up for retention in Ketchikan Superior Court. 
The council issued no recommendation for Carpeneti’s retention. She has served on the Juneau Superior Court since 2021. Three council members voted not to retain, two voted to retain and two members abstained. While Carpeneti largely met performance standards, she received low marks from peace officers and probation officers who rated her integrity and judicial temperament as “below acceptable,” according to the evaluation. 
In the Second Judicial District, which covers the northern region from Nome to Utgiavik, David L. Roghair is standing for retention in the Utgiavik Superior Court.
In the Third Judicial District, which covers Southcentral, the Kenai Peninsula, Prince William Sound, Kodiak and the Aleutian Islands, twelve judges are up for retention. In Anchorage Superior Court, Lara Hartz, Yvonne Lamoreux, Jack R. McKenna, David A. Nesbitt, Christina Rankin, and Ian Wheeles are standing for retention. Jonathan A. Woodman is up for retention in Palmer Superior Court, and Christina “Tina” Reigh is up for retention to the Dillingham Superior Court. 
Lawson and Fallon are standing for retention in Kenai Superior Court and Kenai District Court, respectively.
Lawson was appointed to the Kenai Superior Court in 2023. This is her first retention election. Upon review, the council found she did not meet performance standards for judicial temperament and integrity. 
“While performing acceptably on the bench, Judge Lawson has lacked patience, dignity, and courtesy in her communications with court employees, creating friction between Judge Lawson, court staff, and other judges to a degree that has impeded the efficient administration of justice,” the evaluation said.
Fallon has served on the Kenai District Court since 2019, and this is his second retention election. The council found Fallon did not meet performance standards related to integrity, diligence and administrative skills. The council found Fallon failed to resolve cases in a timely manner — in one case leaving parties waiting for a decision for more than seven months. 
Under state law, a judge cannot collect a paycheck if they have any decision undecided or uncompleted for more than six months. But Fallon signed pay affidavits during that time saying that to the best of his knowledge there were no cases referred to him that were undecided for more than six months. “Judge Fallon acted in a manner that did not promote public confidence in the integrity of the judiciary and created an appearance of impropriety,” the evaluation said. 
In District Court, Chris Darnell is standing for retention in Anchorage and Shawn D. Traini is standing in Palmer. 
In the Fourth Judicial District, covering the Interior region and west to Hooper Bay and the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Nathaniel Peters is standing for retention in Bethel Superior Court, and Kirk Schwalm and Amy Welch are up for retention in Fairbanks Superior Court. 
In the Fairbanks District Court, Benjamin A. Seekins is standing for retention. 
Voters will have the opportunity to vote on judges in the judicial district for which they are registered from now until the polls close at 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Husband of RI Democratic Party leader indicted on federal fraud charges in Ohio
text:
Rhode Island Democratic gubernatorial nominee Helena Buonanno Foulkes, right, is shown at her victory celebration in Providence on the night of the Sept. 9 primary, with state Democratic Party Chair Liz Beretta-Perik, left. Foulkes has called for Perik to step down after Perik's husband was indicted on 12 felony charges in Ohio. (Rhode Island Democratic Party Instagram post)Rhode Island Democratic Party Chair Liz Beretta-Perik is facing calls to step down in the wake of her husband’s indictment by an Ohio grand jury on felony fraud and racketeering charges.
Michael Perik, of Jamestown, is one of three people facing charges of stealing $20 million in federal grants and aid intended to support students at the now-closed Eastern Gateway Community College in Ohio. Ohio Auditor General Keith Faber announced the grand jury indictment on Oct. 8, which includes 12 felony charges against Perik for theft, fraud, bribery, money laundering and corruption.
Beretta-Perik declined to comment. In a text message Monday, she said the charges were unrelated to her or her work as chair of the state party. 
Perik’s attorney has denied any criminal wrongdoing, calling the investigation “purely political payback” from a change in federal administration.
Helena Buonanno Foulkes, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, on Monday night called for Beretta-Perik to step down from her elected position as party leader, citing the upcoming Nov. 3 election.
“These are serious and concerning allegations,” Foulkes said in a statement. “While everyone is entitled to due process, we are weeks away from a pivotal election that will determine the future of our state for years to come. I thank Liz for her service, but in the best interest of the future of Rhode Island, she should step aside at this time.” 
As party chair, Beretta-Perik plays a key role in raising money for and awareness of Rhode Island’s state and local Democratic candidates, including Foulkes. Elected unanimously by the Democratic Party State Committee in 2023, Beretta-Perik is the first woman to lead the state party. 
Campaign finance records show her husband, Michael Perik has donated to dozens of high-ranking Democratic politicians in Rhode Island, including $2,000 to Foulkes during her first gubernatorial campaign in 2022. Angelika Pellegrino, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ campaign, did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the donations from Perik. 
Across the aisle, Aaron Guckian, the Republican gubernatorial candidate, also called for Beretta-Perik to resign. And GOP Party Chairman Allyn Meyers urged Democratic party officials to address the allegations publicly. 
“While the Democratic Party Chairwoman has not been charged with any wrongdoing, Rhode Islanders deserve transparency when allegations of corruption of this magnitude involve the immediate family of our state’s top Democratic Party official,” Meyers said in a statement Monday.
Calling the charges against Perik “disgraceful,” Meyers said the allegations, if proven, are a “staggering betrayal of public trust.”
Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block opted not to enter the fray. Block said he would “leave it up to Democrats” to decide party leadership.
Katherine Riordan, executive director for the Rhode Island Democratic Party, declined to comment.
Joe Paolino Jr., the state party’s national commiteeman, defended Beretta-Perik.
“This is her husband, not her,” Paolino said in an interview Tuesday. “Why get penalized by her spouse?”
Paolino, a former Providence mayor and prominent downtown developer, also said there was a double standard for women in high-ranking positions.
“If her husband had been Democratic state chair, and she had been indicted, I don’t know if anybody would ask for his resignation,” Paolino said.
As former CEO of an education consulting firm, Perik worked with the Ohio community college, overseeing a tuition discount program for students who belonged to or had family members in unions.
The program, which included online options available to students nationwide , contributed to “enormous” enrollment growth at the Steubenville, Ohio, college until 2021, when state and federal education regulators put the college on probation amid evidence of mishandling federal financial aid.
Enrollment plummeted, and the college closed in October 2024. A year later, the state auditor, now the state’s Republican attorney general nominee, released an audit showing serious recordkeeping problems at the college, including more than $17 million in federal Pell Grants.
The 23-page indictment against Perik, his business partner and the former college president traces the federal financial aid through a series of business entities owned by Perik, alleging the shell companies were set up expressly to take advantage of the college’s federal grants and aid over a six-year period, ending in March 2022.
“They hid behind contracts to fool regulators and then disregarded those contracts and engaged in activities to control enrollment and financial aid for the purpose of maximizing their incentive compensation in violation of Federal law,” the indictment states. “Students were led to believe that they were receiving a Union-funded scholarship, when in fact their Federal financial aid dollars were taken and used to pay the education of less-needy students, and for unlawful incentive compensation payments.”
It also alleges that Perik violated the terms of the pandemic-era Paycheck Protection Program, applying for forgivable federal loans for costs already covered by the college through the grant programs.
Perik sold his company in 2021, prompting two federal lawsuits by the buyer, who alleged Perik failed to disclose that the Ohio community college that the business derived most of its revenue from was in financial trouble, the Providence Journal reported.
He pleaded not guilty in an initial court appearance last week, according to news reports. 
“There was no crime or lack of transparency,” Brad Barbin, Perik’s attorney, said in a statement to Rhode Island Current Monday.
Barbin noted that the college’s financial operations were reviewed by multiple state and federal regulators for more than a decade, ending in 2024 when the Department of Justice dropped a lawsuit against the college.
“Through no fault of his own, Michael Perik followed all the protocols and received signoffs from agency lawyers,” Barbin said. “When the administrative reviewers changed, so did the interpretation of its legality.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah sues Kalshi for ‘brazen pattern’ of violating state’s gambling ban
text:
Kalshi photo illustration, Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed a lawsuit against the major prediction market platform Kalshi on Tuesday, seeking to block the company from taking bets from Utahns. 
“Utah has said no to gambling since statehood in 1896, and that didn’t change when betting moved onto cellphones,” Brown said during a news conference at the Utah Capitol announcing the lawsuit. “Effectively, Kalshi bet today that Utah would not enforce its gambling laws. Well, we are enforcing it. So on that point, Kalshi has now lost their bet.” 
Kalshi is subject to Utah’s anti-gambling law, judge rules

The lawsuit filed in 3rd District Court alleges Kalshi has been violating state law and the Utah Constitution, which bans gambling in all forms. It also accuses the company of a “brazen pattern of unlawful conduct” that has “inflicted serious harm” on Utah and its residents, including “gambling-related” harm to Utahns’ mental health. 
To pay for those damages, the Utah Attorney General’s Office is asking a judge to force the company to pay the state “unjustly acquired profits,” plus restitution for other damages that the court deems fair. 
Kalshi and its affiliated companies acts like “the manager of a back-alley gambling den,” the complaint says, “by hosting and facilitating the gambling events and by taking a percentage fee (or ‘rake’) of amounts gambled.” 
Kalshi did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
The attorney general’s office estimates that Kalshi has made between about $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees from “illegal wagers” placed by Utah accounts as of Monday — “a number that is increasing each day in which the Kalshi Enterprise operates in the state,” the complaint says. 
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown speaks to reporters after a news conference announcing Utah’s lawsuit against Kalshi at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Oct. 20, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
That number is based on the fee Kalshi rakes in — which the complaint says is $0.01 to $0.02 per wager — and the estimated more than $3 billion in wagers Utah accounts have placed across Kalshi’s lifetime. The complaint also says that Kalshi has more than 32,000 verified users in Utah, with more than $1 million “invested” on the exchange. 
“Based on the rapid increase in volume on the Kalshi platform, the actual volume attributable to Utah accounts is likely much greater,” the complaint says. 
Brown said that those profit estimates included in the complaint could grow as the lawsuit uncovers more information.
“The reality is, as we get discovery in the course of this civil complaint, we anticipate having more information that will help us understand exactly what it is that they’ve made and how they’ve done it in the course of effectively breaking Utah law,” Brown said.
Prediction market exchange Kalshi sues Utah over proposed prop betting ban

The Utah Attorney General’s Office said that even though Kalshi is “well aware that sports bets and other forms of gambling bets are illegal under Utah law,” the company “chose to begin offering gambling bets” to Utahns by as early as September 2024. 
That’s despite a recent federal order rejected Kalshi’s argument that it doesn’t need to adhere to Utah law, the complaint notes. The company has appealed, arguing it falls under federal, not state, jurisdiction. That federal lawsuit is ongoing. 
In the meantime, Utah’s lawsuit seeking tens of millions in damages is now positioned to play out in the state’s district court. 
When asked why his office filed a civil complaint rather than criminal charges against Kalshi for breaking Utah law, Brown told reporters that — for now — they’re focusing on a civil filing while they’ve been conducting research in “pretty extensive detail” on the company.
“When it comes to potential criminal filings … we don’t comment on existing criminal investigations or potential criminal investigations,” Brown said. 
Asked why his office is targeting Kalshi and not other prediction markets or gambling platforms, Brown also said that his office is “focusing on Kalshi” for now, “but for other companies that are operating here in Utah,” he urged them to read the complaint and follow Utah law. 
He also noted that Kalshi sued Utah in federal court, “and they effectively lost that action” when the federal court made it clear Utah can, in fact, enforce its regulations on the company. 
“Ultimately, this is part of a larger investigation,” Brown said. “But the reality is, Utah law is very specific. And under our system of government, every state can choose how they treat this issue.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Aging farmers and the government want to save farms, but for many the cost is too high
text:
Dan Kuebler walks along a path on Aug. 13, 2026, in Ashland, Mo. He recently put an easement on his land to protect it from development. (Kate Cassady/Missouri News Network)Dan Kuebler is out on a hot August morning on what used to be his farm.
Kuebler grew fruits and vegetables on 30 acres in Ashland, Missouri, and for decades he sold his produce at the Columbia Farmers Market. 
“Ashland was a little, bitty, sleepy town in ’77 when we bought it,” Kuebler said. 
Then, small towns in southern Boone County started becoming homes to those working in nearby Columbia or Jefferson City. Kuebler watched farmland on his 2-mile dead end road get sold and broken up into parcels. As he neared retirement, he needed to come up with a plan for the future of his farmland. 
“I don’t want it split up into five acre plots … and become a development. That is just like — that’s sacrilege,” he said. 
Kuebler began farming at the age of 40. For the next 33 years, he grew dozens of varieties of vegetables and eventually branched out into making fermented foods such as sauerkraut, pickles and kimchi. He balanced managing the farm along with his other job as an in-home physical therapist. 
Kuebler is passionate about local farmers providing food for their community. He was an active seller at the farmers market and advocated for the permanent shelter that now houses the market on the west side of Columbia. 
As new development encroached on his neighborhood, Kuebler wanted to protect his farm from being broken up.
“I don’t want to sell it to the highest bidder. I want it to stay in farmland. So how should I do that?” he said.
A bird flies over Dan Kuebler’s equipment Aug. 13, 2026, in Ashland, Mo. When Kuebler sold his land in 2025, he placed an easement on the property that protects it from development but allows him to use a cabin for the rest of his life. (Kate Cassady/Missouri News Network)
The demand for more housing often comes at the expense of farmland. Flat, cleared fields are ideal for development. 
Now some agriculture advocates are encouraging farmers and landowners to use a legal tool to ensure their land remains farmable. 
They believe the need is critical. At least 50 million acres of farmland in the Midwest is set to change hands by the end of the decade due in part to the average age of farmers and landowners.
Kuebler worked with a local land trust to attach what’s known as a conservation or agriculture easement to his property deed. It dictates that the farmland must remain farmland no matter who owns it — forever.
“You cannot subdivide it, you cannot sell it off for residential development or commercial development. That is the guiding principle,” said Nick Shapiro, executive director of the Greenbelt Land Trust of Mid-Missouri, the organization Kuebler worked with. 
Land trusts do the work of ensuring current and future property owners follow the stipulations laid out in agriculture easements. 
“The initial landowner who donates the easement knows, not only is there this legal document out there that binds future owners, there is also an organization out there that is required to look after that easement in perpetuity and to defend it and to make sure that it is upheld and respected,” Shapiro said.
‘Best use’ of land
In recent years, about 2,000 acres of American farmland a day has been lost or compromised by development, according to American Farmland Trust, a national land preservation organization. The group estimates another 18.4 million acres — an area almost the size of South Carolina — will be converted by 2040.
Development pressures come from urban sprawl, when metropolitan areas continue to creep outward, paving over once-rural places. But what’s known as “low-density residential” development is also a threat. 
Housing built in the country on large plots of former farmland repurposed nearly 7 million acres of agricultural land between 2001 and 2016. 
American Farmland Trust’s analysis shows rural housing development is especially high in Tennessee, where 148,000 acres of agricultural land was converted to urban and highly developed land use between 2001 and 2016. Such land conversion was similarly high in other Southeastern states and the Midwest.
Josh Wright is with American Farmland Trust, where he helps landowners through the often yearslong legal and financial process of securing an easement to protect land from development.
“People who have spent their entire lives working their land, whether it be in their family for many generations or not, you become so attached to it and all of your effort could be snatched up and paved over as soon as you sell the property,” he said. 
But placing development restrictions on a piece of land could reduce its value by up to 65%. Exactly how much depends on a number of factors, including location, nearby development pressures and how restrictive the easement is.
“Whenever you go to sell your property, it’s going to be appraised, and that’s going to be judged at best, highest dollar — and they call it best use in the industry,” Wright said. 
In other words, the most profitable use, which farming generally isn’t.
“Unfortunately, it’s probably considered the worst use,” he said. 
Twelve years ago, Congress expanded federal easement initiatives, setting aside about $450 million a year to compensate farm owners for a portion of reduced value of their land through a program known as ACEP-ALE, which stands for Agricultural Conservation Easement Program – Agricultural Land Easements.
That funding, which has since been increased to $650 million annually, filters through nonprofit organizations, such as land trusts, state and local agencies, or tribal governments, to essentially buy a property’s development rights from the farm owner.
Eric Gramlich works with Ozark Land Trust, a conservation organization focused on preserving land in Arkansas and Missouri. 
Although the government can provide a financial cushion to soften the blow of the drop in value a piece of property under easement will experience, Gramlich said it’s unlikely to be the landowner’s most lucrative option. 
“Even those payments would struggle to keep up with the demand and the price of land for commercial development or large scale subdivision development,” Gramlich said. “So I think the financial means, even for willing land owners, that’s a big challenge for them, and also a big challenge for us to rise up and … be on some sort of a playing field with the other competing interests for that land.”
Missouri, Tennessee and neighboring states make up just 8% of acres enrolled in the federal Agricultural Conservation Easement Program. (Graphic by Laiba Zai, Mariia Novoselia and Trevor Grandin/Missouri News Network)
More than 1 million acres of farmland have been preserved through easements since the federal program began in 2014. But more than half of that land is in just three states: Montana, Wyoming and Colorado. 
Currently, Tennessee has 422 acres of farmland under permanent easements as part of the ACEP-ALE program. Illinois has 445 acres, and Iowa has 2,320 acres. No farmland in Missouri has been restricted from development under the federal program.
Gramlich said that’s because there still aren’t that many land trust organizations in Missouri, and the agricultural community is still learning about the option. 
“I’d like to think that we’ll be gaining more efficiencies in the program now that it’s been established, but it is generally a multiyear process to get the application in, the contracting paperwork, and then to actually do the boots-on-the-ground work of getting the easement in place,” he said. 
President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill increased the federal easement program funding to $650 million annually, to be used to preserve both farmland and wetlands. 
Private landowners in Tennessee conserved thousands of acres of land in 2025 through conservation easements, though it’s not clear how much of that land is farmland. 
Tennessee’s General Assembly passed the Farmland Preservation Act in 2025, setting aside $25 million for grants for farmland and forest owners who place their land in conservation easements. The state’s resulting Preserving Land for Agriculture Now program began accepting its first round of applications in September. The Land Trust for Tennessee and TennGreen Land Conservancy, nonprofits that serve as easement holders, said in January they had received overwhelming interest in the state grants.
But preserving farmland through easements is time consuming, while losing farmland to development can happen rapidly. 
A few years ago the Natural Resources Conservation Service, the agency that administers the easement program, made an effort to “streamline” multiple parts of the process including land appraisals, surveys and certifying organizations such as land trusts. 
In mid-Missouri, Shapiro hopes the land owners out there who value their farm’s legacy will consider preserving it with an easement.
“The older farmers who are looking to get out might be willing to take less than top dollar if they know that there is someone who really wants to take their land and run it and manage it in a way that is consistent with their shared values,” Shapiro said.
His organization, Green Belt Land Trust, was formed to preserve natural areas such as forests and wetlands. It expanded its work to farmland as development pressures increased.
“So much of mid-Missouri’s not just economy, but culture and heritage is based in farming,” Shapiro said. “There is an important role for us to play in helping to preserve that heritage as well.” 
Giving up the farm
On the north side of Kansas City, Kansas, Rick Mareske has been growing berries and forest farming on 40 acres of land for the past 20 years. His food gets to local customers through a community supported agriculture, or CSA, subscription program. 
Mareske and his wife are weighing options for the future of their business and farmland. They considered an easement for their property.
“The cons are, it’s expensive,” he said. “It’s like 20, 25 thousand dollars just to do it, and then you lose money.”
Mareske’s land is a financial asset he’s counting on for retirement income. He said he doesn’t want the years he spent caring for his land to be erased, but he can’t afford to sell for less.
“We’re trying to make it as beautiful as possible and as enticing as possible for someone to buy it and keep it going the way we have it,” he said.
With or without an easement, Mareske hopes the future of his land includes farming.
Liz Graznak, owner of Happy Hollow Farm, hands Dan Kuebler a bouquet of flowers after paying for vegetables on Aug. 29, 2026, in Columbia, Mo. Kuebler sold produce at the Columbia Farmers Market for more than three decades. (Cory MacNeil/Missouri News Network)
Meanwhile, in Boone County, after 33 years Dan Kuebler has stopped selling produce and preserves at the farmers market. He still goes each Saturday to buy his food for the week and catch up with his former customers as he shops. 
“I see them and we talk, and it’s like I really didn’t lose my community,” he said. 
Kuebler estimates that it cost him about $20,000 to place an easement on his land, most of that cost coming from the land survey and appraisal. He didn’t take advantage of the federal ACEP-ALE program and its compensation offer, even though his 30 acres of fields, forest and pastures dropped about $90,000 in value once development rights were stripped. 
He sold the land to another local farmer last year. The easement requires the land remain in agriculture and that the methods used to grow crops are sustainable or regenerative. 
There’s a small, old cabin on the property, and one of the more unique stipulations of the easement is that Kuebler gets to spend time there, and on the land, until he dies. 
“I really couldn’t give up the farm totally because I (am) so attached to it,” he said.
Cassandra Stephenson contributed.
