Food banks cannot possibly make up for the losses this preventable crisis is causing. Greta Faworski from Kalamazoo Loaves and Fishes told us her pantry has seen a 56% jump in people asking for help. Last November, when the federal shutdown delayed SNAP benefits, they went from serving about 800 people a day to 1,200 a day. That meant adding staff and buying more food when shortages and rising prices made things even harder, especially in northern and rural counties where the percentage of children facing food insecurity is often over 20%.
As of October 1, the federal administration now requires states to pay a larger share of SNAP’s administrative costs. In Michigan, that adds up to $95 million this year alone. By next October, the cost could rise to $400 million a year. Where will we come up with that money? It will mean cuts to something Michiganders need.
But Congress has an opportunity to turn this around for the people they serve. Michigan members of Congress  can protect SNAP and delay these devastating cost shifts by acting by the end of this year. For the sake of every community in our state, we hope they do the right thing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Westport Museum for History & Culture sends out funding SOS
text:
When the Westport Museum for History & Culture announced a new strategic plan eight years ago, the organization reimagined what Westport’s history could look like. Now, Executive Director Ramin Ganeshram and board members are putting out an emergency fundraising appeal, without which the organization may have to leave its historic building by next year.  
That news came from the museum last week, as it launched a campaign to raise $750,000 by the end of the calendar year, funding that will sustain its already scaled-down operations and let it stay in the Bradley-Wheeler House, a 1795 home out of which it has operated since 1985. The organization itself dates back to 1889, when it was recognized as the Westport Historical Society (it has also operated as the Saugatuck Historical Society and the Westport-Weston Historical Society). 
“I think people don’t realize the value of the institution,” said Ganeshram, a journalist and scholar who stepped into her position in January 2018. “It’s no longer a historical society with a house museum,” but a space with interactive, rotating exhibitions and installations backed by research. 
She nodded to the museum’s tag line, “Making History Whole,” then continued, “Our approach to history is to respect our visitors’ intellect enough to be able to share with them complex ideas.”
The reason for the appeal, and its urgency in this moment, is multi-pronged, Ganeshram said in an interview last week. For years, she and members of the museum’s staff and board have fought the misconception that the organization receives funding from the town of Westport, the municipal hub just a minute away across Myrtle Street.
While the Town of Westport does provide support to civic institutions such as the Westport Public Library, it does not provide operating funds to the museum. In 2022, it regranted $20,000 of Westport’s overall $8.4 million federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds to the organization, for project-based funding that has since supported “The Real Revolution,” an exhibition that celebrates and explores the full breadth of America’s semiquincentennial.
Per a series of guidelines that the town implemented around the grants, the museum hired local illustrators and writers, and worked on a ​​”a reusable resource packet for fifth graders,” Ganeshram said. Like many other small museums and historical societies across Connecticut, the Westport Museum for History & Culture also does not receive any dedicated line item funding through the state.    
“We’re completely private,” and reliant on grants, institutional funders, and individual donations to raise a $400,000 annual operating budget, Ganeshram said. Despite small grants from organizations like CT Humanities ($1,000 for a dinner and dialogue last year, for instance, or $2,715.15 for summer youth programming in 2024) and more significant donations from the Daniel E. Offutt III Charitable Trust, that still leaves Ganeshram with hundreds of thousands of dollars to raise each year.   
“I haven’t cracked the code,” Ganeshram said. “Funders, grantmakers, as well as donors believe that Westport has money, and therefore should be funding its institution.” 
When asked Monday, Westport First Selectman Kevin Christie confirmed that the museum, as an independent and private organization, does not receive funding from the town, which has allowed it to maintain “the autonomy that comes from being privately funded and outside the municipal budget process.”
“There have been some informal inquiries about potential Town support, but I have not proposed municipal funding,” he said in an email Monday afternoon, adding that “the museum plays an important role in preserving Westport’s history,” and he does hope it is successful in its emergency appeal. “Any such funding would need to go through the Town’s established budget and appropriation process, including review and approval by the appropriate funding bodies.” 
“With the cost of living an increasing concern for many residents, as well as significant financial obligations and competing priorities facing the Town, we need to be disciplined about the use of taxpayer dollars. That applies to funding requests from any independent organization, including those that make important contributions to our community.” 
The call for funding comes after eight years of growth and transition for the museum, including a name change, several capital improvement projects, a new museological approach that includes rotating exhibitions, new gallery spaces, and historical markers that acknowledge Connecticut’s history of enslavement and its original inhabitants, members of the Paugesset Tribe who stewarded the land for generations.
After her tenure began in 2018, Ganeshram built and streamlined the collections management process, began planning exhibitions that pulled from the museum’s extensive archives, and focused on all of Westport’s residents, including those who had long been pushed to the historical margins (in 2024, she held a formal dedication to the Black and Indigenous residents of Westport, including the Golden Hill Paugussett Tribe, framing the history as one that continues to evolve). 
In 2019, one year after her appointment, the museum opened the exhibition “Remembered: The History of African-Americans in Westport,” an exhibition that received recognition from the Institute for Museum and Library Services (ILMS), American Association for State and Local History, and Connecticut League of History Organizations. 
The mission was not just to bring attention to Connecticut’s history of enslavement, which remained legal until 1848, but also shine a light on the long and sometimes fraught history of Black residents of the town, and the way their local stories intersected with national history. 
Zach Terrillion, who grew up in Westport and worked on the exhibition as a high school intern, remembered the thrill of discovering history through the museum’s archives, and the ways in which the exhibition opened his eyes to facts about Westport that he had missed out on in the city’s public schools. He learned, for instance, that both the civil rights activist Martin Luther King, Jr. and the prophetic Black writer James Baldwin had visited and spoken at Westport’s Temple Israel, next to which he attended elementary school, in the 1960s. 
He, and other visitors to the exhibition, also learned that the state’s history of enslavement was more complicated than it had seemed in school, where slavery was largely framed as something that happened in the American South. In fact, slavery was legal in Connecticut through 1848; the last known sale of enslaved people took place on the New Haven Green in 1825. 
In Westport, Greens Farms Parish records from the eighteenth and nineteenth century indicate almost 250 enslaved people, including children, between 1742 and 1822 — a fact that the museum included in the exhibition, and has since commemorated in a brick walkway that leads up to the historic house. 
“It was this moment of local history connecting to national history” that later informed his decision to study public humanities at Oberlin College, Terrillion said. He added that “understanding those uglier parts of the local history are very very important, but I think the museum touched upon excellency and success” of Black Westport residents in a way that made, and continues to make, him proud.   
During those first years of Ganeshram’s tenure, which coincided with the Covid-19 pandemic and a move to increased digital content, the museum also raised $3 million that allowed it to tackle long-deferred maintenance projects on its grounds and building. That included, for instance, a $500,000 restoration of the 1846 Bradley Wheeler Cobblestone Barn by the Middletown-based company Kronenberger & Sons Restoration, $450,000 in updates to the museum’s grounds, including the addition of free WiFi, and updates to the museum’s collections management systems. 
Ganeshram pointed to the importance of protecting and preserving archives that date back to the 1670s, and are often the foundation for the museum’s exhibitions as staff and volunteers do research, and tie in Westport’s history. She said that another chunk of that funding went toward general operating support, including utilities and building needs that can be as much as $150,000 in a given year. 
In recent years, though, raising funds to keep the museum going has become harder, due in part to a nonprofit landscape in which both state and federal dollars are drying up after an ARPA boom, and individual donors are giving less money, less frequently. In the last year, the museum staff has shrunk from six full- and part-time employees to just three, including Ganeshram and two part-time staffers. 
The museum now operates just two days per week, on Fridays and Saturdays. It has continued to run limited programming, which brings in a very small percent of its annual income stream. 
Even as Ganeshram has brought in new visitors, including several young volunteers eager to get to work in the archives, she said she’s also seen significant pushback to the museum’s expanded mission, including its new gallery spaces and focus on Black, Indigenous, and LGBTQ+ people often excluded from historical narratives of the town.
 According to the CT Data Collaborative, 78 percent of Westport is white. Ganeshram, whose mother is Iranian and whose father is Trinidadian, acknowledged the discomfort the museum’s expanded mission can create for people who have not had to reckon with their own history, or the history of their ancestors. 
“Our tagline is ‘Making History Whole,’ and it’s just too much for some people,” she said. But history, by its very nature, “is uncomfortable … [and] it’s more painful to ignore it than to explore it.”  

The Westport Museum for History and Culture is undertaking an emergency fundraising appeal in an effort to raise $750,000 by the end of the year. Credit: Photo courtesy of Westport Museum for History and Culture / Westport Museum for History and Culture

If the museum does not raise $750,000 by the end of the year, Ganeshram added, it will likely mean that “we would sell the asset [the Bradley-Wheeler House] and keep the mission.” Because the museum’s archives include almost 400 years of town history, the organization would probably move into a smaller space where it could preserve those documents, keep its research mission, and continue to offer programming, including out of its newly-restored barn. 
If it is able to raise those funds (Ganeshram pointed to an upcoming fundraiser on November 13), the museum will continue programming, stay open for a limited number of days per week in its current spot, and likely hire a professional fundraiser while working on a new strategic plan. Ganeshram said that the museum would not be able to return to full staffing capacity immediately.  
“I think it’s pretty devastating,” Terrillion said, remembering field trips that he took to the museum as a kid. “Even before I started volunteering at the museum,  I understood the importance of the space … the space is at basically the heart of the community. It’s hard to imagine what it would be like if there was not a museum, a historical space within that historical home, there.” 
“I think it is a space that is worth investing in,” he added, lauding the diversity of visitors, community events, and programs that he’s seen and been a part of during his young adulthood. 
Kathy Nixon, a lifelong resident of Westport who has volunteered, served on the board of, and worked at the museum over the last three and half decades (she is currently one of two part-time staff members left), said that she would likewise be crushed to see it leave its longtime home. 
After growing up in Westport, and wearing multiple professional hats at the museum, she sees it as a vital space for learning the full history of the place that she calls home. She never knew, for instance, that in 1950 — just a decade after her own parents had put down roots in Westport — that a housing complex on the town’s Main Street caught fire, displacing dozens of the town’s Black residents, some of whom permanently left the town.
It was an example of how Westport, often heralded for its Blue Ribbon Schools and progressive ideals, was part of a larger narrative of direct and indirect “slum clearance” efforts, some removed from federal housing policy of the same name, that took place in the mid-twentieth century. Nixon (who suspects that the fire was arson, although that has never been confirmed) was both surprised and not surprised at all that she’d grown up in the town and never known.     
“When they [board members] hired her [Ganeshram] and some people had left, I thought, ‘I just am gonna stick this out and see what she can accomplish,’” she said in a phone call Thursday evening. “And she has accomplished everything they wanted her to do.” 
She added that Ganeshram has become not only a colleague, but a friend. “I’m proud of all of that,” she said. “I’m proud of sticking it out. I’m thrilled to be working with Ramin.”  
In a press release sent out by the organization earlier this week, TEAM Westport Chair Harold Bailey echoed that sense of urgency, championing the work that Ganeshram has done to fold in voices from all of Westport’s residents. TEAM Westport is a committee within the town’s government “with the mission to make the Town of Westport increasingly welcoming with respect to race, ethnicity, religion and LGBTQIA+,” according to its website.
“The innovative approach Ramin has brought to presenting and interpreting subject matter has added remarkable new dimensions of breadth, depth, and relevance to museum exhibitions locally, regionally, and nationally,” he said. “Her work has enabled generations of visitors—both longtime museumgoers and new audiences—to encounter familiar subjects through fresh, compelling, and often unexpected perspectives.” 
In the meantime, Ganeshram has continued to keep programming running, including an upcoming workshop for Connecticut K-12 educators in collaboration with George Washington’s Mount Vernon. Titled “Setting Down Liberty: Washington and the Black Experience in the Founding Era,” the workshop is a day of learning for educators at the museum, centered on the country’s semiquincentennial. Ganeshram is a library fellow at Mount Vernon, which has made the programming possible.

name: California
title: Gavin Newsom’s legacy: Big promises  undercut by costly mismanagement
text:
Whatever accomplishments Gavin Newsom might claim from his eight years as governor, he will also leave a legacy of mismanagement that has squandered untold billions of taxpayers’ dollars.
There is a running thread in that record — grandiose, self-serving promises of benefits and sloppy, sometimes fraudulent implementation.
The largest managerial mess, in terms of both dollars and impact, has been the state budget.
Newsom inherited a workable budget in 2019 from predecessor Jerry Brown, who had cleaned up a fiscal disaster, including a “wall of debt” left over from the Great Recession. However, Newsom and legislators have habitually overspent revenues and built a new wall of debt several times larger than the one Brown faced.
In 2022, Newsom proclaimed the state had a $97.5 billion surplus, boasting “No other state in American history has ever experienced a surplus as large as this.”
He and the Legislature immediately increased spending, such as extending Medi-Cal health benefits to undocumented immigrants. But that cost $6-billion more than Newsom estimated, and state Auditor Grant Parks, in a recent report, says the Department of Health Care Services has failed to stop pervasive abuse and fraud in Medi-Cal.
Eventually, Newsom’s administration acknowledged that the phantom surplus resulted from a $165 billion error in estimating future revenue. The state is left with a “structural deficit” that’s expected to remain at least through the next governor’s first term.
When the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020, Newsom assumed one-man control of the emergency. He issued decrees to shut down schools and many businesses and spent billions of dollars on no-bid contracts.
Money was being shoveled out the door to vendors with scanty or no credentials. Meanwhile, Newsom’s Employment Development Department was granting billions of dollars in unemployment insurance benefits to fraudsters, some of them inmates of state prisons.
While Newsom was telling Californians to avoid human contact, he attended a birthday dinner at a Napa restaurant where no one wore a mask. When his hypocrisy was exposed, Newsom apologized, but it didn’t explain why he had willingly done what he had told everyone else not to do.
More recently, Newsom has also acknowledged he went overboard in shutting schools, which worsened achievement in a state that already was faring poorly in tests of academic skills, such as reading and math.
Newsom has often touted the state’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but specific projects have been plagued by mismanagement.
Newsom at first hinted that he might throttle back the state’s bullet train project, then backtracked and shored it up with billions of new dollars. The project is stuck in neutral, and its inspector general reported recently that the High Speed Rail Authority had blown nearly $600,000 on travel to “questionable locations that appear unrelated to state business,” such as gyms, a nightclub, a tiki bar and a cigar lounge.
Meanwhile, the Los Angeles Times revealed that the state has spent more than $1 billion to subsidize purchases of zero emission buses and trucks, but the program has been riddled with fraud.
Finally, there’s homelessness.
Upon becoming governor, Newsom named himself a czar to attack the crisis and began castigating local governments for not spending state grants effectively. However, in 2024, state Auditor Parks said Newsom’s Interagency Council on Homelessness had failed to effectively oversee programs. Despite more than $20 billion in state spending, the crisis remains at least as serious as it was when Newsom took office.
There are many other examples. Taken as a whole, they reveal an administration that doesn’t administer very well, though it has promised much.

name: California
title: Trump’s attacks on California elections endanger democracy, repeating a pattern
text:
The Trump administration’s attack on California’s ongoing elections is merely one episode in a long and dismal series of efforts to undermine confidence in the integrity of the American democratic system. And it’s an attempt to manufacture a rationale for attacks still to come.
For context, it might be helpful to catalog Trump’s previous evidence-free and often outright disproven allegations that elections were “rigged” against him, either by crooked local and state election officials, crooked voting machine manufacturers, crooked reporters or thousands upon thousands of crooked Californians who aren’t lawfully allowed to vote but do so anyway.
For the present, though, and just as a refresher, let’s recall Trump’s denial that he had lost the 2020 election, his demand that Georgia officials “find” him enough votes to deliver a different outcome, his demand that Vice President Mike Pence not certify the election results and the shameful Jan. 6, 2021 mob attack on the Capitol that Trump egged on.
Recall that four years earlier, when he won the electoral vote and therefore the presidency in 2016, Trump was so incensed that he lost the popular vote to Hillary Clinton that he declared he’d actually won it and that evidence to the contrary was fake. 
To “prove” it he established the Voter Fraud Commission, or more formally the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity. There was a brief period in which observers thought a productive and bipartisan effort was possible, and that the panel could ferret out improper voting and get to the bottom of allegations that Russia and other adversaries interfered with the election.
But the commission produced nothing.

President Donald Trump talks to reporters about an executive order on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games, in the White House in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 5, 2025. Photo by Demetrius Freeman, The Washington Post via Getty Images

And recall that even before that, when asked whether he would respect the 2016 election outcome, Trump responded, “If I win.” It was vintage Trump — a headline-grabbing statement that committed him to no particular position and could be taken either as a jest or a warning, or both at the same time.
It has been widely asserted that Trump sees no distinction between statements that are true or false and considers only whether a statement will or will not serve him.
If that’s the case, he may not care whether there was any fraud or misconduct at the polls.  He may see no difference between that position and the conviction that there absolutely must have been fraud or misconduct — because how else could he possibly have lost? 
That belief — we can only lose if the system is rigged — has roots in California, 2008, and redistricting reform.
Moderate Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor after defeating Gray Davis in the historic recall five years before, but Republican candidates were making no headway in state legislative or congressional races. 
It’s because of your politics, the governor told the party. Candidates had to move toward the center if they wanted support from California voters. “We’re dying at the box office,” he famously told them.
But others in the party said that there must be some other reason they weren’t winning. Many sincerely believed Democrats must be cheating, or at least gaming the system when they use their majority legislative power to draw district lines. Why else could Republicans possibly be losing?
Good-government advocates from inside and outside both major parties agreed it would be best for a nonpartisan, or at least bipartisan, panel to draw district lines. Together they wrote Proposition 11, which changed redistricting in both houses of the Legislature, but not Congress.
Former Democratic Assembly Speaker Willie Brown warned his party’s leaders that the measure was dangerous. Defeating Proposition 11 and electing Barack Obama were equally important, he told the state’s delegation at the Democratic national convention in Denver.
Republicans up and down the state embraced the measure as a way to bring fairness, and perhaps some Republican-controlled seats, to the Legislature. Two years after Prop 11 passed  backers returned with Proposition 20, a measure to apply the same redistricting commission process to congressional elections.
But Republican candidates continued to die at the box office. Schwarzenegger, who supported a range of reforms in a quest to break a toughening partisan stalemate, had been right that candidate positions needed to change as well. But they didn’t.
Redistricting reform went the other way in Texas, which last year altered its rules in an attempt to award congressional Republicans more seats in the current midterm election. California Gov. Gavin Newsom responded with Proposition 50, which (ahem) “temporarily” suspends Proposition 20 to allow midterm redistricting to favor Democrats, because of the emergency created by Texas.
No doubt we will face continuing partisan emergencies in future elections, and California voters will be asked to repeatedly suspend Proposition 20. If that’s the case, we may return permanently to a scenario in which control of Congress is no longer seen merely as a contest between political and policy rivals and will become instead a permanently Trump-flavored electoral civil war. 
The Department of Homeland Security’s recent demand that California election officials set aside some 20,000 ballots cast by voters on a list that supposedly names people who registered but are ineligible to vote, and the Department of Justice’s follow-up lawsuit, may be shots — or perhaps just blanks — in that war.
Also armed troops already gather around ballot dropboxes in the District of Columbia. The director of the FBI won’t rule out sending armed agents to polling places. And Trump supporters openly talk of martial law as the only response to an election that does not go their way. 
Like Trump’s 2016 answer about accepting the election outcome, it’s hard to know whether to take these things as very bad jokes or very serious warnings. Either way, they serve to dissuade people from voting at all, which is likely the point.
Surely there were people who stormed the Capitol in the sincere belief that Trump had won the 2020 election, and that they were standing up against Democratic Party cheating and for the truth. And surely at least some of them now see they were duped into destroying a formerly shared faith in the system and the truth, and the conviction that we could and would unite after the votes are counted.
And there certainly are some Americans who believe California and Democrats are engaged in a criminal conspiracy to get noncitizens and other ineligible voters to the polls — despite the long list of evidence to the contrary, the court rulings that repeatedly reject such allegations, Trump’s previous lies about election fraud, the 2020 pressure on Georgia officials, the Supreme Court’s ruling last month rejecting a similar assault on Nevada’s election and the fact that the attack on California’s vote is taking place in the middle of the election, for maximum impact on public opinion.
That’s the darkness of Trump’s assault on California’s elections. Losing Congress on Nov. 3, by his reasoning, supplies proof that the state is cheating, because how else could he possibly be defeated? 
We need not worry if he actually believes that. The tragedy for American democracy would be if a substantial number of voters also believe it.

name: California
title: Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
text:
In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.


It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country. 
Supporters call Proposition 37 an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers. 
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget.
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything. 
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 and 38, would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest. 
If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults. 
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it. 
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000. 
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest or lowest homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it. 
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help. 
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey. The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview. 
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California political debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible. 
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters, according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis. 
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify. 



There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income, first-generation or veteran homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said. 
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California, worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.  
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities. 
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Three conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be built by a “qualified builder.”
That’s a builder that agrees to abide by the price cap, build inside existing cities and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements. 
In exchange, they would get to build the second mortgage-eligible homes. They also would shield themselves from construction defect lawsuits if they repair a mistake to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The program would probably make the best business sense in parts of the state where home prices are lower and where there are plenty of middle-income borrowers, said Dan Dunmoyer, president of the California Building Industry Association. That’s likely to be cities in places like the Inland Empire and the Central Valley.
The third condition is that the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.
Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique of down payment assistance programs. 
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
The actual number depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of each home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure. 
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans. 
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7%. Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis. 
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly. 
But Hertzberg said he has a plan. 
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards.
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion, Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited. 
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.

name: California
title: Is this America’s most normal congressional race? San Diego candidates run on classic platforms
text:
In summary
Democrat Marni von Wilpert and Republican Jim Desmond are sticking to conventional centrist platforms in the closely watched San Diego House race.


Democratic socialists. Carhartt-wearing farmers. Populist physicians.
The insurgent left has come in all forms in California and across the country this cycle.
But a different story is playing out in the open 48th Congressional District, which straddles San Diego and Riverside counties. 
Democrat Marni von Wilpert, a San Diego city councilmember, is running as a true blue establishment type in one of California’s most competitive House races. She faces Republican Jim Desmond, who is running as a budget-hawk style conservative. 
Case in point: Former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for von Wilpert last month, while Democrats elsewhere have been fearful she’d turn off swing voters still bitter about the previous election.
And Desmond, a San Diego county supervisor, has made slashing taxes and reducing energy prices his main platform while maintaining a healthy distance from President Donald Trump to avoid alienating undecided voters.
Whether cookie-cutter liberal politics or fiscal conservatism will be enough to energize the base and pick up independents in the purple, albeit Democratic-leaning district, is the real question. 
Internal polling from the campaigns suggests the race is close. Von Wilpert, leads fundraising at $4.5 million. Desmond has hauled in $3 million. 
Councilmember Marni von Wilpert during a San Diego City Council meeting at San Diego City Hall on April 14, 2026. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters
Over $6 million in outside spending has poured in, more than virtually every other House race in California — nearly all of it for Von Wilpert. That includes more than $4 million from Democrats’ House Majority PAC and $2 million from the Democratic Majority for Israel, a pro-Israeli PAC that boosts Democratic candidates.Trump’s newly formed No Going Back PAC has given more than $330,000 so far to support Desmond.
The independent expenditure spending is third in California behind the closely watched 22nd Congressional District in the San Joaquin Valley between incumbent GOP Rep. David Valadao and Democrat Randy Villegas that’s attracted $19 million from outside groups, and the Stockton-area House race between Democratic Rep. Adam Gray and Republican Kevin Lincoln, which has drawn $7 million, according to California Target Book. 
Money will likely be a decisive factor between two candidates who are equally matched, said Paul Mitchell, a Democratic political strategist who drew the new Democratic-leaning maps that reshaped the district.
It’s one of a handful of competitive congressional races in California after Democrats’ 2025 redistricting measure turned Republican Rep. Darrell Issa’s safe Republican seat into a left-leaning battleground. Affluent, conservative voters in Temecula and Fallbrook were joined with voters in Oceanside and Palm Springs, where Harris won the last presidential contest by double-digit margins.
Issa, who has represented the area for more than two decades, briefly flirted with the idea of running in Texas before dropping his reelection bid. 
Without an incumbent defending the seat, Democrats see it as ripe for a flip in an election year when they are expected to retake the House from Republicans. 
“The 48th is a real matchup between two fairly equally positioned candidates and the challenge is going to be that Desmond is going to have to win against this massive headwind of a pending blue wave,”  Mitchell said.
Running with the establishment
Von Wilpert is sticking to her record as a moderate, pro-Israel Democrat, pointing to her ability to pick up her then-red city council seat as a selling point to both liberals and conservatives in the district. And she’s tapped mainstream Democrats such as Harris and California Sen. Adam Schiff to help make that pitch.
At a rally in Escondido last week, Schiff said San Diego County’s high cost of living makes 48th District voters receptive to von Wilpert’s anti-war stance and fiscal arguments, in which she has cast herself as an opponent to Trump, eager to vote for resolutions to end the war in Iran and repudiate his tariff policies.
“This is a district where people are acutely attuned to the high cost of living, the high cost of food and medicine, and are also deeply in tune with military families and concerned about the war in Iran,” Schiff told CalMatters in an interview.
Von Wilpert’s just one of a handful of Democrats who accepted Harris’ help in a time where her unpopularity is still viewed as toxic by some, including candidates in Texas, Kansas and Alaska who rebuffed the former vice president’s support on the campaign trail. The two appeared together at another Escondido rally last month. 
“She’s very popular in our district, and people are sick of the Trump White House,” von Wilpert said.
It’s a different approach a few hundred miles north in the toss-up Central Valley seat where the Democratic newcomer Villegas has embraced anti-billionaire, populist messaging alongside Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders in an effort to oust Valadao. But whether von Wilpert’s strategy to play a safe, routine Democratic campaign in a key swing district is up for debate. 
Harris’ appearance on the campaign trail can be risky in parts of the country where she lost, but that’s not the case in San Diego, political consultant Evan McClaughlin said. Democrats gave themselves a three percentage point registration advantage when they redrew the district.
“I’ve seen people write that story about, ‘Well, oh my goodness, nobody wants her in the district,’” McClaughlin said. “That might be true in some places where she didn’t win, but she won this district.”
Keeping it hyperlocal 
A former mayor of San Marcos, Desmond has campaigned as a textbook fiscal conservative concerned about burdensome regulations and high taxes. He is one of two Republican votes on the county board of supervisors, often declining to be a contrarian voice on cultural issues but weighing in on immigration, as he did when he opposed the county’s plan to ban federal agents from using its firing ranges.
He’s worked overtime to distance himself from Trump, despite receiving the president’s endorsement. Instead, he focuses on local issues such as opposing a Temecula power line project.
Spokesperson Sam Oh emphasized as much, saying Desmond supports Trump but will act independently of the president in Congress. He said Desmond’s rebuke of Trump’s remarks earlier this month that Iran could “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles was an example. 
San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond listens to speakers during a TRUTH Act Forum at the San Diego County Administration Center on March 24, 2026. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments,” he posted on social media. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should be treated as collateral damage.”
“We are talking to voters about the things they care about. If they want us to talk to us about the president, we are happy to talk about the president,” Oh said.
Oh did not make Desmond available for an interview with CalMatters after repeated requests through email, phone calls and text messages.
But campaigns can only control the narrative so far, and while Desmond wishes to focus on local issues, it’ll be difficult to overcome Trump’s unpopularity, UC San Diego political science professor Thad Kousser said.
“It seems like it would take something extraordinary to mobilize enough Republicans or swing enough independent voters to overcome the geography of the district, but most importantly the national picture of this midterm,” Kousser said.

name: California
title: This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
text:
In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money. 


The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.Public statements and public records CalMatters obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and by far the largest donor to its political campaign. 
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted to cut existing and future federal science grants.The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly. 
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024.  Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.  
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.  
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute. 
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses. 
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility. The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health. 
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute. 
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.  
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing. 
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure. 
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.
Money raised in support of Prop. 38 now exceeds $66 million, including at least $61.2 million in contributions from Michelson and his policy institute. Roughly $14 million of that includes loans from Michelson. The no camp has raised about $8,800

name: Nevada Current
title: Iran war, rising costs threaten Nevada revenue outlook, state economic panel warned
text:
Wage growth is no longer keeping up with inflation, which will put financial pressures on both Nevadans and the non-Nevadans that Nevada relies on to be tourists. (Photo of Reid International Airport: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)The United States, and Nevada, for the past two years has traversed “relatively gracefully” over economic policy shocks brought on by unprecedented restrictions on trade and immigration. But economists warn that the next two years may bring a more difficult, flatter road for revenue.
Kumael Bilgrami, an associate economist at Moody’s Analytics, told the Nevada Economic Forum last week that strength in consumer spending and the AI buildout have been “important tailwinds” but are soon expected to weaken.
“While we expect growth will remain on stable ground” going forward “its progress will remain relatively flat as these supports begin to weaken,” he said. “A major reason behind this is … the conflict in the Middle East and the resulting surge in energy prices.”
Wage growth is no longer keeping up with inflation, which will put financial pressures on both Nevadans and the non-Nevadans that Nevada relies on to be tourists. Personal savings rates have “dropped dramatically” this year, noted Bilgrami. 
While Moody’s and state-based economists are currently projecting sales tax revenue collection to rise in the upcoming fiscal years, they acknowledged that growth will be driven almost entirely by the cost of goods being higher and not by people buying more things.
The K-shaped economy — where higher income households are faring fine while lower income households are struggling — is becoming more pronounced, Bilgrami emphasized, echoing earlier presentations the Economic Forum has had this year. Tourists to Las Vegas in the past three years especially have skewed toward much higher household incomes.
Moody’s expects domestic visitation to remain “downbeat,” and noted that the recent decline has been sharper than the declines felt after the 2008 crisis and 9/11. International tourism shows “early signs” of moving in the right direction for Nevada but Bilgrami said it was too soon to tell whether it would stabilize.
Bilgrami said Moody’s baseline assumes the conflict in the Middle East “begins to wind down in upcoming months” and leads that toward the “back end of next year” things will improve.
“But that recovery will be gradual,” he added.
Bilgrami cautioned against seeing the massive investment in AI as a long-term solution to economic woes, saying the “wealth effects” as a result of the “lift to the stock market…will be more limited given the current state of stretched market valuations.”
While Nevada is a player in the data center boom, there are “a lot of downside risks,” he added.
For one, it will bring short-term construction jobs but very few permanent ones.
It may also lead to people losing their jobs. Nevada is seen as having “below average exposure” to direct job loss because of AI, Bilgrami told the forum. But if AI were to usher in mass layoffs elsewhere and kick off a recession, Nevada would feel it acutely because of its tourism-based economy.
Nevada’s Economic Forum is a five-member appointed panel that approves the state’s biennial revenue forecast, which serves as the base for the governor’s recommended budget, which the governor presents to the Nevada State Legislature. The Legislature must pass the budget, which is subject to gubernatorial veto, by the end of its 120-day session.
The forum is scheduled to meet again on Nov. 16 to officially approve the revenue forecast. The 2027 Legislative Session begins in February.

name: Nevada Current
title: Data center project proposed on federal land gets sent back to square one
text:
President Donald Trump's July 2025 executive order directs agencies to accelerate permitting for data centers and support energy infrastructure to make federal land available for development. (Bureau of Land Management photo)Approval for the first-ever commercial data center on U.S. public lands was formally rejected on Thursday after a federal appeals board affirmed the Bureau of Land Management must conduct a separate environmental review, which in turn would have to be approved, before proceeding with the project.
In June, BLM approved the construction of the Townsite Data Center near Boulder City without preparing a new or revised environmental assessment after determining the data center project was “essentially like” a previously approved solar project proposed for the same site and would have “similar anticipated impacts.”
The agency relied on its 2023 review of the solar project to assess data center impacts, noting both projects would occupy the “exact same location, same acreage and same perimeter” and described both as industrial uses involving “predominantly electrical” technologies.
Boulder City, the Center for Biological Diversity and Sierra Club appealed the decision in July.
The Interior Board of Appeals temporarily halted construction of the data center in September after finding federal land managers likely violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) by using a previously approved but materially different project to authorize the new project.
That same month, BLM officials asked the federal appeals board to dismiss the agency’s approval of the data center in order “to allow the agency to conduct additional review of the application.” 
Townsite Solar 2 LLC, the data center developer, did not oppose the motion and Center for Biological Diversity and Sierra Club took no position. Boulder City opposed the motion, requesting a ruling on whether BLM’s decision was lawful under environmental law. 
Boulder City welcomed the appeals board decision to revoke approval for the data center and supports a comprehensive environmental review, said Lisa LaPlante, the communications manager for the city.
“It remains the City’s position that the BLM must follow federal law in approving of such a use and provide the City and the public with meaningful opportunity to be involved in if, how, when, where and why these facilities are authorized,” LaPlante said.
Townsite Solar 2 LLC did not respond to a request for comment. 
Patrick Donnelly, the Great Basin Director for the Center for Biological Diversity, said they are now waiting on the BLM’s next move.
 “We got the approval thrown out, so we feel pretty good about that,” Donnelly said. “We’re kind of waiting for next steps or what’s going to be happening from BLM or the developer, but we know they’re starting from ground zero.” 
Donnelly said there’s no precedent for a data center on federal land, raising questions on how the federal government will analyze enviromental impacts, including noise, wildlife habitat, air quality, and socioeconomic issues. 
“These are all pressing questions that we raised in our appeal that they’re going to have to answer if they expect to permit one of these projects,” Donnelly said. 
As more local governments push back against data centers, public land will become more attractive to developers, said Donnelly. The Townsite Data Center could influence how future projects are permitted on public lands, he added. 
“It’s actually getting kind of difficult to put data centers on private land because county commissions are getting swayed by their angry constituents. But meanwhile, this administration is taking a battering ram to all of our federal environmental statutes, paving the way for seemingly very easy development of data centers on public land,” Donnelly said.
President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order directs federal agencies to accelerate the construction of large data centers and supporting energy infrastructure on federal land.
BLM invoked the policy in its initial approval of Townsite, saying the development “supports federal efforts to accelerate permitting for data center infrastructure.”
If implemented on BLM lands, the plan could have major implications for public lands throughout the West, and especially in Nevada where about 80% of the land is managed by the federal government.

name: Nevada Current
title: A midwife solution to Nevada’s maternity care problem
authors: Lorraine M. Garcia, PhD, WHNP-BC, CNM
text:
(Photo: Catherine Delahaye/Getty Images)Nevada recently received an overall failing grade on the March of Dimes 2025 Report Card for key indicators of maternal and infant health. March of Dimes is a leading U.S. nonprofit organization that works to improve the health of moms and babies with a focus on ending preventable morbidity and mortality and correcting inequitable outcomes. The report card for Nevada shows poor grades for preterm birth rates, adequacy of prenatal care, the low-risk cesarean birth rate, infant death rates, and the maternal death rate. Notably, Carson City and Las Vegas are called out for their F grades on preterm birth rates.
Nevada state lawmakers have rightly made improving maternal and infant outcomes a priority as they prepare for the upcoming legislative session, with maternal health provisions proposed in a state “momnibus” bill. But for these efforts to be effective, our legislative and policy leaders need to expand and strengthen two underused and previously overlooked solutions: accredited freestanding birth centers and integrated access to licensed midwives.
Birth centers are freestanding health care facilities focused on providing midwifery-led maternity care services. Birth centers offer highly personalized attention, holistic support programs and comprehensive midwifery care, while coordinating consultations with physicians and hospital transfers as needed.
Research consistently shows that low-risk women who receive care at accredited, freestanding birth centers have better outcomes when compared with similar women who receive hospital-based maternity care. That’s why leading organizations like The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society of Maternal-Fetal Medicine recognize accredited birth centers as an integral part of the health care system in the U.S.
Midwifery care through birth centers also lowers costs. Most savings come from lower cesarean rates for low-risk women, lower preterm birth rates, and lower rates of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions, all of which can be costly for families and society. For example, in Nevada it is estimated that the annual cost associated with each preterm birth is around $65,000. According to the think tank Heartland Forward, the total workplace productivity lost due to preterm births cost the state $6,648,863 each year between 2014-2020.
Midwifery care—whether in homes, hospitals, or birth centers—has also been shown to provide better experiences for mothers, with lower rates of reported mistreatment, disrespect, and abuse. This is particularly true for Black women and other minoritized groups who experience harm at higher rates during pregnancy, birth, and postpartum.
Better access to midwives and birth centers isn’t a solution by itself. To work safely, midwives must consult with physicians and make coordinated transfers to obstetricians and hospitals for medically complex pregnancies and births, and in cases of rare obstetric or newborn emergencies.
That’s why it’s important for Nevada to improve its integration of midwives across all birth settings, meaning that women have routine access to midwifery care for home births, birth center births, and hospital births without discrimination. While Nevada is a strong parental rights state where the right to home birth with any chosen birth attendant has been defended in previous legislative sessions, our ranking for midwifery integration is the lowest among the Western states.
In addition to low midwifery integration, Nevada has one of the smallest midwifery workforces in the country. Nevada continues to be the only state in our region with no pathway to licensure for Certified Professional Midwives who focus on births in homes and birth centers. Meanwhile, Certified Nurse Midwives, who mostly attend childbirth in hospitals, do have an autonomous licensure pathway, but often face restricted hospital privileges, are excluded by insurance payers, and receive unsustainable reimbursement rates.
This matters because where midwives have greater integration in a healthcare system, mothers and newborns have better outcomes on a host of quality measures, including many of the ones for which Nevada is graded so poorly. Our fellow Western states of Washington and Oregon, for example, have seen great successes with high midwifery integration and the resulting association with better perinatal outcomes.
Expanding access to midwifery and freestanding birth centers can also address the lack of childbirth providers across the large rural and frontier areas of Nevada. A March of Dimes report shows that 47.1% of counties in Nevada are maternity care deserts, which means they lack a hospital or birth center offering childbirth services by a licensed midwife, obstetrician, or family physician.
Nevada has the capacity to scale up its midwifery workforce and the capability to support freestanding birth centers in areas of need. The UNLV School of Nursing has had a Master of Science Nurse-Midwifery program since the fall of 2023. State-directed funds that support the ability of UNLV to continue to educate and retain Certified Nurse Midwives to work in Nevada are vitally important. Nevada also has the opportunity in the upcoming legislative session to pass an optional licensure bill for community-based Certified Professional Midwives, who are already popular and practicing throughout Nevada, but who currently remain without a pathway to licensure which limits their ability to work with more families and be a recognized part of the healthcare system.
There are promising developments already happening in our state that demonstrate solutions for how we can improve the health and happiness of our moms and babies. For one, Nevada already has an existing facility model for how to provide excellent maternal and newborn outcomes in the community: Serenity Birth Center in Las Vegas, the only freestanding birth center in the state. Serenity is also where I am a co-medical director and work as a midwife. Midwives at Serenity have attended over 1,200 births since the center opened five years ago and the performance outcomes for the moms and babies at Serenity earn an A-grade by the same March of Dimes indicators for which Nevada is failing.
Additional encouraging news is that the Nevada Health Authority is working to support access to birth center care for women and their newborns who rely on Medicaid. Currently, state Medicaid programs must cover licensed freestanding birth centers, but without reasonable contract rates for essential services, birth centers are forced to deny services to Medicaid-covered clients due to an inadequate payment structure that does not cover the costs of care.
The evidence is clear. Nevada needs to increase midwifery integration through updated regulatory and payment structures that recognize licensed midwives and community-based birth options as essential parts of the solution to our state’s maternity care crisis. If we continue to neglect these proven solutions, we will continue to be an outlier among the Western states with more money spent while Nevada moms and babies continue to suffer from avoidable pregnancy and childbirth-related harms.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: ICE in the crosshairs as NJ Democrats fight to win back control of Congress
text:
New Jersey Democrats say more hearings probing immigration enforcement and less money for ICE are in the cards if their party wins control of Congress. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]New Jersey Democrats who have spent more than a year clashing with the Trump administration over the president’s mass deportation effort say winning the House in November could give them real power to probe what they call the administration’s immigration enforcement abuses.
They have protested outside Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall, fought the feds’ plan to build a detention center in Morris County, and held a shadow hearing to reveal what they say is the human cost of immigration enforcement and detention.
“Part of the reason you do those is to clearly demonstrate what you would do if you had the gavels and what type of hearings you would have,” said Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08), who is running for his third term in November with no Republican opponent.
The Nov. 3 midterm elections will decide whether Republicans retain control of Congress or whether President Donald Trump’s plunging approval ratings will allow Democrats to flip the House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate, or both. Here in New Jersey, Sen. Cory Booker (D) is on the ballot, as are all 12 House seats.
A Democratic victory could force more Trump administration officials to testify in front of Congress at hearings controlled by Democrats, and it could give the party a stronger hand in deciding how much money U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement receives in the future.
New Jersey has made national news for being on the front lines of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with Delaney Hall becoming a flashpoint in the debate earlier this year when protests erupted outside the facility. Morris County residents, too, saw themselves at the center of the debate when the administration said it would open an immigrant processing center in Roxbury, a plan that quickly became the target of a lawsuit by the Sherrill administration and Roxbury’s GOP leadership. And Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) is set to stand trial on federal assault charges related to one of her oversight visits to Delaney Hall last year, a trial she said is part of the president’s crusade against his administration’s critics.
New Jersey Democrats have touted the work they’ve already done as the party in the minority, including regular oversight visits to Delaney and Elizabeth Detention Center. Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-11) said she found a constituent in detention during one of those visits, a Morristown small business owner with a work permit who paid taxes and who had been detained and “given a quarter of her diabetes medication.” Mejia won a special election in April to represent the 11th District in the House and is running next month to remain in the seat for the 120th Congress, which begins its term in January.
“As we prepare for the 120th, we need to ensure that we’re creating a roadmap, a pathway to citizenship, to as many law-abiding people that actually build and support our economy, our nation, our democracy,” she said.
Her Republican opponent, Joe Hathaway, said he worries a Democratic majority would lead to a rise in power for the party’s left-leaning faction. Hathaway, a councilman in Randolph, said those Democrats want “no jails, no Supreme Court, no borders.”
“That group will have now an outsized influence when it comes to legislation,” he warned.
At a recent town hall in Bloomfield, Mejia told voters she does indeed believe the nation should have borders.
“It is important for us to realize, however, that our immigration system, one, it has evolved,” she said. “Part of the problem that we are seeing is that people stay in limbo for over a decade, even if you’re following the law. And so what I have advocated for is we should invest in a system — if you can fill out a credit card application and in 15 seconds you are determined credit-worthy, that means that it shouldn’t take a decade to investigate someone’s background to make sure we understand who they are and whether or not we want to absorb them, welcome them into the fabric of the United States.”
Much of the conversation about New Jersey’s role in the national debate on immigration has focused on Delaney Hall. But it has reverberated statewide, even down to the 2nd Congressional District.
Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock (D), left, is running to unseat Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District. (Mullock photo courtesy of his campaign/Van Drew photo by Anne-Marie Caruso)
Rep. Jeff Van Drew flipped that district to Democratic control in 2018 before he changed parties and became a Republican. Van Drew visited Delaney Hall back in June and said critics of conditions inside the jail are lying about what they’ve seen. Democrats “continue to choose the side of illegal immigrants over the American people,” he said during a congressional hearing in July.
This week, Van Drew said an alleged drunk driver who struck and seriously injured a Middle Township police officer on Friday has an active ICE detainer. He called the incident another in a line of “preventable tragedies.”
“Just weeks ago, a baby was killed in a New Jersey parking lot by an unlicensed driver who was in this country illegally. Then a six-year-old girl was kidnapped and sexually assaulted by a man who should have been deported. Now we have a young South Jersey police officer fighting to recover from devastating injuries. When is enough enough?” Van Drew said in a statement.
Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock, the Democrat challenging Van Drew, in an interview blasted the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort and Van Drew’s support of expanded enforcement.
“He represents an area where we need immigrants. We need them in our restaurants. We need them on our farms. They are out there right now farming in South Jersey, and he would like you to ignore that,” he said.
Mullock said he supports a strong border but said he would return “decency and respect” to immigration enforcement efforts. He also would ban private prisons in New Jersey, expand transparency around immigrant detention, and work to expand pathways to citizenship.
“We should decide who and who isn’t invited into our country. There’s no doubt about that. Full stop. Period. Strong border. However, we were supposed to be going after the worst of the worst, and that is not what’s happening,” Mullock said. “People who are washing dishes or working on a home on my own street are being arrested by ICE with basically no criminal history. That is insane.”
Rachel Peace, a Democrat hoping to unseat Rep. Chris Smith, the Republican incumbent in the 4th District, said she’s heard from voters that immigrants need to come to the U.S. “the right way,” but she thinks that misunderstands American immigration rules, which have become overly complicated.
“It used to be very simple: You come to Ellis Island, you provide them with your name and information, and you’re allowed entry,” Peace said.
But people emigrating here now face varying caps on who can come from what countries and other restrictions where missteps can result in reentry bans or worse, she said.
“Instead of making it so hard for people to ‘do things the right way,’ can we not modernize our process?” Peace said.
Making immigrants gain citizenship “the right way” is a campaign talking point for Michael McGuire, a Republican hoping to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway (D) in the 3rd District. McGuire released a video this week calling for a strong border and a path to citizenship for “people who follow our laws.”
“This is about being smart and fair, securing our border while giving people who do it the right way a real chance to become citizens,” McGuire said in a statement.
Ryan Michael Kelly, an independent also running in the 3rd District, said this message means little “when the system itself is broken.”
“When Congress begins its new term in January, I want to see real immigration reform. That means fixing processing delays, improving legal pathways, protecting asylum seekers and families, and restoring strong civil rights oversight” at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Kelly said. “I also support abolishing ICE and replacing it with an accountable enforcement system that focuses on real public safety while respecting the Constitution.”
Hathaway has also called for immigration reform. He said he supports a path to green cards for long-term residents who contribute to the economy, raise their families here, and do not have a criminal background. People who commit crimes, he said, should be deported.
